profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2026-03-14T05:06:04.331+09:00 by CH Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Chén Zhòngjǔ's words served as a model for scholars,
his conduct as a standard for the world.
Upon mounting his carriage and grasping the reins,
he harbored the ambition to cleanse the empire.
The *Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán* states:
"Chén Fān, styled Zhòngjǔ,
was a man of Píngyú in Rǔnán.
He had a room
that was left overgrown and unswept.
He said:
'A true man should sweep clean the empire for the state.'
At the end of Hàn Emperor Huán's reign,
eunuchs held power,
and imperial relatives were arrogant and domineering.
When he was appointed Grand Tutor,
he plotted with General-in-Chief Dòu Wǔ to eliminate the eunuchs,
but was instead killed by them."
When he became Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng,
the *Biographies of Former Worthies Throughout the Land* states:
"Fān was a Secretary.
Because his loyalty and integrity offended the powerful relatives,
he could not remain in the central administration and was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng."
Upon arrival,
he immediately asked where Xú Rúzǐ was,
wishing to visit him first.
Xiè Chéng's *History of the Later Hàn* states:
"Xú Zhì, styled Rúzǐ,
was a man of Nánchāng in Yùzhāng.
Pure, refined, and lofty in bearing,
he transcended the world and stood apart from the vulgar.
He was repeatedly recruited by various high officials,
but never took office.
Yet when they died,
he would travel thousands of miles to offer condolences.
He would often prepare a roasted chicken in advance,
soak silk in wine,
dry it in the sun,
and use it to wrap the chicken.
Going directly to the tomb path of the deceased,
he would moisten the silk with water,
prepare a peck of rice,
use white cogon grass as a mat,
and place the chicken in front.
After pouring a libation of wine,
he would leave his card and depart immediately,
without meeting the bereaved family."
The Registrar reported:
"Everyone wishes that you, Prefect, would first enter the official residence."
Chén said:
"King Wǔ bowed at the lane of Shāng Róng,
not even pausing to warm his mat.
Xǔ Shūzhòng said:
'Shāng Róng,
a worthy man of the Yīn dynasty,
was Lǎozi's teacher.'
Kneeling in the carriage is called 'shì' (bowing).
In my honoring the worthy,
what is there that cannot be done!"
Yuán Hóng's *Annals of the Hàn* states:
"While in Yùzhāng,
Fān set up a special couch for Zhì alone.
When he left, it would be hung up.
Such was the respect shown to him."
Zhōu Zǐjū often said:
"If I do not see Huáng Shūdù for a few months,
then my mean and petty thoughts begin to arise again."
Zǐjū is treated separately elsewhere.
The *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"Huáng Xiàn, styled Shūdù,
was a man of Shènyáng in Rǔnán.
Contemporaries all said
'Yánzǐ has been reborn.'
Yet his clan was humble and obscure,
his father being an ox doctor.
Xún Jìhé of Yǐngchuān took Xiàn's hand and said:
'You, sir, are my model.'
Later, when he met Yuán Fènggāo, he said:
'In your commandery there is a Yánzǐ,
do you know of him?'
Fènggāo said:
'Have you met my Shūdù?'
Dài Liáng rarely submitted to anyone,
but upon meeting Xiàn, he felt himself diminished and shallow,
disconsolate as if having lost something.
His mother asked:
'Why are you unhappy?
Have you come again from the ox doctor's son?'
Liáng said:
'Gazing at him, he seems ahead;
suddenly, he is behind.
This is what is called my true teacher.'"
Guō Línzōng arrived in Rǔnán
to visit Yuán Fènggāo.
The *Continued History of the Hàn* states:
"Guō Tài, styled Línzōng,
was a man of Jièxiū in Tàiyuán.
Tài was orphaned young.
At age twenty,
while traveling for study, he reached Chénggāo
and the retreat of Qū Bóyàn.
He lacked food,
his clothes did not cover his form,
yet he lived simply and savored the Way,
never altering his joy.
Lǐ Yuánlǐ, upon seeing him once, praised him, saying:
'I have seen many scholars,
but none like Línzōng.'
After his death,
Cài Bóyē composed his epitaph,
saying:
'When I compose inscriptions for others,
I am never without a sense of shame,
except for the *Eulogy for the Stele of Guō Yǒudào*, which I wrote without compunction.'
Initially,
he was summoned as a gentleman of the Way.
Tài said:
'Observing celestial signs and human affairs,
what Heaven has abandoned cannot be supported.'
He thus declined on grounds of illness."
The *Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán* states:
"Yuán Hóng, styled Fènggāo,
was a man of Shènyáng.
He befriended Huáng Shūdù in childhood
and recommended Chén Zhòngjǔ from his own neighborhood.
He died."
When recruited as an aide to the Grand Commandant,
his carriage wheels did not stop rolling,
the bells on his yoke did not cease ringing.
But when he went to visit Huáng Shūdù,
he would stay for days, even two nights.
Someone asked the reason.
Línzōng said:
"Shūdù is vast and deep
like a lake of ten thousand qǐng.
Clarify it, and it does not become clear;
disturb it, and it does not become turbid.
His capacity is profound and broad,
difficult to measure."
The *Separate Biography of Tài* states:
"When Xuē Gōngzǔ asked about it,
Tài said:
'Fènggāo's capacity
can be compared to an overflowing stream;
though clear, it is easily ladled.'"
Lǐ Yuánlǐ's style and character were elegant and upright.
He held himself to a high standard
and wished to take upon himself the responsibility for the fame and teachings of the world, and for judging right and wrong.
Xuē Yíng's *History of the Later Hàn* states:
"Lǐ Yīng, styled Yuánlǐ,
was a man of Xiāngchéng in Yǐngchuān.
He upheld a pure and refined will,
possessing outstanding civil and military talent.
He was promoted to Colonel-Director of Retainers
and committed suicide due to the Faction Incident."
Scholars of later generations
who gained access to his hall
all considered it like ascending the Dragon Gate.
Commentary: The *Records of Sān Qín* states:
"The Dragon Gate,
also called Héjīn,
is nine hundred lǐ from Cháng'ān.
The waterfall is sheer,
and creatures like turtles and fish cannot ascend it.
Those that do ascend transform into dragons."
Lǐ Yuánlǐ once praised Xún Shū and Zhōng Hào.
The *Accounts of Conduct of Former Worthies* states:
"Xún Shū, styled Jìhé,
was a man of Yǐngyīn in Yǐngchuān.
Those he promoted from among the coarse-clothed, herding folk,
and clerks holding documents and writing brushes,
all became outstanding talents.
Recommended as Upright and Direct,
he was appointed Chancellor to the Marquis of Lǎnglíng.
Wherever he served, he transformed the people through his influence.
Zhōng Hào, styled Jìmíng,
was a man of Chángshè in Yǐngchuān. His father and grandfather were renowned for their supreme virtue.
Hào inherited the lofty character of his forebears.
He was appointed Magistrate of Línlǜ,
but did not take up the post.
His official rank was insufficient,
but his heavenly nobility was abundant."
He said:
"Master Xún's clear discernment is difficult to surpass;
Master Zhōng's supreme virtue is worthy of emulation."
The *Biographies of Former Worthies Throughout the Land* states:
"The senior worthies of Yǐngchuān,
who were models for the entire land, were:
Chén Zhìshū of Dìnglíng,
Xún Shū of Yǐngyīn, and Zhōng Hào of Chángshè.
Chamberlain for the Palace Revenues Lǐ Yīng revered these three gentlemen,
often saying:
'Master Xún's clear discernment is difficult to surpass;
Masters Chén and Zhōng's supreme virtue is worthy of emulation.'"
Chén Tàiqiū visited Xún Lǎnglíng,
being poor and frugal, he had no servants.
The "Biography of Chén Shí" states:
"Shí, styled Zhònggōng,
was a man of Xǔchāng in Yǐngchuān.
He served as Magistrate of Wénxǐ
and Chief of Tàiqiū,
spreading moral influence far and wide."
Thus, he had Yuánfāng drive the carriage,
The "Accounts of Former Worthies' Conduct" states:
"Chén Jì, styled Yuánfāng,
was the eldest son of Shí.
His supreme virtue transcended the common,
and his high reputation matched that of Shí,
while his younger brother Chén also complemented him.
Whenever the official bureaus summoned them,
gifts of lambs and geese arrived in flocks,
and the world hailed them as
'The Three Lords',
with their portraits displayed in every city."
Jìfāng followed behind, holding a staff.
Chángwén was still young,
and was placed in the carriage.
Upon arrival,
Xún had Shūcí greet them at the gate,
Címíng serve the wine,
and the remaining six dragons serve the food.
Zhāng Fán's "Records of the Hàn" states:
"Shū had eight sons:
Jiǎn, Kūn,
Jìng, Tāo,
Wāng, Shuǎng,
Sù, Fū.
Shū lived in Xīháo Village,
and the county magistrate Yuàn Kāng said,
'In ancient times, Gāoyángshì had eight talented sons',
so he renamed the village Gāoyáng Village.
People of the time called them the Eight Dragons."
Wénruò was also young,
and sat in front of the knees.
At that time, the Grand Astrologer reported:
"True men are traveling east."
Tán Dàoluán's "Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng Autumn" states:
"Chén Zhònggōng, along with his sons and nephews, visited the Xún father and sons.
At that time, virtuous stars gathered,
and the Grand Astrologer reported:
'Worthy men are gathering within five hundred li.'"
A guest asked Chén Jìfāng:
The "Biographies of Worthies Within the Seas" states:
"Chén Chén, styled Jìfāng,
was the youngest son of Shí.
He was knowledgeable and broad-minded,
and though summoned by the Minister of Works with a public carriage,
he did not accept."
"Your honored father, Tàiqiū,
what merits and virtues does he possess
to bear such a great reputation in the world?"
Jìfāng said:
"My father is like a cassia tree growing in the embrace of Mount Tài,
above, it has the height of ten thousand ren,
below, it has unfathomable depths;
above, it is moistened by sweet dew,
below, it is nourished by deep springs.
At such a time,
how can the cassia tree know the height of Mount Tài,
or the depth of the springs?
It does not know whether it has merits and virtues or not!"
Chén Yuánfāng's son Chángwén had outstanding talent,
The "Book of Wèi" states:
"Chén Qún, styled Chángwén,
his grandfather was Shí,
who once said to his clansmen:
'This child will surely bring prosperity to our clan.'
When he grew up,
he possessed insight and judgment.
Those he befriended
were all his father's associates."
Together with Jìfāng's son Xiàoxiān,
The "Chén Clan Genealogy" states:
"Chén's son Zhōng,
styled Xiàoxiān.
He was summoned by the province but did not accept."
Each debated their fathers' merits and virtues,
and the dispute could not be resolved,
so they consulted Tàiqiū.
Tàiqiū said:
"Yuánfāng is hard to be the elder brother,
Jìfāng is hard to be the younger brother."
Another version reads:
"Yuánfāng is hard to be the younger brother,
Jìfāng is hard to be the elder brother."
Xún Jùbó traveled far to visit a sick friend,
The "Xún Clan Family Records" states:
"Jùbó
was a man of Emperor Huán of Hàn's time.
He also hailed from Yǐngchuān,
but his origins and end are unknown."
He encountered Hu bandits attacking the commandery,
and his friend said to Jùbó:
"I am about to die now,
you should leave!"
Jùbó said:
"I came from afar to see you,
and now you tell me to leave;
to abandon righteousness for the sake of survival,
is that what Xún Jùbó would do?"
When the bandits arrived,
they said to Jùbó:
"The great army has come,
the entire commandery is empty,
what kind of man are you,
to dare stay alone?"
Jùbó said:
"My friend is ill,
I cannot bear to abandon him;
I would rather give my life in place of my friend's."
The bandits said to each other:
"We are unrighteous men,
yet we have entered a righteous land!"
So they withdrew their army and left,
and the entire commandery was preserved.
Huà Xīn treated his sons and younger brothers with great formality,
even within private rooms,
as strict as court ceremonies.
The "Records of Wèi" states:
"Xīn, styled Zǐyú,
was from Gāotáng in Píngyuán."
The "Brief History of Wèi" states:
"During Emperor Líng's time, he studied together with Bǐng Yuán of Běihǎi
and Guǎn Níng, and they were close friends.
People of the time called the three of them a single dragon,
with Xīn as the dragon's head,
Níng as the dragon's belly,
and Yuán as the dragon's tail."
Chén Yuánfāng and his brothers practiced gentle affection,
and within the two households,
neither lost the path of harmony and prosperity.
Guǎn Níng and Huà Xīn were hoeing vegetables together in the garden,
The "Writings of Fù" states:
"Níng, styled Yòu'ān,
was from Zhūxū in Běihǎi,
a descendant of Guǎn Zhòng, Prime Minister of Qí."
They saw a piece of gold on the ground,
Guǎn swung his hoe as if it were tile or stone,
while Huà picked it up and threw it away.
They also once shared a mat while reading,
when a carriage with official insignia passed by the gate,
Níng continued reading as before,
while Xīn put down his book and went out to look.
Níng cut the mat and separated their seats, saying:
"You are not my friend."
The "Brief History of Wèi" states:
"Níng was quiet and calm from youth,
often laughing at Bǐng Yuán and Huà Zǐyú for their desire to become officials.
When Xīn became Minister of Education,
he submitted a memorial recommending Níng.
Níng heard this and laughed:
'Zǐyú originally wanted to be an old official,
so he glorifies it.'"
Wáng Lǎng often praised Huà Xīn for his insight and judgment.
The "Book of Wèi" states:
"Lǎng, styled Jǐngxīng,
was from Tán in Dōnghǎi,
and served as Minister of Education of Wèi."
On the day of the Zhà sacrifice,
The "Book of Rites" states:
"The Son of Heaven holds the great Zhà sacrifice in the eighth month,
Yīqíshì first established the Zhà.
Zhà means to seek.
In the twelfth month of the year,
all things are gathered and offered in sacrifice."
The "Essentials of the Five Classics" states:
"The three dynasties named the Là differently:
Xià called it Jiāpíng,
Yīn called it Qīngsì,
Zhōu called it Dàzhà,
all collectively referred to as Là."
The Jìn dynasty Erudite Zhāng Liàng discussed:
"Zhà is
gathering all things and offering them in sacrifice,
a year-end rest for the elderly and relief for the people.
Là is
sacrificing to the ancestral temple and the five household gods.
The 'Commentary' states:
'Là
means to connect.'
The sacrifice connects the old and the new.
Since Qín and Hàn times,
the day after Là is called Zhùsuì,
an ancient saying."
He once gathered his sons and nephews for a feast,
and Wáng also imitated this.
Someone told Zhāng Huà about this,
and Zhāng said:
"Wáng's imitation of Huà
is all in external form,
which is why he strays even further from it."
Huà Xīn and Wáng Lǎng were both fleeing by boat to escape danger,
when a man wanted to join them.
Huà Xīn immediately expressed difficulty with this.
Wáng Lǎng said:
"Fortunately, the boat is still spacious.
Why can't we take him?"
Later, when bandits pursued and caught up,
Wáng wanted to abandon the man they had taken aboard.
Huà Xīn said:
"The very reason I hesitated earlier
was precisely because of this situation.
Since we have already accepted his request to rely on us,
how can we abandon him in an emergency?"
So they carried and rescued him as before.
The world used this to judge the superiority and inferiority of Huà and Wáng.
Huà Qiáo's "Genealogical Account" states:
"Huà Xīn was the magistrate of Xiàguī.
When the Hàn dynasty was in turmoil,
he went into seclusion with six or seven like-minded scholars, including Zhèng Tài.
They exited through Wǔguān Pass.
On the road, they encountered a man traveling alone
who wished to accompany them.
They all pitied him and agreed.
Huà Xīn alone said:
'We cannot.
We are currently in danger.
Fortune, misfortune, calamity, and harm
should be shared as a matter of righteousness.
Now, to accept him without cause,
not knowing his principles,
if we face advance or retreat,
could we abandon him midway?'
The others could not bear to refuse,
and in the end, they traveled together.
This man fell into a well along the way,
and they all wanted to abandon him.
Huà Xīn then said:
'We have already traveled with him;
to abandon him is unrighteous.'
In the end, they all returned together,
pulled him out, and only then parted ways."
Wáng Xiáng served his stepmother, Lady Zhū, with utmost respect.
"Praise of the Jìn Nobles" states:
"Wáng Xiáng, styled Xiūzhēng,
was from Línyí in Lángyá."
"Wáng Xiáng's Family History" states:
"Wáng Xiáng's father, Róng,
married a woman from the Xuē clan of Gāopíng,
who gave birth to Xiáng.
He then took a woman from the Zhū clan of Lújiāng as his second wife,
who gave birth to Lǎn."
"Jìnyāng Qiū" states:
"The stepmother repeatedly slandered Wáng Xiáng
and often made unreasonable demands of him.
His younger brother, Lǎn, would always join Xiáng in these tasks.
She also mistreated Wáng Xiáng's wife,
and Lǎn's wife would also rush to share in the work.
When the stepmother fell ill,
during a time of severe cold and freezing ice,
she desired fresh fish.
Wáng Xiáng removed his clothes and was about to break the ice to seek fish,
when suddenly, a spot in the ice cracked slightly,
and fish emerged."
Xiāo Guǎngjì's "Biographies of Filial Sons" states:
"Wáng Xiáng's stepmother suddenly desired roasted yellow sparrows.
Wáng Xiáng thought it would be difficult to obtain them quickly.
In a moment,
dozens of yellow sparrows flew into their tent.
Whatever his mother needed,
he would personally rush to obtain it,
and nothing was beyond his reach.
His sincerity reached such heights."
There was a plum tree in their household,
which bore exceptionally fine fruit.
His mother often made him guard it.
When wind and rain suddenly arrived,
Wáng Xiáng hugged the tree and wept.
Xiāo Guǎngjì's "Biographies of Filial Sons" states:
"There was a plum tree in the courtyard of Wáng Xiáng's stepmother.
When it first bore fruit,
she made Wáng Xiáng watch for birds and sparrows during the day
and chase away mice at night.
One night,
a great wind and rainstorm arrived.
Wáng Xiáng hugged the tree and wept until dawn.
When his mother saw this, she was moved with pity."
Wáng Xiáng once slept on a separate bed.
His mother went in the dark to hack at him with an axe,
but it happened that Wáng Xiáng had gotten up privately,
so she only struck the empty bedding.
After returning,
knowing that his mother still resented him,
he knelt before her and begged for death.
His mother was then moved and awakened,
and loved him as her own son.
Yú Yù's "Book of Jìn" states:
"Because of his stepmother, Wáng Xiáng
delayed entering official service.
Approaching sixty years of age,
he was summoned by Inspector Lǚ Qián to serve as his Assistant.
People of the time sang of him:
'The peace of Hǎiyí
truly relies on Wáng Xiáng;
the state is not empty,
thanks to the Assistant's merit!'
He eventually rose to become Grand Guardian."
Jìn Wénwáng praised Ruǎn Sìzōng as being supremely cautious.
Whenever he spoke with him,
his words were all profound and far-reaching,
and he never praised or criticized individuals.
"Book of Wèi" states:
"Wénwáng's personal name was Zhāo,
styled Zǐshàng.
He was the second son of Xuāndì."
"Wèishì Chūnqiū" states:
"Ruǎn Jí, styled Sìzōng,
was from Wèishì in Chénliú.
He was the son of Ruǎn Yǔ. He was broad-minded and unrestrained,
unbound by rituals and customs.
Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Wáng Chǎng, requested to meet with him,
but throughout the day, he could not get a word from him.
Wáng Chǎng sighed in shame,
believing himself incapable of understanding him.
He did not discuss affairs,
yet naturally possessed lofty detachment."
Lǐ Kāng's "Family Admonitions" states:
"I once attended upon the late Emperor.
At that time, three senior officials were all received.
As they were about to take their leave and depart,
the Emperor said:
'To be an official, one must be upright,
cautious, and diligent.
Cultivate these three,
and why worry about governance not being orderly?'
They all received the edict.
The Emperor turned to us and said:
'If forced to abandon one,
which of these three would come first?'
Someone replied:
'Uprightness is certainly fundamental.'
He asked me again, and I replied:
'The ways of uprightness and caution
complement each other to achieve success.
If forced to choose,
caution is the greater.'
The Emperor said:
'Your words capture it.
Can you name someone in recent times who exemplifies caution?'
I then named the former Grand Commandant Xún Jǐngqiàn,
Minister Dǒng Zhòngdá, and Vice Director Wáng Gōngzhòng.
The Emperor said:
'These individuals
are gentle and respectful morning and night,
diligent in their duties,
and each exemplifies caution.
However, the most supremely cautious person in the world
must be Ruǎn Sìzōng!
Whenever I speak with him,
his words touch upon the profound and far-reaching,
yet he never comments on current affairs
or praises or criticizes individuals.
Can he not be called supremely cautious!'"
Wáng Róng said:
"I lived with Jī Kāng for twenty years
and never saw an expression of joy or anger on his face."
"Preface to Jī Kāng's Collected Works" states:
"Jī Kāng, styled Shūyè,
was from Zhì in Qiáoguó." Wáng Yǐn's "Book of Jìn" states:
"The Jī family originally had the surname Xī.
Their ancestors moved to Shàngyú to escape enmity,
then relocated to Zhì County in Qiáoguó.
Because they originated from Kuàijī,
they took one part of the character for 'state,'
which, in sound, remained the same as their original surname Xī."
Yú Yù's "Book of Jìn" states:
"In Zhì, there is Mount Jī.
They settled by its side
and thus took it as their surname."
"Separate Biography of Jī Kāng" states:
"Jī Kāng's nature contained and concealed flaws,
love and hatred did not contend in his heart,
joy and anger were not displayed on his face.
His acquaintance Wáng Jùnchōng, while in Xiāngchéng,
met him hundreds of times
and never saw him raise his voice or flush with anger.
This too is a fine model within the square,
a superior achievement in human relations."
"Record of Literary Works" states:
"Jī Kāng, as the son-in-law of the Wèi Chánglè Pavilion Princess, was promoted to Gentleman of the Interior
and appointed as a Palace Attendant."
Wáng Róng and Hé Qiào simultaneously suffered great mourning,
and both were praised for their filial piety.
Wáng was emaciated to the bone, propped up in bed,
while Hé wept and observed all the rituals.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Róng, styled Jùnchōng,
was from Lángyá.
He was of the same clan as Grand Guardian Xiáng.
When Emperor Wén was assisting in governance,
Zhōng Huì recommended him, saying:
'Péi Kǎi is pure and penetrating,
Wáng Róng is concise and essential.'
They were both immediately appointed as assistants.
When Jìn ascended the throne,
he was promoted successively to Governor of Jīngzhōu.
For his merit in pacifying Wú,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānfēng."
The "Jìn Yáng Qiū" states:
"When Róng was Governor of Yùzhōu,
he encountered the mourning for his mother.
His nature was extremely filial.
He did not adhere to ritual conventions,
drinking wine and eating meat,
or sometimes watching chess games,
yet his appearance was haggard and worn,
and he needed a staff to rise.
At that time, Hé Qiáo of Rǔnán,
also a famous scholar,
maintained himself through ritual propriety.
While in deep mourning,
he measured his rice for meals,
yet his emaciation and grief-stricken appearance
did not reach Róng's level."
Emperor Wǔ said to Liú Zhòngxióng:
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Liú Yì, styled Zhòngxióng,
was from Yè, Dōnglái.
He was a descendant of the Jīng King of Chéngyáng of the Hàn.
He was upright, honest, and incorruptible.
Whenever he saw something improper,
he would certainly comment on it.
Nobles and high officials
feared him from afar.
He resided in Yángpíng,
where Governor Dù Shù appointed him as a Merit Official,
and he dismissed over three hundred county clerks.
The people of Sānwèi all said:
'We only hear of Merit Official Liú,
not of Governor Dù.'
He was promoted successively to Imperial Secretary
and Colonel-Director of Retainers."
"Have you visited Wáng and Hé several times?
I hear Hé's grief and suffering exceed ritual propriety,
which worries people."
Zhòngxióng said:
"Although Hé Qiáo fulfills the rituals,
his spirit and energy are not diminished;
although Wáng Róng does not fulfill the rituals,
he is grief-stricken to the point of being skin and bones.
I consider Hé Qiáo's filial piety as that of the living,
and Wáng Róng's as that of the dead.
Your Majesty should not worry about Qiáo,
but should worry about Róng."
The "Jìn Yáng Qiū" states:
"The contemporary discussions of the time esteemed Róng for this."
Prince Liáng and Prince Zhào,
Zhū Fèng's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Lady Zhāng of Emperor Xuān gave birth to Prince Liáng Xiào, Tóng,
styled Zǐhuī,
who reached the position of Grand Steward.
Lady Huán gave birth to Prince Zhào, Lún,
styled Zǐyí,
who reached the position of Chancellor."
They were close relatives of the state, esteemed and powerful at the time.
Minister Péi
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Péi Kǎi, styled Shūzé,
was from Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
He was the younger brother of Minister Xiù.
His father, Huī,
was Governor of Jìzhōu,
and possessed outstanding discernment.
Kǎi was particularly proficient in the meaning of the 'Yì Jīng'.
He was promoted successively to Governor of Hénán
and died in office."
As Central Secretariat Director,
he requested several million in tax revenue from the two princedoms each year
to aid impoverished relatives.
Some criticized him, saying:
"Why do you beg for things to bestow kindness?"
Péi said:
"Reduce the surplus,
supplement the insufficient,
this is the way of Heaven."
The "Míngshì Zhuàn" states:
"Kǎi conducted himself in giving and taking,
acting according to his heart.
Though praise and blame came,
he remained calm and composed.
All were of this kind."
Wáng Róng said:
"The Grand Guardian, during the Zhèngshǐ era,
was not among those known for eloquence.
But when speaking with him,
his reasoning was clear and profound.
Is it not that his virtue overshadowed his words?"
The "Jìn Yáng Qiū" states:
"Xiáng had fine virtue and conduct from a young age."
When Marquis Ānfēng Wáng encountered hardship,
his innate nature surpassed others.
Minister Péi went to offer condolences, saying:
"If a single outburst of grief could truly harm a person,
Jùnchōng would certainly not escape the criticism of destroying one's nature."
The "Qū Lǐ" states:
"The rites of mourning
should not lead to emaciation that deforms the body,
nor should sight and hearing decline.
If one cannot bear the mourning,
it is comparable to being unfilial and unkind."
The "Xiào Jīng" states:
"Do not let grief destroy one's nature;
this is the teaching of the sages."
Wáng Róng's father, Hún, had a fine reputation,
and his official rank reached Governor of Liángzhōu.
The "Shì Yǔ" states:
"Hún, styled Chángyuán,
had talent and prestige.
He served as Imperial Secretary
and Governor of Liángzhōu."
When Hún died,
the righteous old acquaintances from the nine commanderies he had governed,
cherishing his virtue and kindness,
collectively contributed several million for the funeral,
but Róng refused to accept any of it.
Yú Yù's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Róng became famous because of this."
Liú Dàozhēn was once a convict laborer.
The "Jìn Bǎiguān Míng" states:
"Liú Bǎo, styled Dàozhēn,
was from Gāopíng.
A convict laborer
is one sentenced to penal servitude."
Prince Fúfēng, Jùn, Yú Yù
The "Jìn Shū" states:
"Jùn, styled Zǐzāng,
was the seventeenth son of Emperor Xuān, fond of learning
and extremely filial."
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Jùn became a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary at age eight,
attending upon King Qí of Wèi for lectures.
When Jìn received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Fúfēng,
garrisoned Guānzhōng,
and his governance was the finest.
He died and was posthumously honored as King Wǔ.
The western region remembered him,
and whenever people saw his stele inscriptions,
they would bow and weep.
Such was the lingering affection for him."
He redeemed him with five hundred bolts of cloth,
and later employed him as a Gentleman of the Bureau of Consultations.
This was considered a fine deed at the time.
Wáng Píngzǐ, Húwú Yànguó, and others
all considered unrestrained freedom as enlightenment,
and some even went naked.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Wáng Chéng, styled Píngzǐ,
had enlightened discernment,
and was Governor of Jīngzhōu."
The "Yǒngjiā Liúrén Míng" states:
"Húwú Fǔzhī, styled Yànguó,
was from Fènggāo, Tàishān,
and was Governor of Xiāngzhōu."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"At the end of the Wèi, Ruǎn Jí
was addicted to wine and unrestrained,
going bareheaded with disheveled hair,
naked and sitting with legs sprawled.
Later, noble youths like Ruǎn Zhān, Wáng Chéng,
Xiè Kūn, and Húwú Fǔzhī
all followed Jí's example,
believing they had grasped the essence of the Great Way.
Thus, they removed their caps,
took off their clothes,
exposing their ugliness,
like beasts.
The more extreme called it 'penetration',
the lesser called it 'enlightenment'."
Yuè Guǎng laughed and said:
"Within the teachings of reputation and propriety, there is naturally a place of joy.
Why must it be like this!"
Lord Xī encountered the Yǒngjiā turmoil,
and in his hometown, he was extremely poor and hungry.
The villagers, due to his reputation and virtue,
took turns providing him food.
He often brought along his elder brother's son, Mài,
and his nephew Zhōu Yì, two young children, to eat.
The villagers said:
"We are all starving and in distress.
Given your virtue,
we wish to help you together,
but fear we cannot save everyone."
The Duke then went alone to eat,
and would hold rice between his cheeks with chopsticks,
then return and spit it out to feed the two children.
Later, they all survived
and crossed the river together.
The *Biography of Xī Jiàn* says:
"Jiàn, styled Dàohuī,
was a native of Jīnxiāng in Gāopíng.
He was a descendant of Xī Lǜ, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief of the Hàn.
From a young age, he was upright in character,
devoted to studying the classics,
and renowned for his Confucian elegance.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
the world was in great turmoil,
and famine was widespread.
From officials down,
all contributed their own resources to support Jiàn.
Emperor Yuán summoned him to serve as General of the Central Army,
and he was later promoted to Minister of Works
and Grand Commandant."
The *Book of the Restoration* says:
"Jiàn's nephew Mài,
styled Sīyuǎn,
had talent and strategy for managing worldly affairs.
He was successively promoted to Minister of the Imperial Treasury
and General of the Central Guards."
After Duke Xī passed away,
Yì, who was serving as the magistrate of Shàn County,
resigned from his post and returned,
spreading straw mats by the Duke's spirit bed,
and observed mourning in his heart for three full years.
The *Genealogy of the Zhōu Clan* says:
"Yì, styled Zǐqīng,
was a native of Chénjùn.
His grandfather was Yì,
Governor of Shànggǔ.
His father was Yōu,
Consultant to the Chariot and Horse General.
He served as Magistrate of Shàn,
Governor of Qīng Province,
and Minister of the Imperial Treasury,
and passed away at the age of sixty-four."
Gù Róng was in Luòyáng,
once attending a banquet,
when he noticed the server of roasted meat had a longing look for the meat,
so he gave up his own portion to him.
Those seated with him mocked him.
Róng said:
"How can one hold it all day
and not know its taste?"
Later, when chaos struck and he crossed the river,
whenever he faced danger,
there was always someone assisting him.
When he asked the reason,
it turned out to be the man who had received the roasted meat.
The *Biographies of Literary Men* says:
"Róng, styled Yànxiān,
was a native of Wújùn.
His ancestors were descendants of King Gōujiàn of Yuè,
enfeoffed at Gùyì,
and their descendants took Gù as their surname,
becoming a prominent family in Wú for generations.
His grandfather Yōng
served as Chancellor of Wú.
His father Mù
was Governor of Yídū.
Róng was intelligent and alert from a young age,
graceful and outstanding in demeanor.
He served as Chief of the Court of Judicial Review.
Once, while drinking with colleagues in the government office,
he noticed a server of roasted meat who seemed different from ordinary servants,
so he cut a piece of meat and gave it to him to eat.
Later, when Prince Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
his son served as General of the Central Army,
and forced Róng to serve as his Chief Clerk.
After Lún was executed,
Róng was also arrested.
More than ten people were executed together.
Someone came to rescue Róng,
and when asked why,
he said:
'I am the servant who received roasted meat in the government office.'
Róng then realized and sighed:
'The kindness of a single meal,
is not forgotten even now.
The ancients did not speak in vain!'"
Zǔ, the Minister of Imperial Entertainments, was orphaned and poor in his youth,
but was extremely filial by nature,
often cooking meals for his mother himself.
Wáng Yǐn's *Book of Jìn* says:
"Zǔ Nà, styled Shìyán,
was a native of Qiú in Fànyáng.
For nine generations, his family had produced Filial and Incorrupt candidates.
Among Nà's uncles and three elder brothers,
he was the most virtuous in conduct,
skilled in pure conversation,
and served as Palace Attendant of the Crown Prince
and Minister of Justice.
He fled to the region south of the Yangtze,
and Wēn Qiáo recommended him as Minister of Imperial Entertainments."
General Wáng Píngběi heard of his fine reputation,
and sent him two maidservants as gifts,
then appointed him as a Palace Attendant.
The *Biography of Wáng Yì* says:
"Yì, styled Shūyuán,
was a native of Línyí in Lángyá.
At that time, Shǔ had just been pacified,
but two generals rebelled,
so Emperor Wén went west to Cháng'ān,
and summoned Yì to serve as Marshal of the State of the Chancellor,
later promoting him to Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
and sending him out to supervise military affairs in Yōuzhōu
as General Who Pacifies the North."
Someone teased him, saying:
"The price of a slave is twice that of a maidservant."
Zǔ said:
"Why must Bǎilǐ Xī be valued less than the price of five ram skins?"
The *Biographies of Virtuous Men of Chǔ* says:
"Bǎilǐ Xī, styled Jǐngbó,
was a native of the state of Chǔ.
In his youth, he served in Yú,
as a Grand Master.
When Jìn sought to borrow a path through Yú to attack Guó,
he advised against it but was not heeded,
so Xī left."
The *Garden of Stories* says:
"Duke Mù of Qín sent merchants to transport salt from Yú,
and the merchants bought Bǎilǐ Xī for five ram skins.
Duke Mù inspected the salt,
and was surprised that the oxen were fat.
When he asked the reason,
the reply was:
'They are fed on time,
and not driven harshly,
so they become fat.'
The Duke ordered officials to bathe him and provide him with clothes.
Gōngsūn Zhī yielded his ministerial position to him,
and he was titled Minister of the Five Rams."
Zhōu Zhěn was relieved of his post as Governor of Línchuān and returned to the capital,
but before he could find lodging,
he moored his boat at Qīngxī Islet.
The *Records of Émigrés of Yǒngjiā* says:
"Zhěn, styled Kāngshí,
was a native of Wèishì in Chénliú.
His grandfather Hé
was the former Magistrate of Gù'ān.
His father Zhèn
served as Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works."
The *Book of the Restoration* says:
"Zhěn was pure, frugal, and had few desires,
and achieved outstanding accomplishments wherever he served."
Chancellor Wáng went to visit him.
The *Biography of the Chancellor* says:
"Wáng Dǎo, styled Màohóng,
was a native of Lángyá.
His grandfather Lǎn
was praised for his virtuous conduct.
His father Cái
served as Palace Censor.
Dǎo was well-known from a young age,
though his family was poor and frugal.
He was content and delighted in the Way,
never troubled by worldly affairs."
It was summer,
and a sudden rainstorm arrived.
The boat was extremely narrow and small,
and also leaked heavily,
leaving almost no place to sit.
Wáng said:
"Even Hú Wēi's purity
could not surpass this!"
He immediately appointed him as Governor of Wúxīng.
The *Autumn of Jìn* says:
"Hú Wēi, styled Bóhǔ,
was a native of Huáinán.
His father Zhì was renowned for his loyalty and integrity.
When Zhì served as Governor of Jīng Province,
Wēi went from the capital to visit him.
When it was time to return,
Zhì gave Wēi a bolt of silk.
Wēi knelt and said:
'Father, you are pure and noble—
how did you obtain this?'
Zhì said:
'This is from my official salary surplus,
so I give it to you for provisions.'
Wēi accepted it and left."
Whenever he arrived at an inn,
he would let his donkey loose and gather firewood to cook.
After finishing his meal,
he would again follow the travelers on the road.
The military inspector under Hú Zhì secretly prepared provisions to intercept him,
and thus became his companion.
He assisted him in every matter,
and also offered him some food.
Hú Wēi grew suspicious,
and secretly questioned him to find out,
only to discover that he was the military inspector.
He thanked him and sent him away.
Later, when he reported this to Hú Zhì,
Hú Zhì had the military inspector beaten one hundred strokes,
and removed him from his official post.
Father and son were both so pure and cautious.
When Hú Wēi served in Xúzhōu,
Emperor Shìzǔ granted him an audience,
and discussed border affairs and his life with him.
The emperor sighed at his father's purity,
and said to Hú Wēi:
"How does your purity compare with your father's?"
He replied: "My purity is not as great."
The emperor said: "In what way is he superior to you?"
He replied: "My father's purity feared being known by others,
while my purity fears not being known by others.
Therefore, I am far inferior."
Dèng Yōu once fled from calamity,
and on the road abandoned his own son,
saving his younger brother's son.
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Yōu, styled Bódào,
was from Xiānglíng in Píngyáng.
At the age of seven, he lost his parents and grandparents,
and observed mourning for nine years.
His nature was pure, cautious, calm, and simple."
Dèng Càn's "Jìn Jì" says:
"During the Yǒngjiā era,
Dèng Yōu was captured by Shí Lè.
Summoned for an audience, he stood under the tent and spoke with him,
persuading him, and was seated and given food.
Where Dèng Yōu's carriage stopped,
it was adjacent to a Hu man's cart.
The Hu man's fire burned the carriage encampment,
and Shí Lè's officials interrogated the Hu man,
who falsely accused Dèng Yōu.
Dèng Yōu reckoned it was impossible to argue,
and said:
'Earlier, I was making porridge for an old woman,
and the fire spread out of control.
My crime deserves ten thousand deaths.'
Shí Lè, knowing the truth, released him.
The falsely accused Hu man deeply felt gratitude toward Dèng Yōu,
and gave him his donkey and horse,
escorting him to ensure his escape."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" says:
"Dèng Yōu, because the road was long,
broke his carriage,
and used oxen and horses to carry his wife and children to flee.
The bandits again plundered his oxen and horses.
Dèng Yōu said to his wife:
'My younger brother died early,
leaving only Yímín.
Now we must walk,
and if we carry both children, they will both die.
It is better to abandon our own child,
and hold Yímín.
We will still have children later.'
His wife obeyed."
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Dèng Yōu abandoned his child in the grass.
The child cried and chased after them,
and by evening caught up again.
The next day, Dèng Yōu tied the child to a tree and left.
They then crossed the river,
and he rose to Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, where he died. His nephew Dèng Suí mourned him in coarse mourning for three years."
After crossing the river,
he took a concubine,
whom he greatly favored.
After several years, he inquired about her background.
The concubine fully explained that she was a northerner who had suffered from the chaos,
and recalled her parents' names.
It turned out she was Dèng Yōu's niece.
Dèng Yōu had always been virtuous and accomplished,
his words and actions without blemish.
Upon hearing this, he grieved and regretted it for the rest of his life,
and thereafter never kept a concubine again.
Wáng Chángyù was a cautious and obedient person,
serving his parents with utmost filial piety.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Wáng Yuè, styled Chángyù,
was the eldest son of Chancellor Wáng Dǎo.
He served as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat."
The chancellor was always pleased to see Chángyù,
but always angry to see Jìngyù.
The "Wénzì Zhì" says:
"Wáng Tián, styled Jìngyù,
was the second son of Wáng Dǎo.
In his youth, he was outstanding and unrestrained,
diligent in learning and fond of martial arts,
and was not highly regarded by Wáng Dǎo.
He rose to Central Army General.
He was multi-talented,
skilled in clerical script,
and was known along with Jiāng Bīn of Jìyáng for being good at chess."
When Chángyù spoke with the chancellor,
he always emphasized caution and secrecy.
When the chancellor returned to the government offices,
and as he was leaving,
Chángyù never failed to escort him to his carriage.
He often helped Lady Cáo organize boxes and trunks.
After Chángyù's death,
when the chancellor returned to the offices,
after boarding his carriage,
he wept all the way to the office gate.
Lady Cáo packed his belongings into a basket,
sealed it, and could not bear to open it.
The "Wángshì Pǔ" says:
"Wáng Dǎo married the daughter of Cáo Sháo of Péngchéng,
named Shū."
Whenever Chancellor Héng heard people speak of Shēngōng,
he would say:
"This gentleman already has an established reputation,
and is praised by earlier worthies,
and was also a close friend of my late father.
It is not appropriate to speak of him."
The "Héng Yí Biézhuàn" says:
"Héng Yí, styled Màolún,
was from Lóngkàng in Qiáoguó,
the tenth-generation descendant of Héng Róng, the Han dynasty's 'Fifth Watcher.'
His father, Héng Yǐng,
had a high reputation.
Héng Yí was orphaned young,
but had clear insight and judgment.
He fled the chaos and crossed the river,
eventually rising to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary."
Monk Fǎshēn,
whose secular surname is unknown,
was likely a descendant of an official family.
His lofty virtue was widely praised,
and his reputation spread east of the mountains.
He was a disciple of Liú Gōng of Zhōngzhōu.
During the Yǒngjiā chaos,
he sought refuge in Yángzhōu,
residing in the capital.
Internally, he upheld the monastic rules;
externally, he fulfilled the expectations of all.
He was a Dharma master who propagated the Way.
Because his practice was compassionate and pure,
and he could not endure worldly dust,
he built a dwelling in the Āo Mountains, two hundred li east of Shàn County.
Over ten companions traveled with him,
dwelling loftily and freely.
Zhī Dàolín admired his style and demeanor,
and in a letter to a Goguryeo monk,
praised his virtuous conduct.
At the age of seventy-nine,
he passed away in the mountains."
Yǔ Gōng had a horse with a white blaze,
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Yǔ Liàng, styled Yuánguī,
was from Yānlíng in Yǐngchuān,
the eldest brother of Empress Míngmù.
He was profound, elegant, and virtuous,
and contemporaries compared him to Xiàhóu Tàichū
and Chén Chángwén.
He accompanied his uncle Yǔ Chēn,
taking refuge in Kuàijī,
where he sat upright and stern,
and the commandery people stood in awe of him.
Those who could meet him
numbered only a few.
He eventually rose to General Who Conquers the West
and Governor of Jīngzhōu."
Bó Lè's "Xiàng Mǎ Jīng" says:
"A horse with a white blaze extending from the forehead into the mouth and reaching the teeth
is called Yúyàn,
also known as Dílú.
If a slave rides it, he will die away from home;
if the master rides it, he will be executed in the marketplace.
It is an inauspicious horse."
Someone advised him to sell it.
The "Yǔ Lín" says:
"Yīn Hào advised Yǔ Gōng to sell the horse."
Yǔ said:
"If I sell it, there will surely be a buyer,
and then it will harm its new master.
How can I shift misfortune from myself to another?
In ancient times, Sūn Shū'áo killed a two-headed snake for the sake of those who would come after,
which is a beautiful tale from antiquity."
Jiǎ Yì's "Xīn Shū" says:
"When Sūn Shū'áo was a child,
he went out on the road
and saw a two-headed snake.
He killed it and buried it.
Returning home, he saw his mother and wept.
She asked him the reason. He replied:
'Those who see a two-headed snake are sure to die.
Now I have seen one, hence this.'"
The mother said: "Where is the snake now?"
He replied: "Fearing that others might see it,
I killed it and buried it."
The mother said: "One who performs hidden acts of virtue,
will surely receive open reward.
You need not worry."
Later, he indeed rose to prominence in the Chǔ court.
When he grew up, he became the Lìngyǐn of Chǔ.
To emulate this,
is that not enlightened!"
Ruǎn Guānglù was in Shàn,
and once had a fine carriage
that he would lend to anyone who asked.
There was a man burying his mother,
who wished to borrow it but dared not speak.
Ruǎn later heard of this,
sighed and said:
"I own a carriage that makes people afraid to borrow it—
what use is such a carriage?"
He then burned it.
The "Bié Zhuàn of Ruǎn Guānglù" says:
"Yù, styled Sīkuàng,
was from Wèishì, Chénliú.
His grandfather Luè
was Nèishǐ of Qíguó.
His father Yǐ,
was Tàishǒu of Rǔnán.
Yù was erudite, penetrating, principled, and discerning,
and rose repeatedly to become Shìzhōng.
Due to illness, he built a house on Shàn Mountain in Kuàijī.
He was summoned to be Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
but did not accept.
He died at age sixty-one."
Xiè Yì served as Lìng of Shàn,
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Xiè Yì, styled Wúyì,
was from Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His grandfather Héng
was Tàizǐ Shǎofù.
His father Póu,
was Lìbù Shàngshū.
Yì showed discernment and judgment from a young age,
was appointed as Tàiwèi Yuàn,
Lìng of Shàn,
and rose repeatedly to become Yùzhōu Cìshǐ."
There was an old man who broke the law,
Xiè punished him with strong wine,
until he became excessively drunk,
and still did not stop.
The Tàifù was seven or eight years old at the time,
wearing blue cloth trousers,
sitting by his elder brother's knee,
and admonished:
"Elder brother! The old man is pitiable,
how can you do this?"
Yì then changed expression and said:
"Ānú, do you wish to let him go?"
He then sent him away.
Xiè Tàifù held Chǔ Gōng in the highest esteem,
often saying:
"Chǔ Jìyě, though he does not speak,
possesses the essence of all four seasons."
The "Wénzì Zhì" says:
"Xiè Ān, styled Ānshí,
was Yì's younger brother.
His family had a tradition of learning and conduct;
Ān was broad-minded, pure, far-reaching,
gentle, refined, and harmonious.
Huán Yí saw him when he was four years old
and praised him, saying:
'This child's demeanor is outstanding and clear;
he will follow in the footsteps of Wáng Dōnghǎi.'
He excelled at Xíngshū calligraphy.
He rose repeatedly to become Tàibǎo,
Lù Shàngshū Shì.
He was posthumously granted Tàifù."
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Chǔ Póu, styled Jìyě,
was from Yángdí, Hénán.
His grandfather Cōng
was Āndōng Jiāngjūn.
His father Zhì
was Wǔchāng Tàishǒu.
Póu had an air of simplicity and nobility from a young age,
and was known for his calm and reticence.
He rose repeatedly to become Cìshǐ of Jiāng
and Yǎn provinces.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng,
Tàifù."
Liú Yǐn was in his commandery,
on his deathbed, weak and fading,
when he heard the drums and dances of a shrine ceremony below the tower.
He sternly said:
"Do not engage in improper sacrifices!"
The "Bié Zhuàn of Liú Yǐn" says:
"Tán, styled Zhēncháng,
was from Xiāo, Pèiguó.
A descendant of the Hàn house.
Zhēncháng possessed refined judgment;
even living in a humble gate and narrow lane,
he was content.
He served as Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ,
Shìzhōng,
Dānyáng Yǐn.
In governance, he emphasized calm, trustworthiness, and sincerity;
worldly turmoil could not sway him."
Someone outside requested to kill an ox from a cart to sacrifice to the gods.
Zhēncháng replied:
"I have been praying for a long time;
do not trouble yourself further."
Bāo's "Lúnyǔ" says:
"Dǎo
means to request."
Kǒng Ānguó said:
"Confucius's usual conduct was in harmony with the spirits,
hence he said:
'I have been praying for a long time.'"
Xiè Gōng's wife was instructing their son
and asked the Tàifù:
"Why have I never seen you instruct our son?"
He replied:
"I am always instructing him by my own example."
The "Xiè Shì Pǔ" says:
"Ān married the daughter of Liú Dān of Pèiguó."
Note:
Tàiwèi Liú Zǐzhēn,
was pure, clean, and had firm principles,
conducting himself according to ritual.
Yet his two sons were untalented,
both committing crimes of bribery and corruption.
Zǐzhēn was implicated and dismissed from office.
A guest asked:
"Why did you not instruct and guide them?"
Zǐzhēn said:
"My actions
are what their ears heard and eyes saw,
yet they did not follow or emulate them.
Could stern instruction have changed them?"
Ānshí's point
is the same as Zǐzhēn's meaning.
When Jìn Jiǎnwén was Fǔjūn,
the "Xù Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"The Emperor's name was Yù,
styled Dàowàn,
the youngest son of Zhōngzōng.
He was known for benevolence and wisdom.
Emperor Mù was young and immature,
so he, as Fǔjūn, assisted in governance.
Dà Sīmǎ Huán Wēn deposed Duke Hǎixī and established him as Emperor.
He reigned for three years before passing away."
The dust on the bed he sat on was not to be swept away;
seeing the tracks of mice,
he considered them fine.
A Cānjūn saw a mouse walking in daylight,
and killed it with his hand tablet.
The Fǔjūn looked displeased,
and his subordinates initiated a reprimand.
He instructed: "The mouse was harmed,
and I still cannot forget it;
now, to harm a person over a mouse—
is that not unacceptable?"
Fàn Xuān was eight years old
when picking vegetables in the back garden,
he accidentally injured his finger
and cried loudly.
Someone asked: "Does it hurt?"
He replied: "It is not because of the pain;
it is that one's body, hair, and skin
should not be carelessly injured—
that is why I cry!"
The "Xuān Bié Zhuàn" says:
"Xuān, styled Zǐxuān,
was from Chénliú,
a descendant of Fàn Dān, the former magistrate of Láiwú of the Hàn.
At age ten,
he could recite the Shī and Shū.
As a child,
if his hand was injured, his expression would change;
his family, considering him young,
all found this remarkable.
He was summoned to be Tàixué Bóshì,
Sànqí Chángshì,
but accepted none of these positions.
He died at age fifty-four."
Xuān was pure in conduct and frugal in life.
Hán Yùzhāng sent him a hundred bolts of silk,
but he did not accept them.
Hán Kāngbó was then serving as the Prefect of Dānyáng.
His mother, Yīn, was in the commandery,
and whenever she heard the weeping of the two Wú brothers,
she would feel deeply sorrowful.
She said to Kāngbó:
"If you ever become an official in charge of appointments,
you must properly take care of these men."
Kāngbó also knew them very well.
Hán later indeed became the Minister of Personnel.
The elder Wú could not avoid the mourning rites,
while the younger Wú eventually achieved great honor and success.
Zhèng Jī's "Biographies of Filial Sons" states:
"Yǐnzhī, styled Chùmò,
was filial from a young age.
When his mother passed away,
he grieved excessively, beyond the rites.
At that time, he lived next to Tàicháng Hán Kāngbó.
Kāngbó's mother was the younger sister of Yángzhōu Governor Yīn Hào,
an intelligent woman.
Whenever Yǐnzhī wept,
Kāngbó's mother would stop what she was doing and shed tears,
overwhelmed with grief,
and this continued throughout the mourning period.
She said to Kāngbó:
'If you later hold a position in charge of appointments,
you should employ men like this.'
Later, when Kāngbó became the Minister of Personnel,
he promoted and employed him."
"The Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn" states:
"Yǐnzhī possessed a profoundly filial nature,
and was moreover incorruptible.
He distributed his salary among his clan,
and in winter had no quilt.
Huán Xuán wished to reform the malpractices in Lǐngnán,
and appointed him as Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Twenty lǐ from the provincial capital was the Greedy Spring;
tradition held that those who drank from it would become insatiably greedy.
Yǐnzhī went to the water's edge,
scooped some up and drank it,
and then composed a poem:
'At Shímén lies the Greedy Spring;
one sip is worth a thousand gold.
If Bóyí and Shūqí were made to drink it,
their hearts would in the end remain unchanged.'
He was attacked by Lú Xún,
and returned to the capital.
He served successively as Minister and
General of the Central Army."
"The Book of the Jìn Restoration" states:
"It was traditionally said:
Those who went to Guǎngzhōu
and drank from the Greedy Spring
lost their incorruptible nature.
When Wú Yǐnzhī became Governor,
he personally scooped and drank from the Greedy Spring,
and inscribed a poem on the stone gate, saying thus."
Biān Wénlǐ met Yuán Fènggāo (Yuán Hóng).
He lost his composure.
"Biographies of Literary Men" states:
"Biān Ràng, styled Wénlǐ,
was from Chénliú.
He was talented, outstanding, eloquent, and unrestrained.
Grand General Hé Jìn heard of his reputation,
summoned him and appointed him as a Clerk,
and received him with courtesy.
Ràng's responses were graceful and refined,
his voice and bearing flowed smoothly,
and all the seated guests admired him.
When Ràng went out to his office,
at that time Kǒng Róng,
Wáng Lǎng, and others had previously served as Assistants,
and they all wrote calling cards to follow Ràng,
and Ràng interacted with them calmly and equally.
He later became the Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng,
and was killed by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi."
Fènggāo said:
"In antiquity, Yáo invited Xǔ Yóu,
and his face showed no shame.
Huángfǔ Mì states:
"Yóu, styled Wǔzhòng,
was from Huáilǐ, Yángchéng.
Yáo and Shùn both treated him as a teacher and learned from him.
Later, he retired into the marshes of Pèi,
and Yáo then offered him the empire and abdicated in his favor.
Yóu was a man who upheld righteousness and trod the straight path;
he would not sit on a mat improperly placed,
nor eat food improperly prepared.
Hearing of Yáo's offer, he departed.
His friend Cháofǔ heard that Yóu had been offered the empire by Yáo,
considering it had defiled him,
went to a pool and washed his ears.
The owner of the pool angrily said:
'Why do you defile my water?'
Yóu thereupon fled to cultivate the land south of the Yǐng River at Zhōngyuè,
at the foot of Jīshān,
and to the end of his life never showed any expression of ruling the empire.
When he died, he was buried atop Jīshān,
ten lǐ south of Yángchéng.
Yáo accordingly went to his grave,
and gave him the title 'Lordly Spirit of Jīshān,'
to be sacrificed to alongside the Five Sacred Mountains,
and he has been worshipped generation after generation,
continuing unbroken to this day."
Why then, sir, are your clothes all in disarray?"
Wénlǐ replied:
"Your Honor has only just arrived,
and the virtue of Yáo is not yet manifest;
therefore this humble subject's clothes are in disarray."
Note: Yuán Hóng died while serving as an Assistant to the Grand Commandant;
he never served as Governor of Rǔnán.
This account is erroneous.
Xú Rúzǐ (Xú Zhì).
At age nine,
he was once playing under the moonlight.
Someone said to him:
"If there were nothing in the moon,
would it be extremely bright?"
"General Discussions on the Five Classics" states:
"Why are there a hare and
a toad in the moon?
The moon is yīn;
the toad
is also yīn;
and together with the hare, they illuminate,
signifying yīn being attached to yáng." Xú said:
"Not so.
It is like the pupil in a person's eye;
without this, it certainly would not be bright."
Kǒng Wénjǔ (Kǒng Róng).
At age ten,
he followed his father to Luòyáng.
At that time, Lǐ Yuánlǐ enjoyed great fame
as the Colonel-Director of Retainers.
Those who visited his gate were all men of outstanding talent and pure reputation,
or his maternal relatives and cousins, before they were admitted.
Wénjǔ arrived at the gate
and said to the clerk:
"I am a relative of Prefect Lǐ." Once admitted,
he went forward and sat down.
Yuánlǐ asked:
"What relation are you to me?"
He replied:
"In the past, my ancestor Zhòngní and your ancestor Bóyáng
had a teacher-student relationship.
Therefore, I and you have been friends for generations."
Yuánlǐ and all his guests were greatly astonished.
Grand Master of Palace Leisure Chén Wěi arrived later,
and someone told him what had been said.
Wěi said:
"Clever as a child,
not necessarily outstanding as an adult!"
Wénjǔ said:
"I imagine you, sir, as a child,
must certainly have been clever!"
Wěi was greatly flustered and embarrassed.
"The Later Book of Hàn" states:
"Kǒng Róng, styled Wénjǔ,
was from the state of Lǔ,
a twenty-fourth generation descendant of Confucius.
His great-grandfather was Shàng,
Grand Administrator of Jùlù.
His father was Zhòu,
Commandant of Tàishān."
"Separate Biography of Róng" states:
"When Róng was four years old,
he and his elder brother were eating pears,
and he always took the smaller ones.
Someone asked him why.
He replied:
'Being the younger child,
it is proper to take the smaller ones.'"
At the age of ten,
he followed his father to the capital.
Lǐ Yīng, the Governor of Hénán, had a great reputation,
and Kǒng Róng wished to observe what kind of person he was,
so he went to visit him.
Yīng asked:
"Did your esteemed father or grandfather
ever associate with me?"
Róng replied:
"Yes.
My ancestor Confucius and your ancestor Lǎo Jūn
shared the same virtue and comparable righteousness,
and were each other's teacher and friend.
Thus, I and you are families connected for generations."
All those present sighed in admiration,
and everyone said:
"What an extraordinary child!"
Chén Wěi, the Grand Master of the Palace, arrived later,
and those sitting with him told him about it.
Wěi said:
"A person who is clever when young
may not necessarily grow up to be remarkable."
Róng responded immediately:
then when you were young,
were you truly intelligent?"
Yīng laughed heartily
and, turning to Róng, said:
"When you grow up, you will surely become a great vessel."
Kǒng Wénjǔ had two sons,
the elder was six years old,
the younger five.
One day when their father was sleeping,
the younger one stole wine from the head of the bed and drank it.
The elder boy said to him:
"Why don't you bow?"
He replied:
"This is stealing, how can one perform the ritual!"
When Kǒng Róng was arrested,
his family, both inside and out, was terrified.
At that time, Róng's elder son was nine,
the younger eight.
The two boys were deliberately playing a nail-tapping game,
showing not the slightest sign of panic.
Róng said to the envoy:
"I hope the punishment stops with me;
can my two sons be spared?"
The boys calmly stepped forward and said:
"Father, have you ever seen under an overturned nest
any eggs that remain intact?"
Soon they too were arrested.
The Wèi Shì Chūnqiū states:
"Róng, in his response to Sūn Quán's envoy, made slanderous remarks,
for which he was sentenced to public execution.
His two sons were just eight and nine years old.
When Róng was arrested,
they sat upright playing chess and did not rise.
Those around them said:
'Your father has been seized.'
The two boys said:
'How could there be an overturned nest with unbroken eggs?'
Thereupon they were both killed."
The Shìyǔ states:
"Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi, due to a poor harvest, prohibited alcohol.
Róng argued that wine is used to complete rituals
and should not be banned.
Because he confused the public with this,
Tàizǔ arrested and punished him.
His two young sons were also arrested. He looked at them and said:
'Why didn't you avoid this?'
The two boys said:
'If even our father is like this,
what is there to avoid?'"
Péi Sōngzhī believed that the Shìyǔ saying Róng's sons did not avoid it,
knowing they would surely die together,
is still somewhat acceptable.
But Sūn Shèng's account
is truly incomprehensible.
How could an eight-year-old child
so clearly foresee disaster,
displaying such exceptional intelligence and insight
far surpassing others?
If their feelings of worry and joy
indeed exceeded those of adults,
how could they see their father arrested
without changing expression,
continuing to play chess without rising,
as if at leisure?
In ancient times, Shēnshēng faced death
yet spoke without forgetting his father,
not abandoning thoughts of his father because he himself was about to die.
If it was so even when the father was safe,
how much more in times of turmoil!
Shèng considers this a beautiful tale,
but is that not harming the gentleman's son?
It is likely due to excessive fondness for the extraordinary
that he did not realize his words violate reason.
The Governor of Yǐngchuān had Chén Zhònggōng's head shaved.
Considering Shí's standing in his hometown,
whenever the commanderies or prefectures had doubtful legal cases they could not decide,
they would all go to Shí.
Some would confess upon arrival,
some would change their statements midway,
some would feign madness or terror,
all saying:
"We would rather suffer punishment
than be condemned by Lord Chén."
How could one whose virtuous influence moved people so profoundly
fail to defend himself,
instead incurring punishment?
This is surely not so!
This is what is called Dōngyě's talk!
A visitor asked Yuánfāng:
"What is the Prefect like?"
Yuánfāng said:
"A wise and brilliant lord."
"And what is your honored father like?"
He said:
"A loyal minister and filial son."
The visitor said:
"The Yì Jīng states:
'When two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut through metal;
words of one mind,
their fragrance is like orchids.'"
Wáng Yì's commentary on the Xì Cí says:
"Metal is extremely hard,
but those of one mind—
their sharpness can penetrate anything.
Orchids are fragrant things
that everyone delights in.
This means that those of one mind—
all things delight in them."
How could a wise and brilliant lord
punish a loyal minister and filial son?"
Yuánfāng said:
"How absurd your words are!
Therefore I will not answer."
The visitor said:
"You are merely feigning humility
because you cannot answer." Yuán-
fāng said:
"In ancient times, Emperor Gāozōng exiled the filial son Xiàojǐ.
The Dìwáng Shìjì states:
'Emperor Gāozōng Wǔ Dīng of Yīn had a worthy son named Xiàojǐ.
His mother died early,
and Gāozōng, misled by his later wife's words,
exiled him, and he died.
The whole empire mourned him.'
Yǐn Jífǔ exiled the filial son Bó Qí.
The Qín Cāo states:
'Lord Jífǔ
was a minister of Zhōu.
He had a son named Bó Qí.
After his mother died, he remarried.
The later wife bore a son named Bó Guī.
She then slandered Bó Qí to Jífǔ,
who thereupon exiled Bó Qí to the wilderness.
When King Xuān went on an excursion,
Jífǔ accompanied him.
Bó Qí then composed a song
to move him with words.
King Xuān heard it and said:
"This is a filial son's words."
Jífǔ then sought Bó Qí in the wilderness
and shot and killed his later wife.'
Dǒng Zhòngshū exiled the filial son Fú Qǐ." (Details unknown.)
"Only these three lords
were wise and brilliant;
only these three sons
were loyal ministers and filial sons."
The visitor withdrew in shame.
Xún Címíng met with Yuán Làng of Rǔnán.
Xún Shuǎng had another name, Xǔ.
The Hànnán Jì states:
"Xǔ was thoroughly versed in all literary works and classical texts.
A contemporary proverb said:
'Of the eight dragons of the Xún family,
Címíng is matchless.'
He lived in seclusion with steadfast determination,
and did not accept any summons or offers of employment."
Zhāng Fán's Hàn Jì states:
"When Dǒng Zhuó held power,
he again summoned Shuǎng.
Shuǎng wanted to flee,
but the officials held him urgently.
Starting as a commoner,
he reached the rank of one of the Three Excellencies in ninety-five days."
When asked about the eminent figures of Yǐngchuān,
Címíng first mentioned his elder brothers.
Chén Làng laughed and said:
"Should scholars only be recommended based on kinship and old acquaintances?"
Címíng replied:
"Sir, your challenge—
on what classic is it based?"
Chén Làng said:
"I was asking about the finest talents of the state,
yet you mentioned your elder brothers,
that is why I find it objectionable."
Címíng said:
"In ancient times, Qí Xī recommended from within without avoiding his own son,
and recommended from without without avoiding his enemy,
and was considered perfectly impartial.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* records:
'Qí Xī was the commander of the central army.
He requested retirement due to old age.
The Marquis of Jìn asked him about a successor.
He recommended Xiè Hú, who was his enemy.
Just as he was about to be appointed, Xiè Hú died.
The Marquis asked again.
He replied: "Wǔ is suitable."
This was his own son.
The gentleman said that Qí Xī could indeed be called capable of recommending the worthy.
Recommending his enemy was not flattery;
establishing his son was not favoritism.'
The odes of the Duke of Zhōu and King Wén
do not discuss the virtue of Yáo and Shùn,
but instead praise King Wén and King Wǔ—
this is the principle of cherishing one's kin.
The principle of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
is to treat one's own state as internal and the various Xià states as external.
Moreover, is it not contrary to virtue
to not love one's own kin but love others?"
Mí Héng was demoted by Wèi Wǔ to the position of drum official.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, he was to test the drums.
Héng raised the drumstick and performed the "Yúyáng Càn Zhuā,"
its deep resonance resembling the sound of metal and stone,
causing all present to change their expressions.
The *Diǎn Lüè* states:
"Héng, styled Zhèngpíng,
was from Bān County in Píngyuán."
The *Wénshì Zhuàn* states:
"Héng's ancestry is unknown;
his exceptional talent was outstanding.
In his youth, he formed a friendship of mutual familiarity with Kǒng Róng,
at a time when Héng was not yet twenty,
and Róng was already fifty.
Róng, admiring Héng's brilliant talent,
established a cordial bond with him,
unable to part ways.
At the beginning of the Jiàn'ān era, he traveled north.
Some advised him to visit the influential nobles in the capital.
Héng carried a name card,
but it eventually wore out from neglect,
and in the end, he visited no one.
Róng repeatedly sent letters to Emperor Wǔ,
praising his talent,
and the Emperor earnestly wished to meet him.
Héng claimed illness and refused to go,
yet frequently made critical remarks.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
but due to Héng's talent and reputation, did not have him killed.
Instead, he plotted to humiliate him,
and ordered him registered as a drum official.
Later, at the court assembly in the eighth month,
there was a grand inspection of drum rhythms.
A three-tiered pavilion was erected,
with guests seated in rows.
Clothing was made from silk and fine cloth:
one tall drumming cap,
one single-layered robe and short trousers.
The drum officials taking their turn
were all to remove their old clothes
and don these new garments.
When it was Héng's turn,
Héng struck the drum with the "Yúyáng Càn Zhuā,"
stepping forward,
his feet stamping rhythmically,
his demeanor and bearing unusual,
the drumbeats exceedingly mournful,
the rhythm exceptionally marvelous.
None of the seated guests failed to be stirred with emotion,
knowing it must be Héng.
After his turn,
he refused to change clothes.
An official scolded him:
'Why does the drum official alone not change his attire?'
Héng then stopped.
Before Emperor Wǔ,
he first removed his trousers,
then removed the rest of his clothes,
standing naked.
Slowly, he then put on the tall cap,
next the single-layered robe,
and finally the trousers.
Finished,
he again struck the drum with the stick and left,
his expression showing no shame.
Emperor Wǔ laughed and said to those present:
'I intended to humiliate Héng,
but Héng has instead humiliated me.'
To this day, the "Yúyáng Càn Zhuā"
originated from Héng.
He was later killed by Huáng Zǔ."
Kǒng Róng said:
"Mí Héng's crime was the same as that of Xū Mí,
yet he could not inspire the dream of an enlightened king."
Huángfǔ Mì's *Dìwáng Shìjì* states:
"Wǔ Dīng dreamed that Heaven bestowed upon him a worthy man.
He had the artisans sketch his likeness,
and searched for him throughout the land.
He saw a convict laborer, Xū Mí,
wearing coarse clothes in the wilds of Fùyán—
this was Fù Yuè."
Zhāng Yàn said:
"Xū Mí
is a type of punishment.
Xū means mutual;
mí means following.
It refers to those who are implicated and receive light punishment."
Wèi Wǔ, ashamed, pardoned him.
Páng Shìyuán of Nánjùn heard
that Sīmǎ Décāo was in Yǐngchuān,
so he traveled two thousand lǐ to visit him.
Upon arrival,
he encountered Décāo picking mulberry leaves.
Shìyuán, from his carriage, said to him:
"I have heard that a great man in the world
should wear gold and purple,
how can one with the capacity of a great river
stoop to the tasks of a silk-weaving woman?"
The *Shǔ Zhì* states:
"Páng Tǒng, styled Shìyuán,
was from Xiāngyáng.
In his youth, he was simple and slow-witted,
and none recognized his worth.
Sīmǎ Huī of Yǐngchuān had the discernment to judge men.
Shìyuán, at the age of twenty, went to see Huī.
Huī was picking mulberry leaves in a tree,
while Shìyuán sat beneath the tree.
They conversed
from day until night.
Huī, amazed, said:
'This young man will surely be the crown of the southern provinces' scholars.'
From then on, he gradually became prominent."
The *Xiāngyáng Jì* states:
"Shìyuán
was the nephew of Dé Gōng.
In his youth, none recognized his worth,
only Dé Gōng valued him.
At eighteen,
he was sent to visit Décāo.
After speaking with him,
Décāo sighed and said:
'Dé Gōng truly knows men;
this is indeed great virtue.'
Later, Liú Bèi consulted Décāo about worldly affairs.
Décāo said:
'How could a vulgar scholar understand the times?
Here we have the Crouching Dragon
and the Young Phoenix.'
He referred to Zhūgě Kǒngmíng and Shìyuán."
The *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
"Liú Bèi appointed Shìyuán as Military Advisor and General of the Household.
While following the attack on Luò,
he was hit by a stray arrow
and died. He was thirty-eight at the time."
Décāo said: The *Sīmǎ Huī Biézhuàn* states:
"Huī, styled Décāo,
was from Yángdí in Yǐngchuān.
He possessed the discernment to judge human character.
He resided in Jīngzhōu.
Knowing that Liú Biǎo's nature was dark,
and that he would certainly harm good men,
he kept his mouth shut and did not discuss or judge contemporaries.
When people asked him about individuals,
he never distinguished their high or low standing,
but always simply said they were excellent.
His wife admonished him:
'When people come to you with their doubts,
you should analyze and discuss,
yet you uniformly say they are all excellent—
is this what people consult you for?'
Huī said:
'What you say is also excellent.'
Such was his gentle and evasive manner.
Once, someone mistakenly claimed Huī's pig as his own,
and Huī simply pushed it to him.
Later, when the man found his own pig,
he came back kowtowing to return it.
Huī again thanked him profusely."
Liú Biǎo's son Cóng went to visit Huī,
sending someone to ask if he was in.
It happened that Huī was hoeing his garden himself,
Cóng's attendants asked: "Is Sīmǎ Jūn here?"
Huī said: "I am he."
Cóng's attendants saw his ugliness,
and scolded: "Wretched laborer,
the general's young masters wish to see Sīmǎ Jūn,
what kind of field slave are you,
that you dare call yourself him!"
Huī went back,
cut his hair, put on a headcloth, and came out to meet them.
Cóng's attendants saw that Huī was indeed the old man from before,
were afraid, and told Cóng about it.
Cóng rose,
kowtowed and apologized.
Huī then said to him:
"You truly should not have,
yet I am deeply ashamed of it.
This matter of hoeing the garden myself,
only you know of it."
Someone came to him when he was tending silkworms, asking for bamboo trays and mats;
Huī abandoned his own silkworms and gave them to him.
Someone said:
"When people harm themselves to aid others,
it is because the other's need is urgent and one's own is not.
Now your situations are exactly equal,
why give to another?"
Huī said: "The man had never asked anything of me before,
if I refused his request, he would be ashamed.
How can one cause another shame over material goods!"
Someone said to Liú Biǎo:
"Sīmǎ Dé Cāo is an extraordinary man,
only he has not yet met his opportunity."
Biǎo later saw him and said:
"People in the world speak nonsense,
this is merely a petty scholar."
His wisdom that could appear foolish was all of this kind.
When Jīngzhōu fell,
he was captured by Cáo Cāo,
Cāo wished to employ him greatly,
but he happened to fall ill and die."
"You, sir, please step down from the carriage,
you only know the speed of the shortcut,
but do not consider the confusion of losing the way.
In ancient times, Bó Chéng plowed in pairs,
not coveting the glory of being a feudal lord;
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
"When Yáo governed the world,
Bó Chéng Zǐ Gāo was established as a feudal lord.
When Yǔ became the Son of Heaven,
Bó Chéng resigned his lordship and plowed in the wilds.
Yǔ went to see him,
hastened to a lower position and asked him.
Zǐ Gāo said:
'In the past when Yáo governed the world,
he did not reward, yet the people were encouraged;
he did not punish, yet the people were in awe.
Now you reward and punish, yet the people are becoming unvirtuous.
Virtue has declined from this time,
punishments have been established from this time.
Why do you not leave, sir? Do not interrupt my work!'"
Yuán Xiàn with his mulberry door-pivot,
would not exchange it for an official's mansion.
The Family Sayings says:
"Yuán Xiàn, styled Zǐ Sī,
was a man of Sòng,
a disciple of Confucius. He lived in Lǔ,
in a room surrounded by earthen walls,
thatched with fresh grass,
with a ragged door incomplete,
a mulberry door-pivot and jar windows,
leaking above and damp below,
yet he sat playing his zither and singing.
Zǐ Gòng with his carriage that could not fit in the alley,
went to see him and said:
'What ailment do you suffer from, sir?'
Xiàn said:
'I have heard that lacking wealth is called poverty,
learning but being unable to practice is called an ailment.
Now I am poor, not ill.
To act conforming to the world,
to befriend through partisanship,
to study for the sake of others,
to teach for one's own sake,
the perversion of benevolence and righteousness,
the adornment of carriages and horses—
I cannot bear to do such things.'"
How can it be that one must sit in a magnificent house,
ride fat horses,
have dozens of serving maids,
and only then be considered extraordinary?
This is why Xǔ, Fù (Xǔ Yóu, Cháo Fǔ)
were so impassioned,
why Yí, Qí (Bó Yí, Shū Qí) sighed deeply.
The Mèngzǐ says:
"Bó Yí and Shū Qí would not look with their eyes at evil sights,
would not listen with their ears to evil sounds.
Living among the villagers,
they felt as if in mire and charcoal,
such was the purity of the sages."
Even if one had the rank stolen from Qín,
the wealth of a thousand teams of horses,
The Ancient Historical Investigations says:
"Lǚ Bùwéi acted for Qín's Zǐ Chǔ,
expending a thousand pieces of gold on goods for Lady Huáyáng,
requesting that Zǐ Chǔ be established as heir.
When Zǐ Chǔ was established,
he enfeoffed Bùwéi with a hundred thousand households in Luòyáng,
bestowing the title Marquis Wénxìn."
He obtained the rank by deceit,
hence it is called stolen.
The Analects says:
"Duke Jǐng of Qí had a thousand teams of horses,
yet the people found no virtue in him to praise."
Kǒng Ānguó said:
"A thousand teams,
means four thousand horses." it is not worthy of honor!"
Shì Yuán said:
"I was born in a remote borderland,
and have seen little of great righteousness.
If I do not once strike the great bell,
beat the thunder drum,
then I will not recognize their sound."
Liú Gōng Gàn incurred offense due to disrespect.
The Diǎn Lüè says:
"Liú Zhēn, styled Gōng Gàn,
was from Níngyáng, Dōngpíng.
In the sixteenth year of the Jiàn'ān era,
when the heir apparent was General of the Household for All Purposes,
he was excellently selected for literary talent,
and was made to attend the crown prince.
During a merry drinking feast,
the lady Zhēn Shì was made to come out and pay respects,
most guests at the feast bowed low,
but Zhēn alone looked straight at her.
Another day, the Duke heard of it,
then arrested Zhēn,
commuting his death sentence to penal servitude in the labor corps."
The Wénshì Zhuàn says:
"Zhēn was eloquent and quick-witted,
answering questions as soon as they were asked.
For looking straight at Lady Zhēn,
he was assigned to the labor corps,
and made to grind stones.
Emperor Wǔ went to the workshop to observe the laborers,
and saw Zhēn sitting upright with a solemn expression grinding a stone.
Emperor Wǔ asked:
'How is the stone?'
Zhēn thus found a metaphor to plead his case,
knelt and replied:
'The stone comes from the peak of the sheer cliffs of Jīngshān,
externally it has the pattern of five colors,
internally it contains the treasure of Biàn Hé.
Grinding it does not increase its luster,
carving it does not add to its pattern.
It is endowed with a firm and steadfast nature,
receiving it from what is so of itself.
Yet its grain is bent, twisted, and coiled, unable to be straightened.'
The Emperor looked at his attendants and laughed heartily,
and pardoned him that very day."
Emperor Wén asked:
"Why were you not careful regarding the laws and regulations?"
Zhēn replied:
"Your subject is indeed mediocre and limited,
but it is also because Your Majesty's legal net is not loose."
The Wèi Zhì says:
"The Emperor's personal name was Pī,
styled Zǐ Huán,
he received the abdication from Hàn."
According to various texts, some say Zhēn was punished during the time of Wǔ of Wèi,
and died of illness in the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān.
Emperor Wén ascended the throne seven years later.
To say that Zhēn offended during the Huángchū era
is erroneous.
Zhōng Yù and Zhōng Huì had fine reputations from youth.
The Wèi Shū says:
"Yù, styled Zhì Shū,
was from Chángshè, Yǐngchuān,
the eldest son of the Chancellor of State, Zhōng Yóu.
At fourteen,
he became a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
quick-witted in conversation and laughter like his father,
and rose to the post of General of Chariots and Cavalry."
At thirteen,
Emperor Wén of Wèi heard of him,
and said to his father Zhōng Yóu
The Wèi Zhì says:
"Yóu, styled Yuán Cháng,
was poor in his household but fond of learning,
and wrote commentaries on the Zhōu Yì
and the Lǎozi.
He served as Chief Judge,
Chancellor of State,
and it is said:
was promoted to Grand Tutor."
"You may have your two sons come."
Thereupon he summoned them for an audience.
Zhōng Yù’s face was sweaty.
The Emperor said:
"Why is your face sweating?"
Yù replied:
"Trembling with fear and anxiety,
sweat pours out like thick soup."
He then asked Huì:
"Why are you not sweating?"
Huì replied:
"Trembling with fear and dread,
sweat dares not come out."
When Zhōng Yù and his brother were young,
they once found their father taking a daytime nap,
so together they secretly drank some medicinal wine.
Their father awoke at the time,
but pretended to be asleep to observe them.
Yù bowed before drinking,
while Huì drank without bowing.
The Records of Wei states:
"Huì, styled Shìjì,
was the youngest son of Zhōng Yáo.
He was intelligent and precocious.
The Central Protector of the Army, Jiǎng Jì, wrote an essay,
claiming that by observing a person's pupils,
one could fully understand their character.
When Huì was five years old,
Yáo sent him to see Jì.
Jì found him extraordinary,
and said:
'This is no ordinary person!'
When he reached adulthood,
he possessed talent and resourcefulness,
was well-versed in philosophical reasoning,
