and rose through the ranks to become a Gentleman Attendant at the Palace Gate.
When Zhūgě Dàn rebelled,
and King Wén campaigned against him,
Huì contributed greatly to the strategy,
and contemporaries called him Zǐfáng.
He was appointed General Who Guards the West.
He led the campaign against Shǔ,
and after Shǔ was pacified,
he was promoted to Minister over the Masses.
Believing his achievements and fame were unmatched in his time,
he felt he could no longer serve under others.
He said to his close associates:
'Since my campaign in Huáinán,
not a single strategy of mine has failed,
this is known throughout the land.
With this, where can I find peace?'
He then plotted rebellion,
was executed,
at the age of forty."
Afterwards, their father asked Yù why he had bowed.
Yù said:
"Wine is used to complete rituals,
I dared not not bow."
He then asked Huì why he had not bowed.
Huì said:
"Stealing is inherently contrary to ritual,
therefore I did not bow."
Emperor Míng of Wèi
built a residence for his maternal grandmother among the Zhēn family.
The Late Wèi Biography states:
"The Emperor's personal name was Ruì,
styled Yuánzhòng,
he was the crown prince of Emperor Wén.
Because his mother was deposed,
he was not initially established as heir.
Once, Emperor Wén went hunting with him,
and they saw a doe with her fawn.
Emperor Wén shot the mother,
and she fell with the twang of the bowstring.
He then ordered the Emperor
to shoot the fawn.
The Emperor set down his bow and wept, saying:
'Your Majesty has already killed its mother,
I cannot bear to kill its child as well.'
Emperor Wén said:
'Such fine words move the heart.'
He was then established as heir.
This was Emperor Míng."
The Wèi History states:
"Empress Zhēn, the Wénzhāo Empress,
was the mother of Emperor Míng.
Her father was Zhēn Yì,
Magistrate of Shàngcài.
When Emperor Lièzōng ascended the throne,
he posthumously enfeoffed him as Lord of Shàngcài.
His legitimate grandson, Zhēn Xiàng, inherited the title.
When Xiàng died,
his son, Zhēn Chàng, succeeded him.
A grand mansion was built,
and the imperial carriage personally visited it."
After the residence was completed,
the Emperor went to inspect it himself,
and said to his attendants:
"What should this residence be named?"
The Palace Attendant, Miào Xí, said:
The Preface to Literary Works states:
"Xí, styled Xībó,
was from Lánlíng in Dōnghǎi.
He was talented and learned,
and rose to become Palace Attendant
and Superintendent of the Imperial Household."
"Your Majesty's sagely thoughts match those of wise kings;
your boundless filial piety surpasses even that of Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Sǔn.
The construction of this residence
stems from your deep affection for your maternal uncle's family.
It should be named 'Wèiyáng'."
The Qín Ode in the Book of Songs says:
"'Wèiyáng'
expresses Duke Kāng's remembrance of his mother.
Duke Kāng's mother
was the daughter of Duke Xiàn of Jìn.
When Duke Wén suffered the calamity caused by Lí Jī,
before he could return, his mother, the Qín princess, died.
Duke Mù welcomed Duke Wén,
and Duke Kāng, then the crown prince,
saw Duke Wén off at the north bank of the Wèi River,
thinking of his mother whom he could no longer see.
'When I see my maternal uncle,
it is as if my mother were still alive.'"
According to the Wèi History:
The Emperor built a tower for Xiàng's mother in the rear garden,
and named the lane Wèiyáng.
However, Xiàng's mother was the Emperor's aunt by marriage (his uncle's wife),
not his maternal grandmother.
Moreover,
using "Wèiyáng"
as the name for the residence
also contradicts the old histories.
Hé Píngshū said:
"Taking the Five Minerals Powder
not only treats illness,
but also makes one feel clear-minded and bright."
The Wèi Lüè states:
"Hé Yàn, styled Píngshū,
was from Wǎn in Nányáng.
He was the grandson of Hé Jìn, the Grand General of Hàn.
Some say he was the grandson of Hé Miáo.
He married a princess,
and was also fond of women,
so during the Huángchū era he held no significant post.
During the Zhèngshǐ era,
Cáo Shuǎng employed him as a Palace Secretary,
in charge of selecting officials.
Many old acquaintances received his help and promotion.
He was executed by Sima Xuānwáng."
Chancellor Qín's Treatise on Cold-Food Powder states:
"Although the formula for Cold-Food Powder originated in the Hàn dynasty,
few used it,
and it was not widely transmitted.
Hé Yàn, the Wèi Minister, was the first to obtain its miraculous effects,
and from then on it became widely popular in the world,
with users following one after another."
Jī Kāng, the Palace Consultant, said to Zhào Jǐngzhēn:
Jī Shào's Account of Zhào Zhì states:
"Zhì, styled Jǐngzhēn,
was from Dàijùn.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
his grandfather wandered and settled as a guest in Gōushì.
When the new magistrate took office,
Zhì was twelve years old,
and he watched from the roadside with his mother.
His mother said:
'Your ancestors were not from a lowly family.
Can you later achieve something like this?'
Zhì said: 'It can be done.'
Upon returning home, he immediately sought a teacher to study books.
One morning, hearing his father shouting at the ox while plowing,
he put down his book and wept.
His teacher asked him why, and he replied:
'I grieve that I cannot attain glory and wealth,
and thus cause my old father to toil without respite.'
At fourteen,
he entered the Grand Academy to observe.
At that time, my late father was at the Academy copying ancient script stone classics.
After finishing his work, he left.
Zhì then followed his carriage and asked my late father his name.
My late father said:
'Young man, why do you ask me?'
Zhì said:
'I observe that your demeanor and bearing are extraordinary,
so I asked.'
My late father told him everything.
At fifteen, Zhì feigned illness,
and repeatedly ran wildly for three or five lǐ,
until his family caught up with him.
They also cauterized over ten places on his body.
At sixteen, he fled from home,
went straight to Luòyáng,
but could not find my late father.
He went to Yè,
where Shǐ Zhònghé of the Pèi state, grandson of the Wèi General of the Central Army Shǐ Huàn,
took him in.
He then changed his name to Yì,
styled Yánghé.
When my late father arrived in Yè,
Zhì recounted in detail the events at the Grand Academy,
and then followed my late father back to Shānyáng for a full year."
He was up to seven chi and three cun tall,
with fair skin and black hair,
red lips and bright eyes,
not much sideburns or beard,
calm and composed,
his body so frail it seemed unable to bear the weight of clothes.
His late father once said to him:
'Your head is small and sharp,
your pupils distinct in black and white,
your gaze steady and discerning—
you have the bearing of Bái Qǐ.'
When it came to discussion, he was clear and eloquent,
possessing the talent of a strategist,
yet he never flaunted it.
Mèng Yuánjī appointed him as an assistant in Liáodōng,
where he adjudicated nine cases in the commandery,
and was praised for his fairness and appropriateness.
Tormented by having abandoned his parents to travel far,
he did not see his mother before her death,
vomited blood and fell ill,
and died before completing the mourning period."
"Your pupils are distinct in black and white,
you have the bearing of Bái Qǐ.
Yán Yóu's 'Account of Three Generals' says:
'Bái Qǐ—
Píngyuán Jūn advised King Xiàochéng of Zhào to accept Féng Tíng's offer.
The king said:
"If we accept it, the Qín army will surely come,
and Wǔ'ān Jūn will certainly lead them.
Who can withstand him?"
He replied:
"At the meeting in Miǎnchí,
I observed that Wǔ'ān Jūn had a small head and sharp features,
pupils distinct in black and white,
and a gaze that did not waver.
A small head and sharp features indicate
daring and decisiveness;
pupils distinct in black and white indicate
clarity of vision;
a gaze that does not waver indicates
strong determination.
One can engage him in a prolonged struggle,
but it is difficult to confront him directly.
As for Lián Pō,
he is brave and fierce, and cares for his soldiers,
knows when to endure hardship and swallow humiliation.
In open-field battles, he is no match,
but in defensive warfare, he is fully capable of holding his ground."
The king followed his advice.'"
Regrettably, his capacity was narrow and limited."
Zhào Yún said:
"A one-chi gnomon can determine the degrees of the celestial sphere.
The 'Zhōu Bì' says:
'At the summer solstice,
the sun is 26,000 lǐ to the north;
at the winter solstice,
it is 135,000 lǐ to the south.
At noon, if a gnomon is erected, it casts no shadow.
The Zhōu Bì is eight chǐ long.
On the day of the summer solstice,
the shadow measures one chǐ and six cùn.
Bì refers to the leg;
guǐ refers to the shadow.
One thousand lǐ due south,
the shadow measures one chǐ and five cùn;
one thousand lǐ due north,
the shadow measures one chǐ and seven cùn.
This is from the book 'Zhōu Bì'.'"
A one-cùn pipe can measure the cyclical movements of qi.
The 'Lǚshì Chūnqiū' says:
"Huángdì sent Líng Lún
to the west of Dàxià and the northern slopes of Kūnlún,
to fetch bamboo from the Xiègǔ Valley,
selecting pieces with uniform thickness in their hollows,
cutting them between two nodes, and blowing through them,
to make the Huángzhōng pitch pipes.
He made twelve tubes,
to listen to the calls of the phoenix.
Six were for the male's calls, six for the female's,
and these became the pitch standards."
The 'Continued Hàn History: Treatise on Harmonics and Calendrics' says:
"The variations of the twelve pitches
extend to sixty,
used to observe the qi through pitch pipes.
The method for observing qi:
build a triple-walled chamber,
close the doors,
seal all cracks thoroughly,
hang dense orange curtains,
place a wooden stand,
set the pitch pipes on it,
and fill them with reed membrane ash.
When moved by the qi,
the ash will scatter.
In this way, it is observed.
Why must it be large?
It only depends on how much one knows!"
When Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng campaigned eastward,
the 'Wèi Shū' says:
"Sīmǎ Shī, styled Zǐyuán,
was the eldest son of Xiànguó Xuānwén Hóu.
Renowned for his pure and unblemished virtue,
he was highly regarded at court,
serving as Grand General
and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
When Wúqiū Jiǎn rebelled,
Shī personally led the campaign against him
and was posthumously honored as Jǐngwáng."
He recruited Lǐ Xǐ from Shàngdǎng
to serve as a Palace Assistant.
He then asked Xǐ:
"In the past, my late father summoned you, but you did not accept.
Now that I have summoned you,
why have you come?"
Xǐ replied:
"Your late father treated me with courtesy,
so I could advance or withdraw with courtesy;
but you, my lord, govern by law,
and I have come out of fear of the law!"
The 'Accounts of the Jìn Nobles' says:
"Xǐ, styled Jìhé,
was from Tóngdī in Shàngdǎng.
In his youth, he was of high conduct
and deeply studied the arts and learning.
When Xuāndì served as Xiànguó,
he summoned Xǐ,
but Xǐ firmly declined due to illness.
When Jǐngdì assisted in governance,
he served as a Palace Assistant,
rising through the ranks to become Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
and Specially Advanced.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Guardian."
Dèng Ài had a stutter,
and when speaking, he would say "Ài, Ài."
The 'Wèi Zhì' says:
"Ài, styled Shìzǎi,
was from Jíyáng.
In his youth, he worked as a cowherd for farmers.
At the age of twelve,
he followed his mother to Yǐngchuān,
where he read the inscription on the stele of the former Grand Chief of Tàiqiū,
which said:
'His words are a model for the age,
his conduct a standard for scholars.'
He then took the name Fàn,
and styled himself Shìzé.
Later, when someone in his clan had the same name,
he changed it.
Whenever he saw high mountains or great marshes,
he would plan and sketch locations for military camps,
and many people at the time laughed at him.
Later, when he met Sīmǎ Xuānwáng,
he was appointed three times as an assistant,
and rose through the ranks to become General Who Conquers the West.
He led a campaign against Shǔ,
and after Shǔ was pacified,
he was promoted to Grand Commandant.
He was killed by Wèi Guàn."
Jìn Wénwáng teased him, saying:
"You say 'Ài, Ài'—
how many Àis is that, exactly?"
He replied:
"'Fèng xī, fèng xī'—
still just one phoenix."
Zhū Fèng's 'Jìn Jì' says:
"Wénwáng, named Zhāo,
styled Zǐshàng,
was the second son of Xuāndì."
The 'Biographies of Immortals' says:
"Lù Tōng,
also known as the Madman of Chǔ, Jiē Yú,
was fond of nurturing his nature and traveled to various famous mountains.
Once, upon encountering Confucius, he sang:
'Phoenix, oh phoenix!
How your virtue has declined!
What is past cannot be admonished,
but what is to come can still be pursued.'
Later, he entered Shǔ
and dwelled in the Éméi Mountains."
After Jī Kāng, the Palace Attendant, was executed,
Xiàng Xiù, as a commandery envoy, entered Luòyáng.
Wénwáng summoned him
and asked:
"I heard you had the ambition to retire to Jīshān.
Why are you here?"
He replied:
"Cháo Fǔ and Xǔ Yóu were reclusive and stubborn men—
not worthy of much admiration."
The *Biography of Xiàng Xiù* states:
"Xiù, styled Zǐqī,
was a man from Hénèi.
In his youth, he was recognized by Shān Tāo from the same commandery,
and was also close friends with Jī Kāng of Qiáo Country
and Lǚ Ān of Dōngpíng.
They all possessed an air that transcended the vulgar,
their comings and goings were never different,
and their undertakings and management of livelihood were also identical.
He often worked at the forge alongside Jī Kāng in Luòyì,
and watered gardens with Lǚ Ān in Shānyáng,
giving no thought to whether his family had possessions or not,
external things being insufficient to disturb his mind.
At the age of twenty, he wrote the *Discourse on Confucianism and Daoism*,
but discarded it and did not keep a copy.
Some enthusiasts may have preserved it.
Some say it was written by a member of his clan,
who, finding himself in straits and unable to advance,
then informed Xiù,
wishing to borrow his name.
Xiù laughed and said:
'That can be done again.'
Later, when Kāng was executed,
Xiù then lost his bearings.
He then responded to the annual recommendation,
went to the capital,
and visited the Great General, Sima Wénwáng.
Wénwáng asked him:
'I have heard that you, sir, had the ambition of retiring to Jīshān;
how is it that you can humble yourself?'
Xiù said:
'I have always said that those men did not understand Yáo's intention;
it was not originally what I admired.'
Everyone present was pleased,
and he was subsequently transferred in turn to the posts of Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gates
and Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry."
When Emperor Wǔ of Jìn first ascended the throne,
he drew a divination slip and got "one".
The *Genealogy of the Jìn Dynasty* states:
"The Posthumous Emperor's taboo name was Yán,
styled Ānyǔ,
who received the abdication from Wèi in the second year of Xiánxī."
The number of generations for a king
hinges on this number.
The Emperor, displeased,
caused the assembled ministers to lose color,
with none able to speak.
The Palace Attendant Péi Kǎi came forward and said:
"Your servant has heard that Heaven, by obtaining the One, becomes clear;
Earth, by obtaining the One, becomes tranquil;
the feudal lords and kings, by obtaining the One, become the rectifiers of the world."
The Emperor was pleased,
and the assembled ministers sighed in admiration.
Wáng Bì's *Commentary on the Laozi* says:
"The One is the beginning of numbers,
the ultimate of things.
Each thing is a single entity,
and this is why it serves as the master.
Each by means of its own oneness
achieves this clarity, tranquility, and rectitude."
Mǎn Fèn feared the wind.
While seated with Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the north window had a glass screen,
which was actually solid but appeared porous.
Fèn showed a troubled expression.
The Emperor laughed at him.
Xún Chuò's *Records of Jìzhōu* states:
"Fèn, styled Wǔqiū,
was a man from Gāopíng,
grandson of the Wèi Grand Commandant Chǒng.
His nature was pure and fair, and he had discernment.
He went from Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel to become Governor of Jìzhōu."
The *Eulogies of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"Fèn's bearing and capacity were pure and elegant,
possessing the manner of his great-grandfather Chǒng.
He was promoted to President of the Imperial Secretariat,
and was harmed by Xún Yǐ."
Fèn replied:
"Your servant is like the ox of Wú,
who pants at the sight of the moon."
Nowadays, water buffalo
are only bred in the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
hence they are called oxen of Wú.
The southern lands are often hot,
and this ox fears the heat.
Seeing the moon, it suspects it is the sun,
which is why it pants at the sight of the moon.
Zhūgě Liàng was in Wú,
at a grand assembly in the court hall.
The *Eulogies of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"Liàng, styled Zhòngsī,
was a man from Lángyá,
youngest son of the Minister of Works Dàn.
He was refined, upright, talented, and esteemed.
Dàn rebelled with Shòuyáng,
and sent Liàng to Wú as a hostage,
where Liàng was made General of the Right
and Grand Marshal."
Sūn Hào asked:
"Your style is Zhòngsī (Second Thought);
what is it that you think about?"
He replied:
"At home, I think of filial piety;
serving the ruler, I think of loyalty;
with friends, I think of trustworthiness;
that is all."
Cài Hóng
The *Collected Records of Hóng* states:
"Hóng, styled Shūkāi,
was a man from Wú Commandery,
talented and eloquent.
He first served in the court of Wú.
During the Tàikāng era,
he was an Attendant in his home province,
and was recommended as a Xiùcái."
Wáng Yǐn's *History of Jìn* states:
"Hóng served up to the post of Magistrate of Sōngzī."
He went to Luòyáng.
People in Luòyáng asked him:
"The command headquarters has just been established;
the various lords are issuing summons and appointments,
seeking outstanding talents from obscure places,
gathering worthy and eminent men from mountain caves.
You, sir, are a scholar from Wú-Chǔ,
a remnant of a fallen state.
What exceptional talent do you possess,
to respond to this summons?"
Cài replied:
"The pearl of night's radiance
need not necessarily come from the river of Mèngjīn;
An old account says:
"The Marquis of Suí was traveling,
and there was a snake that had been cut and severed in the middle.
The Marquis connected and mended it,

Later, it brought a bright moon pearl to repay his virtue,
its radiance illuminating the night like day,
hence it was called the Suí pearl."
What Zuǒ Sī's *Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ* refers to as
"The Marquis of Suí disdained its night radiance."
A jade disc that fills the grasp
need not necessarily be mined from the mountains of Kūnlún.
Hán Shì said:
"The jade disc of Héshì
came from within the village well."
The Great Yǔ was born among the Eastern Barbarians,
King Wén was born among the Western Qiāng.

a man of the Eastern Barbarians;

Thus, the Eastern Barbarians refer to Shùn, not Yǔ.
Where sages and worthies emerge from,

In the past, King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,

The *Book of Documents* states:
"When Chéngzhōu was completed,

Kǒng Ānguó's *Commentary* states:

Could it be that you gentlemen are their descendants?"
Note: Huà Lìngsī, upon being recommended as Xiùcái and entering Luòyáng,

Various famous scholars went together to amuse themselves at the Luò River.

I, together with Wáng Ānfēng (Róng),

Wáng Wǔzǐ,

Sūn Zǐjīng,

Minister of Education Yuè's daughter married Chéngdū Wáng Sīmǎ Yǐng, the Great General.

"Yuè Guǎng, styled Yànfǔ,

"Tales of the Eight Princes" states:

All those at court

Minister of Education Yuè, being esteemed by the court,

"The Autumn Annals of Jìn" states:

Wǔzǐ had placed several hu of sheep's milk cheese in front of him,

In the central court, there was a young boy

The master of the house asked about the illness,

The master said: "Your honored father is a virtuous gentleman,

Common tradition holds that the malaria ghost is small,

Therefore, Emperor Guāngwǔ once said to Jǐng Dān:

He replied: "It comes to afflict the gentleman,

Cuī Zhèngxióng visited the commandery capital.

"Register of Jìn Officials" states:

When Emperor Yuán first crossed the Jiāng,

"Rules for Posthumous Names" states:

He said to Gù Piàoqí:

Róng knelt and replied:

therefore Gěng and Bó had no fixed abode,

This is now Yǎnshī.

Those who crossed the river,

Zhōu Hóu, that is Yǐ.

They all looked at each other and shed tears.
Only Chancellor Wáng, that is Dǎo,

When Wèi Xiǎnmǎ first intended to cross the river,

Sīkōng Gù was not yet known,

"His body is slightly unwell,

Hè Shēng of Kuàijī,

Now, although the Jìn dynasty's fortunes have declined,

Wēn replied:

Wēn, newly arrived,

recited a foreign prayer of several thousand words,
his voice loud and clear.
Afterward, he wiped away his tears and ceased weeping.
His expressions of grief and joy, cessation and initiation, were all of this kind.
His nature was lofty and reserved;
he did not learn the Jìn language.
When the various gentlemen spoke with him,
it was all through interpreters.
Yet he grasped the spirit and understood the meaning,
instantly, even before the words were spoken."
The "Record of Pagodas and Temples" states:
"Shīlímì was called Gāozuò in Sòng times,
located at Shízǐgāng.
He often practiced asceticism,
died at Méigāng,
and was buried there.
Emperor Yuán of Jìn established a temple by his grave,
hence named Gāozuò."
Vice Director Zhōu was dignified and fond of proper appearance.
When visiting Wáng Gōng,
upon first alighting from the carriage,
he was supported by several attendants.
Wáng Gōng watched him with a smile.
After taking his seat,
he proudly chanted and recited.
Wáng Gōng said:
"Do you aspire to emulate Jī [Kāng] and
Ruǎn [Jí]?"
He replied:
"How dare I forsake the illustrious lord nearby,
to emulate Jī and
Ruǎn afar!"
Dèng Càn's "Annals of Jìn" states:
"Bórén's appearance was grand and imposing;
he excelled in bowing and responding,
his spirit sufficient to overshadow several men.
He deeply maintained his composure,
able to attract others,
yet never went to them."
Yǔ Gōng once entered a Buddhist temple,
and saw a reclining Buddha.
The "Nirvana Sutra" states:
"The Tathāgata had back pain,
and lay with his head to the north between twin trees;
therefore later painters and sculptors depict this image."
He said:
"This gentleman is weary from ferrying across."
At the time, this was considered a famous saying.
Zhì Zhān once served as governor of four commanderies,
and as Registrar of the Grand General's household,
then went out again to serve as Neishi.
The "Genealogy of the Zhì Clan" states:
"Zhān, styled Jǐngyóu,
was from Cháng'ān, Jīngzhào.
He was the nephew of Tàicháng Yú.
His father was Yù,
Governor of Liángzhōu.
In his youth, Zhān excelled at literary composition,
and began his career as a Gentleman of Writings.
During the chaos of the central court,
he relied on Wáng Dūn, serving as Registrar of the household.
He successively served as Governor of Ānfēng,
Xīncài,
and Xīyáng.
He saw Wáng Dūn give an old, worn fur robe to an elderly, sick outer area commander.
Zhān admonished him, saying:
'Though the noble fur robe is old,
it is not suitable to give to a minor official.'
Dūn said:
'Why is it not permissible?'
Zhān, being drunk at the time,
said:
'If upper garments can all be given as gifts,
then could the marten-tail hats also be given to subordinates?'
Dūn said:
'This is not a proper analogy;
citing such things,
you are unfit to be a two-thousand-bushel official.'
Zhān said:
'I regard leaving Xīyáng
as easy as discarding worn shoes!'
When Dūn rebelled,
he was demoted to Neishi of Suí Commandery."
He was only twenty-nine years old.
Once, when bidding farewell to Wáng Dūn,
Dūn said to Zhān:
"You are not yet thirty,
and already hold a ten-thousand-bushel post;
this is too early."
Zhān replied:
"Compared to the General,
it is somewhat too early;
compared to Gān Luó,
it is already too old."
The "Genealogy of the Zhì Clan" states:
"Zhān was lofty, upright, and had moral integrity;
therefore he answered Dūn thus.
Later, he realized Dūn had rebellious intentions.
In the fourth year of Jiànxīng,
together with Dì Wǔ Qí, he occupied Jīngzhōu to resist Dūn,
and was ultimately killed by him."
The "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"Gān Luó
was the grandson of Qín Chancellor Gān Mào.
At age twelve,
when Qín Chancellor Lǚ Bùwéi wanted to send Zhāng Táng to serve as Chancellor of Yān,
Táng was unwilling to go.
Gān Luó persuaded him, and he went.
He also requested five chariots to serve as envoy to Zhào.
Upon returning and reporting to Qín,
Qín enfeoffed Gān Luó as Senior Minister,
and bestowed upon him the fields and residences of Gān Mào."
There was a son of the Yáng family of Liáng State,
nine years old,
very intelligent.
Kǒng Jūnpíng (Wáng Yǐn's "History of Jìn" states:
"Kǒng Tǎn, styled Jūnpíng,
was from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
He was proficient in the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
and skilled in literary debate.
He served as Gentleman of the Heir Apparent,
and successively rose to become Chief Commandant of Justice.")
visited his father.
The father was not home,
so he called the boy out,
and set out fruit for him.
Among the fruit were bayberries.
Kǒng pointed to them and said to the boy:
"These are your family's fruit."
The boy immediately replied:
"I have not heard that the peacock is the Master's family bird."
Commandant of Justice Kǒng gave a fur robe to his younger cousin Shěn.
The "Genealogy of the Kǒng Clan" states:
"Shěn, styled Dédù,
was from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His grandfather was Yì,
Magistrate of Quánjiāo.
His father was Qún,
Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Shěn attained the post of Literary Scholar to the Prince of Lángyá."
Shěn declined and would not accept it.
The Commandant of Justice said:
"Yàn Píngzhòng was frugal;
when sacrificing to his ancestors,
the pig's shoulder did not cover the sacrificial vessel,
yet he still wore a fox-fur robe for several decades.
Liú Xiàng's "Separate Records" states:
"Yàn Píngzhòng's name was Yīng,
from Yíwéi, Dōnglái.
He served under Duke Líng and
Duke Zhuāng of Qí,
and was esteemed in Qí for his frugality and diligent conduct."
The "Book of Rites" states:
"Yàn Píngzhòng sacrificed to his ancestors;
the pig's shoulder did not cover the sacrificial vessel,
and gentlemen considered him frugal."
It also says:
"Master Yàn wore one fox-fur robe for thirty years;
how could Master Yàn know the rites?"
The "Commentary" states:
"The pig,
is the sacrificial offering.
The vessel is one foot in diameter.
This means the two shoulders of the pig together could not cover the vessel,
illustrating its smallness."
Why do you still decline this?"
Thereupon, he accepted it and wore it.
Fótú Chéng associated with the various members of the Shí family,
The Biography of Chéng states:
"The monk Fótú Chéng,
it is unknown where he was from,
he emerged from Dūnhuáng,
was devoted to Buddhism,
and became a monk.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he arrived in Luòyáng,
but encountered turmoil in the capital,
so he hid in the wilderness.
Hearing that Shí Lè was formidable and fond of killing,
he managed to meet Lè through Lè's general Guō Mò.
He would apply sesame oil to his palm
to divine good and bad omens.
He could hear the bells of pagodas from hundreds of miles away
and predict fortune and misfortune.
Lè greatly revered and trusted him.
When Shí Hǔ ascended the throne,
he also took Chéng as his teacher,
calling him the Great Monk.
Knowing the day of his own death,
when his coffin was opened, there was no corpse,
only his monk's robes remained."
Lín Gōng said:
"Chéng regarded Shí Hǔ as a seagull."
The Book of Zhào states:
"Hǔ, styled Jìlóng,
was Lè's cousin.
In campaigns, he often beheaded enemy generals and captured their flags.
After Lè's death,
he killed Lè's sons
and seized the throne."
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"There was a man by the sea who loved seagulls;
every morning he would go to the sea,
and the seagulls would flock around him,
hundreds of them without end.
His father said:
'I hear the seagulls follow you;
catch one for me to play with.'
The next day, when he went to the sea,
the seagulls danced in the air but would not land."
Xiè Rénzǔ was eight years old,
the son of Xiè Yùzhāng (Xiè Kūn),
see separate biography.
When seeing off guests,
his speech already showed remarkable insight,
placing him among the elite.
Everyone praised him, saying:
"He is the Yán Huí of this gathering."
Rénzǔ replied:
"Without Confucius present,
how can one distinguish Yán Huí?"
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Xiè Shàng, styled Rénzǔ,
was from Chénjùn,
the son of Xiè Kūn.
He lost his elder brother in childhood,
and his grief surpassed that of others.
When his father died,
Wēn Qiáo came to offer condolences,
and Shàng wailed with extreme sorrow.
But then he wiped his tears and spoke,
unlike an ordinary child.
Qiáo found him extraordinary,
and thus he became known,
rising to the positions of General Who Guards the West and
Governor of Yùzhōu."
When Táo Gōng was critically ill,
he offered no advice on governance,
and court officials considered this regrettable.
The Account of the Táo Family states:
"Kǎn, styled Shìhéng,
his ancestors were from Póyáng,
but later moved to Xúnyáng.
From a young age, Kǎn had grand ambitions to govern the world.
Recommended as Xiàolián, he entered Luòyáng,
where the Minister of Works Zhāng Huá saw him and said:
'In the future, to assist the ruler and bring peace to the people,
you are the man.'
When Liú Hóng governed south of the Miǎn River,
he appointed Kǎn as his Chief Clerk,
saying to him:
'When I served as an aide to Grand Tutor Yáng,
he told me:
"You will later hold a high position."
Now observing you,
I see the same.'
He was promoted successively to Governor of Xiāng,
Guǎng, and Jīng Provinces,
granted feather canopies and military bands,
enfeoffed as Duke of Chángshā Commandery,
and made Grand General.
He was exempt from announcing his name at court,
and could wear his sword and shoes in the palace.
He was promoted to Grand Commandant,
posthumously granted Grand Marshal,
and given the posthumous title Duke Huán."
According to Wáng Yǐn's Book of Jìn, which records Kǎn's "Final Memorial," it states:
"I grew up orphaned and poor,
with limited aspirations,
but I was excessively favored by successive reigns of the previous dynasty.
Now approaching eighty,
having reached the highest rank among subjects,
with hands and feet intact,
what regrets could I have!
But because the remaining rebels are not yet eliminated,
and the imperial tombs are not yet restored,
I am filled with indignation and sorrow,
only for this reason!
I still hope that my remaining years
could be slightly extended,
so I could for Your Majesty swallow Shí Hǔ in the north,
and eliminate Lǐ Xióng in the west,
but my strength has waned,
and these fine plans are forever stilled.
As I write this, my wrist trembles,
and tears stream down.
I humbly hope you will carefully select a successor,
ensuring he is truly talented,
capable of promoting the royal way,
and continuing this ambitious enterprise.
Then even in death,
I will feel as if alive."
With such a memorial,
it cannot be said he offered no advice.
Rénzǔ, hearing of this, said:
"Because there was no Shù Diāo at the time,
Táo Gōng left no such words."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū states:
"When Guǎn Zhòng was ill,
Duke Huán asked:
'If you should pass away,
who will replace you as prime minister?
What about Shù Diāo?'
Guǎn Zhòng said:
'He castrated himself to serve his lord,
which goes against human nature;
he must not be used!'
Later, he indeed brought chaos to Qí."
The worthies of the time considered this wise counsel.
When Zhú Fǎshēn was in Jiǎnwén's company,
Governor Liú asked:
"Why does a monk frequent vermilion gates?"
He replied:
"You see them as vermilion gates,
but to this humble monk, it is like visiting a thatched hut."
The Biographies of Lofty and Reclusive Monks states:
"The Master resided in Kuàijī,
and the emperor, valuing his virtue and demeanor,
sent an envoy to welcome him.
The Master temporarily left to respond to the summons.
The Minister of Works, the Prince of Kuàijī, was by nature detached and serene,
and formed a warm friendship with the Master.
Though the Master ascended crimson steps
and entered vermilion mansions,
he remained utterly open-minded,
no different than in a thatched dwelling."
Some say it was Biàn Lìng.
See separate biography.
Sūn Shèng served as Yǔ Gōng's Record Office Army Advisor,
The Book of the Restoration states:
"Shèng, styled Ānguó,
was from Zhōngdū, Tàiyuán.
He was widely learned and had a strong memory,
served as Editorial Director,
and Magistrate of Liúyáng.
When Yǔ Liàng governed Jīngzhōu,
he appointed him as Chief Clerk of the Western Expedition,
and he was promoted to Palace Library Director."
He went hunting,
bringing both his sons along.
Yǔ Gōng did not know,
but suddenly saw Qí Zhuāng in the hunting grounds,
who was then seven or eight years old.
Yǔ said to him:
"You came too?"
He immediately replied:
"As the saying goes,
'Be they small or great,
they follow the duke on his march.'"
Sūn Qíyóu and
Sūn Qízhuāng, when they were young, went to visit Yǔ Hào.
Yǔ Hào asked,
"What is Qíyóu's courtesy name?"
He replied,
"My courtesy name is Qíyóu."
Yǔ Hào said,
"Whom do you wish to emulate?"
He said,
"I wish to emulate Xǔ Yóu."
The *Jìn Bǎiguān Míng* states:
"Sūn Qián's courtesy name was Qíyóu,
a man from Tàiyuán."
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Qián was
the eldest son of Shèng.
When Yīn Zhòngkān, Governor of Yùzhāng, marched down to attack Wáng Guóbǎo,
Qián was in the commandery at the time,
and was pressured to become an Advisory Army Consultant,
but he firmly declined and did not take the post,
and subsequently died of sorrow."
"What is Qízhuāng's courtesy name?"
He replied,
"My courtesy name is Qízhuāng."
Yǔ Hào said,
"Whom do you wish to emulate?"
He said,
"I wish to emulate Zhuāng Zhōu."
Yǔ Hào said,
"Why do you not admire Zhòngní, but admire Zhuāng Zhōu?"
He replied,
"The sage is born with knowledge,
so he is difficult to emulate and admire."
Yǔ Hào was greatly pleased with the boy's reply.
The *Sūn Fàng Biézhuàn* states:
"Fàng's courtesy name was Qízhuāng,
the second son of the Inspector.
At the age of eight,
he was summoned for an audience by Grand Commandant Yǔ Hào.
Fàng was handsome and refined,
and Yǔ Hào wished to test him,
so he gave him paper and brush and ordered him to write.
Fàng then wrote his own name.
Yǔ Hào wrote a question afterward and asked him,
'Do you wish to admire Zhuāng Zhōu?'
Fàng wrote in reply,
'My intention is to admire him.'
Yǔ Hào said,
'Why do you not admire Zhòngní, but admire Zhuāng Zhōu?'
Fàng said,
'Zhòngní was born with knowledge,
which is beyond what one can hope to attain;
as for Zhuāng Zhōu,
he is the next level,
so I admire him.'
Yǔ Hào said to his guests,
'Even Wáng Fǔsì in his responses
would likely not surpass him.'
He eventually became Chancellor to the Prince of Chángshā."
Zhāng Xuánzhī and
Gù Fū
were the grandson and maternal grandson, respectively, of Gù Hé.
Both were intelligent and clever from a young age.
Hé knew them both well,
but often said that Gù was superior.
His affection and esteem were particularly directed toward him,
which Zhāng found rather displeasing.
Fū is separately mentioned elsewhere.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Zhāng Xuánzhī's courtesy name was Zǔxī,
grandson of Zhāng Chéng, Governor of Wú Commandery.
From a young age, he was renowned for his learning.
He served as Minister of Personnel,
and later was appointed General of the Champion and
Governor of Wúxīng.
Xiè Xuán, Governor of Kuàijī, was appointed to his commandery at the same time,
and commentators considered them the hopes of the north and south.
Xuánzhī's reputation was second only to Xiè Xuán's,
and they were also called the Two Xuáns of North and South.
He died in his commandery."
At that time, Zhāng was nine years old,
and Gù was seven.
Hé took them both to a temple.
They saw a statue of the Buddha entering Nirvana,
with some disciples weeping
and others not weeping.
Hé used this to question his two grandsons.
Xuánzhī said,
"Those who were loved wept,
those who were not loved did not weep."
Fū said,
"That is not so.
It must be that those who could forget emotions did not weep,
while those who could not forget emotions wept."
The *Dàzhìdù Lùn* states:
"When the Buddha entered Nirvana between the twin *śāla* trees in the Śītavana Grove,
he lay with his head to the north,
and the earth shook.
All those who were still learners
were deeply saddened,
and wept in sorrow.
But those who were no longer learners
merely contemplated the Dharma,
that all things are impermanent."
Yǔ Fǎchàng went to visit Grand Commandant Yǔ Liàng.
He was holding a very fine duster.
Yǔ Liàng said,
"This is extremely fine.
How is it that it remains in your possession?"
Fǎchàng said,
"The incorruptible do not seek it,
and the greedy are not given it,
so it remains with me."
Fǎchàng's clan and origins are not detailed.
Fǎchàng wrote the *Rénwù Lùn*,
in which he described his own virtues, saying:
"My insight is sharp and divine,
my talent in rhetoric and debate is penetrating."
When Yǔ Zhìgōng was in Jīngzhōu,
the *Yǔ Yì Biézhuàn* states:
"Yì's courtesy name was Zhìgōng,
a man from Yǎnlíng, Yǐngchuān.
From a young age, he had great magnanimity,
and contemporary opinion credited him with strategic ability.
When his elder brother, Grand Commandant Liàng, died,
the court deliberated on talent,
and appointed Yì as Commander of Seven Provinces.
He was promoted to General Who Conquers the South and
Governor of Jīngzhōu."
he presented a feather fan to Emperor Wǔ.
The Emperor suspected it was an old item.
Fù Xián's *Yǔshàn Fù Xù* states:
"In the past, the people of Wú would simply cut bird wings and wave them;
the wind was no less than that from square or round fans,
and their effectiveness was not inferior,
yet in the Central Plains, no one took an interest.
After Wú was conquered,
they suddenly became prized,
and everyone used them."
According to records, Yǔ Yì presented a white feather fan to Emperor Wǔ,
and the Emperor, disliking that it was not new,
returned it.
There is no record of Yì doing so.
Palace Attendant Liú Shào said,
the *Wénzì Zhì* states:
"Shào's courtesy name was Yànzǔ,
a man from Cóngtíng, Péngchéng.
His grandfather was Nè,
who served as Colonel-Director of the Capital.
His father was Sōng,
Magistrate of Chénggāo.
Shào was erudite and fond of learning,
skilled in many arts,
and excelled in cursive and clerical script.
He first served as Army Consultant to the General of the Guards.
When the Grand Tutor went east,
Shào predicted that the capital Luòyáng would surely be in danger,
so he rode alone to Yángzhōu.
He served as Palace Attendant and
Governor of Yùzhāng."
"When the Bǎiliáng Terrace was built high into the clouds,
the craftsmen first dwelt beneath it;
when pipes and strings play in rich harmony,
Zhōng and Kuí first listen to the music.
Zhōng refers to Zhōng Qī.
Kuí was Shùn's Director of Music.
Zhìgōng presented the fan
for its quality, not its newness."
Yǔ later heard of this and said,
"This man should be by the Emperor's side."
After Cavalry General-in-Chief Hé died,
Hé Chōng is separately mentioned elsewhere.
Chǔ Tǎn was summoned to the capital.
When he reached Shítóu,
Chief Clerk Wáng
and Governor Liú went together to visit Chǔ.
Chǔ said,
"Zhēncháng, how do you propose to place me?"
Zhēncháng looked at Wáng and said,
"This young man can speak."
Chǔ then looked at Wáng.
Wáng said,
"The state already has its Duke of Zhōu."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"After Chōng's death,
some councilors suggested that the Empress Dowager's father, Chǔ Póu, should take charge of the government.
Póu came to court from Dāndú.
Minister of Personnel Liú Xiá advised Póu, saying,
'The Prince of Kuàijī is virtuous,
he is the Duke of Zhōu of our state.
You, sir, should entrust the great affairs of state to him.'
Póu's Chief Clerk, Wáng Húzhī, also urged him to return to his fief,
so he firmly declined and returned to the capital."
Duke Huán went on a northern campaign and passed through Jīnchéng.
Seeing the willows he had planted when he was the Administrator of Lángyé,
which had already grown to ten arm-spans in girth,
he sighed with emotion and said:
"If even trees are like this,
how can a man endure!"
Grasping the branches and twigs,
his tears fell in streams.
The *Bié Zhuàn of Huán Wēn* says:
"Wēn, styled Yuánzǐ,
was a man of Lóngkàng in Qiáo Guó,
a descendant of Huán Róng, the 'Fifth Elder' of the Hàn.
His father, Yí,
possessed insight and discernment.
Wēn was bold and unrestrained in his youth,
and was recognized by Wēn Qiáo.
He rose through the ranks to become the Interior Historian of Lángyé,
was promoted to General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West,
and garrisoned Western Xià.
At that time, the rebellious Hú had not yet been exterminated,
and the remaining embers still smoldered.
Wēn personally commanded the commandery troops,
raised banners and launched a punitive expedition,
cleansing and pacifying Yī and
Luò, and paying respects at the imperial tombs.
He died and was posthumously titled Marquis Xuānwǔ."
When Jiǎnwén was serving as General Who Pacifies the Army,
he once entered court together with Huán Xuānwǔ,
and they repeatedly yielded to each other, each urging the other to go first.
Xuānwǔ, unable to proceed forward, eventually went ahead first,
and then said:
"My elder holds the shū,
acting as the king's vanguard."
This is from the *Odes of Wèi*.
The shū is twelve feet long,
and has no blade.
Jiǎnwén said:
"This is what is called
'Be they small or great,
they follow the duke on his march.'"
Gù Yuè was the same age as Jiǎnwén,
but his hair turned white early.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Yuè, styled Jūnshū,
was a man of Jìnlíng.
He first served as Yīn Hào's Assistant in Yángzhōu.
After Hào's death,
he submitted a memorial pleading Hào's case.
Some advised him that since Hào had been deposed by Tàizōng,
his plea would certainly not be granted,
but Yuè firmly insisted on it.
Hào's case was indeed vindicated,
and public opinion praised him for it.
He later rose to the position of Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat."
Jiǎnwén said:
"Why has your hair turned white first?"
He replied:
"The nature of the willow,
is to wither at the approach of autumn;
the substance of the pine and cypress,
grows more luxuriant after enduring frost."
Gù Kǎizhī, in his father's biography, wrote:
"My father, with his upright conduct, met with decline in his time.
When he had an audience with the Prince,
the Prince's hair showed not a single strand of gray,
while my father's was already streaked with white.
The Prince asked his age,
and then said:
'Why has your hair turned white so early?'
My father said:
'The nature of the pine and cypress,
remains luxuriant even after enduring frost;
your servant is of the substance of the willow,
which withers first at the approach of autumn.
This is a difference in innate endowment.'
The Prince praised him for a long time."
Duke Huán entered the Gorges,
where sheer cliffs hung from the sky,
and surging waves raced with swift urgency.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"In the second year of the Yǒnghé era, Wēn
led over seven thousand men under his command to campaign against Shǔ,
presenting a memorial and then departing immediately."
He then sighed and said:
"Since one is a loyal minister,
one cannot be a filial son.
What is to be done?"
The *Hàn Shū* says:
"Wáng Yáng was the Inspector of Yìzhōu.
While touring his district, he reached the Jiǔzhébǎn slope at Qióngbó,
and sighed, saying:
'I have received this body from my ancestors;
how can I repeatedly traverse such peril!'
He resigned from his post due to illness.
Later, Wáng Zūn became Inspector.
When he reached that slope,
he asked his subordinate:
'Isn't this the path that Wáng Yáng feared?'
The subordinate said:
'It is!'
He then shouted to his driver:
'Drive on!
Wáng Yáng was a filial son,
Wáng Zūn is a loyal minister.'"
Initially,
the planet Mars entered the Tàiwēi constellation,
and soon after, Hǎixī was deposed.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"In the intercalary tenth month of the sixth year of the Tàihé era,
Mars stationed itself at the Duānmén gate of the Tàiwēi constellation.
In the eleventh month,
the Grand Marshal Huán Wēn deposed the Emperor, making him the Duke of Hǎixī."
The *Jìn Āndì Jì* says:
"After Huán Wēn's defeat and flight at Fāngtóu,
knowing that popular support had turned from him,
he executed Yuán Zhēn at Shòuyáng.
Afterwards, he said to Xì Chāo:
'Is this enough to wash away the shame of Fāngtóu?'
Chāo said:
'It has not satisfied the sentiments of those with discernment.
You, at sixty years of age,
suffered a major defeat in a grand campaign.
Without establishing a merit surpassing this age,
you will not be able to suppress and satisfy popular expectation.'
He then advised Wēn on the matter of deposing and establishing an emperor.
Wēn had long harbored such a plan,
and deeply accepted Chāo's words.
Subsequently, he deposed Hǎixī."
When Jiǎnwén ascended the throne,
Mars again entered the Tàiwēi constellation.
The Emperor was troubled by this.
Xú Guǎng's *Jìn Jì* says:
"In the twelfth month of the first year of the Xián'ān era,
Mars moved retrograde and entered the Tàiwēi constellation.
By the seventh month of the second year,
it was still there.
The Emperor, mindful of the Hǎixī incident,
was deeply worried.
At that time, Xì Chāo, as a Palace Secretary, was on duty.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Chāo, styled Jǐngxīng,
was a man of Gāopíng,
the son of the Minister of Works, Xì Yīn.
From youth, he was outstanding and unrestrained,
possessing a breadth of spirit unmatched in his generation.
He rose through the ranks to become a Palace Gentleman,
and then Left Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education."
The Emperor summoned Chāo in and said:
"The length of one's life span, as decreed by Heaven,
is certainly not something one can plan for.
But surely there will not be a repeat of the recent events, will there?"
Chāo said:
"The Grand Marshal is currently occupied with securing the borders externally,
and safeguarding the altars of state internally.
There certainly will be no cause for such concerns.
Your servant guarantees it to Your Majesty with the lives of his hundred-strong family."
The Emperor then recited a poem by Yǔ Zhòngchū (Yǔ Chǎn's *Poem on Following an Expedition*),
saying:
"The man of purpose grieves at the court's peril,
The loyal minister laments his lord's disgrace."
His voice was exceedingly mournful and intense.
When Xì Chāo was granted leave to return east,
the Emperor said:
"Convey my regards to your honored father.
That affairs of family and state
have come to this!
It is because I, in my person, have been unable to uphold the Way and protect them,
to think of perils and take preventive measures.
The depth of my shame and regret,
how can words possibly express?"
With this, his tears fell, soaking his lapels.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"The Emperor was oppressed by powerful ministers from without,
and, aggrieved and resentful, unable to fulfill his ambitions,
he passed away after two years on the throne."
Jiǎnwén was sitting in a dark room,
and summoned Xuānwǔ.
When Xuānwǔ arrived,
he asked where His Majesty was.
Jiǎnwén said:
"I am here."
People of the time considered him capable.
The *Analects* says:
"When Master Miǎn came for an audience,
as he reached the steps,
the Master said:
'Here are the steps.'
When he reached the mat,
the Master said:
'Here is the mat.'
When all were seated,
the Master informed him, saying:
'So-and-so is here,
so-and-so is here.'"
The *Commentary* states:
"He went through and informed him of all the people seated there."
Jiǎnwén entered the Huálín Garden,
looked around and said to his attendants:
"The place that resonates with one's heart
need not be far away.
Amidst these secluded woods and waters,
one naturally has thoughts of the Hǎo
and Pú rivers.
Hǎo and Pú
are the names of two rivers.
The *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ were strolling on the bridge over the Hǎo River.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'The minnows are swimming about so freely and easily—
this is the happiness of the fish.'
Huìzǐ said:
'You are not a fish;
how do you know the happiness of the fish?'
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'You are not I;
how do you know that I do not know the happiness of the fish?'"
"Zhuāng Zhōu was fishing in the Pú River.
The King of Chǔ sent two high officials to visit him,
saying:
'We wish to entrust the affairs of our state to you, Master Zhuāng.'
Zhuāngzǐ, holding his fishing rod, did not even look back,
and said:
'I have heard that in Chǔ there is a sacred turtle,
dead for three thousand years already,
kept wrapped in cloth and stored in a box in the ancestral temple.
or would it rather leave its bones behind and be honored?'
The two high officials said:
'It would rather drag its tail in the mud.'
Zhuāngzǐ said:
'Go away!
I too would rather drag my tail in the mud.'"
He felt that birds, beasts, fowl, and fish
all naturally drew near to people."
Grand Tutor Xiè said to General of the Right Army Wáng:
"In middle age, wounded by sorrows and joys,
whenever I part from relatives and friends,
for several days afterward I feel unwell."
Wáng said:
The *Wénzì Zhì* says:
"Wáng Xīzhī, styled Yìshǎo,
was from Línyí in Lángyá.
His father was Kuàng,
Governor of Huáinán.
Xīzhī was intelligent and outstanding from a young age,
and was appreciated by his uncle, Yì.
He excelled at cursive and clerical script,
and successively rose to the posts of Governor of Jiāng Province,
General of the Right Army,
and Governor of Kuàijī."
"When one's years reach the mulberry and elm [i.e., old age],
it naturally comes to this.
One must precisely rely on string and wind instruments to mold and express [one's feelings].
I constantly fear that the younger generation will become aware [of this melancholy]
and diminish the delight and pleasure of it."
Zhī Dàolín often kept several horses.
Some said it was unbecoming for a monk to keep horses.
Zhī said:
"This humble monk values their divine vigor."
The *Gāoyì Shāmén Zhuàn* says:
"Zhī Dùn, styled Dàolín,
was from Línlǜ in Hénèi,
or some say from Chénliú.
His original surname was Guān.
From youth, he followed his own heart and went his own way;
his bearing and aspirations were lofty and bright.
His family for generations had upheld the Dharma.
He once contemplated the practice of the Way on the Yúháng Mountains,
feeling a refreshing clarity and solitary freedom.
At twenty-five, he finally shed his form and entered the Way.
He died at fifty-three in Luòyáng."
Administrator Liú and Xuānwǔ Huán together attended a lecture on the *Book of Rites*.
Huán said:
"At times there were points that entered one's heart,
and one immediately felt the Gate of Mystery was just inches away."
Liú said:
"This does not yet touch upon the ultimate,
it is merely talk from the Jīnhuá Hall."
The *Hànshū Xùzhuàn* says:
"Bān Bó in his youth studied the *Book of Songs* under Shī Dān.
Grand General Wáng Fèng recommended Bó to Emperor Chéng,
saying he should be encouraged in his studies.
He was summoned for an audience and intimate banquet,
and appointed as a Regular Palace Attendant.
At that time, the Emperor was inclined toward learning,
and Zhèng Kuānzhōng
and Zhāng Yǔ would enter morning and evening to expound the *Book of Documents*
and the *Analects* in the Jīnhuá Hall.
The Emperor commanded Bó to receive instruction from them."
Yáng Bǐng served as an aide to the General Who Pacifies the Army.
He died young,
and had a fine reputation.
The Marquis of Yōu, Xiàoruo, composed a eulogy for him,
praising and mourning him to the utmost.
The *Yáng Bǐng Xù* says:
"Bǐng, styled Chángdá,
was from Píngyáng in Tàishān.
He was the great-grandson of Xù, Governor of Nányáng in the Hàn.
His grandfather, the Prefect of Wèijùn,
was the eldest son of Yuán, an aide to the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
The Prefect's wife, Lady Zhèng, had no sons,
so she adopted Bǐng.
Even as a young child he was excellent,
careful, respectful, and cautious.
At ten, Lady Zhèng passed away.
Bǐng, longing for her countenance, expressed his grief fully.
Soon after, the Prefect's aide and his wife both died.
Bǐng and his cousins (
father's side) upheld the rites in succession,
and people did not perceive any distance in their closeness,
so harmonious were they.
He served as an aide to the General Who Pacifies the Army.
He was about to unleash the hooves that gallop a thousand *li*,
and spread wings that soar to the sky.
Alas, he died at the age of thirty-two.
In ancient times, when Hǎn Hǔ died,
Zǐchǎn felt there was no one with whom to do good.
Since the passing of our Master [Bǐng],
we have had Zǐchǎn's lament!
After his death, he had a son, but he too did not live.
How is it that one who acted so well met with such frequent misfortune?
Is this not what left Sīmǎ [Qiān] perplexed?"
Yáng Quán served as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and attended upon Jiǎnwén.
The Emperor asked:
"Xiàhóu Zhàn (see elsewhere)
composed the *Yáng Bǐng Xù*, which is utterly evocative.
What relation was he to you?
Did he have descendants?"
The *Yángshì Pǔ* says:
"Quán, styled Dàoyú,
was the son of Chén, Governor of Xú Province.
He rose to the post of Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs."
Quán, with tears streaming down, replied:
"My late uncle's fine reputation was illustrious from early on,
yet he had no heir to continue his line.
Although his name spread to the imperial ear,
his lineage was cut off in this sage age."
The Emperor sighed with emotion for a long time.
After they had parted and later met again, Chief Secretary Wáng said to Liú Zhēncháng,
The Biography of Chief Secretary Wáng says:
"Méng, styled Zhòngzǔ,
was from Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
His ancestors originated from the Zhōu royal house,
passing through the Hàn
and Wèi dynasties, and for generations were a great clan.
His grandfather, Zuǒ,
was Commandant of the Northern Army.
His father, Nè,
was Magistrate of Yè.
Méng's spirit and energy were pure and refined;
when he was over ten years old,
he was unrestrained and unconventional.
Upon reaching adulthood, he cultivated integrity,
possessing an elegant and upright demeanor,
outwardly shunning glory and competition,
and inwardly having few private desires.
He was appointed as an Assistant in the Ministry of Education and
a Gentleman in the Central Secretariat,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments due to being the emperor's father-in-law."
Wáng said to Liú:
"You have made even greater progress."
He replied:
"This is just like the sky being naturally high."
The Forest of Sayings says:
"Zhòngzǔ said to Zhēncháng:
'You have recently made great progress.'
Liú said:
'Are you looking up?'
Wáng asked what he meant.
Liú said:
'If not,
how could one measure the height of the sky?'"
Prefect Liú said:
"People imagine that Wáng Jīngchǎn is excellent;
this is just like imagining that beneath tall pine trees there must be a clear breeze."
Jīngchǎn
was the childhood name of Wáng Wēi.
The Genealogy of the Wáng Clan says:
"Wēi, styled Yòurén,
was from Lángyé.
His grandfather, Yì,
was General Who Pacifies the North;
his father, Chéng,
was Governor of Jīng Province.
Wēi served successively as Gentleman in the Imperial Secretariat
and Army Major to the General of the Right."
Wáng Zhòngzǔ heard a foreign language and did not understand it;
perplexed, he said:
"If Jiè Gélú were to come to court,
he certainly would not be ignorant of this language."
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
"Jiè Gélú came to Lǔ to pay court,
and upon hearing an ox lowing, said:
'This one gave birth to three sacrificial oxen,
and all have been used.'
That is what its sound says."
Upon inquiry, it was found to be true."
Dù Yù's Commentary says:
"Jiè,
an eastern barbarian state.
Gélú,
the name of its ruler."
When Liú Zhēncháng was Prefect of Dānyáng,
Xǔ Xuándù left the capital and went to stay with Liú.
The Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng says:
"Xǔ Xún, styled Xuándù,
was from Gāoyáng,
a great-great-grandson of Xǔ Yǔn, General of the Central Army of Wèi.
In his youth, he was intelligent and clever,
and was praised by all as a child prodigy.
As an adult, his demeanor was simple and unadorned.
He was appointed as an Assistant in the Ministry of Education,
but did not accept the post,
and died young."
The bed curtains were new and beautiful,
and the food and drink were abundant and sweet.
Xǔ said:
"If one could preserve this place,
it would far surpass Dōngshān."
Liú said:
"If you believe that fortune and misfortune depend on people,
how could I not preserve this!"
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
"Fortune and misfortune have no gate;
they are summoned only by people."
Wáng Yìshào, who was present, said:
"If Cháo Fǔ
and Xǔ Yóu had met Jì
and Xiè, they would certainly not have spoken thus."
Both men looked ashamed.
General of the Right Wáng and Grand Tutor Xiè together ascended Yěchéng.
The Records of Yángzhōu says:
"Yěchéng
was a place for casting and smelting during the Wú period.
After Wú was pacified,
it was still not abandoned.
It was administered by Wáng Màohóng."
Xiè, lost in distant thought,
had aspirations transcending the mundane world.
Wáng said to Xiè:
"Xià Yǔ toiled for his king,
his hands and feet calloused;
The Annals of Emperors and Kings says:
"Yǔ controlled the floodwaters,
his hands and feet calloused.
It is traditionally said that Yǔ suffered from hemiplegia,
his feet could not cross over each other,
which is why his gait is now called 'Yǔ's step.'"
King Wén ate late,
with no time to spare.
The Book of Documents says:
"King Wén, from morning until sunset,
had no leisure to eat."
Now, the outskirts are filled with fortifications,
The Book of Rites says:
"When the outskirts are filled with fortifications,
it is a disgrace for the ministers and high officials."
Everyone should exert themselves.
Yet empty talk neglects duties,
and frivolous writing hinders essentials;
I fear this is not appropriate for the present time."
Xiè replied:
"Qín employed Shāng Yāng,
yet perished in the second generation.
The Strategies of the Warring States says:
"Shāng Yāng of Wèi,
a son of a concubine among the many sons,
named Yāng,
of the Gōngsūn clan.
In his youth, he was fond of the School of Names and Law;
he became chancellor to Duke Xiào of Qín,
and was enfeoffed at Shāng."
Could it be that refined discourse brought about disaster?"
On a cold, snowy day, Grand Tutor Xiè gathered his family indoors,
and together with the younger generation, discussed literary principles.
Suddenly, the snow fell heavily.
The Duke cheerfully said:
"To what can the swirling white snow be compared?"
His elder brother's son, Hú'ér, said:
Hú'ér
was the childhood name of Xiè Lǎng.
The Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng says:
"Lǎng, styled Chángdù,
was the eldest son of Ān's elder brother, Jù.
Ān recognized his talent early.
His literary talent was brilliant and flourishing;
his fame was second only to Xuán's.
He served as Governor of Dōngyáng."
"Sprinkling salt in the air is somewhat comparable."
His elder brother's daughter said:
"Not as good as willow catkins borne by the wind."
The Duke laughed heartily with delight.
She was the daughter of the Duke's eldest brother, Wúyì,
and the wife of General of the Left Wáng Níngzhī.
The Genealogy of the Wáng Clan says:
"Níngzhī, styled Shūpíng,
was the second son of General of the Right Yìzhī.
He served successively as Governor of Jiāng Province,
General of the Left,
and Prefect of Kuàijī."
The Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn says:
"Níngzhī practiced the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice.
When Sūn Ēn attacked Kuàijī,
Níngzhī said to the officials and people:
'There is no need to prepare defenses;
I have already petitioned the Great Way,
and it has promised to send ghost soldiers to assist us;
the bandits will be defeated of their own accord.'
Since he made no preparations,
he was subsequently killed by Ēn."
The Collected Works of Women says:
"Lady Xiè, named Dàoyùn,
was talented in literature.
The poems,
rhapsodies, elegies,
and eulogies she wrote have been handed down through the ages."
Wáng Zhōngláng ordered Fú Xuándù and
Xí Zàochǐ to discuss the eminent figures of Qīng and Chǔ. The "Wáng Zhōngláng Biography" states:
"Tǎnzhī, styled Wéndù,
was from Jìnyáng, Tàiyuán.
His grandfather was Chéng, Governor of Dōnghǎi,
pure and detached in character.
His father, Shù,
was upright, noble, simple, and correct.
Tǎnzhī's capacity and depth were genuine and profound,
his filial piety and fraternal love were heaven-sent,
his reputation gathered praise both at court and among the common people,
and he was a model of his time.
He successively rose to Shìzhōng,
Zhōngshū Lìng,
concurrently held the position of Běi Zhōngláng Jiàng,
and served as Governor of Xú and Yǎn provinces."
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Fú Tāo,
styled Xuándù,
was from Ānqiū, Píngchāng.
From a young age, he was talented and learned,
and was recommended as a Xiùcái.
He served as Cānjūn under Grand Marshal Huán Wēn,
concurrently held the position of Chief Compiler,
oversaw the state history,
served as Yóujī Jiāngjūn,
and then passed away. Xí Zàochǐ, styled Yànwēi,
was from Xiāngyáng.
From a young age, he was praised for his literary talent,
and excelled at writing letters.
When Huán Wēn was in Jīngzhōu,
he recruited him as a Cóngshì.
He successively served as Zhìzhōng and Biéjià,
and was promoted to Governor of Xíngyáng."
They discussed the eminent figures of Qīng and
Chǔ.
The "Tāo Collection" records the outline of his discussion as follows:
"Tāo considers the following from the Spring and Autumn period: Bào Shū,
Guǎn Zhòng,
Xí Péng,
Shào Hū,
Lún Biǎn,
Níng Qī,
the Màiqiū man,
Páng Chǒufù,
Yàn Yīng,
Juānzǐ;
from the Warring States period: Gōngyáng Gāo,
Mèng Kē,
Zōu Yǎn,
Tián Dān,
Xún Qīng,
Zōu Shì,
the Jǔ Grand Master,
Tián Zǐfāng,
Tánzǐ,
Lǔ Lián,
Chúnyú Kūn,
Pànzǐ,
Tián Guāng,
Yán Chù,
Qiánzǐ,
Yúlíng Zhòngzǐ,
Wáng Shū,
the Jímò Grand Master;
from the Former Hàn period: Fú Zhēngjūn,
Zhōng Jūn,
Dōngguō Xiānshēng,
Shūsūn Tōng,
Wàn Shí Jūn,
Dōngfāng Shuò,
Ānqī Xiānshēng;
from the Later Hàn period: Grand Minister over the Masses Fú Sānlǎo,
Jiāng Gé,
Páng Méng,
Qín Qìng,
Chéng Yòuzǐ,
Xú Fáng,
Xuē Fāng,
Zhèng Kāngchéng,
Zhōu Mèngyù,
Liú Zǔróng,
Lín Xiàocún,
Shìqí,
Yuán Jǔ,
Sūn Bīnshuò,
Liú Zhōngmóu,
Liú Gōngshān,
Wáng Yíbó,
Láng Zōng,
Mí Zhèngpíng,
Liú Chéngguó;
from the Wèi period: Guǎn Yòu'ān,
Bǐng Gēnjǔ,
Huà Zǐyú,
Xú Wèicháng,
Rèn Zhāoxiān,
Fú Gāoyáng.
These are all talented and virtuous individuals from Qīng Province.
Zàochǐ believes that Shénnóng was born in Qiánzhōng,
the "Shào Nán" odes praise its refined culture,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" speak of its many talents,
the customs of Hànguǎng
differ from the pieces like 'Jī Míng',
Zǐ Wén,
Shū Áo,
would be ashamed to compare their virtue with Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng.
Jiē Yú's song 'Fèng Xī',
the Fisherman's chant 'Cāng Láng',
the Hànyīn elder's refutation of Zǐgòng,
Shìnán Yìliáo,
Túyáng Yuè's refusal to bend for profit,
Lǔ Zhònglián is not equal to Lǎo Lái and his wife,
Tián Guāng compared to Qū Yuán,
Dèng Yǔ,
Zhuó Mào are unmatched in the world,
Guǎn Yòu'ān does not surpass Páng Gōng,
Páng Shìyuán does not defer to Huà Zǐyú,
the two Ministers Hé and Dèng,
stood alone in the Wèi court,
Yuè Lìng had no match in the Jìn era.
In ancient times, Fúxī was buried in Nánjùn,
Shǎohào was buried in Chángshā,
and Shùn was buried in Línglíng.
Comparing its people,
the standard is thus;
discussing its land,
it is where many sages are buried;
examining its customs,
they are what the poets sang of;
seeking its affairs,
there have been no rebels like the Red Eyebrows or Yellow Turbans.
How does this compare to Qīng Province?"
Tāo and he exchanged arguments back and forth,
and Zàochǐ had nothing to reply.
When it was completed,
it was shown to Hán Kāngbó.
Kāngbó said nothing at all,
and Wáng said:
"Why do you not speak?"
Hán said:
"There is nothing that must be, and nothing that must not be."
Mǎ Róng's commentary on the "Analects" says:
"Only righteousness determines it."
Liú Yǐn said:
"On clear breezes and bright moons,
I often think of Xuándù."
The "Jìn Zhōngxīng Shìrén Shū" states:
"Xǔ Xún was skilled in pure conversation,
and at that time, all scholars admired and looked up to him with affection."
Xún Zhōngláng was in Jīngkǒu,
The Jìn Yáng Qiū says:
"Xún Xiàn, styled Lìngzé,
was from Yǐngchuān,
the son of Guānglù Dàfū Sōng.
He was pure, harmonious, and had discernment and judgment.
In his youth, as the emperor's son-in-law, he was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
At that time, Yīn Hào was participating in the administration of all affairs,
and he recruited Xiàn as support,
who frequently governed Yìxīng,
Wújùn,
and was exceptionally appointed Běi Zhōngláng Jiàng,
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
to serve as a protective screen."
The Zhōngxīng Shū says:
"Xiàn was twenty-eight years old
when he was appointed to govern Xú
and Yǎn, two provinces.
Among the young provincial governors of the Restoration,
none were like Xiàn."
He ascended Běigù and gazed at the sea, saying:
The Nán Xúzhōu Jì says:
"Northwest of the city, there is a separate ridge extending into the river,
with three sides facing the water,
tens of zhàng high,
called Běigù."
"Although I have not seen the Three Mountains,
it naturally makes one feel as if soaring above the clouds.
If it were the rulers of Qín
and Hàn,
they would surely lift their robes and wet their feet."
The Shǐjì Fēngshàn Shū says:
"Pénglái,
Fāngzhàng,
and Yíngzhōu, these three mountains,
are traditionally said to be in the sea,
not far from people.
There have been those who reached them,
saying that the immortals' elixir of immortality is there.
The palaces are made of gold and silver,
the plants, animals, and birds are all white,
and from a distance, they look like clouds.
But when one arrives,
they are actually beneath the water.
When one tries to approach,
the wind blows the boat away,
and ultimately, no one can reach them.
Qín Shǐhuáng ascended Kuàijī,
and traveled along the coast,
hoping to encounter the miraculous herbs of the three divine mountains.
Hàn Wǔdì, after performing the fēngshàn ceremony on Tàishān,
with no wind or rain changes occurring,
the fāngshì further claimed that the herbs of Pénglái could be obtained,
so the emperor joyfully went east to the sea,
hoping to obtain those of Pénglái."
Xiè Gōng said:
"The sages and worthies are not far from people;
the distance between them is also close."
His sons and nephews did not agree with this.
Xiè Gōng sighed and said:
"If Chī Chāo heard these words,
he would certainly not think them far-fetched."
The Chāo Biézhuàn says:
"Chāo was profound in principles and righteousness,
and the Buddhist monk Zhī Dàolín considered him outstanding for his time."
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
Jiān Wú asked Lián Shū:
"I heard words from Jiē Yú,
grand but impractical,
going on without turning back.
I found his words strange and frightening,
like the Milky Way, boundless and endless."
Zhī Gōng was fond of cranes,
and lived on Āngshān east of Shàn.
The Zhī Gōng Shū says:
"The mountain is two hundred lǐ from Kuàijī."
Someone gave him a pair of cranes,
and after a while, their wings grew long, and they wanted to fly.
Zhī, regretting this,
clipped their flight feathers.
The cranes could no longer fly, though they stretched their wings,
and they looked back at their wings,
hanging their heads to gaze at them,
as if with a sense of懊喪.
Zhī Dàolín said:
"Since they have the bearing to soar to the heavens,
how could they be willing to serve as mere playthings for people's eyes and ears?"
He nurtured them until their feathers grew back,
and then set them free to fly away.
Xiè Zhōngláng passed by Qū'ā Hòuhú,
and asked his attendants:
"What body of water is this?"
The Zhōngxīng Shū says:
"Xiè Wàn, styled Wànshí,
was the younger brother of Tàifù Ān.
He was highly talented and outstanding,
and became well-known early on.
He served as Lìbù Láng,
Xī Zhōngláng Jiàng,
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Sànqí Chángshì."
They replied:
"Qū'ā Lake."
The Tàikāng Dìjì says:
"Qū'ā was originally called Yúnyáng.
Qín Shǐhuáng, because it had royal aura,
had Běikēngshān excavated to break its momentum,
cutting off its straight path,
making it curved,
hence it was called Qū'ā.
During Wú, it was restored to Yúnyáng,
but now it is again named Qū'ā."
Xiè said:
"So it must be a deep, pooling accumulation,
containing without flowing."
Jìn Wǔdì often gave Shān Táo very little in rewards.
Xiè Tàifù, that is, Ān.
He asked his sons and nephews about this,
Chējì, that is, Xuán.
He replied:
"It must be because the one who desires does not want much,
and thus makes the giver forget the small amount."
The Xiè Chējì Jiāzhuàn says:
"Xuán, styled Yòudù,
was the third son of Zhènxī Yì.
He was intelligent and outstanding in spirit and reason,
and skilled in subtle discourse.
His uncle, Tàifù, once gathered with his sons and nephews at a banquet,
and asked:
'Wǔdì entrusted Shāngōng with three matters,
appointing officials.
As for rewards,
they were no more than a jīn or a gě.
Was there a purpose to this?'
Xuán replied:
'There was an elegant reasoning behind it.'"
Xiè Hú'ér said to Yǔ Dàojì:
Dàojì,
was the childhood name of Yǔ Hé.
Xú Guǎng's Jìn Jì says:
"Hé, styled Dàojì,
was the son of Tàiwèi Liàng.
He was straightforward and perceptive in demeanor,
and was praised at the time for his literary conversations.
He served up to Dānyáng Yǐn,
concurrently Zhōng Lǐngjūn."
"Various people are sure to come to you for conversation;
you should fortify your defenses."
Yǔ said:
"If Wéndù comes,
I will meet him with a flank force;
if Kāngbó comes,
I will cross the river and burn my boats."
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn says:
"The Earl of Qín attacked Jìn,
crossed the river and burned his boats."
Dù Yù said:
"To show he was determined to die."
Lǐ Hóngdù often lamented not being given opportunities.
The Zhōngxīng Shū says:
"Lǐ Chōng, styled Hóngdù,
was from Méng, Jiāngxià.
His grandfather Kāng
and father Jǔ
both had fine reputations.
Chōng was initially appointed as Chéngxiàng Yuàn,
Jìshì Cānjūn.
Due to poverty,
he sought a position in Shànxiàn,
and was later promoted to Dà Zhùzuò,
Zhōngshū Láng."
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Yīn, that is, Yīn Hào, see separately.
Knowing his family was poor,
he asked:
"Could you lower your ambitions to govern a small district?"
Lǐ replied:
"The lament of 'Běimén,'
has long been heard by those above.
The Wèi Shī:
'Běimén,'
satirizes an official's lack of fulfillment.
A desperate ape fleeing to the forest,
has no time to choose its tree!"
Thus, he was appointed to Shànxiàn.
Sīzhōu Governor Wáng went to Yìnzhǔ in Wúxīng to view the scenery.
The Biography of Wáng Húzhī states:
"Húzhī, styled Xiūlíng,
was a native of Línyí in Lángyá.
He was the son of Wáng Yì.
He served as Governor of Wúxīng,
was summoned to serve as Palace Attendant,
Governor of Dānyáng,
and Director of the Imperial Library,
but declined all appointments.
He was appointed as Commissioner with Special Powers,
Military Governor of Sīzhōu,
Western General of the Household,
and Governor of Sīzhōu."
The Records of Wúxīng states:
"Seventy lǐ east of Yúqián County,
there is Yìnzhǔ.
Beside the islet stands Báishí Mountain,
with steep cliffs forty zhàng high.
Yìnzhǔ is where all the streams converge downstream.
From Yìnzhǔ upward to the county seat,
the waterways are full of rocky rapids and treacherous paths,
making navigation impossible.
Below Yìnzhǔ,
the waterways are free of hazards,
so travelers gather here."
He sighed and said:
"Not only does it cleanse one's heart and mind,
but it also makes the sun and moon seem brighter and clearer."
When Xiè Wàn was appointed Military Governor of Yùzhōu,
newly commissioned,
he was about to travel west to his post.
People saw him off for several days,
and Xiè grew weary.
At that time, Palace Attendant Gāo went to see him.
The Records of the Restoration states:
"Gāo Sōng, styled Màoyǎn,
was a native of Guǎnglíng.
His father, Kuī,
served as Grand Master of the Palace with Discretionary Authority.
Sōng loved learning from a young age
and excelled in history and biographies.
He rose through the ranks to become Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel
and Palace Attendant,
but was dismissed from office due to public affairs."
He went straight to Xiè's seat
and asked:
"Now that you wield authority over a region,
and are tasked with governing the western frontier,
how do you plan to administer it?"
Xiè briefly outlined his ideas.
Gāo then explained the situation to Xiè,
speaking for several hundred words.
Xiè then sat up straight.
After Gāo left,
Xiè remarked afterward:
"Ālíng indeed has some talent."
Ālíng
was Sōng's childhood name.
Thanks to this, Xiè was able to sit through the farewell.
Yuán Yànbó served as Military Advisor to Xiè Fèng, Governor of Ānnán.
Ānnán
refers to Xiè Fèng,
whose biography appears elsewhere.
People from the capital escorted him as far as Làixiāng.
As they were about to part,
he felt melancholy and wistful,
sighing:
"The rivers and mountains stretch far and wide,
truly possessing the grandeur of ten thousand lǐ."
The Continued Annals of Jìnyáng states:
"Yuán Hóng, styled Yànbó,
was a native of Chénjùn,
a sixth-generation descendant of Huàn, the Gentleman of the Palace of the Wèi dynasty.
His grandfather, Yóu,
served as Palace Attendant.
His father, Xù,
served as Magistrate of Línrǔ.
Hóng began his career as a Military Advisor to the General Who Establishes Might
and later served as Military Advisor and Registrar to the Governor of Ānnán.
Grand Tutor Xiè Ān admired Hóng's wit and eloquence.
When Hóng was appointed Governor of Dōngyáng Commandery from his post as Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
Xiè Ān hosted a farewell banquet for him at Yě Pavilion,
where all the worthies of the time gathered.
Ān wanted to test him on the spot,
so as they held hands to bid farewell,
he turned to his attendants and took a fan to give to Hóng.
Hóng immediately replied:
'I shall uphold and spread your benevolent influence,
bringing comfort to the common people.'
All those present praised his quick wit.
Due to his straightforward and upright nature,
he never attained a prominent position.
He died while serving in the commandery."
Sūn Chuò composed the "Suìchū" rhapsody,
built a house by the Quǎn River,
and declared that he had found contentment in knowing his limits.
The Records of the Restoration states:
"Chuò, styled Xìnggōng,
was a native of Zhōngdū in Tàiyuán.
From a young age, he was renowned for his literary talent.
He served as Erudite of the Grand Academy,
Grand Archivist,
and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary."
The preface to the "Suìchū" rhapsody states:
"In my youth, I admired the teachings of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
and long revered their refined ways.
Later, moved by the words of the virtuous wife of Yǔlíng,
I was struck with sudden realization.
Thus, I began building a retreat on the eastern hill,
establishing a five-acre estate,
nestled against long ridges,
and leaning upon lush forests.
How can this be compared to the pleasures of sitting under ornate canopies and striking bells and drums!"
In front of his study, he planted a pine tree,
which he personally tended to.
Gāo Shìyuǎn was his neighbor at the time.
Shìyuǎn
was the style name of Gāo Róu.
His biography appears elsewhere.
He said to Sūn:
"This young pine tree is not without its delicate charm,
but it will never be of use as a pillar or beam!"
Sūn replied:
"Even if a maple or willow grows thick enough to embrace,
what use is it?"
Military Governor Huán of the West built the walls of Jiānglíng into a magnificent sight.
Shèng Hóngzhī's Records of Jīngzhōu states:
"The city of Jīngzhōu overlooks the Hàn River,
and was governed by the Prince of Línjiāng.
When the prince was summoned to the capital,
he exited through the north gate, and his carriage axle broke.
The elders wept and said:
'Our prince leaves and will never return!'
Since then, the north gate has remained closed."
He gathered his guests and subordinates and went to Jiāngjīn to view it,
saying:
"Whoever can describe this city will be rewarded."
Gù Chángkāng was a guest at the time,
and was present.
He described it thus:
"Gazing from afar at the layered walls,
the crimson towers resemble rosy clouds."
Huán immediately rewarded him with two maidservants.
Wáng Zǐjìng said to Wáng Xiàobó:
"Yáng Shūzǐ is indeed admirable,
but what does he have to do with us?"
The Praises of the Jìn Nobles states:
"Yáng Hù, styled Shūzǐ,
was a native of Píngyáng in Tàishān.
For generations, his family had served as officials with salaries of two thousand shí.
By Hù's time, it was the ninth generation,
and they were praised for their integrity and virtue.
As a child,
he was playing by the Wèn River,
when a passing elder stopped to observe him.
He sighed and said:
'This young scholar has an excellent appearance.
If he applies himself well,
before he turns sixty,
he will accomplish great deeds for the world.
Once he attains wealth and honor,
do not forget me.'
He then left,
and no one knew where he went.
Hù rose through the ranks to become Military Governor of Jīngzhōu.
While stationed in the southern regions,
he won the admiration of the people of Wú,
who respectfully called him Lord Yáng,
never daring to address him by name.
When the people of the southern provinces heard of his death,
they wept and closed the markets in mourning."
"Thus, he is not as good as the courtesans on the Bronze Sparrow Terrace."
Cáo Cāo's "Final Instructions" states:
"After my death, have my concubines and courtesans reside on the Bronze Sparrow Terrace,
where a six-foot bed with fine silk curtains shall be set up.
On the first and fifteenth days of each month,
have them perform music and dance facing the curtain."
Master Lín saw the Cháng Mountain in Dōngyáng and said:
"How vast and undulating it is!"
The Gazetteer of Kuàijī states:
"The mountain stretches long and undulating,
and the county is named after it."
Gù Chángkāng paid respects at Huán Xuānwǔ's tomb,
and composed a poem that said:
"When mountains crumble and the dark sea dries up,
where will the fish and birds rely?"
Sòng Míngdì's "Wénzhāng Zhì" states:
"Kǎizhī served as Huán Wēn's military advisor,
and was greatly favored and close to him."
Someone asked him:
"You relied so heavily on Huán;
can you describe how you wept for him?"
Gù said:
"My nose was like the vast desert's long wind,
my eyes like a hanging river bursting its banks."
"Chūnqiū Kǎoyì Yóu" states:
"Forty-five days after the Bùzhōu wind,
the Guǎngmò wind arrives.
Guǎngmò means
essence and greatness are fully prepared.
It is the north wind,
also called the cold wind."
Some say:
"The sound was like thunder shattering mountains,
the tears like a pouring river flooding the sea."
Máo Bóchéng, proud of his talent and spirit,
often declared:
"I would rather be an orchid crushed or jade broken,
than be wormwood flourishing and mugwort thriving."
"Zhēngxī Liáoshǔ Míng" states:
"Máo Xuán, courtesy name Bóchéng,
was from Yǐngchuān.
He served up to the rank of marching army advisor under the General of the West."
When Fàn Nìng served as governor of Yùzhāng,
"Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Nìng, courtesy name Wǔzǐ,
was from Shènyáng County.
Broadly learned and widely read,
he rose through the ranks to become a palace secretary,
and governor of Yùzhāng."
On the eighth day, he invited Buddhist monks with a wooden tablet.
The monks were uncertain,
some wanting to respond.
A young novice monk seated at the end said:
"If the World-Honored One remains silent,
then it means he permits it."
The assembly followed his interpretation.
Grand Tutor Sīmǎ sat at night in his studio,
"Xiàowén Wáng Zhuàn" states:
"The prince, personal name Dàozǐ,
was the fifth son of Emperor Jiǎnwén.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Kuàijī,
served as Minister of Education,
Governor of Yángzhōu,
and was promoted to Grand Tutor.
He was killed by Huán Xuán,
and posthumously honored as Chancellor."
At that time, the sky and moon were bright and clear,
with not a wisp of cloud.
The Grand Tutor sighed, considering it beautiful.
Xiè Jǐngchóng was present,
