"Xù Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"Xiè Chóng, courtesy name Jǐngchóng,
was from Chénjùn.
His father, Lǎng,
was governor of Dōngyáng.
Chóng was intelligent, outstanding, and talented,
and ended his career as Chief Clerk to the General of the Rapid as Tigers."
He replied:
"I think it would be even better with a few wisps of cloud as embellishment."
The Grand Tutor then teased Xiè, saying:
"Your mind is not pure;
must you insist on staining the great clarity?"
Wáng Zhōngláng greatly admired Zhāng Tiānxī,
and asked him:
"Observing those who crossed the river and their governance,
the ways of Jiāngzuǒ,
what is particularly remarkable?
And the later talents,
how do they compare to those of the Central Plains?"
Zhāng said:
"In delving into profound depths,
since Wáng and
Hé onward;
in establishing institutions according to the times,
the style of Xún and Yuè."
Xún Yǐ and
Xún Xù established and revised laws and institutions,
but nothing is heard of Yuè.
Wáng said:
"Your knowledge and insight are more than sufficient;
why then were you controlled by Fú Jiān?"
Zhāng Zī's "Liángzhōu Jì" states:
"Tiānxī was perceptive and brilliant,
and his fine reputation was established early."
He replied:
"When yang wanes and yin waxes,
thus the steps of heaven are beset with difficulties;
when obstruction and decay form an image,
is it worthy of much ridicule?"
Xiè Jǐngchóng's daughter married Wáng Xiàobó's son,
and the two families' elders greatly admired each other.
"Xiè Shì Pǔ" states:
"Chóng's daughter Yuèjìng
married Wáng Gōng's son Yīnzhī."
Xiè served as Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor,
and was impeached;
Wáng immediately appointed him as his own Chief Clerk,
concurrently governing Jìnlíng Commandery.
The Grand Tutor had already developed resentment against Xiàobó,
and did not want him to obtain Xiè's service,
so he took Xiè back and made him a consultant.
Outwardly showing restraint,
but actually to create discord between them.
After Xiàobó's defeat,
the Grand Tutor was taking his medicinal powder walk around the walls of the Eastern Administration,
"Dānyáng Jì" states:
"West of the Eastern Administration walls
was the residence of Jiǎnwén when he was Prince of Kuàijī,
and east was the residence of Prince Xiàowén Dàozǐ.
Dàozǐ served as Governor of Yángzhōu,
and still resided in his former residence,
hence it was commonly called the Eastern Administration."
His subordinates were all gathered at the south gate, hoping to greet and pay respects.
At that time, he said to Xiè:
"Wáng Níng had rebellious plans;
Ā Níng—
Wáng Gōng's childhood name—
they say you were the one who devised the plan for him."
Xiè showed not a trace of fear,
straightened his tablet, and replied:
"Yuè Yànfǔ once said:
'Would I trade five sons for one daughter?'"
The Grand Tutor praised his reply,
and raising a cup to toast him, said:
"Truly excellent!
Truly excellent!"
After Huán Xuán returned from Yìxīng,
he went to see Grand Tutor Sīmǎ.
The Grand Tutor was already drunk,
and there were many guests present.
He asked someone:
"Huán Wēn came wanting to become a traitor;
what about that?"
"Jìn Āndì Jì" states:
"Wēn was in Gūshú,
hinting to the court
that he sought the Nine Bestowments.
Xiè Ān had the Ministry of Personnel official Yuán Hóng draft the text,
and showed it to Vice Director of the Secretariat Wáng Biāozhī.
Biāozhī changed countenance and said:
'How can a gentleman speak of such matters to others?'
Ān calmly asked his plan.
Biāozhī said:
'I hear his illness is already severe;
we can delay this matter for now.'
Ān followed his advice,
so it did not proceed."
Huán Xuán prostrated himself and dared not rise.
Xiè Jǐngchóng, then serving as Chief Clerk,
raised his tablet and replied:
"Thus, Duke Xuānwǔ deposed the dim and dark,
elevated the sage and enlightened,
his merit surpassing Yī and
Huò. The various conflicting opinions
are to be judged by Your Sagely Discernment."
The Grand Tutor said:
"I know!
I know!"
Then raising his cup, he said:
"Huán of Yìxīng,
I offer you wine."
Huán went out and apologized.
Tán Dàoluán commented on this:
"Dàozǐ can be said to have spoken too easily,
but Xiè Chóng was able to resolve the conflict."
When Xuānwǔ (Huán Wēn) moved his headquarters to Nánzhōu,
he had the streets laid out straight and level.
Someone said to Wáng Dōngtíng (Wáng Xún),
as recorded in the Biography of Minister Wáng:
"Wáng Xún, styled Yuánlín,
was the grandson of Chancellor Dǎo (Wáng Dǎo),
and the son of Army Supervisor Qià (Wáng Qià).
In his youth, he was praised for his purity and refinement.
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn recruited him as his Chief Clerk,
and he followed Wēn in the campaign against Yuán Zhēn.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngtíng in Wànghǎi County, Jiāozhǐ,
and rose successively to Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
in charge of official selection,
and was promoted to President of the Imperial Secretariat."
"When the Chancellor (Wáng Dǎo) first planned and built Jiànkāng,
he had no precedent to follow,
and the layout was winding and circuitous;
compared to this (Nánzhōu), it was inferior."
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"After Sū Jùn was executed,
and the major turmoil was quelled,
the capital lay in ruins.
Wēn Qiáo proposed moving the capital to Yùzhāng,
to be close to abundant and secure resources.
Court officials and the powerful families of Sānwú
argued that the capital could be moved to Kuàijī.
Only Wáng Dǎo maintained
'the capital should not be moved.
Jiànyè,
formerly known as Mòlíng,
in ancient times already showed signs of being a place ruled by emperors;
moreover, Sūn Zhòngmóu (Sūn Quán)
and Liú Xuándé (Liú Bèi) both said it was a king's dwelling.
Now, although it is devastated,
we should apply the principle of diligent restoration and gradual stabilization,
to calm the sentiments of the masses.
Moreover, if all the walls are being built,
why worry that it cannot be restored!'
The eventual peace and prosperity
was due to Dǎo's strategy."
Dōngtíng (Wáng Xún) said:
"This is precisely why the Chancellor was ingenious.
The land south of the Yangtze is cramped,
unlike the Central Plains;
if the roads and fields were laid out in straight, open lines,
everything would be seen at a glance.
Therefore, the winding and circuitous layout
makes it seem unfathomable."
Huán Xuán visited Yīn Jīngzhōu (Yīn Zhòngkǎn).
Yīn was taking a daytime nap in his concubine's room,
and his attendants declined to announce Huán.
Later, Huán mentioned this incident,
and Yīn said:
"I was not sleeping at all;
even if I were,
would I not
'esteem virtue in place of beauty'?"
Kǒng Ānguó's Commentary on the Analects states:
"It means if one uses the heart that loves beauty to love virtuous men, then it is good."
Huán Xuán asked Yáng Fú:
The Genealogy of the Yáng Clan states:
"Fú, styled Zǐdào,
was from Tàishān.
His grandfather was Kǎi,
a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
His father was Suí,
a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
Fú served as Erudite of the Grand Academy,
Assistant to the Regional Inspector,
and Army Advisor to the Grand Commandant.
He died at the age of forty-six."
"Why is Wú-style music so highly esteemed?"
Yáng said:
"It must be because it is enchanting and frivolous."
Xiè Hùn asked Yáng Fú:
"Why are ritual vessels (hú liǎn) used as an analogy for a person?"
The Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn states:
"Hùn, styled Shūyuán,
was from Chénjùn.
He was the youngest son of Minister of Works Yǎn (Xiè Yǎn).
He established his reputation through literary cultivation.
He rose successively to President of the Central Secretariat,
and Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was implicated in Liú Yì's faction and executed."
The Analects states:
"Zǐgòng asked:
'What about Cì (myself)?'
The Master said:
'You are a vessel.'
He asked:
'What kind of vessel?'
The Master said:
'A hú liǎn.'"
Zhèng Xuán's Commentary states:
"Vessels for millet.
Called hú in the Xià dynasty,
called liǎn in the Yīn dynasty."
Yáng said:
"It must be because they are vessels for communicating with the spirits."
After Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
his imperial throne slightly sank,
and the assembled ministers turned pale.
Palace Attendant Yīn Zhòngwén stepped forward and said:
The Continued Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Zhòngwén, styled Zhòngwén,
was from Chénjùn.
His grandfather was Róng,
Minister of Ceremonies.
His father was Kāng,
Governor of Wúxīng.
When Zhòngwén heard that Xuán had pacified the capital region,
he abandoned his commandery and went to join him.
Xuán was very pleased with him,
appointing him as Advisory Army Advisor.
At that time, Wáng Mì was treated with respect but not intimacy,
while Biàn Fànzhī was intimate but shown little respect.
The favor and treatment Yīn received
surpassed both Wáng
and Biàn.
After Xuán usurped the throne,
as a close and honored supporter of the accession,
he richly ennobled and exalted himself.
His carriages, horses, utensils, and clothing
were extremely luxurious and beautiful.
He had several dozen singing girls and concubines in his rear chambers,
with the sounds of strings and bamboo never ceasing.
His nature was very greedy and stingy,
accepting many bribes;
his household accumulated vast wealth,
yet he always seemed unsatisfied.
After Xuán's defeat,
he first surrendered to the loyalist army.
He rose successively to Palace Attendant and Imperial Secretary.
He was executed for his crimes."
"It must be because Your Majesty's virtue is so profound and weighty
that even the thick earth cannot bear it."
People of the time praised this remark.
After Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
he intended to reorganize the duty offices,
and asked his attendants:
"Where should the Bureau of the Leader of the Palace Guard be located?"
Someone replied:
"There is no separate bureau."
This answer greatly contradicted the emperor's intention at the time.
He asked:
"How do you know there isn't one?"
The reply was:
"Pān Yuè's Preface to the 'Rhapsody on Autumn Inspiration' states:
'I served concurrently as Leader of the Palace Guard,
and was assigned to duty in the Bureau of the Cavalier Attendants.'
Pān Yuè appears elsewhere.
His Preface to the Rhapsody states:
"In the fourteenth year of Jìn,
I was thirty-two years old and first saw grey hairs.
Serving as an Assistant to the Grand Commandant and concurrently as Leader of the Palace Guard,
I was assigned to duty in the Bureau of the Cavalier Attendants.
High pavilions connected to the clouds,
rarely touched by sunlight.
I am a man of the wilds,
yet presumptuously placed among the court ranks,
like a fish in a pond or a bird in a cage!
I long for the rivers, lakes, mountains, and marshes.
So I dipped my brush and took up paper,
and with emotion composed this rhapsody.
It was autumn then,
hence I titled it 'Autumn Inspiration.'"
Xuán sighed in admiration and praised it.
Liú Qiānzhī's Annals of Jìn states:
"Xuán wanted to restore the position of Leader of the Palace Guard,
but was uncertain whether it should have a duty assignment or not.
He consulted his staff,
but none could decide.
Army Advisor Liú Jiǎnzhī replied:
'In the past, Pān Yuè's Preface to the "Rhapsody on Autumn Inspiration" says:
"I served concurrently as Leader of the Palace Guard,
and was assigned to duty in the Bureau of the Cavalier Attendants."
From this,
it should have a duty assignment.'
Xuán happily followed this."
This account differs slightly,
and the respondent's name is unknown,
so it is recorded here in detail.
Xiè Língyùn was fond of wearing a hat with a curved handle.
Qiū Yuānzhī's *New Collection Record* states:
"Língyùn
was a man of Yángxià in Chénjùn.
His grandfather, Xuán,
was General of Chariots and Cavalry.
His father, Huàn,
was a Gentleman of the Imperial Library.
Língyùn successively held the posts of Supervisor of the Imperial Library,
Palace Attendant,
and Governor of Línchuān.
He was executed for his crimes.
The Recluse Kǒng said to him:
'You aspire to lofty and distant ideals,
so why can't you discard the appearance of the curved canopy?'"
*The Book of Sòng* states:
"Kǒng Chúnzhī, styled Yǎnshēn,
was a man of the State of Lǔ.
From youth, he spurned glory and embraced simplicity.
He did not respond to any summons or offers of appointment.
In the early Yuánjiā era,
he was summoned to be a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
but did not go.
He retired to Shàngyú Mountain."
Xiè replied:
"It is those who do not fear their shadow
who have not yet been able to forget themselves."
*The Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"The Old Fisherman said to Confucius:
'There was a man who, fearing his shadow and hating his footprints, tried to run away from them.
The more he lifted his feet, the more footprints he made;
the faster he ran, the more his shadow kept pace.
Thinking he was still too slow,
he ran even faster without stopping,
until his strength gave out and he died.
He did not know that by staying in the shade he could have rested his shadow,
and by staying still he could have ceased his footprints.
How exceedingly foolish!
If you, sir, cultivate your mind and preserve your genuineness,
returning things to others,
then there will be no such distinctions.
Not cultivating yourself but demanding it of others—
is this not focusing on external matters?'"
Chén Zhònggōng was the Magistrate of Tàiqiū.
At that time, a clerk falsely claimed his mother was ill to request leave.
When the matter was discovered, he was arrested,
and the magistrate ordered the clerk to be executed.
The Registrar requested he be handed over to the prison
for investigation into other possible crimes.
Zhònggōng said:
"To deceive one's lord is disloyal;
to feign his mother's illness is unfilial.
Disloyalty and unfiliality—
no crime is greater than these.
What further crimes could investigating uncover
that would surpass this?"
(Chén Shí has been treated separately elsewhere.)
Chén Zhònggōng was the Magistrate of Tàiqiū.
There was a case of bandits killing a wealthy man.
The authorities arrested them.
Before reaching the scene of the crime,
he heard on the road of a commoner who had a child born on the straw
but did not raise it.
He turned his carriage around to go and deal with that case.
The Registrar said:
"The bandit case is major; we should first investigate and pursue it."
Zhònggōng said:
"How does bandits killing a wealthy man
compare to flesh and blood harming each other?"
(According to records, Jiǎ Biāo in the Later Hàn had such a case;
it is not heard of regarding Shí.)
When Chén Yuánfāng was eleven years old,
(Chén Jì has been mentioned before.)
he paid a visit to Lord Yuán.
Lord Yuán asked him:
"Your worthy father served in Tàiqiū.
Far and near praised him.
What did he practice and implement?"
Yuánfāng said:
"My old father in Tàiqiū
pacified the strong with virtue,
comforted the weak with benevolence,
letting them settle as they wished,
so that over time they respected him even more."
Yuán Hóng's *Annals of the Hàn* states:
"When Shí was in Tàiqiū,
his governance was not harsh yet order was achieved,
and the common people respected him."
Lord Yuán said:
"I formerly served as Magistrate of Yè
and practiced exactly these things.
I wonder, did your esteemed father model himself on me,
or did I model myself on your father?"
(Checking various *Books of the Hàn*,
among the Yuán lords,
it is unknown who served as Magistrate of Yè.
Therefore, the text is left blank here awaiting someone of broad knowledge.)
Yuánfāng said:
"The Duke of Zhōu and Confucius
appeared in different ages,
yet in their movements and stillness, their dealings with the world,
they were as one across ten thousand *lǐ*.
The Duke of Zhōu did not take Confucius as his teacher,
nor did Confucius take the Duke of Zhōu as his teacher."
Grand Tutor Hè served as Administrator of Wú Commandery.
At first, he never went out his gate.
The powerful clans of Wúzhōng looked down on him
and wrote on the gate of his office:
"A Jī from Kuàijī,
cannot crow."
Huán Jì's *Record of Wú* states:
"Hè Shào, styled Xìngbó,
was a man of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
His grandfather, Qí,
and father, Jǐng,
both held fine offices.
Shào served successively as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
then went out to serve as Administrator of Wú Commandery.
Later, he was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent."
Hè, hearing of this, then went out on a tour.
Reaching the gate, he looked back,
asked for a brush, and completed the verse:
"Cannot crow?
It will kill the sons of Wú!"
Thereupon, he went to the various manors and estates,
inspected and checked the conscription of government troops by the various Gù and
Lù families, and their harboring of fugitives.
He reported all matters to the throne,
and many were found guilty.
Lù Kàng was at that time the Military Commissioner of Jiānglíng.
*The Record of Wú* states:
"Kàng, styled Yòujié,
was a man of Wú Commandery.
He was the son of Chancellor Xùn,
and the grandson of Sūn Cè on his mother's side.
He served as Military Commissioner of Jiānglíng,
and was successively promoted to Grand Marshal and
Governor of Jīng Province."
Therefore, he sent a petition down to Sūn Hào,
and only then were they released.
Lord Shān, esteemed for his ability and court reputation,
even past the age of seventy,
still knew how to manage the affairs of the time.
Yú Yù's *Book of Jìn* states:
"Shān Tāo, styled Jùyuán,
was a man of Huái in Hénèi.
His grandfather, Běn,
was a Filial and Incorrupt of the commandery.
His father, Yào,
was Magistrate of Yuānqú.
Tāo was orphaned early and was poor,
but from youth had capacity and tolerance;
even established scholars did not slight him.
At seventeen,
a clansman said to Emperor Xuān:
'Tāo should together with Jǐng and Wén uphold the
governance of the world.'
The Emperor said in jest:
'Yours is a minor clan;
how could it produce such an outstanding man?'
He loved the *Zhuāngzǐ* and *Lǎozǐ*,
and was close to Jī Kāng.
While serving as an Assistant in Hénèi,
he shared a relay station lodging with Shí Jiàn.
Tāo rose at night and nudged Jiàn, saying:
'What times are these that you can sleep!
Do you know why the Grand Tutor is lying low?'
Jiàn said:
'If the Chancellor does not attend court for three days,
he is ordered with an imperial edict to return to his residence.
What is there for you to worry about?'
Tāo said:
'Bah! Master Shí,
there is no peace even between a horse's hooves.'
He threw down his credentials and left.
Indeed, the affair of Cáo Shuǎng occurred,
so he withdrew from the world and did not engage in worldly affairs.
He was successively promoted to Minister of Personnel,
Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of Education.
He died at seventy-nine,
and was posthumously titled Marquis Kāng."
Noble and influential young men,
such as Hé, Péi, Wáng and their like,
all together revered and praised him.
Someone wrote on a pillar of the pavilion:
"East of the pavilion,
there is a great ox.
Hé Qiáo is the yoke,
Péi Kǎi the traces,
Wáng Jì goads and harries it without rest."
Wáng Yǐn's *History of the Jìn* states:
"Initially, when Shān Tāo headed the Ministry of Personnel,
Pān Yuè privately disapproved of him.
He secretly composed a ditty, saying:
'East of the gate, there is a great ox.
Wáng Jì holds the yoke,
Péi Kǎi grips the traces,
Hé Qiào is driven frantically without rest.'"
The *Discourses on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove* states:
"Regarding Tāo's conduct of selections,
hopes for advancement were cut off,
hence this saying was left behind."
Some say: Pān Ní composed it.
The *Biographies of Literary Men* states:
"Ní's courtesy name was Zhèngshū,
a man of Xíngyáng.
His grandfather was Xù,
Left Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat.
His father was Mǎn,
Governor of Píngyuán.
Both were renowned for their literary learning.
Ní was gifted with pure talent from a young age,
his literary style was gentle and elegant.
He first accepted provincial appointment,
and ended his career as Minister of Ceremonies."
When Jiǎ Chōng first established laws and ordinances,
the *Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"Chōng's courtesy name was Gōnglǘ,
a man of Xiānglíng.
His father was Kuí,
Governor of Yù Province under Wèi.
Chōng was well-known from an early age,
he began his career as a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat,
was promoted to Chamberlain for Law Enforcement,
and was praised for the fairness of his adjudications.
When Jìn received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Lǔ Commandery.
Chōng possessed talent and insight,
was clear-sighted and understood the principles of governance,
and was additionally skilled in penal law.
Because of this, he collaborated with the Regular Attendant-in-Waiting Péi Kǎi to establish statutes and ordinances,
removing intricate legal entanglements,
to create the *Jìn Code*.
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor."
He consulted with Yáng Hù and the Grand Tutor Zhèng Chōng.
Wáng Yǐn's *History of the Jìn* states:
"Chōng's courtesy name was Wénhé,
a man of Kāifēng in Xíngyáng.
He possessed a rigorous and practiced talent,
was pure, detached, and had few desires.
He delighted in discussing the Classics and histories.
Wearing straw garments and coarse padded robes,
he did not consider it a hardship.
He rose successively to become Minister over the Masses,
and Grand Guardian.
When Jìn received the abdication,
he was advanced to Grand Tutor."
Chōng said:
"The profound intent of Gāo Yáo's strictness and clarity
is not something a dim and timid fellow like myself can fathom."
Yáng said:
"His Majesty's intention is to have you add a bit of broad embellishment."
Chōng then roughly set down his ideas.
The *Continued Annals of Jìnyáng* states:
"Initially,
Emperor Wén commanded Xún Xù,
Jiǎ Chōng, Péi Xiù, and others
to separately determine rituals, ceremonies, laws, and ordinances.
They all first consulted Zhèng Chōng,
and only then implemented them."
Minister Shān, in his successive selections,
almost encompassed all the officials,
and none of his recommendations failed in talent.
In all cases where he evaluated and nominated someone,
they turned out just as he said.
Only in the appointment of Lù Liàng
was it done by imperial decree,
differing from the Duke's opinion.
He argued against it but was not heeded.
Liàng also soon fell due to bribery.
The *Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"Liàng's courtesy name was Chángxīng,
a man of Yěwáng in Hénèi.
He was the elder brother of Lù Yì, the Minister of Ceremonies.
His nature was intelligent and forthright,
and he was treated with intimacy by Jiǎ Chōng.
Shān Tāo was Left Executive of the Imperial Secretariat and concurrently in charge of selections.
Tāo's conduct and principles differed from Chōng's,
and considering himself respected by the Ancestral Emperor,
in matters of selection and appointment,
he would consult and discuss with Chōng,
but Chōng often failed to get what he wanted.
Busybodies advised Chōng:
'You should recommend a trusted confidant as Minister of Personnel,
to participate jointly in selections.
If opinions do not align,
and matters cannot be harmonized,
wouldn't it be possible to not summon the Duke for selections,
yet actually manage to arrange things according to your wishes?'
Chōng considered this correct.
He then memorialized that Liàng was public-spirited and without private motives.
Tāo, believing Liàng would oppose him,
and also fearing his collusion would be improper,
repeatedly memorialized that Liàng could serve as Left Assistant, initially
unsuitable as a selection official.
The Ancestral Emperor did not permit it,
so Tāo pleaded illness and returned home.
Liàng indeed proved incompetent in his post,
and was dismissed from office due to an offense."
After Jī Kāng was executed,
Duke Shān recommended Kāng's son Shào for the position of Assistant Director of the Palace Library.
The *Memorials of Duke Shān* states:
"An edict ordered the selection of an Assistant Director of the Palace Library.
Tāo recommended, saying:
'Shào is even-tempered, simple, gentle, and perceptive,
possesses literary thought,
and also understands music.
He should achieve success.
It would still be appropriate for him to first become a Gentleman of the Palace Library.'
The edict stated:
'If Shào is as described,
he may directly become Assistant Director;
there is no need for him to be a Gentleman first.'"
The *Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"Twenty years after Kāng's incident,
Shào was then promoted by Tāo."
Wáng Yǐn's *History of the Jìn* states:
"At that time, because Shào's father Kāng had been punished by law,
selection officials did not dare to recommend him.
At age twenty-eight,
Shān Tāo memorialized to employ him.
The Ancestral Emperor issued an edict,
appointing him Assistant Director of the Palace Library."
Shào consulted the Duke about whether to take office or remain in retirement.
The *Discourses on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove* states:
"Shào feared he would not be accepted,
and was about to take off his commoner's clothes [for office],
so he consulted Tāo about it." The Duke said:
"I have been thinking about this for you for a long time!
Heaven, earth, and the four seasons
still have their waxing and waning,
how much more so for a man?"
Wáng Yǐn's *History of the Jìn* states:
"Shào's courtesy name was Yánzǔ, elegantly
possessing literary talent.
Shān Tāo memorialized to Emperor Wǔ, saying thus and so."
When Wáng Ānqī governed Dōnghǎi Commandery,
the *Biographies of Famous Gentlemen* states:
"Wáng Chéng's courtesy name was Ānqī,
a man of Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
His father was Zhàn,
Governor of Rǔnán.
Chéng was serene, detached, and had few desires,
with nothing he particularly followed or esteemed.
He rose successively to become Interior Minister of Dōnghǎi.
His administration was clear and tranquil,
and the officials and people cherished him.
He crossed the river to avoid the chaos.
At that time, the roads were plagued by bandits,
and people were filled with worry and fear.
Whenever Chéng encountered hardship or danger,
he faced it with composure.
When Emperor Yuán was General Who Guards the East,
he recruited him as a Gentleman in Service."
A minor clerk stole fish from the pond,
and the Registrar investigated him.
Wáng said:
"King Wén's park
was shared with the multitude.
The *Mèngzǐ* says:
'King Xuān of Qí asked:
"King Wén's park
was seventy li square, was it not?
Was it really that large?"
Mèngzǐ replied:
"The people still considered it small."
The King said:
"My park
is forty li square,
yet the people still consider it large.
Why is that?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"In King Wén's park,
grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers went there;
he shared it with the people.
The people considering it small—
was that not fitting?
Now, in Your Majesty's park,
those who kill deer are treated as if guilty of murder.
Thus, these forty li become a pitfall within the state.
The people considering it large—
is that not fitting?"'
What is there to regret about pond fish!"
When Wáng Ānqī served as the administrator of Dōnghǎi Commandery,
an officer apprehended a person who had violated the curfew and brought him in.
Wáng asked:
"Where have you come from?"
The man replied:
"I was returning from my teacher's house after receiving instruction,
and did not notice how late it had become."
Wáng said:
"To whip a Nìng Yuè in order to establish one's authority and reputation,
I fear is not the fundamental way to achieve good governance."
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states:
"Nìng Yuè was
a humble man from Zhōngmóu.
Suffering from the toil of plowing and sowing,
he said to his friend:
'What can I do to avoid this hardship?'
His friend said:
'Nothing is better than to study.
Study for thirty years,
and then you can achieve success.'
Nìng Yuè said:
'I ask to do it in fifteen years.
When others are about to rest,
I dare not rest;
when others are about to sleep,
I dare not sleep.'
He studied for fifteen years and became the teacher of Duke Wēi of Zhōu."
Wáng had the officer escort the man and send him home.
When Emperor Chéng was at Shítóu,
the *Jìn Shì Pǔ* states:
"The Emperor's personal name was Yǎn,
his courtesy name was Shìgēn,
and he was the crown prince of Emperor Míng.
He passed away at the age of twenty-two."
Rèn Ràng, in the Emperor's presence,
killed the Palace Attendant Zhōng Yǎ.
The *Jìn Yáng Qiū* states:
"Ràng was
a man from Lè'ān,
a descendant of the various Rèn clans.
He followed Sū Jùn in rebellion."
The *Bié Zhuàn of Zhōng Yǎ* states:
"Yǎ's courtesy name was Yànzhòu,
he was from Chángshè, Yǐngchuān,
and was the great-great-grandson of Zhòng Cháng, the younger brother of Zhōng Yáo, the Grand Tutor of Wèi.
From a young age, he had talent and ambition,
and rose through the ranks to become Palace Attendant."
He also killed the General of the Right Guard, Liú Chāo.
The *Jìn Yáng Qiū* states:
"Chāo's courtesy name was Shìyú,
he was from Lángyá,
and was a sixth-generation descendant of Jǐng, the King of Chéngyáng of the Hàn dynasty.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Cíxiāng in Línyí,
and thus made his home there.
His father, Zhēng, was the Senior General of the Kingdom of Lángyá.
Chāo served as a minor clerk in the county,
and gradually rose to the positions of Registrar Clerk
and Gentleman of the Palace of Āndōng.
Loyal, incorruptible, cautious, and discreet,
he was promoted by Emperor Zhōngzōng.
Believing that his duties lay within the Secretariat,
he absolutely refused to engage in correspondence or dealings with others,
closed his doors and did not receive guests,
and his household had not even a peck or a bushel of stored grain.
For his merit in the campaign against Wáng Dūn,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Língyáng,
and served as the Administrator of Yìxīng.
Yet, when he received his appointments and traveled to and from the court,
no one knew of it,
such was his caution and silence.
He was promoted to Great General of the Right Guard."
The Emperor wept and said:
"Return my Palace Attendant to me!"
Ràng did not obey the decree,
and proceeded to behead Chāo and Yǎ.
The *Bié Zhuàn of Zhōng Yǎ* states:
"When Sū Jùn forced the sovereign to go to Shítóu,
Yǎ and Liú Chāo both attended by the Emperor's side to protect and defend him,
and secretly arranged with people inside Shítóu to rescue His Majesty and get him out.
The plot was discovered, and they were killed."
After the incident was pacified,
Minister Táo, who had an old acquaintance with Ràng,
wished to pardon him.
Xǔ Liǔ—
the *Xǔ Shì Pǔ* states:
"Liǔ's courtesy name was Jìzǔ,
he was from Gāoyáng.
His grandfather was Yǔn,
Central Army Commander of Wèi.
His father was Měng,
a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel."
Liú Qiānzhī's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Liǔ's wife
was the daughter of Zǔ Huàn, son of Zǔ Tì.
When Sū Jùn recruited Zǔ Yuē to join the rebellion,
Yuē sent Liǔ with troops to join Jùn.
After they captured the capital,
he was appointed as the Governor of Dānyáng.
Later, he was executed for his crimes."
—had a son, Sībǐ, who was exceptionally talented,
and the various ministers wished to spare him.
The *Xǔ Shì Pǔ* states:
"Yǒng's courtesy name was Sībǐ."
If Sībǐ were to be spared,
then they would have no choice but to spare Ràng for Táo's sake,
so they wished to pardon both of them.
When the matter was presented to the Emperor, he said:
"Ràng is the one who killed my Palace Attendant.
He cannot be pardoned!"
The ministers, considering that the young sovereign's will could not be opposed,
executed both men.
When Chancellor Wáng was appointed to Yángzhōu,
he received and treated several hundred guests,
and everyone wore a pleased expression.
Only one guest from Línhǎi named Rèn—
the *Yǔ Lín* states:
"Rèn's given name was Yóng,
at the time he held an office in the capital,
and was present at Lord Wáng's gathering."
—and several Hú people felt they had not been adequately engaged.
The Chancellor then casually went over to Rèn's side
and said: "When you, sir, are absent,
Línhǎi truly has no one else."
Rèn was greatly pleased and delighted.
Then he went before the Hú people, snapped his fingers, and said:
"Lánshé, lánshé."
The group of Hú people laughed together,
and all those present were joyful.
The *Jìn Yáng Qiū* states:
"Wáng Dǎo received and guided people, responding to situations,
and there were few who found him disagreeable.
Even casual acquaintances and ordinary guests,
upon meeting him once, mostly felt he poured out sincerity,
and considered themselves treated exceptionally well by Dǎo,
on par with old intimates."
Grand Commandant Lù went to Chancellor Wáng to consult on matters,
but afterward would often change his stance.
Lord Wáng found this strange,
and later asked Lù about it.
The *Bié Zhuàn of Lù Wán* states:
"Wán's courtesy name was Shìyáo,
he was from Wú, Wú Commandery.
His grandfather was Mào,
his father was Yīng,
both served in the commandery with good reputations.
Wán was refined and of generous capacity,
he rose through the ranks to become Palace Attendant,
Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat and enfeoffed,
Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Commandant."
Lù said:
"Your Lordship is lofty, and I, a commoner, am lowly.
In the moment, I did not know what to say,
but afterward, I realized it was not appropriate."
The Chancellor once went to Shítóu in the summer to see Lord Yǔ.
Yǔ was just then managing affairs,
and the Chancellor said:
"In the heat, you could simplify things a bit."
Lord Yǔ said:
"Your Lordship's neglect of affairs
is also not considered appropriate by the world."
The *Yán Xíng of Yīn Xiàn* states:
"After Lord Wáng passed away,
Yǔ Bīng succeeded him as Chancellor,
and his legal net was dense, his punishments severe.
Xiàn was traveling at the time,
and encountering people being arrested on the road,
he sighed with emotion, saying:
'Bǐng Jí inquired about an ox panting;
this seems unlike that!'
He once said to Bīng in a relaxed manner:
'You people certainly ensure that the meshes of the net do not miss anything,
but these are all minor methods and petty virtues.
As for someone like Lord Wáng,
he was truly capable of acting without being bound by rigid principles.'
Xiè Ānshí often sighed and praised this statement.
Yǔ Chìyù once asked Xiàn:
'How was Lord Wáng's governance?
Was it truly his strength?'
Xiàn said:
'His other fine achievements
need not be mentioned again.
However, it was three times seizing and three times governing,
three times resting and three times failing.'"
In his later years, the Chancellor
largely ceased attending to affairs,
merely sealing documents and giving his approval.
He sighed to himself, saying:
"People say I am muddled,
but later generations will long for this muddledness."
Xú Guǎng's *Lì Jì* states:
"Dǎo served as chief minister for three reigns,
managing both peace and peril,
his governance was lenient and forgiving,
and he followed simple and easy methods in handling affairs,
thus leaving behind a reputation of cherished benevolence."
Minister Táo was by nature strict and meticulous,
and diligent in his duties.
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Kǎn was meticulous in examining all matters,
diligently attending to farming.
Even military officers and soldiers
he encouraged and motivated.
When someone presented him with gifts,
he would always ask how they were obtained.
If they came from labor,
he would joyfully accept them and reward the giver;
if obtained otherwise,
he would scold and return them.
Therefore, both the army and civilians were diligent in farming,
and every household was well-supplied and people were content.
He was meticulous and inquisitive by nature,
quite similar to Zhào Guǎnghàn.
Once, he assigned the task of planting willows,
and Commandant Xià Shī secretly uprooted those planted at the west gate of Wǔchāng Commandery.
Later, Kǎn went out himself,
stopped his carriage at Shī's gate,
and asked:
'This is the willow from the west gate of Wǔchāng,
why did you steal it?'
Shī was terrified and confessed,
and the entire army praised his keen observation.
Kǎn was diligent and orderly,
striving tirelessly to improve himself.
He also enjoyed supervising and encouraging others,
often saying:
'The livelihood of the people lies in diligence.
Even the great sage Yǔ
still cherished every inch of time;
as for ordinary people,
they should cherish every fraction of time.
How can one indulge in leisure and idleness,
living without contributing to the times,
dying without leaving a legacy for posterity?
This is self-abandonment.
Moreover, the superficiality of Lǎozhuāng
is not the words of the ancient kings and should not be practiced.
A gentleman should adjust his attire and hat,
maintain a dignified demeanor.
How can one appear disheveled while cultivating a reputation,
claiming to be broad-minded and enlightened?'"
The Zhōngxīng Shū states:
"Kǎn once inspected his subordinate officials,
and if he found gambling tools like chūpú or board games,
he would throw them away, saying:
'Chūpú was created by Lǎozi when he entered the barbarian lands,
merely a foreign game.
Wéiqí
was used by Yáo and Shùn to teach their foolish sons.
Gambling games were created by Zhòu.
You gentlemen are pillars of the state;
why engage in such things?
If you have leisure from official duties,
and are troubled by boredom,
why don't scholars read books?
Why don't warriors practice archery?'
Those who discussed this had no way to refute him."
When he served as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
he ordered the ship officials to collect all sawdust,
regardless of quantity.
No one understood his intention.
Later, during the New Year's assembly,
it happened that after snowfall the weather cleared,
and the ground in front of the audience hall was still wet after the snow was cleared.
Then he used the sawdust to cover it all,
and there was no hindrance at all.
He also ordered that the thick ends of bamboo used for official purposes be collected,
piling them up like a mountain.
Later, when Huán Xuānwǔ campaigned against Shǔ,
for shipbuilding,
they were all used to make nails.
It is also said:
Once, when inspecting locally produced bamboo poles,
there was an official who took them with roots attached,
using them as is for poles,
so he promoted him two ranks.

When Wèi Jiè was young, he asked Yuè Guǎng about "dreams."
Yuè said, "They are thoughts."
Wèi said:
"When form and spirit are not connected, how can dreams be thoughts?"
Yuè said:
"They are based on causes.
One never dreams of riding a carriage into a mouse hole
or pounding minced vegetables and eating an iron pestle,
because there are no thoughts and no causes for such things."
The *Zhōulǐ* lists six types of dreams:
The first is the regular dream,
which occurs without any stimulation,
in peaceful sleep.
The second is the frightening dream,
which occurs due to alarm or fear.
The third is the thoughtful dream,
which arises from thoughts while awake.
The fourth is the waking dream,
which occurs when one speaks of something while awake and then dreams of it.
The fifth is the joyful dream,
which arises from happiness.
The sixth is the fearful dream,
which arises from fear.
According to what Yuè said,
"thoughts"
likely refer to thoughtful dreams.
"Causes"
likely refer to regular dreams.
Wèi pondered the "causes,"
and after a whole day could not understand,
he fell ill.
Yuè heard of this
and thus had his carriage prepared to go and analyze it for him.

"This child surely will never suffer from incurable illnesses in his heart!"

A guest asked Commandant Yuè about the phrase “the point does not arrive.”
Yuè did not analyze the wording further,
but simply tapped the table with the handle of his yak-tail whisk, saying:
“Does it arrive?”
The guest said: “It arrives!”
Yuè then raised the whisk again and said:
“If it arrives, how can it depart?”
For, hiding a boat by stealthily moving it,
or crossing arms in constant farewell,
not a moment lingers,
suddenly there is birth and extinction.
Thus, the shadow of a flying bird
is never seen to shift;
the wheels of a speeding chariot
never seem to cover the ground.
Therefore, if departure is not departure,
how can there be arrival?
If arrival is not arrival,
how can there be departure?
Yet, the former arrival is no different from the latter arrival,
hence the name ‘arrival’ arises;
the former departure is no different from the latter departure,
hence the name ‘departure’ is established.
Now, if in the world there is no departure,
then is not ‘departure’ a fiction?
Since it is a fiction,
then can ‘arrival’ be real?
Thereupon, the guest was enlightened and convinced.
Yuè’s words were concise yet their meaning profound,
all of this kind.
Initially, there were several tens of scholars who annotated the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
but none could grasp its essential meaning.
Xiàng Xiù, apart from the old annotations, composed an interpretation,
wondrously analyzing its extraordinary purport,
greatly promoting the profound style.
The *Separate Biography of Xiù* says:
“Xiù was a friend of Jī Kāng and Lǚ Ān,

Jī Kāng was arrogant toward the world and unrestrained;

The other two often ridiculed him for this.
Later, when Xiù was about to annotate the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
he first told Kāng and Ān.
Kāng and Ān both said:
‘Does this book really need annotation?
It merely ruins people’s enjoyment!’
When it was completed,
he showed it to the two.
Kāng said:
‘So, are you still superior or not?’
Ān then exclaimed in surprise:
‘Zhuāng Zhōu has not died!’
Later, he annotated the *Zhōuyì*,
its main ideas were commendable,
but compared to the various Confucian scholars of the Hàn dynasty, there were points of agreement and disagreement,
not equaling the peerlessness of his hidden *Zhuāng* [annotations].”
Some accounts in Xiù’s main biography say
that Xiù wandered and relied on several worthies,
passing his years in quiet obscurity,
with no annotations or writings at all.
He only loved the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
and merely responded to Cuī Zhuàn’s annotations,
to aid his memory, it is said.
The *Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove* says:
“Xiù expounded this meaning;
those who read it all felt transcendent,
as if they had already emerged from the dust and glimpsed the ultimate obscurity,

There is a divine virtue and profound wisdom

and set aside the myriad things.
Even if it made competitive and striving people look back upon what they pursue,
they would all feel regretful and naturally have a sentiment of self-uplifting.”
Only the two chapters “Autumn Floods” and “Perfect Happiness” were unfinished when Xiù died.
Xiù’s son was young,
and the meaning was thus scattered and lost,
yet there still existed another version.
As for Guō Xiàng,
he was a man of shallow conduct,
but possessed outstanding talent.
The *Biographies of Literary Men* says:
“Xiàng, styled Zǐxuán,
was from Hénán.

Seeing that Xiù’s meaning was not transmitted in the world,
he then stole it and made it his own annotation.
He then personally annotated the two chapters “Autumn Floods” and “Perfect Happiness”,
and also altered the chapter “Horses’ Hooves”,
