hence they are named 'Pratyekabuddha' (solitary realizers).
Bodhisattvas are
people of the Great Way.
As an expedient means, they practice the Six Pāramitās;
in the true teaching, they cultivate all ten thousand virtues.
Their merit is not for themselves;
their aspiration is to broadly aid all beings.
Therefore, they are named after the Great Way."
This refers to Attendant Xǔ, Xǔ Xún.
When he was young,
people compared him to Wáng Gǒuzi.
Gǒuzi
was the childhood name of Wáng Xiū.
The "Record of Calligraphy" says:
"Xiū's courtesy name was Jìngrén,
a man of Jìnyáng in Tàiyuán.
His father was Wáng Méng,
Left Chief Clerk of the Minister Over the Masses.
Xiū was intelligent, outstanding, and had a fine reputation.
He excelled at clerical and running script,
and was praised as
'flowing elegance, pure and lofty.'
He began his career as Assistant Gentleman of Writings,
then became Literary Scholar to the Prince of Lángyé,
and was transferred to be Army Advisor to the Central Army.
He died before assuming the post,
at the age of twenty-four.
In the past, when Wáng Bì died,
he was the same age as Xiū.
Therefore, Xiū's younger brother Xī sighed, saying:
'He is无愧於古人,
and his age matched theirs.'"
Xǔ Xún was greatly displeased.
At that time, various gentlemen and Dharma Master
were all lecturing at the Western Temple in Kuàijī,
and Wáng Xiū was also there.
Xǔ, feeling very indignant,
went to the Western Temple to debate principles with Wáng,
to determine who was superior.
After intense mutual refutation,
Wáng was thoroughly defeated.
Then Xǔ took up Wáng's arguments,
and Wáng took up Xǔ's arguments,
and they exchanged and elaborated further;
Wáng was defeated again.
Xǔ said to Dharma Master Zhī:
"How was my discourse just now?"
Zhī replied calmly:
"Your discourse was excellent, indeed excellent,
but why did you have to press him so hard?
Was that really a discussion seeking the balanced truth!"
The Venerable Lín visited Xiè Ān.
Xiè Lǎng (Dōngyáng) was still a youth at the time,
having just recovered from an illness,
and his body could not yet bear strain.
He engaged in discussion with the Venerable Lín,
which became quite intense.
Dōngyáng
was Xiè Lǎng,
already mentioned.
The "Records of the Restoration" says:
"Lǎng had broad knowledge and outstanding talent,
and was skilled in discoursing on profound principles."
His mother, Lady Wáng, was listening behind the wall.
She twice sent a messenger to have him return,
but the Grand Tutor (Xiè Ān) detained him.
Lady Wáng then came out herself and said:
"This humble wife suffered family misfortune in her youth;
all my hopes in this life
rest solely on this child."
She then wept, embraced her son, and took him back.
Xiè Ān said to those seated with him:
"My sister-in-law's words were deeply moving and impassioned;
they truly deserve to be passed on.
It is a pity that the court officials could not see her."
The "Xiè Clan Genealogy" says:
"Lǎng's father was Xiè Jù,
who married Wáng Tāo's daughter from Tàikāng,
named Suí."
Zhī Dàolín, Attendant Xǔ, and others
were together at Prince of Kuàijī's studio.
(This was Jiǎnwén.)
Zhī served as the Dharma Master,
and Xǔ served as the Lecturer.
The "Biographies of Lofty and Reclusive Monks" says:
"Dàolín was lecturing on the 'Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra' at the time."
Whenever Zhī explained a principle,
all those seated were deeply satisfied.
Whenever Xǔ posed a difficult question,
everyone could not help but clap and dance for joy.
They only jointly praised the excellence of both masters,
without discerning where the true principle lay.
When General of Chariots and Cavalry Xiè Xuán was in mourning for Ānxī,
Ānxī
was Xiè Yì.
Already mentioned.
The Venerable Lín went to converse with him,
and did not leave until evening.
Someone who saw him on the road asked:
"Where have you come from, sir?"
He replied:
"Today I had a vigorous discussion with Xiào of the Xiè family for a while."
The "Separate Biography of Xuán" says:
"Xuán was capable of pure conversation,
skilled in name and principle."
When Zhī Dàolín first came from the east,
he stayed at the Dōng'ān Temple.
The "Biographies of Lofty and Reclusive Monks" says:
"Dùn resided in Kuàijī.
Emperor Āi of Jìn admired his style and character,
and sent a palace envoy east to summon him.
Dùn then left his mountain retreat,
and strode loftily to the capital."
Chief Clerk Wáng (Wáng Méng) had prepared profound principles in advance,
and had also polished his literary talent,
and went to converse with Zhī.
It was not a very well-matched dialogue.
Wáng presented his ideas in several hundred words,
believing them to be extraordinary principles and marvelous rhetoric.
Zhī slowly said to him:
"I have been parted from you for many years,
but your understanding of principle and discourse has not improved at all."
Wáng retired in great shame.
General of the Central Army Yīn Hào read the "Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra" (Xiǎopǐn).
Among the Buddhist "Discourses on Emptiness" scriptures,
some are detailed,
some are abbreviated.
The detailed one is the "Larger Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra" (Dàpǐn),
the abbreviated one is the "Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra" (Xiǎopǐn).
He made over two hundred tags
on points that were all subtle and profound,
obscurities of the world.
He once wished to debate them with Zhī Dàolín,
but ultimately did not get the chance.
The "Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra" still exists today.
The "Biographies of Lofty and Reclusive Monks" says:
"Yīn Hào was skilled in discoursing on name and principle,
but felt there were things he did not fully understand,
and wished to consult Dùn about them.
He happened to miss meeting him,
and deeply regretted it.
The esteem and appreciation he received from famous connoisseurs
was of the highest degree."
The "Forest of Conversations" says:
"Hào had some unresolved questions regarding Buddhist scriptures,
so he sent someone to invite the Venerable Lín.
Lín humbly intended to go.
General of the Right Wáng Xīzhī stopped him, saying:
'Yuānyuán's (Yīn Hào's) thinking is profound and rich.
He is not easily matched as an opponent.
Moreover, what you yourself do not understand,
the Venerable One may not necessarily comprehend either.
Even if you submit to him,
it will not increase your reputation.
If you happen to disagree,
you will lose the standing you have preserved for ten years.
You need not go!'
The Venerable Lín also thought this was right,
and so desisted."
Buddhist scriptures hold that by purifying and refining the spirit,
one can attain sagehood.
The Buddhist scriptures say:
"All sentient beings
possess Buddha-nature.
If one can cultivate wisdom,
sever afflictions,
and perfect all practices,
one will attain Buddhahood."
Jiǎnwén said:
"I wonder if one can immediately reach the ultimate peak?
However, the effort of tempering and refinement
cannot be dismissed."
Yú Fǎkāi initially contended with Zhī Dàonlín for fame.
Later, sentiment gradually favored Zhī,
which Yú deeply resented.
He then withdrew to Shànxià.
He sent a disciple to the capital,
instructing him to pass by Kuàijī.
At that time, Zhī Dàonlín was lecturing on the *Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Yú Fǎkāi cautioned his disciple:
"When Dàolín lectures, by the time you arrive,
he should be on a certain section."
He then provided several dozen points of refutation and difficulty,
saying:
"Traditionally, these points are considered irresolvable."
The disciple went to Zhī Dàonlín as instructed.
He happened upon the lecture
and carefully presented Yú Fǎkāi's arguments.
After extensive debate,
Dàolín was ultimately defeated.
He raised his voice and said:
"Why must you carry another's baggage here!"
*Titles of Famous and Virtuous Monks* says:
"Yú Fǎkāi was eloquent and resourceful,
using numerology to propagate the teachings."
*Biographies of Eminent and Reclusive Monks* says:
"Fǎkāi first gained fame for his doctrinal studies.
Later, he had a rivalry with Zhī Dùn,
so Dùn resided in Shàn County
and further studied medicine."
Yīn Hào asked:
"If nature is without intention in endowment,
why are truly good people few,
and evil people many?"
No one present could answer.
Liú Tǎn replied:
"It is like pouring water onto the ground.
It simply flows and spreads freely,
with hardly any forming perfect squares or circles."
Everyone sighed in admiration at the time,
considering it a famous and penetrating statement.
*Zhuāngzǐ* says:
"The piping of heaven
blows through the myriad things differently,
yet lets each be itself."
Guō Xiàng's *Commentary* says:
"Non-being is non-being;
thus it cannot give birth to being.
Being, before it is born,
also cannot give birth to itself.
Then who is it that gives birth to life?
It spontaneously generates of itself,
not generated by me.
I do not generate things,
things do not generate me.
Thus, what is natural is simply so,
and is called 'heavenly.'
The heavenly is not deliberate action;
therefore, it is spoken of as 'heaven,'
to clarify that it is natural."
When Kāng Sēngyuān first crossed the river,
no one knew him.
He often wandered the markets,
begging to sustain himself.
He once went to Yīn Yuānyuán's place,
where there happened to be many guests.
Yīn had him sit,
briefly exchanged pleasantries,
and then turned to doctrinal principles.
Sēngyuān's speech and expression
showed no sign of shame.
He grasped the main points
and delved directly into profound understanding.
From then on, he became known. Regarding Sēng
yuān's clan and
origins,
it is unclear;
he is suspected to be a foreigner.
Shàngshū Lìng Shěn Yuē, in compiling the *Jìn Shū*,
also praised him for his doctrinal learning.
Yīn, Xiè, and others gathered together.
Yīn Hào and Xiè Ān.
Xiè asked Yīn:
"Does the eye go out to engage the myriad forms,
or do the myriad forms enter the eye?"
*The Satyasiddhi Śāstra* says:
"Visual consciousness perceives without reaching [the object].
It relies on space and light,
thus enabling the seeing of form.
If the eye reached the form,
there would be no space or light between form and eye.
Just as if the eye touched the eyeball,
it could not see it.
One should know that visual consciousness perceives without reaching."
According to this explanation,
the eye does not go out,
nor do forms enter;
perception occurs through remote engagement.
Xiè posed the question,
but Yīn gave no answer.
This is suspected to be a textual omission.
Someone asked Yīn Hào:
"Why is it that
when about to obtain an official position, one dreams of a coffin,
and when about to obtain wealth,
one dreams of excrement and filth?"
Yīn said:
"Official positions are inherently putrid,
hence dreaming of coffins and corpses when about to obtain one;
wealth is inherently dung and dirt,
hence dreaming of filth when about to obtain it."
People of the time considered this a famous and penetrating statement.
When Yīn Hào was dismissed and exiled to Dōngyáng,
(the matter of Hào's dismissal
is recorded elsewhere.)
he began reading Buddhist scriptures.
First, he looked at the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Sēng Zhào's *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says:
"Vimalakīrti,
in Chinese, means 'Pure Name.'
He is a great being of the Dharma-body
who manifests in this world
to propagate the Dharma."
He felt the *Prajñāpāramitā*
was too extensive.
Later, upon seeing the *Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
he regretted his earlier statement.
Pāramitā
means 'reaching the other shore.'
The scripture says:
"There are six kinds of reaching:
First, dāna;
dāna means
giving.
Second, śīla;
śīla means
morality.
Third, kṣānti;
kṣānti means
patience.
Fourth, vīrya;
vīrya means
vigor.
Fifth, dhyāna;
dhyāna means
meditation.
Sixth, prajñā;
prajñā means
wisdom.
Thus, the first five are like the boat,
and prajñā is the helmsman.
The helmsman guides all beyond the stream of characteristics
to ascend to the shore of no-characteristics.
Therefore, it is called pāramitā."
Yīn Yuānyuán had not yet grasped its essence,
so at first he doubted its length;
later, upon investigating its core,
he found its brevity regrettable.
Zhī Dàolín and Yīn Yuānyuán were both at Xiàngwáng's place.
(Jiǎnwén.)
Xiàngwáng said to the two:
"You may try a debate.
However, on the topic of 'Talent and Nature,'
Yuānyuán's defense is nearly as impregnable as
the fortifications of Xiáo and
Hán.
(Xiáo refers to the region of the two ridges;
Hán is Hángǔ Pass.
Both are Qin's strategic strongholds,
fit for a king's residence.
Zuǒ Sī's *Rhapsody on the Capital of Wèi* says:
'Xiáo and Hán are the abode of emperors and kings.')
You must be careful!"
Zhī initially changed his approach, keeping his distance.
After several exchanges,
he unwittingly entered Yīn's profound realm.
Xiàngwáng patted his shoulder and laughed:
"This is naturally his field of mastery;
how can one contend with him!"
Xiè Ān, taking advantage of a gathering of his younger relatives,
È Chēng said:
"It is the childhood name of Xiè Xuán."
Already seen.
"Long ago when I set out,
the willows were swaying softly;
now that I return,
the snow falls thick and fast."
The Duke said:
"Great plans determine fate,
far-reaching strategies are announced in due season."
This is from the "Dàyǎ" poems.
Mǎo Cháng's commentary says:
"Xū means great.
Mó means planning.
Chén means time."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says:
"Yóu means scheme.
Great plans determine fate,
meaning that at the beginning of harmony in the first month,
governance is proclaimed to the states and cities."
He said this line particularly possesses the profound elegance of the refined.
Zhāng Píng was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate and left the capital,
relying on his talent and spirit,
believing he would certainly join the elite of the time.
He wished to visit Administrator Liú,
but his fellow villagers and those recommended together all laughed at him.
Zhāng then went to see Liú.
Liú was washing and attending to affairs,
placed him in a low seat,
only exchanging greetings about the weather,
his mind not engaged.
Zhāng wanted to initiate conversation but found no opening.
After a while, Chief Clerk and other worthies came for pure conversation.
Where host and guests reached an impasse,
Zhāng from his distant low seat adjudicated the matter,
his words concise and meaning profound,
fully satisfying both parties' thoughts,
astonishing everyone present.
Zhēncháng invited him to the upper seat,
and they conversed purely all day,
so he stayed overnight until dawn.
As Zhāng withdrew, Liú said:
"You go ahead for now,
I shall certainly fetch you to go together to see the Military Governor."
Zhāng returned to his boat,
his companions asked where he had stayed?
Zhāng smiled and did not answer.
Shortly after,
Zhēncháng sent a messenger to find Zhāng Xiàolián's boat,
his companions were regretful and astonished.
Then they rode together to see the Military Governor.
Upon reaching the gate,
Liú went ahead and said to the Military Governor:
"This humble official today has obtained for you
an excellent choice for a Court Academician!"
Once brought forward,
the Military Governor conversed with him,
sighed in admiration and praised him, saying:
"Zhāng Píng's profound thoughts are a treasury of principles."
He was immediately appointed Court Academician.
Sòng Míngdì's "Record of Literary Figures" says:
"Píng, styled Zhǎngzōng,
was from Wújùn.
He had spirit and integrity,
praised by his local community.
In learning and pursuits,
he was quick-witted and cultured.
The Grand Administrator recommended him as Filial and Incorrupt for his talent,
he passed the examination with high rank.
Recommended by Tán,
he was appointed Court Academician.
Progressively promoted to Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and then Palace Censor."
Master Tǎ Fǎshī said:
"'Six Penetrations' and
'Three Clarities' converge,
they are merely different names."
"Biography of Master Ān" says:
"Zhú Fǎtài,
his nature broad and simple,
his understanding of the Way profoundly attained,
Master Ān befriended and esteemed him."
One account says Fǎtài was a disciple of Master Ān.
The sūtra says: "The Six Penetrations are
the merits of the Three Vehicles.
First, divine eye penetration,
seeing distant forms;
second, divine ear penetration,
hearing sounds beyond barriers;
third, bodily penetration,
flying, appearing and disappearing;
fourth, penetration of others' minds,
reflecting all thoughts like water in a mirror;
fifth, penetration of past lives,
spiritually knowing the past;
sixth, penetration of the extinction of outflows,
wisdom understanding successive lifetimes.
The Three Clarities are:
liberation in the mind,
illuminating the three periods of time."
Thus, divine eye, divine ear, bodily,
others' minds, and extinction of outflows—these five
are all clarities of the present mind.
Past lives is the clarity of the past mind.
Through divine eye arises wisdom of the future,
which is the clarity of the future mind.
Converging with different names,
the meaning lies herein.
Zhī Dàolín, Xǔ, and Xiè, men of great virtue,
gathered together at Wáng's house.
Xǔ Xún, Xiè Ān, Wáng Méng.
Xiè looked at everyone and said:
"Today can be called a gathering of worthies,
since time cannot be detained,
such gatherings are indeed hard to maintain.
We should converse and recite together,
to express our feelings."
Xǔ then asked the host if he had the "Zhuāngzǐ"?
Only the "Fisherman" chapter was found.
The "Zhuāngzǐ" says:
"Confucius was wandering in the forest of black canopies,
resting seated upon the Apricot Altar.
Confucius played the zither and sang,
before the melody was half finished,
a fisherman came down from his boat,
his beard and eyebrows all white,
hair loose, sleeves waving,
walking up from the plain,
stopping upon reaching the high ground,
left hand on knee,
right hand supporting his chin to listen.
When the song ended, he beckoned Zǐgòng and
Zǐlù, asking:
'Who is that man?'
They said:
'It is Master Kǒng.'
He asked:
'What does Master Kǒng cultivate?'
Zǐgòng said:
'He upholds loyalty and trustworthiness,
practices benevolence and righteousness,
adorns rites and music,
selects among human relationships,
these are what Master Kǒng cultivates.'
He said:
'Is he a ruler with land?'
They said:
'No.'
The fisherman said:
'Benevolent he is indeed,
but I fear he cannot avoid harm to himself.'
Confucius heard and sought to question him,
whereupon he spoke of eight faults and
four evils,
to admonish Confucius."
Xiè looked at the topic,
then had each person present explicate it.
Zhī Dàolín explicated first,
speaking about seven hundred words,
his exposition refined and beautiful,
talent and rhetoric extraordinary,
all praised him.
Then each person present finished expressing their thoughts.
Xiè asked:
"Have you all finished?"
All said: "Today's discussion,
few have not exhausted themselves."
Xiè then roughly challenged them,
and proceeded to expound his own ideas,
speaking over ten thousand words,
his talent's peak elegant and transcendent.
"Record of Calligraphy" says:
"Ān's spirit and demeanor were outstandingly perceptive,
skilled in discussing profound and distant matters."
Since he himself was hard to surpass,
added with his spirited bearing and lofty manner,
serene and self-satisfied,
all present were deeply satisfied.
Zhī said to Xiè:
"You directly rushed to the summit,
thus naturally excellent."
General Yīn, Sūn Ānguó, Wáng, and Xiè—
all worthies skilled in discourse—
were all at Prince of Kuàijī's place.
Yīn and Sūn together discussed
"The Profundity of the Yì's Images Lies in Revealing Form."
Their argument roughly said:
"The sage knew observing vessels is insufficient to comprehend change,
therefore he manifested the circular response through divination stalks and tortoise shells.
The circular response cannot be taken as fixed rules,
therefore he entrusted the wondrous traces to the six lines.
The six lines circulate,
adapting only to transformation,
thus although a single line,
both auspicious and inauspicious are revealed,
missing the one would be an error.
Imitating vessels and entrusting images,
yet fortune and misfortune are jointly manifest,
clinging to vessels would be an error."
Yáng Fú's younger brother married Wáng Yǒngyán's daughter.
Fú's younger brother,
is Fǔ.
The "Genealogy of the Yáng Clan" states:
"Fǔ, styled Yòurén,
was from Tàishān.
His grandfather was Kǎi,
a Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat.
His father was Suí,
a Secretary in the Central Secretariat.
Fǔ served up to the position of Merit Officer in the Guard Army.
He married the daughter of Lángyá's Wáng Nèzhī,
styled Sēngshǒu."
When the Wáng family met the son-in-law,
Fú accompanied his brother there.
At that time, Yǒngyán's father, the Governor of Dōngyáng, was still alive.
The "Genealogy of the Wáng Clan" states:
"Nèzhī, styled Yǒngyán,
was from Lángyá.
His grandfather was Biāozhī,
a Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments.
His father was Línzhī,
Governor of Dōngyáng.
Nèzhī served successively as Left Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief."
Yīn Zhòngkān was the son-in-law of the Governor of Dōngyáng,
and was also present.
The "Genealogy of the Yīn Clan" states:
"Zhòngkān married the daughter of Lángyá's Wáng Línzhī,
styled Yīngyàn."
Fú was exceptionally skilled in philosophical reasoning,
and thus discussed the "Qí Wù" with Zhòngkān.
It is a chapter of the "Zhuāngzǐ."
Yīn challenged him,
and Yáng said:
"After four rounds of debate,
you will come to agree with me."
Yīn laughed and said:
"We can debate to the fullest,
why must we agree?"
Only after four rounds did they reach a consensus.
Yīn sighed and said:
"I have nothing further to differ on."
He praised him as a newly emerged talent for a long time.
Yīn Zhòngkān said:
"If I do not read the 'Dàodé Jīng' for three days,
I feel my tongue stiffen."
The "Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn" states:
"Zhòngkān was thoughtful and logical,
and skilled in pure conversation."
When Típó first arrived,
he lectured on the "Abhidharma" at Dōngtíng's residence.
The "Preface to the Translated Scriptures" states:
"Sengjia Típó,
from Jìbīn,
surname Qiútán.
He was brilliant and insightful,
and when Fú Jiān arrived in Cháng'ān,
he produced various scriptures.
Later, he crossed the river,
and Master Yuǎn requested him to translate the 'Abhidharma.'"
Master Yuǎn's "Preface to the Abhidharma" states:
"The 'Abhidharma Heart'
is the essence of the 'Three Baskets,'
the subtle words for chanting.
Its origins are vast and profound,
encompassing all scriptures,
capturing their essential principles,
hence the author named it 'Heart.'
There was a renunciant scholar named Fǎshèng,
who, because the 'Abhidharma' was vast and profound,
and difficult to fully explore,
extracted this section,
comprising 250 verses in total,
as a concise explanation,
calling it
'Heart.'
The monk Sengjia Típó from Jìbīn,
having studied this text from a young age,
was requested to translate it."
Abhidharma,
in Jìn language, means the Great Dharma.
Master Dàobiāo said:
"Abhidharma,
in Qín language, means the Incomparable Dharma."
When the lecture began,
and only half the audience was seated,
Sēngmí said:
"I already understand it all."
He then divided four interested monks in the audience
and went to another room to lecture himself.
After Típó finished his lecture,
Dōngtíng asked Monk Fǎgāng:
"Fǎgāng,
his clan is unknown. I, your disciple, do not understand it at all,
how could Āmí already understand it?
What did he grasp?"
He replied:
"Broadly speaking, it is all correct,
but there are minor points that are not yet precise."
The "Preface to the Translated Scriptures" states:
"Típó traveled to the capital in the early years of Lóng'ān,
and Marquis Wáng Xún of Dōngjīng welcomed him to his residence to lecture on the 'Abhidharma.'
Típó's doctrinal principles were clear,
and he elucidated the profound meanings,
Wáng Sēngmí understood after one hearing and lectured himself,
such was his clarity in explaining principles and inspiring others.
The year of his death is unknown."
Marquis Huán of Nánjùn and Governor Yīn of Jīngzhōu often debated together,
frequently challenging each other.
After over a year,
they only debated once or twice.
Huán sighed that his talent and thinking were declining.
Yīn said:
"This is because you have come to a deeper understanding."
Zhōu Zhī's "Records of Lóng'ān" states:
"Xuán was skilled in discussing principles,
he abandoned his commandery and returned to his fief,
often engaging in continuous discussions with Governor Yīn Zhòngkān of Jīngzhōu all day."
Emperor Wén once ordered the Prince of Dōng'ā to compose a poem within seven steps,
or face severe punishment.
He immediately responded with a poem:
"Boil beans to make a soup,
filter the beans to extract the juice.
The beanstalks burn beneath the pot,
the beans weep within the pot.
Born from the same root,
why such urgent torment?"
The Emperor was deeply ashamed.
The "Records of Wèi" states:
"Prince Sī of Chén, Cáo Zhí, styled Zǐjiàn,
was the younger brother of Emperor Wén by the same mother.
At over ten years old, he could recite poetry and discourses
as well as tens of thousands of words of rhapsodies and fu.
He excelled in writing,
and Tàizǔ once looked at his writings and said:
'Did you have someone ghostwrite for you?'
Zhí knelt and said:
'I speak to debate,
I write to compose,
you can test me face to face,
why would I need a ghostwriter?'
At that time, the newly built Tóngquè Terrace in Yè was completed,
Tàizǔ took all his sons to ascend it,
and ordered each to compose a fu.
Zhí took up his brush and completed it instantly,
which was admirable.
He was simple and unassuming by nature,
not concerned with dignity and demeanor,
his carriages, horses, and clothing
were not extravagant.
Whenever faced with difficult questions,
he responded immediately,
and Tàizǔ favored him greatly,
nearly making him crown prince several times.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Juànchéng,
later moved to Yōngqiū,
and again enfeoffed as Prince of Dōng'ā.
Zhí often sought opportunities to prove himself but was denied,
and his fief was frequently relocated,
leaving him anxious and joyless.
He died at the age of forty-one."
The Wèi court enfeoffed Prince Wén of Jìn as a Duke,
bestowing upon him the nine bestowals with full ceremony,
but Prince Wén firmly declined to accept.
The high officials and generals were to go to his residence to urge him.
Minister of Works Zhèng Chōng (Chōng has been mentioned before)
sent a messenger to Ruǎn Jí to request a composition.
Jí was at Yuán Xiàoní's home at the time.
The "Yuán Clan Chronicles" state:
"Zhǔn, styled Xiàoní,
was from Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His father was Huàn,
a Gentleman of the Palace of Wèi.
Zhǔn was loyal, trustworthy, and upright,
not ashamed to ask those below him,
only fearing that others could not surpass him.
As worldly affairs were often perilous,
he remained modest and did not seek advancement.
He wrote over a hundred thousand words of works."
Xún Chuò's "Records of Yǎnzhōu" states:
"Zhǔn had outstanding talent,
during the Tàishǐ era,
he served as a Palace Attendant."
Still drunk from the previous night, he was helped up,
and wrote the draft,
without any corrections,
then copied it and gave it to the messenger.
People at the time considered it a divine composition.
Gù Kǎizhī's "Records of Jìn Literature" states:
"Ruǎn Jí's 'Exhortation to Advance,'
is lofty and grand in style,
with a gradual and restrained progression in its arguments."
A commentary on Ruǎn Jí's "Exhortation to Accept Advancement" briefly states:
"I have heard that Your Excellency firmly declines,
but Chōng and others are deeply concerned,
and indeed harbor a foolish thought.
We believe that when a sage king establishes institutions,
they set a precedent for a hundred generations;
praising virtue and rewarding merit
has been a practice since ancient times.
The Duke of Zhōu relied on an already accomplished foundation,
and occupied a secure position,
illuminating Qūfù,
and possessing the lands of Guīméng.
Your Excellency should follow the sacred decree,
and accept this great blessing."
When Zuǒ Tàichōng first completed his "Rhapsody on the Three Capitals,"
the "Biography of Sī" states:
"Sī, styled Tàichōng,
was a native of Línzī in the state of Qí.
His father, Yōng, rose from clerical work,
was well-versed in many affairs,
and served as Palace Censor.
Sī lost his mother early,
and Yōng, pitying him,
did not strictly teach him reading and writing.
When he grew up,
he extensively read famous writings,
and perused the works of the hundred schools.
Minister of Works Zhāng Huá appointed him as Libationer,
and Jiǎ Mì recommended him as a Secretary Gentleman.
After Mì was executed,
he returned to his hometown,
and devoted himself to writing.
Prince of Qí Jiǒng invited him to serve as Record Officer and Army Advisor,
but he did not accept.
At that time, his 'Rhapsody on the Three Capitals' was not yet finished.
Several years later, he died of illness.
His revisions to the 'Rhapsody on the Three Capitals'
continued until his death.
Initially, in his 'Rhapsody on the Shǔ Capital,' he wrote:
'The Golden Horse flashes like lightning on the high ridge,
the Jade Pheasant spreads its wings and parts the clouds.
Ghost bullets fly like pellets, striking with force,
the fire well blazes with radiant light.'
Now there are no ghost bullets,
so his rhapsody often differs.
Sī lacked administrative talent but had literary ability,
and he also took pride in his imperial consort connections,
so the people of Qí did not esteem him."
At the time, people criticized and disparaged each other,
and Sī was dissatisfied.
Later, he showed it to Lord Zhāng.
Zhāng Huá has been mentioned earlier.
Zhāng said:
"This can stand alongside the 'Two Capitals' rhapsodies,
but your work is not yet esteemed in the world;
you should seek the endorsement of a renowned scholar."
Sī then sought out Huángfǔ Mì.
Wáng Yǐn's "History of Jìn" states:
"Mì, styled Shì'ān,
was a native of Zhāonà in Āndìng,
and the great-great-grandson of Hàn Grand Commandant Sōng.
His grandfather, Shūxiàn,
served as Magistrate of Bàlíng.
His father, Shūhóu,
was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt.
Mì's clan members were wealthy and noble for generations,
but he alone remained in humble circumstances.
His foster aunt sighed and said:
'In the past, Mèng's mother moved three times to educate her son,
and Zēng's father taught by cooking a pig.
Is it because I did not choose my neighbors wisely
that you are so dull?
Cultivating oneself and studying diligently—
these you must achieve on your own;
what have I to do with it?'
She then wept before him,
and Mì was deeply moved.
At over twenty years old,
he studied under Xí Tǎn in his hometown,
asking everyone he met questions,
with few peaceful days.
Emperor Wǔ lent him two cartloads of books,
and he thus read extensively.
He was summoned as a Palace Attendant
and Consultant Gentleman,
but he declined both,
and died at home."
Mì saw it and sighed in admiration,
then wrote a "Preface" for it.
Thereafter, those who had previously criticized or opposed it
all respectfully praised and discussed it.
The "Biography of Sī" states:
"Sī visited Zhāng Zǎi,
inquiring about matters of Mín and Shǔ,
but their interaction was also brief.
Huángfǔ Mì was a lofty scholar of the Western Region,
and Zhì Zhòngzhì was a renowned veteran Confucian—
neither were Sī's peers.
Liú Yuānlín and Wèi Bóyú both died early,
and neither wrote prefaces or annotations for Sī's rhapsody.
All the annotations were done by Sī himself;
he wanted to enhance the prestige of his work,
so he borrowed the names of contemporary figures."
Liú Líng wrote "In Praise of the Virtue of Wine,"
expressing his sentiments and aspirations.
The "Biographies of Famous Scholars" states:
"Líng, styled Bólún,
was a native of Pèi Commandery.
He indulged in unrestrained freedom,
considering the universe too narrow.
He often rode in a deer-drawn cart,
carrying a jug of wine,
with someone following him carrying a shovel,
saying:
'When I die, just dig a hole and bury me.'
His body was like earth and wood,
as he roamed carefree through life."
The "Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove" states:
"Líng existed between heaven and earth,
drifting aimlessly,
with no particular concerns.
Once, he offended a vulgar scholar,
who rolled up his sleeves and rose,
intent on beating him.
Líng calmly replied:
'My chicken ribs are hardly worthy of your esteemed fist!'
The man, disarmed, withdrew.
He never paid attention to writing,
and throughout his life,
he only composed one piece,
'In Praise of the Virtue of Wine.'
Its text reads:
'There is a Great Man, a Master,
who regards heaven and earth as a single morning,
ten thousand years as a fleeting moment,
the sun and moon as his windows,
and the eight directions as his courtyard and roads.
He leaves no wheel tracks when traveling,
dwells in no house or hut,
with the sky as his canopy and the earth as his mat,
going wherever his heart desires.
When walking, he holds a goblet and a ladle;
when moving, he carries a flask and a jug,
concerned only with wine,
what does he know of other things?
There are
noble young lords,
gentlemen and recluses,
who hear of my ways,
and debate their merits.
They roll up their sleeves and pull at their collars,
glaring with anger and gnashing their teeth,
expounding on ritual and law,
with arguments flying like spear points.
The Master then
holds a jar to catch the dregs,
sips from his cup and savors the wine,
strokes his beard and sits with legs sprawled,
resting on the lees and leaning on the dregs.
Without thought or worry,
his joy is boundless.
He becomes dazed and drunk,
then suddenly awakens,
hearing no thunderclaps when listening quietly,
seeing no Mount Tài when gazing intently,
feeling neither cold nor heat on his skin,
nor stirred by desires for gain.
Looking down at the bustling myriad things,
they seem like duckweed floating on the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
Two proud men stand by his side,
like parasitic wasps with their host caterpillars.'"
Minister Yuè was skilled in pure conversation,
but not adept at writing.
When he was about to decline the post of Governor of Hénán,
he asked Pān Yuè to draft the memorial for him.
"The Autumn Annals of Jìn" states:
"Yuè, styled Ānrén,
was a native of Xíngyáng.
From an early age, he gained fame for his talent and intelligence.
He excelled at composing prose,
his style pure and exquisite, unmatched in his time—
even Cài Yōng could not surpass him.
He rose to the position of Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates,
but was later killed by Sūn Xiù."
Pān said:
"I can write it,
but I must grasp your intent."
Yuè explained his reasons for declining,
outlining about two hundred words.
Pān directly reorganized and refined them,
and produced a renowned piece.
People at the time all said:
"If Yuè had not borrowed Pān's literary skill,
and Pān had not adopted Yuè's ideas,
this work could never have been accomplished."
Xiàhóu Zhàn completed his composition of the "Zhōu Shī" (Zhou Poems).
The "Wénshì Zhuàn" (Biographies of Literary Figures) states:
"Zhàn, styled Xiàoruò,
was from the state of Qiáo.
He was the great-grandson of Xiàhóu Yuān, General Who Conquers the West of the Wei dynasty.
He possessed outstanding talent,
his writings were cleverly conceived,
he excelled at supplementing elegant lyrics,
and his reputation was second only to Pān Yuè.
He served as Vice Director of the Secretariat."
Zhàn's collected works contain his "Preface," which states:
"The 'Zhōu Shī'
refers to the six poems: 'Nángāi,'
'Báihuá,'
'Huáshǔ,'
'Yóugēng,'
'Chóngqiū,'
and 'Yóuyí.'
Their meanings existed, but their texts were lost.
Zhàn continued what was lost,
hence they are called the 'Zhōu Shī.'"
He showed it to Pān Ānrén.
Ānrén said:
"These are not merely gentle and elegant;
they further reveal the nature of filial piety and fraternal duty."
The poem says:
"Since being earnest in this devotion,
I look up and speak of the great grace.
At night I settle, at dawn I inquire,
serving at court morning and dusk.
At midnight I announce my retirement,
by cockcrow I am at the gate.
Diligent and respectful in instruction,
day and night I am earnest."
Pān, because of this, then composed his "Jiāfēng Shī" (Family Tradition Poem).
Yuè's "Jiāfēng Shī" records the virtues of his ancestors and his own admonitions.
Sūn Zǐjīng, after removing his mourning garments for his wife,
composed a poem and showed it to Wáng Wǔzǐ.
Sūn Chǔ's collected works state:
"The wife was from the Húwú clan."
His poem says:
"Time advances without pause,
sun and moon flow like a current.
Her spirit, bright, has ascended afar,
suddenly a full cycle has passed.
The rites prescribe an order,
I announce removal at the spirit mound.
Facing the shrine, feeling the pain,
my heart feels as if wrung."
Wáng said:
"I cannot tell whether the writing is born of the feeling,
or the feeling is born of the writing.
One version reads:
'Writing is born of feeling,
feeling is born of writing.'
Reading it is sorrowful,
increasing the weight of the marital bond."
Tàishū Guǎng was very eloquent,
while Zhì Zhòngzhì excelled at writing,
both served as high ministers.
Whenever they were at public gatherings,
Guǎng would talk,
and Zhòngzhì could not respond.
Retiring, he would write to challenge Guǎng,
and Guǎng in turn could not reply.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Guǎng, styled Jìsī,
was from Dōngpíng.
He was appointed as Grand Tutor to the Prince of Chéngdū.
When ordered to go to Luòyáng,
as many of Guǎng's sons and grandsons were in Luòyáng,
he feared harm would come to them,
and so took his own life.
Zhì Yú, styled Zhòngzhì,
was from Cháng'ān, Jīngzhào.
His grandfather, Mào,
was a Xiùcái (Distinguished Scholar).
His father, Mó,
was Minister of the Imperial Stud.
Yú loved learning from youth,
studied under Huángfǔ Mì,
excelled at collating and refining literary meanings,
and authored many works.
He served as Director of the Palace Library,
and Minister of Ceremonies.
he then became displaced between Hù
and Dù.
He had a fondness for antiquity,
but his books and writings were all lost.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
during the great famine in Luòyáng,
he starved to death.
Yú and Guǎng had roughly equal fame and rank.
Guǎng excelled in oral skill,
Yú excelled in writing skill,
both were somewhat lacking in administrative affairs.
In gatherings, when Guǎng talked,
Yú could not respond;
when Yú retired and wrote to challenge Guǎng,
Guǎng could not reply.
Thus they ridiculed each other,
and this became widely known.
Guǎng left nothing notable to record,
while Yú produced many writings;
in this, Yú was superior."
In the region east of the Yangtze, Minister of Ceremonies Yīn and his son
were both able to discuss principles,
yet there was also a difference in eloquence and reticence between them.
The Governor of Yángzhōu (Yīn Hào) was extremely sharp in debate,
and the Minister of Ceremonies (Yīn Róng) would often say:
"Think further on my argument."
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Yīn Róng, styled Hóngyuǎn,
was from Chénjùn commandery.
Huán Yí had a discerning eye for judging character,
and upon meeting Róng, greatly admired and praised him.
He wrote 'Xiàng Bù Jìn Yì' (The Image Does Not Exhaust the Meaning)
and 'Dàxián Xū Yì Lùn' (On the Great Worthy Needing the Changes),
their principles and meanings subtle and profound,
praised by those who discussed them.
His elder brother's son, Hào, was also skilled in pure conversation.
Whenever he debated with Hào,
he was sometimes bested,
but retiring to write treatises,
Róng was again superior.
He served as Assistant to the Left of the Minister of Education.
He enjoyed drinking and was good at dancing,
whistling and chanting poetry all day long,
never burdening himself with worldly affairs.
He rose through the ranks to become Minister of Personnel and Minister of Ceremonies,
and died in office."
Yǔ Zǐsōng completed his composition of the "Yì Fù" (Rhapsody on Meaning).
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"Yǐ was killed by Shí Lè during the Yǒngjiā period.
Previously, Yǐ, seeing the many troubles of the royal house,
knew he would eventually be caught up in the disaster,
so he composed the 'Yì Fù' to express his feelings."
His nephew Wénkāng saw it and asked:
"If it has meaning,
then a rhapsody cannot exhaust it;
if it has no meaning,
then what is there to compose a rhapsody about?"
He replied:
"It lies precisely between having meaning and having no meaning."
Guō Jǐngchún's poem says:
"In the woods, no tree is still;
in the rivers, no water stops flowing."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Guō Pú, styled Jǐngchún,
was from Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
His father, Yuàn,
was Governor of Jiànpíng."
The "Bié Zhuàn of Pú" states:
"Pú was extraordinarily learned and broadly knowledgeable,
his literary style brilliant and beautiful,
his talent and learning admirable and ample,
fully ranking among the upper class.
His poems, rhapsodies, elegies, and eulogies
were all transmitted in the world, yet he was reticent in speech.
His casual recitations and utterances
were no different from ordinary people's.
Moreover, he did not uphold formal decorum;
his appearance and substance were slovenly and dissipated,
indulging his passions and being lazy and disrespectful,
often guilty of the faults of drunkenness and gluttony.
His friend Gān Lìngshēng admonished him:
'These are axes that hack away at one's nature.'
Pú said:
'What I have received is allotted;
I constantly fear I will not use it all up—
how can wine and women harm me!'
Wáng Dūn appointed him as an Army Advisor.
When Dūn mobilized troops in the capital region,
he consulted Pú on major affairs.
Pú spoke exhaustively on success and failure,
not yielding or bending.
Dūn, resentful, had him killed."
The poem is from Pú's "Yōusī Piān" (Chapter on Profound Thoughts).
Ruǎn Fú said:
Liú Xiàobiāo's note: "Ruǎn Fú appears elsewhere."
"Profound and towering, desolate and austere,
it truly cannot be expressed in words.
Whenever I read this piece,
I feel my spirit transcend and my form leap beyond."
Yǔ Chǎn first composed the "Yángdū Fù" (Rhapsody on Yangdu).
Speaking of Wēn and Yǔ, it says:
"Wēn stands as the standard of righteousness,
Yǔ is the hope of the people.
Compared to sound, they are like the chime of metal;
compared in virtue, they are like the brightness of jade."
Minister Yǔ, hearing the rhapsody was completed,
asked to see it and also gave him gifts.
Chǎn then changed "hope" to "brilliance,"
and changed "brightness" to "luster."
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Chǎn, styled Zhòngchū,
was a man of Yǐngchuān,
a clansman of the Grand Commandant Liàng.
He was orphaned young,
and by age nine could already compose writings.
He was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and concurrently held the position of Grand Archivist.
He composed the *Yángdū Fù* (Rhapsody on the Yang Capital),
which was unsurpassed in its time.
He died at age fifty-four."
Sūn Xìnggōng composed the *Yǔ Gōng Lěi* (Dirge for Duke Yǔ).
Yuán Yáng said:
"Seeing this, one feels both tension and relaxation."
At the time, this was considered a famous and discerning comment.
The *Yuánshì Jiāzhuàn* states:
"Qiáo possessed literary talent."
When Yǔ Zhòngchū completed his composition of the *Yángdū Fù*,
he presented it to Yǔ Liàng.
Out of familial affection,
Liàng greatly praised its reputation and value, saying:
"It can rank with the *Èr Jīng* (Two Capitals) as a third,
and with the *Sān Dū* (Three Metropolises) as a fourth."
Thereupon, everyone vied to copy it,
and paper in the capital became expensive because of it.
Grand Tutor Xiè said:
"It should not be so.
This is merely building a house under a house.
In every matter it imitates and learns,
yet cannot avoid being meager and narrow."
Wáng Yǐn's *Discussion of Yáng Xióng's Tàixuán Jīng* states:
"Although the *Xuán Jīng* is subtle,
it is not beneficial.
Therefore, the ancients called it 'building a house under a house'."
Xí Zàochǐ's talent as a historian was extraordinary.
Xuānwǔ held him in very high esteem.
Before he was thirty,
he was already appointed as Assistant to the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Zàochǐ expressed his gratitude in a memorial, also saying:
"Had I not encountered Your Excellency,
I would have remained an old Assistant in Jīngzhōu!"
Later, he went to the capital and met Jiǎnwén.
Upon returning to report,
Xuānwǔ asked him,
"How was seeing the Prince-Chancellor?"
He replied:
"In my whole life, I have never seen such a man!"
From then on, he offended the imperial will,
and was sent out to serve as Governor of Héngyáng Commandery.
His mind and temperament then became disordered.
While ill, he still composed the *Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū*,
its judgments and critiques outstanding and extraordinary.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Zàochǐ was erudite from a young age,
his talent and sensibility elegant and transcendent.
Wēn regarded him as highly exceptional.
Within a year, he was promoted three times from Assistant in the province to Assistant to the Governor.
Later, because he offended the imperial will,
he was demoted to Household Registrar and
Governor of Héngyáng.
While in the commandery, he wrote the *Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū*,
to censure Wēn's covetous ambitions."
The *Zàochǐ Collection* records his argument,
which roughly states:
"Those who calmed the successive generations of strife at the end of the Hàn,
cleared the darkness that shrouded the Nine Regions,
and firmly established the glorious achievements of a thousand years,
were all members of the Sīmǎ clan.
If one considers that Wèi possessed the virtue to replace the kingly house,
then it was insufficient;
if one considers its merit in quelling chaos,
then Sūn
and Liú stood in tripartite division,
and even Gòngwáng
and Qín Shǐhuáng,
are still not listed among the true emperors and kings.
How much less so one who only temporarily controlled the masses of a few provinces?
Moreover, if the Hàn had the legacy connecting it to Zhōu,
then Jìn had no succession to trace from Wèi.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Wú and Chǔ called themselves kings.
If one were to push for those with virtue,
they would necessarily connect themselves to Zhōu;
one would not push for Wú
and Chǔ.
Furthermore, holding the long reins in the court,
settling both Wú and Shǔ,
this is the merit of unifying the realm."
Sūn Xìnggōng said:
"The *Sān Dū* and *Èr Jīng*
are the鼓吹 (musical accompaniment) of the *Five Classics*."
Meaning these five rhapsodies are the wings and feathers of the classics.
Grand Tutor Xiè asked his Registrar, Lù Tuì,
The *Lùshì Pǔ* states:
"Tuì, styled Límín,
was a man of Wú Commandery.
His great-great-grandfather was Kǎi,
Chancellor of Wú.
His grandfather was Yǎng,
a Director in the Ministry of Personnel.
His father was Yī,
a Registrar in the province.
Tuì served up to the post of Imperial Household Grand Master."
"Why did Zhāng Píng compose a dirge for his mother,
but not one for his father?"
Tuì replied:
"It must be because a husband's virtue
is manifested in his actions and conduct;
whereas a woman's virtue
is not revealed without a dirge."
The *Lùshì Pǔ* states:
"Tuì
was Píng's son-in-law."
Wáng Jìngrén, at age thirteen,
composed the *Discourse on the Worthy Man*.
The Chief Administrator sent it to show Zhēncháng.
Zhēncháng replied:
"Seeing the discourse Jìngrén composed,
one can see it is sufficient to partake in subtle discourse."
The *Xiū Collection* records his discourse as follows:
"Someone asked:
'The *Yì* speaks of the worthy man,
"Yellow lower garment, supremely auspicious."
If one is unable to silently accord with principle,
how can one not seek penetration?
Seeking penetration involves loss,
and if there is loss, then will the designation "supremely auspicious" be an empty phrase?'
The reply was:
'The worthy man, truly unable to silently accord with principle,
should be content to follow others.
Compared to the exhaustion of principle,
it is like a single hair supporting a beam,
a single hair supporting a beam.
Although there is loss regarding principle,
it is insufficient to bend the beam.
The worthy man has the utmost paucity of emotion,
the hair has the utmost smallness of form.
If the hair does not reach the point of bending the beam,
what loss is there for the worthy man?'"
Sūn Xìnggōng said:
"Pān's writings blaze like brocade being unfurled,
with no part not excellent;"
The *Xù Wénzhāng Zhì* states:
"Yuè's writings selected words and composed chapters,
pure and beautiful beyond compare."
"Lù's writings are like sifting sand to select gold,
where one often finds treasure."
The *Wénzhāng Zhuàn* states:
"Jī was skilled at composing writings.
When Minister of Works Zhāng Huá saw his literary works,
he praised each piece as excellent,
yet still criticized his writing as being overly polished.
He said to him:
'For others in writing,
the worry is lack of talent;
for you in writing,
the worry is rather too much talent.'"
Jiǎnwén praised Attendant Xǔ, saying:
"Xuándù's pentasyllabic poetry
can be said to be rarely unmatched by his contemporaries."
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Xún possessed literary talent and grace,
and was skilled at composing writings.
From the various worthies Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, Wáng Bāo, and Yáng Xióng onward,
the age esteemed rhapsodies and eulogies,
all modeling their style on the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry) and *Sāo* (Songs of the South),
while broadly synthesizing the words of the Hundred Schools.
By the time of Jiàn'ān,
poetry flourished greatly.
Reaching the end of the Western Court,
figures like Pān and Lù, although sometimes their substance and ornamentation varied,
their fundamental allegiance did not differ.
During the Zhèngshǐ era,
Wáng Bì and Hé Yàn favored the mystically superior discourse of *Zhuāng* and *Lǎo*,
and the age then esteemed it.
After crossing the river, Buddhist principles became especially prominent.
Therefore, Guō Pǔ's pentasyllabic poems
began to blend Daoist sayings and give them rhyme.
Xún and Tàiyuán's Sūn Chuò successively honored and followed this,
and further added the terminology of the Three Ages (past, present, future),
and the style of the *Shī* and *Sāo* was exhausted.
Xún and Chuò together became the literary leaders of their time,
and from then on, all writers modeled themselves on them.
By the Yìxī era,
Xiè Hùn began to change it."
Sūn Xīnggōng, having completed his "Rhapsody on Tiāntāi,"
showed it to Fàn Róngqī.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Fàn Qǐ, styled Róngqī,
was from Shènyáng.
His father, Jiān,
served as Protector of the Army.
Qǐ became renowned in his time for his talent and integrity,
and his official career reached the post of Gentleman of the Yellow Gate."
[Sūn] said:
"Try throwing it on the ground,
and it should make a sound like metal or stone."
Fàn said:
"I fear the metal and stone of your piece
may not be in tune with the pentatonic scale!"
Yet, whenever he came to an excellent line,
such as "Red walls of rosy clouds rise to mark the heights,
The waterfall flies down to bound the path."

Yuán Hǔ was poor in his youth.
Hǔ was the childhood name of Yuán Hóng.
He once worked for others, hiring himself out to transport rent grain.
Xiè Zhènxī was traveling by boat.
That night, with a clear breeze and bright moon,
he heard from a merchant's boat among the river islets the sound of someone reciting poetry,
which was full of charming sentiment.
The pentasyllabic verse being recited
was also something he had never heard before,
and he could not stop sighing in admiration.
He immediately sent someone to discreetly inquire,
and it turned out to be Yuán himself reciting his own composition, the "Poems on History."
Because of this, he invited him over,
and greatly appreciated and befriended him.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:

He was orphaned young and poor,
and made his living transporting rent grain.
Zhènxī Xiè Shàng,
who was stationed at Niúzhǔ at the time,
taking advantage of the fine autumn breeze and moonlight,
casually went with his attendants in plain clothes for a boat ride on the river.
He happened upon Hǔ reciting poetry in a rent transport boat.
His voice was both clear and harmonious,
and the diction was also ornate and outstanding.
Shàng had never heard anything like it,
so he stopped to listen,
and then sent someone to inquire.
The reply was:
'It is the son of the Governor of Línrǔ, Yuán, reciting poetry,
namely his composition "On History."'
Shàng admired his forthrightness and exceptional charm,
and immediately sent an invitation to welcome him.
They conversed until dawn.
From then on, his reputation grew daily."

When the time came,
he sent off his wife.
Tens of thousands of people wept, wailed, and pursued her.
After traveling several tens of lǐ,
Guō Huái then ordered his attendants to pursue and bring his wife back.
Thereupon, the officials raced forth,
as if rushing to save their own heads.
After she returned,
Guō Huái wrote to Xuānwáng:
"My five sons grieve and yearn,
longing for their mother.
If their mother perishes,
then there will be no five sons.
If the five sons are lost,
then there will also be no Guō Huái."
Xuānwáng then submitted a memorial,
and specially pardoned Guō Huái's wife.
"Tales of the World" states:
"Guō Huái's wife was to be implicated and executed.
An Attendant Censor was sent to arrest her.
Several thousand commanders and Qiāng-Hú tribal leaders kowtowed,
begging Guō Huái to submit a memorial to spare his wife,
but Guō Huái refused.
When his wife set out on the road,
none failed to shed tears.
Everyone wrung their wrists,
wishing to seize and detain her.
Guō Huái's five sons kowtowed until their heads bled, pleading with Guō Huái.
Guō Huái could not bear to watch,
and so ordered her pursued.
Thereupon, several thousand cavalry went to pursue and bring her back.
Guō Huái wrote to inform Sīmǎ Xuānwáng:
'My five sons grieve for their mother,
not sparing themselves.
If they lose their mother,
they are lost.
If the five sons perish,
then I too am lost.
I have now presumptuously had her brought back.
If this is not permissible by law,
I shall accept punishment from the authorities.'
When the letter arrived,
Xuānwáng submitted a memorial and pardoned her."
When Zhūgě Liàng advanced to the banks of the Wei River,
the Guānzhōng region was shaken.
The Records of Shu states:
"Liàng's courtesy name was Kǒngmíng,
a native of Yángdū in Lángyá.
He sojourned in Jīngzhōu,
personally tilled the fields,
and was fond of singing the 'Liángfǔ Yín'.
He was eight chǐ tall,
and often compared himself to Guǎn Zhòng
and Yuè Yì,
but people of the time did not acknowledge this.
Only Cuī Zhōupíng of Bólíng
and Xú Yuánzhí of Yǐngchuān considered it truly so.
When the Former Sovereign was stationed at Xīnyě,
Xú Shù went to see the Former Sovereign and said:
'Zhūgě Kǒngmíng
is a sleeping dragon.
Would you, General, wish to meet him?'
The Former Sovereign said:
'You and he should come together.'
Shù said:
'This man can be visited,
but cannot be summoned against his will.'
The Former Sovereign then went to see Liàng,
and said to Guān Yǔ
and Zhāng Fēi:
'My having Kǒngmíng
is like a fish having water.'
He was promoted successively to Chancellor,
and Governor of Yìzhōu.
He led the masses on a northern campaign,
and died south of the Wei River."
Emperor Míng of Wèi deeply feared that Jìn Xuānwáng would engage in battle,
so he sent Xīn Pí to be Army Marshal.
The Records of Wei states:
"Pí's courtesy name was Zuǒzhì,
a native of Yángdí in Yǐngchuān.
He was promoted successively to Commandant of the Guards."
After Xuānwáng and Liàng faced each other across the Wei River and deployed their forces,
Liàng employed countless schemes of enticement and deception.
Xuānwáng indeed became greatly enraged,
and was about to respond with a massive army.
Liàng sent a spy to observe them,
who returned and said:
"There is an old man,
resolutely holding a yellow battle-axe,
standing at the army gate,
and the army cannot exit."
Liàng said:
"This must be Xīn Zuǒzhì."
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"When Zhūgě Liàng invaded Méi,
occupying the southern plain of the Wei River,
an edict ordered Gāozǔ to resist him.
Liàng was skilled at comforting and commanding his troops,
and his military administration was strict and clear.
Moreover, his army was an expeditionary force far from home,
with difficult and strained grain transport,
making open-field battle advantageous for him.
Whenever the imperial court heard he was advancing,
they wished to subdue him without fighting,
and Gāozǔ also considered this appropriate.
However, commanding a great army to defend against insult from outside,
it was not fitting to reveal a timid and weak appearance from afar, thereby damaging the grand momentum.
Therefore, he fed his horses and sat in armor,
constantly displaying a formidable, devouring presence.
Although Liàng challenged to battle,
he once sent Gāozǔ women's headgear.
The headgear
was women's adornment,
intended to provoke anger,
hoping to gain an advantage like Cáo Jiù's.
The imperial court feared Gāozǔ would be unable to control his indignation and rage,
and since the Commandant of the Guards, Xīn Pí, was an outspoken and upright minister,
the Emperor then sent Pí, bearing the imperial tally, to be Gāozǔ's Army Marshal.
Liàng indeed challenged again,
and Gāozǔ then became fiercely angry,
about to go out and respond.
Pí, bearing the tally, stood at the central gate,
and Gāozǔ then stopped.
The officers and soldiers who saw and heard this became even more courageous and sharp.
Those with insight considered that although a subject commands a multitude of thousands, he submits to the Emperor's envoy;
the grand strategy was profound and far-reaching,
all of this kind."
After Xiàhóu Xuán had been shackled,
the Wèishì Chūnqiū states:
"Xuán's courtesy name was Tàichū,
a native of Qiáoguó,
the son of Xiàhóu Shàng,
and the elder brother of the Grand General's former wife.
His style was lofty and bright,
his discourse broad and fluent.
During the Zhèngshǐ era,
he was Protector of the Army.
After Cáo Shuǎng was executed,
he was summoned to be Chamberlain for Ceremonials.
Knowing inwardly he could not escape,
he did not engage in social affairs,
and did not keep writing brushes or inkstones.
When the Grand Tutor died,
Xǔ Yǔn said to Xuán:
'You need not worry anymore!'
Xuán sighed and said:
'Shìzōng,
why do you not see the situation?
This man was still able to treat me as a young man from a family with longstanding ties;
Zǐyuán
and Zǐshàng will not tolerate me.'
Later, the Palace Secretary Lǐ Fēng despised the Grand General's control of the government,
and thus plotted to replace him with Xuán.
The Grand General heard of the plot,
executed Fēng,
and arrested Xuán, sending him to the Commandant of Justice."
Gān Bǎo's Jìn Jì states:
"Initially,
when Fēng plotted,
he sent word to inform Xuán.
Xuán replied:
'You should deliberate carefully on this,
but do not let it be heard.'
Therefore, he was implicated in the disaster."
At that time, Zhōng Yù was the Commandant of Justice.
Zhōng Huì had not previously been acquainted with Xuán,
and took the opportunity to become familiar with him.
Xuán said:
"Although I am a man condemned to punishment,
I dare not heed your command!"
The Shìyǔ states:
"When Xuán arrived at the Commandant of Justice's office,
he refused to give a statement.
The Commandant of Justice, Zhōng Yù, personally came to interrogate Xuán.
Xuán said with a stern expression:
'What statement should I give?
Am I to be interrogated by a clerk?
You may compose it for me.'
Yù, considering Xuán a famous scholar
of unyielding integrity,
and as the case needed to be concluded,
composed a statement at night,
making it consistent with the facts.
He tearfully showed it to Xuán.
Xuán looked at it and said:
'Should it not be like this?'
Zhōng Huì was younger than Xuán,
and Xuán did not associate with him.
That day, at Yù's seat, Huì became familiar with Xuán.
Xuán said with a stern expression:
'Lord Zhōng,
how can you be like this!'"
The Míngshì Zhuàn states:
"Initially,
because Zhōng Yù's aspirations and interests differed,
Xuán did not associate with him.
When Xuán was arrested,
Yù was the Commandant of Justice.
He took Xuán's hand and said:
'Tàichū, how did it come to this?'
Xuán said with a stern expression:
'Although I am a man condemned to punishment,
I cannot associate with you.'"
Note: Guō Bān was a man of Western Jìn,
close in time to that era,
and wrote the Jìn Wèi Shìyǔ,
in which events are mostly detailed and verified.
People like Sūn Shèng all adopted it for their writings,
and all say Xuán rebuffed Zhōng Huì.
However, Yuán Hóng's Míngshì Zhuàn appeared last,
not following previous histories,
and considered it to be Zhōng Yù,
which can be called erroneous.
Under interrogation and torture, he initially did not utter a single word.
When facing execution at the Eastern Market,
his countenance did not change.
The Records of Wei states:
"Xuán's capacity and magnanimity were vast and far-reaching.
At the moment of execution,
his countenance did not change,
and his demeanor was as usual."
Xiàhóu Tàichū was on good terms with Chén Běn of Guǎnglíng.
Běn and Xuán were feasting and drinking in front of Běn's mother,
the Shìyǔ states:
"Běn's courtesy name was Xiūyuán,
a native of Dōngyáng in Línhuái."
The Wèi Zhì states:
"Běn,
a native of Dōngyáng in Guǎnglíng.
His father, Jiǎo,
was Minister over the Masses.
Běn served successively as Commandery Administrator,
Commandant of Justice.
Wherever he served, he grasped the essential principles,
focused on the main aspects,
and was able to make his subordinates exert themselves fully.
He possessed the talent for leadership and command.
He did not involve himself in minor matters,
nor did he study laws and statutes,
yet he earned the reputation of a Commandant of Justice.
He was promoted to General Who Guards the North."
Běn's younger brother, Qiān, the Jìn Yángqiū states:
"Qiān's courtesy name was Xiūyuān,
the second son of the Minister over the Masses.
He lacked an upright and outspoken character,
but was witty and full of clever schemes.
He rose to the position of Grand Marshal."
As he returned from his journey,
he went straight in,
reaching the hall's entrance.
Tàichū then rose and said:
"One can associate with equals,
but not mix with those of a different kind."
The Míngshì Zhuàn states:
"Xuán, in his local community, valued seniority,
regardless of virtue or rank;
he would always bow to those older than himself.
While drinking in front of Chén Běn's mother,
Qiān arrived and came out.
This is a case of 'one can associate with equals,
but not mix with those of a different kind.'"
When the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng passed away,
there was clamor both inside and outside the court.
The Wèi Zhì states:
"The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng, personal name Máo,
courtesy name Yànshì,
was the grandson of Emperor Wén,
son of Dōnghǎi Dìng Prince Lín.
He was first enfeoffed as Marquis of Tán County.
The Duke of Gāoguìxiāng was studious and precocious.
When the Prince of Qí was deposed,
the ministers welcomed him,
and he ascended the imperial throne."
The Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū states:
"After the affair of Cáo Fāng,
the men of Wèi reduced and relaxed the palace guards,
no longer wearing armor;
the soldiers at the various gates
were merely old and weak.
Cáo Máo, seeing his authority diminishing day by day,
could not contain his indignation.
He summoned Palace Attendant Wáng Shěn,
Imperial Secretary Wáng Jīng,
and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Wáng Yè, and said to them:
'Sīmǎ Zhāo's intentions
are known even to passersby.
I cannot sit and await deposition and disgrace.
Today, I shall personally lead you out to attack him.'
Wáng Jīng remonstrated, but he would not listen.
Then he took out the written order from his bosom and threw it to the ground, saying:
'The action is decided!
Even if it means death,
what regret would I have?
Moreover, death is not certain!'
Thereupon, he went in to inform the Empress Dowager.
Shěn and Yè ran to report to Zhāo,
and Zhāo made preparations.
Máo then led several hundred servants and retainers,
beating drums and shouting as they went out.
Zhāo's younger brother, Colonel of Garrison Cavalry Zhòu, entered
and encountered Máo at the Eastern Carriage-Stopping Gate.
Máo's attendants shouted at him,
and Zhòu's men fled.
Central Protector Jiǎ Chōng again confronted Máo,
and they fought south of the palace gate.
Máo wielded his sword himself,
and the crowd wanted to retreat.
Gentleman of the Household of the Heir Apparent Chéng Jì asked Chōng:
'The situation is critical!
What should we do?'
Chōng said:
'The Duke has nurtured you all,
precisely for a day like today.
As for today's affair,
there is no need to ask.'
Jì then stepped forward and stabbed Máo,
the blade coming out through his back."
The Wèishì Chūnqiū states:
"The Emperor intended to kill the Grand General.
He issued an edict to the relevant officials to again promote him to the position of Chancellor of State,
and bestow the Nine Distinctions upon him.
The Emperor personally led the Supernumerary Attendant Lǐ Zhāo,
the Attendant Official of the Yellow Gate Jiāo Bó, and others down from the Língyún Terrace at night,
donned armor and distributed weapons,
intending to seize the opportunity
to send out envoys to launch an attack.
However, it rained and they withdrew.
The next day,
he then met with Wáng Jīng and others,
took out a yellow silk edict from his bosom, and said:
'If this can be tolerated,
what cannot?
Now we must decisively carry out this action.'
The Emperor then drew his sword, mounted his carriage,
led the palace guards and servant officials,
beat the war drums,
and went out through the Yúnlóng Gate.
Jiǎ Chōng came in from outside,
the Emperor's troops scattered,
but the Emperor still proclaimed himself the Son of Heaven,
brandishing his sword and striking fiercely,
and none dared to press close.
Chōng urged and encouraged his officers and men.
Cavalry Commander Chéng Cuì
and his younger brother Jì advanced with their spears,
and the Emperor perished in the fray.
At that time, there was a torrential downpour,
with thunder, lightning, and darkness."
Sīmǎ Wénwáng asked Palace Attendant Chén Tài:
The Wèi Zhì states:
"Tài's courtesy name was Xuánbó,
son of Minister of Works Qún."
"How can we pacify this?"
Tài said:
"Only by killing Jiǎ Chōng
to apologize to the world."
Wénwáng said:
"Can we consider something less severe than this?"
He replied:
"I only see what is above this,
I do not see what is below."
Gān Bǎo's Jìn Jì states:
"After the killing of the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng,
Sīmǎ Wénwáng summoned the court officials to discuss the matter.
The Minister of Ceremonies, Chén Tài, did not come.
He sent Tài's maternal uncle, Xún Yǐ, to summon him,
informing him that it was permissible not to attend.
Tài said:
'Those who discuss matters in the world
compare me to my uncle,
but now my uncle is not as good as I am.'
His sons, younger brothers, and relatives both inside and outside all pressured him,
and he entered with tears streaming down his face.
Wénwáng received him in a secluded chamber,
and said to him:
'Xuánbó,
how do you think I should handle this?'
He replied:
'You can execute Jiǎ Chōng to apologize to the world.'
Wénwáng said:
'For my sake, consider the next best option.'
Tài said:
'There is only what is more severe than this,
I do not know what is next best.'
Wénwáng then stopped."
The Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū states:
"When Cáo Máo passed away,
Sīmǎ Zhāo heard of it,
threw himself to the ground, and said:
'What will the world think of me?'
Thereupon, he summoned the hundred officials to discuss the matter.
Zhāo, with tears streaming down, asked Chén Tài:
'How should I position myself?'
Tài said:
'You, Duke, have brilliantly assisted several reigns,
your achievements overshadow the world.
It was said that you would match the ancients in deeds,
leaving a beautiful reputation for later generations.
Yet suddenly there is this affair of killing a sovereign—
is it not a pity!
Quickly behead Jiǎ Chōng,
and you may still be able to clear yourself.'
Zhāo said:
'Gōnglǘ cannot be killed.
Consider another plan.'
Tài said sternly:
'My opinion is that there is only what is more severe than this,
nothing else is worth considering.'
He returned home and committed suicide."
The Wèishì Chūnqiū states:
"Tài urged the Grand General to execute Jiǎ Chōng.
The Grand General said:
'Consider other options.'
Tài said:
'How can you make me speak again afterward?'
He then vomited blood and died."
Hé Qiáo was favored and esteemed by Emperor Wǔ.
The Emperor said to Hé Qiáo:
"The Crown Prince has recently seemed to make further progress.
You should go and see for yourself."
Upon his return, the Emperor asked,
"How was he?"
Hé Qiáo replied:
"The Crown Prince's inherent qualities remain as before."
*The Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"Qiáo, styled Chángyú,
was a man of Xīpíng in Rǔnán.
His father was Hé Yōu,
who served as Grand Master of Ceremonies
and was well-known.
Hé Qiáo was praised from a young age for his dignified composure,
and was deeply appreciated by Jiǎ Chōng,
who often praised him to Shìzǔ (Emperor Wǔ).
He served successively as President of the Imperial Secretariat and
Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince."
Gān Bǎo's *Annals of Jìn* states:
"The Crown Prince possessed the pure and ancient style,
excelling in trust and acceptance.
Palace Attendant-in-ordinary Hé Qiáo spoke to the Emperor several times, saying:
'This late age is full of deceit,
yet the Crown Prince still trusts others.
He is not fit to be the ruler of all under heaven.
I worry that the Crown Prince will not be able to manage Your Majesty's family affairs.
I hope you will reconsider the succession as did King Wén and
King Wǔ.'
The Emperor, valuing the eldest son's right of succession,
and also mindful of the Prince of Qí,
did not accept these factional arguments.
Later, the Emperor said to Hé Qiáo:
'The Crown Prince recently came to court,
and I thought he had somewhat improved.
You may go with Attendant-in-ordinary Xún to speak with him.'
When Xún Yǐ returned after receiving the edict,
he replied to the Emperor:
'The Crown Prince's insight is broad and fresh,
just as Your Majesty's enlightened edict stated.'
The Emperor asked Hé Qiáo,
and Hé Qiáo replied:
'His inherent qualities remain as before.'
The Emperor fell silent."
*The Autumn of Jìn* states:
"Shìzǔ doubted whether Emperor Huì could inherit the great enterprise,
and sent Hé Qiáo
and Xún Xù to observe him.
After meeting him,
Xún Xù praised him, saying:
'The Crown Prince's virtue has grown even more splendid,
different from before.'
Hé Qiáo said:
'The Crown Prince's inherent qualities remain as before.
This is Your Majesty's family affair,
not something your servant can fully comprehend.'
When the world heard of this,
none failed to praise Hé Qiáo for his loyalty,
and wished to reduce Xún Xù to ashes."
Note: Xún Yǐ was pure and refined,
and his nature was not given to flattery.
Comparing the two accounts,
Sūn Shèng's version is the more accurate.
Zhūgě Liàng later entered Jìn,
and was appointed Grand Marshal,
but declined the summons and did not take office.
Because he bore a grudge against the Jìn imperial house,
he often sat with his back to the Luò River.
He had an old acquaintance with Emperor Wǔ,
and the Emperor wished to see him but had no reason,
so he requested Princess Zhūgě to summon Liàng.
After he arrived,
the Emperor went to the Princess's quarters to meet him.
After the formalities were completed,
and they were warmed with wine,
the Emperor said:
"Do you still remember our friendship from our bamboo-horse days?"
Liàng said:
"Your servant cannot swallow charcoal and lacquer his body (to disguise himself for revenge),
and yet today I see Your Majesty's holy countenance again."
Thereupon, tears streamed down his face in a hundred lines.
The Emperor, ashamed and regretful, then departed.
*The Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"After Wú's destruction,
Liàng entered Luòyáng.
Because his father, Zhūgě Dàn, had been killed by Tàizǔ (Sīmǎ Zhāo),
he vowed not to see Shìzǔ (Emperor Wǔ).
Shìzǔ's aunt, the Princess of Lángyá,
was Liàng's elder sister.
The Emperor later took advantage of Liàng being at his sister's place
and went to see him.
Liàng fled into the toilet,
and thereby became famous for his extreme filial piety.
At that time, Jī Kāng had also been executed,
and Kāng's son, Jī Shào, died in the battle of Dàngyīn.
Commentators all said:
'Observing Shào
and Liàng, these two men,
one then understands the Way of Loyalty and Filial Piety,
and how they are distinctly different.'"
Emperor Wǔ said to Hé Qiáo:
"I intend first to bitterly reprimand Wáng Wǔzǐ,
and then enfeoff him."
Hé Qiáo said:
"Wǔzǐ is talented and forthright;
I fear he cannot be forced to submit."
The Emperor then summoned Wáng Wǔzǐ,
harshly reproached him,
and then said:
"Do you know shame or not?"
*The Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"When the Prince of Qí was about to leave for his fief,
Wáng Jì remonstrated and pleaded countless times.
He also repeatedly sent Princess Chángshān and his wife, Princess Chángguǎng, together to kowtow
and beg for him to be retained.
Shìzǔ was very angry
and said to Wáng Róng:
'My brothers are my closest kin.
Now that the Prince of Qí is being sent out,
it is my own family affair.
Yet Zhēn Dé
and Wáng Jì keep sending their wives in here to wail over a living person?
If Jì and others act thus,
what about the rest?'
From then on, Jì was reprimanded
and demoted to Chancellor of the National University."
Wǔzǐ said:
"The ballad of
'A foot of cloth, a peck of grain'
always makes me feel ashamed for Your Majesty!
*The Book of Hàn* states:
'Liǔ Cháng, Prince Lì of Huáinán,
was a younger son of Emperor Gāozǔ.
Having committed a crime,
Emperor Wén exiled him to Shǔ,
where he died without eating.
The people made a song, saying:
"A foot of cloth
can still be sewn;
a peck of grain
can still be hulled.
But two brothers
cannot tolerate each other."'
Zàn's *Commentary* states:
'It means a foot of cloth
can be sewn to make shared clothing;
a peck of rice or grain
can be hulled for shared food.
How much more, with the vastness of the empire,
should they not be able to tolerate each other?'"
Others can cause the estrangement of kin,
but your servant cannot cause kin to become estranged.
For this, I feel ashamed for Your Majesty."
When Dù Yù was appointed to Jīngzhōu,
he halted at Qīlǐ Bridge,
and all the court officials came to bid him farewell.
Wáng Yǐn’s *History of the Jìn* states:
"Yù, styled Yuánkǎi,
was a native of Dùlíng in Jīngzhào.
He was the eleventh-generation descendant of Dù Yánnián, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief of the Hàn.
His grandfather, Dù Jī,
served as Grand Guardian of Wèi.
His father, Dù Shù,
was Governor of Yōuzhōu
and Jīngzhōu.
Yù was profound in wisdom and strategy,
clear-sighted about order and chaos.
He often said that establishing virtue was beyond his reach,
but achieving merit
and establishing words were what he might aspire to.
He rose through the ranks to become Governor of Hénán,
was appointed General Who Guards the South,
Commander of the Military Affairs of Jīngzhōu,
and stationed in Xiāngyáng.
For his merit in pacifying Wú, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dāngyáng.
Yù had no skill in arts or crafts,
did not ride horseback,
and his archery could not pierce armor,
yet whenever major events occurred,
he was always counted among the generals and commanders.
He was posthumously granted the title of General Who Conquers the South,
with honors equivalent to the Three Excellencies."
In his youth, Yù was of low status,
fond of heroic gallantry,
and not approved by others.
Yáng Jì, being from a renowned family,
was so imposing and outstanding that he could not bear it,
and left without taking a seat.
*Tales of the Eight Princes* states:
"Jì, styled Wéntōng,
was a native of Hóngnóng,
and the younger brother of Yáng Jùn.
He had talent and insight,
rose to become Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent,
and was executed along with Jùn."
After a short while,
Hé Chángyú arrived
and asked:
"Where is the Right Guard General Yáng?"
A guest replied:
"He was here earlier,
but left without sitting down."
Chángyú said:
"He must be riding his horse in circles under the Great Summer Gate."
He went to the Great Summer Gate,
and indeed found him reviewing cavalry on a large scale.
Chángyú embraced him and put him into the carriage,
and they rode back together,
sitting as before.
When Dù Yù was appointed General Who Guards the South,
all the court officials came,
and they all sat on connected couches.
*Forest of Conversations* states:
"When a regional commander of the central court returned,
he would not share a seat with Yuánkǎi.
After Yù returned from the campaign against Wú,
he used a single couch,
and did not share it with guests."
At the time, Péi Shūzé was also present.
Yáng Zhìshū arrived later
and said:
"Dù Yuánkǎi actually has guests sitting on connected couches!"
He left without sitting down.
*Praise of the Jìn Nobles* states:
"Yáng Xiù, styled Zhìshū,
was a native of Tàishān.
He was resourceful and capable,
and was on good terms with Shìzǔ since they were the same age.
He said to Shìzǔ:
'When you become wealthy and noble later,
appoint me as Commander and Protector of the Army for ten years each.'
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he rose to Left General
and Special Counselor."
Dù asked Péi to pursue him,
and after Yáng had gone several *lǐ*, he halted his horse.
Soon after, they both returned to Dù’s place.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Xún Xù served as Director of the Central Secretariat.
Yú Yù’s *History of the Jìn* states:
"Xù, styled Gōngzēng,
was a native of Yǐngyīn in Yǐngchuān,
and the great-grandson of Xún Shuǎng, the Minister of Works of the Hàn.
By the age of over ten, he could compose essays.
His maternal grandfather, Zhōng Yáo, said:
'This child will match his great-grandfather.'
He served as Magistrate of Ānyáng,
and the people built a shrine for him while he was still alive.
He rose to become Palace Attendant
and Director of the Central Secretariat."
Hé Qiáo served as Commandant.
According to precedent,
the Director and Commandant had always shared a carriage.
Qiáo was upright and refined by nature,
and often detested Xù’s flattery.
Wáng Yǐn’s *History of the Jìn* states:
"Xù was sycophantic and ingratiating by nature.
He praised the Crown Prince,
and had the Prince of Qí sent away.
Contemporary private discussions held that
he harmed the state and the people,
and was comparable to Sūn and Liú.
If there were good historians in later ages,
they should place him in the *Biographies of Sycophants and Favorites*."
Later, when the official carriage arrived,
Qiáo immediately boarded it,
sat squarely facing forward,
and left no room for Xù.
Xù had to find another carriage,
and only then could he leave.
From this began the practice of providing separate carriages for the Director and Commandant.
Cáo Jiāzhī’s *Annals of the Jìn* (from the *Yǐng Sòng* edition of *A New Account of Tales of the World*, Volume 1, page
7, *Collated Notes on A New Account of Tales of the World*) states:
"The Director and Commandant of the Central Secretariat often rode in the same carriage to court.
When Hé Qiáo became Commandant
and Xún Xù was Director,
Qiáo, being strong-willed and resistant,
took the carriage for himself.
This led to the Director
and Commandant using separate carriages,
which began from this time."
Shān Tāo’s eldest son wore a short cap
and leaned in the carriage.
Emperor Wǔ wished to see him,
but Shān Tāo dared not refuse.
He asked his son,
but the son was unwilling to go.
Contemporary opinion then held that he surpassed Shān Tāo.
*Praise of the Jìn Nobles* states:
"Shān Gāi, styled Bólún,
was the eldest son of Minister Shān Tāo.
He was imposing and had foresight,
and served up to Left Guard General."
Xiàng Xióng served as the Registrar of Hénèi Commandery.
There was an official matter that did not involve Xiàng Xióng,
yet the Grand Administrator Liú Huái became unreasonably furious,
and consequently had him caned and dismissed.
Later, Xiàng Xióng became a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and Liú became a Palace Attendant.
