Initially, they did not speak to each other.
Emperor Wǔ heard of this,
and ordered Xiàng Xióng to restore the proper relationship between ruler and minister.
Xiàng Xióng had no choice,
so he went to see Liú,
bowed twice, and said:
"I have come here having received an imperial edict,
but the bond between ruler and minister is already severed.
What is to be done?"
With that, he immediately left.
Emperor Wǔ heard they were still not reconciled,
and angrily questioned Xiàng Xióng, saying:
"I ordered you to restore the proper relationship between ruler and minister.
Why is it still severed?"
The *Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū* states:
"Xiàng Xióng's courtesy name was Màobó,
and he was from Hénèi."
The *Shìyǔ* states:
"Xiàng Xióng had integrity and moral courage.
He served in office up to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate
and General Who Protects the Army."
Note: Wáng Yǐn and
Sūn Shèng, in their *Discussion on Not Communicating with a Former Ruler*, said:
"In the early years of Jìn,
Xiàng Xióng, the Commandant of Schools in Wēn County, Hénèi,
was delivering sacrificial oxen for imperial use.
He did not first present them to the commandery,
but proceeded directly to send them to Luòyáng.
It happened that the weather was extremely hot,
and many of the oxen sent by the commandery died of heatstroke.
The penalties under the central government's laws were very severe.
The Grand Administrator Wú Fèn summoned Xiàng Xióng to cane him,
but Xiàng Xióng refused to accept the caning,
saying:
'The commandery's oxen would have died anyway;
presenting the oxen would also have resulted in death.'
Fèn was greatly enraged,
threw Xiàng Xióng into prison,
and intended to punish him severely.
It happened that the Director of the Imperial Secretariat appointed Xiàng Xióng as an Assistant in the Capital Officials Section.
After several years,
he became a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate.
Fèn became a Palace Attendant.
They were in the same department,
but avoided and did not see each other.
Emperor Wǔ heard of this,
provided Xiàng Xióng with wine and gifts,
and sent him to Fèn to resolve the matter.
Xiàng Xióng then accepted the edict."
This account, however, does not involve Liú Huái.
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* states:
"Huái's courtesy name was Jūnpíng,
and he was from Zhùqiū in the Principality of Pèi.
From youth, he was praised for his integrity and uprightness.
He rose through the ranks to become Grand Administrator of Hénèi,
Palace Attendant,
Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Minister over the Masses."
Xiàng Xióng said:
"The noble men of antiquity
advanced others according to ritual,
and dismissed others according to ritual.
The noble men of today
advance others as if placing them upon one's knee,
and dismiss others as if pushing them into an abyss.
As for my relationship with Liú of Hénèi,
if I do not become the leader of an armed revolt against him,
that is already most fortunate.
How could the proper relationship between ruler and minister be restored?"
Emperor Wǔ accepted his view.
The *Lǐjì* states:
"Duke Mù asked Zǐsī:
'Is it ancient practice to wear mourning for a former ruler?'
Zǐsī replied:
'The noble men of antiquity
advanced others according to ritual,
and dismissed others according to ritual.
Therefore, there was the ritual of wearing mourning for a former ruler.
The noble men of today
advance others as if placing them upon one's knee,
and dismiss others as if pushing them into an abyss.
If one does not become the leader of an armed revolt against him,
is that not good enough?
What need is there for wearing mourning?'"
Zhèng Xuán commented:
"To be the leader in raising troops to attack,
is therefore called 'róng shǒu' (leader of armed revolt)."
Prince Qí, Jiǒng, served as Grand Marshal and assisted in government.
Yú Yù's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Jiǒng's courtesy name was Jǐngzhì,
and he was the son of Prince Yōu of Qí.
He was intelligent and clever from a young age,
and upon growing up, was modest, restrained, and fond of giving.
When Prince Zhào, Lún, usurped the throne,
Jiǒng raised a righteous army and executed Lún.
He was appointed Grand Marshal,
granted the Nine Bestowments,
and all government decisions were made by him.
However, he indulged in employing petty men,
and ceased attending court audiences.
Consequently, he was executed by Prince Chángshā."
Jī Shào was a Palace Attendant,
and went to Jiǒng to consult on matters.
Jiǒng was hosting a feast for his officials,
and summoned Gé Yú. The *Qí Wáng Guānshǔ Míng* states:
"Yú's courtesy name was Xūyú,
and he was a Gentleman in Attendance of Prince Qí."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"When Prince Qí raised his righteous army,
he was transferred to Chief Clerk.
After defeating Prince Zhào Lún,
he, along with Dǒng Ài and others, monopolized power and authority.
When Jiǒng fell,
he was executed."
Dǒng Ài and others. The *Bā Wáng Gùshì* states:
"Ài's courtesy name was Shūzhì,
and he was from Hóngnóng.
His grandfather, Yù,
was a Palace Attendant of Wèi.
His father, Suí,
was Director of the Palace Library.
Ài, from a young age, was fond of fame and achievement,
and did not cultivate the conduct of a scholar.
When Prince Qí raised his righteous army,
Ài was Magistrate of Xīnjí.
He joined the army,
and was appointed to command the Right Army.
When the Prince was defeated,
he was executed."
They all discussed current affairs.
Yú and others said to Jiǒng:
"Palace Attendant Jī is skilled in string and wind instruments.
Your Highness could have him play them."
They then sent over musical instruments.
Jī Shào declined and would not accept.
Jiǒng said:
"Today we are gathered for enjoyment.
Why do you refuse?"
Jī Shào said:
"Your Highness assists and supports the imperial house,
and should make your actions worthy of emulation.
Although my official rank is low,
my position is that of a regular senior attendant.
Playing string and bamboo instruments
is the business of music officials.
One cannot, wearing the ceremonial robes of the former kings,
engage in the occupation of an entertainer.
Now, compelled by your esteemed command,
I dare not refuse lightly.
I should remove my official cap and robes,
and put on private clothing.
This is my intention."
Yú and the others, feeling discomfited, withdrew.
Lú Zhì, in the presence of the assembled company, as recorded in Shìyǔ, said:
"Zhì, styled Zǐtōng,
was from Fànyáng.
He was the youngest son of Lú Tǐng, a Minister of Works.
He was renowned from a young age.
He began his career as Magistrate of Yè,
and successively served as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Chéngdū,
Commandant of the Guards,
and Gentleman of the Masters of Writing."
He asked Lù Shìhéng:
"What relation are Lù Xùn
and Lù Kàng
to you?"
Kàng has already been mentioned.
The Wúshū states:
"Xùn, styled Bóyán,
was from Wú Commandery,
and his family had for generations been a leading clan.
He first served as Magistrate of Hǎichāng,
and was called a 'Divine Lord'.
He rose to become Chancellor."
Shìhéng replied:
"Just as Lú Yù
and Lú Tǐng are to you."
The Wèizhì states:
"Yù, styled Zǐjiā,
was from Zhuō.
His father, Zhí,
was famous in his time.
He rose to become Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel,
and then Minister of Works.
In selecting officials,
he prioritized character and conduct over eloquence and talent.
He was promoted to Minister of Works.
Tǐng, during the Xiánxī era, served as Grand Administrator of Tàishān.
He was styled Zǐhù,
and his rank reached that of Minister of Works."
Shìlóng's countenance changed.
Yún is treated separately.
Once they had left the room,
he said to his elder brother:
"Why go to such lengths?
Perhaps he genuinely did not know?"
Shìhéng said with a stern expression:
"My father and grandfather's names are known throughout the land;
how could he not know?
How dare that ghost's descendant act like this!"
The Kǒngshì Zhìguài states:
"There was a man named Lú Chōng,
from Fànyáng.
Thirty lǐ west of his home was the tomb of Assistant Minister of the Imperial Clan Cuī.
One day before the winter solstice,
Chōng went hunting west of his home.
He saw a river deer,
raised his bow and shot,
hitting it immediately.
The deer fell but then got up again.
Chōng pursued it,
unaware of how far he had gone.
Suddenly he saw a village gate resembling a government office.
Inside the gate, under a bell, someone announced the arrival of a guest.
Chōng asked:
'What office is this?'
The reply was:
'It is the office of the Assistant Minister of the Imperial Clan.'
Chōng said:
'My clothes are shabby;
how can I see a noble person?'
Immediately someone came with a bundle of new clothes to welcome him.
Chōng put them on, and they fit perfectly.
He then went in to see the Assistant Minister,
and stated his name.
After several rounds of wine and food had been served,
Cuī said:
'I recently received a letter from your esteemed father,
seeking a marriage with my young daughter for you,
hence I have invited you here.'
He then showed the letter to Chōng.
Although Chōng was young when his father died,
he had seen his father's handwriting,
and he sighed deeply, unable to speak.
Cuī then gave orders within,
instructing the young lady to adorn herself,
and had Chōng go to the eastern corridor.
When Chōng arrived,
the lady had already alighted from her carriage.
She stood at the head of the mat,
and they bowed together.
After the three-day ceremony was completed,
he went to see Cuī again.
Cuī said:
'You may return now.
My daughter shows signs of pregnancy.
If she bears a son,
I will return him to you;
if a daughter,
I will keep and raise her myself.'
He ordered the outside attendants to prepare a carriage to send the guest off.
Cuī escorted him to the gate,
grasped his hand, and shed tears.
The feeling of parting
was no different from that among the living.
He also gave him a set of clothes
and a set of bedding.
Chōng then boarded the carriage,
which departed like a flash of lightning.
In a moment, he reached home.
His family saw him,
and amidst joy and sorrow, pressed him with questions.
Learning that Cuī was a deceased person
and that he had entered his tomb,
they felt regret and distress.
Four years later,
on the third day of the third month, while playing by the water,
he suddenly saw an ox-drawn carriage,
now floating, now submerging.
Once it reached the shore,
Chōng went and opened the rear door of the carriage.
He saw the Cuī lady and a three-year-old boy inside together.
Chōng was overjoyed to see them
and wanted to grasp her hand.
The lady raised her hand and pointed to the carriage behind, saying:
'The Assistant Minister wishes to see you.'
He then saw the Assistant Minister,
and Chōng went to greet him.
The lady handed the child to Chōng,
and also gave him a golden bowl.
Upon parting, she also presented him with a poem, which said:
'Brilliant, the substance of the numinous mushroom,
How radiant and luxuriant its splendor!
Its glorious beauty was prominent in its time,
Its wondrous excellence displayed its divine marvel.
Holding its bloom, not yet in full flower,
In midsummer, it met frost and withered.
Its glory and luster long vanished in obscurity,
Its path in the world forever without application.
Not foreseeing the workings of yīn and yáng,
A wise man suddenly came in proper form.
Our meeting was brief, our parting swift,
All due to spirits and deities.
What shall I give to my dear one?
A golden bowl to nourish the child.
Love and grace part from here,
Severance wounds liver and spleen.'
Chōng took the child, the bowl, and the poem,
and suddenly the two carriages were nowhere to be seen.
He brought the child back.
All those present thought it was a ghostly apparition,
and they all spat from a distance,
but its form remained as before.
They asked the child:
'Who is your father?'
The child went straight into Chōng's arms.
The crowd, initially suspicious and repelled,
passed around and examined the poem,
and sighed deeply at the mysterious connection between life and death.
Chōng went to the market to sell the bowl,
setting the price very high
because he did not wish to sell it quickly,
hoping someone who recognized it would appear.
Suddenly an old maidservant
asked Chōng how he obtained the bowl.
She went back and reported to her mistress,
who was the lady's maternal aunt.
She sent someone to look,
and it was indeed the bowl.
She said to Chōng:
'My elder sister,
the daughter of Assistant Minister Cuī,
died before she was married.
Her family grieved for her,
and placed a golden bowl,
inside her coffin.
Now looking at your bowl, it is very similar.
May I hear the whole story of how you obtained it?'
Chōng told her what had happened.
She then went to Chōng's home to fetch the child.
The child had the appearance of the Cuī family,
and also resembled Chōng.
The aunt said:
'My sister's child was born at the end of the third month.
Her father said, "Spring warmth,
means 'wēn' (warm),
may he be blessed and strong."
He was thus named Wēnxiū.
Wēnxiū is probably a hidden reference to the ghostly marriage.
The omen was already apparent beforehand.
The child later became an accomplished man of talent.
He served as a governor of several commanderies,
and in each he achieved merit.
His descendant was Zhí,
who became a Minister of Works of the Hàn.
Zhí's son was Yù,
who became Minister of Works of the Wèi.
Their official caps and carriage canopies have been passed down to the present day.'"
Discussions were held doubting which of the two Lùs was superior.
Xiè Gōng used this incident to settle the matter.
Yáng Chén's nature was extremely upright and resolute.
When Zhào Wáng Sīmǎ Lún became Chancellor of State,
Chén was serving as Senior Clerk to the Grand Tutor.
Lún then issued a placard appointing him to participate in the military affairs of the Chancellor of State.
The envoy arrived suddenly.
Chén deeply feared being implicated in disaster,
and had no time to saddle his horse.
He therefore mounted bareback and fled.
The envoy pursued him.
Chén was skilled at archery.
He shot arrows to the left and right.
The envoy did not dare advance,
and thus he managed to escape.
The *Wénzì Zhì* says:
"Chén's courtesy name was Chánghé.
He also had another name, Táo.
He was from Píngyáng in Tàishān.
His family for generations was a leading clan.
His father was Yóu,
who served as an Assistant in the Chariot and Cavalry.
Chén served successively as Senior Clerk to the Grand Tutor,
Governor of Yángzhōu,
and was promoted to Palace Attendant.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
he encountered the turmoil and was killed,
aged over fifty."
Minister Wáng did not associate with Yǔ Zǐsōng.
(Wáng Yífǔ
and Yǔ Ái.)
Yǔ kept addressing him as 'Qīng' without stopping.
Wáng said:
"You may not act like this."
Yǔ said:
"You address me as 'Jūn',
I address you as 'Qīng'.
I use my own method,
you use your own method."
Ruǎn Xuānzǐ cut down the altar tree.
(Ruǎn Xiū has been seen previously.)
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says:
"Gònggōngshì had a son named Gōulóng,
who became Hòutǔ (Lord of the Earth).
Hòutǔ is the Earth Altar (Shè)."
The *Fēngsú Tōng* says:
"The *Xiàojīng* states:
'Shè means earth.
It is vast and broad, making complete reverence impossible,
so a mound of earth is taken to make the Shè and sacrifices are offered to it to repay its merits.'
However, the Shè originally sacrifices to Gōulóng;
it is not a sacrifice to the earth itself."
Someone stopped him.
Xuānzǐ said:
"If the altar exists and there is a tree,
cutting down the tree means the altar perishes.
If the tree exists and becomes the altar,
cutting down the tree means the altar is moved."
Ruǎn Xuānzǐ discussed whether ghosts and spirits exist.
Some people believe that when a person dies, they become a ghost.
Xuānzǐ alone believed they do not,
saying:
"Those who claim to see ghosts now
say they are wearing the clothes they wore in life.
If when a person dies there is a ghost,
do the clothes also have a ghost?"
The *Lùnhéng* says:
"The world says that when a person dies, they become a ghost.
This is not so.
When a person dies, they do not become a ghost;
they have no consciousness,
and cannot harm people.
If ghosts truly are the essence-spirit of dead people,
people seeing them should see their naked, uncovered forms.
There is no reason to see their belts and garments.
Why?
Clothes have no essence-spirit.
From this perspective,
if the clothes seen resemble a person,
then the physical form also resembles a person.
Resembling a person,
we know it is not the essence-spirit of a dead person.
All ghosts that exist between heaven and earth
are not the essence-spirit of dead people."
After Emperor Yuán ascended the throne,
due to his favor for Empress Zhèng,
he wished to bypass Crown Prince Míng and establish Jiǎnwén.
Opinion at the time all held that:
"Bypassing the elder and establishing the younger
is not only unreasonable in principle,
and moreover, Crown Prince Míng, with his intelligence, brightness, and heroic decisiveness,
is even more suitable to be the heir apparent."
The various dukes, Zhōu and Wáng,
all bitterly and earnestly contended.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Empress Dowager Zhèng's courtesy name was Āchūn.
She was from Xíngyáng.
She was orphaned young.
She first married into the Tián family.
After her husband died,
she relied on her maternal uncle of the Wú family.
At that time, Emperor Zhōngzōng's Empress Yú had already passed away.
When he was about to take a lady of the Wú family,
the Empress was strolling in the rear garden with the Wú family's daughter.
Someone spoke of this to Zhōngzōng.
He took her as a Lady,
and favored her greatly.
She gave birth to Jiǎnwén.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he honored her as Empress Dowager Wénxuān."
Only Diāo Xuánliàng alone wished to support the young heir,
to curry favor with the Emperor's intention.
Emperor Yuán then wished to implement it,
but was concerned the various dukes would not accept the edict.
He therefore first summoned Marquis Zhōu
and the Chancellor in,
then intended to bring out the edict and give it to Diāo.
(Diāo Xié.)
After Zhōu and Wáng entered,
just as they reached the head of the stairs,
the Emperor sent a transmitting edict official ahead to
intercept them and have them go to the eastern wing.
Marquis Zhōu, not yet understanding,
immediately retreated and descended the stairs.
The Chancellor pushed aside the transmitting edict official,
went straight to the front of the imperial couch, and said:
"I do not understand why Your Majesty has summoned your servant."
The Emperor was silent and speechless.
He then took out the yellow paper edict from his bosom, tore it up, and threw it away.
From this, the imperial heir was settled.
Marquis Zhōu then sighed with emotion and regret, saying:
"I often said to myself that I surpassed Màohóng.
Now I finally know I am not his equal!"
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Emperor Yuán considered that neither Crown Prince Míng nor Lángyé Wáng Póu were born of Empress Yú.
He believed Póu had the bearing of great accomplishment,
superior to Crown Prince Míng.
He therefore casually asked Wáng Dǎo:
'Establishing a son is based on virtue, not age.
Now, which of the two sons is more worthy?'
Dǎo said:
'The heir apparent
and Xuānchéng both possess bright and intelligent virtue.
None can be deemed superior or inferior.
Being so,
it should therefore be based on age.'
He then further enfeoffed Póu as Prince of Lángyé."
But this account and the *Shìshuō* differ.
However, Fǎshèng collected anecdotes and典故.
Which should be considered factual?
Moreover, a casual and admonishing remonstrance
is reasonable and perhaps acceptable.
How could it be that with a single statement upon ascending the stairs,
without any extraordinary argument,
he then changed his plan because of it?"
When Chancellor Wáng first arrived in Jiāngzuǒ,
he wished to forge alliances with the Wú people.
He sought a marriage alliance with Commandant Lù.
The latter replied:
"Mounds and hillocks have no pine or cypress;
fragrant and foul herbs do not share the same vessel."
(Dù Yù's *Zuǒzhuàn* commentary says:
"Péilǒu are small mounds.
Pines and cypresses are great trees.
Xūn is fragrant grass.
Yóu is foul-smelling grass.")
"Although Wán lacks talent,
in principle, I will not be the one to start violating proper human relations."
(Wán has been seen previously.)
Zhūgě Huī's eldest daughter was married to the son of Grand Commandant Yǔ Liàng.
The "Biography of Huī" states:
"Huī, styled Dàomíng,
was from Yángdū in Lángyá.
His grandfather, Dàn,
served as Minister of Works.
His father, Liàng,
was also well-known.
Huī was renowned from a young age,
praised as wise and virtuous.
He fled the turmoil to the region south of the Yangtze,
where Emperor Yuán appointed him as Chief Clerk,
and he eventually rose to the position of President of the Imperial Secretariat."
The "Genealogy of the Yǔ Clan" states:
"Yǔ Liàng's son, Huì,
married Huī's daughter,
named Wénbiāo."
Yǔ Huì is mentioned elsewhere.
His second daughter was married to the son of Xúzhōu Governor Yáng Chén.
The "Genealogy of the Yáng Clan" states:
"Yáng Kǎi, styled Dàomào.
His grandfather, Yáo,
served as a Cavalry Officer.
His father, Chén,
served as Palace Attendant.
Kǎi served as a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
He married Zhūgě Huī's second daughter."
Yǔ Liàng's son was killed by Sū Jùn,
and she remarried Jiāng Bīn.
Bīn is mentioned elsewhere.
Huī's son married the daughter of Dèng Yōu.
The "Genealogy of the Zhūgě Clan" states:
"Huī's son, Héng,
styled Jùnwén,
served as the Governor of Yíngyáng.
He married the daughter of Dèng Yōu from Hénán."
At that time, Minister of Personnel Xiè sought to arrange a marriage with his youngest daughter.
Huī then said:
"The Yáng and
Dèng families have intermarried with ours for generations,
the Jiāng family looks up to me,
and the Yǔ family and I respect each other.
I cannot arrange a marriage with Xiè Póu's son."
The "Record of Notable Figures of Yǒngjiā" states:
"Póu, styled Yòurú,
was from Chénjùn.
His father, Héng,
was an Erudite.
Póu served as Palace Attendant,
Minister of Personnel,
and Governor of Wú Commandery."
After Huī's death,
the marriage took place. The "Genealogy of the Xiè Clan" states:
"Póu's son, Shí,
married Huī's youngest daughter,
named Wénxióng.
The "Records of the Restoration" states:
"Shí, styled Shínú,
served as President of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was insatiably greedy,
earning the ridicule of his contemporaries."
Then, Right General Wáng went to the Xiè family to see the new bride.
She still retained the demeanor passed down from Huī,
dignified and composed in her bearing,
with a radiant and tidy appearance.
Wáng sighed and said:
"When I sent off my daughter, she was just like this!"
Zhōu Shūzhì was appointed as the Governor of Jìnlíng.
Zhōu Hóu
and Zhòngzhì went to bid him farewell.
Shūzhì, because of the impending farewell,
wept uncontrollably.
Zhòngzhì angrily said to him:
"This man is like a woman,
only weeping when parting with others!"
He then left.
Dèng Càn's "Records of Jìn" states:
"Zhōu Mó, styled Shūzhì,
was the second younger brother of Yǐ.
He served as Central Protector of the Army.
Sōng, styled Zhòngzhì,
was Mó's elder brother.
He was cunning, straightforward, and decisive,
often intimidating others with his talent and arrogance.
When Yǐ was killed,
Wáng Dūn sent someone to offer condolences.
Sōng said:
'My deceased brother
was a righteous man of the world,
killed by an unrighteous man of the world.
What condolences are there to offer?'
Dūn deeply resented him.
Nevertheless, he appointed him as an Assistant Officer,
and later had him executed on some pretext."
"The Autumn Annals of Jìn" states:
"Sōng was devoted to Buddhism,
and even at his execution, he recited scriptures."
Zhōu Hóu alone stayed behind,
drinking and conversing with him.
At parting, he shed tears,
patted his back, and said:
'Take good care of yourself, Ānú.'"
Ānú
was Mó's childhood name.
Zhōu Bórén served as Minister of Personnel.
One night in the ministry, he fell critically ill.
At the time, Diāo Xuánliàng was President of the Imperial Secretariat,
and he spared no effort in rescuing him, showing utmost affection and goodwill.
After a long while, Bórén's condition slightly improved.
Yú Yù's "History of Jìn" states:
"Diāo Xié, styled Xuánliàng,
was from Ráo'ān in Bóhǎi.
He loved learning from a young age,
though not deeply studied,
he was widely knowledgeable.
The institutions of the Restoration
were all established under his guidance.
He rose to the position of President of the Imperial Secretariat,
and was trusted and valued by Emperor Yuán.
He was resented by Wáng Dūn,
who raised an army against him.
Xié fled to the region south of the Yangtze,
where he was defeated and killed."
The next morning,
news was sent to Zhòngzhì,
who hurried over in a fluster.
As soon as he entered the door,
Diāo got up from his seat and wept bitterly before him,
describing Bórén's critical condition from the previous night.
Zhòngzhì slapped him with his hand,
causing Diāo to retreat to the side of the door.
After approaching,
Zhòngzhì did not inquire about the illness at all,
but directly said:
"You, in the central court,
were as famous as Hé Chángyú.
How could you have affection for a flatterer like Diāo Xié?"
He then turned and left.
Wáng Hán served as the Governor of Lújiāng Commandery,
where he was notoriously corrupt and disorderly.
Wáng Dūn shielded his elder brother,
so in front of everyone, he declared:
"My elder brother's governance of the commandery is certainly excellent,
and the people of Lújiāng all praise him!"
At the time, Hé Chōng was Dūn's Chief Clerk,
and he was present.
With a stern expression, he said:
"I am from Lújiāng,
and what I have heard is different from this!"
Dūn fell silent.
Others present felt uneasy,
but Chōng remained calm,
composed and unperturbed.
The "Records of the Restoration" states:
"Wáng Dūn, with his awe-inspiring authority,
gathered talented individuals,
appointing Chōng as his Chief Clerk.
Chōng knew Dūn had rebellious intentions,
and kept a respectful distance.
When Dūn praised Hán for his benevolent governance,
everyone present feared Dūn,
and merely applauded,
but Chōng alone opposed him.
At that moment, everyone present turned pale.
Because of this, he offended Dūn,
and Dūn demoted him to the position of Literary Scholar to the Prince of Dōnghǎi."
Gù Mèngzhù once offered wine to Zhōu Bórén,
but Bórén declined.
Gù then moved to offer wine to a pillar,
and said to the pillar:
"How can you consider yourself a pillar and beam?"
Zhōu was delighted upon hearing this,
and they became close friends.
Xú Guǎng's "Records of Jìn" states:
"Gù Xiǎn, styled Mèngzhù,
was from Wú Commandery,
the nephew of Cavalry General Róng.
He was highly renowned from a young age,
and during the Tàixīng era, he served as a Cavalry Officer.
He died early,
and was deeply mourned at the time."
Emperor Míng was in the Western Hall,
gathering the various lords for a drinking session.
Before becoming heavily intoxicated,
the Emperor asked:
"Now that famous ministers are gathered together,
how do we compare to Yáo and
Shùn?"
At that time, Zhōu Bóren was the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He thus said sternly:
"Although today we share the same ruler,
how can we be equated with the governance of the sages!"
The Emperor was greatly angered,
returned to the inner chambers,
wrote an imperial edict filling a sheet of yellow paper,
and then handed it to the Commandant of Justice, ordering his arrest,
intending to kill him.
According to historical records, Emperor Míng had not yet ascended the throne
when Yǐ had already been killed by Wáng Dūn,
so this account is incorrect.
Several days later,
an edict was issued releasing Zhōu,
and the assembled ministers went to inquire after him.
Zhōu said:
"I recently realized I should not die,
my crime was not sufficient to warrant this."
When the Grand General Wáng was about to march down,
everyone at the time said there was no reason for it.
Bóren said:
"Our current ruler is not Yáo or
Shùn, how can he be without faults?
Moreover, how can a subject raise arms against the court?
Chùzhòng is arrogant, stubborn, and headstrong;
where is Wáng Píngzǐ?"
The "Biography of Yǐ" states:
"When Wáng Dūn campaigned against Liú Wěi,
at that time Wēn Tàizhēn was an Attendant of the Eastern Palace,
and outside the Chénghuá Gate,
he met with Yǐ,
saying:
'The Grand General's actions have their reasons,
they are righteous and not indiscriminate.'
Yǐ said:
'You are young,
and have little experience in affairs.
Has there ever been a subject like this who did not rebel,
or who, after years of mutual support and acclaim, would act in this manner?
Chùzhòng is arrogant and strongly jealous;
where is Píngzǐ?'"
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"When Wáng Chéng was in Jīngzhōu,
bandits arose together,
so he fled to Yùzhāng.
Relying on his established reputation,
he still insulted and bullied Dūn.
Dūn had his brave warrior Lù Róng and others strangle and kill him."
The "Péizǐ" states:
"When Píngzǐ came down from Jīngzhōu,
the Grand General intended to kill him.
Píngzǐ had around twenty attendants,
very robust,
all holding iron shields and horsewhips.
Píngzǐ always carried a jade pillow.
The Grand General then feasted the civil and military officials of Jīngzhōu.
The twenty men ate and drank heavily,
and all became unable to move.
Then he borrowed Píngzǐ's jade pillow,
and had him taken down from the bed.
Píngzǐ grabbed the Grand General's belt, tearing it off,
and struggled fiercely with the strongmen,
finally managing to climb onto the roof,
where after a long while he died."
After Wáng Dūn marched down,
he stationed his ships at Shítóu,
intending to depose Emperor Míng.
Guests filled the seats.
Dūn knew the Emperor was intelligent,
and wanted to depose him on grounds of unfiliality.
Whenever he spoke of the Emperor's unfilial behavior,
he always said it was what Wēn Tàizhēn had reported.
Wēn had once been the Director of the Eastern Palace,
and later became my Adjutant,
so he was very familiar with these matters.
After a short while,
Wēn arrived.
Dūn then put on a stern and imposing demeanor,
and asked Wēn:
"What kind of person is the Crown Prince?"
Wēn said:
"A petty man cannot measure a gentleman."
Dūn's voice and expression turned severe,
wanting to use his authority to force compliance,
so he asked Wēn again:
"Why is the Crown Prince considered excellent?"
Wēn said:
"His depth and far-reaching vision
are likely beyond the measure of shallow understanding.
However, in serving his relatives with propriety,
he can be called filial."
Liú Qiānzhī's "Jìn Jì" states:
"Dūn wanted to depose Emperor Míng,
and said to the crowd:
'The Crown Prince is deficient in his duties as a son;
Adjutant Wēn was formerly in the Eastern Palace and knows all about it.'
After Qiáo spoke forthrightly,
Dūn was angry and ashamed."
After the Grand General Wáng rebelled,
upon reaching Shítóu,
Zhōu Bóren went to see him.
He said to Zhōu:
"Why have you betrayed me?"
Zhōu replied:
"Your Lordship's army has violated what is right;
I, though unworthy, led the imperial forces,
yet the royal army was not victorious.
For this I have failed you."
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"After Wáng Dūn marched down,
the imperial forces were defeated.
Yǐ's Chief Clerk Hǎo Gǔ and the civil and military officials around him urged Yǐ to flee from danger.
Yǐ said:
'I hold the position of a high minister;
with the court in turmoil and collapse,
how can I seek survival in the wilderness
or throw myself to the barbarians?'
He then went with court officials to see Dūn.
Dūn said:
'Recently in battle, did you have strength to spare?'
He replied:
'I regret my strength was insufficient;
how could there have been any to spare?'"
After Sū Jùn reached Shítóu,
the hundred officials fled and scattered.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Jùn, styled Zìgāo,
was from Yè County in Chángguǎng.
In his youth, he had talent and learning,
served as the Registrar of the Commandery,
and was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt.
During the chaos in the Central Plains,
he gathered and assembled three thousand households of displaced people,
built a fortress in his home county,
proclaimed the king's transformative influence,
collected and buried exposed bones.
People far and near were moved by his kindness and righteousness,
and all revered him.
He had merit in campaigning against Wáng Dūn,
was enfeoffed as a Duke,
and promoted to Prefect of Lìyáng.
An officer from Jùn's outer camp reported:
'The drum sounded by itself.'
Jùn personally cut the drum and said:
'In my hometown,
when this happened, it meant an empty city.'
After a while,
an imperial edict summoned Jùn.
Jùn said:
'The court says I am rebelling;
if I rebel, how can I survive?
I would rather look from the mountaintop toward the Court of Justice,
than have the Court of Justice look toward the mountaintop.'
He then rebelled."
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"Jùn led twenty thousand troops,
crossed from Héngjiāng
to Jiǎngshān,
and the royal forces were defeated."
Only the Palace Attendant Zhōng Yǎ remained alone by the Emperor's side.
Someone said to Zhōng:
"Advance when you see an opportunity,
retreat when you know it is difficult—
this is the way of antiquity.
Your nature is upright and honest;
you will certainly not be tolerated by the enemy.
Why not adapt to the circumstances
instead of sitting and awaiting disaster?"
Zhōng said:
"When the state is in chaos and I cannot set it right,
when the ruler is in danger and I cannot save him,
and if each of us retreats and flees to seek escape,
I fear Dǒng Hú will take up his bamboo slips and come forward!"
When Yǔ Gōng was about to depart,
he turned and spoke to Zhōng about the matters that would follow,
deeply entrusting them to him.
Zhōng said:
"If the ridgepole breaks and the rafters collapse,
whose responsibility is it?"
Yǔ said:
"As for today's affairs,
there is no room for further discussion.
You should only expect the effect of restoration!"
Zhōng said:
"I trust that you, sir, will not be ashamed of Xún Línfù."
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* states:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ besieged Zhèng,
and Jìn sent Xún Línfù to lead an army to rescue Zhèng.
He fought with Chǔ at Bì,
and the Jìn army was defeated.
Huánzǐ returned
and requested death.
Duke Píng of Jìn was about to grant it,
but Shì Zhēnzǐ remonstrated and stopped him.
Later, Línfù defeated the Red Dí at Qūliáng,
and rewarded Huánzǐ
with a thousand households of Dí captives,
and also rewarded Shì Bó with the fields of Guāyǎn,
saying:
'I obtained the Dí fields
through your merit.
Without you,
I would have lost Bóshì.'"
During Sū Jùn's time,
Kǒng Qún was in Héngtáng and was pressured by Kuāng Shù.
Chancellor Wáng preserved Shù.
The *Records of Later Worthies of Kuàijī* states:
"Qún, styled Jìngxiū,
was a man of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
His grandfather was Zhú,
Governor of Yùzhāng in Wú.
His father was Yì,
Magistrate of Quánjiāo.
Qún had wisdom and capability,
and served up to Palace Aide to the Censor-in-chief."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Kuāng Shù was Magistrate of Fùlíng,
but fled and lacked virtue.
When Yǔ Liàng summoned Sū Jùn,
Shù urged Jùn to kill Liàng,
and thus rebelled together with Jùn.
Later, he surrendered with Wǎnchéng.
Taking advantage of a gathering where people were jesting,
he had Shù urge Qún to drink,
to dispel the resentment from Héngtáng.
Qún replied:
'My virtue is not that of Confucius,
yet my distress is like that of the men of Kuāng.'
The *Family Sayings* states:
"When Confucius went to Sòng,
Kuāng Jiǎnzǐ surrounded him with armored soldiers.
Zǐlù was enraged,
raised his halberd, and was about to fight.
Confucius stopped him, saying:
'If the *Odes* and *Documents* are not expounded,
and *Rites* and *Music* are not practiced,
that is Qiū's fault.
But if recounting the way of the former kings brings blame,
that is not Qiū's crime.
It is fate!
Sing, and I will join you.'
Zǐlù plucked his sword,
and Confucius joined him.
After three songs ended,
the men of Kuāng removed their armor and dispersed."
Although the warm air of spring spreads,
and eagles transform into doves,
to those with discernment,
their eyes are still detested."
The *Monthly Ordinances* of the *Book of Rites* states:
"In the second month of spring,
eagles transform into doves."
Zhèng Xuán said:
"Doves
are sowers of grain."
The *Xiǎo Zhèng of Xià* states:
"Eagles then become doves.
Eagles
are creatures of killing times;
doves
are not creatures of killing times.
They are good at changing and turning to benevolence,
hence they are recorded."
After Sū Zǐgāo's affair was settled,
the *Spirit Ghost Records: Prophecies and Omens* states:
"At the beginning of Emperor Míng's reign,
there was a prophecy:
'The high mountain collapses,
the stone breaks itself.'
The high mountain
is Jùn.
Shuò is Jùn's younger brother.
Later, when the various lords executed Jùn,
Shuò still occupied Shítóu,
but his forces scattered and he fled,
and was pursued and beheaded."
Wáng, Yǔ, and the other lords wanted to appoint Censor-in-chief Kǒng as Administrator of Dānyáng.
Kǒng Tǎn.
After the chaos and upheaval,
the common people were impoverished and exhausted.
Kǒng said with emotion:
"Previously, when Sùzǔ was on his deathbed,
you gentlemen personally ascended the imperial couch,
and all received his affectionate recognition,
jointly receiving the final edict.
Kǒng Tǎn is distant and lowly,
and was not among those entrusted with the command.
Now that there are difficulties,
you put a minor official like me in the forefront.
I am now like rotten meat on the chopping block,
to be sliced and diced at others' whim!"
Thereupon, he flicked his sleeves and left,
and the lords also stopped.
According to Wáng Yǐn's *History of Jìn*:
"After Sū Jùn's affair was settled,
Táo Kǎn wanted to appoint Tǎn,
and the court appointed him as Governor of Yùzhāng.
Tǎn declined due to his elderly mother and did not go.
The court then considered him for Wú Commandery.
Wú Commandery had many famous clans,
and Tǎn was young,
so he was appointed as Neishi of Wúxīng.
There is no record of him administering the capital."
Chariot and Horse General Kǒng and the Censor-in-chief were traveling together.
The *Separate Biography of Kǒng Yú* states:
"Yú, styled Kàng,
was a man of Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
He was first recruited as Adjutant to Zhōngzōng,
and for his merit in suppressing Huá Yì,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yú Bù Tíng.
When Yú was young, he once obtained a turtle
and released it into the Yú Bù Stream.
Midway, the turtle looked back to the left several times.
Later, when casting his seal,
the turtle looked left,
and even after recasting, it was still so.
The seal master reported this,
and Yú understood,
took it, and wore it.
He rose through the ranks to Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and was posthumously granted the title of Chariot and Horse General."
The Censor-in-chief
was Kǒng Qún.
On the imperial road, they encountered Kuāng Shù,
whose retinue was very numerous.
Shù then went to speak with the Chariot and Horse General.
The Censor-in-chief did not look at him at all,
and said directly:
"Eagles transform into doves,
but all birds still detest their eyes."
Shù was greatly angered
and wanted to kill him with a blade.
The Chariot and Horse General descended from his carriage,
embraced Shù, and said:
"My clansman has gone mad;
please forgive him for my sake!"
Only then was his head preserved.
Méi Yí once did a favor for Duke Táo.
Later, when Méi Yí served as the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng,
a matter arose,
and Prime Minister Wáng dispatched men to arrest him.
Táo Kǎn said:
"The Son of Heaven is young in years,
and all affairs of state issue from the feudal lords.
Since Duke Wáng has been able to have him arrested,
why can Duke Táo not have him released?"
He then sent men to seize him at the river mouth.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" says:
"Yí, styled Zhòngzhēn,
was a man of Xīpíng in Rǔnán.
In his youth, he loved learning and lived in seclusion,
yet sought advancement based on his true merits."
The "Yǒngjiā Liúrén Míng" says:
"Yí
held the position of Army Supervisor.
Yí's younger brother, Táo,
styled Shūzhēn."
Dèng Càn's "Jìn Jì" says:
"Initially,
there were those who slandered Kǎn to Wáng Dūn,
so Dūn replaced Kǎn as Governor of Jīngzhōu with his cousin Yì,
and demoted Kǎn to Guǎngzhōu.
Kǎn's civil and military officers resisted Yì and sought Kǎn's return,
which greatly angered Dūn when he heard.
When Kǎn was about to proceed to Guǎngzhōu,
he passed by Dūn,
who arrayed troops intending to harm Kǎn.
Dūn's Military Consultant Méi Táo remonstrated with Dūn,
who then stopped,
and sent Kǎn off with generous gifts."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" also records the same.
According to the accounts in these two books,
the one who did the favor for Táo was Méi Táo,
not Yí.
When Yí met Duke Táo,
he bowed, but Duke Táo stopped him.
Yí said:
"Can Méi Zhòngzhēn's knees
bend again tomorrow?"
Prime Minister Wáng arranged for female entertainers,
setting out mats and seats.
Duke Cài was present first,
but, displeased, he left,
and Wáng did not detain him either.
The "Biography of Minister Cài" says:
"Mó, styled Dàomíng,
was a man of Kǎochéng in Jìyáng.
He was erudite and discerning,
took refuge south of the Yangtze,
and successively served as Left General of the Palace Guard,
Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Governor of Yángzhōu.
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works."
Hé Cìdào
and Yǔ Jìjiān both served as chief ministers.
The "Jìn Yángqiū" says:
"Yǔ Bīng, styled Jìjiān,
was the younger brother of Grand Commandant Liàng.
From a young age, he was disciplined and principled,
and his elder brother Liàng often held him in high regard,
saying:
'He is the Yàn Píngzhòng of our family.'
He rose successively to General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and Governor of Jiāngzhōu."
When Emperor Chéng first passed away,
at that time the heir had not been decided,
Hé wished to establish the crown prince,
but Yǔ and the court argued that as foreign enemies were strong,
and the crown prince was young,
they instead established Emperor Kāng.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"The Emperor's personal name was Yuè,
styled Shìtóng,
and he was the younger brother of the same mother as Emperor Chéng.
When Emperor Chéng passed away,
he ascended the throne,
at the age of twenty-two."
When Emperor Kāng ascended the throne,
he met with his ministers
and said to Hé:
"On whose proposal is it that I now inherit the great enterprise?"
Hé replied:
"Your Majesty's dragon-flight ascent
is due to the merit of Yǔ Bīng,
not to my efforts.
Had my humble proposal been followed then,
we would not witness this glorious age today."
The "Jìn Yángqiū" says:
"Initially,
when the late Emperor was critically ill,
Yǔ Bīng proposed establishing an elder ruler,
while Hé Chòng argued that the imperial prince should be supported.
Failing to win the argument,
Chòng felt uneasy
and requested an external appointment.
When Bīng went out to garrison Wǔchāng,
Chòng hurried back from the capital
and said to the Emperor:
'Bīng should not have been sent out.
In the past, when Your Majesty ascended the throne,
it was Bīng's merit
that caused the virtue of Jìn to flourish again.
I had no part in it.'"
The Emperor showed a look of shame.
Junior Officer Jiāng was young,
and Prime Minister Wáng called him to play a game of Go together.
Wáng's skill was usually about two stones inferior,
but he wanted to play on equal terms,
to test and observe him.
Jiāng did not immediately make a move.
Wáng said:
"Why aren't you playing?"
Jiāng said:
"I'm afraid it cannot be done."
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Jì" says:
"Jiāng Bīn, styled Sīxuán,
was a man of Chénliú.
He was erudite and well-known,
and also excelled at Go,
being the best of the Restoration era.
He rose successively to Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and General of the Guards."
A guest nearby said:
"This young man's play is not bad."
Wáng slowly raised his head and said:
"This young man is not only superior in Go."
Fàn Wāng's "Qípǐn" says:
"Bīn and Wáng Tián, etc.,
were ranked first class in Go,
while Dǎo was fifth class."
When Kǒng Jūnpíng was critically ill,
Minister Yǔ, as the Inspector of Kuàijī,
went to visit him.
Yǔ Bīng
inquired after him most solicitously,
shedding tears for him.
After Yǔ had stepped down from the bed,
Kǒng said with emotion:
"A great man is about to die,
and instead of asking about methods to secure the state and bring peace to the family,
you engage in the kind of inquiries typical of women and children!"
When Yǔ heard this,
he turned back to apologize,
and requested his words of advice.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" says:
"Tǎn was upright and principled, and enjoyed high esteem."
Grand Marshal Huán visited Governor Liú,
who remained lying down and did not get up.
Huán bent his slingshot and shot at Liú's pillow,
the pellet shattering against the bed matting.
Liú, with a changed expression, rose and said:
"How can a Regional Inspector like you
possibly seek victory through combat?"
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Wēn once served as Governor of Xúzhōu."
The state of Pèi belonged to Xúzhōu,
hence he addressed Wēn as 'Regional Inspector.'
'Combat'
refers to Wēn being a general.
Huán wore a very resentful expression.
Governor Liú,
Zhēncháng.
Previously mentioned.
Later youths
often spoke of Reverend Shēn.
Reverend Shēn said to them:
"Young fledglings,
do not comment on seasoned scholars.
In the past, I associated with the two Emperors Yuán and Míng,
and with Dukes Wáng and Yǔ."
The "Biographies of Lofty Hermits Among Monks" says:
"The two Jìn Emperors Yuán and Míng
devoted their minds to the mysterious and profound,
entrusting their sentiments to the flavor of the Way,
and treated the Dharma Master with the courtesy due a guest and friend.
Dukes Wáng and Yǔ
turned their hearts and inclined their seats toward him,
sharing the same tastes and inclinations."
When Wáng Tǎnzhī was young,
Tǎnzhī,
already mentioned.
Jiāng Bīn served as Vice Director of the Left in charge of personnel selection,
and intended to appoint him as a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel.
Someone informed Wáng.
Wáng said:
"Since crossing the river,
the position of Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel has been filled by men of second rank,
how can you consider me?"
Jiāng heard this and stopped.
According to the "Biography of Wáng Biāozhī" it says:
"Wáng Biāozhī's paternal uncle Dǎo said to Biāozhī:
'The Ministry of Personnel has recommended you as a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel,
are you fortunate enough to serve as an assistant to the princes?'"
This shows that the position of Gentleman,
was considered a humble and low-ranking post.
Wáng Shù was transferred to the position of President of the Ministry of Personnel,
and as soon as the matter was settled, he was to assume the post.
Wéndù said:
"You should still yield to Dù Xǔ."
Lántián said:
"Do you think I am capable of this or not?"
Wéndù said:
"Why wouldn't you be capable!
But yielding is naturally a virtuous act,
and I fear it should not be omitted."
Lántián said with emotion:
"Since you say I am capable,
why should I yield again?
People say you surpass me,
but you certainly do not."
The "Biography of Shù" says:
"Shù often believed that when people conduct themselves in the world,
they should first assess themselves and then act,
and there is no reason for empty yielding,
therefore, when declining, one should firmly hold to principle.
His integrity and uprightness, never overstepping, were all of this kind."
Sūn Xìnggōng composed the "Eulogy for Duke Yǔ,"
the text contained many words of entrustment and sentiment.
The "Collection of Chuò" records the eulogy text as:
"I consult with you, Duke,
our refinement and elegance share the same end.
Measuring and entrusting feelings,
I regard you as a teacher.
The friendship of gentlemen,
is mutual and without selfishness.
Emptying oneself to accept what is right,
speaking sincerely to admonish against wrong.
Though I am indeed not clever,
I respectfully cherish the bowstring and leather.
Forever treasuring your words,
reciting them by mouth, grieving in heart."
After it was completed,
he showed it to Yǔ Dào'ēn.
Yǔ saw it,
and with emotion returned it,
saying:
"My late father and you,
were certainly not like this."
Dào'ēn,
is the childhood name of Yǔ Xī.
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Annals" says:
"Xī,
courtesy name Shūhé,
the third son of Grand Commandant Liàng.
Promoted to the position of General Who Pacifies the Army.
Held the positions of General Who Establishes Might,
and Governor of Wú Commandery."
Chief Clerk Wáng sought the post of Governor of Dōngyáng,
Jiǎnwén.
Later, when Wáng was critically ill,
on his deathbed,
the General of Pacifying the Army sighed sorrowfully and said:
"I will have wronged Zhòngzǔ in this matter,"
and ordered his appointment.
Chief Clerk said:
"People say the Prince of Kuàijī is foolish,
truly foolish."
Wáng Méng,
already mentioned.
Liú Jiǎn served as Adjutant to Huán Xuānwǔ,
later becoming a Military Adviser of the Eastern Bureau,
the "Genealogy of the Liú Clan" says:
"Jiǎn, courtesy name Zhòngyuē,
a man of Nányáng.
Grandfather Qiáo,
Governor of Yù Province.
Father Tǐng,
Governor of Yǐngchuān.
Jiǎn served up to the position of Army Adviser to the Grand Marshal."
He was rather alienated due to his firm and upright nature.
Once, during a briefing,
Jiǎn said nothing at all.
Xuānwǔ asked:
"Why does Military Adviser Liú of the Eastern Bureau not offer his opinion?"
He replied:
"It would not be used anyway."
Xuānwǔ also showed no expression of surprise.
Liú Zhēncháng
and Wáng Zhòngzǔ were traveling together,
and as the day grew late, they had not eaten.
A lowly acquaintance offered them a meal,
with a lavish spread of dishes,
Zhēncháng declined.
Zhòngzǔ said:
"Just to fill our emptiness,
why trouble to decline?"
Zhēncháng said:
"One should not form any connection with lowly persons."
Confucius said:
"Only women and lowly persons are hard to deal with.
If you are familiar with them, they become insolent.
If you keep them at a distance, they resent it."
Prefect Liú's meaning,
likely follows these words.
Wáng Xiūlíng once lived in Dōngshān and was very poor.
Regional Inspector of Sī Province,
already mentioned.
Táo Húnú served as Magistrate of Wúchéng,
Húnú,
is the childhood name of Táo Fàn.
The "Biography of Táo Kǎn" says:
"Fàn, courtesy name Dàozé,
the tenth son of Kǎn.
The most renowned among Kǎn's sons.
Served as President of the Ministry of Personnel,
and Director of the Palace Library."
Hé Fǎshèng considered him the ninth son.
He sent a boatload of rice to give to him,
but Wáng refused to accept it.
He directly replied, saying:
"If Wáng Xiūlíng is hungry,
he will naturally go to Xiè Rénzǔ to ask for food,
and does not need Táo Húnú's rice."
Ruǎn Guānglù, Ruǎn Yù,
already mentioned.
He went to the imperial mausoleum,
arrived in the capital,
but did not visit the residences of Yīn
or Liú,
and after attending to the matter, returned.
The various gentlemen went together to pursue him,
Ruǎn also knew that the fashionable crowd would certainly chase after him,
so he hurried away swiftly,
reaching Fāngshān before they could catch up.
The "History of the Restoration" says:
"Yù was listless all day,
without any deliberate arrangements,
yet people naturally revered him."
Prefect Liú at that time sought to detain him,
and then sighed, saying:
"When I enter, I should moor at Ānshí's bank.
I dare not approach Sīkuàng's side again,
for he can indeed take a staff and beat people,
not easy."
Wáng,
Liú, and Duke Huán went together to Fùzhōu Mountain to view.
After becoming intoxicated with wine,
Liú lifted his foot and placed it on Duke Huán's neck.
Duke Huán could hardly bear it,
and raised his hand to push it away.
After returning,
Chief Clerk Wáng said to Liú:
"How could he impose his physical manner on others?"
The "Biography of Wēn" says:
"Wēn had a bold and unrestrained demeanor."
Duke Huán asked Huán Zǐyě:
"Xiè Ānshí knew that Wànshí would certainly be defeated,
why did he not remonstrate?"
Zǐyě
was the childhood name of Huán Yī.
The *Continued Annals of Jìnyáng* states:
"Yī, styled Shūxià,
was from Zhì in Qiáo Commandery.
His father, Jǐng,
was General of the Protecting Army.
Yī showed talent and skill from a young age,
and was also skilled in music and temperament.
Furthermore, he was perceptive, understanding, frugal, and straightforward,
and was recognized by Wáng Méng
and Liú Tán.
He rose through the ranks to become Inspector of Yù Province,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Right."
Zǐyě replied:
"Surely it was because he was difficult to confront!"
Duke Huán, changing countenance, said:
"Wànshí was a weak, mediocre talent;
what stern demeanor did he have that was difficult to confront?"
Luó Jūnzhāng was once at someone's home,
and the host instructed him to converse with the guests seated there.
He replied:
"I am already acquainted with many;
there is no need to trouble further."
The *Separate Biography of Prefect Luó* states:
"Hán, styled Jūnzhāng,
was from Zǎoyáng in Guìyáng.
He was a descendant of the Xióng surname of Chǔ,
who opened up the territory of the state of Luó,
and thus took it as their clan name.
Later, they settled in the Xiāng region,
hence he was a man of Guìyáng.
Hán was the great-grandson of Yàn, Governor of Línhǎi,
and the youngest son of Suí, Governor of Xíngyáng.
Duke Huán Xuānwǔ recruited him as Assistant Officer.
Finding the official residence noisy and disruptive,
he built a thatched hut on a small islet in the western city pond,
cut wood to make a bed,
wove reeds into a mat,
wore plain clothes and ate simple food,
yet was content and seemed to have more than enough.
Duke Huán once said to the assembled company:
'This man is truly among the refined and outstanding of Jiāngzuǒ;
how could he be limited to just Jīng-Chǔ!'
He rose through the ranks to become Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
Minister of Justice,
and Chancellor of Chángshā.
Upon retiring from office,
he was appointed a Palace Attendant,
and a barrier was erected before his gate.
While Hán was still in his official residence,
a white sparrow came to roost in the hall.
And when he retired and returned home,
orchids and chrysanthemums suddenly sprang up in his courtyard.
Was this not an omen of his utmost virtue?"
Hán Kāngbó was ill,
and leaning on a staff, he strolled in the front courtyard.
Hán Bó
has been mentioned previously.
Seeing that all the Xiè family members were wealthy and noble,
with carriages rumbling and filling the roads,
he sighed and said:
"How is this any different from the time of Wáng Mǎng?"
The *History of the Hàn* states:
"Wáng Mǎng's clan had a total of ten marquises
and five Grand Marshals."
When Wáng Wéndù was Chief Clerk to Duke Huán,
Duke Huán sought a daughter of Wáng's for his son,
and Wáng promised to consult Lántián.
Wáng Tǎnzhī
and Wáng Shù have both been mentioned previously.
After returning,
Lántián, out of affection for Wéndù,
even though he was grown, still held him on his lap.
Wéndù then mentioned that Duke Huán sought his daughter in marriage.
Lántián flew into a rage,
pushed Wéndù off his lap, and said:
"It's detestable!
Wéndù has become foolish again;
he fears Duke Huán's face.
A military man—how could we marry a daughter to him!"
Wéndù went back and reported:
"In my humble household, a marriage arrangement has already been made."
Duke Huán said:
"I understand;
it is simply that your esteemed father is unwilling."
Later, Duke Huán's daughter married Wéndù's son.
The *Genealogy of the Wáng Clan* states:
"Tǎnzhī's son, Kǎi,
married Duke Huán's second daughter,
whose courtesy name was Bózǐ."
The *Records of the Restoration* states:
"Kǎi, styled Màorén,
served successively as Governor of Wú Commandery,
Governor of Dānyáng,
and was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Ceremonies."
When Wáng Zǐjìng was several years old,
he once watched some retainers playing *chūpú*.
Seeing there were wins and losses,
he then said:
" 'The South Wind' is not strong."
The *Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* states:
"When Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
Master Kuàng said:
'It is not harmful.
I repeatedly sang the South Wind.'
'The South Wind' is not strong,
containing many notes of death;
Chǔ will certainly achieve nothing."
Dù Yù states:
"The singer blows the pitch-pipes,
to intone the eight winds.
The sound of 'The South Wind' is faint,
therefore it is said to be not strong."
The retainers, looking down on him for being a child,
then said:
"This young gentleman is also like looking at a leopard through a tube,
occasionally seeing a spot."
Zǐjìng glared and said:
"From afar, I am ashamed before Xún Fèngqiàn;
from near, I am ashamed before Liú Zhēncháng!"
Then he flicked his sleeves and left.
Xún and Liú
have been mentioned previously.
Duke Xiè heard that Yáng Suí was excellent,
and sent word inviting him to come,
but he ultimately refused to visit.
The *Genealogy of the Yáng Clan* states:
"Suí, styled Zhòngyàn,
was from Tàishān.
His father, Kǎi,
was a Gentleman in the Imperial Secretariat.
Suí served up to Vice Director of the Central Secretariat."
Later, Suí became an Erudite of the Grand Academy.
Due to some business, he met Duke Xiè,
and Duke Xiè immediately appointed him as his Registrar.
Wáng Yòujūn and Duke Xiè went to visit Duke Ruǎn,
that is, Ruǎn Sīkuàng.
Upon reaching the gate, he said to Xiè:
"We should certainly both defer to our host."
Xiè said:
"Deferring to others is precisely difficult."
The Governor of Yùzhāng, Gù Shào,
Huán Jì's "Wú Jì" states:
"Shào, styled Xiàozé,
was a man of Wú Commandery.
At twenty-seven, he began his career as Governor of Yùzhāng,
promoting the virtuous to educate the people,
and moral transformation flourished greatly."
He was the son of Gù Yōng.
Shào died in the commandery,
and Yōng was hosting a grand gathering of his subordinates,
playing wéiqí himself.
"Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn" states:
"Yōng, styled Yuántàn,
once studied under Cài Bójiē,
who admired and considered him exceptional,
giving him his own name."
"Wú Zhì" states:
"Yōng was promoted repeatedly to Shàngshū Lìng,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángsuìxiāng,
and upon receiving the marquisate and returning to his residence,
his family did not know of it.
He did not drink alcohol,
and spoke little.
Sūn Quán once said:
'When Marquis Gù is present,
it makes people unhappy.'
He rose to the position of Chéngxiàng."
A messenger arrived from outside,
but there was no letter from his son.
Although his expression did not change,
he understood the reason in his heart.
He dug his nails into his palm,
and blood flowed, staining the mat.
After the guests had dispersed,
he sighed and said:
"I already lack the nobility of Yánlíng,
how could I bear the blame for losing my sight?"
"Lǐjì" states:
"Yánlíng Jìzǐ went to Qí,
and upon his return,
his eldest son had died,
and was buried between Yíng
and Bó.
Confucius said:
'Yánlíng Jìzǐ
is one from Wú well-versed in ritual.'
He went to observe the burial.
The grave was not dug deep enough to reach the springs,
and the burial clothes were of the season.
After the burial, the mound was raised,
covering the pit in width and length,
its height such that one could lean against it.
After raising the mound,
he bared his left arm,
walked around the mound to the right,
and wailed three times,
saying:
'Flesh and bones return to the earth,
such is fate.
As for the soul's energy,
it goes everywhere.'
And then he departed.
Confucius said:
'Yánlíng Jìzǐ's actions regarding ritual,
are they not in accordance!'
Zǐxià lost his son and then lost his sight.
Zēngzǐ went to console him,
saying:
'When a friend loses his sight, one weeps for him.'
Zēngzǐ wept,
and Zǐxià also wept,
saying:
'Heaven!
I am without fault.'
Zēngzǐ angrily said:
'Shāng,
how can you be without fault?
I and you served our Master between the Zhū
and Sì rivers,
and you retired to grow old above the Xīhé,
causing the people of Xīhé
to compare you to our Master—
this is your first fault.
Losing your parent,
you gave the people nothing to hear of—
this is your second fault.
Losing your son,
you lost your sight—
this is your third fault.'
Zǐxià threw down his staff and bowed, saying:
'I was wrong!
I was wrong!'"
Thereupon, he released his emotions and dispersed his grief,
and his countenance remained as usual.
Jī Zhōngsǎn faced execution at the Eastern Market,
his spirit unchanged.
He asked for a qín and played it,
performing the "Guǎnglíng Sǎn".
When the piece ended, he said:
"Yuán Xiàoní once requested to learn this piece,
but I was stingy and did not give it to him.
The 'Guǎnglíng Sǎn' is now extinct!"
"Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"Initially,
Kāng was close with Lǚ Ān of Dōngpíng.
Ān's elder brother Xùn violated Ān's wife, Madame Xú.
Ān wanted to accuse Xùn and divorce his wife,
and consulted Kāng about it.
Kāng advised and restrained him.
Xùn, uneasy within,
secretly accused Ān of striking his mother,
and petitioned to be exiled to the border.
Ān was to be exiled,
and appealed on his own behalf,
his statement implicating Kāng."
"Wénshì Zhuàn" states:
"Lǚ Ān encountered trouble,
and Kāng went to prison to clarify matters for him.
Zhōng Huì argued against Kāng in court,
saying:
'Now the imperial way is open and bright,
all within the four seas follows the wind,
the borders have no deceitful people,
the streets and alleys have no dissenting opinions.
Yet Kāng above does not serve the Son of Heaven,
below does not serve the princes and marquises,
disdains the times and scorns the world,
is of no use to things,
brings no benefit to the present,
and corrupts the customs.
In the past, Tàigōng executed Huáshì,
and Confucius killed Shàozhèng Mǎo,
because they relied on their talents to disrupt groups and confuse the masses.
If we do not execute Kāng now,
there will be no way to purify the Kingly Way.'
Thereupon, they recorded Kāng's case and imprisoned him.
Facing death,
his brothers and relatives all came to bid him farewell.
Kāng's countenance did not change,
and he asked his elder brother:
'Did you bring the qín earlier?'
His brother said:
'I brought it.'
Kāng tuned it,
played the 'Tàipíng Yǐn',
and when the piece was finished,
he sighed and said:
'The "Tàipíng Yǐn" is now extinct!'"
Three thousand Imperial College students submitted a petition,
requesting to take him as their teacher,
but it was not granted.
King Wén also soon regretted it.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"When Kāng was imprisoned,
several thousand Imperial College students petitioned for him.
At that time, many outstanding figures followed Kāng into prison,
but all were persuaded and explained to,
and dispersed at once.
Kāng was ultimately executed along with Ān."
Xiàhóu Tàichū once leaned against a pillar while writing.
At the time, there was heavy rain,
and a thunderbolt struck the pillar he was leaning against,
scorching his clothes,
but his expression did not change,
and he continued writing as before.
The guests and attendants around him
all stumbled and could not stay still.
See Gù Kǎizhī's "Shū Zàn".
"Yǔlín" states:
"Tàichū followed the Wèi Emperor to pay respects at the imperial tombs,
accompanying the ranks beneath the pines and cypresses.
At that time, a violent storm brought thunderbolts,
striking the tree where he stood.
His hat and crown were scorched and damaged,
and those around him, seeing this, all prostrated themselves,
but Tàichū's countenance did not change."
Zāng Róngxù, however, believed it was Zhūgě Dàn."
Wáng Róng, at seven years old,
once went out to play with several children.
They saw a plum tree by the roadside with many fruits bending the branches.
The other children raced to pick them,
but only Róng did not move.
Someone asked him,
and he replied:
"The tree is by the roadside and has many fruits;
these must be bitter plums."
They picked them,
and indeed it was so.
"Míngshì Zhuàn" states:
"Róng from this gained a reputation for divine understanding even in childhood."
Emperor Míng of Wèi had a tiger's claws and teeth removed at the Xuānwǔ Arena,
and allowed the common people to watch.
Wáng Róng was seven years old at the time,
and also went to see.
The tiger seized an opportunity, climbed the railing, and roared;
its voice shook the ground,
and all the spectators were startled and fell over.
Róng remained calm and unmoving,
showing not the slightest sign of fear.
The "Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove" says:
"Emperor Míng, looking down from the pavilion,
sent someone to ask Róng's name and was greatly impressed by him."
Wáng Róng served as Palace Attendant.
Liú Zhào, the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn Commandery, sent him five bolts of fine silk in a tube.
Although Róng did not accept it,
he sent a generous letter in reply.
The "Autumn of Jìn" says:
"The Colonel-Director of Retainers Liú Yì memorialized:
'Liú Zhào, Grand Administrator of Nánjùn Commandery, sent fifty bolts of silk and other sundries to the former Inspector of Yùzhōu, Wáng Róng.
I request that he be arrested in a cage-cart, sent to the Commandant of Justice for trial,
and dismissed from office for life.'
Róng was not implicated because the letter had not yet arrived."
The "Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove" says:
"When Róng replied to Zhào's letter,
the critics all considered it sarcastic.
Emperor Shìzǔ was troubled by this,
and so issued an oral edict saying:
'With Róng's character as a gentleman,
how could he harbor selfish motives?'
The critics then fell silent,
and Róng also did not offer thanks."
Péi Shūzé was arrested,
but his spirit and expression showed no change,
and his demeanor was as composed as ever.
He asked for paper and brush to write a letter.
After the letter was finished,
many people came to his rescue,
and he was thus spared.
Later, he attained the position of General of the Three Excellencies with Equal Honors.
The "Eulogies of the Various Dignitaries of Jìn" says:
"Péi Kǎi's son, Zàn,
married the daughter of Yáng Jùn.
After Jùn was executed,
because Kǎi was related by marriage,
he was arrested and handed over to the Commandant of Justice.
The Palace Attendant Fù Zhī testified that Kǎi had always been well-intentioned,
and he was thus spared."
The "Biographies of Famous Gentlemen" says:
"During the troubles of the Prince of Chǔ,
Lǐ Zhào, jealous of Kǎi's great reputation,
had him arrested intending to harm him.
Kǎi's expression and spirit showed no change,
and his actions remained composed as usual.
Various people pleaded for his rescue,
and he was spared."
The "Autumn of Jìn" says:
"Kǎi and Wáng Róng were both granted the title of General of the Three Excellencies with Equal Honors."
Wáng Yīfǔ once entrusted a matter to a clansman,
but after some time it had not been done.
Meeting him at a drinking banquet,
Yīfǔ then said to him:
"I recently entrusted you with an important matter;
how is it that it hasn't been done?"
The clansman became greatly enraged,
and immediately picked up a fruit tray and threw it at his face.
Yīfǔ said nothing at all;
after washing up,
he took Chancellor Wáng's arm,
and rode away with him in the carriage.
In the carriage, looking in a mirror, he said to the Chancellor:
"Look at the gleam in my eyes;
it comes from above the ox's back."
Wáng Yīfǔ probably considered himself to have a handsome and distinguished demeanor,
and not one to stoop to quarreling with others.
Péi Xiá was at Zhōu Fù's place,
and Fù was acting as host.
Dèng Càn's "Annals of Jìn" says:
"Fù, styled Zǔxuān,
was from Rǔnán.
He succeeded Liú Huái as General Who Guards the East,
stationed at Shòuyáng.
He issued a proclamation to all quarters,
intending to welcome the Son of Heaven.
Emperor Yuánhuáng sent Gān Zhuó to attack him.
Fù fled,
and died on the road."
Xiá was playing weiqi with someone,
and Fù's Adjutant was serving wine.
Xiá was in the middle of the game,
and did not drink at the proper time.
The Adjutant became angry,
and dragged Xiá to the ground.
Xiá returned to his seat,
his demeanor as usual,
his expression unchanged,
and resumed playing as before.
Wáng Yīfǔ asked Xiá,
"How were you able to keep your expression unchanged at that time?"
He replied:
"It was simply because I was absorbed in the game, that's all."
Another version says: "It was simply because I was absorbed, that's all."
Another version says: "It was truly because I was a fighter, that's all."
Liú Qìngsūn was in the Grand Tutor's office.
At that time, many gentlemen
were framed by him.
Only Yǔ Zǐsōng gave free rein to his mind beyond worldly affairs,
leaving no trace for him to exploit.
Later, because of his frugal nature and wealthy family,
[Qìngsūn] persuaded the Grand Tutor to order him to exchange ten million cash,
hoping he would be stingy,
so that he could take advantage of the situation.
The "Autumn of Jìn" says:
"Liú Yú, styled Qìngsūn,
was from Zhōngshān.
He had the talent and cunning of a gallant knight,
and was skilled at forming connections.
He was favored by Fànyáng Prince Xiāo.
After Xiāo died,
the Grand Tutor summoned him,
greatly entrusted and relied on him,
and appointed him as Chief Clerk."
The "Tales of the Eight Princes" says:
"Sīmǎ Yuè, styled Yuánchāo,
was the eldest son of Prince Tài of Gāomì.
In his youth, he upheld the conduct of a commoner,
and was esteemed both within and outside the court.
He rose successively to Minister of Works,
and Grand Tutor."
The Grand Tutor asked Yǔ in front of everyone,
Yǔ at the time was already drunk and listless,
his headscarf had fallen onto the table,
and he was bending his head to put it back on.
Slowly he replied:
"My humble household indeed may have something like twenty million;
take as much as you wish, sir."
Only then was [Qìngsūn] convinced.
Later, someone mentioned this to Yǔ,
and Yǔ said:
"It can be said that he measured the heart of a gentleman
with the concerns of a petty man."
Wáng Yīfǔ and Péi Jǐngshēng had different aspirations and tastes.
Jǐngshēng disliked him and wanted to win him over,
but ultimately could not change him.
So he deliberately visited Wáng,
ranted and cursed him to the extreme,
demanding that Wáng respond to him,
intending to share the blame.
Wáng did not change his expression,
and slowly said:
"The white-eyed boy is acting up again."
The "Eulogies of the Various Dignitaries of Jìn" says:
"Péi Miǎo, styled Jǐngshēng,
was from Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
In his youth, he had broad talents.
His elder cousin Péi Wěi appreciated and esteemed him;
whenever they engaged in pure conversation,
it lasted from day until dawn.
He himself believed his reasoning and constructs were often superior,
and would often apologize for it,
yet he could not surpass [Wěi].
He served successively as Gentleman of the Grand Tutor's Staff,
Marshal of the Left,
and Supervisor of the Prince of Dōnghǎi's military affairs.
In his youth, he was a man of letters,
but later in life he served as a general.
Although it was not his true talent,
he was praised for being rarely seen and esteemed."
Wáng Yīfǔ was four years older than Péi Chénggōng,
but they were not close.
Once they gathered together at the same place,
all being famous gentlemen of the time,
they said to Wáng:
"What does Péi Lìng's fine reputation amount to!"
Wáng then addressed Péi familiarly as "qīng."
Péi said:
"I can certainly fulfill your elegant intention."
Péi Wěi
has been mentioned previously.
There were people coming and going who said:
Yǔ Gōng intended to come down east.
Someone told Wáng Gōng:
"You should secretly make some preparations,
to guard against unexpected events."
Wáng Gōng said:
"Although Yuán Guī and I are both ministers of the king,
we originally cherished the friendship of commoners.
If he wishes to come,
I will simply put on my square scarf and return directly to Wūyī.
The *Dānyáng Jì* says:
"The rise of Wūyī,
was the location of the Wūyī camp during the time of Wú.
When Jiāngzuǒ was first established,
it was where the various princes of Lángyá resided."
What preparations are needed?"
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Thus, the dust of turmoil dissipated on its own,
and both inside and outside, there was harmony and peace."
The Registrar of Chancellor Wáng wanted to inspect and audit the accounts.
The Duke told the Registrar:
"I wish to engage with you, Registrar,
do not concern yourself with the affairs on other people's desks."
Zǔ Shìshǎo loved wealth,
Ruǎn Yáojí loved clogs,
and both constantly managed their own affairs,
equally a burden,
yet it was not judged which was superior or inferior.
The *Zǔ Yuē Biézhuàn* says:
"Yuē, styled Shìshǎo,
was from Qiú, Fànyáng.
He successively rose to the positions of General Who Pacifies the West,
Governor of Yùzhōu,
stationed at Shòuyáng.
He rebelled with Sū Jùn,
after Jùn's defeat,
Yuē defected to Shí Lè.
Yuē was originally from a prominent family in Yōuzhōu,
his guests filled the gates,
Lè climbed high and saw the carriages and cavalry,
and was greatly alarmed.
He also seized the fields and lands of his ancestors in his hometown,
and many landowners harbored resentment.
Lè despised him,
and subsequently executed Yuē."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Ruǎn Fú, styled Yáojí,
was from Chénliú,
the second son of Ruǎn Xián.
From a young age, he had wisdom and tact,
but was not exceptionally outstanding.
He successively rose to the positions of Palace Attendant,
Minister of Personnel,
and Governor of Guǎngzhōu."
Someone went to visit Zǔ,
and saw him sorting and inspecting his wealth and goods.
When the guest arrived,
he had not finished putting them away,
with two small baskets remaining behind his back,
he leaned over to block them,
his mind unsettled.
Someone went to visit Ruǎn,
and saw him blowing on the fire to wax his clogs,
and then sighing, saying:
"I wonder how many pairs of clogs one wears in a lifetime?"
His expression was calm and relaxed.
Thus, the superiority and inferiority began to be distinguished.
The *Fú Biézhuàn* says:
"Fú had an elegant and unrestrained demeanor,
and from a young age, he possessed the family style."
Attendant Xǔ and
Minister of Works Gù both served as Attendants to the Chancellor,
at that time, they were already favored,
when traveling, feasting, and gathering,
there was almost no difference.
The *Jìn Bǎiguān Míng* says:
"Xǔ Zǎo, styled Sīwén,
was from Yángxiàn, Yìxīng."
The *Xǔ Shì Pǔ* says:
"Zǎo's grandfather was Yàn,
styled Zǐliáng,
Magistrate of Yǒngxīng.
His father was Péi,
styled Jìxiǎn,
Magistrate of Wúchéng.
Zǎo served up to Vice Minister of Personnel."
Once, they went to the Chancellor's place at night for amusement,
the two were extremely joyful,
and the Chancellor then ordered them to enter his own tent to sleep.
Gù tossed and turned until dawn,
unable to sleep soundly.
Xǔ got onto the bed and immediately snored loudly.
The Chancellor looked at the guests and said:
"It is also difficult to find a place to sleep here."
Gù Hé, styled Jūnxiào,
was renowned from a young age.
His clansman Gù Róng said:
"This is the qílín of our family,
he will surely bring prosperity to our clan."
He served up to President of the Imperial Secretariat.
He had five sons:
Zhì, Kuí,
Chún, Lǚzhī.
Grand Commandant Yǔ was majestic in demeanor and appearance,
not acting lightly,
people of the time all thought it was affected.
Liàng had an elder son, a few years old,
possessing an inherently dignified and serious nature,
just like this from the start,
people knew it was innate.
Wēn Tàizhēn once hid behind a curtain to startle him,
this child's expression remained calm,
and then he slowly knelt and said:
"Why does the lord do this?"
Commentators said he was not inferior to Liàng.
He was killed during the time of Sū Jùn.
The *Yǔ Shì Pǔ* says:
"Huì, styled Huìzōng,
was the eldest son of Grand Commandant Liàng.
At nineteen years old,
he was killed in the sixth year of Xiánhé."
Some said:
"Seeing Ā Gōng,
one knows Yuán Guī is not affected."
Ā Gōng,
was Huì's childhood name.
Chǔ Gōng was promoted from Magistrate of Zhāng'ān to Registrar and Army Advisor of the Grand Commandant,
according to Yǔ Liàng's *Qǐ Cānzuǒ Míng*:
"Póu at that time was directly an Army Advisor,
not in charge of the Registrar's office."
His name was already renowned, but his position was lowly,
and not many people recognized him.
The Duke traveled east,
riding on a merchant boat,
and several old subordinates sent him off to stay at the Qiántáng Pavilion.
The *Qiántáng Xiàn Jì* says:
"The county is near the sea,
and was washed away by the tides,
the prominent families of the county,
collected money to hire people,
to transport soil and build an embankment,
hence the name."
At that time, Shěn Chōng of Wúxīng was the county magistrate,
details unknown.
He was sending off guests across the Zhèjiāng River,
when the guests departed,
the pavilion clerk drove the Duke to move under the ox shed.
When the tide came,
Magistrate Shěn got up and paced restlessly,
asking:
"Who is that under the ox shed?"
The clerk said:
"Yesterday, a coarse northerner came to stay in the pavilion,
the *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"The people of Wú called people from the Central Plains 'cāng'."
There were noble guests,
so we temporarily moved him."
The magistrate, under the influence of alcohol,
thus asked from afar:
"Does the coarse northerner want to eat cake?
What is his surname?
We can speak together."
Chǔ then raised his hand and replied:
"Hénán Chǔ Jìyě."
Far and wide had long known the Duke's name,
the magistrate was then greatly flustered,
not daring to move the Duke,
so he prepared a name card under the ox shed to visit the Duke.
He further slaughtered animals to prepare a feast,
set it before the Duke,
whipped the pavilion clerk,
wishing to apologize and show his shame.
The Duke drank and feasted with him,
his words and expression unchanged,
as if unaware.
The magistrate escorted the Duke to the boundary.
Grand Tutor Xī, while in Jīngkǒu,
sent a disciple with a letter to Chancellor Wáng,
seeking a son-in-law.
The chancellor told Xī's messenger:
"Go to the east wing,
and choose freely."
The disciple returned
and reported to Xī:
"All the young gentlemen of the Wáng family
are commendable,
but hearing that someone had come to seek a son-in-law,
they all became reserved and formal.
Only one young gentleman
lay on an eastern bed, baring his belly,
as if he hadn't heard."
Lord Xī said:
"That's exactly the right one!"
Upon inquiry,
it turned out to be Yìshǎo,
so he married his daughter to him.
The "Wáng Shì Pǔ" says:
"Yìshǎo
is the childhood name of Xīzhī.
Xīzhī's wife
was the daughter of Grand Tutor Xī Jiàn,
named Xuán,
courtesy name Zǐfáng."
At the beginning of crossing the river,
when receiving official appointments,
carriages were decorated and feasts were provided.
Yáng Màn was appointed as Governor of Dānyáng,
and guests who arrived early
all received excellent arrangements.
As the day grew late, supplies gradually ran out,
and the fare was no longer refined;
it depended on when the guests arrived,
regardless of their status.
The "Màn Bié Zhuàn" says:
"Màn, courtesy name Yánzǔ,
was from Nánchéng in Tàishān.
His father, Jì,
was the Governor of Yángpíng.
Màn was unrestrained and broad-minded,
indulgent in drinking and unconventional,
and together with Ruǎn Fàng of Chénliú and others, was known as one of the 'Eight Free Spirits of Yǎnzhōu.'
He rose through the ranks to become Governor of Dānyáng,
and was killed by Sū Jùn."
Yáng Gù was appointed to Línhǎi,
and throughout the day, he provided sumptuous feasts.
Even those who arrived late
still received lavish meals.
Contemporary opinion held that Gù's extravagance
was inferior to Màn's genuine simplicity.
The "Míngdì Dōnggōng Liáoshǔ Míng" says:
"Gù, courtesy name Dào'ān,
was from Tàishān."
The "Wénzì Zhì" says:
"Gù's father, Tǎn,
was the Chief Clerk of the Chariot and Cavalry General.
Gù excelled in cursive and running script,
and was renowned for a time.
Fleeing the turmoil, he crossed the river,
and rose to become Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Praised for his integrity and frugality,
he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Herald."
Zhōu Zhòngzhì got drunk while drinking,
glared and turned to Bórén, saying:
"Your talent is inferior to your younger brother's,
