yet you undeservedly gained a great reputation!"
Moments later,
he picked up a candle and threw it at Bórén.
Bórén laughed and said:
"Little brother, using fire as an attack
is certainly a poor strategy!"
The "Sūnzǐ Bīngfǎ" says:
"There are five types of fire attacks:
first, burning personnel;
second, burning supplies;
third, burning transport vehicles;
fourth, burning storehouses;
fifth, burning supply lines.
Any army must understand the variations of these five fires,
so those who use fire attacks
must be clear about them."
Gù Hé first served as an Attendant Officer in Yángzhōu.
On the first day of the month, when he was due to attend court,
before entering,
he stopped his carriage outside the provincial gate.
Marquis Zhōu was on his way to see the chancellor,
and passed by Hé's carriage.
The "Yǔ Lín" says:
"Marquis Zhōu was already drunk from drinking,
wearing a white lined jacket,
and leaning on two attendants as he went to see the chancellor."
Hé was searching for lice,
remaining calm and unmoved.
After Zhōu had passed,
he turned back,
pointed at Gù's chest, and said:
"What is in here?"
Gù continued catching lice as before,
and slowly replied:
"This is the most unpredictable place."
After Marquis Zhōu entered,
he said to the chancellor:
"Among your provincial officials, there is one with the talent to become a minister."
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Hé had integrity and judgment,
and became well-known by the age of twenty."
Grand Marshal Yǔ fought against Sū Jùn,
was defeated, and led a dozen or so attendants,
fleeing west in a small boat.
The "Jìn Yáng Qiū" says:
"Sū Jùn rebelled,
and an edict ordered Liàng to command the campaign against him.
They fought outside the Jiànyáng Gate,
and the imperial forces were defeated.
Liàng fled from the battlefield with his three younger brothers to Wēn Qiáo."
Disorderly soldiers were plundering and robbing,
and an arrow mistakenly hit the helmsman,
who fell as the bowstring twanged.
Everyone on the boat panicked and scattered,
but Liàng remained unperturbed,
and slowly said:
"How could such a hand be used against bandits!"
Only then did the crowd calm down.
Yǔ Xiǎo Zhēngxī once went out and had not yet returned.
His mother-in-law, Ruǎn, was the wife of Liú Wàn'ān.
The "Liú Shì Pǔ" says:
"Liú Suí's wife was the daughter of Ruǎn Fān of Chénliú,
courtesy name Yòu'é."
Suí is mentioned elsewhere.
She went with her daughter up to the tower of Ānlíng City.
Shortly after, Yì returned,
riding a fine horse,
with a splendid entourage.
Ruǎn said to her daughter:
"I've heard that your husband Yǔ is skilled at riding;
how can I get to see it?"
The wife told Yì,
The "Yǔ Shì Pǔ Zhuàn" says:
"Yì married the daughter of Liú Suí of Gāopíng,
courtesy name Jìngnǚ."
Yì then performed a cavalry display with his ceremonial guard on the road.
After just two turns,
he fell from his horse to the ground,
but his expression remained composed.
Xuānwǔ, Chancellor Huán Wēn,
was riding together with Jiǎnwén
and Grand Steward, Prince Wǔlíng, Xī.
They shared a carriage,
and Huán secretly ordered people to beat drums and shout loudly in front of and behind the carriage.
The ceremonial guard was thrown into chaos,
and the Grand Steward, terrified, begged to get down from the carriage.
Looking at Jiǎnwén,
he was serene and calm.
Xuānwǔ said to others:
"So there is still such a worthy man in the court."
The "Xù Jìn Yáng Qiū" says:
"The Emperor was gentle and profound by nature,
truly poised and steady.
Once, he rode together with Huán Wēn
and Grand Steward, Prince Wǔlíng, Xī.
When they reached Bǎnqiáo,
Huán secretly ordered horns to be blown and drums beaten without cause,
causing the troops to panic and scatter.
Huán pretended to be alarmed,
while Xī was greatly shaken.
The Emperor, however, remained composed,
his voice and expression unchanged.
Huán often praised his virtue and magnanimity for this reason,
so commentators say that Huán was both admiring and wary of him."
Wáng Shào and
Wáng Huì went together to visit Xuānwǔ (Huán Wēn).
The "Bié Zhuàn of Shào and Huì" says:
"Shào, styled Jìnglún,
was the fifth son of Chancellor Dǎo.
He was noble, pure, simple, and unadorned,
and deeply savored the profound mysteries.
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn praised him as a 'phoenix chick.'
He rose through the ranks to become Shàngshū Púyè and
Administrator of Wú Commandery.
Huì, styled Jìngwén,
was the youngest son of the Chancellor.
He had a reputation for purity,
was calm and peaceful, free from contention,
and served up to the position of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn."
It happened to be when (Huán Wēn's men) were arresting Yǔ Xī's family.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Xī, styled Shǐyàn,
was the eldest son of Minister of Works Yǔ Bīng.
He rose through the ranks to become Regional Inspector of Xú and
Yǎn provinces.
The Xī brothers were noble and powerful,
and Huán Wēn was jealous of them.
He hinted that Xī should be dismissed from office,
so Xī fled to Jìyáng.
Earlier, Guō Pǔ had divined that Bīng's descendants would certainly meet with disaster,
and only by firmly holding the three 'yáng' places could they have posterity.
Therefore, Xī sought to be stationed in Shānyáng,
his younger brother Yǒu was in Dōngyáng,
and Xī himself was in Jìyáng.
When Wēn executed Xī,
his younger brothers Róu and
Qiàn heard of Xī's calamity
and fled to Hǎilíng.
Later, they returned to Jīngkǒu to gather followers,
but the affair failed,
and they were executed by Wēn."
Huì felt uneasy,
hesitating and wanting to leave;
Shào sat firmly without moving,
waiting until the arresting officers returned,
and only after learning the outcome did he leave.
Commentators considered Shào superior.
Huán Xuānwǔ and Xī Chāo discussed eliminating court ministers.
After the list was finalized,
they stayed together that night.
The "Xù Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Chāo believed Wēn was heroic and martial,
and that he was destined for a time when people would gladly support him,
so he deeply committed himself to him.
Wēn also deeply valued and esteemed him,
so all secret plans and schemes
involved him."
The next morning,
Wēn called Xiè Ān and
Wáng Tǎnzhī in,
and threw the memorandum to show them.
Xī was still inside the tent.
Xiè said nothing at all,
Wáng simply threw it back,
saying: "Too many!"
Xuānwǔ took up a brush to delete some,
and Xī, unaware, secretly spoke to Xuānwǔ from within the tent.
Xiè said with a smile:
"Master Xī can truly be called the 'guest within the tent.'"
Tent, some versions say curtain.
When Grand Tutor Xiè was leisurely staying at Dōngshān,
he went sailing on the sea for amusement with Sūn Xìnggōng and others.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Ān originally resided in Kuàijī,
and spent time traveling with Zhī Dàolín,
Wáng Xīzhī,
and Xǔ Xún.
Outdoors, they fished and hunted in the mountains and waters;
indoors, they conversed and composed writings,
never having any intention of engaging in worldly affairs."
The wind rose and waves swelled.
Sūn, Wáng, and the others all looked alarmed,
and immediately called to turn back.
The Grand Tutor's spirit was just then vigorous,
chanting and whistling without speaking.
The boatman, seeing the Duke's appearance calm and his mood pleased,
continued onward without stopping.
When the wind grew fiercer
and the waves more violent,
everyone was clamoring and restless, unable to sit still.
The Duke slowly said:
"If it's like this,
shouldn't we go back!"
The others immediately followed his words and turned back.
From this, they understood his composure
was sufficient to pacify both court and country.
Duke Huán set up concealed armed guards and prepared a feast,
widely inviting court officials,
intending thereby to kill Xiè Ān and
Wáng Tǎnzhī.
The "Jìn Āndì Jì" says:
"When Jiǎnwén passed away,
his final edict ordered Huán Wēn to follow the precedents of Zhūgě Liàng and
Wáng Dǎo.
Wēn was greatly angered,
believing this diminished his power,
and that it was the doing of Xiè Ān and
Wáng Tǎnzhī.
When he came to attend the imperial funeral,
the officials bowed by the roadside.
Those in positions of authority who saw him
trembled and lost their composure.
Some say it was from this point he intended to kill Wáng and
Xiè."
Wáng was very alarmed,
and asked Xiè:
"What plan should we make?"
Xiè's expression and demeanor did not change.
He said to Wéndù (Wáng Tǎnzhī):
"The survival or fall of the Jìn dynasty
rests on this one trip."
They went forward together.
Wáng's fearful state
became increasingly evident in his expression.
Xiè's composure
was even more apparent in his bearing.
Approaching the steps and hastening to the mats,
he began to chant in the Luòyáng style,
reciting
"Vast, mighty flow."
Huán was daunted by his broad-mindedness and detachment,
and hastily dismissed the soldiers.
According to Sòng Míngdì's "Wénzhāng Zhì":
"Ān could perform the Luòyáng scholar's chant,
but he had a slight nasal ailment from youth,
making his speech sound thick.
Later, many famous figures imitated his chant,
but could not match it,
so they would cover their noses while chanting.
Huán Wēn halted at Xīntíng,
arraying his soldiers and guards on a large scale,
and summoned Ān and Tǎnzhī,
intending to harm them at the gathering.
Upon entering, Wáng lost his composure,
holding his tablet upside down,
sweat soaking his clothes.
Ān's demeanor and movements
were no different from usual.
He looked around at all the guards at Wēn's side,
and said to Wēn:
'Ān has heard that when a feudal lord possesses the Way,
his defense lies with the four neighboring states.
Why does Your Lordship have these fellows posted behind the wall?'
Wēn laughed and said:
'It's simply that I cannot help but do so.'
Thereupon, his stern and solemn intent vanished completely.
He ordered his attendants,
urging them to proceed with the feast and pass the wine cups,
and they talked and laughed for a long time."
Wáng and Xiè were formerly equally famous,
but from this their superiority and inferiority were first distinguished.
Grand Tutor Xiè and Wáng Wéndù went together to visit Xī Chāo.
As the day grew late and they still had not been admitted,
Wáng wanted to leave.
Xiè said:
"Can you not endure a moment for the sake of your life?"
Chāo enjoyed Huán Wēn's favor,
and wielded the exclusive authority over life and death.
Zhī Dàolín returned to the east.
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* says:
“Dùn was welcomed by Emperor Āi,
and after traveling in the capital for a long time,
his heart remained in his old mountains.
So he brushed off his sleeves in the royal capital
and returned to his cave dwelling.”
The worthies of the time all saw him off at Zhēnglǔ Pavilion.
The *Records of Dānyáng* says:
“During the Tài’ān era,
General Zhēnglǔ Xiè Ān built this pavilion,
and thus it was named after him.”
Cài Zǐshū arrived first
and sat close to Master Lín.
The *Book of the Restoration* says:
“Cài Xì, styled Zǐshū,
was from Jìyáng.
He was the second son of Minister Cài Mó.
He was cultured and principled
and served up to the position of Chief Clerk to the General of Pacification.”
Xiè Wànshí arrived later
and sat a little farther away.
Cài got up briefly,
and Xiè moved to his spot.
When Cài returned,
he saw Xiè sitting there,
so he gathered up the mat and threw Xiè to the ground,
then sat back down himself.
Xiè’s cap and headcloth were knocked askew,
but he slowly got up, shook out his clothes, and returned to his seat.
His expression and mood were very calm,
showing no sign of anger or dismay.
After he was seated,
he said to Cài:
“You are a strange man—
you nearly ruined my face.”
Cài replied:
“I never considered your face in the first place.”
Afterward,
neither of them bore any grudge.
Xī Jiābīn admired and revered Shì Dào’ān’s virtuous reputation.
The *Biography of the Venerable Ān* says:
“Shì Dào’ān
was from Bóliǔ in Chángshān.
His original surname was Wèi.
At age twelve, he became a monk.
He was exceptionally intelligent but extremely ugly in appearance.
Fótúchéng held him in high esteem.
During the rebellion of the Shí clan,
he lived on wild plants and pursued his studies at Lùhún Mountain.
Pressured by Mùróng Jùn,
he then settled in Xiāngyáng.
Because the Buddhist teachings had spread eastward
and the scriptures were full of errors,
he reorganized them into chapters,
arranged the sections and titles,
and provided commentaries.
Even masters like Zhī Dàolín all respected his principles.
He died without illness.”
Xī sent him a thousand *hú* of rice
and wrote a long letter
expressing deep sincerity.
Dào’ān replied simply:
“You have diminished your rice.”
This made Xī feel even more keenly the burdens of worldly attachments.
Xiè Ānnán was dismissed from the post of Minister of Personnel and returned to the east.
The *Official Roster of the Jin* says:
“Xiè Fèng, styled Hóngdào,
was from Shānyīn in Kuàijī.”
The *Genealogy of the Xiè Clan* says:
“Fèng’s grandfather was Duān,
a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
His father was Fèng,
Chief Clerk to the Chancellor.
Fèng served as General Ānnán,
Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
and Minister of Personnel.”
When Grand Tutor Xiè was traveling west to take up his post as Marshal under Duke Huán,
they met at Pògǎng.
Since they were about to part for a long time,
they stopped for three days to talk.
The Grand Tutor wanted to console him over his loss of office,
but Ānnán kept steering the conversation to other topics.
Though they spent two nights on the road together,
he never mentioned the matter.
The Grand Tutor deeply regretted not fully expressing his feelings,
and said to his fellow travelers:
“Xiè Fèng is truly an extraordinary man.”
When Dài Gōng came out from the east,
Grand Tutor Xiè went to see him.
Xiè had originally looked down on Dài,
but when they met, he only discussed *qin* and calligraphy.
Dài showed no reluctance,
and his discourse on *qin* and calligraphy grew even more exquisite.
Xiè then calmly realized his depth.
The *Annals of Emperor Ān of Jin* says:
“Dài Kuí, styled Āndào,
was from Qiáoguó.
In his youth, he had pure integrity,
was serene, harmonious, and open-minded,
and was recognized by Liú Zhēncháng.
His nature was very unrestrained and free,
and he took great pleasure in life.
He loved playing the *qin*,
was skilled in writing,
and especially enjoyed outings and banquets.
He often associated with elegant and cultured men from prominent families,
and commentators praised him as a reclusive yet worldly figure.
He repeatedly declined official summons,
thus earning a reputation for lofty integrity.”
Xiè Gōng was playing *weiqi* with someone
when a messenger from Xiè Xuán at the Huái River arrived.
After reading the letter,
he remained silent,
then slowly turned back to the board.
A guest asked about the situation at the Huái front:
He replied:
“The youngsters have soundly defeated the enemy.”
His expression and demeanor
were no different than usual.
The *Continued Annals of Jìnyáng* says:
“Initially,
when Fú Jiān invaded south,
the capital was in great alarm.
Xiè Ān showed no fear;
instead, he ordered his carriage to go to his country villa,
where he played *weiqi* with his nephew Xuán.
Only after returning that night did he issue directives,
and within a few days, everything was settled.
Even after the enemy was defeated, he showed no sign of joy.
Such was his lofty composure.”
The *Biography of General Xiè* says:
“The Dí rebel Fú Jiān
mobilized his entire country for a massive campaign,
with forces reportedly numbering a million.
The court dispatched various armies to resist him,
totaling eighty thousand men.
Jiān advanced and stationed his troops at Shòuyáng.
Xuán served as Vanguard Commander
and, together with his cousin Yǎn and others, selected elite troops for a decisive battle.
They wounded Jiān with arrows,
captured tens of thousands of prisoners,
seized the enemy’s imperial carriage and mica-decorated chariot,
amassed treasures like mountains,
obtained tens of thousands of rolls of brocade and felt,
and captured oxen, horses,
donkeys, mules,
and camels totaling a hundred thousand head.”
Wáng Zǐyóu
and Zǐjìng were once sitting together in a room
when a fire suddenly broke out above.
Zǐyóu hurriedly fled to avoid it,
not even having time to put on his clogs.
The *Official Roster of the Jin* says:
“Wáng Huīzhī,
styled Zǐyóu.”
The *Book of the Restoration* says:
“Huīzhī
was the fifth son of Wáng Xīzhī.
He was outstanding and unrestrained,
aspiring to be lofty and unconventional.
He served up to the position of Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.”
Zǐjìng’s expression remained calm and composed.
He slowly called to his attendants,
leaned on them, and walked out,
no different than usual.
The *Continued Annals of Jìnyáng* says:
“Although Xiànzhī did not adhere to conventional norms,
his demeanor and conduct were never improper.”
The world used this to judge the spiritual bearing of the two Wángs.
Fú Jiān’s lingering forces were approaching the border.
(Jiān—see elsewhere.)
Grand Tutor Xiè said to Zǐjìng:
“We should take charge of the axis
and settle matters here.”
When Lord Cáo was young, he met Qiáo Xuán.
Xuán said to him:
"The world is in chaos,
with powerful figures contending like tigers.
To bring order and govern it—
is it not you?
Yet you are truly a hero in times of chaos,
but a treacherous villain in times of peace.
I regret that I am old,
and will not see your wealth and honor.
I shall entrust my descendants to you."
The *Continued Book of Hàn* states:
"Xuán's courtesy name was Gōngzǔ,
a man of Suīyáng in the state of Liáng.
In his youth, he studied the *Rites* and the *Spring and Autumn Annals* of the Yán family.
He rose through the ranks to become Prefect of the Masters of Writing.
Xuán was stern, clear-sighted, and talented in strategy,
skilled at recognizing people.
Earlier, when Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was still a student,
and not yet known,
Xuán regarded him as extraordinary."
The *Book of Wèi* states:
"Xuán met the Grand Ancestor and said:
'I have seen many gentlemen,
but none like you!
The world is about to fall into chaos;
without a talent destined for the age, it cannot be saved.
The one who can bring peace to it—
is it not you?'"
According to the *Tales of the World*:
"Xuán said to the Grand Ancestor:
'You are not yet known;
you should befriend Xǔ Zijiāng.'
The Grand Ancestor then visited Zijiāng,
and Zijiāng accepted him."
Sūn Shèng's *Miscellaneous Sayings* states:
"The Grand Ancestor once asked Xǔ Zijiāng:
'What kind of person am I?'
He insisted on asking,
and then Zijiāng replied:
'A capable minister in times of peace,
a treacherous hero in times of chaos.'
The Grand Ancestor laughed heartily."
What the *Shìshuō* says is erroneous.
Lord Cáo asked Péi Qián:
"You once stayed with Liú Bèi in Jīngzhōu;
what do you think of Bèi's talent?"
Qián said:
"If he were to reside in the Central Plains,
he could cause disorder among people,
but could not bring governance.
If he were to guard the borders and hold strategic points,
he would be sufficient to be a ruler of one region."
The *Records of Wèi* states:
"Qián's courtesy name was Wénxíng,
a man of Hédōng.
He took refuge from chaos in Jīngzhōu,
where Liú Biǎo treated him with the courtesy due a guest.
Qián privately said to Wáng Càn
and Sīmǎ Zhī:
'Governor Liú lacks the talent of a hegemon or king,
yet he wishes to position himself as a Western Earl;
his downfall is not far off!'
He then crossed south,
and went to Chángshā."
Hé Yàn,
Dèng Yáng,
and Xiàhóu Xuán all sought friendship with Fù Gǔ,
but Gǔ never agreed.
The *Brief History of Wèi* states:
"Dèng Yáng's courtesy name was Xuánmào,
a man of Wǎn in Nányáng,
a descendant of Dèng Yǔ.
In his youth, he gained a reputation among scholars.
During Emperor Míng's reign, he served as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
but was dismissed for forming a clique with Lǐ Shèng and others.
During the Zhèngshǐ era,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant and Master of Writing.
He was fond of wealth;
Zāng Ài gave his father's concubine to Yáng,
and obtained a prominent office.
The capital had a saying about him:
'Exchanging office for wealth—Dèng Xuánmào.'
Hé Yàn's selection of officials was improper,
largely due to Yáng.
He was executed for allying with Cáo Shuǎng."
These men then used Xún Càn to mediate and reconcile,
saying to Gǔ:
"Xiàhóu Tàichū is an outstanding talent of the time;
he is open-minded toward you,
yet you harbor unwillingness.
If friendship is established, goodwill follows;
if not, it leads to discord.
If two worthies are harmonious,
it is a blessing for the state.
This is why Lìn Xiàngrú yielded to Lián Pō."
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"Xiàngrú was appointed Senior Minister due to his great achievements,
ranking above Lián Pō.
Pō was angry
and wanted to humiliate him.
Xiàngrú often claimed illness;
when he saw Pō,
he turned his carriage to avoid him.
His retainers wanted to leave him,
but Xiàngrú said:
'Even with the King of Qín's might, I rebuked him in court—
why should I fear General Lián?
But consider: Qín is strong, Zhào is weak;
because of the two of us, Qín dares not attack Zhào.
Now if two tigers fight,
they cannot both survive.
I put the state's urgency before private grudges.'
Pō heard this
and apologized."
Fù said:
"Xiàhóu Tàichū
has great ambitions but a troubled mind;
he can gather empty praise,
truly what is called a person whose sharp tongue overturns states.
Hé Yàn
and Dèng Yáng are capable but rash,
broad but lacking focus,
fond of profit outwardly but without restraint inwardly,
valuing conformity and disliking difference,
talkative and envious of those ahead.
Talkativeness brings many faults;
envy of those ahead leaves one without close friends.
In my view:
these three worthies
are all people of ruined virtue!
Keeping away from them, I still fear encountering disaster—
how could I possibly be close to them?"
Later events all turned out as he said.
The *Book of Fù* states:
"At that time, Hé Yàn was prominent for his talent and eloquence among the noble relatives;
Dèng Yáng was fond of social connections,
forming factions,
and selling his reputation in the alleys.
Xiàhóu Xuán, as the son of a high minister,
had a weighty reputation from youth.
They all sought friendship with Gǔ,
but Gǔ did not accept them.
Gǔ's friend Xún Càn had clear insight and lofty aspirations,
yet still urged Gǔ to befriend them."
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn conducted a military review at Xuānwǔ Field.
The emperor wished to cease warfare and cultivate the arts,
and personally attended the event,
summoning all his ministers.
Shān Tāo said this was not appropriate,
and thus discussed with the various Shàngshū the original intent behind the military strategies of Sūn and Wú.
He then delved into a thorough discussion,
and everyone present sighed in admiration.
They all said:
"Shān Shǎofù's words are truly the wise sayings of the world."
Liú Xiàobiāo's note:
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Sūn Wǔ was from Qí.
Wú Qǐ was from Wèi.
Both were skilled in military strategy."
The Treatise on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove states:
"During the Xiánníng era,
after Wú was pacified,
the emperor intended to undertake affairs at Táolín and Huàshān,
halting military campaigns and ceasing warfare,
to demonstrate great peace to the world.
Thus, the provinces and commanderies all disbanded their troops,
with large commanderies retaining only a hundred military officials,
and small commanderies fifty.
At that time, the capital still held military reviews,
and Shān Tāo thus discussed the original intent behind the military strategies of Sūn and Wú.
Shān Tāo was a man of simplicity and silence,
believing that a state must not forget warfare,
hence his remarks."
The Biographies of Famous Scholars states:
"Shān Tāo lived during the transition from Wèi to Jìn,
without making any notable distinctions.
He once discussed the original intent of military strategy with Shàngshū Lú Qīn.
Emperor Wǔ heard of this
and said:
'Shān Shǎofù's words are indeed wise.'"
Later, the various princes grew arrogant and extravagant,
lightly provoking disasters and calamities.
As a result, bandits and rebels gathered like ants everywhere,
and many commanderies and principalities, lacking preparedness,
were unable to suppress them.
Thus, the turmoil gradually intensified,
just as Shān Tāo had predicted.
People of the time believed that Shān Tāo had not studied Sūn or Wú,
yet his understanding aligned with their principles in an unspoken manner.
Wáng Yífǔ also sighed and said:
"His understanding aligns with the Way in an unspoken manner."
The Treatise on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove states:
"After the Yǒngníng era,
when the various princes conspired to create disasters,
and cunning enemies suddenly arose,
it all unfolded as Shān Tāo had predicted."
The Biographies of Famous Scholars states:
"Wáng Yífǔ praised Shān Tāo,
saying, 'His profound understanding aligns with the Way in an unspoken manner;
its depth is immeasurable.'
All such remarks are of this kind."
Wáng Yífǔ's father, Wáng Yì, served as General Who Pacifies the North.
There was an official matter
for which he sent an envoy to argue but failed.
At the time, Wáng Yífǔ was in the capital
and ordered his carriage to visit Vice Director Yáng Hù and Shàngshū Shān Tāo.
Wáng Yífǔ was then still a youth,
with outstanding talent and exceptional appearance.
His presentation was both swift
and logically sound,
greatly astonishing Shān Tāo.
After he left,
Shān Tāo could not take his eyes off him
and sighed, saying:
"Shouldn't one's son be like Wáng Yífǔ?"
Yáng Hù said:
"The one who will bring chaos to the world
is surely this boy!"
The Autumn Annals of Jìn states:
"Wáng Yífǔ's father, Wáng Yì,
faced an official document
that would lead to his dismissal from office.
Wáng Yífǔ, then seventeen,
visited his stepmother's cousin Yáng Hù
to explain the situation,
his words exceptionally eloquent and impressive.
Yáng Hù disagreed with him,
and Wáng Yífǔ flicked his sleeves and rose to leave.
Yáng Hù turned to his guests and said:
'This man will surely achieve great fame and hold high positions in his time,
but the one who will corrupt customs and harm moral transformation
is undoubtedly this man!'"
The Spring and Autumn Annals of Hàn and Jìn states:
"Initially, Yáng Hù intended to execute Wáng Róng according to military law.
Wáng Yífǔ also resented Yáng Hù for saying he would surely fail,
and they did not hold each other in high regard.
People of the time said of this:
'When the two Wángs are in court,
no one in the world dares to praise Lord Yáng for his virtue.'"
Pān Yángzhòng saw Wáng Dūn when he was young
and said to him:
"Your bee-like eyes are already revealed,
but your wolf-like voice has not yet resonated.
You will surely devour others,
and you will also be devoured by others."
The Autumn Annals of Jìn states:
"Pān Tāo, styled Yángzhòng,
was from Xíngyáng,
the nephew of Tàicháng Pān Ní.
He possessed literary talent and insight.
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
he served as Governor of Hénán
and was killed."
The Spring and Autumn Annals of Hàn and Jìn states:
"Initially, Wáng Yífǔ spoke to Prince Yuè of Dōnghǎi,
who transferred Wáng Dūn to Yángzhōu.
Pān Tāo, then serving as Senior Clerk to the Grand Tutor,
said to the Grand Tutor:
'Wáng Chùzhòng's bee-like eyes are already revealed,
and his wolf-like voice has not yet sounded.
Now, placing him beyond the Jiāng,
where he can indulge his fierce and ambitious heart,
is to make a rebel of him.'"
The Autumn Annals of Jìn states:
"Wáng Dūn served as a Gentleman of the Heir Apparent,
and was a colleague of Pān Tāo,
hence these words."
The accounts of Xí and Sūn
show slight variations.
The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
"Chǔ's Lingyǐn Zǐshàng said of the heir Shāngchén:
'He has bee-like eyes and a wolf-like voice;
he is a cruel man.'"
Shí Lè was illiterate.
The Biography of Shí Lè states:
"Shí Lè, styled Shìlóng,
was from Wǔxiāng in Shàngdǎng,
a descendant of the Xiōngnú.
He was brave, fond of horseback riding and archery.
During the Yuánkāng era of Jìn,
he wandered east of the mountains,
working as a laborer for Shī Huān of Chípíng in Píngyuán.
His ears often heard the sounds of drums, horns, and bells,
and Shí Lè privately found this strange.
Initially, in Shí Lè's hometown, stones grew from the earth on the plains,
resembling iron cavalry.
Ginseng grew in the state,
with lush flowers and leaves.
At that time, the elders and physiognomists all said:
'This Hú man's physique and appearance are extraordinary,
and his future is unknowable.'
They urged the townspeople to treat him well,
but many laughed and did not believe.
At the beginning of the Yǒngjiā era,
when heroes rose together,
he and Hú Wángyáng and seventeen others rode to Jí Sāng,
where he was appointed Left Vanguard Commander.
After Jí Sāng's defeat,
they jointly elected Shí Lè as their leader.
He captured provinces and counties
and established his capital at Xiāngguó.
Later, he usurped the imperial title,
and upon his death, was posthumously titled Emperor Míng."
He had someone read the Book of Hàn to him.
Upon hearing that Lì Yìjī advised establishing the descendants of the six states,
and that seals were carved to confer them,
he was greatly alarmed and said:
"This method is bound to fail.
How then could one ultimately possess the world?"
When it came to Liú Hóu's remonstrance,
he then said:
"It is only thanks to this!"
Dèng Càn's Annals of Jìn states:
"Shí Lè could not write with his hands
and was illiterate.
In the army, he often had people read aloud,
and by listening,
he understood the meaning."
The Book of Hàn states:
"Xiàng Yǔ urgently besieged the King of Hàn at Xíngyáng.
The King of Hàn plotted with Lì Yìjī to weaken Chǔ's power.
Lì Yìjī advised establishing the descendants of the six states,
and the king ordered seals to be carved quickly.
Zhāng Liáng entered to remonstrate,
believing it impermissible.
The king stopped eating, spat out his food,
and scolded Lì Yìjī, saying:
'This petty Confucian nearly ruined your lord's affairs!'
He then ordered the seals destroyed."
Wèi Jiè was five years old,
his spirit and demeanor were lovable.
His grandfather, the Grand Guardian, said:
"This child is extraordinary;
it's just that I am old,
and will not live to see him grow up!"
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* says:
"Guàn, styled Bóyù,
was from Ānyì in Hédōng.
From youth, he was praised for his clear insight and fair judgment.
Fù Gǔ held him in the highest esteem,
calling him Níng Wǔzǐ.
He served up to the position of Grand Guardian,
and was killed by Chǔwáng Wěi."
The *Wèi Jiè Biézhuàn* says:
"Jiè possessed outstanding elegance and grace,
a pure and transcendent air.
Among his peers,
he stood out with the promise of an exceptional person.
His grandfather, the Grand Guardian, seeing Jiè at five years old, said:
'This child's spirit is keen and his intelligence remarkable,
greatly different from the crowd.
I fear I am old,
and will not live to see it.'"
Liú Yuèshí said:
"Huá Yànxià's discernment and ability are insufficient,
but his stubbornness and determination are excessive."
Yú Yù's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Huá Yì, styled Yànxià,
was from Píngyuán.
He was the great-grandson of Wèi's Grand Commandant Huá Xīn.
He rose through the ranks to become Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
He devoted himself to treating scholars with respect,
and greatly won their favor.
He was executed for not obeying Yuánhuáng's orders."
The *Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū* says:
"Liú Kūn knew Yì would certainly fail,
saying he brought it upon himself."
Zhāng Jìyīng was appointed as Qíwáng's Eastern Bureau Officer.
While in Luòyáng, he saw the autumn wind rise,
and thus thought of the water-shield soup and
perch mince
from Wúzhōng, saying:
"In life, what is valuable is to follow one's heart's desire.
How can one be an official bound thousands of miles away just to seek fame and rank!"
He then ordered his carriage and returned home.
Soon after, Qíwáng was defeated,
and people of the time all said he had foresight.
The *Wénshì Zhuàn* says:
"Zhāng Hàn, styled Jìyīng.
His father was Yǎn,
Grand Herald of Wú.
Hàn had pure talent and fine reputation,
was widely learned and skilled at writing,
composing swiftly,
with fresh and clear language and meaning.
Grand Marshal Qíwáng Jiǒng appointed him as Eastern Bureau Officer.
Hàn said to his fellow townsman Gù Róng:
'The world is in turmoil without end.
Those who have fame throughout the land
find it truly hard to retire.
I am originally a man of the mountains and forests,
with no hopes for the times for a long while.
You, my friend, are good at using clarity to guard against what lies ahead,
and wisdom to consider what comes after.'
Róng grasped his hand,
sadly saying:
'I too shall gather bracken on the southern hills with you,
and drink from the Three Rivers!'
Hàn returned home due to illness,
and the administration removed his name from the official roster for leaving without permission.
He was extremely filial by nature.
When his mother passed away,
he grieved to the point of damaging his health, exceeding ritual norms.
Considering himself advanced in years,
he did not seek involvement in worldly affairs,
and died at home from illness."
When Zhūgě Dàomíng first crossed to the left of the river,
he gave himself the style Dàomíng.
His reputation was second only to Wáng and
Yǔ.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Huī fled the troubles and crossed the river.
Together with Xún Dàomíng of Yǐngchuān and
Cài Dàomíng of Chénliú, they all had repute,
and were called
'The Three Míng of the Restoration'.
People of the time said of them:
'The capital's three Míng each have their fame;
the Cài is refined and elegant, the Xún and
Zhūgě are pure.'"
He first served as Magistrate of Línyí.
The Prime Minister said to him:
"Your Honor will surely become a 'black-haired duke'."
The *Yǔlín* says:
"When the Prime Minister was appointed as Minister of Works,
Zhūgě Dàomíng was among the guests.
Pointing to the official cap and headdress, he said:
'You will wear this again.'"
Wáng Píngzǐ had never thought much of Méizǐ,
saying:
"His ambition exceeds his capacity;
he will ultimately die within fortress walls."
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* says:
"Wáng Xuán, styled Méizǐ,
was the son of Yífǔ.
Dōnghǎiwáng Yuè appointed him as an officer,
and he later served as Administrator of Chénliú.
He exercised severe punishments extensively,
and was killed by the fortress people."
When the Grand General Wáng first marched down,
Yáng Lǎng bitterly advised against it but was not heeded.
He then exerted effort for Wáng,
riding
in a 'Cloud-Dew Chariot with Central Bell'
straight to the front, saying:
"Listen to the beat of my drum,
and with one advance we will triumph."
Wáng first grasped his hand, saying:
"When the matter succeeds,
I will appoint you to Jīngzhōu."
Later he forgot this,
and appointed him to Nánjùn.
The *Jìn Bǎiguān Míng* says:
"Lǎng, styled Shìyàn,
was from Hóngnóng."
The *Yángshì Pǔ* says:
"Lǎng's grandfather was Xiāo,
Commandant of the Palace Guard.
His father was Huái,
Governor of Jìzhōu."
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Lǎng had the capacity, insight, talent, and measure,
and was adept at handling contemporary affairs.
He served up to the position of Governor of Yōngzhōu."
After Wáng's defeat,
Emperor Míng arrested Lǎng,
intending to kill him.
The Emperor soon passed away,
and he was spared.
Later, he concurrently headed the Three Dukes office,
appointing several dozen people as his subordinates.
These individuals were all unknown at the time,
but later all received recognition and favor,
and he was praised for his discernment of people.
Zhōu Bórén's mother, on the winter solstice, raised a cup of wine and bestowed it upon her three sons, saying:
"I originally thought that crossing the river, we would have no place to set foot.
But our family has fortune,
and you are all arrayed before me.
What more is there to worry about?"
Zhōu Sōng rose,
knelt upright and wept, saying:
"It is not as Mother says.
Bórén's character: his ambition is great but his talent short;
his fame is heavy but his insight dim.
He likes to take advantage of others' weaknesses—
this is not the way to preserve oneself.
As for Sōng, my nature is arrogant and unyielding,
and I too will not be tolerated by the world.
Only Ānú, mediocre as he is,
will likely remain under Mother's gaze!"
Dèng Càn's *Jìn Jì* says:
"Ānú
is Sōng's younger brother, Zhōu Mó."
The three Zhōus have all been previously mentioned.
After the Grand General Wáng Dūn had died,
Wáng Yìng wanted to seek refuge with Wáng Bīn,
who was the Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Wáng Hán wanted to seek refuge with Wáng Shū,
who was the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Hán said to Yìng:
"How did the Grand General usually get along with the Governor of Jiāngzhōu?
And yet you want to go to him."
Yìng replied:
"That is precisely why we should go.
The Jìn Yáng Qiū states:
"Yìng, styled Ānqī,
was the son of Hán.
Dūn had no sons,
so he adopted him as his heir.
He appointed him as General of the Martial Guards,
using him as his deputy,
and he was later executed."
When the Governor of Jiāngzhōu was in a position of strength,
he was able to uphold his differing views,
which is not something an ordinary person would do.
When he sees others in decline and distress,
he will certainly feel compassion.
The Bié Zhuàn of Wáng Bīn states:
"Bīn, styled Shìrú,
was from Lángyá.
His grandfather was Lǎn,
his father was Zhèng,
both were renowned for their virtue.
Bīn possessed an upright and outstanding character,
with an elegant and proper demeanor.
He was a maternal cousin of Emperor Yuán,
and assisted in the imperial enterprise,
rising to the position of Palace Attendant.
When his elder cousin Dūn captured Shítóu,
and killed Zhōu Yǐ,
Bīn, who had always been close to Yǐ,
went to mourn over his corpse,
grieving deeply.
Afterward, he went to see Dūn,
who was surprised by his sorrowful expression and asked him about it.
He replied:
'I was mourning Zhōu Yǐ,
and could not contain my emotions.'
Dūn said:
'Yǐ brought his execution upon himself,
what are you doing?'
Bīn said:
'Yǐ was a man of pure reputation,
what crime did he commit?'
He then reproached Dūn, saying:
'Raising banners against the sovereign,
killing loyal and good men!'
His words were impassioned,
and tears streamed down his face.
Dūn was extremely angry.
The Chancellor was present,
and, fearing for Bīn,
commanded him:
'Bow and apologize.'
Bīn said:
'I have a foot ailment.
Lately, I cannot even bow when seeing the Son of Heaven,
why should I kneel?'
Dūn said:
'How does a foot ailment compare to a neck ailment?'
Because of their kinship, he did not harm him.
He later rose to become Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of the Guards."
The Governor of Jīngzhōu adheres strictly to rules,
how could he act beyond expectations?"
Hán did not listen,
and together they sought refuge with Shū.
Shū indeed drowned Hán and his son in the river.
The Zhuàn of Wáng Shū states:
"Shū, styled Chǔmíng,
was from Lángyá.
His grandfather was Lǎn,
a man of renown.
His father was Huì,
a Censor.
Shū was simple and unadorned in character and ability,
possessing both civil and military talents.
Emperor Zhōngzōng appointed him as General of the Northern Garrison,
Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was later appointed as Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
Because his father's name was Huì,
he repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to be reassigned.
He contributed to the suppression of Sū Jùn's rebellion,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Péngzé,
and posthumously granted the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry."
When Bīn heard that Yìng was coming,
he secretly prepared a boat to wait for him,
but in the end, he did not come,
which Bīn deeply regretted.
When Hán sought refuge with Shū,
Shū sent troops to meet him,
and Hán and his son drowned themselves.
In the past, Lì Jì was criticized for betraying a friend,
how much more so for selling out a brother to seek safety?
Shū is not a human being!
In Wǔchāng, Mèng Jiā served as an Attendant under Grand Marshal Yǔ Liàng in the province,
and was already well-known.
Grand Tutor Chǔ Póu had the insight to recognize talent,
and upon returning from being relieved of his post in Yùzhāng,
passed through Wǔchāng,
and asked Yǔ:
"I hear that Attendant Mèng is excellent,
is he here now?"
Yǔ said:
"Try to find him yourself."
Chǔ looked around for a long time,
then pointed at Jiā and said:
"This gentleman is slightly different,
could it be him?"
Yǔ laughed heartily and said:
"Indeed!"
At that time, people admired Chǔ's silent discernment,
and were also pleased that Jiā was recognized.
The Bié Zhuàn of Jiā states:
"Jiā, styled Wànnián,
was from Méng, Jiāngxià.
His great-grandfather was Zōng,
who served as Minister of Works in Wú.
His grandfather was Yī,
who served as Grand Administrator of Lúlíng in Jìn.
Zōng was buried in Yángxīn County, Wǔchāng,
and his descendants settled there.
Jiā was known for his integrity and conduct from a young age.
Grand Marshal Yǔ Liàng,
while overseeing Jiāngzhōu,
recruited Jiā as an Attendant in Lúlíng.
Upon returning to the capital,
Liàng questioned him about local customs and governance.
He replied:
'Wait until I return,
and I will ask the local officials.'
Liàng covered his mouth with his whisk and laughed,
and said to his younger brother Yì:
'Mèng Jiā is truly a man of great virtue.'
He was later transferred to the position of Educational Attendant.
Grand Tutor Chǔ Póu was a man of insight and discernment.
During a grand assembly on New Year's Day hosted by Liàng,
Póu asked Liàng:
'I hear there is a Mèng Jiā in Jiāngzhōu,
where is he?'
Liàng said:
'He is among the guests,
you can look for him yourself.'
Póu looked around for a long time,
then pointed at Jiā and said:
'Could it be him?'
Liàng smiled happily,
pleased that Póu had recognized Jiā,
and impressed that Jiā had been recognized by Póu,
and thus held him in even higher regard.
Later, he served as an Adjutant under Huán Wēn, the General of the Western Expedition.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, Wēn was touring Lóngshān,
and all his subordinates were gathered.
At that time, the officials were all wearing military attire,
and the wind blew Jiā's hat off.
Wēn warned those around him not to speak,
to observe his reaction.
Jiā did not notice at first,
but after a while, when he went to the restroom,
he ordered someone to retrieve it for him.
Wēn had Sūn Shèng write a satirical essay about it,
and when it was finished, placed it on Jiā's seat.
When Jiā returned, he immediately replied,
and all those present sighed in admiration.
Jiā enjoyed drinking to the fullest,
but no matter how much he drank, he remained composed.
Wēn asked:
'What is so good about wine?
That you are so fond of it.'
Jiā replied:
'My lord, you have not yet discovered the delight within wine.'
Wēn asked again:
'When listening to music,
string instruments are not as good as wind instruments,
and wind instruments are not as good as the human voice,
why is that?'
He replied:
'Because it is closer to nature.'
He was later transferred to the position of Chief Attendant,
and promoted to Chief Clerk.
He died at the age of fifty-three."
Dài Āndào was over ten years old,
painting at the Wǎguān Temple.
Minister Wáng Chángshǐ saw him and said:
"This child is not only capable of painting,
The *Continued Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Kuí excelled in painting,
mastering the art of colors."
He will also ultimately achieve fame.
It is regrettable that I am old,
and will not see his prime!"
Wáng Zhòngzǔ,
Xiè Rénzǔ,
and Liú Zhēncháng all went to the tomb in Dānyáng to pay respects to Governor Yīn Yángzhōu,
who held a firm and resolute ambition.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Hào lived in seclusion for many years,
repeatedly declining official appointments."
After returning,
Wáng and Xiè said to each other:
"If Yuānyuán does not rise to office,
what will become of the common people?"
They deeply worried and sighed.
Liú said:
"Are you gentlemen truly worried that Yuānyuán will not rise to office?"
On his deathbed,
Xiǎo Yù submitted a memorial recommending his son Yuánkè as his successor.
Yuánkè
was the childhood name of Àizhī.
The *Yǔ Shì Pǔ* states:
"Àizhī's courtesy name was Zhòngzhēn,
the second son of Yì's younger brother."
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Àizhī had the demeanor of his father Yì,
and Huán Wēn relocated him to Yùzhāng.
He died at the age of thirty-six."
The court was concerned that he would not comply with orders,
and did not know whom to send,
so they collectively decided to appoint Huán Wēn.
Governor Liú said:
"If he is sent,
he will certainly be able to pacify Western Chǔ,
but I fear he may become uncontrollable."
The *Táo Kǎn Biézhuàn* states:
"After Yǔ Yì's death,
he recommended his son Àizhī to succeed him as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Hé Chōng said:
'Lord Táo was a man of great merit,
yet he humbly declined on his deathbed.
Before the Chancellor passed away,
Jìngyù was a fourth-rank general,
and this has not changed to this day.
As for relatives, Dào'ēn
leisurely served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and no one has ever received such an exceptional appointment.'
Thus, Huán Wēn, Governor of Xúzhōu, was appointed General of Peaceful the West and
Governor of Jīngzhōu."
Emperor Sòng Míngdì's *Wénzhāng Zhì* states:
"Yì recommended his son to succeed him,
and the court feared him.
The councilors wanted to appoint Huán Wēn.
At that time, Jiǎnwén was assisting in governance,
and he agreed.
Liú Tán said:
'If Wēn goes, he will certainly pacify Western Chǔ,
but I fear he may become uncontrollable.
I hope Your Highness will personally oversee the upper reaches,
and I, Tán, request to serve as an Army Marshal.'
Jiǎnwén did not permit it.
Wēn later indeed acted as Tán had predicted."
Lord Huán was about to campaign against Shǔ,
and all the worthy officials involved believed that Lǐ Shì had been in Shǔ for a long time,
inheriting power over generations,
and moreover, he occupied the strategic upper reaches,
making the Three Gorges difficult to conquer.
Only Governor Liú said:
"He will certainly conquer Shǔ.
Observing his gambling,
if he is not certain to win,
he will not act."
The *Huáyáng Guózhì* states:
"Lǐ Shì's courtesy name was Zǐrén,
a native of Luòyáng Línwèi.
Originally, he was a Cóng person from Dàngqú, Bāxī.
His ancestor was Lǐ Tè,
who seized Shǔ during the Jìn turmoil.
Tè's son, Xióng,
proclaimed himself ruler in Chéngdū.
Shì's grandfather, Xiāng,
was Tè's younger brother.
Xiāng fathered Shòu,
and Shòu usurped the throne and declared himself ruler.
Shì was Shòu's son.
The Jìn General of Peaceful the West campaigned against Shǔ,
and Shì surrendered,
relocating to Yángzhōu.
From its rise to its fall,
it lasted six generations and thirty-seven years."
The *Wēn Biézhuàn* states:
"Initially,
the court believed Shǔ was remote and perilous,
and Wēn's forces were few,
advancing deep into enemy territory,
causing great concern and fear.
Yet Wēn marched directly to Chéngdū,
and Lǐ Shì surrendered with his hands bound."
The *Yǔlín* states:
"Governor Liú observed that Lord Huán always sought victory in every game,
and said to him:
'You are so fond of profit,
why not burn your head?'
When he campaigned against Shǔ,
this remark was recalled."
Lord Xiè kept singing girls at Dōngshān,
and Jiǎnwén said:
"Ānshí will certainly emerge.
Since he shares joy with others,
he cannot avoid sharing worries with others."
Emperor Sòng Míngdì's *Wénzhāng Zhì* states:
"Ān indulged in matters beyond worldly affairs,
neglecting conventional etiquette.
He often kept singing girls,
taking them along for leisurely outings."
Xī Chāo and Xiè Xuán did not get along.
Fú Jiān was about to challenge Jìn's sovereignty,
having already wolfishly devoured Liáng and
Qí, and was now eyeing Huáiyīn like a tiger.
Chē Pín's "Book of Qín" states:
"Fú Jiān, courtesy name Yǒnggù,
was a Dí person from Wǔdū.
His original surname was Pú.
His grandfather, Hóng,
falsely claimed an auspicious prophecy,
and changed it to
'Fú'.
It meant he was destined to be king,
responding to the mandate of the prophecy.
When Jiān was born,
a red light flowed through his room.
At his birth,
red markings rose faintly on his back,
resembling seal script.
From childhood, he had a noble demeanor.
Shí Hǔ's Sīlì, Xú Zhèngmíng, was skilled at judging character.
When Jiān was six years old,
he was once playing in the street.
Zhèng saw him and found him remarkable,
asking:
'Young Master Fú!
This is an official street.
A child playing here,
are you not afraid of being bound?'
Jiān replied:
'Officials bind the guilty,
they do not bind children.'
Zhèng said to those around him:
'This child has the bearing of a king or hegemon.'
During the chaos of the Shí clan,
his uncle Jiàn and father Xióng went west into Guānzhōng.
Jiàn dreamed of a heavenly envoy in red robes and cap,
who appointed Jiāntóu as General Dragon Soaring.
Jiāntóu
was Jiān's childhood name.
Jiàn then appointed him as General Dragon Soaring,
to fulfill the divine command.
Later, Jiān usurped the imperial title.
After his death, his son Shēng succeeded,
but he was cruel and violent.
The ministers killed him and established Jiān.
After Jiān had ruled for fifteen years,
he sent the Duke of Chánglè, Pī, to attack and capture Xiāngyáng.
In the nineteenth year,
he raised a massive army to attack Jìn,
his forces reportedly numbering a million,
advancing by both water and land,
and encamped at Xiàngchéng.
From Xiàngchéng to Cháng'ān,
banners stretched for a thousand lǐ,
unbroken from front to rear.
He then sent a message to Jìn, saying:
'I have already built a grand mansion for the Jìn ruler within Cháng'ān's walls.
Now I am launching this great campaign across the river to welcome you,
and on the appointed day, you shall take residence.'"
At that time, the court deliberated on sending Xuán north to campaign,
and among the people, there were quite differing opinions.
Only Chāo said:
"He is certain to accomplish the task.
I once served with him in Huán Xuānwǔ's administration,
and I saw that he utilized talent to the fullest.
Even in matters as trivial as shoes and clogs,
he assigned them appropriately.
From this I infer,
he is likely capable of achieving merit."
After the great feat was accomplished,
people of the time all sighed in admiration of Chāo's foresight,
and further respected him for not letting personal likes and dislikes obscure good judgment.
"The Book of the Restoration" states:
"At that time, the Dí bandits were powerful and strong,
and the court deliberated on finding a capable civil and military general who could pacify the north.
Grand General Wèi Ān said:
'Only my elder brother's son, Xuán, is fit for this task.'
Secretariat Gentleman Xī Chāo heard this and sighed:
'Ān going against the crowd to recommend a relative
shows his clarity.
Xuán will certainly not fail his recommendation.'"
Hán Kāngbó and Xiè Xuán also were not particularly close.
After Xuán's northern campaign,
street gossip doubted his effectiveness.
Kāngbó said:
"This man cares for reputation,
he will certainly fight well."
"The Continued Annals of Jìnyáng Autumn" states:
"Xuán's judgment was upright and steadfast,
possessing the talent and strategy to govern the state."
Xuán heard this and was very indignant,
often saying with a stern expression among the crowd:
"A man leading a thousand troops,
entering a deadly situation,
does so to serve his lord and family—that is the reason for action,
one cannot say it is for reputation."
When Chǔ Qīshēng was young,
Xiè Gōng thought very highly of him,
constantly saying:
"If Chǔ Qīshēng does not turn out well,
I will never again judge men of talent."
Qīshēng
was the childhood name of Chǔ Shuǎng.
"The Continued Annals of Jìnyáng Autumn" states:
"Shuǎng, courtesy name Màohóng,
was from Hénán.
Grandson of Grand Tutor Chǔ Póu,
son of Secretariat Director Chǔ Sháo.
When Grand Tutor Xiè Ān saw him in his youth,
he sighed:
'If Qīshēng does not turn out well,
I will never again discuss men of talent.'
When he grew up,
he indeed proved outstanding and spirited, with a distinguished manner.
He admired the teachings of Lǎozi and
Zhuāngzi,
and disdained
the honors and praise of his time.
He was only close with Yīn Zhòngkān.
He rose through the ranks to become Secretariat Gentleman,
and Governor of Yìxīng.
His daughter became Empress to Emperor Gōng."
Xī Chāo associated with Fù Yuàn,
and Yuàn introduced his two sons, both with their hair tied up.
Chāo observed them for a long time,
then said to Yuàn:
"The younger one surpasses in talent and reputation,
but the one who will ultimately protect your family
will be the elder brother."
These were the brothers Fù Liàng.
"The Fù Clan Genealogy" states:
"Yuàn, courtesy name Shūyù,
was from Língzhōu in Běidì.
He served as Chief Clerk of the Protector General
and Governor of Ānchéng."
"The Book of Sòng" states:
"Dí, courtesy name Chángyóu,
was the eldest son of Yuàn.
He rose to the position of Minister of War.
He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Chamberlain."
Qiū Yuānzhī's "Record of Literary Works" states:
"Liàng, courtesy name Jìyǒu,
was Dí's younger brother.
He served as President of the Secretariat
and Grand Master of the Left with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
In the third year of Yuánjiā,
he was executed for his crimes."
Wáng Gōng was with his father in Kuàijī,
when Wáng Dà came from the capital to pay respects at the tombs.
Gōng's father, Yùn,
and Wáng Chén
have both been mentioned previously.
Gōng went briefly to the tombs to see him,
and as the two had always been close,
he stayed over ten days before returning.
His father asked Gōng:
"Why were you gone so many days?"
He replied:
"Conversing with Ā Dà,
the talk was continuous and I couldn't return."
His father then told him:
"I fear Ā Dà is not your friend."
In the end, their affection turned to discord,
just as he predicted.
Chén and Gōng were estranged by Wáng Xù's machinations,
eventually becoming bitter enemies.
See elsewhere.
Xiè Zǐwēi saw the brothers Xǔ Zǐjiāng and said:
"In the depths of Píngyú,
there are two dragons."
When he saw Xǔ Zǐzhèng in his youth,
he sighed and said:
"As for Xǔ Zǐzhèng,
he possesses the capacity to govern the state.
With upright demeanor and loyal integrity,
he is the equal of Chén Zhòngjǔ;
The *Biographies of Former Worthies of Rǔnán* says:
"Xiè Zhēn, styled Zǐwēi,
was from Shàolíng in Rǔnán.
He was discerning in human relationships,
even Guō Línzōng could not match Zhēn's insight.
When he saw the brothers Xǔ Zǐjiāng in their youth,
he said:
'In the depths of Píngyú there are two dragons.'
He served as an Attendant in Yùzhāng.
Xǔ Qián, styled Zǐzhèng,
was from Píngyú.
His character esteemed loftiness and purity,
elegant, upright, broad-minded, and bright.
Xiè Zǐwēi, upon seeing the Qián brothers, sighed and said:
'As for Xǔ Zǐzhèng,
he is a vessel for governing the state.'
Qián's younger brother Shào,
before his reputation had spread,
was considered by contemporaries as not equal to Qián.
Qián often patted his thigh praising Shào,
considering himself inferior.
He first took office as a Commandery Merit Officer,
dismissed the treacherous and removed the wicked,
bringing solemn order to the entire commandery.
He died at age thirty-five."
The *Biographies of Former Worthies Within the Seas* says:
"Xǔ Shào, styled Zǐjiāng,
was Qián's younger brother.
He stood firm as a mountain and was deep as an abyss,
his conduct matched the models of propriety.
Xiè Zǐwēi of Shàolíng, with high talent and far-reaching insight,
upon seeing Shào at age ten,
sighed and said:
'This is a rare great man of the age.'
Initially, Shào elevated Fán Zǐzhāo from the marketplace,
brought out Yú Chéngxián from a guesthouse,
summoned Lǐ Shūcái from obscurity,
promoted Guō Zǐyú from a minor clerk.
Xú Mènběn of Guǎnglíng came to govern Rǔnán,
hearing of Shào's high reputation,
summoned him as Merit Officer.
At that time, Yuán Shào, as a scion of the ducal house, was Magistrate of Púyáng,
but abandoned his office and returned.
With a secondary carriage and accompanying riders,
as he was about to enter the commandery borders,
he sighed and said:
'Xǔ Zǐjiāng upholds pure standards;
how can I meet him with my carriage and trappings?'
So he returned with a single horse.
He was recruited as a Commandery Officer,
but declined all earnest summons.
He took refuge south of the Yangtze,
and died in Yùzhāng."
In punishing the wicked and dismissing the unworthy,
he had the style of Fàn Mèngbó."
Zhāng Fán's *Annals of the Hàn* says:
"Fàn Pāng, styled Mèngbó,
was from Yīyáng in Rǔnán.
He served as Merit Officer,
and was recruited as a Commandery Officer.
Mounting his carriage and taking the reins,
he had the ambition to clarify all under heaven.
Hearing of Pāng's high reputation, the officials of a hundred cities
all removed their seals and ribbons and left.
He was executed due to the Partisan Proscriptions."
Gōngsūn Dù described Bǐng Yuán:
"What is called a white crane among the clouds,
cannot be caught by the nets meant for swallows and sparrows."
The *Wèi Shū* says:
"Dù, styled Shūjì,
was from Xiāngpíng.
He rose successively to Governor of Jìzhōu,
and Grand Administrator of Liáodōng."
The *Separate Biography of Bǐng Yuán* says:
"Yuán, styled Gēnjǔ,
was from Zhūxū in Dōngguǎn.
He was orphaned young.
When several years old, he passed by a schoolhouse and wept.
The teacher asked:
'Child, why do you weep?'
Yuán said:
'All those who can study
have parents.
second, I envy their chance to study.
My heart is grieved,
therefore I weep.'
The teacher, moved with pity, said:
'If you wish to learn,
no tuition is needed.'
Thereupon he began his studies.
When grown, he was widely read and knowledgeable,
his conduct like gold and jade.
Knowing the world was heading toward chaos,
he took refuge in Liáodōng.
Gōngsūn Dù treated him with great courtesy.
When the Central Plains were pacified,
he wished to return to his hometown,
but Dù prevented him.
Yuán secretly prepared for travel,
and said to his tribesmen:
'Let us move to a commandery near the north,
to observe his intention.'
They all said:
'We are willing to move.'
Yuán originally had a large fishing boat.
He invited people from the villages,
got them thoroughly drunk,
and left under cover of night.
After several days,
Dù realized it,
and his officers wanted to pursue him.
Dù said:
'Bǐng Jūn is what is called a white crane among the clouds,
not to be caught by the nets meant for quails and sparrows.'
The King of Wèi recruited him as Libationer,
and he rose successively to Chief Clerk of the Gentleman of the Five Offices."
Zhōng Shìjì described Wáng Ānfēng:
"Ā Rōng thoroughly understands people's minds."
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Róng was intelligent and perceptive from youth."
Speaking of Péi Gōng's conversation,
it lasted all day without exhausting.
Péi Wěi has been mentioned previously.
When a post in the Ministry of Personnel was vacant,
Emperor Wén asked Zhōng Huì about a candidate.
Huì said:
"Péi Kǎi is pure and penetrating,
Wáng Róng is concise and essential;
both are suitable candidates."
Thereupon Péi was appointed.
According to various texts:
Zhōng Huì recommended Péi Kǎi and
Wáng Róng to King Wén of Jìn,
and the King recruited them as Officers,
but it is not heard that they became Ministry of Personnel Gentlemen.
Wáng Jùnchōng
and Péi Shūzé, the two of them,
visited Zhōng Shìjì in their youth.
Shortly after they left,
a guest asked Zhōng:
"What about those two boys just now?"
Zhōng said:
"Péi Kǎi is pure and penetrating,
Wáng Róng is concise and essential.
Twenty years from now,
these two worthies should become Presidents of the Ministry of Personnel,
hoping that by then no talent under heaven will be left unused."
*Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"When Róng was a child,
Zhōng Huì considered him exceptional."
A saying went:
"Among later leaders, there is Péi Xiù."
Yú Yù's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Xiù, styled Jìyàn,
was from Wénxǐ in Hédōng.
His father Qián,
was Grand Master of Ceremonies for Wèi.
Xiù had dignified bearing and conduct,
and could write essays at age eight.
His paternal uncle Huī,
was renowned.
When Xiù was over ten years old,
guests visiting Huī,
upon leaving would call on Xiù.
Contemporaries said of him:
'Among later leaders, there is Péi Xiù.'
The Grand General recruited him as an Officer.
When his father died,
he yielded the property to his elder brother.
At age twenty-five,
he was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
When Jìn received the abdication,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Jùlù.
Later he rose successively to Left Brilliantly Virtuous,
and Minister of Works.
He died at forty-eight,
posthumously titled Duke Yuán,
and was enshrined in the ancestral temple."
Minister Péi assessed Xiàhóu Tàichū:
"Solemn and stately, as if entering the ancestral temple and court;
though he does not cultivate reverence, people naturally feel reverence."
The Book of Rites states:
"Zhōu Fēng said to Duke Āi of Lǔ:
'Within the ancestral temple and altars of state,
though no reverence is imposed, the people naturally feel reverence.'"
Another version says:
"As if entering the ancestral temple,
one sees only the gleaming ritual vessels and musical instruments.
Seeing Zhōng Shìjì,
is like viewing an armory,
where one sees only spears and halberds.
Seeing Fù Lánshuò,
is like a vast treasury where nothing is lacking.
Seeing Shān Jùyuán,
is like climbing a mountain and looking down,
serene and profoundly deep."
(Xiàhóu) Xuán, (Zhōng) Huì,
(Fù) Gǔ, (Shān) Tāo,
have all been mentioned previously.
When Lord Yáng returned to Luòyáng,
Guō Yì was the Magistrate of Yěwáng.
The Praise of Jin Nobles states:
"Yì, styled Tàiyè,
was from Yángqǔ, Tàiyuán.
His family was an established clan for generations.
Yì had talent and reputation,
serving successively as Governor of Yōng Province,
and Secretary.
When Yáng reached the border,
(Guō) sent someone to invite him.
Guō then went himself.
After meeting him,
he sighed, saying:
'Why must Yáng Shūzǐ be inferior to Guō Tàiyè!'
He went again to Yáng's place,
stayed briefly and returned,
and sighed again, saying:
'Yáng Shūzǐ is far beyond ordinary men!'
After Yáng had left,
Guō saw him off for a full day,
traveling several hundred li in one journey,
and was consequently dismissed from his post for leaving his jurisdiction.
He sighed again, saying:
'Why must Yáng Shūzǐ be inferior to Yánzǐ!'
Wáng Róng assessed Shān Jùyuán:
"Like unpolished jade or unrefined gold,
everyone admires his preciousness,
but none can name his true vessel."
Gù Kǎizhī's Eulogy on Paintings states:
"Tāo made no ostentatious display,
pure, deep, serene, and silent.
No one could see his limits,
and his capacity also entered the realm of the Way.
Therefore, those who saw him could not find words to describe him,
yet submitted to his great measure."
Yáng Chánghé's father, Yóu,
was a cousin of Grand Tutor Hù and they were close friends.
He served as Assistant to the Chariot and Horse General.
He died young.
Chánghé and his brothers, five in total,
were orphaned in childhood.
The Genealogy of the Yáng Clan states:
"Yóu, styled Kānfǔ,
was from Tàishān.
His grandfather Xù,
was appointed Grand Commandant of Hàn,
but did not accept the post.
His father Mì,
was Governor of Jīngzhào.
Yóu served as Assistant to the Chariot and Horse General.
He married the daughter of Yuè Guózhēn,
and had five sons:
Bǐng, Qià,
Shì, Liàng,
and Yuè."
Hù came to mourn,
and seeing Chánghé's sorrowful demeanor and comportment,
exactly like an adult's,
he sighed and said:
"My cousin is not dead!"
Shān Gōng recommended Ruǎn Xián for the post of Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
assessing him thus:
"Pure and genuine, with few desires;
the myriad things cannot sway him."
The Biographies of Famous Scholars states:
"Xián, styled Zhòngróng,
was from Chénliú,
the nephew of (Ruǎn) Jí.
Unrestrained and unconventional,
his contemporaries all thought his behavior strange.
But when they associated with him,
and his feelings of sorrow and joy were profound and genuine,
surpassing ordinary people.
Afterwards, they all forgot their previous criticisms.
He served as Gentleman Cavalier Attendant.
Shān Tāo recommended him for the Ministry of Personnel,
but Emperor Wǔ did not employ him.
Guō Yì of Tàiyuán saw him and was utterly captivated,
unconsciously sighing in admiration.
He understood music,
loved wine, and died in office.
Shān Tāo's Memorial states:
"The post of Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, Shǐ Yào, is vacant due to his departure,
and a selection must be made.
Tāo recommended Xián, saying:
'Genuine and simple, with few desires,
deeply discerning purity and impurity,
the myriad things cannot sway him.
If placed in an office responsible for appointing officials,
he would certainly be supremely excellent for his time.'
An edict appointed Lù Liàng instead."
The Chronicles of Jìn states:
"Xián's conduct often violated ritual norms.
Tāo recommended him for Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
but the Ancestral Emperor (Emperor Wǔ) did not permit it."
The Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove states:
"Shān Tāo's recommendation of Ruǎn Xián
certainly knew that the Emperor would not employ him,
but it was out of regret for a talent unmatched in his generation,
fearing that none would recognize his true worth.
Considering Xián's transgressions,
they pertained to matters beyond conventional norms.
Praising his purity, genuineness, and few desires,
then the meaning beyond his outward traces becomes self-evident."
Wáng Róng assessed Ruǎn Wényè:
"Pure in ethical judgment and possessing discerning insight;
since the time of Emperor Yuán of Hàn,
there has been no one like him."
Dù Dǔ's New Book states:
"Ruǎn Wǔ, styled Wényè,
was from Wèishì, Chénliú.
His father Chén,
served as Palace Attendant.
Wǔ was broad-minded, expansive, erudite, and penetrating,
a profound and elegant scholar."
The Records of Chénliú state:
"Wǔ,
served as Governor of Héqīng in the late Wèi period.
His clansman (Ruǎn) Jí,
in his youth was still unknown,
but Wǔ saw him and considered him exceptional,
believing he surpassed himself.
His understanding of people was often like this.
He authored a work in eighteen chapters,
called The Master Ruǎn,
and died at home."
Guō Tài's friend Sòng Zǐjùn praised Tài:
"Since the time of Emperor Yuán of Hàn,
there has been no match for Línzōng (Guō Tài)."
Wǔ Yuánxià assessed Péi (Kǎi) and
Wáng (Róng), saying:
"Róng values conciseness,
Kǎi is pure and penetrating."
Yú Yù's History of Jìn states:
"Wǔ Gāi, styled Yuánxià,
was from Zhúyì, Pèi State.
His father Zhōu,
served as Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments of Wèi.
Gāi and his two younger brothers, Xīn and
Mào, were all praised from childhood,
each possessing capacity and reputation.
The elders of their hometown
could not discern which was superior.
At that time, Liú Gōngróng of the same commandery was famous for judging people.
He once visited Zhōu,
and Zhōu presented his three sons.
Gōngróng said:
'Your three sons are all men of state talent.
Yuánxià's capacity and measure is the finest,
possessing the bearing of a chief minister.
If he pursues an official career,
he could become Vice-Duke.
Shūxià and
Jìxià are no less than regular chamberlains or remonstrance officials.'
Gāi rose to Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat."
Yǔ Zǐsōng assessed Hé Qiáo:
"Towering like a thousand-zhang pine;
though it has knots and irregularities,
when used for a great hall,
it serves as pillar and beam."
The Praise of Jin Nobles states:
"Qiáo often admired the character of his maternal uncle Xiàhóu Xuán,
therefore among court officials he stood lofty and apart from the crowd,
and his contemporaries feared his upright character and integrity."
Wáng Róng said:
"The Grand Commandant's divine bearing is lofty and pure,
like jade trees in a jasper forest,
naturally a being beyond the mundane world."
The *Biographies of Famous Scholars* states:
"Yífǔ's natural form was extraordinary,
bright and elegant like a deity."
The *Tales of the Eight Princes* states:
"When Shí Lè saw Yífǔ,
he said to his Chief Clerk Kǒng Cháng:
'I have traveled the world extensively!
Never have I seen such a man;
can he be spared?'
Cháng said:
'He is one of the Three Dukes of Jìn,
and will not serve us.'
Lè said:
'Even so,
we must not subject him to the blade.'
That night, he had him killed by pushing a wall over him."
After Wáng Rùnnán had completed mourning for his birth mother,
he remained at the gravesite.
His elder brother's son Jì would come each time to pay respects at the tomb,
barely acknowledging his uncle,
and his uncle also did not wait upon him.
When Jì occasionally visited,
they exchanged only the briefest pleasantries.
Later, Jì casually tried asking about recent affairs,
and his responses were remarkably eloquent and articulate,
surprising Jì beyond expectation,
leaving him utterly astonished.
He then conversed with him further,
and the discussion turned increasingly profound and subtle.
Jì had initially shown almost no respect due to an uncle,
but after hearing his words,
he could not help but feel awed,
his mind and demeanor both turning solemn.
He then stayed to converse with him,
for days and nights on end.
Though Jì was brilliant and forthright,
he felt himself lacking in comparison,
and sighed with admiration, saying:
"To have such a renowned scholar in the family,
and not know it for thirty years!"
When Jì departed,
his uncle saw him to the gate.
Among Jì's mounted attendants was a horse
extremely difficult to ride,
with few able to handle it.
Jì casually asked his uncle:
"Do you enjoy riding?"
He replied:
"I do enjoy it as well."
Jì then had him ride the difficult horse,
and his uncle's posture and form were so exquisite,
turning the whip as if winding silk,
that even famed riders could not surpass him.
Jì marveled even more at his unfathomable depth,
which was not limited to just one matter.
Dèng Càn's *Jìn Annals* states:
"Wáng Zhàn, styled Chǔchōng,
was from Tàiyuán.
He concealed his virtue,
and none knew of it;
even his brothers and clan
considered him foolish,
only his father Wǎng Chǎng regarded him differently.
After Chǎng's death,
he resided by the tomb,
and his elder brother's son Jì went to visit Zhàn.
Seeing the *Book of Changes* by his bedside,
Jì said to Zhàn:
'Uncle, what use do you have for this?
Have you ever read it?'
Zhàn smiled and said:
'When I am in good health,
I occasionally read it.
Today, I shall discuss it with you.'
Thus they conversed together about the *Changes*.
His analysis penetrated the subtle,
with wondrous words and extraordinary insights,
unheard of by Jì,
who sighed, unable to fathom him.
Jì had a fondness for horses,
and the horse he rode was swift and spirited,
which he cherished greatly.
Zhàn said:
'Though this horse is somewhat swift,
its strength is weak and cannot endure hardship.
Recently, I saw the postal inspector's horse,
which should surpass this one,
but it is not properly cared for.'
Jì took the postal inspector's horse and fed it grain for over ten days,
then tested it with Zhàn.
Zhàn had never ridden a horse before,
yet suddenly he galloped off,
his pace and movements no different from Jì's,
and the horse could not outdo him.
Zhàn said:
'Now we are merely riding on a straight road;
how can we distinguish which horse is superior?
Only by riding over an anthill mound!'
Thereupon, they rode in circles over an anthill mound,
and indeed the horse stumbled and fell,
such was his keen discernment and natural talent."
After returning,
Hún asked Jì:
"Why were you away for so many days?"
Jì said:
"I have just discovered an uncle."
Hún asked the reason,
and Jì recounted everything with admiration.
Hún said:
"How does he compare to me?"
Jì said:
"He surpasses me."
Whenever Emperor Wǔ saw Jì,
he would tease him about Zhàn, saying:
"Has your foolish uncle died yet?"
Jì often had no reply.
After discovering his uncle,
when the Emperor asked again as before,
Jì said:
"My uncle is not foolish."
And praised his true excellence.
The Emperor said:
"To whom can he be compared?"
Jì said:
"Below Shān Tāo,
above Wèi Shū."
The *Jìnyáng Autumn* states:
"Jì had a discerning eye for judging character,
and his distinctions between refinement and vulgarity, right and wrong,
were rarely influenced by bias.
Upon meeting Zhàn,
he sighed in admiration of his moral character.
People of the time said of Zhàn:
'Above, he falls short of Shān Tāo;
below, he surpasses Wèi Shū.'
Zhàn, hearing this, said:
'Do they intend to place me between Jì and Mèng?'"
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn History* states:
"Wèi Shū, styled Yángyuán,
was from Rènchéng.
Orphaned in childhood,
he was raised by his maternal Nìng family.
When the Nìngs were building a residence,
a physiognomist said:
'A noble nephew shall emerge from this house.'
His maternal grandmother thought that her grandson from the Shèng family, though young, was intelligent,
and believed he was the one referred to.
Shū said:
'I shall fulfill this physiognomy for my maternal family.'
In youth, he was known as slow-witted.
His paternal uncle Héng had him guard the water-powered trip-hammer,
often saying:
'If Shū can become a village head of eight hundred households,
my wishes will be fulfilled.'
Shū did not take it to heart.
He stood eight feet two inches tall,
and did not bother with ordinary mundane affairs.
Skilled in archery from a young age,
he would wear leather clothing and enter the mountains and marshes,
always returning from hunts with great success.
He served as Chief Clerk to the Rear General Zhōng Yù.
When Yù and his aides engaged in archery games,
Shū often sat and tallied the scores.
Later, when they were short of participants,
they had Shū make up the number,
whereupon he never missed a shot,
and his demeanor was composed and elegant,
nearly perfect in skill.
Yù sighed and apologized to him, saying:
'My shortcomings
are fully compensated by your archery!'
He was transferred to be an Army Advisor to the Chancellor.
Whenever the Prince of Jìn concluded court,
he would watch him depart and say:
'Wèi Shū is majestic and dignified,
a leader among men!'
He rose successively to Palace Attendant
and Minister over the Masses."
Thus he became renowned.
At the age of twenty-eight,
he began his official career.
The Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Péi was regarded by contemporaries as a forest and marsh of conversation.
The *Annals of Emperor Huì* states:
"Wěi's reasoning was profoundly erudite,
abundant in debate and refutation."
Zhāng Huà saw Chǔ Táo,
and said to Lù Píngyuán:
"You and your brother are like dragons leaping at the river crossing,
and Gù Yànxiān is like a phoenix singing at sunrise.
I thought the treasures of the southeast were already exhausted,
but unexpectedly I see Chǔ Táo again."
Lù said:
"You have not seen those who neither sing nor leap!"
The "Chǔ Family Biography" says:
"Táo, styled Jìyǎ,
was a man of Qiántáng in Wújùn,
a descendant of Master Chǔ.
Táo was exceptionally intelligent and wise,
at the age of thirteen,
he composed two rhapsodies: 'The Seagull'
and 'The Water Weight.'
Yán Zhòngbì of Wǎnlíng saw them and marveled, saying:
'Master Chǔ has been reborn!'
He was gentle and not fond of frivolity,
engaging in refined conversation and quiet contemplation,
finding amusement in the 'Fén'
and 'Diǎn' classics.
He said to his close ones:
'The sages and worthies are fully contained in the yellow scrolls;
what else should one seek beyond this?'
He declined invitations from the commandery and prefecture.
When Wú surrendered to the Shìzǔ of the Guīmìng era,
he was appointed as a Táiláng,
and later as Jiànzhōng Xiàowèi.
Minister Zhāng Huà wrote to Táo, saying:
'The two Lùs are like dragons leaping in the Jiāng
and Hàn rivers, and Yànxiān is like a phoenix singing at sunrise.
Since then,
I have often feared that the southern gold was exhausted,
but now I have found it again in you!
Thus I know that the virtue of Yánzhōu is not solitary,
and the treasures of Yuān and Dài are not depleted.'
He served up to the position of Zhōngwèi."
Someone asked the Xiùcai:
"What were the old families of Wú like?"
He replied:
"Wú Fǔjūn is the venerable elder of a sage king,
the outstanding talent of an enlightened era.
Zhū Yǒngcháng possesses the highest virtue in governing affairs,
and the lofty reputation of a pure selection.
Yán Zhòngbì is the singing crane of the nine marshes,
the white steed of the empty valley.
Gù Yànxiān is the qín and sè among the eight tones,
the dragon's pattern among the five colors.
Zhāng Wēibó is the luxuriant pine in the winter cold,
the escaping light in the dark night.
Lù Shìhéng
and Shìlóng are the soaring swan geese,
the hanging drum awaiting the mallet.
The Xiùcai
was Cài Hóng.
The 'Collection' records a letter from Hóng to Inspector Zhōu Jùn, saying:
"One day while attending in your presence,
the conversation turned to the scholars of Wú,
and you inquired among the humble,
thus posing this question to me.
In haste and facing your countenance,
I was unable to articulate a response,
so you ordered me to list their names and descriptions.
Upon retiring, I pondered it.
Now I shall briefly recount what I know:
Wú Zhǎn, styled Shìjì,
was a man of Xiàpī.
His loyalty was sufficient to correct wrongs,
his purity sufficient to inspire customs,
his trustworthiness sufficient to forge divine bonds,
his talent sufficient to manage the world.
He served Wú as Governor of Guǎngzhōu
and Prefect of Wújùn.
After Wú's pacification,
he returned to Xiàpī,
shut his doors and kept to himself,
not associating with guests.
Truly, he is the venerable elder of a sage king,
the outstanding talent of an enlightened era.
Zhū Dàn, styled Yǒngcháng,
was a man of Wújùn.
His demeanor was clear and harmonious,
yellow-centered and penetrating in principle.
He was recommended as Xiánliáng by the Wú court,
progressively promoted to Yìláng,
and now has retired to his home.
Truly, he possesses the highest virtue in governing affairs,
and the lofty reputation of a pure selection.
Yán Yǐn, styled Zhòngbì,
was a man of Wújùn.
He was endowed with a clear and pure disposition,
with profound and grand thoughts.
He was recommended as Xiánliáng by the Wú court,
and served as Magistrate of Wǎnlíng.
After Wú's pacification,
he left his post.
He is the singing crane of the nine marshes,
the white steed of the empty valley.
Zhāng Chàng, styled Wēibó,
was a man of Wújùn.
His nature was firm and bright,
his aspirations and conduct clear and upright.
Even amidst grinding and staining,
he suffered no loss of purity or resilience.
He is the pine and cypress in the winter cold,
the escaping light in the dark night."
The "Biography of Lù Yún" says:
"Yún, styled Shìlóng,
was the fifth son of Lù Kàng, the Grand Marshal of Wú,
and the younger brother of Lù Jī by the same mother.
He was refined and elegant, possessing outstanding talent,
with a majestic and imposing appearance,
eloquent and skilled in conversation,
widely learned and with a strong memory.
He excelled in writing,
and at the age of six could already compose poetry,
so that contemporaries regarded him as the equal of Xiàng Tuō
and Yáng Wū.
At the age of eighteen,
Inspector Zhōu Jùn appointed him as Zhǔbù.
Jùn often sighed, saying:
'Lù Shìlóng is the Yán Yuān of our time!'
He was progressively promoted to Crown Prince's Attendant
and Prefect of Qīnghé.
He was killed by the Prince of Chéngdū."
All these gentlemen:
took their writing brushes as plows and hoes,
and paper and slips as fertile fields.
They regarded profound silence as their cultivation,
and righteousness and principle as their bountiful harvest.
They considered discourse as their blossoms,
and loyalty and forgiveness as their treasures.
They crafted writings as brocade and embroidery,
and stored the Five Classics as silk and cloth.
They sat upon humility as their mat and cushion,
and spread righteousness and deference as their curtains and canopies.
They practiced benevolence and righteousness as their dwelling,
and cultivated virtue and morality as their vast mansion."
Note: The sixteen scholars discussed by Cài
did not include Lù Jī and his brother,
