and also lacked
"all these gentlemen"
and what follows.
It is suspected to have been added later.
Someone asked Wáng Yífǔ:
"How is Shān Jùyuán in terms of righteousness and principle?
To whom can he be compared?"
Wáng said:
"This man initially refused to regard himself as a conversationalist,
yet without reading the 'Lǎo'
or 'Zhuāng,'
when one occasionally hears his recitations,
they often align with their essence."
Gù Kǎizhī's "Painting Eulogy" says:
"Tāo possessed but did not boast,
all of this kind."
In Luòyáng, the elegant and refined Yǎyǎ included the three Gǔs:
Liú Cuì, styled Chúngǔ,
Liú Hóng, styled Zhōnggǔ,
and Liú Mò, styled Chōnggǔ,
who were blood brothers.
They were nephews of Wáng Ānfēng,
and all were sons-in-law of Wáng Ānfēng.
Hóng was the grandfather of Zhēncháng.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Cuì,
was from the Pèi commandery.
He served successively as Palace Attendant,
and General of the Southern Palace Guard.
Hóng served successively as Director of the Palace Library,
and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness."
The "Jìn Hòu Lüè" states:
"Mò was renowned from a young age for his clear discernment.
He was friendly with Wáng Yífǔ,
and both took delight in evaluating human character,
thus contemporaries praised them for their talent and wisdom.
He went from being the Senior Administrator of the Right of the Chancellor of State to become the Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
He was praised for his nobility and simplicity."
According to the "Liú Shì Pǔ," the wife of Liú Bīn,
was the daughter of Wǔ Zhōu,
and gave birth to Cuì,
Hóng, and Mò.
They were not nephews of the Wáng family.
In Luòyáng, the outstanding Féng Huìqīng,
named Sūn,
was the son of Bō.
The "Jìn Hòu Lüè" states:
"Bō, styled Yǒushēng,
was from Chánglè.
He reached the position of Grand Minister of the Imperial Clan,
and fathered Sūn."
The "Bā Wáng Gùshì" states:
"Sūn was known from a young age for his talent and insight,
understanding the exigencies of his time.
He early on held pure offices,
serving up to Palace Attendant.
He was killed by the Prince of Chángshā.
Sūn and Xíng Qiáo were both grandsons of the Minister of Education Lǐ Yìn,
and along with Yìn's son Shùn, they were all well-known.
It was said at the time:
'Féng's talent is pure,
Lǐ's talent is bright,
and Xíng is flawless.'"
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Qiáo, styled Zēngbó,
was from Héjiān.
He possessed talent and learning,
and served up to Colonel Director of the Retainers.
Shùn, styled Màncháng,
served up to Chamberlain for the Imperial Stud."
Wèi Bóyù, serving as President of the Imperial Secretariat,
saw Yuè Guǎng discussing with famous scholars of the central court,
and marveled, saying:
"Since the passing of those gentlemen of old,
I have often feared that subtle discourse would be cut off.
Now I hear such words from you again!"
He ordered his sons and younger brothers to visit him, saying:
"This man
is a mirror of water to people;
seeing him is like parting the clouds and mist to gaze upon the blue sky."
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"President of the Imperial Secretariat Wèi Guàn, upon seeing Guǎng, said:
'Since the passing of Hé Píngshū and others,
I often thought that pure discourse had ended,
but now I hear it again from you!'"
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Wèi Guàn was skilled in philosophical reasoning,
and when he discussed with Hé Yàn,
Dèng Yáng, and others on several occasions,
upon seeing Guǎng, he marveled, saying:
'Each time I see this man,
it is brilliantly clear, as if parting the clouds and mist to gaze upon the blue sky.'"
The Grand Commandant Wáng said:
"Seeing Minister Péi's brilliance and clarity,
he towers above others,
which is no ordinary insight.
If the dead could rise again,
I would wish to follow him."
Some say these were the words of Wáng Róng.
The "Lǐjì" states:
"Zhào Wénzǐ and Shū Yù observed at Jiǔyuán,
Wénzǐ said:
'If the dead could rise again,
with whom would I wish to associate?'"
Zhèng Xuán notes:
"'Zuò'
means to rise."
Wáng Yífǔ sighed to himself:
"Whenever I converse with Minister Yuè,
I cannot help but feel my words are verbose."
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"Yuè Guǎng was adept at using concise words to satisfy people's minds;
regarding what he did not know,
he remained silent.
Grand Commandant Wáng Yífǔ
and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Péi Shūzé were skilled in pure discourse,
and often said:
'When conversing with Master Yuè,
one feels his simplicity and directness,
while we all seem verbose.'"
Guō Zǐxuán possessed outstanding talent,
and was skilled in discussing the "Lǎozǐ"
and "Zhuāngzǐ."
Yǔ Kǎi once praised him,
frequently saying:
"Why must Guō Zǐxuán be inferior to Yǔ Zǐsōng!"
The "Míngshì Zhuàn" states:
"Guō Xiàng, styled Zǐxuán,
from the position of Gentleman of the Yellow Gate became the Registrar of the Grand Tutor,
wielding authority and influence,
and swayed the entire administration.
Kǎi said to Xiàng:
'You are indeed a great talent of our time;
my former intentions
are now entirely exhausted!'
His submission to principle and sincere admiration
were all of this kind."
Wáng Píngzǐ appraised the Grand Commandant:
"Elder brother's appearance resembles the Way,
but his spirit and edge are too sharp."
The Grand Commandant replied:
"I truly am not as composed and serene as you."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Chéng was clear and perceptive, fond of evaluating human character,
and his emotions were unattached."
The Grand Tutor had three talents:
Liú Qìngsūn, a talent of administration,
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"When the Grand Tutor was about to summon Liú Yú,
someone said:
'Yú is like grease;
approaching will soil people.'
The Grand Tutor became suspicious and kept him at a distance.
Yú then secretly examined the military registers of the realm,
the locations of all garrisons and storehouses,
the amounts of grain,
oxen, horses, and equipment,
and the terrain of land and water routes,
memorizing them all.
At that time, military and state affairs were numerous,
and whenever matters were discussed in meetings,
from Pān Tāo downwards, none knew how to respond.
Yú would then count on his fingers and calculate,
the locations for deploying troops and weapons,
the transport of grain supplies,
and matters proceeded without obstruction.
Thereupon, the Grand Tutor entrusted him with authority."
Pān Yángzhòng, a talent of great capacity,
and Péi Jǐngshēng, a talent of purity.
The "Bā Wáng Gùshì" states:
"Liú Yú's talent lay in comprehensive administration and verification,
Pān Tāo was renowned for his broad learning,
Péi Miǎo was strong-willed and upright,
all were favored by the Prince of Dōnghǎi,
and were prominent in the same administration.
Therefore, contemporaries praised them, saying:
Yú, a talent of administration,
Tāo, a talent of great capacity,
and Miǎo, a talent of purity."
The worthies beneath the grove
each had a talented son.
Jí Kǎng's son Jí Shào
was broad-minded and magnanimous.
The Shìyǔ states:
"Shào, styled Chángchéng,
was pure, empty, and had few desires.
He attained the position of Palace Attendant to the Heir Apparent."
Jí Kǎng's son Jí Shào
was pure, far-reaching, elegant, and upright.
Already seen."
Shān Tāo's son Shān Jiǎn
was open-minded, penetrating, lofty, and plain.
Yú Yù's Jìn Shū states:
"Jiǎn, styled Jìlún,
was even-tempered and elegant, possessing his father's manner.
He was equally famous with Jí Shào
and Liú Mò, among others.
He was promoted to Secretary,
and went out to serve as General Who Conquers the South."
Ruǎn Xián's son Ruǎn Zhān
was empty, peaceful, and had far-reaching aspirations.
Zhān's younger brother Ruǎn Fú
was bright and clear, and left many things behind.
The Míngshì Zhuàn states:
"Zhān, styled Qiānlǐ,
was peaceful and responsible, with few cravings or desires.
He did not cultivate fame or conduct,
but was self-content in his bosom.
When reading books, he did not deeply research or seek,
yet grasped their essentials.
He served as a Gentleman of the Heir Apparent's Household.
He died at age thirty."
The Zhōngxīng Shū states:
"Fú's demeanor was open-minded and unrestrained;
from youth he had the family style.
Initially serving as Adjutant to the General Who Pacifies the East,
with disheveled hair and drinking wine,
he did not let princely affairs burden his heart."
Xiàng Xiù's sons Xiàng Chún
and Xiàng Tì were both virtuous and had pure reputations.
The Zhúlín Qī Xián Lùn states:
"Chún, styled Chángtì,
attained the position of Palace Attendant.
Tì, styled Shūxùn,
attained the position of Palace Censor."
The Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn states:
"When Luòyáng fell,
Chún and Tì fled,
and were killed by bandits."
Wáng Róng's son Wáng Wànzi
had the manner of great accomplishment,
but sprouted without flowering.
The Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn states:
"Wáng Suí, styled Wànzi,
was recruited as Clerk to the Grand Commandant,
but did not take the post.
He died at age nineteen."
The Jìn Shū states:
"Róng's son Wàn
had a fine reputation but was too fat.
Róng ordered him to eat chaff,
but he grew even fatter."
Only Liú Líng's son left no record.
Among all these sons,
only Zhān was the foremost,
and Shào and Jiǎn were also esteemed in their time.
Yǔ Zǐgōng had a disability,
yet was very well-known.
His home was west of the city,
and it was called the Ducal Mansion West of the City.
Yú Yù's Jìn Shū states:
"Cóng, styled Zǐgōng,
was from Yǐngchuān,
the second son of the Minister of Ceremonies Jùn,
and served as Clerk to the Grand Commandant."
Wáng Yífǔ said to Music Commandant Yuè:
"True famous scholars are not many,
so we should allow Píngzǐ to know them."
The Wáng Chéng Biézhuàn states:
"Chéng's demeanor was lofty and penetrating,
his will and spirit unmatched.
His elder cousin Róng
and elder brother Yífǔ
were the most famous of their time.
When men from all within the four seas
were once evaluated by Chéng,
then his two elder brothers would no longer pay attention,
saying
'they have already been assessed by Píngzǐ.'
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
Thus his fame grew ever greater,
and all under heaven, whether they knew him or not,
none failed to admire him.
Later, Chéng's deeds did not match up,
and court and commoners were disappointed.
Yet those who had known him from earlier travels and acquaintance
still said:
'He is a famous scholar of the present age.'"
Grand Commandant Wáng said:
"Guō Zǐxuán's discourse is like a waterfall pouring water,
gushing forth without exhaustion."
The Míngshì Zhuàn states:
"Zǐxuán had outstanding talent,
and could discourse on the Zhuāngzǐ
and Lǎozǐ."
Grand Tutor Sīmǎ's headquarters had many famous scholars,
outstanding talents of the time.
Yǔ Wénkāng said:
"Seeing Zǐsōng among them,
I often feel my spirit naturally exalted."
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Yǐ served as Adjutant to the Grand Tutor."
Grand Tutor, the Prince of Dōnghǎi, garrisoned Xǔchāng,

Yǔ Liàng asked where he was,
and Huán immediately recounted the story.
Xú Níng was promoted successively to Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
General of the Left,
and Governor of Jiāng Province."
Huán Màolún said:
"Chǔ Jìyě has the *Spring and Autumn Annals* within his skin."
This means he judges with fairness.
*The Spring and Autumn Annals of Jìn* states:
"Chǔ Póu was simple, solemn, and possessed insight."
Therefore, he was thus described by Huán Yí.
Hé Cìdào once escorted some people from the east,
and looking ahead, he saw Jiǎ Níng in a carriage behind,
saying:
"If this man does not die,
he will eventually become a valued guest of the feudal lords."
*The Spring and Autumn Annals of Jìn* states:
"Jiǎ Níng, courtesy name Jiànníng,
was from Chánglè,
an illegitimate son of the Jiǎ family.
Initially, he associated himself with Wáng Yīng
and Zhūgě Yáo.
After Wáng Yīng's downfall,
he wandered in Wú and Kuàijī,
where the people of Wú all insulted him.
Hearing of the turmoil in the capital,
he rushed out and joined Sū Jùn,
who grew very close to him,
making him his chief strategist.
When Sū Jùn heard that the righteous army was rising,
he moved from Gūzhú to garrison Shítóu—
this was Jiǎ Níng's plan.
After Sū Jùn's defeat,
Jiǎ Níng surrendered first.
He served up to the position of Prefect of Xīn'ān."
When Dù Hóngzhì's tomb collapsed,
his expression of grief was deemed inappropriate.
Yǔ Liàng turned to the guests and said:
"Hóngzhì is extremely frail,
and cannot be expected to show intense grief."
*The Spring and Autumn Annals of Jìn* states:
"Dù Yì, courtesy name Hóngzhì,
was from Jīngzhào.
His grandfather Dù Yù
and father Dù Xī
were renowned in previous reigns.
Dù Yì had a fine reputation from a young age,
served as Assistant Magistrate of Dānyáng,
and died early.
Emperor Chéng took Dù Yì's daughter as his empress."
It also says:
"Hóngzhì's weeping should not be overly sorrowful."
The world praised
"Yǔ Wénkāng as the jade of a bountiful year,
and Yǔ Zhìgōng as the grain of a famine year."
The Yǔ family discussion states that Wénkāng praised
"Zhìgōng as the grain of a famine year,
and Yǔ Chángrén as the jade of a bountiful year."
This means Yǔ Liàng had the capacity for high office,
and Yǔ Yì had the talent to save the world,
each being useful in their own way.
The world described
"Dù Hóngzhì as outstandingly brilliant,
and Chǔ Jìyě as solemn and youthful."
*Biographies of Famous Gentlemen of Jiāngzuǒ* states:
"Dù Yì
was of pure and outstanding character, a fine gentleman."
Someone described Dù Hóngzhì:
"Outstandingly brilliant and pure,
with the demeanor of abundant virtue,
worthy of joyful praise."
*Forest of Conversations* states:
"Someone described Dù Hóngzhì,
as outstandingly brilliant and very pure,
initially appearing cheerful and pleasant,
yet his countenance lacked charm,
but his demeanor of abundant virtue,
is worthy of joyful praise."
Yǔ Liàng said:
"Wáng Yìshǎo is acclaimed by the state."
Therefore, Yǔ Ní wrote in his epitaph:
"Outstandingly eminent, acclaimed by the state."
Ní was the childhood name of Yǔ Qiàn.
Xú Guǎng's *Annals of Jìn* states:
"Yǔ Qiàn, courtesy name Shǎoyàn,
was the son of Minister of Works Yǔ Bīng,
and the elder brother of the empress.
He possessed talent and ability,
and served up to Chief Clerk to the Grand Tutor.
Huán Wēn, because his clan was powerful,
had King Huǎng of Xiàpī falsely accuse him of plotting rebellion and had him executed."
Yǔ Zhìgōng wrote to Huán Wēn,
praising
"Liú Dàoshēng attends to affairs day and night,
handling matters great and small with exceptional efficiency.
His sense of righteousness and capacity for enjoyment are both excellent,
and moreover, he is fully capable of being a friend.
Truly, he is a fine vessel indeed.
I recommend him to you,
as one who can join you in overcoming hardships."
Emperor Míng of Sòng's *Record of Literary Works* states:
"Liú Huī, courtesy name Dàoshēng,
was from Pèi State.
He had clear and comprehensive judgment,
and possessed both civil and military talents.
Wáng Méng often praised his profound and thorough reasoning,
considering him an excellent choice for a frontier defender.
He served as Marshal of the Chariots and Cavalry.
He died at the age of thirty-six,
and was posthumously awarded the title of Former General."
When Wáng Lántián was appointed Governor of Yáng Province,
his Registrar requested the taboos (names to be avoided),
and he instructed:
"My late ancestors and father
are renowned throughout the land,
known far and wide.
The taboos for female relatives are not to be disclosed outside,
as *The Book of Rites* says:
'The taboos for women do not go beyond the gate.'
Beyond that, there are no other taboos."
Xiāo Zhōngláng
was the father-in-law of Sūn Chénggōng.
When Liú Yǐn was at Fǔjūn's place,
at that time Xiāo was being considered for the position of Tàicháng.
Liú Yǐn said:
"I don't know if Xiāo Zǔzhōu can become one of the Three Dukes or not?
But for any position below that,
there is nothing he is not capable of."
The "Jìn Bǎiguān Míng" says:
"Xiāo Lún, styled Zǔzhōu,
was from Lè'ān."
Liú Qiānzhī's "Jìn Jì" says:
"Lún had talent and learning,
excelling in the 'Three Rituals',
and served successively as Chángshì
and Guózǐ Bóshì."
Before Xiè Tàifù had reached the age of capping,
he first went west,
to visit Wáng Zhǎngshǐ.
They engaged in pure conversation for a long time.
After he left,
Xúnzǐ asked:
Wáng Méng
and Zǐxiū have both already been introduced.
"How does the guest who just left compare to you, father?"
Zhǎngshǐ said:
"That guest was earnest and diligent,
his manner was imposing."
Wáng Yòujūn said to Liú Yǐn:
"We should indeed jointly recommend Ānshí."
Liú Yǐn said:
"If Ānshí establishes his resolve on Dōngshān,
then we should join with all under heaven to recommend him."
"Xù Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Initially,
Xiè settled his family in Shàngyú County, Kuàijī,
leisurely enjoying the mountains and forests.
For six or seven years,
imperial summonses did not reach him.
Although memorials of impeachment were submitted one after another,
followed by confinement,
he remained calm and unperturbed."
Xiè Gōng praised Lántián:
"Even when you peel off his skin, it's all genuine."
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Jì" says:
"Shù was sincere and careful,
his true intentions were not outwardly displayed."
Huán Wēn was traveling and passed by Wáng Dūn's tomb.
Looking at it, he said:
"A likable man!
A likable man!"
Sūn Chuò wrote in his "Jiān" to Yǔ Liàng:
"The designation of Wáng Dūn as a 'likable man',
has lasted for several decades."
Yīn Zhōngjūn said of Wáng Yòujūn:
"Yìshǎo is a pure and noble man.
I treat him with the utmost regard,
at present, there is no one I place after him."
"Wénzhāng Zhì" says:
"Xīzhī was lofty and forthright, possessing an air of distinction,
not like the common crowd."
Wáng Zhòngzǔ praised Yīn Yuānyuán:
"Not only does he surpass others with his strengths,
he also surpasses others in how he handles his strengths."
"Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Hào was adept at interacting with others through harmony and understanding."
Wáng Sīzhōu was conversing with Yīn Zhōngjūn.
He sighed and said:
"The depths of my own storehouse,
were long ago poured out and revealed.
But Yīn's array is vast and boundless,
its many sources cannot be fathomed."
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Jì" says:
"Hào's pure conversation and marvelous debate reached profound subtleties.
The famous figures of the time,
all praised him highly."
Wáng Zhǎngshǐ said to Lín Gōng:
"Zhēncháng can truly be said to have a hall full of gold and jade."
Lín Gōng said:
"If the hall is full of gold and jade,
then why is he so selective in speech?"
Wáng said:
"It's not that he selects his words,
it's just that the place from which his words come forth is naturally sparse."
This means that the words of an auspicious man are few,
not that he chooses his words before speaking.
Wáng Zhǎngshǐ said of Jiāng Dàoqún:
"What others ought to have,
he does not necessarily have;
what others ought not to have,
he definitely does not have."
"Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Jiāng Guàn, styled Dàoqún,
was from Chénliú.
He was the younger cousin of Púshè Bīn.
He had talent and ability.
His fame was second only to that of his elder cousin Yóu.
He served as Shàngshū
and Zhōnghùjūn."
Kuàijī's Kǒng Chén,
Wèi Yǐ,
Yú Qiú,
Yú Cún,
and Xiè Fèng,
were all outstanding men of these four clans,
the heroes of their time.
Chén, Cún,
Yǐ, and Fèng are all mentioned elsewhere.
"Yú Shì Pǔ" says:
"Qiú, styled Hélín,
was from Yúyáo, Kuàijī.
His grandfather Shòu
was Governor of Guǎngzhōu under Wú.
His father Jī
was Yòujūn Sīmǎ.
Qiú served up to the position of Huángmén Shìláng."
Sūn Xìnggōng described them thus:
"Chén is the gold of the Kǒng family,
Yǐ is the jade of the Wèi family,
Yú is the leader of Cháng
and Lín's clan,
Xiè is the one who bows to Hóngdào."
Cháng and Lín
are the styles of Cún and Qiú respectively.
Hóngdào
is the style of Xiè Fèng.
This means the Yú clan reveres the talent of Cháng
and Lín,
and the Xiè clan bows to the virtue of Hóngdào.
Wáng Zhòngzǔ
and Liú Zhēncháng went to visit Yīn Zhōngjūn for conversation.
After the conversation ended,
they rode in the same carriage away.
Liú said to Wáng:
"Yuānyuán is truly commendable."
Wáng said:
"You have fallen into his clouds and mist."
"Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Hào was skilled in discussing principles,
his discourse was subtle and profound.
He excelled in the "Lǎozi"
and "Yìjīng",
so those of refined taste all revered and followed him."
Liú Yǐn often praised Wáng Zhǎngshǐ, saying:
"His nature is supremely open,
yet he is naturally restrained."
"Méng Biézhuàn" says:
"In his interactions with others, Méng
emptied himself to accept goodness,
considered carefully before acting,
and rarely showed signs of joy or anger.
Anyone who met him even once,
could not but respect and love him.
However, he was orphaned young,
and served his various mothers with great respect.
He was devoted to righteousness and harmonious with his clan,
did not fuss over minor matters of purity,
and was praised for his pure poverty."
Wáng Yòujūn said of Xiè Wànshí
"amidst forests and marshes,
he is naturally vigorous and lofty."
He praised Lín Gōng
"his capacity is bright, his spirit outstanding."
"Zhī Dùn Biézhuàn" says:
"Dùn followed his heart and went his own way,
his bearing and aspirations were lofty and bright."
He said of Zǔ Shìshǎo
"the wind in his bearing, his hair and bones,
I fear I will not see such a man again in this lifetime."
He said of Liú Zhēncháng
"marks the cloudy branches, yet does not rely on spreading foliage."
"Liú Yǐn Biézhuàn" says:
"Dàn already possessed fine reputation,
and was related by marriage to the imperial house,
thus he repeatedly held high office.
However, his nature was not to conform to vulgar customs,
his heart was indifferent to glory and profit.
Although he personally ascended to prominent rank,
he often remained humble and restrained,
quietly and calmly maintaining his own integrity."
Jiǎnwén appraised Yǔ Chìyù:
"He is straightforward and unaffected, and handles affairs with ease."
Xiè Rénzǔ said:
"Yǔ Chìyù harbors no old grievances in his heart."
Chìyù
was the childhood name of Yǔ Tǒng.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Tǒng's courtesy name was Chángrén,
a man of Yǐngchuān,
son of the General of the Guards, Yì.
He enjoyed a fine reputation from a young age,
and his official career reached the post of Xúnyáng Commandant."
Yīn Zhōngjūn spoke of Hán Tàicháng, saying:
"Kāngbó set high standards for himself from youth,
and was indeed an outstanding talent.
When he speaks and expresses himself,
it is often full of charm and feeling."
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Kāngbó was pure, harmonious, and thoughtful,
praised by his maternal uncle Yīn Hào from childhood."
Jiǎnwén spoke of Wáng Huáizǔ:
"His talent is not great,
nor is he indifferent to fame and profit;
yet simply by being genuinely straightforward in small measure,
he is more than enough to match others in great measure."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Shù was poor and frugal in his youth,
living in a humble lane with simple food and drink,
not seeking fame or advancement,
and thus was esteemed by those of discernment."
Lín Gōng said to Wáng Yòujūn:
"When Chángshǐ speaks several hundred words,
they are all virtuous words,
only it is a pity they are not 'bitter'."
'Bitter' means to press someone hard with words.
Wáng said:
"Chángshǐ himself does not wish to press others hard."
Yīn Zhōngjūn, in a letter to someone,
said of Xiè Wàn
"his literary reasoning grows ever more vigorous,
achieving this is truly not easy."
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Wàn was talented, capable, and outstanding,
skilled at promoting himself,
thus gaining timely praise.
He was also skilled at composing literature,
able to engage in discourse,
and was praised by his contemporaries."
Wáng Chángshǐ said:
"Jiāng Sīquān's breadth of thought and understanding
is not limited to the Confucian realm."
Xú Guǎng's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Jiāng Dūn, courtesy name Sīquān,
a man of Chénliú,
younger brother of the Vice Director, Bīn.
He was diligent in study by nature,
never letting books leave his hand,
widely read in the ancient classics,
synthesizing both Confucianism and Daoism.
He did not accept any summons to office,
and died at the age of forty-nine."
When Xǔ Xuándù was seeing his mother off,
just as he left the capital,
someone asked Liú Yǐn:
"Does Xuándù truly live up to what we have heard?"
Liú said:
"His talent and sensibility exceed what we have heard."
The *Xǔ Shì Pǔ* states:
"Xuándù's mother
was the daughter of Huá Yì."
According to the *Xún Collection*,
Xún left the capital to welcome his elder sister,
and composed a poem on the road;
the *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* also states this.
Yet here it says he was seeing his mother off,
which is likely an error.
Ruǎn Guānglù said:
"The Wáng family has three young men:
Yòujūn,
Ānqī,
and Chángyù."
Ruǎn Yù,
Wáng Yuè,
Ānqī,
and Wáng Yīng have all been mentioned previously.
Xiè Gōng spoke of Yùzhāng:
"If he encountered the Seven Worthies,
he would certainly take them by the arm and enter the forest."
The *Jiāngzuǒ Míngshì Zhuàn* states:
"Kūn was straightforward, simple, and discerning,
not cultivating a dignified manner.
He loved ease and freedom, yet his mind was orderly;
his appearance was coarse, yet his speech was refined.
He lived as if in filth,
yet his actions were not burdened by loftiness.
A neighbor had a daughter,
whom he once went to provoke.
The girl was weaving at the time,
and threw her shuttle, breaking two of his teeth.
After returning home,
he proudly let out a long whistle and said:
'It still doesn't stop me from whistling and singing.'
Such was his disregard for physical form."
Wáng Chángshǐ praised Lín Gōng:
"His achievement in probing the subtle
is no less than Fǔsì's."
The *Zhī Dùn Biézhuàn* states:
"Dùn's spirit and mind were alert and perceptive,
his pure discernment profound and far-reaching.
When he once went to the capital,
Wáng Zhòngzǔ praised his achievement in reaching the subtle,
as no different from Wáng Bì."
Yīn Yuānyuán remained at the family graves for nearly ten years.
At that time, both court and commoners compared him to Guǎn [Zhòng] and [Zhūgě] Liàng,
and whether he would take office or not
was used to prognosticate the rise and fall of Jiāngzuǒ.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"At that time, Emperor Mù was young,
and the Empress Dowager presided over the court.
Jiǎnwén, being close to the worthy and enjoying the people's hopes,
was appointed to the post of Chief Minister.
Huán Wēn had the merit of pacifying Shǔ
and Luò,
and wielded power in the western region.
The Emperor, considering himself weak in civil affairs,
had no means to oppose him.
Yīn Hào of Chénjùn
had long enjoyed great fame,
and contemporary opinion compared him to Guǎn [Zhòng] and [Zhūgě] Liàng.
Therefore, Hào was summoned to be Governor of Yángzhōu.
Wēn knew the intent was to oppose himself,
and was greatly angered by it."
Yīn Zhōngjūn spoke of Wáng Yòujūn:
"His pure discernment is noble and essential."
The *Jìn Āndì Jì* states:
"Xīzhī's bearing and character were pure and outstanding."
Xiè Tàifù served as Marshal for Duke Huán.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Initially,
Ān wandered leisurely among mountains and waters,
amusing himself with composing writings and analyzing principles.
Huán Wēn, stationed in the western frontier,
admired his great reputation,
and hinted to the court to invite him to serve as Marshal.
As the way of the world was not yet peaceful,
his will lay in aiding and saving it.
At the age of forty,
he began his official career to attend to affairs."
Huán visited Xiè,
finding Xiè combing his hair.
Xiè hastily fetched his robe and cap,
but Duke Huán said:
"Why trouble yourself with this."
Thereupon, they sat down and talked until dusk.
After leaving,
Huán said to his attendants:
"Have you ever seen such a man before?"
When Xiè Gōng served as Marshal for Xuānwǔ,
he entrusted several tens of his disciples to Tiáncáo Vice Director Zhào Yuèzǐ.
Fú Tāo's *Dàsīmǎ Liáoshǔ Míng* states:
"Yuè, courtesy name Yuèzǐ,
a man of Xiàpī.
He successively held the posts of Dàsīmǎ Army Advisor
and General of the Left Guard."
Yuèzǐ reported this to Xuānwǔ,
and Xuānwǔ said:
"Use half for now."
Zhào soon employed them all,
saying:
"In the past, when Ānshí was at Dōngshān,
the gentry urgently pressed him,
fearing he would not participate in human affairs;
how much more now, when he himself selects from his hometown,
should I go against his wishes?"
Huan Xuānwǔ's "Memorial" states:
"Xiè Shàng possesses a spirit of uprightness and forthrightness,
and from youth has garnered the people's acclaim."
The "Collection of Wēn" records his "Memorial on Pacifying Luò" as follows:
"Now that the Central Provinces are pacified,
it is timely to bring about stability.
General Zhènxī and Governor of Yùzhōu, Shàng,
possesses a spirit of uprightness and forthrightness,
and from youth has garnered people's acclaim.
Therefore, he has entered to assist the myriad officials,
and gone out to guard the regional administration.
It is fitting that he advance and occupy Luòyáng,
to pacify and soothe the common people.
It is proposed that he retain his current office and be appointed Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Sīzhōu."
The world regarded Xiè Shàng as refined and enlightened.
Ruǎn Yáojí said:
"His clarity and expansiveness resemble enlightenment."
Some said:
"Shàng is naturally refined and superior."
"Jìn Yáng Qiū" states:
"Shàng was straightforward, forthright, and enlightened,
attracting understanding and refined superiority."
Grand Marshal Huán was ill.
Xiè Gōng went to visit him in his illness,
entering through the eastern gate.
Wēn was at Gūshú at the time.
Duke Huán gazed from afar,
and sighed, saying:
"It has been long since I have seen such a person within my gates!"
Jiǎnwén characterized Jìngyù as
"bright and joyful."
Wáng Tián has been previously mentioned.
"Wénzì Zhì" states:
"Tián understood principles clearly and esteemed them,
and was the crown among the younger generation."
Sūn Xìnggōng served as Yǔ Gōng's army advisor,
and together they traveled to Báishí Mountain.
Wèi Jūnzhǎng was present.
"Wèi Shì Pǔ" states:
"Yǒng, styled Jūnzhǎng,
was from Chéngyáng,
and his rank reached Left Army Chief Clerk."
Sūn said:
"This man's spirit and emotions are not at all concerned with mountains and waters,
yet he is capable of composing writings."
Yǔ Gōng said:
"Although Wèi's grace and charm are not equal to you gentlemen,
the places where he captivates are also not shallow."
Sūn then immersed himself in these words.
Wáng Yòujūn characterized Chén Xuánbó:
"He has accumulated substance and proper bone."
Chén Tài has been previously mentioned.
Chief Clerk Wáng said:
"Administrator Liú knows me,
better than I know myself."
"Méng Biézhuàn" states:
"Méng and Liú Tán of the Peì State were equally renowned.
People of the time compared Méng to Yuán Yàoqīng,
and Tán to Xún Fèngqiàn,
and they befriended each other,
greatly appreciating and understanding one another."
Wáng and
Liú listened to Reverend Lín lecture.
Wáng said to Liú:
"That person on the high seat just now,
is indeed a formidable figure."
Listening further,
Wáng again said:
"He is truly a latter-day Wáng and
Hé after the alms bowl."
"Gāoyì Shāmén Zhuàn" states:
"Wáng Méng often sought out Dùn.
Encountering him lecturing at the Zhīhuán Temple,
he was precisely on the high seat.
Each time he raised his yak-tail whisk,
he would often expound several hundred words,
with both principle and sentiment flowing freely.
Over a hundred people were present in the seats,
all holding their tongues and listening intently.
Méng said, 'Among the monks listening to the lecture,
that person on the high seat
is a latter-day Wáng and
Hé after the alms bowl.'"
Xǔ Xuándù said:
"As stated in the 'Ode to the Lute':
'If one is not of the utmost refinement,
one cannot analyze principles with him.'
Administrator Liú is such a man;
'If one is not profoundly tranquil,
one cannot dwell in leisure with him,'
Jiǎnwén is such a man."
This is from Jī Shūyè's "Ode to the Lute."
Liú Tán, styled Zhēncháng,
was Administrator of Dānyáng.
The Wèi Yǐn brothers,
from youth possessed learning and righteousness.
"Wèi Shì Pǔ" states:
"Yǐn, styled Ānshí,
was from Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
He served successively as Governor of Yìxīng,
and Palace Censor.
His younger brother Dàng,
was a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate."
In their youth, they visited Xiè Fèng.
Fèng spoke with them,
and was greatly pleased,
saying:
"Although the main lineage has declined,
the Wèi clan already again has worthy men."
Jiǎnwén said:
"Yuānyuán's speech does not reach extraordinary heights of conciseness;
however, in the areas of managing affairs and pondering,
he indeed has structure and arrangement."
Initially,
Fǎtài came from the north and was not yet known.
Chē Pín's "Qín Shū" states:
"Shì Dào'ān was captured by Mùróng Jìn,
and wished to go to Xiāngyáng.
Upon reaching Xīnyě,
he gathered the assembly to deliberate, saying:
'Now we encounter a calamitous year;
if we do not rely on a ruler of a state,
then Buddhist affairs will be difficult to establish.'
He then divided the monastic community,
sending Zhú Fǎtài to Yángzhōu,
saying:
'There are many gentlemen there,
a superior region where we may go.'
Fǎtài then crossed the river,
and reached the land of Yáng."
Commander-in-Chief Wáng provided for him.
"Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Wáng Qià, styled Jìnghé,
was the third son of Chancellor Dǎo's younger brother.
He successively rose to be Governor of Wú Commandery,
and was cherished by the gentry and common people.
He was summoned and appointed as Central Commander-in-Chief,
and soon additionally as Central Secretariat Director,
but did not accept the appointment.
He died at the age of twenty-six."
Whenever [Commander-in-Chief Wáng] socialized,
going to visit famous and distinguished persons,
he would always take [Fǎtài] along.
If he could not get Tài,
he would stop his carriage and not proceed.
Because of this, [Fǎtài's] reputation subsequently became great.
"Míngdé Shāmén Tímù" states:
"Fǎtài was lofty, bright, open, and enlightened."
Sūn Chuò composed a "Eulogy" for Tài, saying:
"A chilly wind sweeps the forest,
bright springs reflect the ravine.
Refreshing and clear, Fǎtài,
examining virtue, without shame.
Detached and carefree beyond worldly affairs,
spirit within, broad and expansive.
Substance arose from the former,
name leapt forward afterward."
"Tàiyuán Qǐjū Zhù" states:
"Fǎtài died at the age of twelve.
Emperor Lièzōng issued an edict, saying:
'Master Fǎtài has passed away,
causing grief and sorrow in our heart.
He may be granted one hundred thousand coins.'"
Chief Clerk Wáng, in a letter to the Grand Marshal,
said of Yuānyuán
"His understanding and disposition are peaceful and settled,
fully matching contemporary discussions."
Xiè Gōng said:
"Administrator Liú's speech is careful and detailed."
Sūn Chuò, in the "Preface to the Dirge for Tán," said:
"His spirit was like an abyssal mirror,
his words were invariably pearls and jade."
Duke Huán said to Jiābīn:
"Ā Yuán possesses both virtue and eloquence.
Had he been made a Director or Vice Director,
he would have been fully capable of serving as a model for the myriad officials.
The court employed him contrary to his talent."
Jiābīn
is the childhood name of Xī Chāo.
Ā Yuán
is Yīn Hào.
Jiǎnwén said to Jiābīn:
"Liú Yǐn's words at the end also differed slightly,
but upon reconsidering his speech,
it was indeed without fault."
Sūn Xìnggōng
and Xǔ Xuándù were together at Báilóu Pavilion.
The *Huìjī Jì* states:
"The pavilion is located at Shānyīn,
overlooking the stream and reflecting the ravines."
They discussed together the famous and accomplished figures of the past.
Lín Gōng was not involved in the topic,
but after listening, he said:
"The two worthies indeed possess talent and sentiment."
Wáng Yòujūn said of Dōngyáng
"Our family's Ā Lín,
his clarity and purity are truly outstanding."
"Lín"
should be
"Lín."
The *Wángshì Pǔ* states:
"Línzhī, styled Zhòngchǎn,
was from Lángyá,
the son of Minister Bīao.
He served as the governor of Dōngyáng."
Wáng Chángshǐ wrote to Liú Yǐn,
saying of Yuānyuán
"he handles affairs with constant ease."
Xiè Zhōngláng said:
"Wáng Xiūzài's carefree nature
comes from his family tradition."
The *Wángshì Pǔ* states:
"Qízhī, styled Xiūzài,
was from Lángyá,
the third son of Yì, the governor of Jīngzhōu.
He served as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
governor of Póyáng,
and Palace Attendant."
Lín Gōng said:
"Wáng Jìngrén is a person of transcendent understanding."
The *Wénzì Zhì* states:
"Xiūzhī was praised from a young age for his outstanding talent."
Liú Yǐn first praised Xiè Zhènxī,
and later Xiè greatly esteemed Liú, saying:
"In the past, I once faced north as his student."
Note: Xiè Shàng was older than Tán,
and his brilliance was evident from an early age,
so saying he faced north as Liú's student
is not credible.
Xiè Tàifù praised Wáng Xiūlíng, saying:
"Sīzhōu is someone with whom one can wander in forests and marshes."
The *Wáng Húzhī Biézhuàn* states:
"Húzhī often disregarded worldly affairs,
cherishing a noble and lofty disposition,
and was on good terms with Xiè Ān."
A saying goes:
"In Yángzhōu, Wáng Wéndù stands alone,
and later, Chī Jiābīn surpasses others."
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Chāo was exceptionally talented from a young age,
transcending his era and defying convention,
not adhering to ordinary norms.
Among those praised by contemporaries as outstanding of their generation,
it was said:
'Great talent, vast and profound, Xiè Jiā'ān;
in Jiāngdōng, Wáng Wéndù stands alone;
with abundant virtue renewed daily, Chī Jiābīn.'"
The wording differs slightly,
so it is recorded here in detail.
Someone asked Wáng Chángshǐ about Jiāng Bīn and his brothers and cousins,
and Wáng replied:
"All the Jiāngs are indeed capable of managing their own lives."
Bīn and his younger brother Chún,
and cousin Guàn,
all possessed moral conduct,
and were well-known in their time.
Xiè Tàifù said of Ānběi:
"Seeing him does not make one weary,
but once he leaves the door,
one does not long for him again."
Ānběi
refers to Wáng Tǎnzhī.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Xiè Ān initially took his young children and like-minded friends,
nurturing his aspirations by the seaside,
his sentiments lofty and unrestrained,
especially fond of music.
Yet he restrained himself with propriety;
in mourning, he could be deeply affected.
After the death of his younger brother Wàn,
he did not listen to music for nearly ten years.
When he became an assistant in government,
he built mansions, gardens, and estates,
adorned carriages and clothing,
and even during the mourning period for close relatives,
he did not cease music and entertainment.
Wáng Tǎnzhī repeatedly admonished him earnestly."
Note: Xiè Gōng likely found Wáng Tǎnzhī too fond of blunt speech,
hence he did not long for him.
Xiè Gōng said:
"Sīzhōu achieves excellence in every decision."
Sòng Míngdì's *Wénzhāng Zhì* states:
"Húzhī had a simple nature,
and was fond of expressing profound metaphysical discourse."
Liú Yǐn said:
"Seeing Hé Cìdào drink
makes one want to pour out all the family's brew."
Chōng could drink while maintaining warmth and restraint.
Xiè Tàifù said to Zhēncháng:
"Ā Líng, in this matter,
truly desires to be too severe."
Xiūlíng
is the childhood name of Wáng Húzhī.
Liú said:
"He is also among the noble and lofty scholars."
The *Húzhī Biézhuàn* states:
"Húzhī cultivated himself with purity and restraint,
and upheld an air of moral integrity."
Wáng Zǐyóu said:
"The world regards Shìshǎo as bright and clear,
and our family also considers him thoroughly bright."
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* states:
"Zǔ Yuē was praised for his purity from a young age."
Xiè Gōng said:
"Chángshǐ speaks very little,
yet it can be said he has admirable words."
The *Wáng Méng Biézhuàn* states:
"Méng's nature was harmonious and unrestrained,
skilled in pure conversation,
discoursing on the Way and valuing reasoned principles,
concise yet meaningful.
Discussing ancient worthies,
in moments of clarity and silence,
his expressions were commendable and admirable,
often possessing lofty sentiments."
Xiè Zhènxī said of Jìngrén:
"His literary talent is sharp and outstanding,
there is nothing he cannot renew."
The *Yǔlín* states:
"Jìngrén had exceptional talent,
and contemporary worthies all esteemed him.
Wáng Yòujūn, while in the commandery, welcomed Jìngrén,
and Shūrén often rode in the same carriage,
always disliking his slowness.
Later, he used a horse to welcome Jìngrén,
and even in wind and rain,
he would not use a carriage."
Liú Yǐn said of Jiāng Dàoqún:
"He cannot speak, yet he is capable of not speaking."
Jiāng Guàn has been mentioned before.
Lín Gōng said:
"Seeing Sīzhōu's alertness and understanding come together,
one cannot help but be captivated,
and even after a whole day, one forgets fatigue."
The *Wáng Húzhī Biézhuàn* states:
"Húzhī had an elegant demeanor from a young age,
his talent and capacity were generally outstanding,
and he was praised for his refined understanding."
The world says:
"Xúnzǐ is outstandingly brilliant,
Ā Xīng is pure and harmonious."
Xúnzǐ has been mentioned before.
Ā Xīng
is the childhood name of Wáng Yùn.
Jiǎnwén said:
"Liú Yǐn, like fine tea, has substantial principles."
Kē, in one version, is written as dǎ,
also as dīng,
and also as dǎ.
Xiè Hú'ér served as a Gentleman of the Imperial Library,
and once wrote a "Biography of Wáng Kān."
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" says:
"Kān, styled Shìzhòu,
was a man from Shòuzhāng in Dōngpíng.
In his youth, he was praised for his lofty integrity and righteous conduct.
He served as Left Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat,
and possessed upright principles and conduct.
He was killed by Shí Lè,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Commandant."
Not knowing what kind of person Kān was,
he consulted Xiè Gōng.
Xiè Gōng replied:
"Shìzhòu was also well-regarded.
Kān was the son of Liè.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" says:
"Liè, styled Yángxiù,
was renowned early on.
During the Wèi dynasty, he served as Censor."
He was a maternal cousin of Ruǎn Qiānlǐ,
and a relative of Pān Ānrén.
As Ānrén's poem says:
'Your mother is my aunt,
my father is your uncle.'
He was also the son-in-law of Xǔ Yǔn."
The "Yuè Collection" says:
"Kān served as Military Marshal for the Prince of Chéngdū.
Yuè saw him off at Běimáng,
and composed a poem:
'Our humble bodies,
are received from our parents.
The lofty princes and nobles,
are the foremost among our kin.
Your mother is my aunt,
my father is your uncle.'"
Grand Tutor Xiè esteemed Attendant-in-Chief Dèng,
often saying,
"Heaven and Earth are without wisdom,
to let Bódào have no son."
The "Jìn Yángqiū" says:
"Dèng Yōu, having abandoned his son,
thus had no further heirs,
which was lamented by those of understanding."
Xiè Gōng wrote to General of the Right Wáng:
"Jìnghé's aspirations and pursuits are excellent."
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says: [49"Qià was the most renowned among the gentlemen,
and shared a fine reputation with Xún Xiàn of Yǐngchuān."
The traditional assessment of the four great families of Wú says:
"The Zhāngs are known for literature,
the Zhūs for military prowess,
the Lùs for loyalty,
and the Gùs for magnanimity."
The "Wú Lù Shìlín" says: [58"In Wú commandery, the Gù,
Lù, Zhū,
and Zhāng families are the four great clans.
During the Three Kingdoms period,
these four families flourished."
Xiè Gōng said to Wáng Xiàobó:
"Your family's Lántián,
in all his conduct, does nothing ordinary."
According to records, although Shù was straightforward,
his nature was not tolerant,
and his anger at flies throwing themselves into the fire
was not excessive.
If not for the Grand Tutor's exaggerated praise,
then the "Shì Shuō" erroneously attributes these words.
Attendant Xǔ once visited Jiǎnwén,
that night the wind was calm and the moon bright,
so they conversed together in a secluded chamber.
Lyrical expressions of sentiment
were particularly Xǔ's forte.
His words were pure and graceful,
surpassing his usual self.
Although Jiǎnwén had always been congenial with him,
this encounter especially made him sigh in admiration.
Unconsciously, they drew close,
clasped hands and talked,
until nearly dawn.
Afterward, he said:
"Xuándù's talent and sentiment
are indeed not easily found in many."
The "Xù Jìn Yángqiū" says:
"Xún was skilled in discussing principles.
Once, he went out of the capital to welcome his elder sister,
and Emperor Jiǎnwén and Liú Zhēncháng spoke of his emotional depth and lyrical expressions.
Each time they drew close in appreciation and conversation,
the night extended into day."
Yīn Yǔn went west,
Xī Chāo wrote to Yuán Hǔ:
"Zǐsī seeks good friends,
and entrusts his goodwill to you.
Do not judge him by the standard of 'open excellence.'"
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Yǔn, styled Zǐsī,
was from Chén commandery,
the sixth son of Tàicháng Kāng's younger brother.
Respectful, plain, modest, and retiring,
he had the demeanor of a Confucian scholar.
He served as President of the Board of Civil Office."
The world regarded Yuán as
"open excellence,"
hence Zǐjìng's poem says:
"Yuán Shēng possesses the measure of open excellence."
General of Chariots and Cavalry Xiè asked Xiè Gōng:
"Zhēncháng's nature is extremely stern;
why is he so esteemed?"
He replied:
"It is because you have not seen him!
Even seeing Zǐjìng
still makes one unable to restrain admiration."
The "Yǔ Lín" says:
"Yáng Lín, due to drunkenness,
patted General of the Left Xiè and said to the Grand Tutor:
'How could this family again produce one like General of the West?'
The Grand Tutor said:
'You, seeing Zǐjìng,
immediately bathe and discuss him as among the elder brothers.'"
Inferring the meaning of these words,
then Ān thought Xuán had not seen Zhēncháng,
hence did not esteem him.
Seeing Zǐjìng, he still esteemed him;
how much more Zhēncháng?
Xiè Gōng held the position of Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat.
Wáng Dōngtíng had matters requiring them to go to the ministry together.
Wáng arrived later,
and seating was cramped.
Although Wáng and Xiè were not on good terms,
the Grand Tutor still drew in his knees to accommodate him.
The matter of Wáng and Xiè not being on good terms
is separately recorded.
Wáng's demeanor was leisurely and unrestrained;
Xiè Gōng gazed at him intently.
Returning, he said to Lady Liú:
"Just now seeing Āguā,
he is indeed not easily matched.
According to records, Wáng Xún's childhood name was Fǎhù,
yet here he is called Āguā,
which is hard to explain;
perhaps he had two childhood names.
Although unrelated,
it truly makes one unable to restrain admiration."
Wáng Zǐjìng said to Xiè Gōng:
"You are truly carefree and unrestrained."
Xiè said:
"I am not carefree and unrestrained.
You describe me most aptly;
I am simply naturally harmonious and unrestrained."
The "Xù Jìn Yángqiū" says:
"Ān was broad-minded and elegant, possessing an aura;
his demeanor and spirit were harmonious and unrestrained."
General of Chariots and Cavalry Xiè first saw Wáng Wéndù and said:
"Seeing Wéndù, although our encounter was carefree and unrestrained,
he again was serene and composed throughout the evening."
Fàn Yùzhāng said to Wáng Jīngzhōu:
Fàn Nìng,
Wáng Chén are both previously mentioned.
"Your elegance and outstanding reputation
truly make you an outstanding later generation."
Wáng said:
"Without such an uncle,
how could there be such a nephew?"
Zǐjìng wrote to Zǐyóu,
saying:
"Elder brother is aloof and rarely sociable,
but when encountering wine, he becomes exhilarated and unrestrained, forgetting to return,
which is indeed admirable."
Zhāng Tiānxī was a regional hegemon in Liángzhōu for generations,
but due to his weakened strength, he came to the capital.
Although he was from a distant and different region,
he was still an outstanding figure among the border people.
(Zhāng Tiānxī has been mentioned previously.)
Hearing that the imperial capital was full of talented individuals,
his admiration and envy grew even stronger.
While he was still staying by the riverbank,
Simǎ the Attendant went to visit him.
(His identity is not detailed.)
His speech and appearance were vulgar and unrefined,
with nothing worth observing or listening to.
Zhāng Tiānxī deeply regretted coming,
thinking that staying in a remote area would have allowed him to remain secure.
Wáng Mí, who possessed outstanding talent and a fine reputation,
heard about this and went to visit him at the time.
The *Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng Autumn* states:
"Wáng Mín was elegant and spirited,
with a rich and ample command of language."
Upon his arrival,
Zhāng Tiānxī saw that his demeanor was pure and refined,
his speech flowed effortlessly,
and whether discussing past or present matters,
he was thoroughly knowledgeable about everything.
He was also well-versed in the lineages of notable figures,
and his accounts were always supported by evidence.
Zhāng Tiānxī was astonished and impressed.
Wáng Gōng initially had a very close relationship with Wáng Jiànwǔ,
but later, due to Yuán Yuè's sowing discord,
suspicions and rifts arose between them.
The *Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn* states:
"Initially,
Wáng Chén and his clansman Wáng Gōng were close from a young age,
and they were praised together for their shared reputation.
After both entered court service,
and both were treated with importance by the ruler and the chancellor,
internal and external discussions began to arise about their lack of harmony.
Wáng Gōng alone was deeply troubled by this,
so he told Wáng Chén:
'The widespread discussions
show considerable differences of opinion,
likely because the General of Agile Cavalry (Wáng Chén) has been neglecting court audiences.
Could it be that no one has candidly spoken to him about this?
If the ruler and chancellor are harmonious,
we can all devote our efforts to this enlightened era—
what further worries would we have?'
Wáng Chén agreed,
but worried he might not be well-received,
so he had Yuán Yuè convey the message in full.
Yuán Yuè, who often sought to create a rift with Wáng Gōng,
then took the opportunity in the prince's presence to reprimand Wáng Gōng, saying:
'Why do you recklessly create divisions and differences,
sowing doubt and confusion in the court and among the people?'
His words were severe and harsh.
Although Wáng Gōng was dismayed and regretful,
he believed Wáng Chén had framed him.
Although Wáng Chén bore no ill will toward Wáng Gōng in his heart,
he had no way to clear himself.
Thus, their affection greatly deteriorated,
and resentment and rift were formed."
However, whenever occasions of heightened feeling arose,
they would still think of each other.
Once, Wáng Gōng was taking his medicinal powder walk and arrived at the archery hall in Jīngkǒu.
At that time, the clear dew was flowing in the morning,
and the new paulownia leaves were just beginning to emerge.
Wáng Gōng looked at them and said:
"Wáng Dà is indeed so fresh and gleaming."
Grand Tutor Simǎ characterized the two Wángs, saying:
"Xiàobó stands tall and straight,
Ādà is open and clear, aloof and unrestrained."
Wáng Gōng was upright, profound, and intense;
Wáng Chén was perceptive, bright, unconventional, and free-spirited.
Wáng Gōng had clear speech and concise ideas;
he was good at narration and discussion,
but having read few books,
he often repeated himself.
The *Records of the Restoration* states:
"Although Wáng Gōng's talent was not extensive,
his clarity in debate surpassed others."
Some said that Xiàobó often had novel ideas,
so one did not find him tedious.
After Yīn Zhòngkān passed away,
Huán Xuán asked Yīn Zhòngwén:
"What kind of person was your clansman Zhòngkān,
exactly?"
Yīn Zhòngwén replied:
"Although he could not achieve illustriousness for a whole generation,
he was sufficient to shine through to the Nine Springs."
The *Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng Autumn* states:
"Yīn Zhòngkān
was the elder cousin of Yīn Zhòngwén,
and had a fine reputation from a young age."
Chén Zhòngjǔ of Rǔnán
and Lǐ Yuánlǐ of Yǐngchuān—
when people discussed their merits and virtues together,
they could not determine who should come first.
Cài Bójiē's *Continued History of the Hàn* states:
"Cài Bójiē
was from Yǔ, Chénliú.
He was perceptive and possessed outstanding talent,
widely learned and skilled in composition.
In arts, crafts, and technical calculations,
there was none he did not master thoroughly.
He served up to the position of General of the Gentlemen of the Left,
and was executed by Wáng Yǔn."
He evaluated them, saying:
"Chén Zhòngjǔ was strong in opposing superiors,
while Lǐ Yuánlǐ was strict in managing subordinates.
Opposing superiors is difficult,
managing subordinates is easy."
Zhāng Fán's *Annals of the Hàn* states:
"People of the time said of them:
'Fearless against the powerful is Chén Zhòngjǔ,
the model for the realm is Lǐ Yuánlǐ.'"
Thus, Chén Zhòngjǔ was placed below the Three Excellencies.
Xiè Chén's *History of the Hàn* states:
"The Three Excellencies were
those esteemed by their time.
Dòu Wǔ,
Liú Shū,
and Chén Fán
possessed lofty conduct from a young age.
The realm respected and praised them,
hence they were designated as such."
Lǐ Yuánlǐ ranked at the top of the Eight Paragons.
Xuē Yíng's *History of the Hàn* states:
"Lǐ Yīng,
Wáng Chàng,
Xún Gǔn,
Zhū Yù,
Wèi Lǎng,
Liú Yòu,
Dù Kǎi,
and Zhào Diǎn were the Eight Paragons."
The *Records of Heroes* states:
"Previously, Zhāng Jiǎn and others together formed the 'Caps and Gowns Impeachment' group.
Members of the group teased each other,
saying:
'Our group truly has its Eight Paragons
and Eight Worthies,
like the ancient Eight Virtuous Ones
and Eight Accomplished Ones of old.'"
Xiè Chén's *Book* states:
"'Paragon'
is a name for those who stand out eminently."
Yáo Xìn's *Discourse on Scholars* states:
"Chén Zhòngjǔ's physical presence and spirit were lofty and intense,
possessing the integrity of a royal minister.
Lǐ Yuánlǐ was loyal, steadfast, upright, and honest,
with the capability to serve the state.
The realm debated without reaching a conclusion,
until Cài Bójiē, with a single statement, shifted the perspective,
and the doubtful debate was then settled."
Páng Shìyuán arrived in Wú,
and the people of Wú all befriended him.
The "Shǔ Zhì" states:
"Zhōu Yú governed Nánjùn,
and Shìyuán served as Registrar.
After Yú's death,
Shìyuán escorted the funeral procession to Wú.
Many in Wú had heard of his reputation,
and when he was about to return west,
they all gathered at Chāngmén to speak with Shìyuán."
He met Lù Jì—
the "Wénshì Zhuàn" states:
"Jì, styled Gōngjì,
was exceptionally bright and talented from a young age,
broadly learned and well-versed.
Páng Shìyuán was older than Jì,
and they became close friends.
Jì served as the Grand Administrator of Yùlín.
He knew the day of his own death,
and passed away at the age of thirty-two."
Gù Shào,
and Quán Cóng—Huán Jì's "Wú Jì" states:
"Cóng, styled Zǐhuáng,
was a man of Qiántáng in Wújùn.
He possessed virtuous conduct and a righteous character,
and served as Grand Marshal."
And he assessed them, saying:
"Master Lù is what one might call a 'mediocre horse' that can still run swiftly;
Master Gù is what one might call a 'mediocre ox' that can bear heavy burdens over long distances."
Someone asked:
"According to your assessment,
is Master Lù superior?"
He replied:
"Though a mediocre horse is swift and precise,
it can only carry one person.
A mediocre ox travels a hundred lǐ in a day—
how many people can it carry?"
The people of Wú had no way to refute him.
"Master Quán is fond of reputation,
similar to Fán Zǐzhāo of Rǔnán."
Jiǎng Jì's "Wànjī Lùn" states:
"Xǔ Zǐjiāng's praise and criticism were unfair,
promoting Fán Zǐzhāo while suppressing Xǔ Wénxiū.
Liú Yè challenged this, saying:
'Zǐzhāo was elevated from being a merchant,
and at the age of seventy,
he could withdraw to preserve tranquility,
and advance without seeking undue gain.'
Jì replied:
'It is true that Zǐzhāo, from youth to adulthood,
maintained a complete and clean appearance.
However, observe his protruding teeth,
his prominent cheekbones,
and his protruding lips—
he is naturally no match for Wénxiū.'"
Gù Shào once stayed overnight conversing with Páng Shìyuán,
and asked:
"I hear you are known for judging people—
between you and me, who is better?"
He replied:
"In molding and refining worldly customs,
and floating or sinking with the times,
I am not as good as you."
The "Wú Zhì" states:
"Shào delighted in human relationships;
from local officials in the provinces to people from all directions,
whenever they met,
some would offer criticism and depart,
others would become friends and part ways.
His reputation spread far and wide,
and he was praised by all, near and far."
"But in discussing the remaining strategies of kings and hegemons,
and observing the critical points of reliance and leverage,
I seem to have a slight advantage."
Shào also accepted his words.
The "Wú Lù" states:
"Shào accepted his words,
and grew even closer to him."
Zhūgě Jǐn, his younger brother Liàng, and his cousin Dàn—
the "Wú Shū" states:
"Jǐn, styled Zǐyú,
his ancestors were of the Gé surname,
from Zhū County in Lángyá.
Later, they moved to Yángdū.
Since there were already people surnamed Gé in Yángdū,
contemporaries referred to them
as 'Zhūgé,'
and they thus adopted it as their surname.
Jǐn was renowned for his utmost filial piety from a young age.
He rose to become Governor of Yùzhōu,
and passed away at the age of sixty-eight."
The "Wèi Zhì" states:
"Dàn, styled Gōngxiū,
served as an official in the Ministry of Personnel.
When people entrusted him with recommendations,
he would openly state their words and promptly employ them.
If later there were cases of unsuitability,
he would publicly discuss their merits and faults,
using this as praise or criticism.
From then on, all officials were cautious in their recommendations.
He rose to become Inspector of Yángzhōu,
General Who Guards the East,
and Minister of Works.
He plotted rebellion,
and was executed."
All three enjoyed great fame,
each in a different state.
Thus, it was said that
"Shǔ obtained the dragon,
Wú obtained the tiger,
and Wèi obtained the dog."
Dàn in Wèi was equally famous as Xiàhóu Xuán;
Jǐn in Wú
was admired by the Wú court for his magnanimity.
The "Wú Shū" states:
"Jǐn crossed the river to escape the chaos,
and the Great Emperor appointed him as Chief Clerk.
When sent as an envoy to Shǔ,
he only met his younger brother Liàng in official gatherings,
and never in private.
Moreover, he possessed dignified appearance and thoughtful demeanor.
Contemporaries admired his magnanimity."
Sīmǎ Wénwáng asked Wǔ Gāi:
"How does Chén Xuánbó compare to his father, the Minister of Works?"
Gāi replied:
"In broad learning and elegant fluency,

He said:
"Pure, lush, simple, and fine."
"What is Wáng Zhòngzǔ like?"
He said:
"Warm, moist, tranquil, and harmonious."
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Jì" states:
"Whenever people spoke of those with refined taste and charm,
they all cited Wáng
and Liú as the models."
"What is Huán Wēn like?"
He said:
"Lofty, forthright, and surpassing."
"What is Xiè Rénzǔ like?"
He said:
"Pure, easy, fine, and penetrating."
"What is Ruǎn Sīkuàng like?"
He said:
"Broad, moist, penetrating, and far-reaching."
"What is Yuán Yáng like?"
He said:
"Flowing, flowing, pure, and facile."
"What is Yīn Hóngyuǎn like?"
He said:
"He has far-reaching, meaningful thoughts."
"How would you compare those you just mentioned?"
He said:
"In terms of the abilities and learning I possess,
I am inferior in all respects to these worthies.
As for weighing the exigencies of the times
and encompassing the contemporary world,
I am also largely inferior.
However, despite my lack of talent,
I occasionally entrust my thoughts to the mystery of the sublime,
chanting distantly of the "Lǎozǐ"
and "Zhuāngzǐ,"
detached and loftily aloof,
not allowing worldly affairs to occupy my mind.
I dare say that in this heart of mine, I yield to no one."
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn arrived at the capital,
and asked Liú Zhēncháng:
"I hear that Prince of Kuàijī's conversation has remarkably advanced,
is that so?"
The Biography of Huán Wēn says:
"In the ninth year of Xīngníng,
because Huán Wēn had recovered the old capital,
and pacified Huáxià,
he was promoted to Commander of All Military Affairs,
Palace Attendant,
and Grand Marshal,
and granted the Yellow Axe,
so that he could participate in court governance."
Liú said:
"It has advanced to the utmost,
but he is still a man of the second rank!"
Huán said:
"Then who are the first rank?"
Liú said:
"Exactly people like us!"
After Marquis Yīn was dismissed from office,
Duke Huán said to everyone:
"When we were young, I used to ride bamboo horses with Yuānyuán,
and whenever I discarded one,
he would always pick it up,
so naturally he is beneath me."
The Continued Chronicles of Jìnyángqiū says:
"When Jiǎnwén assisted in governance,
he appointed Yīn Hào as Governor of Yángzhōu,
intending to use him to oppose Huán.
Huán had always looked down on Hào,
and was not afraid of him."
Someone asked the General of Pacification:
"How is Yīn Hào's conversation after all?"
He replied:
"He cannot surpass others,
but he is somewhat capable of satisfying the hearts of the crowd."
Jiǎnwén said:
"Xiè Fèngnán is not as pure and refined as his younger brother,
Xiè Fèngnán,
is Xiè Fèng.
Already mentioned.
The Xiè Clan Genealogy says:
"Fèng's younger brother Pìn,
courtesy name Hóngyuǎn.
Served as Palace Attendant,
and Chief Minister of Justice."
In learning and righteousness, he is not equal to Kǒng Yán.
The Records of the Restoration says:
"Yán, courtesy name Péngzǔ,
was from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His father Jiǎn,
was a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates.
Yán had talent and learning,
served as Governor of Dānyáng,
Imperial Secretary,
and Marquis of Xīyáng.
At court, he often corrected matters.
As Governor of Wúxīng,
he greatly won the harmony of the people.
Later, he died at home."
Yet he naturally surpasses them."
This means Fèng followed his natural disposition.
Before Duke Hǎixī was deposed,
Wáng Yuánlín asked Huán Yuánzǐ:
"Jīzǐ and
Bǐgān,
their actions differed but their hearts were the same.
I wonder, my lord, which one is right and which is wrong?"
He said:
"In terms of benevolence, they are not different,
but I would rather be Guǎn Zhòng."
The Analects says:
"Wēizǐ left him,
Jīzǐ became his slave,
Bǐgān remonstrated and died.
The Master said:
'There were three benevolent men in Yīn.'"
"Zǐlù said:
'Duke Huán killed Prince Jiǔ,
Zhào Hū died for him,
but Guǎn Zhòng did not die.
Can it be said he was not benevolent?'
The Master said:
'Duke Huán assembled the feudal lords nine times,
and brought order to all under heaven,
without the use of arms and chariots—
this was through the strength of Guǎn Zhòng.
Such is his benevolence!
Such is his benevolence!'"
Liú Dānyáng and
Prefect Wáng gathered at Wǎguān Temple,
and General Huán was also present.
Huán Yí has already been mentioned.
Together they discussed figures from the Western Court and those south of the river.
Someone asked:
"How is Dù Hóngzhì compared to Wèi Hǔ?"
Huán replied:
"Hóngzhì is pure in appearance,
while Wèi Hǔ is radiant and divine in spirit."
Wáng and Liú praised his words.
Hǔ was the childhood name of Wèi Jiè.
The Biography of Jiè says:
"During the Yǒnghé era,
Liú Zhēncháng and
Xiè Rénzǔ together discussed figures of the central court.
Someone asked:
'Can Dù Hóngzhì be compared to Wèi Xiǎnmǎ?'
Xiè said:
'How can they be compared!
Several people could fit between them.'"
The Biographies of Famous Gentlemen South of the River says:
"Liú Zhēncháng said:
'Let me evaluate them:
Hóngzhì is pure in appearance,
while Shūbǎo is pure in spirit.'
Commentators considered this a perceptive statement."
Prefect Liú patted Prefect Wáng on the back and said:
"Ānú compared to the Chancellor,
only has elegance and refinement."
Ānú
was the childhood name of Méng.
Dū means elegant.
The Biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú says:
"Leisurely and elegant, very refined."
The Forest of Sayings says:
"Liú Zhēncháng did not get along with the Chancellor,
and often said:
'Ānú compared to the Chancellor,
is clear and refined.'"
Prefect Liú and
Prefect Wáng were sitting together,
and the Prefect, while drunk, began to dance.
Prefect Liú said:
"Ānú today is no less than Xiàng Zǐqī."
This resembles Xiù's unrestrained nature.
Duke Huán asked Kǒng Xīyáng:
"How is Ānshí compared to Zhòngwén?"
Xīyáng was Kǒng Yán.
Kǒng Sī did not answer,
but instead asked the Duke:
"What do you think?"
He replied:
"Ānshí naturally cannot be trampled upon in his position,
and therefore he is superior."
Duke Xiè was enjoying conversation with the worthies of the time,
È and Hú'ér were both present.
The Duke asked Lǐ Hóngdù:
"How is your family's Píngyáng
compared to Yuè Lìng?"
The Praises of the Jìn Nobles says:
"Lǐ Chóng, courtesy name Màozēng,
was from Zhōngwǔ, Jiàngxià.
In his youth, he was praised for his purity and integrity.
He served as Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and Governor of Píngyáng."
At this, Lǐ shed tears and said:
"When King Zhào usurped the throne,
Yuè Lìng personally presented the imperial seal and ribbon.
The Chronicles of Jìnyángqiū says:
"When King Zhào Lún usurped the throne,
Yuè Guǎng, together with Mǎn Fèn and
Cuī Suí, presented the imperial seal and ribbon."
My late uncle was upright and correct,
and ashamed to serve in a chaotic court,
so he eventually took poison.
I fear it is difficult to compare them!
This is evident from the facts,
and not the words of a biased relative."
The Praises of the Jìn Nobles says:
"When King Zhào became Chancellor of State,
he appointed Chóng as Left Marshal.
Chóng, because Lún was about to usurp the throne,
declined on grounds of illness and did not take office.
When urged and persuaded,
Chóng no longer took care of himself,
until he became gravely ill.
Supported and dragged, he accepted the appointment,
and died a few days later.
People of the time lamented him.
He was posthumously granted the title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary."
Duke Xiè said to Hú'ér:
"A man of discernment indeed does not disappoint one's expectations."
Wáng Xiūlíng asked Chángshǐ Wáng Měng:
"How does my family's Línchuān compare to your family's Wǎnlíng?"
Chángshǐ did not reply,
and Xiūlíng said:
"Línchuān is honored by praise."
Chángshǐ said:
"Wǎnlíng is not without honor."
The Book of the Restoration of Jin states:
"Xīzhī, from being an Advisor to the Prince of Kuàijī,
was transferred and appointed as Governor of Línchuān.
Yù Shù, from being a Registrar of the Cavalry General,
went out to serve as Magistrate of Wǎnlíng.
When Shù was at Wǎnlíng,
he extensively prepared household furnishings,
initially drawing complaints of hardship.
Chéngxiàng Wáng Dǎo sent someone to tell him:
'The son of a famous father,
condescending to a small county,
is most inappropriate.'
Shù replied:
'It will stop when it is enough.'
People of the time did not understand him.
Later, he repeatedly governed commanderies and provinces,
and did nothing of the sort,
and the world finally sighed in admiration of him."
Administrator Liú went to Chángshǐ Wáng's place for pure conversation.
At that time, Xúnzǐ was thirteen years old,
leaning by the bed listening.
After he left,
he asked his father:
"How are Administrator Liú's words compared to yours?"
Chángshǐ said:
"In melodious voice and elegant diction,
he is not as good as I;
but in hitting the mark whenever he speaks,
he surpasses me."
The Separate Biography of Liú Tán states:
"Tán had outstanding talent.
In his discussions and appreciations of metaphysical excellence,
and in the principles he grasped and where they led,
he was roughly similar to Wáng Měng,
but his manner of exposition surpassed him,
and his words were apt."
After Xiè Wàn was defeated at Shòuchūn,
Jiǎnwén asked Xī Chāo:
"Wàn could certainly be defeated,
but how could he so lose the affection of his officers and men?"
Chāo said:
"With his unrestrained and indulgent nature,
he sought to distinguish between wisdom and courage."
The Book of the Restoration of Jin states:
"When Wàn was in Yùzhōu,
the Dí and Qiāng violently plundered Sīzhōu and
Yùzhōu, and the Xiānbēi massed in Bīngzhōu and
Jìzhōu. Wàn, having received authority over the region,
personally led his troops into Yǐng
to aid Luòyáng.
Wàn was arrogant and contemptuous of others,
losing the hearts of his officers and men.
Lieutenant General of the North Xī Tán returned to Péngchéng due to illness.
Wàn thought he retreated because the enemy was strong,
so he turned back south,
and his army then collapsed into disorder.
In disarray, he returned alone.
Tàizōng reprimanded him
and demoted him to commoner."
Administrator Liú said to Xiè Rénzǔ:
"Since I have my four friends,
my disciples have become more intimate."
He said to Xǔ Xuándù:
"Since I have my Zǐlù,
harsh words no longer reach my ears."
Both men accepted this without resentment.
The Great Commentary to the Book of Documents states:
"Confucius said:
'King Wén had four friends.
Since I got Yán Huí,
my disciples have become more intimate—
is this not 'mutual attachment'?
Since I got Duānmuā Cì,
scholars from distant places have come—
is this not 'running to serve'?
Since I got Rǎn Qiú,
there is radiance in front,
and light behind—
is this not 'vanguard and rearguard'?
Since I got Zhòng Yóu,
harsh words do not enter my ears—
is this not 'warding off insults'?'"
The world appraised General Yīn of the Central Army:
"The threads of his thought are profound and penetrating,
comparable to Yáng Shūzǐ."
Yáng Hù's virtue surpassed a generation,
and his talent had experienced both peace and peril.
The glow of Yuānyuán's lampwick—
how could it compare to the brightness of the sun and moon?
Someone asked Duke Huán about the relative merits of Xiè Ānshí and
Wáng Tǎnzhī.
Duke Huán paused, about to speak,
then regretted it mid-way and said:
"You delight in spreading people's words,
so I cannot tell you."
Lieutenant General Wáng once asked Liú of Chángshā:
"How do I compare to Xúnzǐ?"
The Roster of Officials of the Grand Marshal states:
"Liú Shì, styled Wénshí,
was from Péngchéng."
The Genealogy of the Liú Clan states:
"Shì's grandfather, Chǎng,
was Governor of Péngchéng.
His father, Jì,
was Magistrate of Línhǎi.
Shì served successively as Consultant to the Chariot and Horse General,
Chancellor of Chángshā,
and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary."
Liú replied:
"Your talent certainly does not surpass Xúnzǐ's,
but you are more adept at making a name for yourself."
Wáng laughed and said:
"Silly!"
Zhī Dàolín asked Sūn Xìnggōng:
"How do you compare to Attendant Xǔ?"
Sūn said:
"In lofty sentiment and far-reaching spirit,
I, your disciple, have long since admired and upheld him;
but in every chant and every ode,
Xǔ would face north as my student."
General of the Right Wáng asked Xǔ Xuándù:
"You yourself say, how do you compare to Ānshí?"
Xǔ did not reply,
and Wáng therefore said:
"Ānshí is of course heroic,
but would Āwàn really glare and contend?"
The Book of the Restoration of Jin states:
"Wàn's capacity was not equal to Ānshí's.
Although he held a regional post,
even when Ān was in private life at home,
his reputation was above Wàn's."
Administrator Liú said:
"People say Jiāng Bīn is a country bumpkin,
but Jiāng actually has his own fields and estates."
Meaning he was capable of producing much.
Xiè Gōng said:
"Among those at the Golden Valley, Sū Shào was the most outstanding."
Shào was the brother-in-law of Shí Chóng,
grandson of Sū Zé,
and son of Sū Yú.
Shí Chóng's "Preface to the Golden Valley Poems" says:
"In the sixth year of Yuánkāng,
I was sent out from the position of Minister of the Imperial Stud to serve as an envoy,
holding the tally as Supervisor of the military affairs of Qīngzhōu and
Xúzhōu,
and General Who Subdues the Caitiffs.
I had a separate lodge within the Golden Valley Stream in Hénán County,
with high and low terrain,
clear springs and lush woods,
various fruits, bamboos, cypresses,
and medicinal herbs,
all fully provided.
There were also water-powered trip-hammers,
fish ponds,
and earthen caves—
everything for pleasing the eye and gladdening the heart was complete.
At that time, Wáng Xǔ, the Libationer of the Great General Who Conquers the West, was about to return to Cháng'ān.
I and various worthies together saw him off within the stream,
feasting and touring day and night,
frequently changing our seats.
Sometimes we climbed high and looked down,
sometimes we sat in rows by the water's edge.
At the time, lutes, zithers, panpipes, and zhus
were all loaded together in the carriages,
and music was played along the road.
When we stopped,
we ordered them to play alternately with the military band.
Then each composed a poem
to express our inner feelings.
Those who could not
were fined three dou of wine.
Moved by the impermanence of life,
and fearing the uncertain time of our decline,
I therefore fully listed the official titles,
names,
and ages of the people of the time,
and also copied the poems afterward.
May later enthusiasts
peruse this!
In all, there were thirty people.
The Tutor to the Prince of Wú,
Court Gentleman for Consultation,
Marquis Within the Passes,
Sū Shào of Wǔgōng in Shǐpíng, styled Shìsì,
aged fifty,
was first."
The "History of Wèi" says:
"Sū Zé, styled Wénshī,
was from Wǔgōng in Fúfēng.
He was upright and detested evil,
often admiring the conduct of Jí Àn.
He served up to Palace Attendant
and Chancellor of Hédōng."
"The Roster of Jìn Officials" says:
"Sū Yú, styled Xiūyù,
was the second son of Zé."
Shān Tāo's "Memorials" says:
"Yú was loyal and righteous, possessing wisdom and insight;
he reached the position of Palace Attendant."
Prefect Liú appraised Gentleman-in-Attendance Yǔ:
"Although his words are not as serene and profound as the Way,
his abruptness somewhat approximates the Way."
"Biographies of Famous Gentlemen" says:
"Yǔkǎi was carefree, profound, and unrestrained;
none could stir his attention."
Sūn Chénggōng said:
"Xiè Gōng is purer than Wúyì,
"The History of the Restoration" says:
"Sūn Tǒng, styled Chénggōng,
was from Tàiyuán.
He excelled at literary composition;
contemporaries said he had the style of his ancestor Sūn Chǔ.
He served up to Magistrate of Yúyáo."
and more polished than Líndào."
"Separate Biography of Chén Kuí" says:
"Kuí, styled Líndào,
was from Xǔchāng in Yǐngchuān.
His grandfather was Chén Huái,
Grand Commandant.
His father was Chén Zhěn,
Palace Attendant.
Kuí showed talent from youth
and established a reputation for purity and acuity.
He inherited the title of Duke of Guǎnglíng,
served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
General of the Western Palace Guard,
and concurrently Administrator of the two commanderies of Liáng
and Huáinán."
Someone asked Reverend Lín:
"How does the Regional Inspector compare to the two Xiès?"
Reverend Lín said:
"He should naturally be ranked above Ān and below Wàn."
"Separate Biography of Wáng Húzhī" says:
"Húzhī enjoyed witty conversation
and excelled at literary composition,
being esteemed by his contemporaries."
Sūn Xìnggōng
and Xǔ Xuándù were both famous figures of their time.
Some valued Xǔ's lofty sentiments,
then despised Sūn's base conduct;
some admired Sūn's literary talent,
but found nothing to praise in Xǔ.
Emperor Míng of Sòng's "Record of Literary Works" says:
"Sūn Chuò broadly studied the classics and histories,
excelling at literary composition.
Both he and Xǔ Xún had unconventional reputations.
Xún ultimately did not lower his aspirations,
while Chuò became entangled in worldly affairs."
"Continued Annals of Jìnyáng" says:
"Although Chuò had literary talent,
he was unrestrained and had many base habits,
which contemporaries despised."
Xī Jiābīn appraised Xiè Gōng:
"His insights, though not profoundly penetrating,
are intricate and thorough."
It is also said:
"The Right Army went to visit Jiābīn."
When Jiābīn heard this, he said:
"One cannot say he 'visited';
it's only proper to say they were companions!"
Xiè Gōng considered Jiābīn's words correct.
Generally, 'penetrating' and 'visiting'
are terms for deep examination.
Xiè was not penetrating,
and Wáng did not visit.
Xiè and Wáng, in terms of principle,
were mutual companions.
Yǔ Dàojì said:
"In orderly and harmonious reasoning,
I am ashamed before Kāngbó;
in strong and upright willpower,
I am ashamed before Wéndù.
As for those below them,
I surpass them all a hundredfold."
Yǔ Hé has already been mentioned.
Wáng Sēng'ēn looked down on Reverend Lín.
Lántián said:
"Don't imitate your elder brother;
your elder brother himself is not his equal."
Sēng'ēn
was the childhood name of Wáng Yīzhī.
"Genealogy of the Wáng Clan" says:
"Yīzhī, styled Wénshào,
was the second son of Wáng Shù.
He was renowned from youth
and married Princess Xúnyáng.
He served up to Gentleman of the Central Secretariat
and died before reaching thirty.
Wáng Tǎnzhī mourned him
and spoke of him to Huán Wēn,
who posthumously awarded him the title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary."
Emperor Jiǎnwén asked Sūn Xìnggōng:
"What is Yuán Yáng like?"
He replied:
"Those who do not know him do not appreciate his talent;
those who know him do not value his character."
This means he had talent but lacked virtue.
Cài Shūzǐ said:
"Although Hán Kāngbó lacks a strong framework,
he still has a respectable appearance."
Xī Jiābīn asked Grand Tutor Xiè:
"How do Reverend Lín's discourses compare to those of Jī?"
Xiè said:
"Jī must diligently exert himself
to just manage to keep up."
"Biography of Zhī Dùn" says:
"Dùn was divinely perceptive and quick-witted;
what he attained through his natural disposition
was spontaneously transcendent."
He also asked:
"How does Yīn compare to Zhī?"
Xiè said:
"Precisely in terms of transcendence,
Zhī surpasses Yīn.
But in tireless debate,
I fear Yīn's eloquence could overwhelm Zhī."
Yǔ Dàojì said:
"Even though Lián Pō and
Lìn Xiàngrú have been dead for a thousand years,
their awe-inspiring presence still seems full of vitality.
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
'Lián Pō was
a fine general of Zhào.
His courage was renowned among the feudal lords.
Lìn Xiàngrú was
a man of Zhào.
During the reign of King Huìwén of Zhào,
he obtained the Héshì jade disc of Chǔ.
King Zhāo of Qín offered fifteen cities in exchange for it.
Zhào sent Xiàngrú to deliver the jade.
Qín received it,
but had no intention of returning the cities.
Xiàngrú requested to show the jade's flaws,
then, holding the jade, he stepped back and leaned against a pillar,
his angry hair standing on end and lifting his cap, saying:
'If Your Majesty presses me,
my head and the jade will shatter together now.'
The King of Qín apologized to him.
Later, the King of Qín had the King of Zhào play the sè,
and Xiàngrú requested the King of Qín to strike the zhù.
Zhào, considering Xiàngrú's great merit,
appointed him Senior Minister,
placing him above Lián Pō.'"
As for Cáo Chú and
Chú, it was the childhood name of Cáo Màozhī.
The Cáo Clan Genealogy states:
"Màozhī, styled Yǒngshì,
was from Péngchéng.
His grandfather Sháo
was General Who Guards the East and Army Supervisor.
His father Màn
was Minister of the Imperial Household.
Màozhī served up to the position of Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat."
Lǐ Zhì's Jin Dynasty Roster of Officials states:
"Zhì, styled Wēnzǔ,
was from Zhōngwǔ, Jiāngxià."
The Lǐ Clan Genealogy states:
"Zhì's grandfather Zhòng
was Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
His father Mù
was Magistrate of Chúnyáng.
Zhì served up to the positions of Extraordinary Attendant-in-Ordinary and
Administrator of Nánkāng."
"Although they are alive today,
they are listless as if they were men from the Nine Springs.
If everyone were like this,
one could govern by knotting ropes,
but I fear the foxes, badgers, and raccoon dogs would devour everything."
This means if everyone were like Cáo and
Lǐ—simple, honest, and sincere—
then there would be no wicked people in the world,
and one could govern by knotting ropes.
However, their talents and wisdom are unheard of,
their achievements and deeds are all extinguished,
their bodies consumed by foxes,
with no renowned names to dominate their age.
Wèi Jūncháng was the elder brother of Xiāo Zǔzhōu's wife.
Xiè Gōng asked Sūn Sēngnú:
Sēngnú
was the childhood name of Sūn Téng.
