The Jin Dynasty Roster of Officials states:
"Téng, styled Bóhǎi,
was from Tàiyuán."
The Records of the Restoration states:
"Téng
was the son of Dǎn.
He was erudite.
He served successively as Palace Attendant,
and Commandant of Justice."
"What do you say about your family's Wèi Jūncháng?"
Sūn said:
"He is said to be a man of inherited profession."
Xiè said:
"That is absolutely not so;
Wèi is naturally a man of principle and righteousness."
At that time, he was compared to Yīn Hóngyuǎn.
Wáng Zǐjìng asked Xiè Gōng:
"How does Lín Gōng compare to Yǔ Gōng?"
Xiè was extremely unwilling to accept the comparison,
and replied:
"The earlier generation originally made no comparisons;
Yǔ Gōng himself is sufficient to surpass Lín Gōng."
The Words and Deeds of Yīn Xiàn states:
"At that time, someone praised Grand Marshal Yǔ for his reasoning.
Xiàn said:
'This lord likes to raise the fundamental principles to strike people down.'"
Xiè È and others were together discussing the relative merits of the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove.
Xiè Gōng said:
"The earlier generation originally did not praise or disparage the Seven Worthies."
The Annals of the Wei Clan states:
"Shān Tāo was open-minded and virtuous;
Xiù, Xián,
Róng, and Líng were intelligent, perceptive, and possessed outstanding talent.
In the discussions of that time,
Ruǎn was placed first,
Wáng Róng second,
and Shān, Xiàng, and their like
were all of their kind."
If it is as Shèng says,
then it is not that there was no praise or disparagement;
this statement is mistaken.
Someone compared Vice Director Wáng to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
The General of Chariots and Cavalry, hearing of it, said:
"He has solid achievements."
The Continued Annals of Jìnyáng states:
"Tánzhī was refined, noble, perceptive, and measured,
his style stern and proper."
Grand Tutor Xiè said to Wáng Xiàobó:
"Administrator Liú also remarkably knew himself,
yet he did not say he surpassed Senior Administrator."
The three brothers of the Huangmen Gentleman Wáng all went to visit Xiè Gōng.
Zǐyóu and
Zǐzhòng spoke mostly of vulgar matters.
The Wáng Clan Genealogy states:
"Cāozhī, styled Zǐzhòng,
was the sixth son of Xīzhī.
He served successively as Director of the Palace Library,
Palace Attendant,
Secretary,
and Governor of Yùzhāng."
Zǐjìng merely exchanged greetings about the weather.
After they left,
a seated guest asked Xiè Gōng:
"Of the three worthies just now, who was superior?"
Xiè Gōng said:
"The youngest was the best."
The guest said:
"How do you know?"
Xiè Gōng said:
"The words of a good man are few;
the words of a restless man are many.
I infer this from that."
Xiè Gōng asked Wáng Zǐjìng:
"How does your calligraphy compare to that of your esteemed father?"
He replied:
"They certainly should be different."
Xiè Gōng said:
"Outside opinions are absolutely not like that."
Wáng said:
"How would outsiders know?"
Emperor Míng of Sòng's Record of Literary Works states:
"Xiànzhī was skilled in clerical script,
changing Right General's method into the modern style.
His brushstrokes were elegant and charming,
wondrously surpassing his contemporaries,
and he gained fame together with his father.
His draft cursive script was sparse and weak,
far inferior to his father's.
Someone once questioned Xiànzhī, saying:
'Is Xīzhī's calligraphy superior or not?'
'No one can judge.'
Someone asked Xīzhī:
'General opinion says your calligraphy does not reach Xiànzhī's?'
He replied:
'That is absolutely not so.'
Another day, seeing Xiànzhī,
he asked:
'How is your esteemed father's calligraphy?'
Xiànzhī did not reply.
He asked again:
'Commentators say
you certainly should be inferior?'
Xiànzhī laughed and replied:
'How could people know?'"
Wáng Xiàobó asked Grand Tutor Xiè:
"How does Lín Gōng compare to Senior Administrator?"
The Grand Tutor said:
"Senior Administrator had elegant inspiration."
He asked:
"How does he compare to Administrator Liú?"
Xiè said:
"Alas!
Administrator Liú was outstanding."
Wáng said:
"If it is as you say,
then he does not equal these two men?"
Xiè said:
"My opinion is precisely so."
Someone asked Grand Tutor Xiè Ān:
"To which of the former worthies might Zǐjìng be compared?"
Xiè replied:
"Ājìng in recent times has gathered the outstanding qualities of Wáng Dàolíng and
Liú Tǎn."
The *Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng* states:
"Xiànzhī's literary talent was not his forte,
yet he was able to gather their finest qualities,
thus gaining renown for a time,
and becoming the crown of the refined and cultured."
Lord Xiè said to Wáng Xiàobó:
"Your grandfather, compared to Prefect Liú,
was indeed his equal."
Xiàobó said:
"It's not that Prefect Liú could not equal him,
it's simply that he did not."
This means Liú Tǎn was substantial in substance,
while Wáng Měng was refined in style.
When Yuán Yànbó became a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel,
Wáng Zǐjìng wrote a letter to Chì Jiābīn saying:
"Yànbó has already entered office,
which is quite enough to dampen the spirit of those who aspire to advance.
Thus, we know that enduring beatings is naturally difficult for a man,
so we hope for a slight retreat,
and then things should improve somewhat."
Wáng Zǐyóu and
Zǐjìng, the brothers, were together appreciating the figures and the *Eulogies* in the *Biographies of Eminent Gentlemen*.
Zǐjìng admired Jǐng Dān for his lofty purity,
while Zǐyóu said:
"He is not as good as Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's disregard for worldly conventions."
Jī Kāng's *Biographies of Eminent Gentlemen* states:
"Dān, styled Dàchūn,
was a man of Méi in Fúfēng.
He was widely learned and lofty in discourse.
The capital had a saying about him:
'The Five Classics in profusion, Jǐng Dàchūn,
who never wrote a visiting card to call on a single person.'
The Five Princes of the Northern Palace repeatedly invited him,
but none could secure his presence.
Marquis Xīnyáng, Yīn Jiù, sent someone to intercept him,
and he had no choice but to go.
The Marquis set out wheat-meal and
scallion-vegetables
to observe his reaction.
Dān pushed them away, saying:
'It was because I thought you, my lord, could provide a fine meal
that I came to visit.
What is the meaning of this?'
Then the Marquis brought out a lavish feast.
The Marquis rose,
and his attendants brought forward a carriage.
Dān laughed and said:
'I have heard that Jié and
Zhòu drove carriages of men.
Is this what is called a carriage of men?'
The Marquis immediately removed the carriage.
The Commandant of the Rapid-as-Storm Cavalry, Liáng Sōng,
whose prestige shook the court,
sought to befriend Dān,
but Dān refused to see him.
Later, Dān contracted a seasonal illness,
and Sōng personally brought a physician to see him.
Long after his recovery,
Sōng lost his eldest son, Lěi.
Dān went once to offer condolences.
At that time, the guests filled the hall.
Dān, in worn fur and coarse cloth,
entered the gate.
All who were seated were awed,
gazing at his countenance.
Dān made a deep bow to the four directions,
then went forward and spoke with Sōng.
After the rituals between guest and host were concluded,
he made a deep bow and sat directly down,
and no one dared to speak with him.
He refused to serve as an official,
and departed directly.
Later, he went into seclusion.
His *Eulogy* says:
'Jǐng Dān, lofty and pure,
did not covet glory or rank.
He maintained his integrity against the Five Princes,
and did not associate with those not his kind.
Openly mocking the carriage,
he made the attendants lose their nerve.
In coarse cloth, making a deep bow,
his righteousness towered over the gathered crowd.'"
"Sīmǎ Xiàngrú
was a man of Chéngdū in Shǔ commandery,
styled Chángqīng.
He first served as a Gentleman,
attending upon Emperor Jǐng.
When King Xiào of Liáng came to court,
accompanied by wandering persuaders such as Zōu Yáng,
Xiàngrú was pleased with them,
and, pleading illness, left his post to wander in Liáng.
Later, passing through Línqióng,
he met the wealthy man Zhuó Wángsūn's daughter, Wénjūn, recently widowed,
who loved music.
Xiàngrú stirred her feelings with the lute,
and Wénjūn eloped with him,
and they returned together to Chéngdū.
Later, living in poverty,
they went to Línqióng to buy a wine shop.
Wénjūn tended the counter,
while Xiàngrú wore calf-nose trousers
and washed vessels in the market.
He was a stutterer,
but excelled at composing literature.
In official service, he did not covet high rank,
often pleading illness to avoid major affairs with the high ministers.
He died at home.
His *Eulogy* says:
'Chángqīng disregarded the world,
transgressing ritual, he indulged himself.
In calf-nose trousers, dwelling in the market,
he was not ashamed of his condition.
Pleading illness to avoid office,
he scorned these ministers and chancellors.
Then he composed the *Rhapsody on the Great Man*,
transcendent, with none to surpass him.'"
Someone asked Attendant-in-Ordinary Yuán (The *Yuán Clan Genealogy* states:
"Kèzhī, styled Yuánzǔ,
was a man of Yángxià in Chén commandery.
His grandfather was Wángsūn,
Gentleman of the Palace Gate in the Ministry of Education.
His father was Lún,
Magistrate of Línrǔ.
Kèzhī served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and in the early Yìxī period became Attendant-in-Ordinary."):
He asked:
"How does Yīn Zhòngkān compare to Hán Kāngbó?"
He replied:
"In terms of understanding of principle and righteousness,
their superiority or inferiority is still not discernible;
however, in the quiet and secluded atmosphere of his household,
Hán indeed possesses the refined air of a famous scholar,
which Yīn does not match."
Therefore, Yīn wrote in his *Dirge*:
"The gate of Jīngzhōu is closed by day,
the quiet courtyard is peaceful and still."
Wáng Zǐjìng asked Lord Xiè:
"How does Jiābīn compare to Dàojì?"
He replied:
"Dàojì indeed gathers and selects with clarity and insight,
but Jiābīn naturally stands above."
This means he was outstanding and transcendent.
When Wáng Xún was ill,
and near his end,
he asked Wáng Wǔgāng (The *History of the Restoration* states:
"Mì, styled Yǎyuǎn,
was the grandson of Chancellor Dǎo,
and son of Chariot and Horse General Shào.
He had talent and ability,
inherited the title of Marquis of Gāng,
and reached the position of Minister of Education."):
"Whom do the opinions of the world compare my family's General of the Central Army to?"
Wǔgāng said:
"The world compares him to the Northern General of the Household Wáng Tǎnzhī."
Dōngtíng turned to lie facing the wall,
and sighed, saying:
"A man indeed cannot be without longevity!"
The General of the Central Army was Wáng Qià,
Xún's father.
He died at twenty-six.
Xún believed that his father's reputation and virtue surpassed Tǎnzhī's, but he lacked longevity,
hence this opinion arose.
Wáng Xiàobó said of Lord Xiè:
"Profound and thorough."
He also said:
"Chief Clerk Wáng is empty,
Prefect Liú is outstanding,
Lord Xiè is harmonious."
This means he was smooth and unimpeded.
Wáng Xiàobó asked Lord Xiè:
"How does Reverend Lín compare to the General of the Right?"
Xiè said:
"The General of the Right surpasses Reverend Lín.
Reverend Lín, compared to Sīzhōu, is also esteemed and penetrating."
He did not say he was like Xīzhī,
but said he surpassed Húzhī.
Huán Xuán served as Grand Tutor,
and held a grand assembly,
where all the court officials gathered.
As soon as they were seated,
he asked Wáng Zhēnzhī:
"How do I compare to your seventh uncle?"
The "Wáng Clan Genealogy" states:
"Zhēnzhī, styled Gōnggàn,
was from Lángyá.
He was the son of Huīzhī.
He served as Palace Attendant,
and Chief Clerk to the Grand Marshal."
The seventh uncle
was Xiànzhī.
At that moment, the guests held their breath.
Wáng slowly replied:
"My late uncle was the paragon of his time,
while you, my lord, are a hero for the ages."
The entire assembly was delighted.
Huán Xuán asked Grand Minister of Ceremonies Liú:
"How do I compare to Grand Tutor Xiè?"
Liú Jǐn's "Collected Narratives" states:
"Jǐn, styled Zhòngzhāng,
was from Nányáng.
His grandfather was Xiá,
and his father was Chàng.
Chàng married the daughter of Wáng Xīzhī,
and gave birth to Jǐn.
Jǐn possessed talent and capability,
serving as Minister of Personnel
and Grand Minister of Ceremonies."
Liú replied:
"You, my lord, are lofty,
while Grand Tutor Xiè is profound."
Huán Xuán then asked:
"How do I compare to your worthy uncle Zǐjìng?"
Liú replied:
"Hawthorn,
pear, orange,
and pomelo—each has its own excellence."
The "Zhuāngzǐ" states:
"Hawthorn,
pear, orange,
and pomelo—their flavors are distinct,
yet all are pleasing to the palate."
It was once customary to compare Huán Qiān to Yīn Zhòngwén.
The "Book of the Restoration" states:
"Qiān, styled Jìngzǔ,
was the third son of Chōng.
He served as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat
and General of the Central Army."
The "Annals of Emperor Ān of Jìn" states:
"Zhòngwén possessed both dignified appearance and talent."
During Huán Xuán's time,
when Zhòngwén entered,
Huán, seeing him from the courtyard,
said to those seated with him:
"How could my family's General of the Central Army
ever compare to this man!"
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's wet nurse once committed an offense outside the palace.
The emperor intended to enforce the law,
so the wet nurse sought help from Dōngfāng Shuò.
The "Book of Hàn" states:
"Shuò, styled Mànqiàn,
was from Yàncì in Píngyuán."
The "Separate Biography of Shuò" states:
"Shuò
was from Bùguǎng Village in Nányáng."
The "Biographies of Immortals" states:
"Shuò was from Chǔ.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign, he submitted a memorial discussing beneficial policies
and was appointed Gentleman of the Interior.
At the beginning of Emperor Xuān's reign,
he abandoned his office and left,
and people believed he was the Year Star."
Shuò said:
"This is not a matter to be resolved by mere words.
If you truly hope for success,
when you are about to leave, you must repeatedly look back at the emperor,
but be careful not to speak!
This might offer a slim chance of hope."
When the wet nurse arrived,
Shuò was also in attendance.
He then said to her:
"You are foolish!
Would the emperor still remember the kindness of your nursing him?"
Although the emperor was talented, ambitious, and resolute,
he was also deeply sentimental.
Moved with pity,
he immediately issued an edict pardoning her offense.
The "Biographies of Jesters" in the "Records of the Grand Historian" states:
"When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was young,
the mother of the Marquis of Dōngwǔ nursed him,
and she was later called the Great Wet Nurse.
Her sons, grandsons, and servants
rampaged through Cháng'ān,
seizing people's belongings in the streets.
The authorities requested to exile the wet nurse to the border,
and the petition was approved.
The wet nurse went to bid farewell.
Guō Shèrén, an entertainer favored by the emperor, spoke up.
Although his words did not align with grand principles,
they pleased the ruler.
The wet nurse appeared first
and wept.
Shèrén said:
'When you go to bid farewell,
do not leave immediately,
but look back repeatedly.'
The wet nurse did as he said.
Shèrén then sharply scolded her:
'Begone!
Old woman,
why are you not leaving quickly?
His Majesty is already grown.
Does he still need a wet nurse to survive?
Why do you keep looking back?'
Thereupon, the ruler took pity on her.
He issued an edict halting the exile
and punished those who had requested it."
Jīng Fáng was discussing with Emperor Yuán of Hàn,
and took the opportunity to ask the Emperor:
"Why did the rulers Yōu
and Lì perish?
Whom did they employ?"
The reply was:
"They employed men who were not loyal."
Fáng said:
"If they knew they were not loyal yet employed them,
why was that?"
The Emperor said:
"The rulers of perished states
each considered their ministers worthy;
how could they have known they were not loyal and still employed them?"
Fáng kowtowed and said:
"I fear that the present viewing the past
is also like the future viewing the present."
The *Book of Hàn* states:
"Jīng Fáng, styled Jūnmíng,
was from Dùnqiū in Dōngjùn.
He was especially fond of bells and pitch-pipes,
understood music and tones,
and became a Gentleman Attendant by recommendation as Filial and Incorrupt.
At that time, the Palace Secretary Shí Xiǎn held exclusive power,
and his friend Wǔlù Chōngzōng was the Imperial Secretary.
They shared the same classical studies with Fáng,
debated and argued over right and wrong,
and these two men were in charge of affairs.
Fáng once had a private audience,
and asked the Emperor:
'Why did the rulers Yōu
and Lì perish?
Whom did they employ?'
The Emperor said:
'The rulers were also unenlightened,
and the ministers were artful and flattering.'
Fáng said:
'Did they know they were artful and flattering and still employed them?
Or did they consider them worthy?'
The Emperor said:
'They considered them worthy.'
Fáng said:
'Then how do we now know they were not worthy?'
The Emperor said:
'We know it from the disorder of their times and the peril of their rulers.'
Fáng said:
'Thus, employing the worthy leads to order,
employing the unworthy leads to disorder;
this is the natural way of things.
Why did Yōu and Lì not awaken and early on employ the worthy?
Why did they end up employing the unworthy to the point of perishing?'
Then the Emperor said:
'The rulers of disorder and ruin
each considered their ministers worthy.
If they had all awakened,
how could there be rulers of disorder and ruin?'
Fáng said:
'Why did Duke Huán of Qí
and the Second Emperor not take warning from Yōu
and Lì,
and still employ Shù Diāo
and Zhào Gāo,
causing governance to grow daily more disordered?'
The Emperor said:
'Only those who possess the Way can use the past to know the future.'
Fáng said:
'Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
bandits and thieves have not been restrained,
and executed criminals fill the markets'
and so on,
and asked the Emperor:
'Is the present era orderly?
Or disordered?'
The Emperor said:
'Yet it is better than those past eras.'
Fáng said:
'The former two rulers were just like this.
I fear that the future viewing the present
will be just like the present viewing the past.'
The Emperor said:
'Who now is causing the disorder?'
Fáng said:
'Those whom Your Majesty trusts and consults with in the planning chamber.'
Fáng was pointing to Shí Xiǎn and Chōngzōng.
Xiǎn and others then proposed
that Fáng should be tested as a commandery governor,
and so Fáng was made governor of Dōngjùn.
Xiǎn exposed his private affairs,
and he was condemned and executed in the marketplace."
Chén Yuánfāng suffered the loss of his father,
wept and wailed in deep grief,
his body emaciated to skin and bones.
His mother pitied him,
and secretly covered him with a brocade quilt.
Guō Línzōng came to offer condolences and saw this,
and said to him:
"You are an outstanding talent within the realm,
a model for all directions.
How can you, while in mourning,
be covered with a brocade quilt?
Confucius said:
'To wear brocade,
to eat fine rice,
would you feel at ease?'
The *Analects* states:
"Zǎi Wǒ asked:
'The three-year mourning period,
one year is already long enough.'
The Master said:
'To eat fine rice,
to wear brocade,
would you feel at ease?
When a gentleman is in mourning,
he finds no sweetness in fine food,
hears no pleasure in music,
feels no comfort in his dwelling;
therefore he does not do these things!
Now if you feel at ease,
then do them.'"
I do not approve of this!"
He shook out his sleeves and left.
Afterwards, for over a hundred days, no guests came.
'Suǒ' is also written as 'xǔ'.
Sūn Xiū was fond of shooting pheasants,
and when the season came, he would leave at dawn and return at dusk.
All the ministers tried to admonish him:
"This is a trivial thing,
why be so engrossed in it?"
Xiū said:
"Although it is a trivial thing,
their uprightness surpasses that of men,
which is why I am fond of them."
Huán Jì's *Record of Wú* states:
"Xiū, styled Zǐliè,
was the sixth son of the Great Emperor of Wú.
He was first enfeoffed as the Prince of Lángyá.
He dreamed of riding a dragon to heaven,
but looking back, could not see its tail.
Sūn Chén deposed the young ruler,
and welcomed Xiū to establish him.
He was keenly devoted to the classics,
wishing to peruse all the works of the Hundred Schools.
He was rather fond of shooting pheasants;
when spring came,
he would go out at dawn and return at dusk,
only at this time putting aside his books.
He passed away and was posthumously titled Emperor Jǐng."
*A Systematic Account of Wú Affairs* states:
"Xiū's conduct in office was exemplary,
with nothing left undone,
only his pheasant shooting being worthy of criticism."
Sūn Hào asked Chancellor Lù Kǎi:
"How many men of your clan hold court positions?"
Lù said:
"Two chancellors,
five marquises,
and over ten generals."
Hào said:
"How flourishing!"
Lù said:
"When the ruler is worthy and the ministers loyal,
that is the flourishing of a state.
When the father is kind and the son filial,
that is the flourishing of a family.
Now governance is neglected and the people are distressed,
we fear overthrow and ruin;
how dare I speak of flourishing!"
*Records of Wú* states:
"Kǎi, styled Jìngfēng,
was from Wú,
a clansman of Chancellor Lù Xùn.
He was loyal, outspoken, and possessed great integrity,
steadfast and fond of learning.
He first served as Commandant Who Establishes Loyalty,
and even with military affairs,
he never set aside his books.
He rose through the ranks to become Left Chancellor.
At that time, the later ruler was tyrannical,
but Kǎi remonstrated with him directly and forcefully.
Because his clan was powerful and flourishing,
the ruler did not dare to execute him."
Hé Yàn and
Dèng Yáng had Guǎn Lù perform a divination,
saying:
"We wonder if we will reach the rank of the Three Excellencies?"
After the hexagram was formed,
Lù cited ancient principles,
deeply cautioning them.
Yáng said:
"These are just the platitudes of an old scholar."
The "Biography of Guǎn Lù" states:
"Lù, styled Gōngmíng,
was a man of Píngyuán.
He was well-versed in the Zhōu Yì,
and his reputation spread throughout Xúzhōu.
Péi Huī, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, recommended him as a Xiùcái,
and said to him:
'The two Ministers Hé and
Dèng possess talent and strategy for governing the state,
and are thoroughly knowledgeable in all principles of things.
Minister Hé's spirit is clear and penetrating,
capable of discerning the finest details.
You should be cautious with him.
He himself says he does not understand nine matters in the Yì,
and will certainly ask you about them.
By the time you reach Luòyáng,
you should be well-prepared and refined in their principles.'
Lù replied:
'If these nine matters all pertain to ultimate principles,
they are not worth laborious thought.
As for matters of yīn and yáng,
I have long delved deeply into them.'
When Lù arrived in Luòyáng,
he was indeed questioned by Minister Hé,
and all nine matters were clarified.
Hé said:
'Your discourse on yīn and yáng
is unmatched in this world.'
At that time, Minister Dèng, who was present, said:
'This gentleman is skilled in the Yì,
yet his speech initially does not discuss the meanings of the Yì's texts.
Why is that?'
Lù answered:
'Those who are truly skilled in the Yì
do not discuss the Yì.'
Minister Hé, smiling, praised him, saying:
'That can be called essential speech without verbosity.'
He then said to Lù:
'I have heard that you are not only skilled in discussing the Yì,
but also in dividing the yarrow stalks and contemplating the lines,
which is also divinely marvelous.
Please try to perform a divination for us,
to know if we are destined to reach the rank of the Three Excellencies?
Also, recently I dreamed of several dozen blue flies coming to the tip of my nose,
and I could not drive them away.
What is the meaning of this?'
Lù said:
'The owl,
is a lowly bird in the world.
But when it eats mulberries in the forest,
it cherishes our beautiful songs.
How much more so I, whose heart surpasses grass and trees,
and whose affection is devoted like sunflowers and beans,
dare I not be utterly loyal?
I only ask you to examine this.
In ancient times, Yuán and
Kǎi assisted Chónghuà,
spreading kindness, benevolence, and harmony,
which was the pinnacle of righteousness and benevolence.
The Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
sitting and waiting for dawn,
which was the pinnacle of reverence and caution.
Therefore, they could radiate light throughout the six directions,
and all states were at peace.
Only then did they stand firm like a tripod's legs and ascend to the golden handle,
harmonizing yīn and yáng to aid the myriad people.
This is the auspicious response of walking the path,
not something divination can clarify.
Now, your lordship's position is as weighty as mountains and peaks,
your power like thunder and lightning.
Gazing at the clouds and chasing the light,
you gallop with the wind for ten thousand lǐ.
But those who cherish your virtue are few,
while those who fear your authority are many.
This is hardly the way of cautious vigilance,
or of a man blessed with abundant fortune.
Moreover, the nose
corresponds to the Gèn hexagram.
This is the mountain in the center of heaven,
high yet not perilous,
and thus it long preserves nobility.
Now, blue flies are foul and odious creatures,
yet they gather upon it.
Those in lofty positions may fall,
the arrogant and reckless may perish—
this is an inevitable outcome.
Although change and transformation give rise to each other,
reaching an extreme brings harm.
Although emptiness and fullness receive each other,
overflow leads to exhaustion.
The sages perceived the nature of yīn and yáng,
understood the principles of survival and demise,
reduced excess and supplemented deficiency to counter decline,
restrained advancement to prepare for retreat.
Therefore, a mountain within the earth is called the Qiān hexagram;
thunder above heaven is called the Dà Zhuàng hexagram.
Qiān means taking from the abundant to supplement the scarce;
Dà Zhuàng means not treading where propriety is lacking.
I humbly wish your lordship to seek above the intent of King Wén's six lines,
and ponder below the meaning of Master Ní's judgments and images.
Then the matter of the Three Excellencies can be decided,
and the blue flies can be driven away.'
Dèng said:
'These are just the platitudes of an old scholar.'
Lù said:
'An old scholar
is one who sees what is not born.
Platitudes
are words that see what is not spoken.'"
Yàn said:
"To know the subtle signs, is that not divine!
The ancients considered it difficult.
To speak sincerely despite a distant relationship,
modern people consider it difficult.
Now, in one meeting, you have fully achieved both these difficult things.
It can be said
'Bright virtue alone is fragrant.'
Does the Shī not say:
'I keep it in my heart,
never forgetting it for a single day!'"
The "Biography of Famous Scholars" states:
"At that time, Cáo Shuǎng was assisting in governance,
and discerning individuals feared there was a crisis.
Yàn had a great reputation,
and was related by marriage to the Wèi house.
Although inwardly worried,
he had no way to retreat.
He composed a poem in five-character lines to express his intent:
'The swan geese fly wing to wing,
flocking and sporting in the great void.
Ever fearing the great net,
that calamity may befall them all at once.
How better to gather at the five lakes,
following the current, nibbling on floating duckweed.
Forever peaceful and open-hearted,
why be startled and alarmed?'
It was likely due to Lù's words
that he, in fear, composed this poem."
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, failing to realize the foolishness of the Crown Prince,
was determined to pass the throne to him.
Many of the famous ministers also offered forthright advice.
The Emperor was once seated on the Língyún Tower,
with Wèi Guàn at his side.
Wishing to express his thoughts,
Guàn pretended to be drunk and knelt before the Emperor,
patting the seat with his hand, saying:
"This seat is a pity."
Although the Emperor understood,
he smiled and said:
"Are you drunk, sir?"
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"Initially,
when Emperor Huì was Crown Prince,
everyone said he was incapable of handling affairs of state.
Wèi Guàn often wished to propose his removal but did not dare.
Later, taking advantage of a gathering while drunk,
he knelt before the Emperor's seat and said:
'Your subject wishes to make a proposal.'
The Emperor said:
'What is it
you wish to say, sir?'
Guàn, wishing to speak, hesitated three times,
then patted the seat with his hand, saying:
'This seat is a pity.'
The Emperor then understood his meaning,
but feigned ignorance, saying:
'You are truly very drunk, sir.'
Later, the Emperor summoned all the officials of the Eastern Palace for a grand assembly,
ordered his attendants to bring memorials from the Imperial Secretariat to show the Crown Prince,
and had him decide on them.
The Crown Prince did not know how to respond.
Consort Jiǎ asked outsiders,
who answered on the Crown Prince's behalf,
often citing ancient texts and meanings.
The attendant Zhāng Hóng said:
'The Crown Prince does not study,
as Your Majesty knows.
He should decide based on the matters presented,
and should not quote from books.'
The Consort followed his advice.
Hóng drafted a memorial,
had the Crown Prince copy it and present it,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased,
showing it to Guàn.
Thereupon, Jiǎ Chōng said to the Consort:
'That old slave Wèi Guàn
nearly ruined your family.'
From then on, the Consort bore a grudge against Guàn,
and later had him executed."
Wáng Yífǔ's wife was the daughter of Guō Tàiníng.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Guō Yù, styled Tàiníng,
was from Tàiyuán.
He served as an aide to the Counselor-in-Chief,
and was well-known.
He died young."
She was untalented yet stubborn by nature,
insatiable in amassing wealth,
and meddled in others' affairs.
Yífǔ was troubled by this but could not stop her.
At that time, their fellow townsman Lǐ Yáng, the Governor of Yōuzhōu,
was a great knight-errant in the capital.
The "Jìn Bǎiguān Míng" states:
"Yáng, styled Jǐngzǔ,
was from Gāopíng.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign, he served as Governor of Yōuzhōu."
The "Yǔlín" states:
"Yáng was by nature a knight-errant.
During the height of summer, he would visit several hundred households in a single day to bid farewell,
and guests coming to say goodbye
often filled his gate.
He eventually died beneath a small table,
so she feared him."
He was like Lóu Hù of the Hàn dynasty.
The "Hànshū·Yóuxiá Zhuàn" states:
"Hù, styled Jūnqīng,
was from Qí.
He studied the classics and commentaries,
and gained considerable fame.
When his mother died,
three thousand carriages attended her funeral.
He served as Governor of Tiānshuǐ."
Lady Guō was afraid of him.
Yífǔ repeatedly admonished her,
and finally said:
"Not only do I say you shouldn't do this,
Lǐ Yáng also says you shouldn't."
Lady Guō then slightly reduced her behavior.
Wáng Yífǔ was refined and esteemed profound detachment,
and often detested his wife's greed and vulgarity.
He never uttered
the word
"money." The "Jìn Yáng Qiū" states:
"Yífǔ was good at giving alms.
For those who had borrowed from his father,
he would burn their promissory notes,
and never engaged in profit-seeking ventures."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìnshū" states:
"Yífǔ sought wealth and obtained wealth;
his assets piled up like mountains,
and he couldn't spend them all.
Why would he need to ask about money?
Yet the world considers his not asking to be lofty—
isn't that also perplexing!"
His wife wanted to test him,
and ordered maids to surround the bed with coins,
so he couldn't walk.
Yífǔ got up in the morning,
saw the coins blocking his way,
and called to the maids:
"Take away these things!"
Wáng Píngzǐ, at fourteen
or fifteen, saw Wáng Yífǔ's wife Guō being greedy,
ordering maids to carry manure on the road.
Píngzǐ admonished her,
and said it was unacceptable.
Guō became furious,
and said to Píngzǐ:
"When your late mother was dying,
she entrusted the young master to your new sister-in-law,
not your new sister-in-law to the young master!"
The "Yǒngjiā Liúrén Míng" states:
"Chéng's father was Yì,
the third son,
who married a daughter of the Rèn family from Lè'ān,
and gave birth to Chéng."
She quickly grabbed his robe,
intending to beat him with a cane.
Píngzǐ was quite strong,
struggled free,
and fled by leaping through a window.
Emperor Yuán, even after crossing the river, still loved wine.
Wáng Màohóng had an old friendship with the Emperor,
and often tearfully admonished him.
The Emperor agreed,
ordered wine to be poured,
drank one hearty round,
and from then on abstained.
Dèng Càn's "Jìn Jì" states:
"The Emperor personally practiced frugality,
to prioritize current affairs.
He had always loved wine.
When about to cross the river,
Wáng Dǎo earnestly admonished him.
The Emperor then ordered attendants to bring a cup,
drank and overturned it,
and from then on never drank again.
Restraining himself and returning to propriety,
he perfected his governance methods,
and thus the restoration of the dynasty flourished."
Xiè Kūn was Governor of Yùzhāng,
and followed the Grand General down to Shítóu.
Dūn said to Kūn:
"I can no longer engage in virtuous deeds."
Kūn said:
"Why is that so?
Just let from now on,
each day pass and each day depart!"
The "Xiè Kūn Biézhuàn" states:
"Kūn's elegant and upright admonitions
were all of this kind."
Dūn also claimed illness and did not attend court.
Kūn advised Dūn:
"Recently,
your actions,
though intended to greatly preserve the state,
yet within the four seas,
people's true feelings are not understood.
If you can attend court to see the Son of Heaven,
so that the officials are relieved,
the hearts of all things
will then be won over.
Rely on the people's hopes to follow public sentiment,
and fully embrace humility to serve the sovereign.
If so,
then your merit will equal that of unifying the realm,
and your name will endure for a thousand years."
Contemporaries considered this a famous saying.
The "Jìn Yáng Qiū" states:
"Kūn was Governor of Yùzhāng.
When Wáng Dūn was about to commit rebellion,
because Kūn had contemporary prestige,
he forced him to go along.
After capturing the capital,
as they were about to return to Wǔchāng,
Kūn said:
'If you do not attend court for an audience,
I fear private criticism throughout the land.'
Dūn said:
'Can you guarantee there will be no change?'
He replied:
'I recently entered for an audience;
the sovereign anxiously awaited,
eager to see you.
The palace was solemn and orderly;
there is certainly no cause for unforeseen worry.
If you enter court,
I request to accompany you.'
Dūn said:
'Even if I kill a few hundred like you,
what harm would it do to the times?'
Thus, he did not attend court and left."
During the reign of Emperor Yuán,
Chief Commandant of Justice Zhāng Kǎi (Gě Hóng's "Ode to the Fùmín Pond" states:
"Kǎi, styled Jìngxù,
was from Dānyáng,
and was the grandson of Zhāng Zhāo.")
The Book of the Restoration states:
"Kǎi,
as the Prefect of Jìnlíng,
was very authoritative and virtuous.
He was later transferred to become Chief Commandant of Justice.")
He lived in the Lesser Market,
and privately built a main gate,
closing it early and opening it late.
The common people were troubled by this,
and went to the provincial government to lodge a complaint,
but received no resolution.
They then proceeded to beat the drum for appealing to the emperor,
yet still received no judgment.
Hearing that Minister of Works Hè was leaving,
and had reached Pògāng,
they jointly went to Hè to present their complaint.
(The Separate Biography of Hè Xún states:
"Xún, styled Yànxiān,
was from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His original surname was Qìng.
His great-great-grandfather, Chún,
avoided the taboo of the Hàn emperor's name,
and changed it to the surname Hè.
His father, Shào,
was the Central Secretariat Director of Wú,
and was killed for his loyalty and integrity.
Xún suffered the family calamity in his youth,
was exiled to a remote border region,
and returned only after Wú was pacified.
He upheld his integrity and rose high.
When Emperor Yuán was the General Pacifying the East,
he recommended Xún to be the Prefect of Wú Commandery.")
Hè said:
"I have been summoned to serve as a ritual official,
and am not involved in this matter."
The common people kowtowed and said:
"If you, Prefect, also do not address this,
then we have nowhere else to appeal."
Hè did not speak,
but told them to leave for now,
saying that when he saw Chief Commandant of Justice Zhāng, he would mention it for them.
When Zhāng heard of this,
he immediately had the gate destroyed,
and personally went to Fāngshān to welcome Hè.
Hè came out to see him and declined, saying:
"This did not necessarily require your attention,
but due to our family friendship,
I felt it was a pity."
Zhāng, ashamed, apologized and said:
"For such a minor matter,
I did not know immediately,
but have already had it destroyed early on."
Grand Marshal Xī, in his later years, enjoyed discussing affairs,
though these were not matters he was truly experienced in,
yet he was very proud of it.
(The Book of the Restoration states:
"Jiàn was fond of learning and widely read from a young age,
though not versed in detailed exegesis,
he had a broad and comprehensive understanding.")
Later, during an audience at court,
believing that Chancellor Wáng in his later years had many regrettable actions,
every time they met,
he would insist on earnestly admonishing him.
Lord Wáng knew his intention,
and each time would steer the conversation to other topics.
Before returning to his garrison,
Xī deliberately had his carriage driven to visit the Chancellor.
The Chancellor, with bristling beard and stern countenance,
sat up and immediately said:
"As we are about to part,
I must speak of what I have observed."
His mind was full but his words heavy,
and his speech was particularly halting.
Lord Wáng, seizing the pause, said:
"The time for our next meeting is uncertain,
and I too wish to express all that is on my mind,
so I hope you will not speak further."
Xī then became greatly angry,
and left with a cold, stiff demeanor,
unable to utter a single word.
When Chancellor Wáng was in Yángzhōu,
he dispatched eight Departmental Assistants to their posts.
Gù Hé at the time was returning from an inspection tour,
and they were all received together.
The various Assistants each reported on the merits and faults of the two-thousand-picul officials and administrators,
but when it came to Hé, he alone said nothing.
Wáng asked Gù:
"What have you heard?"
He replied:
"With you, Illustrious Lord, as chief minister,
would you rather let the net be so loose that it allows a boat-swallowing fish to escape?
Why then gather hearsay,
to implement a government of petty scrutiny?"
The Chancellor sighed in admiration and praised it as excellent,
and the various Assistants felt themselves lacking.
Sū Jùn was marching east to attack Shěn Chōng,
(The Autumn Annals of Jìn states:
"Chōng, styled Shìjū,
was from Wúxīng.
In his youth, he was fond of military affairs,
and flattered Wáng Dūn.
When Dūn captured the capital region,
he appointed Chōng as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
concurrently holding the post of Prefect of Wú Commandery.
When Emperor Míng attacked Wáng Dūn,
Chōng led his troops to join Wáng Hán,
and said to his wife:
'If a man does not establish a leopard-tail banner,
he will not return!'
After Dūn's death,
Chōng was beheaded in the capital by Wú Rú.")
He requested that the Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, Lù Mài, accompany him.
(The Stele Inscription for Lù states:
"Mài, styled Gōnggāo,
was from Wú Commandery.
His talent and insight were clear and sharp,
and his conduct and self-restraint were pure and stern.
He rose successively to General Who Inspires Awe and Administrator,
and Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.")
As they were about to reach Wú,
Jùn secretly ordered his attendants
to enter the Chāng Gate and set a fire to demonstrate his power.
Lù knew his intention,
and said to Jùn:
"Wú has not been peaceful for long,
and there is sure to be disorder.
If you wish to create a step towards chaos,
please start from my household."
Jùn then stopped.
Lù Wán was appointed as Minister of Works.
(The Separate Biography of Wán states:
"At that time, Wáng Dǎo,
Xī Jiàn,
and Yǔ Liàng had successively passed away,
causing anxiety and fear in the court and among the people.
Because of Wán's virtue and reputation,
he was appointed Minister of Works.
Wán declined and yielded but could not avoid it,
and then sighed, saying to his friends:
'For someone like me to become one of the Three Dukes
means there is no one left in the empire.'
People of the time considered this a perceptive statement.")
Someone went to see him,
asked for fine wine,
and upon receiving it, stood up himself,
poured it on the ground between the beams and pillars,
and prayed, saying:
"Nowadays there is a lack of talent,
and you are being used as pillars and cornerstones.
Do not topple the beams and pillars of others."
Wán said with a smile:
"I take note of your excellent admonition."
When Xiǎo Yǔ was in Jīngzhōu,
during a grand assembly of officials,
he asked his various aides:
"I wish to be like Hàn Gāozǔ or
Wèi Wǔ, what do you think?"
(Yì's separate biography is seen elsewhere.)
Sòng Míngdì's Record of Literary Works states:
"Considering Yǔ Yì's standing and reputation,
how could he have been so presumptuous and unrestrained?
If such words were spoken at the time,
it must also be an error of those who transmitted the account.")
No one in the assembly answered,
until Chief Clerk Jiāng Bīn said:
"I hope you, Illustrious Lord, will undertake the affairs of Huán and
Wén,
and not wish to become like Hàn Gāozǔ or
Wèi Wǔ."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi once passed by the stele of Cáo É,
with Yáng Xiū accompanying him.
On the back of the stele, they saw an inscription that read
"Huáng juǎn yòu fù,
wài sūn jī jiù"
— eight characters in total.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi asked Xiū:
"Do you understand it?"
He replied:
"I do."
Emperor Wǔ said:
"Do not speak yet,
let me think about it."
After traveling thirty lǐ,
Emperor Wǔ then said:
"I have figured it out."
He ordered Xiū to separately write down what he understood.
Xiū said:
"Huáng juǎn
means 'colored silk,'
which forms the character 'jué' (绝).
Yòu fù
means 'young woman,'
which forms the character 'miào' (妙).
Wài sūn
means 'daughter's son,'
which forms the character 'hǎo' (好).
Jī jiù
means 'receiving pungent things,'
which forms the character 'cí' (辭).
Altogether, it means
'jué miào hǎo cí'
— 'exquisite and beautiful words.'"
Emperor Wǔ also wrote it down,
and it matched Xiū's interpretation.
He then sighed and said:
"My talent is not equal to yours;
it took me thirty lǐ to realize it."
The "Kuàijī Diǎn Lù" states:
"The filial daughter Cáo É
was a person of Shàngyú.
Her father, Xū,
could beat time and sing along,
dancing to entertain the gods.
In the second year of the Hàn'ān era,
while welcoming the spirit of Wǔ Jūn,
he went upstream against the waves,
was drowned by the water,
and his body was not recovered.
É, at the age of fourteen,
wept in longing for Xū,
and threw a melon into the river,
saying to locate her father's body:
'If my father is here,
the melon should sink.'
After seventeen days,
the melon happened to sink,
so she threw herself into the river and died.
The county magistrate Dù Shàng, moved by her righteousness,
had her reburied,
and ordered his disciple Hándān Zǐlǐ to compose a 'Stele' for her."
Note: The stele of Cáo É is in Kuàijī,
but Emperor Wǔ of Wèi
and Yáng Xiū never crossed the river.
The "Yì Yuàn" states:
"Càiliú's Cài Yōng, fleeing trouble, passed through Wú,
read the stele's text,
and thought it was the work of a poet,
without deceit or falsehood.
Thus, he carved eight characters beside the stone.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi saw it but could not understand,
so he asked his officials,
and none could explain it.
There was a woman washing clothes at Fénzhǔ,
who said:
'The fourth carriage understands.'
Shortly after,
it was Mí Zhèngpíng.
Héng immediately explained it using the method of character decomposition.
Some say this woman was the spirit of É."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was campaigning against Yuán Běnchū,
preparing equipment,
and there were several tens of hú of bamboo strips left over,
each several inches long.
Everyone said they were unusable,
and were about to order them burned.
Tàizǔ pondered how to use them,
thinking they could be made into bamboo shields,
but did not voice this idea.
He sent a messenger to ask his Registrar Yáng Dézǔ.
Dézǔ answered immediately,
matching the emperor's thoughts.
Everyone admired his quick wit.
Wáng Dūn led his army almost to the Great Bridge,
and Emperor Míng personally went to the central hall.
Wēn Qiáo was the Governor of Dānyáng,
and the emperor ordered the Great Bridge destroyed,
but it had not yet been destroyed.
The emperor was furious,
glaring fiercely,
and everyone around was terrified.
According to the "Jìnyáng Qiū"
and Dèng's "Records," both state:
As Dūn approached,
Qiáo burned the Zhūquè Bridge to hinder his troops.
But it is said the Great Bridge was not destroyed,
causing the emperor's anger,
which is a great error.
One version says
"The emperor personally urged Qiáo to enter,"
another version says
"He drank to quell the emperor's anger,"
which is closer to the truth.
He summoned the various lords.
Qiáo arrived without apologizing,
only asking for wine and roasted meat.
Wáng Dǎo arrived shortly after,
barefoot and stepping down,
apologizing:
"The majesty of heaven is upon your face,
causing Wēn Qiáo to be unable to apologize."
Qiáo then apologized,
and the emperor calmed down.
The lords of old admired Wáng's clever and famous words.
Minister of Works Xī was in the Northern Administration,
and Huán Xuānwǔ disliked his holding military power.
The "Nán Xúzhōu Jì" states:
"The people of Xúzhōu are strong and fierce,
known as elite soldiers,
so Huán Wēn often said:
'In Jīngkǒu, the wine is drinkable,
the thorns are usable,
the soldiers are deployable.'"
Xī was always slow to grasp critical matters,
and sent a letter to Huán:
"I wish to jointly support the royal house,
and restore the imperial tombs."
His eldest son, Jiābīn, was traveling,
and on the road heard a messenger had arrived,
urgently took the letter,
read it through,
tore it into tiny pieces,
and turned back.
He returned and rewrote the letter,
stating on his own behalf that he was old and ill,
unfit for worldly affairs,
and wished to beg for a quiet place to retire.
Xuānwǔ was delighted upon receiving the letter,
and immediately issued an edict transferring the Duke to oversee five commanderies,
as Governor of Kuàijī.
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"The Grand Marshal was about to campaign against Mùróng Wěi,
and submitted a request urging General Píngběi Yīn and Yuán Zhēn, among others, to prepare strictly.
Yīn, due to frail health, requested to retire,
and an edict ordered the Grand Marshal to assume Yīn's duties."
According to the "Zhōngxīng Shū":
Yīn declined this mission,
Wēn reprimanded him for not complying,
and transferred him to Kuàijī.
The "Shì Shuō" is mistaken.
Wáng Dōngtíng served as Xuānwǔ's Registrar,
and once in spring went horseback riding in the suburbs with Shítóu and his brothers.
The talented companions of the time
rode side by side, advancing together.
Shítóu
was the childhood name of Huán Xiá.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Xiá, styled Bódào,
was Wēn's eldest son.
He served up to Governor of Yùzhōu."
Only Dōngtíng consistently rode ahead,
leading by several tens of paces,
and no one understood why.
Shítóu and the others grew tired,
and soon returned by carriage,
everyone looking like attendants,
only Dōngtíng remained spirited and ahead.
Such was his quick wit.
Wáng Chùzhòng was acclaimed by his contemporaries as a man of lofty character.
He once indulged recklessly in sensual pleasures,
to the point that his health deteriorated.
His attendants admonished him,
and Chùzhòng said:
"I was simply unaware of it.
If that is the case,
it is very easy to remedy!"
He then opened the rear chambers,
drove out several dozen maids and concubines onto the road,
and let them go wherever they wished.
People of the time sighed in admiration.
Dèng Càn's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Dūn was by nature straightforward and unrestrained,
and never spoke of wealth.
His conduct was of such a standard."
The Grand General Wáng himself described himself as:
"Lofty and clear-minded, unrestrained and direct,
with a scholarly mastery of the *Zuǒzhuàn*."
*Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"From a young age, Dūn was praised as lofty, direct, penetrating, and clear-minded,
possessing discernment and judgment."
Wáng Chùzhòng, after drinking wine, would often recite
"An old steed in the stable may still aspire to gallop a thousand miles;
A hero in his twilight years never abandons his lofty ambitions."
From Wèi Wǔdì's *Yuèfǔ* poems.
He would strike his spittoon with a *rúyì* scepter,
until the mouth of the spittoon was completely chipped away.
Jìn Míngdì wished to construct a pond and terrace,
but Yuándì would not permit it.
The Emperor, then Crown Prince,
was fond of nurturing warriors.
One night, they constructed a pond,
and by dawn it was completed.
This is the present-day Crown Prince's West Pond.
*Dānyáng Jì* states:
"The West Pond
was originally created by Sūn Dēng,
and is the West Garden mentioned in *Wú Shǐ*.
Míngdì merely restored it."
When Grand General Wáng first intended to march to the capital,
to make arrangements and establish his authority,
he first sent an aide to inform the court,
hinting at his intentions to the eminent men of the time.
Zǔ Chēqí had not yet been stationed in Shòuchūn;
glaring and speaking in a stern voice to the messenger, he said:
"You tell Ā Hēi:
Dūn's childhood name.
How dare he be so insolent!
Urge him to pack up and leave at once.
If he delays even a moment,
I will lead three thousand troops
and spear him all the way back up!"
Wáng, upon hearing this, desisted.
Yǔ Zhìgōng had long harbored the ambition to recover the Central Plains.
During Wénkāng's time, when power was concentrated,
it was not in his hands.
When Jìjiān became chancellor,
fearing military conflict and calamity,
he and Zhìgōng debated their differences for a long time
before finally taking action.
Mobilizing the full strength of Jīngzhōu and Hànzhōng,
and exhausting the capacity of boats and chariots,
he stationed his army at Xiāngyáng.
*Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū* states:
"Yì's demeanor was elegant and commendable,
his talents abundant and ample.
From a young age, he possessed great strategic vision.
After succeeding his elder brother Liàng in governing a key province,
he held the ambition to uphold order both internally and externally,
and to sweep away the various hostile forces.
At that time,
Dù Yì,
Yīn Hào, and others enjoyed great fame, renowned throughout the age,
but Yì did not value them.
He often said:
'Such men should be put on the high shelf;
wait until the world is pacified and settled,
then discuss what posts they should hold!'
Such was his spirit.
He was only close friends with Huán Wēn,
mutually committed to the task of bringing peace and order to the realm.
Initially, Yì mobilized the servants under his command and tens of thousands of chariots and horses,
leading a great army into the Miǎn region,
planning to campaign against the northern tribes,
and thus stationed his forces at Xiāngyáng."
*Yì Biézhuàn* states:
"As Governor of Jīngzhōu,
Yì truly had great ambitions.
He often felt that given his family's prestigious status
and the high positions granted to his brothers,
if he did not exert his strength and devote his utmost loyalty,
how could he repay the state?
Although Shǔ relied on treacherous terrain,
and the northern tribes possessed fierce military power,
both were tyrannical and cruel, without the Way,
and could easily be taken advantage of and destroyed.
If at this time he could not eradicate these two enemies
and restore the royal enterprise,
he would not be a true man.
Thereupon, he levied troops from three provinces,
exhausted their treasuries and resources,
assembled a force of fifty thousand men,
and additionally led recently submitted border tribes,
marshaling his troops for a major campaign,
directly aiming at Wèi and Zhào.
His army stationed at Xiāngyáng,
displaying its might north of the Hàn River."
He convened a grand assembly of his officers,
displayed his banners and armor,
and personally drew his bow, saying:
"This campaign of mine
is like this shot!"
He then shot three times, each hitting the target in succession.
The assembled troops watched intently,
and their morale increased tenfold.
When Huán Xuānwǔ pacified Shǔ,
he gathered his subordinates and held a banquet in Lǐ Shì's palace hall.
The gentry of Bā and Shǔ
all came to gather.
Huán, who always possessed a heroic spirit and forthright demeanor,
on that day was particularly eloquent and inspiring in his speech.
He discussed how success and failure throughout history depended on people,
and survival or destruction hinged on talent.
His manner was open and magnificent,
earning the admiration of all present.
After the gathering dispersed,
many pondered and savored his remaining words.
At that time, Zhōu Fù of Xúnyáng said:
"It is a pity that you gentlemen never saw the Grand General Wáng."
*Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Fù
was the grandson of Zhōu Fǔ,
courtesy name Zhànyǐn.
He had military talent,
and once served as an aide to Dūn."
Duke Huán was reading *Gāoshì Zhuàn*,
and when he reached Yúlíng Zhòngzǐ,
he threw the book aside and said:
"Who can bear to live in such a harsh and severe manner!"
Huángfǔ Mì's *Gāoshì Zhuàn* states:
"Chén Zhòngzǐ, courtesy name Zǐzhōng,
was a man of Qí.
His elder brother Dài served as Chancellor of Qí,
enjoying a salary of ten thousand *zhōng*.
Zhòngzǐ considered his brother's salary unrighteous,
so he went to Chǔ
and lived in Yúlíng.
Once he went without food for three days;
crawling, he ate the fruit of a wild plum tree by the well,
swallowing three times before he could see again.
He wove sandals himself
and had his wife split hemp fibers,
to exchange for clothing and food.
Once he returned to visit his mother,
and someone had presented his brother with a live goose.
Zhòngzǐ frowned and said:
'What use is this honking creature?'
Later, his mother killed the goose,
and Zhòngzǐ, unaware, ate it.
His brother came in from outside and said:
'Is this the honking creature's meat?'
Zhòngzǐ rushed out the door
and vomited it up.
The King of Chǔ, hearing of his reputation,
invited him to serve as chancellor,
but he and his wife fled,
and worked watering gardens for others."
Huán Shíqián was the eldest son of a concubine of Sikōng Huò.
The "Biography of Huò" states:
"Huò, styled Lǎngzǐ,
was the younger brother of Huán Wēn.
He rose through the ranks to become the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and was posthumously granted the title of Sikōng."
Huán Shíqián's childhood name was Zhèn'è.
At the age of seventeen or eighteen, before he had been officially recommended for office,
the servants and attendants already called him 'Young Master Zhèn'è.'
He once stayed at Xuānwǔ's (Huán Wēn's) headquarters.
While following the campaign to Fángtóu,
the Chējì (General of Chariots and Cavalry) Chōng (Huán Chōng) fell into the enemy ranks,
and none of the attendants around him could rescue him first.
Xuānwǔ said to him:
"Your uncle has fallen into the hands of the enemy,
do you know?"
Shíqián heard this,
and his spirit was greatly roused.
He ordered Zhū Pì as his deputy,
spurred his horse into the midst of tens of thousands of enemy troops,
and none could resist him.
He directly brought Chōng back,
and the entire army sighed in admiration.
Later, north of the Yellow River, they used his name to cure malaria.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Shíqián had talent and ability,
was knowledgeable in history,
and repeatedly achieved military merits.
He served up to the position of Governor of Yùzhōu,
and was posthumously granted the title of General of the Rear Army."
Chén Líndào was on the western bank.
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"Kuí served as the General of the Western Central Army,
concurrently holding the position of Tàishǒu of Huáinán,
and garrisoned Lìyáng."
Various people from the capital invited him to a gathering at Niúzhǔ.
Since Chén's reasoning was excellent,
people wanted to debate and refute him together.
Chén rested his cheek on a ruyi scepter,
gazed at Jīlóng Mountain and sighed, saying:
"Sūn Bófú's ambitions and achievements were not fulfilled!"
The "Wú Lù" states:
"The King of Chángshā, posthumously named Cè,
styled Bófú,
was from Fùchūn, Wújùn.
From a young age, he had a heroic appearance and imposing demeanor.
At the age of nineteen, he inherited the family enterprise,
and the masses called him 'Young Master Sūn.'
He pacified Jiāngdōng.
He was shot in the face by an assassin sent by Xǔ Gòng,
took a mirror to look at himself,
and said to his attendants:
'With a face like this,
how can I achieve further merits?'
Then he said to Zhāng Zhāo:
'The Central Plains are in chaos.
With the masses of Wú and
Yuè,
and the natural defenses of the Three Rivers,
it is enough to observe the successes and failures.
You, gentlemen, must assist my younger brother well.'
He called the Great Emperor and handed him the seal and ribbon, saying:
'To lead the masses of Jiāngdōng
and make decisive moves between two battle arrays,
you are not as good as I;
but in appointing the worthy and employing the capable,
enabling each to give their utmost loyalty,
I am not as good as you.
Be careful not to cross north!'
After speaking these words, he passed away,
at the age of twenty-six."
Thus, for the entire gathering, no one could engage in conversation.
Sīzhōu Wáng was at Xiè Gōng's gathering,
and recited
"Entering without a word, leaving without a farewell,
riding the whirlwind, bearing cloud banners."
These are lines from the "Lísāo," the "Jiǔgē," specifically the "Shǎosīmìng."
He told others:
"At that moment,
I felt as if there was no one else in the entire gathering."
Huán Xuán went down the river westward,
and entered Shítóu.
A report came from outside:
"Sīmǎ, the Prince of Liáng, has fled and rebelled."
The "Xù Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"The Prince of Liáng, Zhēnzhī, styled Jǐngdù."
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Initially,
when Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
a man of the state named Kǒng Pú
escorted Zhēnzhī to flee to Xúnyáng.
After the righteous banners were raised,
he returned to the court,
served up to the position of Tàicháng Qīng,
and was executed for a crime."
At that time, Huán Xuán's situation was already settled,
and on the Píngchéng boat, reed pipes and drums were played together.
He directly chanted aloud:
"The flutes and pipes still carry lingering tunes,
but where is the Prince of Liáng now?"
These are lines from Ruǎn Jí's "Yǒnghuái" poems.
Wèi Wǔ (Cáo Cāo) was about to receive an envoy from the Xiōngnú.
He considered himself physically unimpressive,
and insufficient to awe a distant state.
The "Wèishì Chūnqiū" states:
"Wǔ Wáng (Cáo Cāo) was short in stature,
but his spirit and intelligence were outstanding."
He had Cuī Jìguī act as his substitute,
while the Emperor himself stood by the head of the bed holding a sword.
After the audience was over,
he sent a spy to ask:
"What did you think of the King of Wèi?"
The Xiōngnú envoy replied:
"The King of Wèi had an exceptionally dignified appearance.
The "Wèi Zhì" states:
"Cuī Yǎn, styled Jìguī,
was from Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé.
His voice and bearing were lofty and resonant,
his eyebrows and eyes clear and bright,
his beard four feet long,
and he had a very imposing and dignified presence."
However, the man holding the sword by the head of the bed,
he is the true hero."
Wèi Wǔ heard this,
and pursued and killed this envoy.
Hé Píngshū had beautiful features and appearance,
and his face was extremely white.
Wèi Míngdì suspected that he applied powder.
It was precisely during the summer,
and he gave him hot soup and noodles.
After he ate them,
great sweat poured out,
and he wiped himself with his red robe.
His complexion became even more radiant.
The "Wèi Lüè" states:
"Yàn was naturally fond of his appearance,
powder and silk never left his hands,
and he walked observing his own shadow."
Note: According to this account,
then Yàn's enchanting beauty
originally relied on external adornment.
Moreover, Yàn was raised within the palace,
and grew up together with the Emperor.
How could he still doubt his physical appearance,
needing to verify it to become clear?
Wèi Míngdì had the younger brother of the Empress, Máo Zēng, sit together with Xiàhóu Xuán.
People of the time said
it was like "reeds leaning against a jade tree."
The "Wèi Zhì" states:
"Xuán served as a Huángmén Shìláng,
and once sat together with Máo Zēng.
Xuán felt deeply ashamed of this,
and his displeasure showed on his face.
Míngdì resented this,
and demoted Xuán to the position of Yǔlín Jiān."
People of the time described Xiàhóu Tàichū as
"brilliant and clear, like the sun and moon entering one's bosom,"
and Lǐ Ānguó as
"unsteady like a jade mountain about to collapse."
The "Wèi Lüè" states:
"Lǐ Fēng, styled Ānguó,
was the son of Commandant of the Guards Lǐ Yì.
He was skilled in discerning people,
and attracted attention throughout the land.
Míngdì obtained a surrendered person from Wú,
and asked, 'In Jiāngdōng, who are the famous scholars of the Central States that are known?'
The person answered with Ānguó's name.
At that time, Fēng was a Huángmén Láng,
and had changed his name to Xuān.
The Emperor asked, 'Where is Ānguó?'
The attending ministers and nobles immediately informed him that it was Fēng.
The Emperor said:
'Fēng's fame has even spread to Wú and
Yuè?'
He served up to the position of Zhōngshū Lìng,
and was executed by the Prince of Jìn."
Jī Kāng was seven feet eight inches tall,
with exceptionally distinguished grace and bearing.
The "Biography of Kāng" states:
"Kāng was seven feet eight inches tall,
with a magnificent countenance.
His physical form was like earth and wood,
without any added adornment or polish,
yet he possessed the elegance of a dragon and the grace of a phoenix,
a natural, heavenly quality.
Even amidst a crowd of people,
one could immediately recognize him as an extraordinary vessel."
Those who saw him sighed, saying:
"Solemn and dignified,
refreshingly bright and clear, elevated."
Some said:
"Solemn like the wind beneath a pine tree,
lofty and gently extending."
Shān Gōng said:
"Jī Shūyè as a person
stands tall and imposing like a solitary pine tree;
when he is drunk,
he totters like a jade mountain about to collapse."
Minister Péi described Wáng Ānfēng as
"having eyes that sparkle brilliantly like lightning beneath a cliff."
Wáng Róng was short and small in stature,
but his eyes were exceptionally clear and bright,
able to gaze at the sun without being dazzled.
Pān Yuè possessed marvelous beauty and grace,
with a delightful spirit and demeanor.
The "Biography of Yuè" states:
"Yuè's appearance and grace were exceedingly beautiful,
his bearing and manner were leisurely and unrestrained."
In his youth, he would go out carrying a slingshot on the roads of Luòyáng,
and whenever women encountered him,
they would all join hands to encircle him.
Zuǒ Tàichōng was extremely ugly.
The "Continuation of the Records of Literary Figures" states:
"Sī's appearance was ugly and haggard,
and he did not maintain proper grooming or adornment."
He also imitated Yuè in wandering about,
whereupon a group of old women all spat at him in disorder,
and he returned utterly exhausted.
The "Forest of Sayings" states:
"Ānrén was extremely beautiful;
every time he went out,
old women would throw fruit at him,
filling his cart.
Zhāng Mèngyáng was extremely ugly;
every time he went out,
children would throw tiles and stones at him,
also filling his cart."
The two accounts differ.
Wáng Yífǔ's appearance was neat and handsome,
and he excelled in discussing profound mysteries.
He often held a white jade-handled yak-tail whisk,
and his hand was indistinguishable from it.
Pān Ānrén
and Xiàhóu Zhàn were both beautifully handsome,
and they enjoyed traveling together.
People of the time called them
"linked jades."
The "Stories of the Eight Princes" states:
"Yuè and Zhàn were close friends,
hence they enjoyed traveling together."
Minister Péi possessed outstanding appearance and grace.
Once, when he was severely ill,
Emperor Huì sent Wáng Yífǔ to visit him.
Péi was lying facing the wall,
and upon hearing that the imperial envoy had arrived,
he forced himself to turn and look.
Wáng went out and told people:
"His pair of eyes sparkled and shone,
like lightning beneath a cliff;
his spirit was vigorous and animated,
though he was indeed somewhat unwell in body."
The "Biographies of Famous Scholars" states:
"When Kǎi was seriously ill,
an edict dispatched the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Wáng Yífǔ, to inquire after him.
Kǎi turned his gaze to Yífǔ and said:
'After all, we have not truly known each other.'
Yífǔ returned
and also sighed at his divine excellence."
Someone said to Wáng Róng:
"Jī Yánzǔ stands out prominently like a wild crane among chickens."
He replied:
"You have not seen his father, that's all!"
Kāng has already been mentioned above.
Minister Péi possessed outstanding appearance and demeanor.
Even when he removed his official cap and robes,
and wore coarse clothes with disheveled hair, he still looked good.
People of the time considered him
"a jade man."
Those who saw him said:
"Seeing Péi Shūzé is like walking on a jade mountain,
his radiance illuminates people."
Liú Líng was six feet tall,
with a very ugly and haggard appearance,
yet he was carefree and absent-minded,
his physical form like earth and wood.
Liáng Zuò's "Unified Records of the State of Wèi" states:
"Liú Líng,
courtesy name Bólún,
had an ugly and unattractive appearance,
and was six feet tall;
yet he indulged freely in unrestrained behavior,
leisurely and solitary, unrestrained.
Content in his own time,
he often felt the universe was too narrow."
Cavalry General Wáng Wǔzǐ was Wèi Jiè's maternal uncle,
outstanding, forthright, and possessing graceful bearing.
Whenever he saw Jiè, he would sigh and say:
"With pearls and jade by my side,
I feel the shabbiness of my own form!"
The "Biography of Jiè" states:
"Cavalry General Wáng Jì,
was Jiè's maternal uncle.
Once, when traveling together,
he told people:
'Yesterday I sat together with my nephew,
it was like having bright pearls by my side,
radiantly illuminating people.'"
Someone visited Minister Wáng,
and encountered Ānfēng,
the Great General,
and the Chancellor all seated there;
then went to another room and saw Jìyìn
and Píngzǐ.
Shí Chóng's "Preface to the Jīngǔ Poems" states:
"Wáng Xǔ, courtesy name Jìyìn,
was from Lángyá."
The "Genealogy of the Wáng Clan" states:
"Xǔ,
was Yífǔ's younger brother,
and served up to the position of Magistrate of Xiūwǔ."
Upon returning, the visitor told people:
"Today's visit,
wherever I looked, I saw a dazzling array of pearls and jades."
Chancellor Wáng, upon seeing Wèi the Palace Aide, said:
"He actually has such a frail form;
even if he were to regulate and harmonize himself all day long,
he still seems unable to bear the weight of fine silks."
The "Biography of Jiè" states:
"Jiè had long suffered from a frail constitution."
The "Rhapsody on the Western Capital" states:
"At first advancing slowly with a frail form,
as if unable to bear the weight of fine silks."
The Great General Wáng praised the Minister:
"Amidst a crowd of people,
he is like pearls and jade among tiles and stones."
Yǔ Zǐsōng was less than seven feet tall,
with a waistband ten spans around,
yet he was carefree and self-indulgent.
Wèi Jiè traveled from Yùzhāng to the lower capital,
and people had long heard of his fame,
so onlookers formed a wall-like crowd.
Jiè already had a frail constitution,
and his body could not endure the strain,
so he fell ill and died.
People of the time said
"they looked Wèi Jiè to death."
The "Biography of Jiè" states:
"Jiè, among the crowd,
truly had the aura of an extraordinary person.
When he was a child,
he rode a white goat cart in the markets of Luòyáng,
and everyone said:
'Whose jade man is this?'
Thus, within his family, district, and community, he was called
'the jade man.'"
According to the "Records of Émigrés in Yǒngjiā":
"Jiè arrived in Yùzhāng on the sixth day of the fifth month of the sixth year of Yǒngjiā,
and died on the twentieth day of the sixth month of that year."
This means Jiè was in Yùzhāng for forty-five days after crossing south;
how could he have had time to go to the lower capital and die there?
Moreover, all the texts state that Jiè died in Yùzhāng,
and do not say he died in the lower capital.
Zhōu Bórén said of Huán Màolún:
"Lofty and rugged, full of character—a laughable man."
Some say it was Xiè Yòuyú who said this.
Marquis Zhōu praised the father of Senior Official Wáng:
The "Genealogy of the Wáng Clan" states:
"Wáng Nè, styled Wénkāi,
was from Tàiyuán.
His grandfather, Mò,
served as a Minister.
His father, Yòu,
served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Nè first crossed the river [to the south]
and served as the magistrate of Xīngàn."
His appearance was imposing,
and his refined demeanor possessed grandeur.
Preserve and employ him,
and he could accomplish many things.
Zǔ Shìshào, upon seeing Wèi Jūncháng, said:
"This man has the bearing of one who holds the ceremonial staff beneath the banner."
During the Shítóu incident,
the imperial court was overthrown.
The "Jìnyāng Qiū" states:
"Sū Jùn advanced from Gūshú to Shítóu,
forcing the emperor to relocate.
Jùn used a granary building as the palace,
and had people guard it."
The "Língguǐ Zhì Yáozhēng" states:
"At the end of Emperor Míng's reign, there was a ballad:
'Cè cè lì,
fàng mǎ chū shān cè.
Dà mǎ sǐ,
xiǎo mǎ è.'
Later, Jùn moved the emperor to Shítóu,
and the imperial meals were not provided."
Wēn Zhōngwǔ and Yǔ Wénkāng went to Táo Gōng to seek help.
Táo Gōng said:
"I was not included in Sùzǔ's final decree,
and moreover, Sū Jùn's rebellion
originated from the Yǔ family.
Executing his brothers
would not suffice to apologize to the realm."
Xú Guǎng's "Jìn Jì" states:
"Sùzǔ's final decree
appointed Yǔ Liàng
and Wáng Dǎo to assist the young ruler and promoted the officials of the great ministers,
but Táo Kǎn
and Zǔ Yuē were not among those listed.
Kǎn and Yuē suspected that Liàng had suppressed the final decree."
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Initially,
Yǔ Liàng wanted to summon Sū Jùn,
but Biǎn Kǔn did not permit it.
Wēn Qiáo and the Sānwú region wanted to raise troops to defend the imperial house,
but Liàng would not listen.
He issued an order stating:
'Those who recklessly raise troops shall be executed!'
Therefore, Jùn was able to rebel in the capital."
At that time, Yǔ, who was behind Wēn on the boat, heard this
and was anxious and terrified, with no plan.
On another day,
Wēn urged Yǔ to see Táo.
Yǔ hesitated and could not bring himself to go.
Wēn said:
"I know that Xī dog well.
You just go see him,
and you will certainly have no worries!"
Yǔ's demeanor and spirit
caused Táo to change his view upon first sight.
They conversed and feasted all day,
and affection and esteem arose immediately.
Grand Marshal Yǔ was in Wǔchāng.
On an autumn night with fine air and clear scenery,
he had his officials Yīn Hào,
Wáng Húzhī, and others ascend the south tower to discuss and recite poetry.
Just as the tones began to grow vigorous,
they heard the sound of clogs on the staircase, very loud,
and knew it must be Lord Yǔ.
Soon, he led about ten attendants on foot.
The various worthies wanted to rise and avoid him.
The lord slowly said:
"Gentlemen, stay a while.
This old man's interest here is not shallow!"
Thereupon, he took a folding chair
and joked and recited with the others.
Throughout the gathering, they greatly enjoyed themselves freely.
Later, Wáng Yìshào went down [to the capital]
and spoke of this matter with the Chancellor.
The Chancellor said:
"Yuánguī's demeanor at that time
could not but be somewhat diminished."
The Right Army General replied:
"Only the hills and valleys remained within him."
Sūn Chuò's "Inscription for Yǔ Liàng's Stele" states:
"The lord's refined tastes found expression
often beyond the dust and grime.
Although his gentle heart responded to the world,
and his tracks were bent like an inchworm,
his inner mind was serene,
firmly facing mountains and waters with profundity."
Wáng Jìngyù had a beautiful appearance.
He went to inquire after Lord Wáng.
Lord Wáng patted his shoulder and said:
"Ānú, it is a pity your talent does not match [your looks]!"
It is also said:
"Jìngyù resembles Lord Wáng in every matter."
The "Yǔlín" states:
"Lord Xiè said:
'When I was young, I saw the Chancellor at a court gathering,
and I felt a clear breeze come to brush against people.'"
The Right Army General Wáng saw Dù Hóngzhì
and sighed, saying:
"His face is like congealed lard,
his eyes like dots of lacquer.
This is a man among immortals."
The "Jiāngzuǒ Míngshì Zhuàn" states:
"During the Yǒnghé era,
Liú Zhēncháng
and Xiè Rénzǔ together discussed the gentlemen of the central court.
Someone said:
'Dù Hóngzhì possesses pure and outstanding qualities,
a beauty among later generations.
Moreover, his face is like congealed lard,
his eyes like dots of lacquer.
Roughly, he can be compared to Wèi Jiè.'"
When people of the time praised the appearance of Senior Official Wáng,
Lord Cài said:
"It is a pity those people have not seen Dù Hóngzhì!"
Prefect Liú said of Lord Huán:
his sideburns were like reversed hedgehog skin,
his eyebrows like purple stone edges.
He was naturally of the same kind as Sūn Zhòngmóu
and Simǎ Xuānwáng.
Emperor Míng of Sòng's "Wénzhāng Zhì" states:
"Wēn was admired by Wēn Qiáo,
hence he was named Wēn."
The "Wú Zhì" states:
"Sūn Quán, styled Zhòngmóu,
was Cè's younger brother.
The Hàn envoy Liú Wǎn said to people:
'I observe the Sūn brothers.
Although all are talented, outstanding, and clear-sighted,
none will enjoy their emoluments and blessings to the end.
Only the middle brother, the Filial and Incorrupt,
has a majestic and imposing appearance,
an extraordinary bone structure and physique,
bearing the signs of great nobility.'"
The "Jìnyāng Qiū" states:
"Xuānwáng's natural talents were outstanding and surpassing,
possessing a hero's strategy."
Wáng Jìnglún's demeanor resembled his father's.
He served as Palace Attendant,
and was sent to confer [an appointment] upon Lord Huán.
He entered through the main gate in court dress.
Lord Huán looked at him
and said:
"Dànú indeed naturally has phoenix feathers."
Dànú
was Wáng Shào.
Previously mentioned.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" states:
"Shào had a beautiful appearance and bearing,
and maintained proper deportment."
Monk Lín commented on Senior Official Wáng:
"When he straightens his collar and comes once,
how lofty and splendid his bearing is!"
The "Yǔlín" states:
"Wáng Zhòngzǔ had a fine appearance.
Whenever he looked at himself in the mirror,
he would say:
'How did Wáng Wénkāi produce such a son!'
People of the time considered him open-minded."
People of the time described the Right Army General Wáng:
"Floating like a wandering cloud,
nimble like a startled dragon."
Senior Official Wáng was once ill,
and no one, close or distant, was admitted.
When Monk Lín came,
the gatekeeper hastily reported, saying:
"There is an unusual person at the gate,
I dare not not report it."
Wáng laughed and said:
"This must be Monk Lín."
According to the "Yǔlín":
"People once invited Ruǎn Guānglù to go together to see Monk Lín.
Ruǎn said:
'I wish to hear his words,
but I loathe to see his face.'"
This shows that Monk Lín's appearance
was indeed ugly and unusual.
Some compared Xiè Rénzǔ to someone,
but not with particular esteem.
Grand Marshal Huán said:
"Gentlemen, do not speak lightly.
When Rénzǔ stood on tiptoe beneath the north window playing the pipa,
he truly evoked the image of a celestial transcendent."
*Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Shàng was skilled in music."
*The Writings of Péi* says:
"The Chancellor once said:
'When Jiānshí lifted his foot and rested his head on a pipa,
he had celestial thoughts.'"
Jiānshí
was Shàng's childhood name.
Chief Secretary Wáng served as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
He went to Jìnghé's place.
Jìnghé,
Wáng Qià, has been mentioned previously.
At that time, snow had accumulated.
The Chief Secretary alighted from his carriage outside the gate,
and walked into the Department of State Affairs,
wearing his official robes.
Jìnghé, gazing from afar,
sighed and said:
"This is no longer like a man of this world!"
When Jiǎnwén was the Prince-Chancellor,
he went with Xiè Gōng to visit Huán Xuānwǔ.
Wáng Xún was already inside.
Huán said to Wáng:
"You have long wished to see the Prince-Chancellor;
you may stay behind the curtain."
After the two guests had left,
Huán asked Wáng:
"What is he truly like?"
Wáng said:
"The Prince-Chancellor as a regent
is naturally profound and majestic like a divine lord."
*The Continued Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"The Emperor possessed elegant grace,
his bearing dignified and composed."
"And Xiè Gōng is also the hope of ten thousand men.
Otherwise,
how could the President of the Left of the Department of State Affairs willingly efface himself?"
The President of the Left,
was Xiè Ān.
During the reign of Hǎixī,
whenever the various lords attended court at dawn,
the court hall was still dark.
Only when the Prince of Kuàijī arrived,
did he appear radiant, like the rising of morning clouds.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Xiè spoke of Xiè Gōng:
"Even when strolling in the marketplace without singing loftily,
merely sitting respectfully, pinching his nose and glancing about,
he naturally possessed the demeanor of one dwelling amidst mountains and marshes."
Xiè Gōng said:
"Seeing Reverend Lín's pair of eyes,
darkly profound and brightly black."
Sūn Xìnggōng, upon seeing Reverend Lín,
said: "Sharp and distinct, revealing his keen intelligence."
Yǔ Chángrén and his younger brothers entered Wú,
wishing to lodge at a roadside pavilion.
His younger brothers went up first,
and saw the place full of common folk,
none showing any intention of making way.
Chángrén said:
"Let me go and have a look."
Then, leaning on his staff and leading a young boy,
he had just entered the gate,
when all the guests, beholding his divine bearing,
immediately retreated and hid.
Chángrén has been mentioned previously;
another account says it was Yǔ Liàng.
Someone praised Wáng Gōng's handsome appearance,
saying:
"Fresh and gleaming like a willow in the spring moon."
When Zhōu Chǔ was young,
he was violent, strong, and chivalrous,
and was considered a plague by his village.
*The Separate Biography of Chǔ* states:
"Chǔ, styled Zǐyǐn,
was a man of Yángxiàn in Wú Commandery.
His father was Fáng,
Governor of Póyáng in Wú.
Chǔ was orphaned young,
and did not attend to minor matters of conduct."
*Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Chǔ was frivolous, impulsive, and of shallow conduct,
shunned by the commandery and province."
Furthermore, in Yìxīng, there was a flood dragon in the water,
and in the mountains, a white-browed tiger (one text says 'a lingering-track tiger'),
and both violently harmed the people.
The people of Yìxīng called them the "Three Scourges,"
with Chǔ being the most severe.
Someone persuaded Chǔ to kill the tiger and behead the dragon,
truly hoping that of the three scourges, only one would remain.
Chǔ then stabbed and killed the tiger,
and also entered the water to attack the dragon.
The dragon sometimes floated, sometimes submerged,
traveling for several tens of *li*,
with Chǔ staying alongside it.
After three days and three nights,
the villagers all thought he had died,
and congratulated each other.
In the end, he killed the dragon and emerged.
Hearing the villagers congratulating each other,
he first realized he was considered a plague by people,
and conceived the intention to reform himself.
*The Records of the Strange by the Kong Clan* states:
"In Yìxīng, there was a lame-footed tiger,
and in the streams and marshes of Cháng Bridge, a blue dragon,
