both devouring many people.
Zhōu of Guōxī
was called at the time the third of the commandery's three banes."
Zhōu refers to Chǔ.
He then went himself to seek out the two Lùs.
Lù Píngyuán was not there;
he only met Lù Qīnghé.
He fully reported the circumstances,
and also said:
"I wish to correct and improve myself,
but my years have already been wasted,
and I fear in the end I will achieve nothing."
Qīnghé said:
"The ancients valued hearing the Way in the morning and dying in the evening.
Moreover, your future prospects are still promising.
And what people should worry about is not establishing their will;
why then worry that a fine reputation will not be made manifest?"
Chǔ then reformed and exerted himself,
and in the end became a loyal minister and a filial son.
*Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Chǔ served Jìn as Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief,
and impeached many.
When the Di rebel Qí Wànnián revolted,
he was ordered to resist Wànnián.
Sun Xiu, General Who Calms the Waves, wished to submit a memorial citing Chǔ's aged mother.
Chǔ said:
'The way of loyalty and filial piety—
how can one attain both fully?'
He then advanced to battle,
beheading enemies by the tens of thousands.
When his bowstring snapped and his arrows were exhausted,
his attendants urged him to retreat.
Chǔ said:
'This is the day I receive my fate.'
He then fought until he fell."
Dài Yuān in his youth was
a wandering knight who did not cultivate proper conduct.
He once roamed between the Jiāng and
Huái rivers, attacking and plundering traveling merchants.
When Lù Jī was returning to Luòyáng after his leave,
his baggage train was very substantial.
Yuān sent young men to rob it.
Yuān himself was on the bank,
sitting on a folding chair,
directing his followers left and right,
all with perfect appropriateness.
Since Yuān possessed a divine and outstanding demeanor,
even while engaged in such base affairs,
his spirit and bearing remained extraordinary.
Jī, from the cabin of his boat, called out to him from afar, saying:
"With talent such as yours,
must you also resort to robbery?"
Yuān then wept,
threw down his sword, and surrendered to Jī.
His words were exceptionally forceful.
Jī esteemed him all the more,
formed a friendship with him,
and wrote a letter recommending him.
Yú Yù's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Jī recommended Yuān to Prince Zhào Lún, saying:
'I have heard that only when the Fánruò bow is employed in the imperial hunt,
does its efficacy against high walls become manifest;
only when the Gūzhú bamboo is placed in the workshop,
does the divine music come to completion.
I humbly observe that the retired scholar Dài Yuān
hones his integrity and establishes his conduct,
possessing the purity of a cleansed well;
he finds contentment in poverty and delights in his aspirations,
free from any longing for worldly fame.
He is truly a lost treasure of the southeast,
a precious uncut jade for the imperial court.
If he is allowed to tread the path of virtue,
he will certainly keep pace with the finest steeds;
if his substance is displayed in the court's halls,
he will certainly radiate the brilliance of fine jade.
The people of the barren shore
are resolute in presenting pearls;
the guests of the moist mountain
are arrayed in offering jade.
For when brightness and darkness take form,
even ordinary discernment can recognize them.'"
Lún then summoned Yuān to office."
After crossing the river,
he served up to the position of General Who Conquers the West.
When Chancellor Wǎng was appointed Minister of Works,
Commandant Huán wore his hair in two buns,
a hempen skirt,
and leaning on a staff,
peered at him from the roadside.
He sighed and said:
"People say Ā Lóng is outstanding;
Ā Lóng is indeed outstanding."
Ā Lóng was
the Chancellor's childhood name.
Unconsciously, he reached the gate of the ministry.
Chancellor Wǎng, after crossing the river,
spoke of how he used to be by the Luò River,
often discussing the Way with worthies such as Péi Chénggōng and
Ruǎn Qiānlǐ.
Yáng Màn said:
"People have long acknowledged this about you;
why must you mention it again?"
Wǎng said:
"It's not that I need to say this,
but simply that such times are now irrecoverable!"
Some texts have "sigh" instead of "desire."
When Wáng Yòujūn heard people compare his *Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Collection* to the *Preface to the Poems of the Golden Valley*,
and also compared himself to Shí Chóng,
he wore a very pleased expression.
Wáng Xīzhī's *Riverside Preface* states:
"In the ninth year of the Yǒnghé era,
the cyclical year being guǐchǒu,
in the first days of late spring,
we gathered at the Orchid Pavilion in Shānyīn of Kuàijī
for the purification ceremony.
All the worthies were present,
young and old alike assembled.
This place had lofty mountains and towering ridges,
dense forests and tall bamboos.
There were also clear streams and rushing rapids,
shining and winding around us.
We channeled the water into a winding stream for floating cups,
and sat in rows along its banks.
On this day,
the sky was clear and the air fresh,
a gentle breeze wafted freely.
Pleasing the eye and freeing the heart,
it was truly a joyful occasion.
Though lacking the grandeur of strings and pipes,
with one cup of wine and one chant of a poem,
it was also sufficient to freely express our deep feelings.
Therefore, I list the participants of the time,
recording their compositions.
Right General Sima, Tàiyuán's Sūn Chénggōng, and twenty-five others
composed poems as follows.
Former Yáoyáo Magistrate Xiè Shèng of Kuàijī and fourteen others
could not compose poems;
they were each fined three dou of wine."
Sīzhōu Wáng first served as Registrar to Duke Yǔ,
and later appointed Yīn Hào as his Chief Clerk.
When Hào first arrived,
Duke Yǔ wanted to send Wáng on a mission down to the capital.
Wáng himself petitioned to stay, saying:
"Your humble official rarely encounters great virtue.
Yuānyuán has just arrived,
and I still crave to spend a few days in his company."
Xī Jiābīn was delighted
when people compared him to Fú Jiān.
Before Mèng Chǎng achieved prominence,
his family was in Jīngkǒu.
*Jìn Āndì Jì* states:
"Chǎng, styled Yàndá,
was from Píngchāng.
His father was Fù,
Central Protector of the Army.
Chǎng was dignified, stern, and had firm conduct.
In his youth, he was recognized by Wáng Gōng.
He contributed to the righteous uprising,
and was promoted to Governor of Dānyáng.
After Lú Xún advanced south,
Chǎng, fearing the enterprise would fail,
took poison and died."
He once saw Wáng Gōng riding in a high carriage,
clad in a crane-feather cloak.
At the time there was a light snowfall.
Chǎng peered at him through a fence
and sighed, saying:
"This is truly a man among immortals!"
Wáng Zhòngxuān was fond of donkey brays.
*Wèi Zhì* states:
"Wáng Càn, styled Zhòngxuān,
was from Gāopíng in Shānyáng.
His great-grandfather Gōng and
father Chàng
both served as the Three Excellencies of Hàn.
Càn went to Cháng'ān to see Cài Yōng.
Yōng thought him extraordinary,
and hurried to greet him, shoes on backwards, saying:
'This is the grandson of Lord Wáng.
He has exceptional talent;
I am not his equal!
All the books in my house
should be given to him.'
He fled the turmoil to Jīngzhōu,
relying on Liú Biǎo.
Because Càn was plain-looking and unconventional,
Biǎo did not highly esteem him.
He accompanied the Grand Progenitor on the campaign against Wú,
and died on the journey."
After he was buried,
Emperor Wén attended his funeral.
Turning to his companions, he said:
"Wáng was fond of donkey brays;
let each of us make one sound to send him off."
All the attending guests each made a donkey bray.
Note: Dài Shūluán's mother was fond of donkey brays,
and Shūluán would often bray like a donkey to please her.
What people are fond of
may perhaps be the same.
When Wáng Jùnchōng served as President of the Imperial Secretariat,
dressed in his official robes,
and riding in a light carriage,
he passed by the foot of Master Huáng's wine shop.
Wéi Zhāo's *Annotations to the Hàn Shū* states:
"A 'lú'
is a wine shop.
It is made of earth built into a platform,
with four sides high like a furnace."
Turning to the guest in the carriage behind, he said:
"I once drank heartily at this shop with Jī Shūyè
and Ruǎn Sìzōng.
The excursions of the Bamboo Grove—
I also participated in their latter days.
Since Jī's untimely death
and Ruǎn's passing,
I have been fettered by worldly affairs.
Today, though this place seems near,
it feels as distant as mountains and rivers."
*Treatise on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove* states:
"This is the popular legend.
Yǐngchuān's Yǔ Àizhī once asked his uncle Wénkāng about it.
Wénkāng said:
'This was unheard of in the central court.
South of the river, this tale suddenly appeared.
It was probably fabricated by busybodies.'"
Sūn Zǐjīng, being a man of talent,
had few whom he admired and respected in his youth,
save for his profound reverence for Wáng Wǔzǐ.
When Wǔzǐ passed away,
all the renowned scholars of the time attended his funeral.
Zǐjīng arrived later,
approached the corpse, and wept bitterly,
causing all the guests to shed tears.
After he finished weeping,
he turned to the spirit bed and said:
"You always enjoyed hearing me imitate a donkey's bray,
so today I shall do it for you."
His imitation was remarkably lifelike,
and all the guests burst into laughter.
Sūn raised his head and said:
"How is it that you all remain alive,
while this man is dead!"
The *Forest of Tales* records:
"When Wáng Wǔzǐ was buried,
Sūn Zǐjīng mourned him with great sorrow,
and all the guests wept.
After he brayed like a donkey,
the guests all laughed.
Sūn said:
'How is it that all of you are still alive,
while Wǔzǐ is dead?'
The guests all became angry."
When Wáng Róng lost his son Wànzǐ,
Shān Jiǎn went to console him.
Wáng was overwhelmed with grief.
Jiǎn said:
"He was but a child in arms;
why grieve to such an extent?"
Wáng replied:
"Sages are beyond emotions,
and the lowest are incapable of deep emotion;
it is precisely among people like us
that emotions are most profoundly felt."
Wáng Yǐn's *History of the Jin* states:
"Róng's son Suí
wished to marry the daughter of Péi Dùn.
After Suí died prematurely,
Róng was excessively grieved and pained,
and would not allow anyone to seek a match for her,
so that she remained unmarried until old age, with none daring to ask for her hand."
Jiǎn was convinced by his words,
and wept even more bitterly for him.
Another account says it was Wáng Yífǔ who lost a son,
and Shān Jiǎn came to offer condolences.
Someone mourned Hé Chángyú, saying:
"It is as if a towering thousand-foot pine has collapsed."
Weì Xǐmǎ died in the sixth year of the Yǒngjiā era.
Xiè Kūn wept for him,
moving passersby with his grief.
The *Register of Figures from the Yǒngjiā Era* states:
"Jiè died on the twentieth day of the sixth month in the sixth year,
and was buried east of Xǔ Zhēng's tomb in Nánchāng City.
When Jiè passed away,
Xiè Yòuyú expressed his grief in Wǔchāng,
overwhelmed with sorrow.
People asked him:
'Why do you grieve so deeply?'
He replied:
'A pillar of the state has fallen;
how can I not mourn?'"
During the Xiánhé era,
Chéngxiàng Wáng Gōng issued an instruction:
"Weì Xǐmǎ should be reburied.
This gentleman was a refined and renowned scholar,
admired throughout the land.
We should prepare a modest sacrifice
to honor our old friendship."
The *Separate Biography of Jiè* records:
"Jiè was reburied in Jiāngníng during the Xiánhé era.
Chéngxiàng Wáng Gōng instructed:
'Xǐmǎ should be reburied tomorrow.
This gentleman was a refined and renowned scholar,
the people's hope throughout the land.
We should prepare a sacrifice of three animals
to honor our old friendship.'"
Gù Yànxiān had always loved the qin in his lifetime.
After his death,
his family often placed a qin on his spirit bed.
Zhāng Jìyīng went to mourn him,
and, unable to contain his grief,
he directly climbed onto the bed,
took up the qin,
played several pieces to their end,
then stroked the qin and said:
"Does Gù Yànxiān still appreciate this?"
Thereupon, he wept bitterly again,
and left without taking the filial son's hand.
Yǔ Liàng's son met his death during the Sū Jùn rebellion.
Zhūgě Dàomíng's daughter was married to Yǔ's son.
After being widowed,
she was about to remarry.
Liàng's son Huì,
and Huì's wife Wén Biāo,
both have been mentioned earlier.
He wrote to Liàng about this matter.
Liàng replied:
"Your virtuous daughter is still young,
so it is fitting for her to remarry.
Yet I think of my deceased son
as if he had just passed away."
When Yǔ Wénkāng died,
Hé Yángzhōu said at the burial:
"Burying a jade tree in the earth—
how can one's feelings bear it!"
The *Records of Searching for the Supernatural* states:
"Initially,
when Yǔ Liàng fell ill,
the diviner Dài Yáng said:
'During the Sū Jùn affair,
you, sir, vowed at the Báishí Shrine to offer an ox from beneath a carriage,
but you never fulfilled it.
You are being punished by this ghost,
and cannot be saved.'
The following year,
Liàng indeed died."
The *Records of Spirit Ghosts and Ballad Portents* states:
"When Wénkāng first garrisoned Wǔchāng,
setting out from Shítóu,
the watching commoners sang from the shore:
'Lord Yǔ goes to Wǔchāng,
soaring like a flying bird;
Lord Yǔ returns to Yángzhōu,
a white horse pulls the funeral banner.'
Another version says:
'When Lord Yǔ first set out,
soaring like a flying crow;
Lord Yǔ returns to Yángzhōu,
a white horse pulls the hearse.'
Later, he was repeatedly summoned but did not enter court,
and soon passed away,
being buried in the lower capital."
When Wáng Chángshǐ was critically ill,
he lay beneath a lamp,
turning his duster and gazing at it,
sighing:
"A man like me
will not even reach forty!"
After his death,
Liú Yǐn attended the funeral,
placed a rhinoceros-handled duster in the coffin,
and wept until he fainted.
The *Separate Biography of Méng* records:
"Méng died in the early years of the Yǒnghé era,
at the age of thirty-nine.
Liú Tán of Pèiguó was Méng's closest friend.
After Méng's death,
Tán deeply mourned him.
Even the love between brothers
could not surpass it."
After Zhī Dàolín lost Fǎ Qián,
his spirit collapsed,
and his demeanor declined.
The "Biography of Zhī Dùn" says:
"Fǎ Qián
was a fellow student of Dàolín.
He was brilliant and principled,
and Dùn esteemed him greatly."
Dùn often said to others:
"In the past, Carpenter Shí discarded his axe after the man of Yǐng died.
The "Zhuangzi" says:
'A man of Yǐng had a speck of plaster on the tip of his nose, as thin as a fly's wing.
He had Carpenter Shí swing his axe to chop it off.
The plaster was entirely removed, yet his nose was unharmed,
and the man of Yǐng stood without changing expression.'
Yá Yá stopped playing the zither after Zhōng Zǐqī died.
The "Han Shi Wai Zhuan" says:
'Bó Yá played the qin,
and Zhōng Zǐqī listened to him.
While he was playing,
his thoughts were on Mount Tài.
Zǐqī said:
"How excellently you play the qin!
Lofty as Mount Tài!"
A short while later,
his thoughts turned to flowing water.
Zǐqī said:
"How excellently you play the qin!
Vast as the flowing waters!"
After Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bó Yá broke his qin and severed its strings.
For the rest of his life he never played again,
believing there was no one left for whom it was worth playing.'
Applying this to myself and looking outward,
it is indeed not unfounded!
Now that my silent confidant is gone,
when I speak, there is no one to appreciate it.
My heart is knotted with sorrow,
I fear I shall perish!"
A little over a year later,
Zhī Dùn indeed passed away.
When Xī Jiābīn died,
his attendants informed Lord Xī
that "the young master has passed away."
Upon hearing this,
he showed no grief.
Instead, he told his attendants:
"Inform me when it is time for the funeral."
When the lord went to attend the funeral,
he wailed in grief, nearly fainting.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"Chāo died at forty-two,
preceding Xīn in death.
The friends Chāo associated with
were all outstanding talents of the time.
On the day of his death,
over forty people, both noble and common, wrote eulogies for him."
The "Xù Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Chāo sided with the Huán clan,
acting as their chief strategist.
Because his father Xīn was loyal to the imperial house,
he did not let him know.
As he was nearing death,
he took out a small box and entrusted it to a disciple,
saying:
'I originally intended to burn this,
but I fear my elderly father,
in his grief and distress, might harm himself.
After I die,
if he suffers greatly, losing sleep and appetite,
then present this box to him.'
Xīn later indeed grieved and fell ill.
The disciple then followed Chāo's instruction
and gave him the secret correspondence with Huán Wēn.
When Xīn saw it, he flew into a rage, saying:
'That scoundrel! I only regret his death came too late!'
After that, he wept no more."
Dài Ānshì saw the tomb of Master Lín Fǎshī.
The "Biography of Zhī Dùn" says:
"Dùn died in the first year of the Tàihé era in Shíchéng Mountain in Shàn,
and was buried there."
He said:
"The sound of his virtuous words has not yet faded,
yet the trees encircling his grave have already grown thick.
I hope his divine principle continues endlessly,
not perishing along with his allotted lifespan!"
Wáng Xún's "Preface to the Poem at the Master's Tomb" says:
"In the second year of the Níngkāng era,
I ordered my carriage to Shíchéng Mountain in Shàn,
which is the Master's burial mound.
The high tomb is overgrown with wild brambles,
the mound transformed into aged weeds.
His traces have not yet vanished,
yet the man himself is already far away.
Reflecting on the past,
everything I touch stirs sorrow in my heart."
Thus he was cherished by the worthy men of his time.
Wáng Zǐjìng was on good terms with Yáng Suí.
Suí was pure, honest, simple, and noble.
He served as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
but died young.
Suí has been mentioned previously.
Wáng deeply mourned and lamented him,
saying to Dōngtíng:
"He was a man the state should regret losing!"
Wáng Dōngtíng and Xiè Ān became enemies.
The "Zhōngxīng Shū" says:
"The Xún brothers were both sons-in-law of the Xiè family,
but due to suspicion and discord, the marriages were dissolved.
After the Grand Tutor severed the marriage ties with Xún,
he also divorced his wife,
and from then on the two families became bitter enemies."
When Wáng, who was in the east, heard of Xiè's death,
he immediately left the capital to visit Zǐjìng and said:
"I wish to mourn Xiè Gōng."
Zǐjìng was initially lying down.
Upon hearing his words,
he startled and rose, saying:
"This is what I had hoped for from Fǎhù."
Fǎhù
was Xún's childhood name.
Wáng then went to mourn.
The commanding officer Diāo Yuē would not let him proceed,
saying:
"When our lord was alive,
he never received this guest."
Wáng did not speak to him either.
He went straight forward,
wept with great sorrow,
and left without taking Mòbì's hand.
Mòbì
was Xiè Yǎn's childhood name.
Yǎn, styled Yuàndù,
was Ān's youngest son.
He was open-minded and magnanimous.
He was killed by Sūn Ēn.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant and Minister of Works.
Wáng Zǐyóu
and Zǐjìng were both critically ill,
and Zǐjìng died first.
Xiànzhī died in the thirteenth year of the Tàiyuán era,
at the age of forty-five.
Zǐyóu asked his attendants:
"Why have I heard no news at all?
He must already be gone!"
As he spoke, he showed no sadness whatsoever.
He then called for a carriage to rush to the funeral,
yet he did not weep at all.
Zǐjìng had always loved the qin.
Zǐyóu went straight in and sat on the spirit bed,
took Zǐjìng's qin to play,
but the strings were out of tune.
He threw it to the ground and said:
"Zǐjìng!
Zǐjìng!
Both the man and the qin are gone forever."
Then he wailed in grief for a long time,
and a little over a month later, he also died.
The "Yōumíng Lù" says:
"During the Tàiyuán era,
there was a master who came from afar,
and no one knew his origin.
He said:
'When a person's destined lifespan ends,
if there is someone living who is willing to take their place,
then the deceased can return to life.
But if one forces someone to seek a substitute,
it also will not last long.'
When people heard this,
they all thought it absurd and unfounded.
Wáng Zǐyóu
and Zǐjìng were brothers
who were especially close and harmonious.
When Zǐjìng's illness was critical,
Zǐyóu said to him:
'My talent is not equal to my younger brother's,
and my official position is also middling.
I ask to use my remaining years to take my brother's place.'
The master said:
'For the living to substitute for the dead,
one must have surplus years in one's own allotted lifespan
to make up for what the deceased lacks.
Now, your worthy brother's life is fated to end,
and your own allotted years are also nearly exhausted.
What is there for you to substitute?
Zǐyóu previously had a back ailment.
When Zǐjìng's illness became critical,
he was constantly prevented from visiting.
Upon hearing of his death,
he clutched his chest in grief and lamentation,
yet could not utter a single sound.
His back then ruptured.
Considering the master's words,
they were indeed credible and true."
Jī Kāng was traveling in the mountains of Jíjùn,
when he met the Daoist priest Sūn Dēng,
and subsequently traveled with him.
As Kāng was about to leave,
Dēng said:
"Your talent is indeed lofty,
but your way of preserving yourself is insufficient."
The preface to the "Collected Works of Kāng" states:
"Sūn Dēng—
it is unknown from where he came.
He had no family,
and lived in an earthen cave on the northern mountain of Jíjùn.
In summer, he wove grass into garments;
in winter, he let his hair down to cover himself.
He enjoyed reading the "Book of Changes,"
and played a single-stringed qín;
all who saw him felt affection and joy towards him."
The "Chronicles of the Wei Clan" states:
"Dēng's nature was without joy or anger;
sometimes he would submerge himself in water,
emerge and look around,
then laugh heartily again.
From time to time, he would come and go among people;
for households that provided him with clothing and food along his way,
he never declined anything,
but upon leaving, he would abandon it all."
The "Biographies of Literary Scholars" states:
"During the Jiāpíng era,
the people of Jí County went together into the mountains,
and saw a man
whose dwelling was on a sheer cliff a hundred rèn high,
amidst dense and flourishing woods,
and whose spirit and intelligence were exceptionally keen.
He himself said:
'My surname is Sūn,
my given name is Dēng,
and my courtesy name is Gōnghé.'
When Kāng heard of this,
he followed and traveled with him for three years.
He asked about Dēng's intentions,
but Dēng never answered.
Yet the profound wisdom he harbored was truly marvelous,
and Kāng often sighed in admiration.
As they were about to part,
Kāng said to him:
'Does the Master truly have nothing to say?'
Dēng then said:
'Do you understand fire?
It is born with light,
yet does not use its light;
its true purpose lies in using the light.
Humans are born with talent,
yet do not use their talent;
their true purpose lies in using the talent.
Therefore, using light depends on obtaining fuel,
so as to preserve its radiance;
using talent depends on understanding things,
so as to preserve one's years.
Now, you have much talent but little understanding;
it will be difficult for you to avoid calamity in this present world!
Do not seek too much!'
Kāng was unable to follow this advice.
When he encountered the affair of Lǚ Ān,
while in prison, he wrote a poem blaming himself, saying:
'In the past, I felt ashamed before Xiàhuì,
today, I am ashamed before Sūn Dēng!'"
Wáng Yǐn's "Book of Jin" states:
"Sūn Dēng was the one whom Ruǎn Jí had seen.
Jī Kāng observed the rites of a disciple and took him as his teacher.
The choices between serving and withdrawing in the Wei and Jin periods
easily gave rise to suspicion,
and both the noble and the lowly perished,
therefore Dēng sometimes remained silent."
Shān Gōng was about to leave the Selection Bureau,
and wished to recommend Jī Kāng;
Kāng sent him a letter severing relations.
The "Separate Biography of Kāng" states:
"Shān Jùyuán was a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel,
promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and recommended Kāng;
Kāng declined it,
and also severed relations with Shān.
Was it that he did not recognize Shān's sincere intention in offering him an official post?
He also wished to demonstrate an unyielding integrity,
in order to stop the mouths of those who recommended him!
Thus he replied to Tāo's letter,
stating himself unfit for the vulgar world,
and disparaging Tāng and Wǔ.
The Grand General heard of this and despised him."
Lǐ Xīn was the fifth son of Màozēng's younger brother,
pure, upright, and possessing lofty conduct,
but from youth he was frail and sickly,
and unwilling to marry or serve as an official.
He resided in Línhǎi,
living at the tomb of his elder brother, the Palace Attendant.
Since he already had a high reputation,
Chancellor Wáng wished to summon and honor him,
and therefore recruited him as an Assistant in his administration.
Xīn received the summons and order,
and said with a laugh:
'Màohóng is actually bestowing an official title upon someone!'"
The "Treatise on Writing" states:
"Xīn, courtesy name Zōngzǐ,
was from Zhōngwǔ, Jiāngxià.
His grandfather, Kāng,
was Governor of Qínzhōu.
His father, Zhòng,
was Governor of Píngyáng.
The family had a renowned reputation.
Xīn was fond of learning,
excelled at cursive and clerical script,
and was equally famous as his elder brother, Shì.
Lame and unable to walk or sit,
he often lay on his back,
playing the qín
and reading aloud without cease.
The Prince of Héjiān recruited him as an Assistant in the Grand Commandant's office,
but due to illness he did not go.
Later, fleeing from troubles,
he followed his elder brother south across the river,
and Minister of Education Wáng Dǎo again recruited him.
Xīn said:
'Màohóng is actually imposing an official title upon someone!'
He died during the Yǒnghé era.
Xīn had once been recruited by two administrations,
hence he was called 'Lord Lǐ of the Administration.'
Wǔ, courtesy name Jǐngzé,
was Xīn's eldest brother.
His thoughts and principles were those of a reclusive scholar,
and he had a reputation for simple integrity.
After crossing the river,
he rose through the ranks to become Governor of Línhǎi,
and Palace Attendant.
He died at the age of fifty-four."
The younger brother of General of Agile Cavalry Hé avoided the world with lofty sentiments,
and the General of Agile Cavalry urged him to take office.
He replied:
"Though I am the fifth in the family,
why must my reputation be inferior to the General of Agile Cavalry?"
The "Book of the Restoration" states:
"Hé Zhǔn, courtesy name Yòudào,
was from Qián, Lújiāng.
He was the fifth younger brother of General of Agile Cavalry Hé Chōng.
He was refined and fond of lofty pursuits,
and did not accept any summons or appointments.
Chōng held the position of Prime Minister,
with power overshadowing the sovereign,
yet Zhǔn wore loose belts at his humble gate,
and paid no heed to worldly affairs.
At that time, men of virtue and reputation all praised him.
He died at the age of forty-seven.
He had a daughter,
who became Empress to Emperor Mù.
He was posthumously awarded the title of Senior Guardian of the Light.
His son, Huī,
declined and did not accept it."
Senior Guardian of the Light Ruǎn lived on the Eastern Mountain,
serene and without affairs,
always inwardly content in his heart.
The "Separate Biography of Ruǎn Yù" states:
"Yù lived on Shàn Mountain in Kuàijī,
his will set on a comfortable retreat."
Someone asked General of the Right Wáng about this,
and the General of the Right said:
"This gentleman is recently undisturbed by favor or disgrace.
The "Lǎozǐ" says:
'Favor and disgrace are like shocks;
gaining them is a shock,
losing them is a shock.'
Even the 'deeply obscure' of ancient times,
how could they surpass this?"
The "Book of Yángzǐ" says:
"The Zhuāng of Shǔ
was deeply obscure."
Lǐ Guǐ's "Commentary" states:
"'Deeply obscure'
is like profound stillness,
the appearance of being utterly extinguished and without trace."
Kǒng Chēqí (Kong Cheqi) had from youth the noble intention of retiring from the world.
Only after he was over forty
did he finally accept the summons of General An Dōng (Andong).
Before he entered government service,
he would often sleep alone,
singing and playing the flute to admonish and instruct himself.
He called himself Master Kǒng (Kong Lang),
and roamed among the famous mountains.
The "Separate Biography of Kǒng Yú (Kong Yu)" says:
"During the great disorder of the Yǒngjiā (Yongjia) era,
Yú entered the mountains of Línhǎi (Linhai),
not seeking fame or advancement.
Emperor Zhōngzōng (Zhongzong) appointed him as an Army Consultant."
The common people believed he possessed the Way and its arts,
and built a temple for him while he was still alive.
Even today there is still a Master Kǒng (Kong Lang) Temple.
Liú Línzhī (Liu Linzhi) of Nányáng (Nanyang)
was lofty, straightforward, and well-versed in histories and commentaries.
He lived in seclusion at Yángqí (Yangqi).
At that time, Fú Jiān (Fu Jian) was pressing upon the Yangtze River.
Huán Chōng (Huan Chong), Governor of Jīngzhōu (Jingzhou), wishing to fully implement his grand strategies,
summoned Línzhī to serve as his Chief Administrator.
He sent a man with a boat to fetch him,
presenting him with very generous gifts.
Upon hearing of the summons,
Línzhī boarded the boat,
but completely refused to accept the gifts offered to him.
Along the way, he distributed them to the poor and destitute,
so that by the time he reached Shàngmíng (Shangming), they were all gone.
As soon as he met Chōng,
he declared himself useless for the task,
and withdrew with an air of detachment.
He lived at Yángqí (Yangqi) for many years.
Whether he had clothing and food or not, he always shared with the villagers.
When he himself was in want,
the villagers treated him likewise.
He was very generous,
and was a source of peace and stability for his village and community.
Dèng Càn's (Deng Can) "Annals of Jìn (Jin)" says:
"Línzhī's courtesy name was Zǐjì (Ziji).
He was from Ānzhòng (Anzhong) in Nányáng (Nanyang).
From youth he esteemed simplicity and plainness,
being modest, retiring, and having few desires.
He loved to wander among mountains and marshes.
His will was set on withdrawal and reclusion.
Huán Chōng (Huan Chong) once went to his home.
Línzhī was just then pruning mulberry trees.
He said to Chōng:
'Since Your Lordship has gone to the trouble of gracing us with your presence,
you should first call upon my father.'
Chōng then went to see his father.
His father summoned Línzhī,
and only then did he return,
brushing off his short coarse jacket to speak with Chōng.
His father had Línzhī personally bring unstrained wine and pickled vegetables to serve the guest.
Chōng ordered his attendants to do it for him.
His father declined, saying:
'If we use your official's servants,
then it is not in keeping with the intention of a rustic man.'
Chōng was deeply moved.
Only at dusk did he leave.
He then asked Línzhī to be his Chief Administrator,
but Línzhī firmly declined.
He lived at Yángqí (Yangqi).
As it was close to the main road,
scholars and gentlemen coming and going
would invariably stop at his house.
Línzhī personally provided for them,
but would accept no gifts offered to him.
A hundred *li* from his home,
there was an old widow who was ill
and about to die.
She said to people:
'Only Chief Administrator Liú will bury me!'
Línzhī personally went to tend to her until her illness ended in death,
and arranged for her coffin and burial.
His acts of humaneness and kindness were all like this.
He died of old age."
Zhái Dàoyuān (Zhai Daoyuan) of Nányáng (Nanyang) and Zhōu Zǐnán (Zhou Zinan) of Rǔnán (Runan) were friends from youth,
and together lived in seclusion at Xúnyáng (Xunyang).
Grand Marshal Yǔ (Yu) persuaded Zhōu (Zhou) concerning the affairs of the contemporary world,
and Zhōu (Zhou) subsequently entered government service,
but Zhái (Zhai) held even more firmly to his resolve.
Afterwards, when Zhōu (Zhou) went to visit Zhái (Zhai),
Zhái (Zhai) would not speak with him.
"The Jìn Yángqiū (Jin Yangqiu)" says:
"Zhái Tāng (Zhai Tang), courtesy name Dàoyuān (Daoyuan),
was a man of Nányáng (Nanyang),
a descendant of Zhái Fāngjìn (Zhai Fangjin) of the Hàn (Han).
He was sincere in conduct, following his innate nature,
righteous, deferential, incorruptible, and honest.
He would accept none of the gifts offered to him.
It happened that during the disorder there were many bandits,
but hearing of Tāng's reputation and virtue,
none dared to molest him."
"The Record of Xúnyáng (Xunyang)" says:
"In the beginning,
when Yǔ Liàng (Yu Liang) came to Jiāngzhōu (Jiangzhou),
he heard of the character of Zhái Tāng (Zhai Tang).
He fastened his belt, put on his clogs, and went to call on him.
Liàng's courtesy was extremely respectful.
Tāng said:
'Your Lordship merely respects a withered tree and rotten stump.'
Liàng praised his eloquent speech,
and submitted a memorial recommending him.
He was summoned to be Erudite of the National University,
but did not go.
His Registrar, Zhāng Xuán (Zhang Xuan), said:
'This gentleman is a reclining dragon;
he cannot be moved.'
He died at home."
Mèng Wànnián (Meng Wannian) and his younger brother, Shàogū (Shaogu),
lived in Yángxīn (Yangxin) County of Wǔchāng (Wuchang).
Wànnián traveled in government service
and had a great reputation in his time.
Shàogū never went out,
so the gentlemen of the capital, wishing to see him,
sent a messenger to report to Shàogū,
saying
"your elder brother is critically ill."
In great haste and confusion, he reached the capital.
The worthy men of the time who saw him
could not but sigh in admiration.
They said to each other:
"With a younger brother like Shàogū,
Wànnián may die."
Yuán Hóng's (Yuan Hong) "Inscription for Recluse Mèng (Meng)" says:
"The recluse's name was Lòu (Lou),
courtesy name Shàogū (Shaogu).
He was from Yángxīn (Yangxin) in Wǔchāng (Wuchang),
a descendant of Mèng Zōng (Meng Zong), Minister of Works of Wú (Wu).
From youth he admired antiquity,
wearing cloth clothes and eating plain food.
He dwelled content beneath a thatched hut,
cut off from the affairs of the human world.
His relatives admired his filial piety.
The Grand General ordered the Prince of Kuàijī (Kuaiji) to summon him to office,
but he pleaded illness and did not go.
For years the ministerial post remained vacant for him,
yet he remained calm and unperturbed,
never lowering his will.
His contemporaries considered him extraordinary."
Kāng Sēngyuān (Kang Sengyuan) was in Yùzhāng (Yuzhang).
Several tens of *li* from the outer wall,
he built a retreat.
It was adjacent to mountain ridges,
girdled by a long stream.
Fragrant groves stood before his veranda and courtyard;
clear flowing water rushed past his hall and chambers.
There he lived in quietude, studying and expounding,
devoting his mind to the subtle principles and savoring them.
Lord Yǔ (Yu) and many others often went to see him.
Observing his application of breath control and meditation,
his grace and refinement grew even better.
Moreover, he dwelt there contentedly,
and also had that by which he found self-satisfaction.
His reputation consequently flourished.
Later, he could not bear it,
and so left.
(Sēngyuān has already appeared [in the text].)
Dài Āndào (Dai Andao) had already disciplined his conduct at Dōngshān (Dongshan).
"The Continued Jìn Yángqiū (Jin Yangqiu)" says:
"Dài Kuí (Dai Kui) took no pleasure in the contemporary world,
but amused himself with the lute and books.
He lived in seclusion at Shàn (Shan) Mountain in Kuàijī (Kuaiji).
He was summoned to be Erudite of the National University,
but did not accept."
Yet his elder brother wished to achieve the merit of repelling [enemies].
"The Dài (Dai) Family Genealogy" says:
"Dài Lù (Dai Lu), courtesy name Ānqiū (Anqiu),
was from Qiáoguó (Qiaoguo).
His grandfather was Shuò (Shuo);
his father was Suí (Sui);
both had repute and rank.
Lù became prominent through his military valor,
achieved merit,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎnglíng (Guangling),
and served up to the post of Minister of Agriculture."
Grand Tutor Xiè (Xie) said:
"The aspirations and pursuits of you brothers—
how can they be so vastly different?"
Dài (Dai) replied:
"This humble official
'could not bear such worries,'
while my younger brother
'did not change his joy.'"
Xǔ Xuándù lived in seclusion in a secluded cave south of Yǒngxīng,
and often received gifts from the various feudal lords from all directions.
Someone said to Xǔ:
"I have heard of the Jīshān recluse,
but it seems he was not like this!"
Xǔ replied:
"Baskets and bundles of gifts
are certainly lighter than the treasure of the empire!"
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the *Book of Rites* states:
"Bāojū
means wrapped meat.
It is wrapped either with reeds
or with rushes."
This means that Xǔ Yóu still received the abdication offer from Emperor Yáo;
gifts in baskets,
are they not indeed light?
Fàn Xuān never entered government offices.
Hán Kāngbó was riding in the same carriage with him
and thus lured him to enter the commandery office together.
Fàn then hurriedly got down from the back of the carriage.
The *Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng* states:
"Xuān, from a young age, admired reclusion and withdrawal,
lived in Yùzhāng,
and established himself through purity and integrity."
Xī Chāo, whenever he heard of someone who wished to live in lofty seclusion and withdrawal,
would always prepare a million in funds for them,
and also build them a residence.
In Shàn, he built a house for Dài Gōng,
which was very fine and well-ordered.
When Dài first went to his old residence,
he wrote to his relatives:
"Recently arrived in Shàn,
it feels like an official residence."
Xī also prepared a million in funds for Fù Yuē,
but Fù's plans for seclusion encountered complications,
so it was not ultimately given.
Yuē was the childhood name of Fù Qióng.
Attendant Xǔ loved to travel through mountains and rivers,
and his physique was suited for climbing and ascending.
People of the time said:
"Xǔ not only has a passion for scenic beauty,
but truly possesses the means to reach it."
Minister Xī and the recluse Xiè were on good terms.
He often said:
"Xiè Qìngxù's insight and understanding, though not surpassing others,
allows him to completely rid himself of all burdens on the mind."
The Minister
was Xī Huī.
See elsewhere.
Tán Dàoluán's *Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng* states:
"Xiè Fū, styled Qìngxù,
was from Kuàijī,
and deeply believed in Buddhism.
Initially, he entered Tàipíng Mountain for over ten years,
devoting himself to long-term vegetarian fasting and support,
attracting like-minded companions,
tirelessly transforming and accepting others.
Due to his mother's old age, he returned to the Ruòyé area in the southern mountains.
The Neishi Xī Yīn submitted a memorial recommending him,
and he was summoned to serve as Erudite,
but he did not accept.
Initially, the moon encroached upon the Shàowēi star,
also known as the Recluse Star.
The divination stated:
'A recluse will bear this.'
At that time, Dài Kuí lived in Shàn;
he was both talented in arts and had connections with the noble and powerful,
and was more famous than Fū,
so people of the time were worried about him.
Soon after, Fū died,
and the scholars of Kuàijī mocked the people of Wú, saying:
'The lofty scholar of Wúzhōng
simply cannot seek death.'"
Chén Yīng
was from Dōngyáng.
From a young age, he cultivated virtuous conduct,
and was renowned in his hometown.
During the great chaos at the end of the Qin dynasty,
the people of Dōngyáng wanted to support Yīng as their leader.
His mother said:
"Do not do this!
Since I became a wife in your family,
we have long experienced poverty and low status.
To suddenly become wealthy and noble
is inauspicious!
It would be better to entrust the troops to someone else:
if the endeavor succeeds,
you will receive some benefit;
if it does not succeed,
the calamity will fall upon others."
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"Yīng was formerly a minor official under the magistrate of Dōngyáng.
He lived in the county,
was always trustworthy,
and was considered an honorable man.
The people of Dōngyáng wanted to establish a leader,
so they invited Yīng.
Yīng's mother advised against it.
He then entrusted the troops to Xiàng Liáng,
and Liáng appointed Yīng as Shàngzhùguó."
Emperor Yuán of Hàn had many palace women,
so he ordered painters to depict them,
intending that when he wished to summon someone,
he would consult the portraits and call for her.
Those of ordinary appearance
all bribed the painters.
Wáng Míngjūn was exceptionally beautiful in appearance,
but she was determined not to seek favor through improper means,
so the painter deliberately marred her likeness.
Later, the Xiōngnú came to seek peace,
and requested a beautiful woman from the Hàn emperor.
The emperor sent Míngjūn to fulfill this request.
After summoning her for an audience, he regretted it.
However, her name had already been sent,
and he did not wish to change it midway,
so she departed.
The *Book of Hàn: Annals of the Xiōngnú* states:
"In the first year of Jìngníng,
Hūhányé Chányú came to court,
and stated that he wished to become a son-in-law of the Hàn to establish kinship.
Emperor Yuán bestowed upon him Wáng Qiáng, styled Míngjūn, a good family girl from the rear palace.
The Chányú was delighted,
and submitted a letter offering to guard the frontiers."
Wén Yǐng stated:
"Zhāojūn was originally from Zǐguī County in Shǔ Commandery."
The *Accounts of the Lute* states:
"Wáng Zhāojūn
was the daughter of Wáng Rǎng of the state of Qí.
At seventeen,
her appearance was peerlessly beautiful,
and her moral integrity was renowned throughout the state.
When elders sought her hand,
her father did not consent to any,
and instead presented her to Emperor Yuán of Hàn.
The emperor, in haste, could not distinguish the women behind the curtains,
and Zhāojūn was resentful and angry about this.
When the Chányú sent an envoy,
the emperor ordered the palace women to dress up and appear.
The envoy requested one woman.
The emperor then said to the women in the palace:
'Whoever wishes to go to the Chányú, stand up.'
Zhāojūn sighed, stepped over the mat, and stood up.
The emperor looked at her
and was greatly astonished and regretful.
At that time, the envoy was also present,
and he could not stop it,
so he bestowed her upon the Chányú.
The Chányú was greatly pleased,
and presented various precious items.
Zhāojūn had a son named Shìwéi.
When the Chányú died,
Shìwéi succeeded him.
According to Hú custom,
when the father dies, the son marries the mother.
Zhāojūn asked Shìwéi:
'Are you Hàn
or Hú?'
Shìwéi said:
'I wish to be Hú.'
Zhāojūn then swallowed poison and killed herself."
Shí Jìlún said:
"Zhāo was changed to Míng
because it violated the personal name taboo of Emperor Wén."
Emperor Chéng of Hàn favored Zhào Fēiyàn.
Fēiyàn slandered Lady Bān Jiéyú, accusing her of cursing others,
so she was interrogated.
Lady Bān replied:
"I have heard that life and death are fated,
and wealth and honor lie with Heaven.
If cultivating goodness still does not bring blessings,
what hope can one have by doing evil?
If ghosts and spirits are aware,
they would not accept the pleas of the wicked and deceitful;
if they are unaware,
what good would complaining to them do?
Therefore, I do not do such things."
The "Hànshū‧Wàiqī Zhuàn" says:
"Emperor Chéng's Empress Zhào
was originally a palace maid in Cháng'ān.
When she was born,
her parents did not raise her,
but after three days she did not die,
so they took her in and raised her.
When she grew up,
she was assigned to the household of the Princess of Héyáng to learn singing and dancing,
and was called Fēiyàn.
The emperor, while traveling incognito, passed by the princess's residence,
saw her and was pleased,
summoned her into the palace,
greatly favored her,
and established her as empress.
Lady Bān Jiéyú
was from Yànmén.
Early in Emperor Chéng's reign,
she was selected to enter the palace,
greatly favored,
and established as a Jiéyú.
When the emperor toured the rear palace,
he once wanted her to share his carriage,
but Lady Jiéyú declined.
Zhào Fēiyàn slandered Empress Xǔ and Lady Jiéyú,
but Lady Jiéyú responded with eloquent reasoning,
so the emperor pitied her
and bestowed a hundred catties of gold.
Fēiyàn was arrogant and jealous,
and Lady Jiéyú, fearing danger,
requested to serve the Empress Dowager in the Chángxìn Palace.
When the emperor passed away,
Lady Jiéyú served at his tomb garden.
She died and was buried in the garden."
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi passed away,
Emperor Wén took all of Emperor Wǔ's palace ladies to attend him.
When the emperor fell critically ill,
Empress Biàn went to see his condition.
Upon entering his chamber,
she saw that the attendants were all the women Emperor Wǔ had once favored.
The empress dowager asked:
"When did they come?"
They replied:
"They were summoned when the soul was being summoned back."
She then did not proceed further and sighed:
"Even dogs and rats would not eat what you leave behind;
death is indeed fitting for you!"
When it came to the imperial tomb,
she ultimately did not attend.
The "Wèishū" says:
"Empress Wǔxuān Biàn
was from Kāiyáng in Lángyá.
Born in the third year of the Yánxī era of Hàn in Báitíng, Qí Commandery,
a yellow aura filled the room all day.
Her father, the Marquis of Jìng, found it strange
and asked the diviner Wáng Yuè.
Yuè said:
'This is auspicious.'
At age twenty,
Tàizǔ took her as a concubine in Qiáo.
Her nature was frugal and simple,
not fond of extravagance,
and she possessed maternal virtue and moral conduct."
Mother Zhào married off her daughter.
As her daughter was about to leave,
she instructed her:
"Be careful not to be too good!"
The daughter said:
"If I shouldn't be good,
should I be bad then?"
The mother said:
"If being good is not advisable,
how much more so being bad?"
The "Liènǚ Zhuàn" says:
"Lady Zhào
was the wife of Yú Wěi, the magistrate of Tóngxiāng in Dōng Commandery,
and a daughter of the Zhào clan of Yǐngchuān.
She was talented, quick-witted, and well-read.
After Wěi passed away,
the great emperor admired her literary talent
and summoned her to the palace.
When the emperor wanted to personally campaign against Gōngsūn Yuān,
Lady Zhào submitted a memorial to advise against it.
She wrote the 'Liènǚ Zhuàn Jiě,'
titled 'Zhàomǔ Zhù,'
comprising hundreds of thousands of words.
She died in the sixth year of the Chìwū era."
The "Huáinánzǐ" says:
"There was a person who, when marrying off his daughter, instructed her:
'If you are good,
good people will resent you.'
She replied:
'Then should I be bad?'
He said:
'If being good is not advisable,
how much more so being bad?'"
Empress Jǐngxiàn Yáng said:
"Though these words are crude,
they can serve as a warning to the world."
Xǔ Yǔn's wife was the daughter of Commandant Ruǎn,
the younger sister of Dé rú.
The "Wèilüè" says:
"Yǔn, styled Shìzōng,
was from Gāoyáng.
In his youth, he and Cuī Zàn of Qīnghé
both gained fame in Jìzhōu.
He served up to the position of General of the Central Army."
The "Chénliú Zhìmíng" says:
"Ruǎn Gòng, styled Bóyàn,
was from Wèishì.
Pure and sincere, he upheld the Way,
and acted with ritual and deference.
He served Wèi
up to the position of Minister of the Imperial Guard.
His youngest son, Kǎn,
styled Dé rú,
was exceptionally talented
and refined in philosophical reasoning.
Elegant and gentle in demeanor,
he was a friend of Jī Kāng.
He served up to the position of Governor of Hénèi."
She was exceptionally ugly.
After the wedding ceremony concluded,
Yǔn showed no intention of entering the bridal chamber,
and his family was deeply worried.
It happened that Yǔn had a guest arrive,
and the wife had a maid look at him.
The maid returned and replied:
"It is Master Huán."
Master Huán was Huán Fàn.
The "Wèilüè" says:
"Fàn, styled Yǔnmíng,
was from Pèi Commandery.
He served up to the position of Minister of Agriculture
and was executed by King Xuān."
The wife said:
"Do not worry;
Huán will surely urge him to enter."
Huán indeed said to Xǔ:
"Since the Ruǎn family has married an ugly daughter to you,
they must have had a reason.
You should consider this."
Xǔ then turned back and entered the inner chamber.
Upon seeing his wife,
he immediately wanted to leave.
The wife anticipated that if he left this time,
he would not return,
so she grabbed his sleeve to stop him.
Xǔ then said to her:
"A woman has four virtues;
how many do you possess?"
The "Zhōulǐ" says:
"The Nine Ladies oversee the methods of women's learning
to teach the Nine Attendants:
womanly virtue,
womanly speech,
womanly appearance,
and womanly work."
Zhèng's commentary says:
"Virtue means chastity and obedience;
speech means eloquence;
appearance means grace and gentleness;
work means silk and hemp weaving."
The wife said:
"What I lack is only appearance.
However, a gentleman has a hundred conducts;
how many do you possess?"
Xǔ said:
"I possess them all."
The wife said:
"Of the hundred conducts, virtue is the foremost.
You favor beauty over virtue;
how can you say you possess them all?"
Yǔn felt ashamed,
and thereafter they respected each other.
Xǔ Yǔn served as the Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and he frequently appointed people from his hometown.
Emperor Míng of Wèi dispatched the Imperial Guard to arrest him.
His wife came out to admonish Yǔn, saying:
"An enlightened ruler can be swayed by reason,
but is difficult to appeal to through emotion."
After he arrived,
the Emperor interrogated him.
Yǔn replied:
"'Recommend those whom you know.'
The people from my hometown
are those I know.
Your Majesty, please investigate to see if they are competent or not.
If they are not competent,
I will accept the punishment."
After the investigation,
it was found that all the officials were suitable for their positions,
so he was released.
Yǔn's clothes were worn out,
and an imperial edict granted him new garments.
Initially, when Yǔn was arrested,
the entire household wailed and cried.
His wife, Madame Ruǎn, remained calm and said:
"Do not worry,
he will return soon."
She prepared millet porridge and waited,
and shortly after, Yǔn arrived.
The *Wèishì Chūnqiū* states:
"Initially,
when Yǔn served in the Ministry of Personnel,
he selected and promoted a commandery governor.
Emperor Míng suspected that his appointment was improper,
and intended to punish him.
Yǔn's wife, Madame Ruǎn, rushed out barefoot
and said to him:
'An enlightened ruler can be swayed by reason,
but cannot be appealed to through emotion.'
Yǔn nodded and entered.
The Emperor angrily questioned him,
and Yǔn replied:
'Although that commandery governor's term limit had expired,
the documents arrived first,
while the term limit came later;
the date limit was earlier.'
The Emperor took the documents and examined them,
and then his anger subsided.
He sent Yǔn out,
and noticing his worn-out clothes,
said:
'He is an honest official.'"
Xǔ Yǔn was executed by Prince Jǐng of Jìn,
and a disciple rushed in to inform his wife.
She was at her loom,
her expression unchanged,
and said:
"I knew this would happen long ago!"
The *Wèizhì* states:
"Initially,
the Commander of the Capital Guards was on close terms with Xiàhóu Xuán
and Lǐ Fēng.
Someone forged an imperial edict,
appointing Xuán as Grand General
and Yǔn as Grand Commandant,
to jointly oversee the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
Not long after,
someone rode a horse before dawn and delivered the edict to Yǔn.
The gatekeeper said:
'There is an imperial edict.'
The messenger then galloped away.
Yǔn threw the document into the fire and burned it,
without reporting it to Prince Jǐng."
The *Wèilüè* states:
"The following year,
Lǐ Fēng was arrested,
and Yǔn intended to visit the Grand General.
After leaving the house,
Yǔn hesitated and wavered,
turning back midway to fetch his trousers.
The Grand General heard of this and found it strange, saying:
'I am only arresting Lǐ Fēng;
why are the scholar-officials so agitated?'
At that time, General Zhènběi Liú Jìng passed away,
and Yǔn was appointed to replace Jìng.
The Grand General wrote to Yǔn, saying:
'Although the duties of Zhènběi are few,
you preside over an entire region.
I imagine you, sir, sounding the magnificent drums,
bearing the vermilion insignia,
and traversing your home province—
this is what is called wearing embroidered robes and walking in broad daylight.'
Then, an official reported that Yǔn had previously misappropriated funds and grain from the official kitchen,
distributing them to entertainers and his subordinates.
His death sentence was reduced to exile to the frontier,
and he died on the journey."
The *Wèishì Chūnqiū* states:
"When Yǔn was appointed as Zhènběi,
he joyfully said to his wife:
'I know I am spared!'
His wife said:
'Disaster lies precisely in this;
how can you be spared?'"
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* states:
"Yǔn held upright sentiments,
and because he was at odds with Emperor Wén,
he was secretly executed."
The *Fùrén Jí* records a letter from Madame Ruǎn to Yǔn,
explaining the origins of his calamities.
The language was deeply sorrowful,
and most of the text is not transcribed here.
The disciples wanted to hide her sons,
but the wife said:
"This has nothing to do with the children."
Later, she moved to reside near the tomb.
Prince Jǐng sent Zhōng Huì to observe them,
and if their talent and bearing matched their father's,
they were to be arrested.
The sons consulted their mother.
The mother said:
"Although you are fine young men,
your talents are not extensive.
Speak with him openly and sincerely,
and there will be nothing to worry about.
Do not grieve excessively;
stop when Huì stops.
Also, ask little about court affairs."
The sons followed her advice.
Huì returned and reported the situation,
and they ultimately avoided harm.
The *Shìyǔ* states:
"Yǔn had two sons:
Qí, styled Zǐtài;
and Měng, styled Zǐbào.
Both were capable in governance."
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* states:
"Qí,
during the Tàishǐ era, served as Assistant to the Minister of Ceremonies.
When Emperor Shìzǔ once performed sacrifices at the ancestral temple,
Qí was supposed to assist in the rituals.
The court, considering that Qí came from a family that had suffered persecution,
did not allow him to approach,
and he was sent out to serve as a Chief Clerk.
Emperor Shìzǔ issued an edict,
recounting Yǔn's longstanding reputation,
and also praising Qí's talent,
promoting him to Director of the Ministry of Rites.
Měng was deeply learned in ritual studies and Confucianism,
and additionally possessed talent and insight.
He served as Governor of Yōuzhōu."
Wáng Gōngyuān married the daughter of Zhūgě Dàn.
Upon entering the bridal chamber,
when conversation began,
Wáng said to his wife:
"Your expression and demeanor are rather humble;
you are nothing like Gōngxiū!"
His wife replied:
"A great husband cannot emulate Yànyún,
yet expects his wife to rival heroes and outstanding figures!"
The *Wèishì Chūnqiū* states:
"Wáng Guǎng, styled Gōngyuān,
was the son of Wáng Líng.
He possessed grace, capacity, and literary talent,
and was highly esteemed in his time.
He engaged in discussions with Fù Gǔ and others on 'The Similarities and Differences of Talent and Nature,'
which circulated widely."
The *Wèizhì* states:
"Guǎng had high aspirations, learning, and conduct.
When Líng was executed,
he was also put to death."
I submit that Wáng Guǎng was a renowned scholar;
how could he jest about his father-in-law?
This statement is incorrect.
Wáng Jīng was poor and struggling in his youth,
but rose in official rank to the two-thousand-bushel level.
His mother said to him:
"You were originally the son of a humble family.
Now you have reached the rank of two thousand bushels.
Can this not be enough to stop?"
Jīng was unable to follow her advice.
He served as a Secretary,
assisting the state of Wei,
but was not loyal to Jin,
and was arrested.
Weeping, he bid farewell to his mother, saying:
"Because I did not obey your instruction,
I have come to this day!"
His mother showed no trace of sorrow,
and said to him:
"As a son, be filial;
as a minister, be loyal.
You have been both filial and loyal.
How have you failed me?"
The *Shìyǔ* says:
"Jīng's courtesy name was Yànwěi,
and he was from Qīnghé.
During the incident with the Duke of Gāoguìxiāng,
Wáng Chén
and Wáng Yè galloped to inform King Wén,
but Jīng, being upright, did not go out.
Because of Chén
and Yè conveying his intent,
he was later executed along with his mother."
The *Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* says:
"When Chén
and Yè were about to leave,
they called out to Jīng,
but he did not follow,
saying:
'You gentlemen, go!'"
The *Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū* says:
"Initially,
when Cáo Máo was about to personally campaign against Sīmǎ Zhāo,
Jīng admonished him, saying:
'In the past, Duke Zhāo of Lǔ could not bear the Jì clan,
was defeated and fled, losing his state,
and became the laughingstock of the world.
Now, power has long been at their gates.
The court and the four directions
all exert themselves to the death for them,
disregarding the principles of obedience and rebellion.
This is not a matter of a single day.
Moreover, the palace guard is empty and lacking,
and there is not a single inch of blade.
What resources does Your Majesty have to rely on?
And to act like this all of a sudden—
is it not like trying to cure a disease but making it deeper?'
Máo did not listen.
Later, Jīng was killed,
along with his mother.
As he was about to die,
he wept and apologized to his mother.
His mother's expression did not change;
she smiled and said to him:
'Who among men does not die?
The reason I stopped you before
was only fear that you would not meet your proper end.
To die together like this—
what regret is there?'"
Gān Bǎo's *Jìn Jì* says:
"Jīng was upright,
but not loyal to us,
so we executed him."
According to the records of Fù Chàng
and Gān Bǎo,
then Jīng was truly loyal and steadfast to Wei.
Yet the *Shìyǔ* says he was upright,
and also says it was because of Chén
and Yè conveying his intent.
How contradictory!
Therefore, the words of these two families capture it well.
Shān Gōng, after just one meeting with Jī
and Ruǎn,
formed a bond as strong as metal and orchid.
Shān's wife, née Hán,
sensed that her husband's friendship with these two men was extraordinary,
and asked him about it.
He said:
"In my present life, those I can consider friends
are only these two gentlemen!"
His wife said:
"The wife of Fù Jī also personally observed Hú
and Zhào. I wish to observe them.
May I?"
Another day,
when the two men came,
the wife urged her husband to have them stay overnight,
and prepared wine and meat.
At night, she bored through the wall to watch them,
and stayed until dawn, forgetting to return.
Her husband entered and said:
"What are the two men like?"
His wife said:
"Your talent and grace are far inferior,
but you are precisely fit to befriend them based on your insight and breadth."
He said:
"They also often consider my breadth superior."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Tāo was elegant, simple, broad-minded, and perceptive,
his measure vast and far-reaching.
His mind dwelled beyond affairs,
yet he accommodated himself to the times.
He once formed a wordless bond with Ruǎn Jí
and Jī Kāng, among others.
As for the other gentlemen,
who struggled and stumbled in the world,
Tāo alone preserved a vast and noble measure."
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Lady Hán had talent and insight.
Before Tāo took office,
he teased her, saying:
'Endure the cold.
I shall become one of the Three Dukes.
I wonder if you are worthy to be a Lady?'"
Wáng Hún's wife, née Zhōng, bore a daughter who was virtuous and beautiful.
Yú Yù's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Hún's courtesy name was Xuánchōng,
from Jìnyáng, Tàiyuán.
He was the son of Wěi's Minister of Education, Chǎng.
He rose to the rank of Minister of Education."
Wǔzǐ sought a simple and excellent match for his sister but had not found one.
There was a son of a military family
who had outstanding talent.
Wishing to marry his sister to him,
he then informed his mother.
The *Wángshì Pǔ* says:
"Lady Zhōng's personal name was Yǎnzhī,
granddaughter of the Grand Tutor, Yáo."
She said:
"If he is truly talented,
his background can be overlooked.
However, you must let me see him."
Wǔzǐ then had the military youth mix among a group of commoners,
and had his mother observe from behind a curtain.
Afterward,
his mother said to Wǔzǐ:
"That person wearing such clothes and with such a bearing—
is he not the one you have in mind?"
Wǔzǐ said:
"It is he."
His mother said:
"This man's talent is sufficient to stand out from the crowd,
but his background is humble.
Unless he has a long life,
he will not be able to fully apply his talents.
Observing his bone structure and appearance,
he will certainly not live long.
He cannot be married."
Wǔzǐ followed her advice.
The military youth died after a few years.
Jiǎ Chōng's former wife
was the daughter of Lǐ Fēng.
After Lǐ Fēng was executed,
they divorced and she was exiled to the frontier.
The *Collected Works of Women* states:
"Jiǎ Chōng's wife, née Lǐ,
was named Wǎn, courtesy name Shūwén.
After Lǐ Fēng's execution,
she was exiled to Lèlàng."
Later, she was pardoned and allowed to return.
By then, Jiǎ Chōng had already married the daughter of Guō Pèi.
The *Genealogy of the Jiǎ Clan* states:
"The Guō woman was named Yùhuáng,
who was the Lady of Guǎngxuān."
Emperor Wǔ specially permitted him to establish left and right wives.
The Lǐ woman lived separately outside,
unwilling to return to Jiǎ Chōng's residence.
The *Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"After Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
the Lǐ woman was pardoned and returned.
The Princess Consort of Qíxiànwáng wished to have Jiǎ Chōng dismiss Guō Shì
and take her mother back instead.
Jiǎ Chōng did not consent.
He built a residence for the Lǐ woman,
but they did not associate with each other.
When Jiǎ Chōng's mother, Liǔ Shì, was nearing death,
Jiǎ Chōng asked her if she had any final words.
Liǔ said:
'I told you to bring back your new wife Lǐ, but you still refused.
Why ask about other matters!'"
Guō Shì said to Jiǎ Chōng:
"I wish to visit Lǐ."
Jiǎ Chōng said:
"She is upright, principled, and talented.
It would be better for you not to go."
The *Separate Biography of Jiǎ Chōng* states:
"The Lǐ woman possessed virtuous nature and fine talent."
Guō Shì then arrayed herself in grand attire and bearing,
bringing many maidservants with her.
Upon arrival,
she entered the doorway.
The Lǐ woman rose to greet her.
Guō unconsciously found her own legs bending,
and she knelt and bowed twice.
After returning,
she told Jiǎ Chōng.
Jiǎ Chōng said:
"What did I tell you?"
According to the *Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn*:
"Shìzǔ, because Lǐ Fēng had offended the Jìn court,
and also because Guō Shì was the mother of the Crown Prince's consort,
there was no reason for divorce and severance.
He therefore issued an edict ordering a cessation,
forbidding them from associating."
However, Wáng Yǐn's *History of Jìn* also states:
"After Jiǎ Chōng divorced Lǐ,
he married the daughter of Guō Pèi, the Administrator of Chéngyáng,
named Huái.
When Lǐ's banishment was lifted,
an edict permitted Jiǎ Chōng to establish left and right wives.
Jiǎ Chōng's mother, Liǔ, also ordered him to bring Lǐ back.
Huái became angry,
rolled up her sleeves, and reproached Jiǎ Chōng, saying:
'You edited and established the laws and ordinances,
achieving the merit of assisting the founding.
I have my share in that.
How can Lǐ be placed on equal footing with me?'
Jiǎ Chōng then built a house in Yǒngnián Lane to settle Lǐ.
Huái only learned of this later.
When Jiǎ Chōng went out,
she would send people to look for him.
An edict permitted Jiǎ Chōng to establish left and right wives.
Jiǎ Chōng replied to the edict with modesty, not daring to accept such a grand ritual."
Since the *Praise of Jìn* states that Shìzǔ issued an edict not allowing Lǐ to return,
while Wáng Yǐn's *History of Jìn* and the *Separate Biography of Jiǎ Chōng* both say the edict permitted the establishment of left and right wives,
and that Jiǎ Chōng feared Guō Shì,
not daring to bring Lǐ back,
the accounts of these three sources differ,
and it is unclear which is correct.
However, Lǐ's not returning
had other reasons,
and the *Shì Shuō* stating
"she herself was unwilling to return"
is erroneous.
Moreover, Guō Huái was fierce and stubborn;
how could she possibly visit Lǐ and bow to her?
These are all fabrications.
Jiǎ Chōng's wife, née Lǐ, composed the *Instructions for Women*,
which circulated in the world.
The daughter of the Lǐ woman
was the Princess Consort of Qíxiànwáng.
The daughter of the Guō woman
was Empress Huìdì.
After Jiǎ Chōng died,
the daughters of Lǐ and Guō each wished to have their own mother buried with him.
For years it remained unresolved.
After Empress Jiǎ was deposed,
the Lǐ woman was then interred with him,
and the burial was thus settled.
The *Praise of the Various Dukes of Jìn* states:
"The Lǐ woman was talented and virtuous.
The world refers to
the '*Instructions of Lady Lǐ*'
. She bore a daughter, Hé,
who was also talented and intelligent,
namely the Princess Consort of Qíwáng."
The *Collected Works of Women* states:
"When the Lǐ woman reached Lèlàng,
she left her two daughters the eight chapters of *Models and Standards*."
Wáng Yǐn's *History of Jìn* states:
"Empress Jiǎ, courtesy name Nánfēng,
was executed by Zhàowáng."
Wáng Rǔnán in his youth had no marriage arranged,
and he himself sought the daughter of Hǎo Pǔ.
The *Genealogy of the Hǎo Clan* states:
"Pǔ, courtesy name Dàokuāng,
was from Xiāngchéng in Tàiyuán.
He served up to the position of Administrator of Luòyáng."
The Minister of Works considered him foolish,
and since there was no marriage prospect for him,
he let him have his way
and consented.
The *Records of the Wèi Clan* states:
"Wáng Chǎng, courtesy name Wénshū,
served up to the position of Minister of Works."
After the marriage,
she indeed possessed fine appearance and virtuous character.
She gave birth to Dōnghǎi,
and thus became the maternal model for the Wáng clan.
Someone asked Wáng Rǔnán how he knew.
He said:
"I once saw her fetching water from the well.
Her movements, demeanor, and bearing never deviated from propriety,
and she never acted contrary to what was observed.
From this, I knew."
The *Separate Biography of Wáng Rǔnán* states:
"Hǎo Zhòngjiāng of Xiāngchéng
came from an extremely isolated and humble family,
not a suitable match for him.
My lord once saw his daughter
and then sought to betroth her.
She indeed proved to be lofty, intelligent, outstanding, and exceptional,
a maternal model who stood out in the clan.
His broad knowledge and ample capacity
were all of this kind."
The wife of Minister of Education Wáng
was a daughter of the Zhōng clan,
the great-great-granddaughter of the Grand Tutor.
The *Genealogy of the Wáng Clan* states:
"The lady
was the daughter of Zhōng Yǎn, a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
She also possessed outstanding talent and womanly virtue."
The *Collected Works of Women* states:
"The lady had literary talent.
Her poems, rhapsodies, eulogies, and elegies circulated in the world."
Zhōng and Hǎo were sisters-in-law,
and they esteemed and were close to each other.
Zhōng did not use her high status to oppress Hǎo,
nor did Hǎo use her low status to defer to Zhōng.
Within the Dōnghǎi household,
the rules of Lady Hǎo were followed.
Within the Jīnglíng household,
the rituals of Lady Zhōng were modeled.
Lǐ Píngyáng,
son of the Governor of Qínzhōu,
Lǐ Zhòng has already been mentioned.
The "Yǒngjiā Exiles' Register" states:
"His courtesy name was Xuánzhòu,
a man from Jiāngxià,
Governor of Qínzhōu under Wei."
He was a renowned scholar of the Central Plains.
At that time, he was compared to Wáng Yífǔ.
Sūn Xiù initially sought to establish his authority,
and everyone said:
"Lè Lìng is too esteemed among the people to be killed,
and killing Lǐ Zhòng would not be worth it either."
The "Accounts of the Jin Nobles" states:
"Sūn Xiù, courtesy name Jùnzhōng,
was a man from Lángyé.
Initially, when Zhào Wáng Lún was enfeoffed in Lángyé,
Xiù served as a minor official in a close position.
Lún often had Xiù draft letters and memorials,
and his literary talent pleased Lún.
When Lún was enfeoffed as the Prince of Zhào,
Xiù moved his household to become a man of Zhào,
was appointed as a Gentleman Attendant,
and was trusted by Lún."
The "Jìn Yángqiū" states:
"When Lún usurped the throne,
Xiù became the Central Secretariat Director,
and all matters were decided by Xiù.
He was executed by Qí Wáng."
He then forced Zhòng to take his own life.
Initially, while Zhòng was at home,
someone rushed in through the gate,
took out a document from their hair knot, and showed it to Zhòng.
Zhòng read it and his expression changed,
went inside to show it to his daughter,
and the daughter immediately cried out
"It's over."
Understanding her meaning,
he went out and took his own life.
According to various records, it is said:
"Zhòng knew that Zhào Wáng Lún was causing chaos,
and, being ill, did not seek treatment,
eventually leading to his death."
Yet this text says he took his own life,
which is very contradictory.
Moreover, Lún and
Xiù were cruel and tyrannical,
often resorting to executions,
and if they wanted to establish authority,
they would have publicly executed him;
why would they force him to take his own life?
This daughter was very wise,
and Zhòng often consulted her.
When Zhōu Jùn served as the General Pacifying the East,
he went hunting,
encountered heavy rain,
and passed by the Lǐ family of Rǔnán.
The Lǐ family was wealthy,
but the men were not at home.
There was a daughter named Luòxiù,
who heard that there were distinguished guests outside,
and with a maidservant, slaughtered pigs and sheep inside,
prepared food for several dozen people,
everything meticulously arranged,
without any sound of people being heard.
Secretly observing,
he saw only one woman,
whose appearance was extraordinary,
and Jùn thus sought to take her as a concubine.
Her father and brothers refused.
Luòxiù said:
"Our family is in decline,
why begrudge one daughter?
If we form a marriage alliance with a noble family,
it may bring great benefits in the future."
Her father and brothers agreed.
The "Tales of the Eight Princes" states:
"Jùn, courtesy name Kāilín,
was a man from Ānchéng in Rǔnán.
He was known for his talent from a young age.
In the early Tàikāng era,
after pacifying Wú,
he went from Palace Censor to Governor of Yángzhōu.
In the early Yuánkāng era,
he was appointed General Pacifying the East."
She then gave birth to Bórén and his brothers.
Luòxiù said to Bórén and the others:
"The reason I humbled myself to become a concubine in your family
was for the sake of our family's standing!
According to the "Zhōu Family Genealogy":
"Jùn married the daughter of Lǐ Bózōng from the same commandery."
This text says she was a concubine,
which is false.
If you do not treat my family as close relatives,
I will not regret the remaining years of my life either."
Bórén and the others all complied.
From then on, the Lǐ family in the world
received proper recognition and treatment.
Táo Gōng had great ambitions from a young age,
but his family was extremely poor,
and he lived with his mother, Zhàn shì.
Fàn Kuí of the same commandery was well-known,
having been recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
but Kuí's details are unclear.
He sought lodging at Kǎn's home.
At that time, snow and ice had accumulated for days,
and Kǎn's house was as empty as a hanging chime,
yet Kuí had many horses and attendants.
Kǎn's mother, Zhàn shì, said to Kǎn:
"You just go out and entertain the guest,
I will handle things myself."
Zhàn's hair reached the ground,
and she cut it into two portions,
one portion made into a wig.
She sold it for several hu of rice,
chopped the house pillars,
split them all in half for firewood,
and shredded the mats for horse fodder.
By evening,
she had prepared fine food,
and none of the attendants lacked anything.
Kuí admired his talent and eloquence,
and deeply appreciated his generous hospitality.
The next morning, as he was leaving,
Kǎn pursued and saw him off without end,
for nearly a hundred li.
Kuí said:
"The road is already far,
you should turn back."
Kǎn still did not return,
and Kuí said:
"You may go now!
When I reach Luòyáng,
I will surely spread a favorable account of you."
Kǎn then returned.
When Kuí reached Luò,
he praised him to Yáng Zhuó,
Gù Róng, and others,
earning him great acclaim.
The "Jìn Yángqiū" states:
"Kǎn's father, Dān,
married a daughter of the Zhàn family from Xīngàn,
and she gave birth to Kǎn.
Zhàn was devout, respectful, and wise,
and because the Táo family was poor and lowly,
she spun and wove to support Kǎn,
enabling him to associate with those better than himself.
Kǎn served as a minor official in Xúnyáng in his youth,
and Fàn Kuí, a Filial and Incorrupt from Póyáng, once sought lodging at Kǎn's home.
At the time, there was heavy snow,
and Kǎn's home had no fodder,
so Zhàn took apart the mats she slept on and shredded them for fodder.
Secretly, she cut off her hair,
sold it to provide for the meal.
Kuí heard of this and sighed.
As Kuí was leaving,
Kǎn pursued and saw him off.
Kuí said:
'Do you wish to serve in office?'
Kǎn said:
'I have the intention to serve in the commandery.'
Kuí said:
'I will surely speak on your behalf.'
Passing through Lújiāng,
he praised him to the Grand Administrator, Zhāng Kuí.
Kǎn was summoned to fill a minor post,
recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
and appointed as a Gentleman of the Interior.
At the time, Gù Róng of Yùzhāng once reproached Yáng Zhuó, saying:
'How can you ride in the same carriage with a lowly person?'
Zhuó said:
'This is a man of humble origins but outstanding talent.'"
Wáng Yǐn's "History of Jin" states:
"After Kǎn's mother cut off her hair to provide for the guest,
those who heard of it sighed:
'Only such a mother could give birth to such a son.'
He was then recommended to Zhāng Kuí.
Yáng Zhuó also took note of him.
Later, when Zhuó served as the Rectifier for ten commanderies,
he recommended Kǎn as the Minor Rectifier of Póyáng,
and only then did he attain the upper grade."
Táo Kǎn in his youth,
served as an official in charge of fish weirs.
Once he sent a jar of pickled fish to his mother.
His mother sealed the jar and returned it with the messenger,
and in reply she reproached Kǎn, saying:
"You are an official,
and you use government property to send me gifts.
Not only is this of no benefit,
it only increases my worries."
The "Biography of Kǎn" says:
"His mother, née Zhàn,
was virtuous, wise, and had strict principles.
When Kǎn was in Wǔchāng,
he would drink leisurely with his subordinates at banquets,
but he always had a drinking limit.
Someone once urged him that he could still drink a little more,
but Kǎn was sorrowful for a long time and said:
'When I was young,
I once made a mistake due to drinking.
My parents set this restriction for me,
so I dare not exceed the limit.'
When Kǎn was mourning his mother's death,
while he was at her gravesite,
suddenly two guests came to offer condolences.
They did not weep but withdrew,
their attire and appearance were strikingly unusual,
and it was known they were no ordinary people.
He sent someone to follow and watch them,
and they only saw a pair of cranes soaring into the sky and flying away."
The "Yōumíng Lù" says:
"Táo Kǎn caught fish at a dam southwest of Xúnyáng,
and he himself called that pond 'Hèmén' (Crane Gate)."
Note: Wú's Minister of Education, Mèng Zōng, served as the supervisor of Léichí,
and he sent pickled fish to his mother,
but his mother did not accept it.
This was not Kǎn.
It is suspected that later people borrowed from Mèng's story to create this account.
Huán Xuānwǔ pacified Shǔ,
and took Lǐ Shì's younger sister as a concubine,
favoring her greatly.
She often stayed behind his study.
His principal wife did not know at first,
but after hearing of it,
she went with several dozen maidservants, drawing white blades to attack her.
The "Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng" says:
"Wēn married Emperor Míng's daughter, Princess Nánkāng."
Just then, Lǐ was combing her hair.
Her hair cascaded down to the ground,
her skin shone like jade,
yet she showed no change in expression.
Calmly she said:
"My country is destroyed, my family lost,
I have no heart to be here.
If I can be killed today,
it would fulfill my original wish."
The principal wife, ashamed, withdrew.
The "Record of Jealousy" says:
"Wēn, after pacifying Shǔ,
took Lǐ Shì's daughter as a concubine.
The princess was fierce and jealous,
and did not know immediately.
Later, when she found out,
she drew a blade and went to Lǐ's place,
intending to strike her.
She saw Lǐ combing her hair by the window.
Her appearance was dignified and beautiful.
Slowly she tied up her hair,
folded her hands toward the princess,
her expression calm and proper,
her words full of sorrow and pathos.
The princess then threw down the knife, stepped forward, and embraced her, saying:
'Ah, child,
even I, upon seeing you, feel pity,
how much more that old rascal!'
Thereafter she treated her well."
Yǔ Yùtái
was Xī's younger brother.
When Xī was executed,
Yùtái was also to be killed.
Xī has been mentioned previously.
Yùtái
was the childhood name of Yǔ Yǒu.
The "Genealogy of the Yǔ Clan" says:
"Yǒu, styled Huìyàn,
was the third son of Minister Bīng.
He served as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
and as Governor of Dōngyáng."
Yùtái's daughter-in-law
was the daughter of Xuānwǔ's younger brother, Huán Huò.
The "Genealogy of the Yǔ Clan" says:
"Yǒu, styled Hóngzhī,
his eldest son Xuān
married the daughter of Xuānwǔ's younger brother Huán Huò,
her childhood name was Nǚyòu."
Barefoot, she sought to enter,
but the gatekeeper barred her and would not let her in.
The woman said sternly:
"What kind of petty person are you?
This is my paternal uncle's gate,
and you won't let me pass!"
Then she rushed in,
wept and pleaded, saying:
"Yǔ Yùtái, because of others, his feet are short by three inches—
could he still possibly be a rebel?"
Xuānwǔ laughed and said:
"The son-in-law is indeed in a hurry."
Thus he pardoned Yùtái and his entire family.
The "Chronicles of the Restoration" says:
"Huán Wēn executed Yǔ Xī's younger brother Qiàn.
Xī, hearing of the trouble, fled.
Xī's younger brother Yǒu was to be executed.
His daughter-in-law, a woman of the Huán clan,
pleaded with Wēn,
and obtained pardon."
Xiè Ān's wife screened off the maidservants
and had them perform music and dance in front,
letting the Grand Tutor see them briefly,
then lowered the screen.
The Grand Tutor asked to open it again,
but his wife said:
"I fear it might harm your great virtue."
Lady Liú has been mentioned previously.
Chariot-riding General Huán disliked wearing new clothes.
After bathing,
his wife deliberately sent new clothes to him.
The "Genealogy of the Huán Clan" says:
"Chōng married the daughter of Lángyá's Wáng Tián,
her childhood name was Nǚzōng."
The General was greatly angered,
urging her to take them away.
His wife took them back but then brought them again,
sending a message, saying:
"If clothes are not worn when new,
how can they become old?"
Lord Huán laughed heartily,
and put them on.
Wáng Xīzhī's wife, Lady Xī, said to her two younger brothers, the Minister of Education and the Gentleman of the Central Secretariat:
The Minister of Education, Xī Yīn, has been mentioned previously.
The "Separate Biography of Xī Tán" says:
"Tán, styled Chóngxī,
was the youngest son of Jiàn.
His nature was principled and substantial,
harmonious, upright, deep, and simple.
He rose through the ranks to become Governor of Dānyáng,
General of the Northern Central Army,
and Governor of Xú and Yǎn provinces."
"When the Wáng family sees the two Xiè brothers,
