they empty their baskets and shelves [to entertain them];
the two Xiè brothers:
Ān and Wàn.
When they see you all coming,
they are merely ordinary.
You need not trouble yourselves to go again."
Wáng Níngzhī's wife, Lady Xiè, after marrying into the Wáng family,
greatly looked down upon Níngzhī.
After returning to the Xiè family,
she was very displeased.
The Grand Tutor comforted and explained to her, saying:
"Young Master Wáng
is the son of Yìshǎo,
and his person is not bad either.
Why do you resent him so?"
She replied:
"Among my uncles in the family,
there are Ādà
and the Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
Among my cousins,
there are Fēng,
Hú, È,
and Mò. Fēng and Hú
are the childhood names of Xiè Sháo.
È and Mò
are the childhood names of Xiè Yuān.
Sháo, styled Mùdù,
was the son of Wàn,
and served as Chariot-riding General's Marshal.
Yuān, styled Shūdù,
was the second son of Yì,
and served as Governor of Yìxīng.
People of the time praised those of outstanding talent and elegance,
sometimes calling them Fēng,
Hú, È,
and Mò. Fēng refers to Lǎng,
È refers to Xuán,
Mò refers to Sháo.
Lǎng, Xuán, and Yuān—
another version says Hú refers to Yuān,
È refers to Xuán,
Mò refers to Sháo.
I never imagined that between heaven and earth,
there could be a young master like Wáng!"
Hán Kāngbó's mother
had an ancient armrest that was worn out.
Biàn Jū saw the armrest was in poor condition
and wanted to replace it.
Jū was Biàn Fànzhī,
the grandson of the mother's daughter.
She replied:
"If I had not kept this hidden,
how would you have been able to see an ancient object?"
Wáng Jiāngzhōu's wife said to Xiè È:
"Why have you made no progress at all?
The wife
was Xuán's younger sister.
Is it because worldly affairs preoccupy your mind,
or is your natural talent limited?"
When Xī Jiābīn passed away,
his wife's brothers wanted to bring their sister back home,
but she adamantly refused to return.
The Xī Clan Genealogy states:
"Chāo married the daughter of Zhōu Mǐn from Rǔnán,
named Mǎtóu."
She said:
"In life, even if I could not share the same room as my husband Xī,
in death, how could I not share the same grave!"
The Book of Songs says:
"In life, we lived in separate rooms;
in death, we share the same grave."
Zhèng Xuán's annotation states:
"The 'grave' refers to the burial pit in the tomb."
Xiè È held his elder sister in the highest esteem,
while Zhāng Xuán often praised his younger sister,
intending to rival him.
There was a nun named Jìní
who visited both the Zhāng
and Xiè households.
When asked about their relative merits,
she replied:
"Lady Wáng possesses a free and open spirit,
truly embodying the grace of a forest recluse.
As for the wife of the Gù family, her pure heart shines like jade,
undoubtedly a paragon of feminine virtue."
Shàngshū Wáng Huì once visited the wife of Yòujūn Wáng.
The Book of Song states:
"Huì, styled Lìngmíng,
was from Lángyá.
He served as Minister of Personnel
and was posthumously honored as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices."
He asked:
"Do your eyes and ears still function well?"
The Anthology of Women's Writings records a Memorial of Gratitude stating:
"I am ninety years old,
my solitary bones alone remain.
I humbly beg for your compassion,
to grant me care and sustenance."
She replied:
"White hair and lost teeth
pertain to the physical body;
but as for the eyes and ears,
they are connected to the spirit and consciousness.
How could they be cut off from others?"
Hán Kāngbó's mother, Yīn,
accompanied her grandson Huìzhī to Héngyáng.
The Hán Clan Genealogy states:
"Huìzhī, styled Jìlún.
His father was Kāngbó,
Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Huìzhī served as the Prefect of Héngyáng."
At Hélú Island, she encountered Nánjùn Huán.
Biàn Jū was her grandson,
and he came to inquire after her.
She said to Jū:
"If I do not die,
I will see this upstart commit treason for two generations!"
After several years in Héngyáng,
Huìzhī met his demise in the disaster caused by Huán Jǐngzhēn.
The Continued Annals of Jìnyáng states:
"Huán Liàng, styled Jǐngzhēn,
was the grandson of Grand Marshal Huán Wēn.
His father was Jì,
a Palace Attendant.
His uncle, Xuán,
was executed for treason.
Liàng gathered followers in Chángshā,
proclaiming himself Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
He killed Grand Steward Zhēn Gōng,
former Prefect of Héngyáng Hán Huìzhī, and over ten others.
He was beheaded by Guō Zhēn, a soldier under Liú Yì's command."
Yīn caressed the corpse and wept, saying:
"When your father was dismissed from Yùzhāng,
he departed the morning the imperial summons arrived.
You left your commandery for several years,
unable to move due to circumstances,
and thus met with disaster.
What more is there to say?"
Xún Xù was skilled in understanding musical tones,
and contemporary opinion regarded him as having an intuitive grasp.
Thus, he adjusted the pitch pipes,
and corrected the ceremonial music.
Whenever the grand assembly was held,
and music was performed in the palace courtyard,
he would personally tune the pitches,
and all were harmonious and in tune.
Ruǎn Xián possessed exquisite discernment,
and was considered divinely perceptive.
Whenever music was performed at official gatherings,
he felt in his heart that it was out of tune.
Since no one spoke in support of Xún,
Xún resented him,
and had Ruǎn demoted to Prefect of Shǐpíng.
Later, an old farmer tilling the fields
found a jade ruler from the Zhōu dynasty,
which was the standard ruler of the realm.
Xún tested it against the bells, drums,
metal and stone instruments,
and string and bamboo instruments he had tuned,
and found all were short by one grain of millet.
Thereupon, he acknowledged Ruǎn's divine perception.
The Later Summary of Jìn states:
"The instruments of pitch and temperament
had fallen into disuse since the end of Zhōu,
and during the reigns of Hàn Chéngdì
and Hàn Āidì,
various scholars restored and managed them.
By the end of the Eastern Hàn,
they were again neglected.
The Wèi court commissioned Dù Kuí, a music master who understood tones, to create them,
but he could not verify them against classical rites,
merely relying on the sounds of contemporary string and wind instruments
and the measurements of the time to make them,
greatly deviating from ritual standards.
Thereupon, Emperor Wǔ ordered Secretariat Director Xún Xù to follow classical regulations
and determine the pitch standards.
After casting the pitch pipes,
he sought out ancient instruments,
obtaining several jade pitch pipes from the Zhōu era.
Compared, they showed no discrepancy.
Moreover, in various commandery granaries,
some old bells from the Hàn era were found.
When measured against the pitch standard,
they resonated without being struck,
their sounds harmonizing perfectly,
as if all were made together."
The Eulogies of Jìn Notables states:
"After the pitch standard was established,
Cavalry Lieutenant Ruǎn Xián said
'Xún's created pitches are too high;
high pitches sound mournful.
The music of a perished state is sorrowful and brooding,
reflecting the hardship of its people.
Now the music does not match the elegance of the classics;
I fear it is not the harmonious sound of virtuous governance.
It must be due to differences in the length of ancient and modern rulers.
However, the bells and chimes currently in use were made by Dù Kuí during the Wèi era,
and do not correspond to Xún's pitch standard.
Their sound is relaxed and elegant,
and since it has long been unknown that Kuí made them,
people of the time consider them adequate
and not in need of alteration.'
Xún, being arrogant by nature,
used an incident to demote Ruǎn to Prefect of Shǐpíng,
where he died of illness.
Later, an ancient bronze ruler was unearthed from the ground.
When used to measure Xún's current ruler,
it was found to be four-tenths of an inch short.
Only then was it clear that Ruǎn indeed understood music,
yet no one could correct it."
Gān Bǎo's Annals of Jìn states:
"Xún Xù first created the dance 'Correct Virtue and Great Image,'
and used the pitch pipes established by Dù Kuí of Wèi to adjust the grand music,
but the fundamental tones were not harmonious.
From the Later Hàn to Wèi,
the ruler was over four-tenths of an inch longer than in antiquity,
and Kuí relied on it,
hence the loss of harmony.
Thus, following the Rites of Zhōu,
he piled millet to establish measures,
used them to measure ancient instruments,
matched the original inscriptions,
and adopted them as the standard,
using them for suburban and ancestral temple ceremonies."
Xún Xù was once dining with Emperor Wǔ of Jìn and eating bamboo shoots with rice.
He said to those present:
"This was cooked with firewood from worn-out cartwheels."
Those present did not believe him,
but upon secretly inquiring,
found that old cart axles had indeed been used.
Someone read the grave of Yáng Hù's father and said,
"Later, a ruler destined to receive the Mandate of Heaven will emerge from here."
Hù detested these words,
so he dug and broke the ground behind the grave,
to ruin its auspicious energy.
The physiognomist stood watching and said:
"Still, a Duke with a broken arm will emerge."
Soon after, Hù fell from a horse and broke his arm,
and his rank indeed reached that of a Duke.
The *Yōumíng Lù* says:
"Yáng Hù was skilled at riding.
He had a son, five or six years old,
intelligent and delightful.
After the grave was dug,
the child died.
At that time, Yáng was the Governor of Xiāngyáng,
and while riding in circles, he fell to the ground,
breaking his arm.
At that time, scholars all sighed in admiration of his loyalty."
Wáng Wǔzi was adept at understanding the nature of horses.
Once he rode a horse
fitted with a linked-coin saddlecloth.
Ahead there was water,
but the horse refused to cross all day.
Wáng said:
"This must be because it cherishes the saddlecloth."
He had someone remove it,
and the horse crossed directly.
The *Yǔlín* says:
"Wǔzi had a fondness for horses,
and was also very discerning about them.
Therefore, Dù Yù said,
'Wáng Wǔzi has a horse obsession,
and Hé Chángyú has a money obsession.'
Emperor Wǔ asked Dù Yù:
'What obsession do you have?'
He replied:
'I have an obsession with the *Zuǒzhuàn*.'"
Chén Shù served as an aide to the Grand General,
and was greatly loved and valued.
When he died,
Guō Pú went to mourn him,
grieving deeply,
and cried out:
"Sìzǔ,
how do you know it is not a blessing!"
Soon after, the Grand General rebelled,
just as he had said.
The *Chén Shì Pǔ* says:
"Shù, styled Sìzǔ,
was from Xǔchāng, Yǐngchuān.
He had a fine reputation."
Jìn Míngdì understood the art of divining graves and dwellings.
Hearing that Guō Pú was conducting a burial for someone,
the Emperor went in plain clothes to observe.
He then asked the host:
"Why bury at the dragon's horn?
This method will bring extermination to the clan!"
The host said:
"Guō said:
'This is burying at the dragon's ear;
within three years,
it will attract the Son of Heaven.'"
The Emperor asked:
"Does that mean an emperor will emerge?"
He replied:
"Not that an emperor will emerge,
but that it will attract the Son of Heaven's inquiry."
The *Xiàng Zhǒng Shū* by Qīngniǎozi says:
"Burying at the dragon's horn
brings sudden wealth and honor,
but later the family will be destroyed."
Guō Jǐngchún crossed the river,
and lived in Jìyáng.
His grave was less than a hundred paces from the water,
and people at the time thought it was too close to the water.
Jǐngchún said:
"It will become land."
The *Pú Biézhuàn* says:
"Pú was fond of classical studies from a young age,
and was skilled in divination.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
as the realm was about to fall into chaos,
Pú cast his divination sticks and sighed:
'The common people will become like different species!'
He then gathered over ten close families,
crossed the river south,
and settled in Jìyáng."
Now, as sand accumulated,
the area tens of *lǐ* from the grave became mulberry fields.
His poem says:
"The northern hills stand tall and fierce,
the vast sea churns and roils;
three graves lie in mounds,
only mother and brothers."
Chancellor Wáng ordered Guō Pú to perform a divination.
After the hexagram was formed,
Guō's expression turned very grim,
and he said:
"You, sir, have a thunder calamity!"
Wáng asked:
"Is there a way to dispel it?"
Guō said:
"Take a carriage westward for several *lǐ*,
find a cypress tree,
cut a piece as tall as you,
place it on the bed where you usually sleep,
and the disaster can be dispelled."
Wáng followed his advice.
Within a few days,
the cypress was indeed shattered by thunder,
and his disciples all celebrated.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Pú dispelled disasters and turned misfortune,
alleviated calamities and selected auspicious sites.
People at the time all said Jīng
and Guǎn were not his equals."
The Grand General said:
"You, sir, have shifted the blame onto a tree."
Duke Huán had a registrar skilled at distinguishing wine,
and whenever there was wine, he would have him taste it first.
Good wine was called
"Qīngzhōu Cóngshì,"
and bad wine was called
"Píngyuán Dūyóu."
Qīngzhōu had the Qí Commandery,
and Píngyuán had the Gé County.
"Cóngshì"
means
"reaching the navel,"
and "Dūyóu"
means
"staying above the diaphragm."
Xī Yīn followed the Daoist faith with great diligence and fervor,
often suffering from an abdominal ailment
that many doctors could not cure.
Hearing that Yú Fǎkāi was renowned,
he went to invite him.
When he arrived,
he took his pulse and said:
"The ailment you suffer, noble sir,
is precisely due to excessive spiritual exertion."
He prepared a dose of decoction for him.
After one dose,
he had a severe bowel movement,
expelling several pieces of paper the size of fists;
upon cutting them open,
they turned out to be previously ingested talismans.
The *Jìn Shū* says:
"Fǎkāi was skilled in medicine.
Once, while traveling,
he sought lodging with a host.
The host's wife was in labor,
but the child would not come out for days.
Fǎkāi said:
'This is easy to treat.'
He had a fat sheep killed,
ate over ten pieces of meat, and then applied acupuncture.
Soon, the child was delivered,
wrapped in the sheep's fat.
His skill was this exquisite."
Yīn Zhōngjūn was profoundly skilled in understanding meridians and pulses,
but in middle age, he abandoned it entirely.
There was a servant who often attended to him,
who suddenly kowtowed until his head bled.
Hào asked the reason,
and he said:
"There is a matter of life and death,
but I cannot speak of it."
After prolonged questioning,
he finally said:
"My mother is nearly a hundred years old,
and has been ill for a long time.
If I could receive a pulse diagnosis from you, sir,
there might be a chance for her to live.
Even if I am executed afterward, I would have no regrets."
Hào was moved by his utmost sincerity,
so he had her carried over,
diagnosed her pulse, and prescribed a formula.
After just one dose of the decoction,
she recovered.
Thereupon, he burned all his medical texts.
The game of Tánqí originated within the palace of Wei,
played with cosmetic boxes.
Fù Xuán’s “Preface to the Rhapsody on Tánqí” states:
“Emperor Chéng of the Hàn was fond of Cùjū,
but Liú Xiàng considered it to exhaust the body
and drain one’s strength,
unsuitable for the supreme ruler to engage in.
Therefore, based on its form, he created Tánqí.
Now, observing its principles,
they are indeed those of Cùjū.”
According to Xuán’s words,
the game of Tánqí
has existed for a long time.
Moreover, the “Biography of Liáng Jì” says:
“Jì excelled at Tánqí
and Géwǔ.”
Thus, to say it originated in the Wei era
is mistaken.
Emperor Wén was exceptionally skilled at this game;
using the corner of a handkerchief to flick the pieces,
he never missed.
A guest once claimed he could do it,
and the emperor had him demonstrate.
The guest used the corner of his géjīn headscarf,
lowered his head to flick the pieces,
surpassing even the emperor in skill.
In the “Diǎnlùn,” the emperor wrote in his own account:
“Among playful diversions,
I had few favorites,
only Tánqí, in which I somewhat mastered its subtleties.
In my youth, I once composed a rhapsody on it.
In former times, the capital had two masters of this art:
Marquis Héxiāng Dōngfāng Shì’ān,
and Zhāng Gōngzǐ.
I have always regretted not being able to play against them.”
The “Bówùzhì” states:
“The emperor excelled at Tánqí,
able to use the corner of a handkerchief.
At that time, there was a scholar
who could also lower his head and use the corner of his géjīn headscarf to flick the pieces.”
The Língyún Tái tower was exquisitely crafted;
first, the weight of all the timber was balanced,
and only then was it constructed,
so that not the slightest imbalance occurred.
Although the tower was lofty and steep,
it often swayed with the wind,
yet it never risked collapsing.
Emperor Míng of Wei ascended the tower,
fearing its precarious state,
and had it reinforced with large timbers.
The tower then collapsed.
Commentators said it was due to an imbalance in weight distribution.
The “Luòyáng Gōngdiàn Bù” states:
“The base of Língyún Tái is thirteen zhàng square,
and nine chǐ high.
The tower itself is four zhàng square,
and five zhàng high.
The ridgepole is thirteen zhàng, five chǐ, seven cùn, and five fēn above the ground.”
Wéi Zhòngjiāng was skilled in calligraphy.
When Emperor Míng of Wei built a hall,
he wanted to install a placard,
so he had Zhòngjiāng climb a ladder to inscribe it.
After descending,
his hair had turned completely white.
He then instructed his descendants:
“Do not study calligraphy anymore.”
The “Wénzhāng Xùlù” states:
“Wéi Dàn, styled Zhòngjiāng,
was from Dùlíng, Jīngzhào.
He was the son of Wéi Duān, the Grand Coachman.
He was learned in literature,
skilled in composition.
He died as Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments.”
Wèi Héng’s “Sìtǐ Shūshì” states:
“Dàn excelled in regular script;
many Wei palace buildings bore his inscriptions.
When Emperor Míng erected the Língxiāo Guàn,
the placard was mistakenly nailed up first,
so Dàn was placed in a cage,
hoisted up with a long rope on a windlass,
to inscribe it on the spot.
It was twenty-five zhàng above the ground,
and Dàn was extremely terrified.
He then warned his descendants
to abandon this method of regular script,
and recorded it in his family instructions.”
Zhōng Huì was the maternal uncle of Xún Jìběi,
but the two were not on good terms.
Xún possessed a precious sword
worth a million coins,
which he often kept with his mother, Lady Zhōng.
The “Kǒngshì Zhìguài” states:
“Xù entrusted the sword to his wife.”
Huì was skilled in handwriting,
and imitated Xún’s script,
writing a letter to his mother to fetch the sword,
then stole it and never returned it.
The “Shìyǔ” states:
“Huì was adept at imitating others’ handwriting.
During the campaign against Shǔ,
at Jiàngé, he intercepted Dèng Ài’s memorials,
altering their wording.
He made the language arrogant,
full of self-praise.
This led to Ài’s arrest.”
Xún Xù knew it was Zhōng but had no way to retrieve it,
so he contemplated how to repay him.
Later, the Zhōng brothers built a mansion costing tens of millions,
newly completed,
extremely exquisite and splendid,
but they had not yet moved in.
Xún was highly skilled in painting,
so he secretly went and painted on the gate hall of the Zhōng mansion
a portrait of the Grand Tutor,
with attire and appearance as in life.
When the two Zhōng brothers entered the gate,
they were overcome with grief,
and the mansion was left vacant and abandoned.
The “Kǒngshì Zhìguài” states:
“At the time, it was said that Xù’s retaliation against Huì
exceeded the loss by several tens of times.
Their calligraphy and painting
were both extremely ingenious.”
Yáng Chánghé was erudite and skilled in calligraphy.
The “Wénzìzhì” states:
“Chén was adept at cursive script,
also skilled in running and clerical scripts,
praised in his time.”
He could ride and shoot,
and excelled at Wéiqí.
Later generations of the Yáng family mostly knew calligraphy,
but in archery
and the art of Wéiqí, none could match him.
Dài Āndào went to study under Fàn Xuān.
The “Zhōngxīng Shū” states:
“Kuí traveled a thousand lǐ without regard for the distance,
going to Yùzhāng to visit Fàn Xuān.
Xuān, upon meeting Kuí,
found him extraordinary,
and married his elder brother’s daughter to him.”
He observed what Fàn did:
when Fàn read, he also read;
when Fàn copied books, he also copied books.
Only in his fondness for painting
did Fàn consider it useless,
and thought it unwise to labor over it.
Dài then painted a scene from the “Rhapsody on the Southern Capital”;
after Fàn viewed it, he sighed in admiration,
considering it highly beneficial,
and began to value painting.
Grand Tutor Xiè said:
“In the paintings of Gù Chángkāng,
there is something never seen since the beginning of humankind.”
The “Xù Jìnyáng Qiū” states:
“Kǎizhī was particularly fond of painting,
supremely skilled in his time.
Once, he entrusted a cabinet of paintings to Huán Xuán,
all his finest works,
which he deeply cherished.
He sealed and labeled the front of the cabinet.
Huán then opened the back of the cabinet and took them out,
carefully restoring them.
Later, when Kǎizhī saw the seals and labels intact as before,
but the paintings were all gone,
he simply said:
‘Exquisite paintings attain spiritual power,
transform and depart,
like humans ascending to immortality.’”
The Jìnyāng Qiū states:
"At that time, his reputation spread throughout the land,
and he is still praised today."
Ruǎn Jí was in mourning for his mother,
yet at the seat of Jìn Wénwáng, he drank wine and ate meat.
Sīlì Hé Zēng was also present.
The Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn states:
"Hé Zēng, styled Yǐngkǎo,
was from Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His father, Kuí,
served as Tàipú under Wèi.
Hé Zēng was known for his lofty elegance,
and additionally, his nature was benevolent and filial.
He rose through the ranks to become Sīlì Xiàowèi.
His intentions were very upright,
and the court was in awe of him.
He served under Jìn, rising to the position of Tàizǎi."
He said:
"Your Excellency governs the realm with filial piety,
yet Ruǎn Jí, in deep mourning,
openly drinks wine and eats meat in Your Excellency's presence.
He should be exiled beyond the seas,
to rectify customs and teachings."
Wénwáng said:
"Sìzōng is so devastated and worn,
and you, sir, cannot share in his sorrow.
What is the meaning of this?
Moreover, drinking wine and eating meat while ill
is indeed in accordance with mourning rites!"
Ruǎn Jí continued eating and drinking without pause,
his expression calm as usual.

Gān Bǎo's Jìn Jì states:
"Hé Zēng once said to Ruǎn Jí:
'You indulge your emotions and follow your whims;
you are a corruptor of customs.
Now loyal and worthy men hold governance,
examining names and realities comprehensively.
How can the likes of you
be allowed to endure long!'
He repeated this to Tàizǔ,
but Ruǎn Jí continued eating and drinking without pause.
Thus, between Wèi and Jìn,
there arose incidents of disheveled hair and barbaric arrogance,
and people who forgot death and life,
yet were paradoxically called practitioners of ritual—
all this was due to Ruǎn Jí."
The Wèishì Chūnqiū states:
"Ruǎn Jí was extremely filial by nature.
Although during mourning he did not follow conventional rites,
he was so devastated he nearly destroyed himself.
Yet he was deeply hated and resented by conventional literati like Hé Zēng.
Grand General Sīmǎ Zhāo admired his brilliance and greatness,
and thus did not harm him."
Liú Líng suffered from wine-sickness;
very thirsty,
he asked his wife for wine.
His wife discarded the wine and destroyed the vessels,
weeping and admonishing him:
"You drink far too much;
it is not the way to nurture life.
You must stop it!"
Liú Líng said: "Very well.
I cannot restrain myself,
so I must only pray to the ghosts and spirits,
and swear an oath to stop it myself!
You may then prepare wine and meat."
His wife said: "I respectfully heed your command."
She offered wine and meat before the spirits,
and asked Liú Líng to pray and swear.
Liú Líng knelt and prayed:
"Heaven gave birth to Liú Líng,
who takes wine as his fame.
With one drink, a hú;
with five dǒu, sober from hangover.
The Máogōng Zhù states:
"Wine-sickness is called chéng."
The words of a woman
must on no account be heeded."
Thereupon he drank the wine and ate the meat,
and soon was toppling drunk.
See the Zhúlín Qī Xián Lùn.
Liú Gōngróng drank with others,
mixing with vulgar and unsuitable company.
Some people criticized him for this.
He replied:
"Those superior to Gōngróng—
I cannot not drink with them;
those inferior to Gōngróng—
I also cannot not drink with them;
those of Gōngróng's own kind—
again, I cannot not drink with them."
Thus he drank all day long until drunk.
The Liúshì Pǔ states:
"Chǎng, styled Gōngróng,
was from the state of Pèi."
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Chǎng was a perceptive and understanding man,
and served up to the position of Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ."
When the position of Infantry Commandant was vacant,
and there were several hundred hú of wine stored in the kitchens,
Ruǎn Jí then requested to be made Infantry Commandant.
The Wénshì Zhuàn states:
"Ruǎn Jí was unrestrained and had an aloof attitude toward the world,
and did not enjoy serving as an official.
Jìn Wéndì was fond of Ruǎn Jí,
often chatting and joking with him,
allowing him his desires,
and not pressuring him with official duties.
Ruǎn Jí once said calmly:
'In my life, I once traveled to Dōngpíng,
and enjoyed its local customs.
I wish to become the Tàishǒu of Dōngpíng.'
Wéndì was pleased and granted his wish.
Ruǎn Jí then rode a donkey straight to the commandery,
had all the walls and partitions of the government offices torn down,
so that inside and outside could see each other,
and then issued clear and peaceful orders.
After more than ten days, he again rode his donkey and left.
Later, hearing that there were three hundred shí of wine in the Infantry kitchens,
he joyfully requested to be Commandant.
Thereupon he entered the government offices,
and drank heartily with Liú Líng."
The Zhúlín Qī Xián Lùn also says:
"Ruǎn Jí and Liú Líng drank together in the Infantry kitchens,
and both died drunk."
This is something said by busybodies.
Ruǎn Jí died during the Jǐngyuán era,
while Liú Líng was still alive during the Tàishǐ era.
Liú Líng often indulged in wine and behaved unrestrainedly.
Sometimes he would take off his clothes and go naked in his house.
When people saw him, they criticized him.
Liú Líng said:
"I take heaven and earth as my house,
and the rooms as my trousers.
Why, gentlemen, do you enter my trousers?"
Dèng Càn's Jìn Jì states:
"A guest came to visit Liú Líng,
and found him naked.
Liú Líng laughed and said:
'I take heaven and earth as my dwelling,
and the house as my trousers.
You gentlemen should not have entered my trousers of your own accord;
why then do you find it offensive?'
He was self-assured to such an extent."
Ruǎn Jí's sister-in-law once returned to her娘家,
and Ruǎn Jí saw her off and bid her farewell.
Some criticized him for this. The Qūlǐ states:
"Brothers and sisters-in-law do not exchange inquiries."
Hence the criticism.
Ruǎn Jí said:
"Are the rites established for people like us?"
There was a neighbor's wife of great beauty near Ruǎn Gōng,
who sold wine at the tavern.
Ruǎn and Wáng Ānfēng often drank with this woman.
When Ruǎn got drunk,
he would sleep beside the woman.
Her husband at first was very suspicious,
but after observing them,
found no other intentions in the end.
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū states:
"There was a young maiden of talent and beauty in Ruǎn Jí's neighborhood,
who died before marrying.
Ruǎn Jí was not related to her,
and had not known her in life.
He went to mourn her,
expressed his utmost grief, and then left.
His broad-mindedness and lack of restraint
were all of this kind."
When Ruǎn Jí was to bury his mother,
he steamed a fat suckling pig,
drank two dǒu of wine,
and then went to bid his final farewell.
He only said, "All is finished!"
He gave one loud cry,
then vomited blood,
and was prostrate and exhausted for a long time.
Dèng Càn's Jìn Jì states:
"When Ruǎn Jí's mother was about to die,
he played weiqi as usual with others.
His opponent asked to stop,
but Ruǎn Jí refused,
insisting on finishing the game.
Afterward, he drank three dǒu of wine,
let out a loud cry,
vomited several shēng of blood,
and was prostrate and exhausted for a long time."
Ruǎn Zhòngróng is Ruǎn Xián.
The Infantry Commandant (Ruǎn Jí) lived south of the road,
while the various Ruǎn clansmen lived north of the road.
The northern Ruǎn were all wealthy,
while the southern Ruǎn were poor.
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
the northern Ruǎn put out their clothes to air in a grand display,
all of them being sheer silks, gauzes, brocades, and damasks.
Zhòngróng used a bamboo pole
to hang a large cloth "calf-nose" loincloth in the central courtyard.
Some people found this strange,
and he replied:
"I am unable to escape convention,
so I am merely following along!"
The "Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove" states:
"All the Ruǎn were Confucian scholars,
skilled in managing their households.
Only the family of Xián esteemed the Way and neglected worldly affairs,
fond of wine and poor.
According to old custom:
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
it was proper to air clothes.
In the courtyards of the various Ruǎn,
brocades and damasks shone brilliantly.
Xián, then still a youth with his hair in tufts,
erected a long pole
and hung a calf-nose loincloth on it."
Ruǎn Infantry Commandant is Ruǎn Jí.
When his mother passed away,
Peì Lìnggōng (Peì Kǎi)
went to offer condolences.
Ruǎn was just then drunk,
with disheveled hair, sitting on his bed,
sprawled with legs apart, not weeping.
When Peì arrived,
he descended from his mat to the ground,
finished weeping and offering condolences,
and then left.
Someone asked Peì:
"Generally, when offering condolences,
the host weeps,
and then the guest performs the rites.
Since Ruǎn did not weep,
why did you, sir, weep?"
Peì said:
"Ruǎn is a man beyond the mundane world,
therefore he does not uphold ritual conventions;
we are people within the mundane world,
therefore we abide by ceremonial rules."
People of the time sighed, considering that both had found their appropriate place.
The "Biographies of Famous Scholars" states:
"When Ruǎn Jí lost a parent,
he did not follow the usual rites.
Peì Kǎi went to offer condolences
and encountered Jí just then drunk,
with disheveled hair, sprawled with legs apart,
as if no one else were present.
Kǎi wept and expressed his grief fully before withdrawing,
showing not the slightest unusual expression.
Such was his ability to accommodate both conformity and nonconformity."
Dài Kuí commented on this, saying:
"As for Peìgōng's offering of condolences,
he wished to transcend the external to protect the internal.
There was in this an expression of understanding,
and a broad-minded defense."
All the Ruǎn could drink wine.
When Zhòngróng went to gather with his clansmen,
they no longer used ordinary cups for pouring,
but instead used a large urn to hold the wine.
Sitting in a circle,
they faced each other and drank heavily.
At that time, a herd of pigs came to drink,
went straight up to it,
and they drank together with them.
When Ruǎn Hún grew up,
his demeanor and bearing resembled his father's,
and he also wished to act with unconventional freedom.
The Infantry Commandant said:
"Zhòngróng has already joined in this;
you may not do so again."
The "Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove" states:
"Jí's restraining of Hún
was likely because Hún did not understand the reason for his own unconventional freedom.
Later, Xián's elder brother's son, Jiǎn,
also considered himself broad-minded and unconventional.
During his father's mourning period, while traveling he encountered heavy snow,
and suffering from cold and freezing, he went to see the Magistrate of Jùnyí.
The magistrate had millet porridge prepared for other guests.
Jiǎn ate it,
and because of this, he was criticized by the pure discourse,
and was dismissed and idle for nearly thirty years.
At that time, although the style of the various worthies of the Bamboo Grove was lofty,
ritual teachings were still strict.
By the Yuánkāng era,
it had reached the point of wantonness and transgression of ritual.
Yuè Guǎng criticized this, saying:
'Within the teaching of names itself there is a place of joy;
why must it come to this?'
Administrator Yuè's words had meaning indeed!
It means that they were not of profound mind,
but merely took advantage of it to indulge themselves wantonly."
Peì Chénggōng's wife
was Wáng Róng's daughter.
Wáng Róng went to their residence in the morning,
and without being announced, went straight in.
Peì came down from the south side of the bed,
and his wife came down from the north side,
facing each other as host and guest,
showing not the slightest unusual expression.
The "Family Biography of the Peì Clan" states:
"Peǐ Wěi married Wáng Róng's eldest daughter."
Ruǎn Zhòngróng had previously been intimate with a Xianbei maidservant at his aunt's home.
When he was in mourning for his mother,
his aunt was about to move far away.
At first she said she would leave the maidservant behind,
but when she departed, she definitely took her along.
Zhòngróng borrowed a guest's donkey, and wearing heavy mourning garments, personally pursued her,
and returned riding together with her.
He said:
"The seed of a man must not be lost!"
This was the mother of Yáojí.
The "Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove" states:
"After Xián pursued the maidservant,
discussions in the world became numerous and varied.
From the end of the Wei dynasty, he sank into obscurity among the lanes and alleys.
It was not until the Xiánníng era of the Jin dynasty
that he began to tread the path of official service."
The "Separate Biography of Ruǎn Fú" states:
"Xián wrote to his aunt, saying:
'The Hu maidservant has given birth to a Hu son.'
His aunt replied in a letter:
'The "Rhapsody on the Hall of Numinous Light of Lǔ" says:
"Hu people gather from afar upon the upper pillars."
He may be styled Yáojí (Gather from Afar).'
Therefore, Fú's style was Yáojí."
After Rèn Kǎi lost his power and influence,
he no longer restrained himself.
Someone said to Hé Qiào:
"Why do you sit by and watch Yuán
póu be ruined without rescuing him?"
Hé said:
"Yuánpóu is like the North Xià Gate;
it is collapsing and about to fall of its own accord;
it is not something a single timber can prop up."
The "Praise of the Various Dukes of Jin" states:
"Kǎi's style was Yuánpóu,
a man of Bóchāng in Lè'ān. He possessed refined discernment and the capacity to manage state affairs.
He oversaw many matters of governance, both great and small.
He was at odds with Jiǎ Chōng.
Chōng then had Kǎi appointed to head the Ministry of Personnel,
and also had the responsible officials impeach Kǎi for using imperial dining vessels.
Kǎi was dismissed from office as a result,
and the affection of Shìzǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Jin) for him consequently waned."
When Liú Dàozhēn was young,
he often fished in the marshes,
and was skilled at singing and whistling.
Those who heard him could not help but linger.
There was an old woman
who recognized that he was no ordinary man,
and greatly delighted in his singing and whistling.
She then killed a piglet and offered it to him.
Dàozhēn ate the entire piglet,
and did not thank her at all.
Seeing he was not full,
the old woman offered another piglet.
He ate half and left half,
and then returned it.
Later, when he became a Vice Director in the Ministry of Personnel,
the old woman's son was a minor clerk.
Dàozhēn promoted and employed him.
Not knowing the reason,
he asked his mother;
his mother told him.
Thereupon, he brought ox meat and wine to visit Dàozhēn.
Dàozhēn said:
"Go away! Go away!
There is no need to repay me further."
Liú Bǎo has already been mentioned.
Ruǎn Xuānzǐ often walked on foot,
hanging a hundred coins on the head of his staff.
When he reached a wine shop,
he would drink alone to his heart's content.
Even those who were noble and powerful in his time
he would not deign to visit.
The "Biographies of Famous Scholars" states:
"Xiū's nature was simple and unrestrained."
Shān Jìlún served as the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and would often go out for unrestrained drinking.
People composed a song about him:
"Lord Shān, whenever he gets drunk,
heads straight for Gāoyáng Pond.
At dusk, he's carried home upside down,
so intoxicated he knows nothing.
Yet he can still mount a fine horse,
wearing his white cap backwards.
Raising his hand, he asks Gé Qiáng,
'How do I compare to a lad from Bīngzhōu?'"
Gāoyáng Pond was located in Xiāngyáng.
Qiáng was his beloved general,
and a native of Bīngzhōu.
The *Records of Xiāngyáng* states:
"During the Hàn, the Palace Attendant Xí Yù, south of Xiàn Mountain,
following Fàn Lǐ's method of fish farming, constructed a fish pond.
Beside the pond was a high embankment,
planted with bamboo and tall catalpa trees.
Lotus and water caltrops covered the water's surface,
making it a famous place for excursions and feasts.
Shān Jiǎn, whenever he visited this pond,
would always return utterly drunk,
saying:
'This is my Gāoyáng Pond!'
The children of Xiāngyáng sang of it."
Zhāng Jìyīng was unrestrained and uninhibited,
and his contemporaries dubbed him 'the Infantry Commander of Jiāngdōng'.
Someone said to him:
"You may indulge your whims for a time,
but do you give no thought to your posthumous reputation?"
He replied:
"If I must have a posthumous reputation,
I'd rather have a single cup of wine right now!"
The *Biographies of Literary Men* states:
"Hàn was self-indulgent and followed his own desires,
seeking nothing from the world of his time.
His contemporaries valued his broad-mindedness and freedom from convention."
Bì Màoshì said:
"With one hand holding a crab claw,
and the other holding a cup of wine,
floating and paddling in a pool of wine—
that would be enough to fulfill a lifetime."
The *Book of the Jin Restoration* states:
"Bì Zhuó, styled Màoshì,
was a man of Xīncài.
In his youth, his proud and unconventional nature was recognized by Húwú Fǔzhī.
Towards the end of the Tàixīng era,
he served as a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel,
but often neglected his duties due to drinking.
When the wine of the Gentleman in the neighboring residence finished fermenting,
Zhuó, being drunk,
went at night to his jars to fetch some to drink.
The master, thinking him a thief,
seized and bound him.
Upon learning he was from the Ministry of Personnel,
he released him.
Zhuó then led the host to feast beside the jars,
drank until drunk, and then left.
Wēn Qiáo had long known and admired Zhuó,
and requested him as his Chief Clerk of Pacifying the South.
He died in that post."
When Minister of Works Hè was traveling to Luòyáng to assume his post,
appointed as a Gentleman of the Heir Apparent's household,
he passed through the Chāng Gate of Wú,
and was playing the qin in his boat.
Zhāng Jìyīng, who did not know him previously,
was at the Jīnchāng Pavilion.
Hearing the clear sound of the strings,
he disembarked and approached Hè,
and they conversed.
Immediately they felt a profound mutual understanding and delight.
He asked Hè, "Where are you bound?"
Hè said, "I am going to Luòyáng to assume my post,
and am just now proceeding on my way."
Zhāng said:
"I also have business in the northern capital."
So, availing himself of the journey, he sought passage,
and set off together with Hè.
He did not inform his family at all,
and they only found out after pursuing and inquiring.
When General of Chariots and Cavalry Zǔ crossed the river,
both public and private resources were scarce and meager,
and there were no fine garments or curios.
Wáng, Yǔ, and the other gentlemen once went together to visit Zǔ,
when suddenly they saw piled fur robes,
and precious ornaments filling the display.
The gentlemen wondered and asked about it.
Zǔ said:
"Last night I made another trip to Nántáng."
At that time, Zǔ often personally sent his strong men to openly plunder and seize goods.
Those in charge of affairs
also tolerated it and did not question him.
The *Jin Autumn Annals* states:
"Zǔ Tì was by nature resourceful and adaptable,
and not constrained by minor proprieties.
Moreover, his retainers and followers were mostly fierce and cunning warriors,
whom Tì treated all like sons and younger brothers.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
refugees numbered in the tens of thousands,
and the Yáng region suffered a great famine.
His guests and followers would attack and plunder,
and Tì would always protect and fully defend them.
Commentators because of this thought little of him,
so for a long time he was not transferred to another post."
The Minister of Ceremonies Kǒng Qún was fond of drinking.
Chancellor Wáng said to him:
"Why do you constantly drink?
Do you not see the cloth covering the wine jars at the tavern,
rotting away day by day?"
Qún said:
"Not so.
Do you not see meat pickled in wine lees—
it actually keeps longer."
Qún once wrote to relatives and old friends:
"This year the fields yielded seven hundred hú of glutinous millet,
but it's still not enough for the business of brewing."
Qún has been mentioned above.
Someone criticized Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Zhōu:
"In conversation and jesting with relatives and friends,
he is vulgar, crude, and without restraint."
Dèng Càn's *Jin Annals* states:
"Wáng Dǎo, Zhōu Yǐ, and court officials
went to the Minister of Personnel Jì Zhān to watch performers.
Zhān had a beloved concubine
who could sing new tunes.
Yǐ, in front of the crowd, wanted to have relations with his concubine,
exposing his ugly and vulgar nature,
yet his face showed no shame.
The responsible officials petitioned to have Yǐ dismissed from office,
but an imperial edict specially pardoned him."
Zhōu said:
"If I am like the ten-thousand *li* Long River,
how can it not have a single bend over a thousand *li*?"
When Wēn Tàizhēn's rank was not yet high,
he often gambled at *chūpú* with merchants from Yángzhōu and the Huái region,
and whenever he played, he did not win.
Once, after a round,
he lost a great deal of goods.
The game ended,
and he had no means to return.
Being on good terms with Yǔ Liàng,
he shouted loudly from the boat to Liàng:
"You must ransom me!"
Yǔ immediately sent the payment,
and only then could he return.
This sort of thing happened several times.
The *Book of the Restoration* states:
"Qiáo had a reputation for being outstanding and bright,
but was not constrained by minor matters of conduct."
Lord Wēn was fond of casual, irreverent talk,
while Commandant Biàn upheld ritual and law as his personal standard.
The *Separate Biography of Biàn Kǔn* states:
"Kǔn maintained a stern demeanor at court,
and all officials strictly feared him.
The sons of noble families
all behaved with reverence and solemnity."
When they were at Lord Yǔ's place,
they fiercely attacked and criticized each other.
Wēn's speech was vulgar and foul.
Lord Yǔ said calmly:
"Tàizhēn, throughout the entire day, has not uttered a single vulgar word."
He valued his broad-mindedness.
Zhōu Bórén's demeanor and virtue were refined and weighty,
and he deeply understood peril and disorder.
After crossing the river for many years,
he constantly drank heavily.
Once he remained drunk for three days without sobering up.
His contemporaries called him 'the Three-Day Vice Director'.
The *Jin Autumn Annals* states:
"Initially, Yǐ, with his refined reputation,
gained great fame throughout the land.
Later, he repeatedly erred due to wine.
Yǔ Liàng said:
'In his later years, Marquis Zhōu
could be said to exemplify the decline of the phoenix's virtue.'"
The *Forest of Conversations* states:
"Bórén was precisely in mourning for his elder sister—
three days drunk; for his aunt's mourning—
two days drunk.
This greatly damaged his standing and reputation.
Whenever he was drunk,
the various gentlemen would often gather to guard him."
Wèi Jūncháng served as Chief Clerk to Lord Wēn,
and Lord Wēn thought very highly of him.
Often, on impulse, Wēn would take wine and dried meat to Wèi's place,
and they would sit with legs sprawled out, facing each other for the whole day.
When Wèi went to Wēn's place, it was also like this.
Wèi Yǒng has been mentioned previously.
During Sū Jùn's rebellion,
the members of the Yǔ family fled and scattered.
Yǔ Bīng was then the governor of Wú Commandery,
and he fled alone,
with all the commoners and officials having deserted him.
Only a commandery soldier alone used a small boat to carry Yǔ Bīng out of the Qiántáng estuary,
covering him with a reed mat.
At that time, Sū Jùn had offered a reward to search for Yǔ Bīng,
and ordered all areas to conduct very urgent searches and inspections.
The soldier left the boat at a market islet,
and, having drunk until intoxicated, returned,
waving his oar towards the boat and saying:
"Where to look for Governor Yǔ of Wú?
He's right here in this one!"
Yǔ Bīng was greatly terrified,
but dared not move.
The supervising officers saw the boat was small and cramped,
and thought the soldier was wildly drunk,
so they did not suspect anything further.
He himself escorted him across the Zhè River,
and placed him with the Wèi family in Shānyīn, where he escaped harm.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Yǔ Bīng was governor of Wú Commandery.
When Sū Jùn rebelled,
he sent troops to attack Yǔ Bīng,
and Yǔ Bīng abandoned the commandery and fled to Kuàijī."
Later, when the affair was settled,
Yǔ Bīng wanted to repay the soldier,
granting him whatever he desired.
The soldier said:
"I come from a menial background,
and do not desire rank and honors.
From youth I suffered from menial service,
and have always worried about not being able to drink to my heart's content.
If I can have enough wine to last me the rest of my years, that will be the end of it,
and I require nothing more."
Yǔ Bīng built a large house for him,
bought male and female servants,
and ensured that within his gates there were a hundred *hú* of wine,
for the rest of his life.
People of the time said this soldier not only had wisdom,
but was also a man of enlightened understanding.
Yīn Hóngqiáo was appointed as governor of Yùzhāng Commandery.
The *Yīn Shì Pǔ* says:
"Yìn Xiàn, styled Hóngqiáo,
was a man of Chén Commandery.
His father was Yìn Shí,
a Sima of the Eastern Garrison.
Yìn Xiàn's official career reached the post of Governor of Yùzhāng." When he was about to leave,
people from the capital entrusted him with about a hundred letters.
When he reached Shítóu,
he threw them all into the water,
and then prayed, saying:
"Let those that sink sink by themselves,
and those that float float by themselves.
Yīn Hóngqiáo cannot
act as a mail carrier."
Chief Clerk Wáng and Xiè Rénzǔ both served as aides to Lord Wáng.
The *Wáng Méng Biézhuàn* says:
"Chancellor Wáng Dǎo recruited famous scholars and worthies of the time,
to assist in the restoration.
Wherever his summons and appointments were directed,
he invariably sought out the talented and outstanding,
and recruited Wáng Méng as an aide."
Chief Clerk [Wáng] said:
"Aide Xiè can perform an unusual dance."
Xiè then rose and danced,
his spirit and expression very relaxed.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Xiè Shàng was by nature open and unrestrained,
and skilled in music."
The *Yǔlín* says:
"After drinking, Xiè Zhènxī,
among the trays and tables,
performed the 'Mynah Dance' of the marketplace entertainers of Luòyáng,
and it was excellent."
Lord Wáng looked at him intently,
and said to the guests:
"He makes one think of Ānfēng."
Wáng Róng was by nature open and unrestrained,
and Xiè Shàng resembled him.
Wáng [Méng] and
Liǔ [Dàn] were together south of the Háng [River],
feasting merrily at Huán Zǐyě's home.
Huán Yǐ has been mentioned previously.
Xiè Zhènxī was returning from visiting the tomb of the Minister,
the 'returning wail' three days after the burial.
The others wanted to invite him,
and first sent a messenger,
but he still did not agree,
though he had already stopped his carriage.
When they pressed the invitation again,
he turned his carriage around.
The others welcomed him outside the gate,
and taking him by the arm, he alighted immediately,
only having time to remove his headcloth and put on a cap.
Halfway through the merry feast,
he then realized he had not removed his mourning garments.
The Minister was
Xiè Póu,
Xiè Shàng's uncle.
He has been mentioned previously.
Sòng Míngdì's *Wénzhāng Zhì* says:
"Xiè Shàng was by nature frivolous and impetuous,
not constrained by minor details of conduct.
After his elder brother's burial,
while returning from the tomb,
Wáng Méng and Liǔ Dàn were together traveling at Xīntíng.
Wáng Méng wanted to summon Xiè Shàng,
and first asked Liǔ Dàn, saying:
'I reckon Rénzǔ probably won't object.'
Liǔ Dàn said:
'From Rénzǔ's temperament, he should naturally come.'
They then sent to invite him.
Xiè Shàng initially declined,
but already had no intention of returning home.
When they requested again,
he immediately turned his carriage around.
Such was his uninhibited nature."
When Huán Xuānwǔ was young, his family was poor.
He gambled and lost heavily,
and the creditors pressed their demands very urgently.
He thought of ways to extricate himself,
but did not know what to do.
Yuán Dān of Chén Commandery
was outstandingly talented and capable in many ways.
The *Yuánshì Jiāzhuàn* says:
"Yuán Dān, styled Yàndào,
was a man of Yángxià in Chén Commandery,
the great-grandson of Yuán Huàn, a Gentleman of the Interior in the Wèi dynasty.
He was stalwart and forthright,
lofty in spirit and outstandingly talented,
unconventional and unrestrained from youth,
possessing extraordinary ability,
and many scholars attached themselves to him.
His official career reached the post of Gentleman of the Masters of Writing in the Ministry of Works."
Huán Xuānwǔ wanted to seek help from Yuán Dān.
Yuán Dān was then in mourning,
and [Huán] feared causing suspicion,
so he tentatively told him about it.
[Yuán Dān] agreed immediately upon hearing,
without the slightest hesitation or reluctance.
He then changed clothes, tucked a cloth cap inside his garments, and went with Wēn [Huán Wēn].
to gamble with the creditor.
Yuán Dān had always had a reputation for skill [in gambling].
The creditor approached the gaming board and said:
"You surely aren't capable of being Yuán Yàndào, are you?"
They then gambled together.
They bet a hundred thousand at a throw,
straight up to several million.
[Yuán Dān] threw down his chips and shouted loudly,
as if no one else was around,
took out the cloth cap and threw it at his opponent, saying:
"Do you finally recognize Yuán Yàndao or not?"
The *Guōzǐ* says:
"Lord Huán was playing *chūpú* [a gambling game]
and lost several hundred *hú* of rice,
and sought help from Yuán Dān.
Yuán Dān was in mourning,
but immediately said:
'Excellent.
I will certainly get the winning throws,
you just shout loudly.'
He then removed his mourning garments,
and they went out the door together.
Noticing he still had a mourning cloth cap on his head,
he threw it off and put on a small cap.
Once they began to gamble,
Yuán's manner was loud and unrestrained,
his throws invariably being the best combinations,
and the two of them shouted together,
causing the opponent to lose several million in a moment."
Guānglù [Minister of the Imperial Stud] Wáng said:
"Wine precisely causes each person to become detached from himself."
Guānglù was
Wáng Yùn.
The *Xù Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Wáng Yùn had always been fond of wine,
and in his later years especially so.
When he was in Kuàijī,
there were very few days when he was slightly sober."
Governor Liǔ said:
"Sūn Chénggōng is a wild eccentric.
Whenever he goes to a place,
he enjoys and savors it for days on end,
or sometimes turns back when halfway on the return journey."
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Sūn Chénggōng was unconventional and unrestrained from youth,
and his home was in Kuàijī.
He was by nature fond of mountains and rivers.
When he sought appointment as magistrate of Yín County,
he neglected petty affairs,
and gave free rein to his inclination to wander and roam,
visiting all the famous hills and scenic rivers,
without exception."
Yuán Yàndào had two younger sisters:
one married to Yīn Yuānyuán,
the other married to Xiè Rénzǔ.
The Yuán Family Genealogy states:
"Dān's elder sister was named Nǚhuáng,
married to Yīn Hào.
The younger sister was named Nǚzhèng,
married to Xiè Shàng."
He said to Huán Xuānwǔ:
"What a pity I don't have another sister to match with you."
When Huán Chēqí was in Jīngzhōu,
Zhāng Xuán served as Shìzhōng,
and was sent to Jiānglíng.
On the way, he passed by Yángqí Village, which
bordered the river,
about two hundred lǐ from Jīngzhōu.
Suddenly he saw a man,
holding half a small basket of live fish,
who came straight to the boat and said:
"I have fish,
and wish to have them sliced into sashimi."
Zhāng then moored the boat and let him aboard.
He asked his name,
and the man said he was Liú Yímín.
The Zhōngxīng Shū states:
"Liú Línzhī,
also known as Yímín."
Already mentioned.
Zhāng had long heard of his name,
and treated him with great delight.
Liú, knowing that Zhāng was on an official mission,
asked: "Are Xiè Ān and Wáng Wéndù both well?"
Zhāng very much wanted to converse,
but Liú showed no intention of staying.
After the sashimi was prepared,
he left immediately,
saying: "I just caught these fish,
and seeing that your boat likely had sashimi utensils,
that's why I came."
With that, he departed.
Zhāng then followed him to Liú's home,
where Liú served wine,
which was not particularly clear or fine.
Zhāng, admiring the man,
had no choice but to drink it.
As they were drinking together,
Liú rose first,
saying: "Now is the time to harvest reeds,
I shouldn't linger too long."
Zhāng had no way to detain him.
Wáng Zǐyóu visited Xī Yōngzhōu.
The Zhōngxīng Shū states:
"Xī Huī, styled Dàoyìn,
was from Gāopíng.
His father, Xī Tán,
served as Northern Central General.
Huī was eight chǐ tall,
with a handsome beard,
and a majestic demeanor.
Emperor Lièzōng valued him,
considering him a pillar of the frontier.
From the position of Crown Prince Left Commander,
he was promoted to Governor of Yōngzhōu."
Yōngzhōu was inside,
and seeing a fine woolen carpet, he said:
"How did Āqǐ get this thing?"
Āqǐ was
Huī's childhood name. He ordered his attendants to send it back home.
Xī went out to look for it,
and Wáng said:
"Just now, a man of great strength carried it away."
The Zhuāngzǐ states:
"To hide a boat in a ravine,
or a mountain in a marsh,
is considered secure.
Yet a man of great strength may carry them away,
and the ignorant would not know."
Xī showed no sign of displeasure.
When Xiè Ān first went west for amusement,
he lost his carriage and ox,
so he walked back with a cane.
On the way, he met Prefect Liú,
who said:
"Ānshí, are you unharmed?"
Xiè then rode back with him in his carriage.
Luó Yǒu of Xiāngyáng had great charm,
but in his youth, many considered him foolish.
Once, he waited for people performing ancestral sacrifices,
hoping to beg for food.
He arrived too early,
and the gate was not yet open.
The host came out to greet the spirits and saw him,
asking why he was there at such an untimely hour.
He replied:
"I heard you were performing sacrifices,
and wanted to beg for a meal."
Then he hid by the side of the gate.
At dawn,
after getting food, he left,
showing no sign of shame.
He had a remarkable memory.
When following Huán Xuānwǔ to pacify Shǔ,
he inspected the city walls, towers, and palaces of Shǔ,
noting the width and narrowness of the roads inside and outside,
and the number of fruit trees and bamboos planted,
all of which he memorized silently.
Later, when Huán Xuānwǔ gathered with Jiǎnwén at Piāozhōu,
Yǒu also attended.
When discussing matters of Shǔ,
some details were forgotten,
but Yǒu listed them all,
without any mistakes or omissions.
Huán Xuānwǔ checked with the Shǔ city records,
and everything matched Yǒu's account.
Those present sighed in admiration.
Xiè Ān said:
"How is Luó Yǒu inferior to Wèi Yángyuán!"
Later, he became Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
When about to assume his post,
Governor Huán Huò invited him to stay overnight.
He replied:
"I already have a prior engagement.
The host is poor,
and there may be expenses for wine and food.
Since we are old acquaintances,
I ask to comply on another day."
Zhēngxī secretly sent someone to observe him.
In the evening,
he went to the home of a clerk under the Governor of Jīngzhōu,
where he stayed contentedly,
no different than with distinguished guests.
In Yìzhōu, he told his son:
"I have dining utensils for five hundred people."
His family was greatly surprised.
He had always been poor,
yet suddenly had such items—
they were surely two hundred and fifty sets of black lacquered trays.
The Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Yǒu, styled Zháirén,
was from Xiāngyáng.
In his youth, he loved learning,
but did not uphold proper conduct.
He had a fondness for wine,
and wherever he went,
he did not distinguish between scholars and commoners.
He also liked to wait for people performing sacrifices,
going to beg for leftover food.
Even in markets and shops,
he felt no shame.
Huán Wēn often reproached him, saying:
'You are too improper!
If you need food,
why not come to me to ask?
Why go to such lengths!'
Yǒu replied arrogantly and disdainfully:
'If I beg from you today,
I may get food,
but tomorrow there will be none again.'
Huán laughed heartily at him.
He first served in Jīngzhōu,
later in Huán's office.
Due to his family's poverty, he sought an official salary.
Although Huán treated him with respect for his talent and learning,
he considered him unrestrained and unconventional,
unfit for governing the people,
so he promised but did not employ him.
Later, when a colleague in the same office obtained a commandery post,
Huán held a farewell banquet.
Yǒu arrived especially late.
When asked why,
Yǒu replied:
'I have a fondness for drinking and fine flavors.
Yesterday, following your instructions,
I set out early in the morning,
but on the way, I met a ghost,
who greatly mocked me, saying:
"I only see you sending others to become governors,
why don't I see anyone sending you to become a governor?"
At first, I was frightened, then ashamed,
so I turned back to resolve this,
and unknowingly incurred the fault of delay.'
Although Huán laughed at his wit,
he felt somewhat ashamed in his heart.
Later, he appointed him as Governor of Xiāngyáng,
and he was successively promoted to Governor of Guǎngzhōu and
Yìzhōu.
In his administration, he focused on the broader principles,
not bothering with minor details,
and was greatly appreciated by officials and people alike.
He died in Yìzhōu."
Whenever Huán Zǐyě heard a clear song,
he would exclaim, "Alas!"
Xiè Ān, hearing of this, said:
"Zǐyě can be said to be deeply devoted in a single moment."
The boat moored at Dízhǔ.
Wáng Dà, after taking the powdered medicine, was already slightly drunk,
and went to visit Huán.
Huán prepared wine for him,
but he could not drink it cold,
and repeatedly said to his attendants:
"Bring warm wine!"
Huán then shed tears and sobbed.
Wáng wanted to leave.
Huán covered his tears with a handkerchief
and said to Wáng:
"You have violated my family taboo,
but what does that have to do with you?"
The Records of Emperor Ān of Jìn states:
"Xuán's sorrows and joys surpassed others;
every time joy or grief arose,
it always led to sobbing."
Wáng sighed and said:
"Língbǎo is indeed open-minded."
Língbǎo was Xuán's childhood name.
The Garden of Marvels states:
"When Xuán was born, light illuminated the room.
A skilled diviner said:
'This child is born with a wondrous radiance;
he should be named Tiānrén.'
Xuānwǔ disliked that it had three characters,
so he proposed 'Shén Língbǎo',
which still used three.
Since it was difficult to repeat the earlier name,
he removed the character 'Shén',
and named him 'Língbǎo'."
The Forest of Conversations states:
"Xuán did not observe death anniversaries by the day,
but only by the hour.
His open-mindedness and lack of restraint
were all of this kind."
Wáng Xiàobó asked Wáng Dà:
"How does Ruǎn Jí compare to Sīmǎ Xiàngrú?"
Wáng Dà said:
"Ruǎn Jí had pent-up frustrations in his heart,
so he needed wine to wash them away."
This means Ruǎn was similar to Xiàngrú,
but differed in his drinking.
Wáng Fódà sighed and said:
"If I don't drink wine for three days,
I feel my body and spirit are no longer in harmony."
The Records of Emperor Ān of Jìn states:
"Chén admired open-mindedness from a young age,
loved wine,
and in Jīngzhōu this grew even more intense.
He would sometimes drink for days without sobering up,
and eventually died from it."
Sòng Míngdì's Record of Literary Works states:
"Chén was addicted to wine;
when drunk, he would often spend the whole day in that state.
He called himself 'Shàngdùn'.
The saying that heavy drinking is called
'Shàngdùn'
originated from Chén."
Wáng Xiàobó said:
"A famous scholar does not necessarily need extraordinary talent.
As long as one can often be free from affairs,
drink wine heartily,
and read the 'Lísāo' thoroughly,
one can be called a famous scholar."
Chief Secretary Wáng ascended Máo Mountain
and wept bitterly, saying:
"Lángyá's Wáng Bóyú
will ultimately die for sentiment."
The Wáng Clan Genealogy states:
"Xīn, styled Bóyú,
was from Lángyá.
His father was Huì,
a general of the guard.
Xīn served as chief secretary to the minister of education."
Zhōu Zhī's Records of Lóng'ān states:
"Initially,
Wáng Gōng was about to raise a righteous army,
and sent messengers to the Three Wú regions.
Xīn was in mourning,
but was appointed as the internal historian of Wú.
After Guóbǎo died,
Gōng disbanded the troops
and ordered Xīn to return to mourning attire.
Xīn was greatly angered
and that very day occupied the capital of Wú to rebel.
Gōng sent Marshal Liú Láozhī to suppress Xīn.
Xīn was defeated
and his whereabouts became unknown."
...BG. his ability would be no less than that of ān ù"
King Wén of Jìn had immense merit and virtue,
and in his seat, he was solemn and revered,
comparable to a king.
The Spring and Autumn Annals of Hàn and Jìn states:
"When King Wén was promoted to king,
Minister of Education Hé Zēng and the court officials all observed full etiquette,
only Wáng Xiáng bowed with hands clasped without prostrating."
Only Ruǎn Jí was present,
sitting with legs sprawled, whistling and singing,
drunk and unrestrained, completely at ease.
Wáng Róng, at the age of twenty, visited Ruǎn Jí,
while Liú Gōngróng was present.
Ruǎn said to Wáng:
"I happen to have two dǒu of fine wine,
which I should share with you.
As for that Gōngróng,
he has no part in it."
The two exchanged cups and drank toasts, so Gōngróng did not get a single
cup.
Yet in conversation and banter,
the three were no different.
Someone asked Ruǎn about this,
and he replied:
"Those superior to Gōngróng
must be given wine to drink;
those inferior to Gōngróng
must not be denied wine;
only Gōngróng
may be denied wine."
The Autumn of Jìn states:
"Róng was fifteen years old
when he followed his father Hún to the official residence.
Ruǎn Jí saw him and took a liking to him.
Every time Ruǎn visited Hún briefly,
he would spend a long time in Róng's room.
He then said to Hún:
'Jùnchōng is pure and noble,
not of your kind.'"
Róng once visited Ruǎn Jí to drink together,
while Liú Chǎng was present but not included.
Chǎng showed no resentment.
Later, Róng asked Ruǎn Jí:
"Who is that person?"
Ruǎn replied:
"That is Liú Gōngróng."
Jùnchōng said:
"Those superior to Gōngróng
must be given wine;
those inferior to Gōngróng
must not be denied wine;
only Gōngróng
may be denied wine."
The Discourse on the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove states:
"Initially,
Ruǎn Jí and Róng's father Hún were both secretaries in the ministry.
Every time Ruǎn visited Hún,
before even sitting down,
he would say:
'Talking with you
is not as good as talking with Ā Róng.'
He would go to Róng
and stay until evening before returning.
Ruǎn Jí was twenty years older than Róng,
but they got along like peers.
Liú Gōngróng was a learned man,
especially fond of wine.
Ruǎn Jí and Róng exchanged toasts all day,
yet Gōngróng did not receive a single cup.
All three were content.
Róng was often praised in public discourse,
and this was typical of him."
Zhōng Shìjì was exceptionally talented and astute,
but initially did not know Jī Kāng.
Zhōng invited the worthy and outstanding scholars of the time,
and together they went to visit Kāng.
Kāng was at that moment forging under a large tree,
with Xiàng Zǐqī assisting by working the bellows.
Kāng continued swinging his hammer without pause,
acting as if no one else was around,
and for a long while did not exchange a single word.
Zhōng rose to leave,
and Kāng said:
"What did you hear that brought you here?
What did you see that makes you leave?"
Zhōng replied:
"I heard what I heard and came,
I saw what I saw and leave."
The *Wénshì Zhuàn* states:
"Kāng was extremely skillful by nature,
able to forge iron.
His home had a flourishing willow tree,
and he channeled water around it,
making it very cool and refreshing in summer.
He often stayed beneath it, proudly amusing himself,
and personally did the forging.
Although his family was poor,
when people came to have items forged,
Kāng would not accept payment.
Only when close friends or relatives came with chicken and wine to drink and eat together,
would he engage in pure conversation."
The *Wèishì Chūnqiū* states:
"Zhōng Huì was favored by the Dàjiāngjūn and his brothers,
and hearing of Kāng's fame, he went to visit him.
Huì was a famous noble scion,
esteemed and favored for his talent and ability,
riding fat horses and wearing light silks,
with a retinue of guests like clouds.
Kāng was sitting with legs sprawled, forging,
and when Huì arrived, he did not show him the proper courtesy.
Huì deeply resented this.
Later, because of the affair with Lǚ Ān,
he slandered Kāng."
Jī Kāng was on good terms with Lǚ Ān.
Whenever one missed the other,
they would order a carriage to travel a thousand *lǐ*.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Ān's courtesy name was Zhōngtì,
a man of Dōngpíng,
the second son of Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāo.
His aspirations and capacity were broad and open,
possessing a demeanor that transcended the vulgar."
Gān Bǎo's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Initially,
when Ān befriended Kāng,
if one missed the other, he would forthrightly order a carriage."
Ān came later,
and finding Kāng not at home,
Jī Xǐ came out the door to invite him in,
but Ān did not enter.
The *Jìn Bǎiguān Míng* states:
"Jī Xǐ's courtesy name was Gōngmù,
he served as Yángzhōu Cìshǐ,
and was Kāng's elder brother.
When Ruǎn Jí was in mourning,
Xǐ went to offer condolences.
Jí could make 'green eyes' and 'white eyes'.
When he saw ordinary, vulgar scholars,
he would face them with white eyes.
When Xǐ went,
Jí did not weep,
and upon seeing him, gave him the white eyes.
Xǐ, displeased, withdrew.
When Kāng heard of this,
he brought wine and, carrying his qin, went to visit Jí,
and thereafter they became close friends."
Gān Bǎo's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Ān once followed Kāng,
and sometimes when they were out,
Kāng's elder brother Xǐ would wipe the mat and wait for him,
but Ān paid no heed,
sitting alone in the carriage.
Kāng's mother then set out wine and food,
and sought to have Kāng's children converse and play with him.
After a long while, he left.
Such was his disregard for the esteemed."
He wrote on the gate
the character "fèng"
and left.
Xǐ did not realize,
and still thought it was complimentary,
hence he displayed it.
The character "fèng"
is composed of '凡' (fán) and '鸟' (niǎo) — an ordinary bird.
Xǔ Shèn's *Shuōwén* states:
"The fèng,
is a divine bird,
its radical is '鸟' (bird),
with '凡' (fán) indicating its sound."
When Lù Shìhéng first entered Luòyáng,
he consulted Zhāng Gōng about whom he should visit;
Liú Dàozhēn was one of them.
Lù went to visit,
but Liú was still in the mourning period.
He was fond of drink by nature.
After the formalities,
initially he said nothing else,
only asking:
"In Eastern Wú, there are long-handled gourds,
did you bring any seeds?"
The Lù brothers were greatly disappointed,
and regretted having gone.
Wáng Píngzǐ was appointed to Jīngzhōu.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"During Emperor Huì's time,
Tàiwèi Wáng Yífǔ spoke to the selection officials,
having his younger brother Chéng appointed as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and his cousin Dūn as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Chéng and Dūn both went to bid farewell to the Tàiwèi.
The Tàiwèi said to them:
'Now the royal house is declining,
therefore I have you brothers stationed in the Qí and
Chǔ regions.
Externally, you can establish hegemonic enterprises;
internally, you can sufficiently support the imperial house.
This is what I hope for from you two brothers!'"
Tàiwèi Wáng and the worthy men of the time seeing him off filled the road.
At that time, there was a large tree in the courtyard,
with a magpie's nest in it.
Píngzǐ took off his outer garment and headcloth,
and directly climbed the tree to get the magpie chicks.
His undergarment got caught on the tree branches,
so he took it off as well.
Having gotten the magpie chicks, he came back down,
played with them,
his expression calm and natural,
as if no one else was around.
Dèng Càn's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Chéng was unrestrained and uninhibited,
contemporaries called him 'unconstrained'."
The Dàorén Gāozuò, while at Chéngxiàng's place,
would often recline at his side.
Upon seeing Biàn Lìng,
he solemnly changed his demeanor, saying:
"He is a man of ritual and law."
The *Gāozuò Zhuàn* states:
"Wáng Gōng once visited the Heshang,
the Heshang loosened his belt and reclined,
conversing with profound understanding.
Upon seeing Shàngshū Lìng Biàn Wàngzhī,
he immediately straightened his collar and composed his demeanor.
People of the time sighed that each was in his proper place."
When Huán Xuānwǔ governed Xúzhōu,
at that time Xiè Yì was in Jìnlíng.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Yì, from the position of Lìbù Láng,
was sent out to be Tàishǒu of Jìnlíng."
Initially, they had a brief, superficial acquaintance,
and there was nothing unusual.
When Huán was transferred to Jīngzhōu,
just before heading west,
his attitude became very earnest,
but Yì did not suspect anything.
Only Xiè Hǔzǐ's wife, Wáng, understood his intent.
Hǔzǐ
was the infant name of Xiè Jù,
Yì's younger brother.
His wife, née Wáng,
has been mentioned before.
She often said:
"The intent of Huán of Jīngzhōu is very unusual,
he will surely take the man of Jìnlíng west with him!"
Soon after, he recruited Yì as his Sīmǎ.
After Yì took up the post,
he still maintained the rapport of a commoner friendship.
When in Wēn's presence,
he would push up his headcloth and whistle or chant poems,
no different from usual days.
Xuānwǔ often said:
"He is my 'otherworldly Sīmǎ'."
Then, because of drink,
he gradually abandoned all daily礼节.
When Huán went inside his residence,
Yì would follow him in.
Later, when Yì was drunk,
Wēn went to his wife's place to avoid him.
The lady said:
"If you didn't have this wild Sīmǎ,
how would I get to see you?"
Xiè Wàn, in front of his elder brother,
wanted to get up and ask for a chamber pot.
At that time, Ruǎn Sīkuàng was present and said:
"A newly risen household,
simple but lacking in propriety."
Xiè Wàn, the Director of the Central Bureau, was the son-in-law of Wáng Lántián (Wáng Shù).
The Xiè Family Genealogy states:
"Wàn married the daughter of Wáng Shù of Tàiyuán,
named Quán."
He once wore a white silk headscarf,
and was carried in a sedan chair directly to the main hall of the Yángzhōu office to see Wáng.
He said bluntly:
"People say you, Lord, are foolish;
you, Lord, truly are foolish."
Lántián replied:
"It's not that there is no such talk,
it's just that I achieved fame late."
The Separate Biography of Wáng Shù states:
"In his youth, Shù was genuinely solitary, retiring, and quiet;
people did not yet know of him,
hence the saying about achieving fame late."
Wáng Zǐyóu served as Cavalry Adjutant to Cavalry General Huán.
Huán asked him:
"Which office are you in?"
He replied:
"I don't know which office.
From time to time I see horses being led in,
so it seems to be the Horse Department."
The Book of the Restoration states:
"Huán Chōng appointed Huīzhī (Wáng Zǐyóu) as Adjutant.
He went about with disheveled hair and loose sash,
and did not attend to the affairs of the office."
Huán also asked:
"How many horses does your office have?"
He replied:
"If one does not ask about the horses,
how can one know their number?"
The Analects says:
"When the stables burned,
Confucius, returning from court, asked:
'Was anyone hurt?'
He did not ask about the horses."
Commentary:
"He valued people and despised animals,
therefore he did not ask."
Huán asked again:
"How many horses have died recently?"
He replied:
"If one does not yet understand life,
how can one understand death?"
The Analects says:
"Zǐlù asked about death.
Confucius said:
'If you do not yet understand life,
how can you understand death?'"
Mǎ Róng's Commentary states:
"Matters of death are difficult to clarify;
speaking of them is of no benefit,
therefore he did not answer."
Xiè Ān once traveled west together with Xiè Wàn,
passing through Wú Commandery.
Āwàn wanted them to go together and gather at Wáng Tián's place.
Tián has been mentioned previously.
At that time he was the Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery.
The Grand Tutor (Xiè Ān) said:
"I'm afraid he may not necessarily entertain you;
it's probably not worth it!"
Wàn still insisted strenuously,
but the Grand Tutor firmly would not change his mind.
Wàn then went alone.
After sitting for a short while,
Wáng Tián went inside the inner door.
Xiè Wàn looked very pleased,
thinking he would be treated generously.
After a long time,
Tián finally came out, having just washed his hair and left it loose.
He did not sit down either,
but instead leaned on a folding chair,
drying his hair in the central courtyard,
his manner proud and aloof,
showing absolutely no intention of engaging in conversation.
Xiè Wàn then returned.
Before reaching the boat,
he called out ahead to the Grand Tutor.
Ān said:
"Āchī didn't put on an act, did he!"
Wáng Tián's
childhood name was Chīhǔ.
Wáng Zǐyóu served as Adjutant to Cavalry General Huán.
Huán said to Wáng:
"You have been in the office for a long time;
it's time I should arrange some duties for you."
At first he did not reply,
but simply gazed into the distance,
resting his cheek on his official tablet and saying:
"The morning breeze from the Western Hills
brings such refreshing air."
When Xiè Wàn went on the northern campaign,
he always considered himself superior through whistling and chanting poetry,
and never comforted or encouraged the troops.
Xiè Ān thought very highly of and loved Wàn,
but recognizing that he would certainly fail,
he accompanied him on the campaign.
Casually, he said to Wàn:
"You are the commander-in-chief;
you should frequently summon the various generals to banquets,
to please the hearts of the men."
Wàn followed his advice.
He then summoned the various generals,
but had nothing to say to them.
He simply pointed his ruyi scepter around at those seated on all sides and said:
"You gentlemen are all stalwart soldiers."
The generals were extremely resentful and angry about this.
Xiè Ān, wishing to deeply establish kindness and trust,
personally visited everyone from the squad leaders and generals on down,
without exception,
humbly apologizing and expressing regret.
When Wàn's campaign failed,
the army wanted to get rid of him because of it.
But they also said:
"We must consider Xiè Ān."
Thus Wàn fortunately escaped harm.
The account of Wàn's defeat is recorded above.
Wáng Zǐjìng and his brothers went to see their uncle, Lord Xī,
wearing slippers to pay their respects,
observing the formalities due to a maternal uncle with great care.
After Jiābīn (Xī Chāo) died,
they all wore high clogs,
their demeanor casual and disrespectful.
When invited to sit,
they all said
"We have matters to attend to,
no time to sit."
After they had left,
Lord Xī said with emotion:
"If Jiābīn were still alive,
would these rodents dare act like this!"
Xī Yīn's son, Chāo,
enjoyed great fame,
and moreover received favor from Huán Wēn,
so they showed respect to Yīn for Chāo's sake.
Wáng Zǐyóu once was traveling through Wúzhōng,
and saw a gentleman's home
that had extremely fine bamboo.
The host already knew that Zǐyóu would be coming,
so he swept and cleaned, made preparations,
and sat waiting in the main hall.
Wáng, in his sedan chair, went directly to the bamboo grove,
and chanted and whistled for a long time.
The host was already disappointed,
but still hoped he would come and communicate upon returning.
Instead, Wáng simply wanted to go straight out the gate.
The host could not bear it any longer,
so he ordered his attendants to close the gate and not let him out.
Wáng, because of this, appreciated the host all the more,
so he stayed and sat down,
and they enjoyed themselves fully before he left.
Wáng Zǐjìng, traveling from Kuàijī through Wú,
heard that Gù Pìjiāng The Gù Family Genealogy states:
"Pìjiāng
was a man of Wú Commandery.
He served successively as Commandery Merit Officer,
and Pingbei Adjutant."
had a famous garden.
Not knowing the host beforehand,
he went directly to his home.
It happened that Gù was just gathering guests and friends for a lively feast.
But after Wáng had finished touring the garden,
he pointed out what was good and bad,
acting as if no one else was around.
Gù, bursting with anger and unable to bear it, said:
"To be arrogant toward your host
is discourteous;
to act proud because of your high status
is unprincipled.
Lacking these two qualities,
you are not worth mentioning—
merely a boor!"
He then drove Wáng's attendants out the gate.
Wáng remained alone in his sedan chair,
turning his head to look around.
After his attendants did not come for a long time,
he then had them sent outside the gate,
perfectly at ease and unconcerned.
When Zhūgě Jǐn was Governor of Yùzhōu,
he sent his Assistant Inspector to the capital,
and Jǐn had already met him.
He said:
"My son knows how to converse;
you may speak with him."
The Assistant Inspector went to visit Kè.
The *Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn* states:
"Kè, styled Yuánxùn,
was Jǐn's eldest son.
From a young age he was renowned for his talent;
his literary brilliance emerged early,
and he could debate responsively,
with no one able to match him.
Sūn Quán saw him and considered him extraordinary,
saying to Jǐn:
'Jade is indeed born in Lántián—
this is no empty saying!'
He served Wú, rising to Grand Tutor.
He was harmed by Sūn Jùn."
Kè did not meet with him.
Later, they encountered each other at Zhāng the Assistant General of Wú's gathering.
Huán Jì's *Wú Jì* states:
"Zhāng Zhāo, styled Zǐbù,
was loyal, upright, talented, and righteous.
He served Wú,
as Assistant General of Wú."
The Assistant Inspector called out to Kè:
"What an impressive young gentleman!"
Kè then mocked him, saying:
"Yùzhōu is in chaos—
what is there to be impressed about?"
He replied:
"The ruler is enlightened, the ministers are worthy—
I have not heard of any chaos."
Kè said:
"In ancient times, Táng Yáo was above,
yet the Four Fiends were below."
He replied:
"Not only were there the Four Fiends—
there was also Dān Zhū."
At this, the entire gathering burst into laughter.
Jìn Wéndì was riding in a carriage with the two Chéns,
and called over Zhōng Huì to ride together,
then drove the carriage away, abandoning him.
By the time Huì came out,
they were already far away.
When they arrived,
they mocked him, saying:
"When one agrees to travel with others,
why be so slow?
We looked for you from afar, but you never arrived."
Huì replied:
"One who stands out with fine virtue—
why must he join the crowd?"
The Emperor again asked Huì:
"What kind of man was Gāo Yáo?"
Huì replied:
"Above, he did not reach Yáo
and Shùn; below, he did not match Zhōu
and Kǒng—yet he was still a fine scholar of his time."
The two Chéns
were Qiān and Tài.
