Huì's father's name was Yáo,
hence they used
"from afar"
to tease him.
Qiān's father was Jiǎo,
Xuāndì's taboo name was Yì,
Tài's father was Qún,
and his grandfather was Shí—
hence Huì responded in this way.
Zhōng Yù served as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate;
he was quick-witted and alert.
Once, he was feasting at Jǐng Wáng's place.
At the time, Chén Qún's son Xuánbó
and Wǔ Zhōu's son Yuánxià were also present.
The *Wèi Zhì* states:
"Wǔ Zhōu, styled Bónán,
was from Zhúyì in the Pèi Kingdom.
He served up to the position of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness."
Together, they teased Yù.
Jǐng Wáng said:
"What kind of man was Gāo Yáo?"
Yù replied:
"A fine scholar of ancient times."
Then, turning to Xuánbó
and Yuánxià, he said:
"A gentleman is broad-minded but not biased,
sociable but not partisan."
Kǒng Ānguó's *Commentary on the Analects* states:
"Loyalty and trustworthiness constitute broad-mindedness;
favoritism and partisanship constitute bias.
Partisanship means aiding one another.
Even if gentlemen are many,
they do not privately aid each other."
Jī,
Ruǎn, Shān,
and Liú were drinking heartily in the Bamboo Grove,
when Wáng Róng arrived later.
the Minister of Infantry said:
"This vulgar creature has come again to spoil our mood!"
The *Wèishì Chūnqiū* states:
"At the time, it was said that Wáng Róng had not transcended vulgarity."
Wáng laughed and said:
"The mood of you lot—
can it even be spoiled?"
Jìn Wǔdì asked Sūn Hào:
The *Wú Lù* states:
"Hào, styled Yuánzōng,
also named Péngzǔ,
was the grandson of the Great Emperor.
When Jǐngdì passed away,
Hào succeeded to the throne.
He was destroyed by Jìn
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Guīmìng."
"I hear southerners enjoy composing 'Ěr Rǔ Songs'—
can you do one?"
Hào was drinking at the time,
so he raised his cup to toast the Emperor and said:
"In the past, I was your neighbor;
now, I am your subject.
I offer you a cup of wine,
may you live ten thousand springs."
The Emperor regretted asking.
When Sūn Zǐjīng was young, he wanted to become a recluse.
He told Wáng Wǔzǐ
"I shall pillow on stone and rinse my mouth with stream water,"
but mistakenly said
"rinse my mouth with stone and pillow on stream water."
Wáng said:
"Can stream water be used as a pillow?
Can stone be used to rinse the mouth?"
Sūn said:
"The reason for pillowing on stream water
is to wash one's ears;
the *Yìshì Zhuàn* states:
"Xǔ Yóu declined Yáo's offer to abdicate to him,
and his friend Cháofù reproached him.
Yóu then went to the clear, cold water to wash his ears and eyes,
saying:
'Having just heard greedy words,
I have betrayed my friend.'"
The reason for rinsing with stone
is to sharpen one's teeth."
The Head Reproaches Qín Zǐyǔ:
Zǐyǔ’s details are unknown.
“You are not even as good as Wēn Yǒng of Tàiyuán,
Xún Yǔ of Yǐngchuān,
Wēn Yǒng has been mentioned previously.
The Xún Clan Genealogy says:
“Yǔ, styled Jǐngbó,
grandfather Shì,
Grand Commandant.
Father Bǎo,
Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief.”
The Shìyǔ says:
“Yǔ was famous from a young age alongside Péi Kǎi,
Wáng Róng,
and Dù Mò.
He served in Jìn,
rising to the post of Shàngshū.”
Zhāng Huà of Fànyáng,
Shìqīng Liú Xǔ,
the Jìn Bǎiguān Míng says:
“Liú Xǔ, styled Wénshēng,
was from Zhuōlù Commandery.
His father, Fàng,
served as General of Agile Cavalry in Wèi.
Xǔ served as Minister of the Imperial Clan under Emperor Huì of Jìn.”
Note: Xǔ and Zhāng Huà were both from Fànyáng,
hence called Shìqīng,
using the terms interchangeably.
Minister of the Imperial Clan,
is also called Shìqīng.
Zōu Zhàn of Yìyáng,
and Zhèng Xǔ of Hénán.
The Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn says:
“Zhàn, styled Rùnfǔ,
was from Xīnyě.
He achieved prominence through literary talent,
serving up to Palace Attendant.
Xǔ, styled Sīyuān,
was from Kāifēng, Xíngyáng,
serving as Minister of the Imperial Guard.
His grandfather, Tài,
was Governor of Yángzhōu.
His father, Bāo,
was Minister of Works.”
These several men,
some stammered without musical tone,
some were frail and reticent,
some were affected and full of postures,
some were clamorous but lacking in wisdom,
some had mouths as if filled with sticky malt sugar,
some had heads like pestles wrapped in cloth.
The Wénshì Zhuàn says:
“Huà as a person lacked dignified bearing,
and was full of postures.”
Inferring the meaning of these words,
then these six lines,
correspond to the six men above,
and “mouth as if filled with sticky malt sugar,”
refers to Zōu Zhàn.
Zhàn was eloquent, brilliant, and erudite,
yet had this epithet.
The details are unknown.
Yet they still, due to their literary talent being noteworthy,
and their thoughts being orderly and detailed,
clung to the dragon and attached to the phoenix,
and together ascended to the heavenly court.”
The Collected Works of Zhāng Mǐn:
records the text “The Head Reproaches Zǐyǔ” as follows:
“I have a friend named Qín,
though he holds the respected status of my brother-in-law,
I have been familiar with him since youth.
Among our close companions of the time,
were Wēn Chángrén Yǒng of Tàiyuán,
Xún Jǐngbó Yǔ of Yǐngchuān,
Zhāng Màoxiān Huà of Fànyáng,
Shìqīng Liú Wénshēng Xǔ,
Zōu Rùnfǔ Zhàn of Nányáng,
and Zhèng Sīyuān Xǔ of Hénán.
Within a few years,
they successively ascended to court positions,
yet this worthy man remained in a humble alley,
repeatedly offered for sale but without a good price,
maintaining his lofty aspirations as ever,
never declining or falling into despair,
which made me sigh with feeling.
Moreover, I wondered why these worthies, already in positions,
had never made the sounds of calling friends while cutting wood,
greatly violating the principle of Wáng and Gòng dusting their caps,
so, taking advantage of Qín’s impressive appearance,
I composed this reproach from his head to tease him,
and also to mock the six men.
Though it seems humorous and playful,
it truly carries deeper meaning.
The text says:
‘In the first year of the Tàishǐ era,
the head reproached Zǐyǔ, saying:
“I have been entrusted to you as your head
for over ten thousand days.
The great mass endowed me with essence,
formed me into shape.
I grew for you hair and skin,
placed nose and ears,
set eyebrows and beard,
inserted teeth,
made pupils gleam with light,
and cheekbones rise prominently.
Whenever you go out or come in,
roaming the markets and neighborhoods,
pedestrians make way in awe,
those seated rise respectfully.
Some address you as lord,
some call you general,
hands clasped, bodies inclined,
standing attentively on uneven ground.
All this,
is precisely because my form is sufficiently imposing.
Yet you wear no crown or official headgear,
adorn yourself with no gold or silver,
use hairpins as mere clasps,
substitute caps for proper headdresses,
taste no fine flavors,
eat millet and vegetables,
huddle brokenly in garden corners,
soiled by manure and grime,
as years end and time passes,
you have never regretted it.
You despise my appearance,
I disdain your attitude.
If this is the case,
it must be a flaw in your own conduct.
You treat me as an enemy,
I regard you as a foe,
living constantly unhappy,
both of us full of worry—
how vulgar this is!
If you wish to be a treasure to others,
then you should be like Gāo Yáo,
Hòu Jì,
Wū Xián,
and Yī Zhì,
protecting and assisting the royal house,
forever seeing your lineage enfeoffed and established.
If you wish for lofty fame,
then you should be like Xǔ Yóu,
Zǐ Zāng,
Biàn Suí,
and Wù Guāng,
washing your ears to escape salary,
leaving a fragrance for a thousand years.
If you wish to be a traveling persuader,
then you should be like Chén Zhěn,
Kuǎi Tōng,
Master Lù,
and Lord Dèng,
turning calamity into fortune,
making your words smooth and composed.
If you wish to advance and strive,
then you should be like Master Jiǎ seeking trial,
or Zhōng Jūn requesting a mission.
Sharpen your edge and point,
to serve the king’s affairs.
If you wish to be tranquil and indifferent,
then you should be like Lǎo Dān guarding the One,
or Zhuāng Zhōu enjoying his own ease.
Vastly free from desires,
your will soaring above clouds and sun.
If you wish to be a recluse,
then you should be like Róng Qī with his rope belt,
or the Fisherman splashing in the stream,
lingering by divine hills,
dangling bait over giant abysses.
This is how a single individual can manifest himself and achieve fame.
Now, you above do not aspire to the Way and Virtue,
in the middle do not emulate Ru or Mohist teachings,
lumpishly poor and lowly,
clinging to this foolish delusion.
Examining your sentiments,
observing your aspirations,
in retreat you do not act as a retired scholar,
in advance you have no hope for the Three Excellencies,
yet you merely waste days and weary your body,
accustoming yourself to what pleases ordinary people—
is this not a mistake!”’
Thereupon, Zǐyǔ, with a grave and thoughtful expression, replied:
“All your instructions,
I respectfully hear and acknowledge.
But constrained by my innate nature,
unfamiliar with ritual and righteousness,
and relying on heaven’s fortune,
that you are entrusted to me.
Now, if you want me to be loyal,
then I should be like Wǔ Xū or Qū Píng.
If you want me to be trustworthy,
then I should kill myself to achieve fame.
If you want me to have integrity and principle,
then I should plunge into water or fire to preserve chastity.
These four things,
are what people fear,
therefore I dare not conceive such intentions.”
The head said:
"What you call the punishment of heaven and the net of earth,
the extreme of rigid virtue,
is either climbing mountains to embrace trees,
or lifting robes to wade into streams.
I wish to teach you about nurturing your nature,
instruct you in leisurely ease,
yet you share the same sentiments as lice,
not heeding my counsel,
how lamentable!
Both dwelling in human form,
yet you alone are the head!
Moreover, comparing you to your peers,
I liken you to your companions.
You are not like Wēn Yóng from Tàiyuán,
Xún Yǔ from Yǐngchuān,
Zhāng Huà from Fànyáng,
Liú Xǔ the Minister of the Masses,
Zōu Zhàn from Nányáng,
or Zhèng Xǔ from Hénán.
These several gentlemen,
some stammer without musicality,
some are frail and reticent,
some are affected with many postures,
some are clamorous with little wisdom,
some have mouths as if filled with sticky candy,
some have heads like pestles wrapped in cloth,
yet they are still considered for their literary brilliance,
their thoughts detailed and orderly,
climbing the dragon and attaching to the phoenix,
all ascending to the heavenly court.
Licking hemorrhoids to obtain carriages,
diving into deep waters to obtain pearls—
how can you, sir, merely cause your lips and tongue to rot,
your hands and feet to be soaked?
Living in a world of affairs,
yet ashamed to be a strategist of power,
is like digging a pond while embracing a jar,
difficult to seek wealth.
Alas, Zǐyǔ!
How different are you from a bear in a cage,
a tiger in a deep pit,
a starving crab among rocks,
a rat in a hole?
Though your efforts are diligent,
the results are bitter.
It is fitting that you are cramped and constrained,
reaching old age without hope.
With a fragmented form,
you can still avoid hardship—
is it not fate?
How can I share the same place with you, sir?"
Wáng Hún and his wife, Madame Zhōng, were sitting together,
when they saw Wǔzǐ passing through the courtyard.
Hún happily said to his wife:
"To have a son like this,
is enough to comfort one's heart."
His wife laughed and said:
"If I had been matched with Cānjūn,
the son born would certainly not be inferior to this!"
The "Wáng Family Genealogy" says:
"Wáng Lún, styled Tàichōng,
was the middle son of the Minister of Works, Marquis Mù,
and the younger brother of Minister of Education Wáng Hún.
Pure, refined, simple, and detached,
he esteemed the teachings of Lǎozi
and Zhuāngzi,
his mind was tranquil and indifferent.
He wrote 'Examples and Summaries of the Lǎozi'
and 'Records of the Zhōu Dynasty.'
In his twenties,
he was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
but did not take office.
He served as a military advisor to the Grand General.
He died at the age of twenty-five,
and the Grand General shed tears for him."
Xún Mínghè
and Lù Shìlóng had not yet met,
when they both attended a gathering at Zhāng Màoxiān's place.
Zhāng asked them to converse.
Since both possessed great talent,
they should not speak in ordinary terms.
Lù raised his hand and said:
"Lù Shìlóng among the clouds."
Xún replied:
"Xún Mínghè under the sun."
Lù said:
"Since the blue clouds have parted and the white pheasant is visible,
why not draw your bow,
and set your arrow?"
Xún replied:
"I thought the cloud dragon was majestic,
but it turns out to be a mountain deer or wild elk.
The beast is weak, the crossbow strong,
hence the delayed shot."
Zhāng then clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
The "Register of Jìn Officials" says:
"Xún Yǐn, styled Mínghè,
was from Yǐngchuān."
The "Xún Family Biography" says:
"Yǐn's grandfather was Xīn,
Governor of Lè'ān.
His father was Yuè,
a Secretary in the Central Secretariat.
Yǐn and Lù Yún conversed at Zhāng Huá's gathering,
engaging in mutual repartee,
with Lù repeatedly bested,
while Yǐn's words were all elegant and beautiful,
and Lord Zhāng praised them.
This text exists in the world,
but I have not yet found it.
He served as a Gentleman of the Heir Apparent,
and as a Judge in the Court of Judicial Review,
and died early."
Grand Commandant Lù visited Chancellor Wáng,
Lù Wán has been mentioned previously.
Lord Wáng served him yogurt.
Lù fell ill upon returning.
The next day, he wrote a note to Wáng:
"Yesterday, I ate a bit too much yogurt,
and was utterly exhausted all night.
Though I am a man of Wú,
I nearly became a ghost of the north."
When Emperor Yuán's son was born,
he bestowed gifts upon all the ministers.
Yīn Hóngqiáo expressed gratitude:
Yīn Xiàn has been mentioned previously.
"The birth of the imperial prince,
is celebrated throughout the land.
I have no merit in this,
yet I presumptuously receive generous rewards."
Emperor Zhōngzōng laughed and said:
"How could this matter allow you to have merit?"
Minister Zhūgě
and Chancellor Wáng were arguing over whose family name came first,
Wáng said:
"Why not say Gé,
Wáng, but instead say Wáng,
Gé?"
The Minister said:
"It's like saying donkey-horse,
not horse-donkey—
does the donkey surpass the horse?"
Zhūgě Huī,
has been mentioned previously.
Liú Zhēncháng first met Chancellor Wáng,
during the height of the summer heat,
the Chancellor pressed his belly against a gaming board,
and said:
"How refreshing!"
People of Wú call cold "qìng."
After Liú left,
someone asked:
"What did you think of Lord Wáng?"
Liú said:
"I saw nothing extraordinary,
only heard him speaking the Wú dialect!"
The "Forest of Conversations" says:
"Zhēncháng said:
'What is remarkable about the Chancellor?
He can only speak the Wú dialect and spit finely.'"
Lord Wáng was drinking with court officials,
he raised a glass bowl and said to Bórén:
"This bowl's belly is quite empty,
yet it is called a precious vessel—
why is that?"
This was to mock Zhōu for his lack of ability.
He replied:
"This bowl is radiant,
truly clear and transparent,
that is why it is precious!"
Xiè Yòuyú said to Marquis Zhōu:
"You resemble the village tree:
from afar,
it towers, brushing against the blue sky;
but upon closer inspection,
its roots are where foxes gather,
with filth accumulated below!"
This was because Zhōu Yǐ was fond of vulgar banter.
He replied:
"Its branches brush the blue sky,
yet it does not consider itself tall;
foxes run amok beneath it,
yet it does not consider itself impure;
the filth accumulated below—
that is what you preserve,
how can you boast of yourself?"
Wáng Chángyù was gentle and agreeable from childhood,
and the Prime Minister doted on him exceedingly.
Whenever they played weiqi together,
if the Prime Minister wanted to move a piece,
Chángyù would press his finger down and not allow it.
The Prime Minister laughed and said:
"How can you do this?
It seems we are connected by some distant relation."
Cài Yōng said:
"'Guā gé'
means distant relatives."
Emperor Míng asked Zhōu Bórén:
"What kind of man is Zhēncháng?"
He replied:
"He is indeed a thousand-jīn castrated bull."
Minister Wáng laughed at his words.
Bórén said:
"He is not as good as a curly-horned cow,
which has a fondness for circling and bowing."
He said this to tease Wáng.
Prime Minister Wáng rested his head on Zhōu Bórén's knee,
pointed at his belly and said:
"What do you have in here?"
He replied:
"It is hollow and empty inside,
yet it can hold several hundred people like you."
Gān Bǎo spoke to Liú Zhēncháng about the *Zhōngxīng Shū*, which says:
"Bǎo, styled Lìngshēng,
was from Xīncài.
His grandfather, Zhèng,
was General of Fierce Might in Wú.
His father, Yíng,
was an Assistant in Dānyáng.
Bǎo was renowned from youth for his broad learning and talent,
and served as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary."
He narrated his *Sōushén Jì*.
The *Kǒngshì Zhìguài* says:
"Bǎo's father had a favored concubine.
Bǎo's mother was extremely jealous,
and when Bǎo's father was buried,
she pushed her into the tomb.
After ten years, when his mother died,
they opened the tomb,
and found the maidservant lying on the coffin.
Upon inspection, she was still warm,
and gradually began to breathe.
They carried her back home,
and by the end of the day she revived.
She said that Bǎo's father often provided her with food and drink,
and shared her bed,
their affection as in life.
Regarding the household's fortunes and misfortunes,
he would tell her of them,
and upon verification, they all proved true.
After recovering for several years, she finally died.
Bǎo therefore wrote the *Sōushén Jì*,
in which he says
'was moved by this'
referring to this event."
Liú said:
"You may be called the Dǒng Hú of ghosts."
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says:
"Zhào Chuān attacked Duke Líng of Jìn at Táoyuán,
and Zhào Xuānzǐ had not yet left the borders when he returned.
The Grand Historian recorded:
'Zhào Dùn assassinated his ruler.'
Xuānzǐ said:
'It was not so.'
He replied:
'You were the chief minister.
When you fled, you did not cross the border;
when you returned, you did not punish the culprit.
If it was not you, then who was it?'
Confucius said:
'Dǒng Hú
was a good historian of antiquity,
and did not conceal the principles of recording.
Zhào Dùn
was a worthy minister of antiquity,
and bore the blame for the sake of the principle.'"
Xǔ Wénsī went to visit Gù Héxǔ.
Gù was already asleep inside his bed curtains.
When Xǔ arrived,
he went straight to the bed, shared the corner pillow, and spoke with him.
Xǔ Chēn has been mentioned previously.
After a while, Xǔ called Gù to go out together,
so Gù ordered his attendants to fetch a new robe from the clothes rack
and change out of the one he was wearing.
Xǔ laughed and said:
"Do you really have a separate set of clothes for going out?"
Kāng Sēngyuān had deep-set eyes and a high nose,
and Prime Minister Wáng often teased him about it.
Sēngyuān said:
"The nose is the mountain of the face.
The *Guǎn Lù Biézhuàn* says:
'The nose is the mountain in the center of heaven.'
The *Xiàngshū* says:
'Where the nose is located is the center of heaven.
The nose has the image of a mountain,
therefore it is called a mountain.'
The eyes are the abyss of the face.
If a mountain is not high, it lacks spirit;
if an abyss is not deep, it lacks clarity.'"
Hé Cìdào went to the Wǎguān Temple to pay his respects very diligently.
Chōng revered Buddhism
and showed it great respect.
Ruǎn Sìkuàng said to him:
"Your ambition is greater than the cosmos.
The *Shīzǐ* says:
'The four directions of heaven and earth are called yǔ,
past and present are called zhòu.'
Your courage surpasses all antiquity."
"Zhōnggǔ"
means ancient times.
The *Chǔcí* says:
"I cannot endure this forever."
Hé said:
"Why do you suddenly praise me today?"
Ruǎn said:
"I aspire to a commandery of several thousand households,
and still cannot obtain it;
yet you aspire to become a Buddha—
is that not grand indeed!"
Sìkuàng
was Yù.
Regional Inspector Yǔ launched a major campaign against the Hú.
After setting out,
he halted and garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Yì led his troops into Miǎn,
planning to attack the Dí.
Upon reaching Xiāngyáng,
the Dí were still strong,
and a decisive battle was not yet possible.
Then Emperor Kāng died,
and his elder brother Bīng passed away,
so he left his eldest son Fāngzhī to guard Xiāngyáng
and hurried back to Xià□."
Yīn Yùzhāng wrote him a letter,
sending a broken-cornered rúyì to tease him.
Yùzhāng
was Yīn Xiàn.
Yǔ replied in a letter:
"I have received what you sent.
Although it is a damaged object,
I still wish to repair it and use it."
Grand Marshal Huán wished to go hunting in the snow,
and first visited the residences of Wáng,
Liú, and others.
Zhēncháng saw that his attire was light and tight-fitting,
and asked:
"You old rascal, what are you planning to do with this getup?"
Huán said:
"If I did not do this,
how could you people sit and chat?"
The *Yǔlín* says:
"When Xuānwǔ returned from campaign,
Prefect Liú welcomed him from several tens of lǐ away.
Huán said nothing at all,
but simply said:
'Wearing long robes,
discoursing on pure conversation—
whose achievement is this, after all?'
Liú replied:
'The virtue of Jìn is vast and enduring;
how could the achievement be yours?'"
The accounts of the two men differ slightly,
so they are recorded here in detail.
Chǔ Jìyě asked Sūn Shèng:
"When will your state history be completed?"
Sūn said:
"It should have been finished long ago,
but official duties leave no leisure,
hence it has dragged on until today."
Chǔ said:
"The ancients
'transmitted without creating',
why must one be in a silkworm chamber?"
The *Hànshū* says:
"Lǐ Líng surrendered to the Xiōngnú,
and Emperor Wǔ was greatly angered.
The Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān strongly praised Líng's loyalty,
and the Emperor believed Qiān was pleading Líng's case,
and sentenced Qiān to castration.
Thereupon he narrated from the times of Táng
and Yú onwards,
up to the capture of the qílín,
composing the *Shǐjì*.
Qiān, in a letter to Rèn Ān, said:
'Lǐ Líng having surrendered alive,
I was further humiliated by being placed in the silkworm chamber.'"
Sū Lín's *Annotation* says:
"For the castration punishment,
they made a sealed chamber containing a fire,
warm like a silkworm chamber.
In former times, Píngyīn had a silkworm chamber prison."
Xiè Gōng was at Dōngshān,
imperial decrees repeatedly descended yet he did not stir.
Later, he went out to serve as Huán Xuānwǔ's Military Marshal,
and as he was about to depart from Xīntíng,
all the court officials came out to gaze upon him and see him off.
Gāo Líng was then a Palace Aide to the Censor-in-chief,
and also went to bid him farewell.
Earlier,
he had drunk a fair amount of wine,
and so, leaning as if drunk,
he jested, saying:
"You repeatedly defied the court's will,
reclining loftily at Dōngshān.
People often said to each other:
'Ānshí refuses to come out,
what is to become of the common people?'
Now, what is to become of you with the common people?"
Xiè laughed but did not reply.
Gāo Líng has already appeared.
The *Collection on Women* records Huán Xuán asking Wáng Níngzhī's wife, Lady Xiè, saying:
"The Grand Tutor was at Dōngshān for over twenty years,
yet in the end did not remain there,
what is the reason for this?"
Lady Xiè replied:
"My late uncle, the Grand Tutor, first rectified himself,
taking 'having no use' as his mind.
Whether to manifest or conceal himself was a matter of superiority or inferiority,
the beginning and end are precisely the difference between action and stillness."
Initially,
when Xiè Ān resided at Dōngshān,
as a commoner,
his brothers had already attained wealth and rank,
gathering splendidly at the family gate,
stirring and moving people.
Lady Liú playfully said to Ān:
"Shouldn't a great man be like this?"
Xiè then pinched his nose and said:
"I only fear I cannot avoid it!"
Zhī Dàolín, through an intermediary, asked Shēn Gōng to sell him Yìn Mountain.
Shēn Gōng replied:
"I have not heard that Cháo
or Yóu bought a mountain to live in seclusion."
The *Biographies of Reclusive Gentlemen* says:
"Cháofù was
a recluse in the time of Yáo.
He dwelt in the mountains,
did not seek worldly profit,
and in old age made a nest in a tree,
sleeping upon it,
hence he was called Cháofù (Nest Father)."
The *Biographies of Lofty and Reclusive Monks* says:
"Dùn, hearing Shēn Gōng's words,
was only ashamed and remorseful."
Wáng
and Liǔ often did not respect Cài Gōng.
The two once visited Cài,
conversed for a long while,
then asked Cài:
"How would you, sir, say you compare to Yífǔ?"
He replied:
"I am not equal to Yífǔ."
Wáng and Liǔ looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"In what respect are you not equal?"
He replied:
"Yífǔ does not have guests like you!"
Zhāng Wúxīng was eight years old,
and had lost a tooth.
Xuánzhī has already appeared.
A senior worthy, knowing he was no ordinary child,
playfully said to him:
"Why is there a dog hole open in your mouth?"
Zhāng replied immediately:
"Precisely so that people like you can go in and out through it!"
Hǎo Lóng, on the seventh day of the seventh month, went out and lay on his back under the sun.
People asked him the reason.
He replied:
"I am sunning my books."
The *Register of Names of the Western Campaign's Staff* says:
"Lóng, styled Zuǒzhì,
was from Jí Commandery.
Served in Wú, rising to Army Advisor to the General of the Western Campaign."
Xiè Gōng initially had the intention to remain at Dōngshān,
but later stern commands repeatedly arrived,
and the situation left him no choice,
so he finally took up the post of Military Marshal under Duke Huán.
At that time, someone sent Duke Huán some medicinal herbs,
among which was
"yuǎnzhì" (Polygala root).
The Duke took it and asked Xiè:
"This herb is also called
'xiǎocǎo' (little grass),
how can one thing have two names?"
The *Běncǎo* says:
"Yuǎnzhì is also called jíwǎn,
its leaves are called xiǎocǎo."
Xiè did not reply immediately.
Hǎo Lóng was then present,
and answered immediately:
"This is very easy to explain:
when dwelling in seclusion, it is 'far-reaching aspiration' (yuǎnzhì);
when coming out, it is 'little grass' (xiǎocǎo)."
Xiè looked very ashamed.
Duke Huán looked at Xiè and laughed, saying:
"Army Advisor Hǎo's remark this time is not bad,
and also hits the mark perfectly."
Yǔ Yuánkè visited Supervisor Sūn,
and found him away,
but saw Qízhuāng outside,
still young,
yet with an intelligent expression.
Yǔ tested him, saying:
"Where is Sūn Ānguó?"
He immediately replied:
"At Yǔ Zhìgōng's house."
Yǔ laughed loudly and said:
"The Sūns are flourishing greatly,
to have a son like this!"
He replied again:
"Not as good as the Yǔs, with their 'winged' prosperity."
Returning, he told people:
"I certainly won,
for I got to call his father's name twice."
The *Biography of Sūn Fàng* says:
"Fàng and his brothers were both outstanding and exceptional,
and studied together with Yǔ Yì's son Yuánkè.
Yuánkè had a fine reputation from youth,
and once, in conversation and jest, teased Fàng, saying:
'The Sūns are now flourishing.'
'Flourishing' (shèng) was the taboo name of Supervisor Sūn.
Fàng immediately replied:
'Not as good as the Yǔs, with their "winged" prosperity.'
Fàng responded to the situation and achieved victory,
and people of the time admired him.
Even Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng,
Chén, Zhōng and the other worthies in their exchanges
could not surpass this."
Fàn Xuánpíng was at Jiǎnwén's gathering,
and in debate was about to be bested,
so he called upon Prefect Wáng, saying:
"Help me."
The *Biography of Fàn Wāng* says:
"Wāng, styled Xuánpíng,
was from Yǐngyáng.
Grandson of General of the Left Lüè.
In youth, he had unusual ambitions,
was intelligent and widely knowledgeable,
extensively studied the classics and texts,
and gained a reputation in his time.
Served as President of the Board of Civil Office,
and Governor of Xú and Yǎn Provinces."
Wáng said:
"This is not something that 'strength to uproot mountains' can help with!"
Liú Xiàobiāo notes:
The *Shǐjì* says:
"Xiàng Yǔ was surrounded by Hàn troops,
and at night rose and sang:
'My strength plucked up mountains, my energy overshadowed the world;
the times are against me, my dappled horse will not run.'"
Hǎo Lóng served as the Southern Barbarian Adjutant under Duke Huán.
On the third day of the third month, there was a gathering,
where they composed poems.
Those who could not
were fined three shēng of wine.
Initially, Hǎo Lóng was fined because he could not compose.
After drinking,
he took up the brush and immediately wrote a line:
"Jūyú leaps in the clear pond."
Duke Huán asked:
"What is jūyú?"
He replied:
"In the barbarian language, fish is called jūyú."
Duke Huán said:
"Why use barbarian language in composing a poem?"
Hǎo Lóng said:
"I traveled a thousand lǐ to serve you,
and only obtained the post of barbarian prefecture adjutant.
How could I not use barbarian language?"
Yuán Yáng once visited Liú Huī,
who was sleeping inside and had not yet risen.
Yuán therefore composed a poem to tease him:
"The horn pillow gleams on the patterned mat,
the brocade quilt shines on the long feast mat."
The "Book of Songs" says:
"Duke Xiàn of Jìn loved warfare,
and many people in the state perished.
The poem says:
'The horn pillow gleams,
the brocade quilt shines;
my beauty is gone from here,
with whom shall I pass the dawn alone?'"
Thus, Yuán was mocking him.
Liú married the daughter of Emperor Míng of Jìn.
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Liú Huī married the Princess of Lúlíng,
named Nándì."
The princess saw the poem
and indignantly said:
"Yuán Yáng
is a madman left over from ancient times!"
Yīn Hóngyuǎn's poem in reply to Sūn Xìnggōng said:
"Let me just play one more tune."
Liú Zhēncháng laughed at the clumsiness of his words,
asking:
"How do you intend to play it?"
Yīn said:
"Tàlà can also be played,
why must it be qiānglíng?"
Yīn Róng has been mentioned previously.
After Duke Huán deposed Hǎixī
and established Jiǎnwén,
the "Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Hǎixī Gōng, personal name Yì,
courtesy name Yánlíng,
was the son of Emperor Chéng.
He ascended the throne during the Xīngníng era.
He suffered from a condition similar to that of a eunuch,
and had palace women and attendants engage in illicit relations to bear children.
Grand Marshal Wēn, returning from Guǎnglíng to Gūshú,
passed through the capital.
By order of the Empress Dowager,
he deposed the emperor, who became Hǎixī Gōng."
The Palace Attendant Xiè Gōng saw Duke Huán and bowed.
Duke Huán exclaimed in surprise and laughter:
"Ānshí,
why have you gone to such lengths?"
Xiè said:
"There has never been a case where the ruler bows in front,
and the subject stands behind!"
Xī Chóngxī wrote to Xiè Gōng,
saying:
"Wáng Jìngrén heard that a young man harbors ambitions of inquiring about the tripods.
Xī Tán and
Wáng Xiū have been mentioned previously.
The "Records of the Grand Historian" says:
"King Zhuāng of Chǔ displayed his troops on the outskirts of Zhōu.
King Dìng of Zhōu sent Wángsūn Mǎn to greet and entertain the King of Chǔ.
The king asked about the size and weight of the tripods.
He replied:
'It depends on virtue, not on the tripods.'
King Zhuāng said:
'Do not hinder me from the Nine Tripods.
The broken hooks of Chǔ
are enough to make the Nine Tripods.'"
I do not know whether Duke Huán's virtue has declined,
or whether the younger generation is truly formidable?"
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" says:
"Duke Huán of Qí attacked Chǔ,
reproaching them for not offering the bundled thatch."
The "Analects" says:
"The younger generation is formidable.
How do we know that those to come will not surpass the present?"
Kǒng Ānguó said:
"The younger generation
refers to the youth."
Zhāng Cāngwú was the grandfather of Zhāng Píng.
He once said to Píng's father:
"I am not as good as you."
Píng's father did not understand why.
Cāngwú said:
"You have a fine son."
The "Stele of Zhāng Cāngwú" says:
"His personal name was Zhèn,
courtesy name Yìyuǎn,
a man of Wú in the state of Wú.
He was loyal, tolerant, broad-minded, and enlightened,
simple, upright, steadfast, and pure.
During the Tài'ān era,
he was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Cāngwú.
He performed meritorious service in suppressing Wáng Hán,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīngdào County."
At that time, Píng was only a few years old.
He clasped his hands and said:
"Grandfather,
how can you use the son to jest with the father?"
Xí Zàochǐ and
Sūn Xìnggōng had not yet met.
They were both seated with Duke Huán.
Duke Huán said to Sūn:
"You may converse with Adjutant Xí."
Sūn said:
"'You ignorant Jīng barbarians,'
how dare you become enemies of a great state?"
Xí said:
"'We attacked the Xiǎnyǔn,'
all the way to Tàiyuán."
This is from the "Minor Odes" of the "Book of Songs."
The "Máo Commentary on the Book of Songs" says:
"'Ignorant'
means to stir.
'Jīng barbarians'
refers to the barbarians of Jīng.
'Xiǎnyǔn'
are the northern barbarians."
Xí Zàochǐ
was from Xiāngyáng.
Sūn Xìnggōng
was from Tàiyuán.
Thus, they used the poems to tease each other.
Huán Bàonú was the nephew of Wáng Dānyáng on his mother's side.
He resembled his maternal uncle in appearance,
which Huán greatly disliked.
Bàonú
was the childhood name of Huán Sì.
The "Records of the Restoration" says:
"Sì, courtesy name Gōngzǔ,
was the son of Chariot and Horse General Chōng.
He had a reputation for purity from a young age.
He served up to the post of Governor of Jiāng Province."
The "Genealogy of the Wáng Clan" says:
"Hùn, courtesy name Fèngzhèng,
was the son of General of the Central Army Tián.
He served up to the post of Governor of Dānyáng."
Xuānwǔ said:
"They are not always alike,
only sometimes alike!
Constant likeness is in form,
occasional likeness is in spirit."
Huán became even more displeased.
Wáng Zǐyóu visited Xiè Wàn.
Master Lín was already seated there,
looking aloof and lofty.
Wáng said:
"If Master Lín had both beard and hair intact,
would his spirit and demeanor surpass this?"
Xiè said:
"Lips and teeth depend on each other,
neither can be missing.
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" says:
'With the lips gone, the teeth are cold.'
What do beard and hair have to do with divine spirit?"
Master Lín was very displeased.
He said:
"This seven-foot body
is today entrusted to you two worthies."
Minister of Works Xī Chāo was appointed to the Northern Administration,
as recorded in the *Annals of Southern Xúzhōu*:
"In the past, the Governor of Xúzhōu was referred to with the title 'Eastern.'
After the Jin court moved south,
Xúzhōu Regional Inspector Wáng Shū was additionally appointed as General of the Northern Headquarters.
The designation 'Northern Administration'
originated from this."
Attendant Gentleman Wáng Xiànzhī went to pay respects at Xī's gate,
saying:
"Adapting to changing circumstances and military strategy
are not his strengths."
He repeatedly chanted this without cease.
Xī Cāng said to Jiābīn:
"My lord received his appointment today,
yet Zǐyóu's words were extremely disrespectful,
utterly intolerable!"
Cāng was the childhood name of Xī Róng.
The *Genealogy of the Xī Clan* states:
"Róng, styled Jǐngshān,
was the second son of Xī Yīn,
summoned to serve as Literary Gentleman to the Prince of Lángyá,
but did not take up the post and died young."
Jiābīn said:
"This is Chén Shòu's evaluation of Zhūgě Liàng.
Chén Shòu's commentary in the *Records of Shǔ* states:
"Liàng mobilized the masses year after year,
yet achieved no success,
likely because adapting to changing circumstances and military strategy
were not his strengths."
Wáng Yǐn's *History of Jin* states:
"Shòu, styled Chéngzuò,
was a man of Ānhàn in Bāxī.
He loved learning
and was skilled at writing.
He served up to the position of Palace Attendant.
Originally, Shòu's father served as an Army Advisor under Mǎ Sù.
When Zhūgě Liàng executed Sù,
he had Shòu's father's head shaved.
Liàng's son Zhān also looked down upon Shòu.
Therefore, when Shòu compiled the *Records of Shǔ*,
he based his evaluations on personal likes and dislikes."
Since people are comparing your family to Military Marquis Zhūgě,
what more is there to say?"
Wáng Zǐyóu visited Xiè Ān,
Xiè asked:
"What about seven-character poetry?"
The *Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò* states:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was at the Bóliáng Terrace,
and had his ministers compose seven-character poems."
Seven-character poetry began from this.
Zǐyóu, responding to the question,
replied:
"Proud and lofty like a thousand-li steed,
floating freely like a duck in the water."
From the *Lísāo*.
Wáng Wéndù
and Fàn Róngqī were both summoned by Jiǎnwén.
Fàn was older but held a lower position,
while Wáng was younger but held a higher position.
As they were about to proceed,
they repeatedly deferred to each other to go first.
After a long delay,
Wáng ended up behind Fàn.
Wáng then said to him:
"When you winnow and toss,
the chaff and husks come to the front."
Fàn replied:
"When you wash and rinse,
the sand and gravel sink to the back."
Wáng Tǎnzhī
and Fàn Qǐ have already been mentioned above.
One version says it was Sūn Chuò
and Xí Zuòchǐ who spoke these lines.
Liú Zūnzǔ in his youth was recognized by General of the Central Army Yīn Hào,
who praised him to Minister Yǔ Liàng.
Minister Yǔ was very pleased,
and immediately recruited him as an assistant.
After meeting him,
he had him sit on a single couch and spoke with him.
Liú that day performed far below expectations,
and Yǔ was somewhat disappointed,
so he nicknamed him
"Lord Yáng's Crane."
In the past, Yáng Shūzǐ had a crane skilled at dancing,
and he often praised it to guests.
When a guest tried to have it driven over,
it just fluffed its feathers and refused to dance.
Hence the comparison.
Xú Guǎng's *Annals of Jin* states:
"Liú Áizhī, styled Zūnzǔ,
was a man of Pèi Commandery.
In his youth, he had talent and learning,
and was skilled in discussing principles.
He served successively as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat
and Governor of Xuānchéng."
Wèi Chángqí was truly dignified and magnanimous,
but talent and learning were not his forte.
When he first took office and was about to depart,
Yú Cún teased him, saying:
"I establish three rules with you:
those who engage in pure conversation shall die,
those who write literary compositions shall be punished,
and those who deliberate on affairs shall be held accountable."
Wèi smiled cheerfully,
showing no sign of offense.
The *Genealogy of the Wèi Clan* states:
"Yǐ, styled Chángqí,
was a man of Kuàijī.
His grandfather Yìn
was a recluse scholar.
His father Yuè
served as Minister of the Imperial Clan.
Yǐ served up to the position of Magistrate of Shānyīn."
The *History of the Former Hàn* states:
"The Lord of Pèi entered Xiányáng,
summoned the elders and said:
'The world has long suffered under the harsh laws of Qín.
Now I establish three rules with you elders:
murderers shall die,
those who injure others or steal shall be held accountable.'"
Yìng Shào's *Commentary* states:
"'Dǐ'
means 'to reach.'
It simply means to be held accountable for the crime."
Xī Jiābīn wrote to Yuán Hǔ,
mentioning Dài Āndào
and Layman Xiè, saying:
"The style of constancy and responsibility
should be promoted."
Because Yuán lacked constancy,
he used this to provoke him.
Yuán, Dài,
and Xiè have all been mentioned previously.
Fàn Qǐ wrote to Xī Jiābīn, saying:
"Zǐjìng's entire body lacks any plumpness or softness;
strip off his skin and there's no extra moisture."
Xī replied:
"An entire body lacking extra moisture—
how does that compare to an entire body that is not genuine?"
Fàn's nature was arrogant, artificial, and often vexing,
hence the mockery.
The two Xīs revered the Dào,
the two Hés revered Buddhism,
both using wealth and bribes.
Central Army Aide Xiè said:
"The two Xīs flatter the Dào,
the two Hés fawn upon Buddhism."
The *History of the Restoration* states:
"Xī Yīn and his younger brother Tán revered the Way of the Celestial Masters."
The *Annals of Jin* states:
"Hé Chōng was by nature fond of Buddhism,
reverently building Buddhist temples
and supporting monks by the hundreds.
Having long been in Yángzhōu,
he levied corvée labor on officials and commoners,
spending tens of thousands on projects and rewards,
for which he was criticized far and wide.
Chōng's younger brother Zhǔn
was also diligent and devoted,
only reading Buddhist scriptures
and managing temple construction."
Wáng Wéndù was in Xīzhōu,
debating with Dharma Master Lín,
with Hán, Sūn, and others all present.
Dharma Master Lín's arguments were often slightly at a disadvantage,
and Sūn Xìnggōng said:
"Today, the Dharma Master is like wearing tattered wadding in a thorny thicket,
snagging and hindered at every touch."
Fàn Róngqī saw that Xī Chāo’s worldly attachments were not yet light,
and teased him, saying:
“Yí,
Qí, Cháo,
Xǔ—each achieved lasting fame with a single visit.
Why must you toil your spirit and strain your body,
propping up your staff and leaning against the wú tree?”
Xī did not reply.
Hán Kāngbó said:
“Why not let the blade roam through emptiness?”
The Zhuāngzǐ says:
“Zhāowén’s playing of the qin,
Shī Kuàng’s propping of the staff,
and Huìzǐ’s leaning against the wú tree—
the wisdom of these three men was nearly perfect,
all were at their peak,
and thus they were recorded.
In later years,
the cook Dīng carved an ox for Lord Wénhuì.
After three years,
he no longer saw a whole ox.
He had used his knife for nineteen years,
carving thousands of oxen,
yet the blade was as if newly sharpened on the whetstone.
Lord Wénhuì asked him about it,
and the cook Dīng said:
‘The joints have spaces,
while the blade has no thickness;
with no thickness entering into spaces,
how ample and roomy there is for the blade to roam!’”
Jiǎnwén was walking in the palace hall,
with Yòujūn and Sūn Xìnggōng behind him.
Yòujūn pointed at Jiǎnwén and said to Sūn:
“This is a fame-devouring guest!”
Jiǎnwén turned and said:
“The world naturally has sharp-toothed fellows.”
Later, when Wáng Guānglù was appointed to Kuàijī,
Xiè Chēqí went out to Qū’ē to see him off.
Wáng Yùn,
Xiè Xuán—already mentioned.
Wáng Xiàobó, dismissed from his post as Secretariat Assistant, was present.
Xiè spoke of this matter,
then looked at Xiàobó and said:
“Assistant Wáng’s teeth seem not to be dull.”
Wáng said:
“Not dull,
and quite proven.”
Xiè È once lay on his back on a summer day.
Xiè Gōng suddenly arrived early in the morning,
and he had no time to put on his clothes.
Barefoot, he rushed outside,
then put on his shoes and greeted him.
Xiè Gōng said:
“You could be called haughty at first and respectful later.”
The Zhànguócè says:
“Sū Qín advised King Huì but was not employed.
His sable fur robe wore out,
a hundred catties of gold were exhausted,
and he returned in great distress.
His parents would not speak to him,
his wife did not leave her loom,
and his sister-in-law did not cook for him.
Later, when he served as leader of the vertical alliance,
passing through Luòyáng,
with many chariots, cavalry, and baggage trains,
Qín’s brothers, wife, and sister-in-law watched sidelong, not daring to look directly.
Qín smiled and said to his sister-in-law:
‘Why so haughty before and respectful now?’
His sister-in-law apologized, saying:
‘I see that Jìzǐ holds high rank and has much gold.’
Qín sighed and said:
‘In one person’s lifetime,
when rich and noble, even relatives fear him;
when poor and lowly, they treat him lightly—
how much more so with others!’”
Gù Chángkāng served as an assistant to Yīn Jīngzhōu,
and requested leave to return east.
At that time, by regulation, cloth sails were not provided,
but Gù pleaded hard for one,
and only then set off.
Upon reaching Pòzhǒng,
he encountered strong winds and suffered great damage.
Zhōu Zhī’s Lóng’ān Jì says:
“Pòzhǒng
is the name of an islet,
located in Huáróng County.”
He wrote a letter to Yīn, saying:
“The place is named Pòzhǒng [‘Broken Tomb’],
and I truly broke out of a tomb.
The traveler is safe and sound,
and the cloth sail is unharmed.”
Fú Lǎng had just crossed the river.
Péi Jǐngrén’s Qín Shū says:
“Lǎng, styled Yuándá,
was a cousin of Fú Jiān.
His nature was broad and unrestrained,
his spirit clear and perceptive.
Jiān often said:
‘He is the thousand-li steed of our family.’
When Jiān was besieged by Mùróng Chōng,
Lǎng surrendered to Xiè Xuán,
who appointed him as an Extraordinary Cavalier Attendant.
The Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, Wáng Chén, and his elder brother Guóbǎo ordered a carriage to visit him.
The monk Fǎtài asked Lǎng:
‘Have you seen the Wáng Vice Director and his brother?’
Lǎng said:
‘Are they not the one with a dog’s face and a human heart,
and the other with a human face and a dog’s heart?’
This was because Chén was ugly but talented,
while Guóbǎo was handsome but cruel.
Lǎng once feasted with court officials.
The worthy men of the time all used spittoons,
but Lǎng, wishing to show off,
had a young servant kneel and open his mouth,
then spat into it and had him hold it before spitting it out.
He was also skilled at discerning flavors.
When Sīmǎ Dàozǐ of Kuàijī prepared a fine feast for him,
after finishing, he asked:
‘How does the food of Guānzhōng
compare with this?’
Lǎng said:
‘Both are good.
Only the salt flavor is slightly raw.’
When they asked the cook,
it was as he said.
Someone once killed a chicken to serve him,
and Lǎng said:
‘This chicken roosted
always half-exposed.’
When asked,
it was verified.
He also ate roasted goose,
and could tell where the white and dark meat were,
having tested and remembered it,
with not the slightest error.
He wrote several tens of chapters of the Fúzǐ,
belonging to the school of Lǎo
and Zhuāng.
Lǎng was arrogant and offended others,
and was not tolerated by the world.
Later, many slandered him, and he was killed.”
Wáng Zīyì was extremely inquisitive,
asking about Central Plains figures and local products,
endlessly and without limit.
The Wángshì Pǔ says:
“Sùzhī, styled Yòugōng,
was the fourth son of General of the Right Wáng Xīzhī.
He served as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
and Cavalry Consultant.”
Lǎng was greatly annoyed by him.
Next, he asked about the price of male and female servants,
and Lǎng said:
“Those who are prudent, honest, and discerning,
of middling quality,
can fetch up to a hundred thousand;
those who ask unintentionally about being servants,
only several thousand.”
The guest lodge of the Eastern Administration was a plank house.
Xiè Jǐngzhòng visited the Grand Tutor,
and at the time the lodge was full of guests.
At first, he did not speak to anyone,
but simply looked up and said:
“The Prince has indeed made his house like those of the Western Róng.”
The preface to the Qín Odes says:
“Duke Xiāng prepared his armor and weapons
to campaign against the Western Róng.
The women pitied their lords,
and thus composed a poem, saying:
‘In his plank house,
my heart is troubled.’
Master Máo’s commentary says:
‘It refers to the plank houses of the Western Róng.’”
Gù Chángkāng ate sugarcane,
starting from the tip.
When asked why,
he said:
“To gradually reach a better state.”
Grand Commandant Wáng asked Méizi:
"Your uncle is a famous scholar,
why don't you respect him?"
Méizi has been mentioned before.
The uncle is Wáng Chéng.
Méizi said:
"How can a famous scholar talk nonsense all day long?"
Yǔ Yuánguī said to Zhōu Bórén:
"Everyone compares you to Lè."
Zhōu said:
"Which Lè?
Do you mean Yuè Yì?"
The Records of the Grand Historian states:
"Yuè Yì,
a man from Zhōngshān.
A worthy man who became General of King Zhāo of Yān,
leading the feudal lords to attack Qí,
and died in Zhào."
Yǔ said:
"Not that one.
It's Lè Lìng!"
Zhōu said:
"Why carve and paint Wúyán,
only to offend Xīzǐ?"
The Biographies of Exemplary Women states:
"Zhōnglí Chūn,
a woman from Wúyán in Qí.
Her ugliness was unparalleled,
with yellow hair and deep-set eyes,
tall and strong with large joints,
a high nose and a protruding Adam's apple,
a thick neck and sparse hair,
a bent waist and protruding chest,
skin as dark as lacquer.
At the age of thirty,
she had nowhere to turn,
and no one would marry her despite her efforts to promote herself.
She then went to King Xuān of Qí herself,
begging to be accepted into the rear palace.
She advised the king on four perils,
and the king appointed her as his principal queen."
The Spring and Autumn Annals of Wú and Yuè states:
"King Gōujiàn of Yuè obtained a woman who gathered firewood in the mountains,
named Xīshī,
and presented her to the King of Wú."
Shēn Gōng said:
"People say Yǔ Yuánguī is a famous scholar,
but in his chest, there are about three pecks of thorns and brambles."
Duke Yǔ held great power,
enough to overwhelm Duke Wáng.
Yǔ was in Shítóu,
while Wáng was seated in Yěchéng.
A strong wind raised dust,
and Wáng used a fan to brush away the dust, saying:
"Yuánguī's dust sullies people!"
According to records, Duke Wáng was magnanimous and resourceful.
When Yǔ Liàng was in Wǔchāng,
rumors spread that he was about to move downriver.
Duke Wáng used his discernment and judgment to manage the situation,
and the clamorous talk naturally ceased.
How could there have been an incident of fanning away dust due to disloyalty or duplicity?
Wáng Yǐn's Book of Jìn, Biography of Dài Yáng states:
"Dàishǒu of Dānyáng, Wáng Dǎo,
asked Yáng about an illness he had suffered for seven years.
Yáng said:
'Your lordship's fate lies in Shēn,
as the master of the land.
Yet you smelt on Shēn,
with flames illuminating the sky.
This is metal and fire scorching each other,
water and fire clashing,
hence the mutual harm.'
Dǎo summoned the smelting official Yì Sùn,
ordering him to move the foundry eastward.
This is the present-day Dōngyě."
The Records of Dānyáng states:
"The Yěchéng of Dānyáng,
three lǐ from the palace,
was a site for casting during the Wú period,
and remained in use even after Wú was pacified."
It also states:
"Sūn Quán built Yěchéng,
as a site for casting."
Since the great fortress of Shítóu had already been established,
it was unnecessary to build this small city nearby.
It must have been that the county seat was moved,
leaving the city empty and establishing the foundry there.
Yěchéng is suspected to be the original administrative center of Jīnlíng.
In the sixth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
he ordered the establishment of counties and towns throughout the land,
so Mòlíng should not have been the only exception.
In his youth, Wáng Yòujūn was very reserved and taciturn.
At the residence of the Grand General,
when Dukes Wáng and Yǔ arrived later,
Yòujūn immediately rose to leave.
The Grand General stopped him, saying:
"Your family's Minister of Works,
Prime Minister Wáng has been mentioned before.
As for Yuánguī,
what difficulty is there?"
Chancellor Wáng Dǎo looked down upon Cài Mò,
saying:
"When I roamed the banks of the Luò River with Ānqī and Qiānlǐ,
where did I ever hear of a son of Cài Chōng?"
《Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn》states:
"Chōng, styled Zǐní,
was from Yōngqiū, Chénliú."
《Cài Chōng Biézhuàn》states:
"Chōng's grandfather was Mù,
grandson of Cài Yōng.
In his youth, Chōng loved learning,
possessed refined tastes,
and had a dignified, imposing appearance.
No one dared to be frivolous or disrespectful in his presence.
Liú Zhěng of Gāopíng had outstanding talent,
but his carriages and attire were extravagant and luxurious.
He once said to others:
'Gauze and crepe are common attire.
Yet once, when I happened to be seated with Cài Zǐní present,
I felt uneasy the entire day.'
Such was the awe he inspired.
At that time,
Chénliú was a large commandery,
with many notable figures.
Wáng Chéng of Lángyá once passed through the commandery and entered its borders,
asking:
'This commandery has many gentlemen;
who are they?'
The clerk replied:
'There are Jiāng Yīngyuán and Cài Zǐní.'
At the time, many from Chénliú held high positions.
Chéng asked:
'Why do you only mention these two?'
The clerk said:
'I assumed you, my lord, were asking about men of character,
not about official rank.'
Chéng laughed and let the matter drop.
Chōng served as the Eastern Bureau Officer under Prince Chéngdū,
hence he was referred to as the Eastern Bureau Officer."
《Dù Jì》states:
"Chancellor Cáo Fūrén was extremely jealous by nature.
She imposed restrictions on the Chancellor,
forbidding him to have any concubines or attendants.
Even the minor servants around him
were subject to her scrutiny and selection.
If any were particularly beautiful or charming,
she would reprimand and blame them.
Lord Wáng could not endure this for long,
so he secretly established a separate residence,
where he assembled numerous concubines,
and children were plentiful.
Later, on the day of the Grand Assembly,
the Lady, from within the Qīngshū Terrace,
saw two or three children riding goats,
all handsome and endearing.
Seeing them from afar,
she felt great affection and fondness for them.
She told a maidservant:
'Go out and ask
whose children these are.'
The attendant, misunderstanding her intent,
replied:
'They are the fourth and fifth young masters, among others.'
Upon hearing this, Lady Cáo
was shocked and enraged.
She ordered her carriage prepared,
and leading twenty eunuchs and maidservants,
each holding a kitchen knife,
she set out personally to search and confront them.
Lord Wáng also hastily ordered his carriage,
whipped the horses out the gate,
yet still worried the ox was too slow.
So, with his left hand gripping the carriage rail,
and his right hand holding a yak-tail whisk,
he used the whisk's handle to help the driver whip the ox.
In a frantic, desperate gallop,
he barely managed to arrive first.
Minister Cài Mò heard of this and laughed at him.
He then deliberately visited Lord Wáng,
saying to him:
'The court intends to bestow upon you the Nine Bestowals;
are you aware of this?'
Wáng, believing it to be true,
began modestly declining the honor.
Cài said:
'I haven't heard of the other items,
only that there is a short-shaft calf cart
and a long-handled yak-tail whisk.'
Wáng was greatly ashamed.
Later, he disparaged Cài, saying:
'In the past, when I was with Ānqī and Qiānlǐ,
gathering together by the Luò River,
I never heard there was a son of Cài Chōng in the world!'
This was precisely due to his lingering resentment over Cài's earlier jest."
When Grand Mentor Chǔ Pí first crossed the river,
he once traveled east,
arriving at Jīnchāng Pavilion.
The powerful gentry of Wú
were feasting in the pavilion.
Xiè Xīn's《Jīnchāng Tíng Shī Xù》states:
"While seeking a teacher,
I came through Wú.
Traveling, I reached Chāng Gate,
and suddenly beheld this pavilion,
situated by a stream and bordering a river.
Its plaque was inscribed
'Jīnchāng'.
Inquiring of the elders,
they said:
'Long ago, Zhū Mǎichén served the Hàn,
and upon returning to serve as Governor of Kuàijī,
encountered the officials sent to welcome him.
The neighboring lodgings
vied with Mǎichén for seating.
Mǎichén produced his official seal and ribbons,
and the assembled officials, ashamed and submitting, took their own lives.
Because of this event, the pavilion was built,
and named
"Jīn Shāng",
though the meaning of the characters has been lost.'"
Although Chǔ had long enjoyed a great reputation,
at that moment, in the haste, they did not recognize him.
They ordered the attendants to give him plenty of tea,
but very few rice dumplings.
As soon as the tea was finished, they would refill it,
ensuring he never got to eat.
After Chǔ finished drinking,
he calmly raised his hands and addressed the company, saying:
"I am Chǔ Jìyě!"
At this, all those seated scattered in alarm,
each in disarray.
When General of the Right Wáng Xīzhī was in the south,
the Chancellor wrote to him,
often lamenting that his sons and nephews were not promising.
He said:
"Hǔtún and Hǔdú
are just as they are."
Hǔtún was the childhood name of Wáng Péngzhī.
《Wángshì Pǔ》states:
"Péngzhī, styled Ānshòu,
was from Lángyá.
His grandfather was Zhèng,
a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
His father was Bīn,
General of the Guards.
Péngzhī served up to Gentleman of the Palace Gate.
Hǔdú
was the childhood name of Wáng Biāozhī.
Biāozhī, styled Shūhǔ,
was Péngzhī's third younger brother.
By age twenty, his hair and beard were already white,
so contemporaries called him 'Wáng the White-Bearded'.
In his youth, he was praised for being capable and substantial.
He rose through the ranks to become Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon."
When Grand Mentor Chǔ was traveling south,
Sūn Chěng of Chánglè observed him from a boat.
Chánglè refers to Sūn Chuò.
In the course of conversation,
they mentioned Liú Zhēncháng's death.
Sūn shed tears
and then recited:
"When men are lost,
the state is afflicted and distressed."
《Dàyǎ Shī Máo Gōng Zhù》states:
"Tiǎn means
'exhausted'. Cuì means
'afflicted'."
Chǔ became furious and said:
"In all his life, Zhēncháng never associated with the likes of you.
And today you put on such a face for others!"
Sūn turned his weeping face to Chǔ and said:
"You should have some consideration for me!"
At the time, everyone laughed at his talent but despised his character.
General of the West Xiè Shàng wrote to Governor Yīn Hào of Yángzhōu,
requesting Kuàijī for Liú Zhēncháng.
Yīn replied:
"Zhēncháng forms cliques and attacks those who differ;
he is a great partisan.
I have always thought it excessive that you, Governor, lowered your standards for him.
How can you now go so far as to run errands for him?"
Duke Huán entered Luòyáng,
crossed the Huái and
Sì Rivers, and set foot on the northern border.
With his various subordinates, he ascended the Píngchéng Tower,
gazed out over the Central Plains,
and sighed with emotion, saying:
"Thus it has caused the Divine Land to sink into ruin,
for a hundred years it has become mounds and ruins.
Wáng Yífǔ and his ilk
cannot escape bearing the blame for this!"
The "Tales of the Eight Princes" states:
"Although Yífǔ held a high ministerial post,
he did not involve himself with practical affairs.
The people of his time were influenced by this,
and it became shameful to speak of the teachings of reputation and duty.
From the court officials downwards,
all esteemed refined silence and inaction,
considering neglect of affairs to be noble.
Though the realm was still peaceful,
those with discernment knew chaos was imminent."
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" states:
"When Yífǔ was about to be killed by Shí Lè,
he said to others:
'If we had not revered and promoted empty talk and impracticality,
we would not have come to this!'"
Yuán Hǔ impulsively replied:
"The fortunes of the state naturally have their decline and rise;
how could it necessarily be the fault of those men?"
Duke Huán, stern and with a changed countenance,
looked around at those seated and said:
"Have you gentlemen perhaps heard of Liú Jǐngshēng?
The 'Inscription for General Liú Zhènnán' says:
'His courtesy name was Jǐngshēng,
a man of Gāopíng in Shānyáng.
He possessed a virtuous nature and understood principles,
was erudite and widely learned.
He served up to the positions of General Who Guards the South and
Governor of Jīng Province.'
He had a great ox weighing a thousand jīn,
which ate ten times more fodder and beans than a regular ox,
yet when carrying heavy loads over long distances,
it could not even match a weak cow.
When Cáo Cāo entered Jīng Province,
he had it cooked to feed his soldiers,
and at that time, none failed to applaud."
His meaning was to use this to analogize Yuán.
All those seated were shocked,
and Yuán also lost color in his face.
Yuán Hǔ and
Fú Tāo were both in Duke Huán's administration.
Whenever Duke Huán went on outings or banquets,
he would always summon Yuán and
Fú. Yuán felt deeply ashamed of this,
and often sighed, saying:
"The Duke's great favor
is not enough to honor a man of true talent!
To be placed shoulder-to-shoulder with Fú Tāo—
what disgrace could be greater than this?"
Gāo Róu was in the east,
and was highly esteemed by Xiè Rénzǔ.
After he came out [to the capital],
he was not recognized by Wáng
or Liǔ.
Rénzǔ said:
"Recently I saw Gāo Róu;
he greatly exerted himself in presenting memorials and arguments,
but achieved nothing."
Zhēncháng (Liǔ Dàn) said:
"So one cannot live in a remote place,
lightly staying in a corner [pronounced *nù jué*],
and then come here to make arguments for others."
Gāo Róu heard this
and said:
"I seek nothing from him."
Someone repeated these words to Zhēncháng,
and Zhēncháng said:
"I truly also have nothing to give him."
However, when on outings or at banquets, he still wrote to others:
"Shall we invite Āngù?"
Āngù was
Gāo Róu.
Sūn Tǒng wrote the "Preface to Gāo Róu's Collected Works," stating:
"Róu's courtesy name was Shìyuǎn,
a man of Lè'ān.
His talent and reasoning were clear and fresh;
he peacefully practiced benevolence and righteousness.
He married a daughter of the Húwú family of Tàishān.
At twenty years of age,
she already possessed the understanding of someone twice her age,
and her appearance was pure and graceful,
nearly that of a woman from the highest circles.
Róu's family circumstances were prosperous and esteemed.
After leaving his post as Adjutant to the Minister of Works and
Magistrate of Āngù,
he built a residence at Fúchuān.
His desires for activity and fame having grown thin,
and being fond of and delighting in his virtuous wife,
he then formed the intention to end his days there.
The President of the Imperial Secretariat Hé Chōng recruited him as Adjutant to the General of the Vanguard.
He reluctantly accepted the appointment,
but was so deeply attached and entangled [with his home life]
that he could not bear to part.
The poems and letters they exchanged
were pure, gentle, fresh, and poignant."
Prefect Liǔ,
Jiāng Bīn,
Wáng Shūhǔ, and
Sūn Xìnggōng were sitting together.
Jiāng and Wáng had expressions of mutual disdain.
Bīn pointed at Shūhǔ and said:
"Cruel official!"
His words and expression were very forceful.
Prefect Liǔ looked over and said:
"Is this anger?
It's not merely ugly words and tone,
or an awkward gaze."
Meaning that Jiāng's words
were not simply ugly and awkward,
but seemed to show resentment towards Wáng.
Sūn Chuò wrote the "Eulogy for the Immortal Shāngqiūzǐ," saying:
"What is it he herds?
It is surely no ordinary pig.
Should it encounter wind and clouds,
it will become a dragon for me to ride."
The "Biographies of Immortals" states:
"Shāngqiūzǐ Jìn
was a man of Shāngyi.
He enjoyed playing the yu and herding pigs.
At seventy years of age,
he had not taken a wife and yet did not age.
When asked the essential method [of his longevity],
he said:
'Only eat old atractylodes,
calamus root,
and drink water.
Doing this, one will not hunger and will not age.'
The noble relatives and wealthy families,
hearing of this, tried it,
but could not persist for a full year and would stop,
saying he must have concealed some technique."
Sūn Chuò wrote the "Eulogy," saying:
'Shāngqiū is outstanding and eminent,
holding a whip and playing the yu.
Thirsty, he drinks from cold springs;
hungry, he eats calamus.
What is it he herds?
It is surely no ordinary pig.
Should it encounter wind and clouds,
it will become a dragon for me to ride.'"
Many people of the time considered him talented.
Wáng Lántián said to someone:
"Recently I saw that son of the Sūn family writing an essay,
talking about 'what thing' and
'ordinary pig.'"
Duke Huán wanted to move the capital,
in order to expand and secure his achievements.
Sūn Chánglè submitted a memorial,
remonstrating against this proposal with very reasonable arguments.
Duke Huán, seeing the memorial, was convinced in his heart,
but was angry that he took a dissenting stance.
He had someone convey a message to Sūn, saying:
"Why don't you, sir, go back to studying your 'Rhapsody on Fulfilling My Original Intent,'
and stop forcing your knowledge into matters of state?"
Sūn Chuò's "Memorial" remonstrated, saying:
"When Emperor Yuán ascended the throne,
he truly relied on the thousand-mile-long Yangtze River,
drawing a line and defending it.
Otherwise,
the Hu cavalry would have long ago trampled the lands of Jiànkāng,
and Jiāngdōng would have become a den of jackals and wolves."
Chuò composed the "Rhapsody on Fulfilling My Original Intent,"
setting forth the principle of knowing contentment.
Sūn Chánglè and his brother went to stay overnight at Xiè Gōng's place.
Their conversation became extremely intimate and miscellaneous.
Lady Liǔ was listening behind the wall
and heard all their words.
The next day, when Xiè Gōng returned,
he asked:
"What were yesterday's guests like?"
Lady Liǔ replied:
"In my late brother's household,
there were never guests like these!"
The lady was
the younger sister of Liǔ Tán.
Xiè wore a deeply ashamed expression.
Jiǎnwén and Xǔ Xuándù were conversing together,
when Xǔ said:
"To choose between one's lord and
one's parent is a difficult matter."
Jiǎnwén then did not respond further.
After Xǔ had left, he remarked:
"Xuándù really should not have gone so far as this!"
According to the Bǐng Yuán Biézhuàn:
"The Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng of Wèi,
once discussed with a group of worthies, saying:
'Now suppose there is one pill of medicine,
capable of curing one person's illness,
and both one's lord and
one's father are sick—
should it be given to the lord,
or to the father?'
The various men debated vigorously,
some saying the father,
some the lord.
Yuán angrily declared:
'Father and son
share the same root;
this is not even a difficult choice.'"
Comparing lord and parent,
has been like this since ancient times.
I do not understand Jiǎnwén's intention in criticizing Xǔ.
After Xiè Wàn was defeated at Shòuchūn,
he returned and wrote to Wáng Yòujūn, saying:
"I am ashamed for failing your long-standing expectations."
Yòujūn pushed the letter away and said:
"This is the self-reproach of Yǔ and
Tāng."
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn states:
"When Yǔ and
Tāng blamed themselves,
their rise was vigorous."
This means that Yǔ and
Tāng, with their sage virtue, blamed themselves,
and thus were able to rise.
Now Wàn, having lost discipline and caused defeat,
even if he again blames himself,
how can it help?
Thus Wáng praised Wàn.
Cài Bójiē saw a rafter suitable for a flute;
Sūn Xìnggōng, while listening to a courtesan,
shook it and broke it off.
Fú Tāo's Chángdí Fù Xù states:
"My colleague Huán Zǐyě had an old long flute,
which the elders passed down, saying:
'It was made by Cài Yōng, Bójiē.'
Initially, Yōng was fleeing hardship south of the river,
and lodged at the Kētíng Inn.
Using bamboo as rafters,
Yōng looked up and gazed at one,
saying:
'This is fine bamboo.'
He took it to make a flute,
and its sound was uniquely superb,
passed down through generations to the present."
Wáng Yòujūn heard of this
and said angrily:
"The musical instruments of the Three Ancestors (or 'platform'),
the musical instruments,
are like earthen tiles (or 'inferior and ordinary').
Alas, the Sūn family fellow broke it."
Wáng Zhōngláng and Lín Gōng were utterly incompatible.
Wáng said Lín Gōng was sophistical in debate;
Lín Gōng said of Wáng:
"Wearing a greasy Yánqià hat,
a coarse cloth single robe,
carrying the Zuǒzhuàn,
chasing after Zhèng Kāngchéng's carriage,
asking what kind of dust-and-grime sack this is!"
Zhōngláng
is Tǎnzhī.
Qià is a hat.
The Péizǐ states:
"Lín Gōng said:
'Wéndù wears a greasy Yán [hat],
carries the Zuǒzhuàn,
chases after Zhèng Kāngchéng,
considering himself a top disciple.
Strictly speaking,
he does not leave the dust-and-grime sack.'"
Sūn Chánglè composed the Wáng Chángshǐ Lěi, saying:
"I and the Master,
our friendship was not based on power or profit;
our hearts were like clear water,
sharing this profound taste."
The Lǐjì states:
"The friendship of gentlemen is as mild as water;
the friendship of petty men is as sweet as sweet wine."
Wáng Xiàobó saw it and said:
"This talented man is disrespectful;
how could my late grandfather have associated with this man!"
Xiè Tàifù said to his sons and nephews:
"Zhōngláng truly is the only one to possess a thousand years!"
Chējì said:
"Zhōngláng's heart and embrace are not yet empty;
how then can he be the only one to possess it?"
Zhōngláng
is Xiè Wàn.
Yǔ Dàojì boasted to Xiè Ān, saying:
"Pei Láng said:
'Xiè Ān remarked that Pei Láng is indeed not bad,
but why does he still drink?'
Yǔ Hé and
Péi Qǐ have been mentioned before.
Pei Láng also said:
'Xiè Ān described Zhī Dàolín
as being like Jiǔfāng Gāo judging horses,
overlooking their black and yellow colors,
and focusing on their outstanding qualities.'"
The "Biography of Zhī Dùn" states:
"Dùn often highlighted the essential principles,
but did not pay attention to imagery and metaphors.
When explaining passages and sentences,
he sometimes missed details,
so scholars
often had doubts about him.
Xiè Ānshí heard about this and praised him, saying:
'This is like Jiǔfāng Gāo judging horses,
overlooking their black and yellow colors,
and focusing on their outstanding qualities.'"
The "Lièzǐ" states:
Bó Lè said to Duke Mù of Qín:
'Among those who share the burdens of carrying ropes and gathering firewood with me,
there is Jiǔfāng Gāo.
When it comes to horses,
he is no less skilled than I am.'
The duke sent him to find a horse.
He returned and said:
'I have found one!
It is a yellow mare.'
Someone was sent to fetch it,
but it turned out to be a black mare.
The duke said:
'He cannot even distinguish the color and gender of a horse;
how can he know anything about horses?'
Bó Lè said:
'When Gāo observes a horse,
he grasps its innate nature.
He captures its essence,
and disregards its coarse aspects.
He focuses on what is inside,
and ignores what is outside.
He sees what he should see,
and does not see what he should not see.
He looks at what he should look at,
and overlooks what he should not look at.
The way he judges
is more valuable than the horse itself.'
Later,
the horse indeed proved to be a thousand-mile steed."
Xiè Ān said:
"I never said these two things;
Pei made up these words himself!"
Yǔ was very displeased by this,
so he presented Wáng Xún's "Rhapsody on Passing by the Wine Shop."
After reading it,
Xiè offered no praise or critique,
but simply said:
"You are just imitating Pei's style!"
From then on, the "Forest of Conversations" fell into disuse.
The copies that exist today
are all earlier transcriptions,
and no longer contain Xiè's remarks.
The "Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng Autumn" states:
"During the Lónghé era of the Jìn dynasty,
Péi Qǐ of Hédōng compiled notable dialogues and responses
from the Hàn and Wèi dynasties up to his own time,
calling it the 'Forest of Conversations.'
Many people at the time enjoyed it,
and the text became widely circulated.
Later, when his account of the Grand Tutor was found to be untrue,
and someone at Xiè's gathering mentioned the story of Huáng Gōng's wine shop,
for which Minister Wáng Xún had composed a rhapsody,
Xiè, due to his discord with Wáng,
said:
'You are just imitating Pei Láng's style.'
From then on, everyone looked down on the work.
A fellow villager of Ān's who had been dismissed from his post in Zhōngsù County came to see Ān,
and Ān asked about his resources for returning home.
He replied:
'Lǐngnán is impoverished,
and I only have fifty thousand palm-leaf fans,
which are out of season and hard to sell.'
Ān then took one of medium quality and held it,
whereupon the scholars and commoners in the capital competed to admire and wear them.
The price increased severalfold,
and within a month, none were left for sale.
What is favored grows feathers;
what is disliked becomes a scar.
With a single remark, Minister Xiè
undermined a fine work for a thousand years,
and with his support,
he elevated the value of a trivial item to a hundred gold pieces.
The likes, dislikes, endorsements, and rejections of those in high positions
must be handled with great care!"
Wáng Tán was not appreciated by Zhī Dàolín,
so he wrote "A Discourse That Monks Cannot Be Lofty Scholars."
The main points were:
"Lofty scholars must be free-spirited and unrestrained,
while monks, though claiming to be beyond worldly concerns,
are instead bound by religious doctrines,
which cannot be called attaining natural disposition."
Someone asked Gù Kǎizhī:
"Why don't you recite in the Luòyáng style?"
He replied:
"Why should I sound like an old maidservant!"
The recitation style of Luòyáng scholars
has a heavy and muddy tone,
hence it is called the "old maidservant's voice."
Yǐn Yǐ and
Yǔ Héng were both grandsons of Xiè Shàng.
The "Xiè Family Genealogy" states:
"Shàng's eldest daughter, Sēngyào, married Yǔ Hé,
and his second daughter, Sēngsháo, married Yǐn Xīn."
Yǐn was clever and perceptive from a young age,
but Yǔ often did not acknowledge him.
Once, they both visited Xiè Ān,
and Xiè Ān looked closely at Yǐn and said:
"Ā Cháo indeed resembles Xiè Shàng."
Cháo was Yǐn Yǐ's childhood name.
Then Yǔ whispered:
"In what way exactly?"
Xiè Ān continued:
"Cháo's cheeks resemble Xiè Shàng's."
Yǔ said again:
"If it's just the cheeks,
is that enough to make him outstanding?"
The "Yǔ Family Genealogy" states:
"Héng, styled Jìngzé,
grandfather Liàng,
father Hé.
Héng served up to the position of Imperial Secretary."
People used to describe Hán Bó as:
"Even if you lift his elbow, there is no strength in his bones."
The "Forest of Sayings" states:
"Fàn Qǐ said:
'Hán Bó is like a meat duck.'"
Fú Hóng rebelled and surrendered to our state.
Grand Tutor Xiè often received and introduced him.
Hóng, considering himself talented,
often liked to surpass others,
and no one at gatherings could refute him.
Once, when Wáng Huīzhī came,
the Grand Tutor had them converse.
Huīzhī simply stared at him for a long time,
then turned to the Grand Tutor and said:
"He is, after all, no different from anyone else!"
Hóng was greatly ashamed and withdrew.
The "Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng Autumn" states:
"Hóng was
the crown prince of Fú Jiān.
He was killed by Yáo Chāng.
Hóng brought his mother and wife to surrender,
and an edict granted him fields and a residence.
Huán Xuán appointed Hóng as a general.
After Xuán's defeat,
Hóng became a bandit in Xiāngzhōng
and was executed."
When Zhī Dàolín went east,
he met Wáng Huīzhī and his brothers.
Upon returning, someone asked:
"How did you find the Wáng brothers?"
He replied:
"I saw a flock of white-necked crows,
hearing nothing but their cawing."
Wáng Tán recommended Xǔ Xún for the position of Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
Xī Chōngxī said:
"The Imperial Chancellor is fond of meddling;
we cannot let Ā Nè sit at the head."
Nè was Xǔ Xún's childhood name.
Wáng Hézhī said that
Xiè Yǎn was as restless as a falconer who has lost his hawk.
The "Records of Yǒngjiā" state:
"Wáng Hézhī, styled Xìngdào,
was from Lángyá.
His grandfather, Yì,
was a General Who Pacifies the South.
His father, Húzhī,
was the Inspector of Sīzhōu.
Hézhī served as the Governor of Yǒngjiā
and Regular Attendant."
Wàngcài
was Xiè Yǎn's childhood name.
Whenever the Duke of Nánjùn, Huán Xuán, saw someone displeased,
he would angrily say:
"If you got the Āi family pears,
would you still steam and eat them?"
An old saying goes:
"In Mòlíng, there was a family named Āi whose pears were extremely delicious,
as large as a shēng measure,
melting in the mouth upon eating."
This means that foolish people cannot distinguish flavors,
and would steam and eat even good pears."
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was young,
he once, along with Yuán Shào, enjoyed playing the wandering knight.
Observing a wedding,
they sneaked into the host's garden,
and at night shouted:
"There is a thief!"
Everyone in the wedding tent came out to look,
and Emperor Wǔ of Wèi then entered,
drew his blade, kidnapped the bride, and returned out with Shào.
Losing their way,
they fell into a thorny thicket.
Shào could not move,
so (Emperor Wǔ) shouted again:
"The thief is here!"
Shào, in panic, threw himself out,
and thus they both escaped.
The Biography of Cáo Mán states:
"Cáo Cāo's childhood name was Ā Mán,
and from a young age he was fond of deceit and trickery,
wandering and indulging without restraint."
Sūn Shèng's Miscellaneous Sayings states:
"Emperor Wǔ was fond of knight-errantry from a young age,
dissolute and not cultivating proper conduct.
He once secretly entered the residence of the Regular Attendant Zhāng Ràng,
and Ràng wielded a halberd in the courtyard,
but (Cáo) vaulted over the wall and escaped,
possessing extraordinary strength,
so no one could harm him."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was on a campaign,
and the route to fetch water was lost.
The army was all thirsty,
so he ordered:
"Ahead there is a large plum forest,
abundant with fruit,
sweet and sour,
which can quench thirst."
When the soldiers heard this,
their mouths all watered,
and taking advantage of this, they managed to reach the water source ahead.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi often said:
"If someone intends to harm me,
I will sense it in my heart."
Thus, he told a close attendant:
"You, carrying a blade, secretly come to my side.
I will certainly say I sense it.
I will have you seized and executed,
but you must not say who sent you.
There is no other issue,
and I will richly reward you!"
The one seized believed him,
and did not fear,
so he was beheaded.
This person died without knowing the truth.
Those around believed it was real,
and those plotting rebellion lost their nerve.
The Biography of Cáo Mán states:
"When Cáo was in the army,
the grain supply was insufficient.
He privately told the officer in charge:
'What to do?'
The officer said:
'We can use a small hú measure to make it sufficient.'
Cáo said:
'Good.'
Later, the army said Cáo was deceiving everyone.
Cáo then labeled that officer,
paraded him with his back exposed, saying:
'Using a small hú measure,
stealing army grain.'
Thus, he was beheaded.
And then said:
'I specifically used your death
to appease the army's discontent.'
His deceit and trickery were all of this kind."
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi often said:
"When I am asleep, do not recklessly approach me.
If approached, I will strike people,
and I will not be aware of it myself.
Those around should be deeply cautious of this!"
Later, he pretended to be asleep,
and a favored attendant secretly covered him with a blanket.
He then struck and killed him.
From then on, whenever he slept,
no one around dared to approach.
When Yuán Shào was young,
he once sent someone at night to throw a sword at Emperor Wǔ of Wèi.
It fell slightly low,
and did not hit.
Emperor Wǔ estimated that
the next one would certainly be high,
so he lay flat on the bed.
The sword indeed came high.
Note: Yuán and
Cáo later became rival powers,
and traces of their estrangement began.
Before this,
there is no record of enmity between them.
What reason could there have been to stab him with a sword?
After the Grand General Wáng Dūn rebelled,
he stationed his army at Gūshú.
Emperor Míng of Jìn, with his heroic and martial talent,
was still wary and fearful of him.
So he put on military attire,
rode a Bācóng horse,
carrying a golden horsewhip,
and secretly observed the military situation.
Before reaching about ten lǐ away,
there was an old woman guest,
living in a shop selling food.
The Emperor passed by and rested there,
and said to the old woman:
"Wáng Dūn is raising troops plotting rebellion,
suspecting and harming loyal and good officials.
The court is alarmed and fearful,
and the state is in peril.
Therefore, I toil day and night,
to secretly observe,
fearing that my traces might be dangerously exposed,
or lead to a desperate situation.
If the day of pursuit comes,
please hide me."
He then gave the old woman guest the horsewhip and left.
He circled Wáng Dūn's camp and left.
The soldiers noticed,
and said:
"This is no ordinary person!"
Dūn, lying down, felt a stirring in his heart,
and said:
"This must be that yellow-bearded Xiānbēi slave coming!"
He ordered cavalry to pursue him,
but he was already many lǐ away.
The pursuing soldiers then asked the old woman from before:
"Didn't you see a yellow-bearded man on horseback pass by here?"
The old woman said:
"He left long ago,
you cannot catch up."
So the cavalry gave up and returned.
The Garden of Marvels states:
"The Emperor personally went to Gūshú.
Dūn was napping during the day,
and suddenly woke up in alarm, saying:
