'A yellow-headed Xiānbēi slave has come to the camp,
why not capture him?'
The Emperor's birth mother was Lady Xún,
from Yānguó,
hence his appearance resembled that."
When Wáng Xīzhī was less than ten years old,
the Grand General (Wáng Dūn) was very fond of him,
and often had him sleep in his tent.
Once, the Grand General went out first,
and Xīzhī had not yet gotten up.
After a while,
Qián Fèng entered,
and dismissed others to discuss matters.
The Autumn of Jìnyáng states:
"Fèng's courtesy name was Shìyí,
son of the commandant of Jiāxīng in Wú.
He was treacherous and fond of profit.
He served as Dūn's Armory Officer,
knew Dūn had disloyal intentions,
and thus offered advice.
Later, when Dūn was defeated,
he was executed."
They completely forgot that Xīzhī was in the tent,
and began discussing plans for rebellion.
Xīzhī woke up,
and upon hearing the discussion,
knew there was no chance of survival.
So he pretended to vomit, soiling his face and bedding,
and feigned deep sleep.
When Dūn's discussion was halfway,
he then remembered that Xīzhī had not gotten up,
and they were greatly alarmed, saying:
"We must eliminate him!"
But when they opened the tent,
they saw vomit all over,
and believed he was truly in deep sleep.
Thus, he was spared.
At that time, he was praised for his wisdom.
Note: Various records all say this was Wáng Yǔn's affair,
but here it says Xīzhī,
which is likely an error.
Duke Táo came from the upper reaches,
heading to the disaster of Sū Jùn,
ordering the execution of Duke Yǔ.
He believed that killing Yǔ
could appease Jùn.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"At that time, Emperor Chéng was still in swaddling clothes,
the Empress Dowager was overseeing the court,
and the Imperial Secretariat Director Yǔ Liàng, as the maternal uncle, assisted in governance,
wishing to use moral influence to regulate governance,
and to rule the four seas.
However, Jùn held troops near the capital,
becoming a haven for fugitives.
Liàng planned to summon Jùn,
but Wáng Dǎo
and Biàn Kǔn both opposed it.
Liàng said:
'Sū Jùn is a jackal,
and will eventually cause disaster and chaos.
As Cháo Cuò said, whether you reduce his power or not, he will rebel.'
Subsequently, a lenient edict was issued,
summoning him as the Minister of Agriculture.
Jùn angrily said:
'Yǔ Liàng wants to lure and kill me.'
He then captured the capital.
Wēn Qiáo, the General Who Pacifies the South, heard of the chaos,
wept and boarded a boat,
sending his aide Wáng Qiānqī to recommend Táo Kǎn, the General Who Conquers the West, as the alliance leader,
and together they headed to the capital.
At that time, Liàng, having been defeated, fled to Qiáo,
and everyone blamed and looked down on him.
Qiáo, however, increasingly respected and valued him,
dividing troops to supply him."
Yǔ wanted to flee,
but could not;
he wanted to meet,
but feared being captured,
having no plan for advance or retreat.
Duke Wēn advised Yǔ to visit Táo,
saying:
"You just need to bow from a distance,
and there will certainly be no trouble.
I will guarantee it for you."
Yǔ followed Wēn's words and went to see Táo.
Upon arrival, he bowed.
Táo himself stood up to stop him,
saying:
"Why should Yuán Guī Yǔ bow to Táo Shì Héng?"
After finishing, he again stepped down to take a lower seat.
Táo himself then invited him to rise and sit together.
Once seated,
Yǔ took the blame upon himself,
deeply apologizing and deferring.
Táo unconsciously felt relieved.
Duke Wēn lost his wife,
and his paternal aunt Liú Shì,
whose family was scattered due to chaos and separation,
had only one daughter,
who was very beautiful and intelligent.
The aunt entrusted the duke with finding a marriage for her.
The duke secretly intended to marry her himself,
and replied:
"A good son-in-law is hard to find,
but what about someone like Qiáo?"
The aunt said:
"In the aftermath of ruin,
I only beg for a rough survival,
enough to comfort my remaining years.
How dare I hope for someone like you?"
A few days later,
the duke reported to his aunt:
"I have found a marriage match,
the family background is roughly acceptable,
the son-in-law's personal reputation and official rank
are no less than Qiáo's."
He then presented a jade mirror stand as a betrothal gift.
The aunt was overjoyed.
After the marriage,
during the exchange of wedding rites,
the girl used her hand to part the gauze fan,
clapped her hands and laughed loudly, saying:
"I suspected it was this old fellow,
and indeed it was as I guessed!"
According to the *Wēn Shì Pǔ*:
"Qiáo first married the daughter of Lǐ Hàn of Gāopíng,
then married the daughter of Wáng Xǔ of Lángyá,
and later married the daughter of Hé Suì of Lújiāng."
There is no record of him marrying a Liú Shì,
so this must be false and erroneous.
Gǔkǒu said:
"Liú Shì
refers precisely to his aunt,
not that the daughter's surname was Liú.
Xiào Biāo's annotation
is also not correct."
The jade mirror stand
was obtained by the duke when he served as Chief Clerk to Liú Yuèshí,
during the northern expedition against Liú Cōng.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"In the second year of Jiànxīng,
Qiáo served as Acting Left Marshal for Liú Kūn,
overseeing the vanguard military affairs,
to campaign against Liú Cōng."
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Cōng also had the name Zǎi,
courtesy name Xuánmíng,
a Túgè person.
His father Yuān
died after raising troops amid chaos.
Cōng inherited his enterprise."
The daughter of Minister Zhūgě,
married into the Yǔ family,
after being widowed,
vowed:
"I will not remarry!"
This woman's nature was very upright and strong,
with no intention of remarrying.
She was the wife of Yǔ Huì, son of Yǔ Liàng, named Wén Biāo,
as mentioned above.
After Huī promised marriage to Jiāng Sīxuán,
he moved his family closer to him.
Initially, he deceived his daughter, saying:
"We should move here."
The family members left at once,
leaving the daughter alone behind.
By the time she realized,
she could no longer get out.
When young master Jiāng came,
the girl cried and scolded even more fiercely,
but gradually calmed down over the days.
Jiāng Bīn entered at dusk to stay,
always sleeping on the opposite bed.
Later, seeing her attitude becoming more settled,
Bīn pretended to have a nightmare,
not waking for a long time,
his breathing becoming more urgent.
The girl then called the maid, saying:
"Wake young master Jiāng up!"
Jiāng then jumped up and approached her, saying:
"I am a man of the world;
having a nightmare, what does it have to do with you that you call me?
Since you are concerned,
you cannot avoid speaking to others."
The girl fell silent in shame,
and their affection then grew deep.
Minister Zhūgě's purity and excellence,
and Lord Jiāng's profound insight,
would certainly not betray the orthodox canons of the sages,
nor adopt the vulgar practices of barbarians.
Kāng Wáng's words
belittle them too much.
The monk Mǐndù initially wanted to cross the river,
and partnered with a northern monk,
planning:
"If we go to Jiāngdōng with the old doctrines,
I fear we won't be able to get food."
So they together established
the "Mindless Doctrine."
Later, this monk did not succeed in crossing,
but Mǐndù indeed lectured on this doctrine for many years.
The *Míngdé Shāmén Tímù* states:
"Zhī Mǐndù's talent and discernment are clear and outstanding."
Sūn Chuò's *Mǐndù Zàn* says:
"Zhīdù is refined and cultured,
fond of innovation.
Both endowed with clear insight,
yet able to surpass others.
The world values outstanding talent,
all compete for such treasures.
Like the solitary tong tree on Yìyáng,
or the floating chime stone by the Sì riverbank."
Later, a northerner came,
and the earlier monk sent a message, saying:
"Convey my regards to Mǐndù:
how can the doctrine of 'no-mind' be established?
The old doctrine says:
'The wisdom of all seeds exists,
and can illuminate perfectly.
Thus, all afflictions are exhausted,
called emptiness;
eternal and unchanging,
called wondrous existence.'
But the no-mind doctrine says:
'The essence of the wisdom of all seeds
is vast like the great void;
void yet capable of knowing,
nonexistent yet capable of responding.
Standing at the pinnacle of principles,
is it not precisely 'nonexistence'?'
This plan
was just a temporary measure to stave off hunger!
Do not ultimately betray the Tathāgata."
Wáng Wéndù's younger brother Āzhì,
was so wicked it was beyond measure,
and when he grew up, no one would marry him.
Sūn Xìnggōng had a daughter,
who was also eccentric and difficult,
and likewise had no prospects for marriage.
He therefore went to see Wéndù,
requesting to meet Āzhì.
After meeting him,
he deliberately said:
"This one is certainly acceptable,
quite unlike what people say;
how could he have remained unmarried until now?
I have a daughter,
who is not bad at all,
but I am a poor scholar,
and it is not fitting for me to discuss this with you,
but I wish to have Āzhì marry her."
Wéndù happily informed Lántián, saying:
"Xìnggōng came just now,
and suddenly said he wants to arrange a marriage with Āzhì."
Lántián was pleasantly surprised.
After the marriage was completed,
the daughter's stubbornness and foolishness
surpassed even Āzhì's.
Only then did they realize Xìnggōng's deceit.
Āzhì
was the childhood name of Wáng Chùzhī.
Qiánzhī's courtesy name was Wénjiāng,
and he was appointed as Assistant to the Regional Inspector,
but did not take up the post.
He married the daughter of Sūn Chuò from Tàiyuán,
whose childhood name was Āhéng.
Fàn Xuánpíng, as a person,
was fond of using clever schemes,
but sometimes lost opportunities due to overcalculating.
Once, having lost his official post, he lived in Dōngyáng,
while Grand Marshal Huán was in Nánzhōu,
so he went to seek refuge with him.
Huán was at that time wanting to recruit those who had been overlooked or stagnant,
in order to undermine the court;
moreover, Xuánpíng in the capital
had always enjoyed a good reputation,
so Huán thought he had come from afar to rely on him,
and was extremely delighted.
When Fàn entered the courtyard,
Huán leaned forward, eagerly looking,
and they talked and laughed very happily.
Turning to Yuán Hǔ, he said:
"Master Fàn could serve as Minister of Ceremonies."
As soon as Fàn sat down,
Huán thanked him for coming from afar.
Although Fàn had indeed come to seek Huán's patronage,
he feared that doing so would damage his reputation as being opportunistic,
so he said:
"Although I cherish the thought of paying homage to you,
it happens that my deceased son is buried here,
so I came to visit his grave."
Huán was disappointed and disheartened;
all the earlier anticipation and respect
vanished in an instant.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Initially,
Huán Wēn invited Fàn Wāng to serve as Chief Clerk to the General of the West,
and later petitioned for him to be appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
but he did not accept either position.
Returning to the capital,
he then requested to be appointed Prefect of Dōngyáng,
which made Huán deeply resent him.
Later, when Wāng was Governor of Xúzhōu,
Huán launched a northern campaign,
ordering Wāng to march from Liángguó,
but he missed the deadline.
Huán, bearing a grudge, petitioned to have Wāng reduced to a commoner.
Wāng lived in Wú,
and later went to Gūshú to see Huán.
Huán said to his subordinates:
'Xuánpíng has come to see me;
I should appoint him as General of the Guards.'
After a few days, Wāng declined and prepared to leave.
Huán asked:
'You just came;
why are you leaving so soon?'
Wāng replied:
'My young son died several years ago;
due to the turmoil in previous years,
he was temporarily buried in this region.
I came to retrieve his remains,
and now that the matter is settled, I am leaving.'
Huán became even angrier with him,
and ultimately did not give him any consideration."
When Xiè È was young,
he liked to wear a purple silk sachet,
dangling over his hand.
The Grand Tutor was troubled by this,
but did not want to hurt his feelings,
so he cunningly gambled with him,
and upon winning it, burned it.
È was the childhood name of Xiè Xuán.
Zhūgé Gōng, while serving in the Western court,
enjoyed a pure reputation from a young age,
and was esteemed by Wáng Yífǔ;
contemporary opinion also compared him to Wáng.
Later, he was slandered by his stepmother's clan,
who falsely accused him of being insane and rebellious.
As he was about to be exiled far away,
his friends, including Wáng Yífǔ,
went to his prison cart to bid him farewell.
Gōng asked:
"Why is the court exiling me?"
Wáng said:
"They say you are insane and rebellious."
Gōng said:
"If rebellious, then I should be executed;
if insane, why exile me?"
Gōng has appeared earlier.
When Duke Huán entered Shǔ,
reaching the midst of the Three Gorges,
someone in the troops captured a baby monkey.
The *Jīngzhōu Jì* states:
"The gorges stretch for seven hundred *li*,
with mountains lining both banks,
almost without interruption,
layered cliffs and overlapping barriers,
obscuring the sky and blocking the sun.
Often, high monkeys emit long cries,
their calls clear and far-reaching.
Fishermen sing:
'In Bādōng, the Three Gorges, Wū Gorge is the longest;
one cry of the monkeys, and tears soak my clothes.'"
Its mother followed along the bank, wailing mournfully,
for over a hundred *li* without leaving,
then leaped onto the boat,
and upon landing, immediately died.
When they cut open her belly to look,
her intestines were all broken into pieces.
Upon hearing this,
the Duke was furious and ordered the man dismissed.
When General Yīn of the Central Army was dismissed from office,
and lived in Xìn'ān,
he would often spend whole days writing characters in the air.
Officials and commoners from Yángzhōu, seeking to understand his meaning, followed him,
and secretly observed
that he only wrote
"Duōduō guàishì" (How strange! How strange!)
these four characters and nothing more.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Initially,
Hào, as General of the Central Army, garrisoned Shòuyáng.
The Qiāng leader Yáo Xiāng submitted a letter surrendering.
Later, having committed an offense,
Hào secretly plotted to kill him.
Meanwhile, there was a change in Guānzhōng;
Fú Jiàn died.
Hào feigned leading the army on a march,
claiming
'to repair the imperial tombs.'
Xiāng, serving as the vanguard,
became fearful and rebelled.
When the army reached Shānsāng,
hearing that Xiāng was approaching,
Hào abandoned the supplies and hurriedly retreated to defend Qiáo.
When Xiāng arrived,
he occupied Shānsāng,
and burned their boats and provisions.
He then advanced to Shòuyáng,
plundered the displaced people, and withdrew.
Many of Hào's soldiers deserted,
so General of the West Wēn petitioned to dismiss Hào,
and the General of the Pacifying Army memorialized to have Hào removed from office,
stripping him of his status and making him a commoner.
Hào hurried back to apologize for his offense.
Later, he was relocated to Xìn'ān County in Dōngyáng."
At Duke Huán's gathering, there was an aide whose chopsticks got stuck while picking up steamed shallots and he could not free them in time;
those sharing the meal did not help him either,
and he kept his chopsticks stuck without letting go,
making everyone at the table laugh.
Duke Huán said:
"When sharing the same plate, you still do not help each other,
let alone in times of danger and difficulty?"
He then ordered the aide dismissed from his post.
After Yīn Hào was dismissed from office,
he resented Jiǎnwén, saying:
"You've put someone up on a hundred-foot tower,
and then taken the ladder away."
*Continued Records of Jìnyáng Autumn* states:
"Although Hào was dismissed and demoted,
he remained composed and accepted his fate,
continuing to recite poetry elegantly.
Even his family members did not see any sorrow of exile in him.
His nephew Hán Bó initially followed him to the place of exile,
and after a year returned to the capital.
Hào had always loved him,
and when seeing him off by the waterside,
he recited Cáo Yán's poem:
'In wealth and honor, others gather;
in poverty and lowliness, even relatives depart.'
Then he shed tears."
The only instance where his grief was outwardly visible
was this one event.
Thus,
the stories of "writing in the air"
and "removing the ladder"
may not all be true.
After Dèng Xiá was dismissed from his post as Jìnglíng Administrator, he attended the imperial tombs.
On his way, he visited Grand Marshal Huán Wēn.
Huán asked him:
"Why have you grown even thinner?"
*Register of Grand Marshal's Subordinates* states:
"Dèng Xiá, courtesy name Yìngxuán,
was from Chénjùn.
He was the son of General Yuè of the Pacifying South.
His courage and strength surpassed others,
and his spirit overshadowed his contemporaries.
People of the time compared him to Fán Kuài.
He served as Huán Wēn's military advisor,
repeatedly following Wēn on campaigns.
He served as the Administrator of Jìnglíng.
During the battle of Fāngtóu,
Wēn, feeling both shame and resentment,
and also fearing Xiá,
dismissed Xiá from his post.
Xiá later fell ill and died."
Dèng replied:
"I feel ashamed compared to Shūdá,
yet I cannot help but regret the broken pot!"
*Separate Biography of Guō Línzōng* states:
"Mèng Mǐn from Jùlù,
courtesy name Shūdá,
was honest, simple, and straightforward.
He lived as a guest in Tàiyuán,
mingling among ordinary people,
and was not yet known.
Once, he went to the market to buy a pot,
and while carrying it on a pole, it fell and broke.
He walked straight away without looking back.
He happened to meet Guō Línzōng,
who saw this and found it remarkable.
He asked:
'It's a pity the pot broke;
why didn't you look back?'
Mèng replied:
'Since the pot is already broken,
what good does looking at it do?'
Línzōng admired his decisiveness,
and from this recognized his virtuous nature,
saying he would surely become a fine scholar.
He encouraged him to study.
After ten years of traveling and learning,
he became well-known.
The three highest offices all sought to recruit him,
but he declined.
The eastern region considered him a virtuous and worthy man."
After Huán Xuānwǔ deposed Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Xī and his son,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"We must cut off close affections
to preserve long-term plans.
If we eliminate Grand Tutor Xī and his son,
there will be no future worries."
Jiǎnwén personally replied to the memorial:
"What is unbearable to say,
how much more unbearable to act upon?"
Xuānwǔ submitted another memorial,
with increasingly urgent and bitter language.
Jiǎnwén replied again:
"If the Jìn dynasty's fortune endures,
you, esteemed sir, should respectfully carry out this edict.
But if the great mandate has departed,
I beg to step aside for the worthy!"
When Huán Wēn read the edict,
his hands trembled and he broke into a sweat.
At this point, he stopped.
Grand Tutor Xī and his son
were exiled to Xīn'ān.
*Biography of Sīmǎ Xī* states:
"Xī, courtesy name Dàoshēng,
was the fourth son of Emperor Yuán.
He was initially enfeoffed as Prince of Wǔlíng
and appointed Grand Tutor.
From a young age, he disliked study
and was fond of martial prowess, violent and unrestrained.
At the time, Tàizōng was assisting in governance,
and Xī, as the senior clansman, resented not holding power.
He often harbored indignation
and planned to kill Huán Wēn when he entered the court.
After Tàizōng ascended the throne,
Prince Xīn of Cài, Huǎng, confessed first,
implicating Xī and his son Zōng in plotting rebellion.
The officials recommended execution for Xī and others,
but the edict pardoned them,
exiling them to Xīn'ān.
Before his downfall,
for four or five years,
Xī enjoyed singing funeral dirges,
shaking a large bell himself,
and having his attendants practice harmonizing.
Also, at banquets,
performers would sing songs of farewell from Xīn'ān,
their voices very sorrowful.
Later, he was indeed exiled to Xīn'ān."
After Huán Xuán's defeat,
Yīn Zhòngwén returned to serve as Grand Marshal's consultant.
His demeanor seemed uncertain,
no longer like before.
In front of the Grand Marshal's office hall,
there was an old locust tree,
very lush and spreading.
On the first day of the month,
while Yīn was in the hall with others,
he gazed at the locust tree for a long time,
sighed, and said:
"This locust tree, though flourishing,
has no more vitality!"
*Records of Jìn Āndì* states:
"After Huán Xuán's defeat,
Yīn Zhòngwén returned to the capital.
Gāozǔ, considering that he had escorted the two empresses
and had publicly proclaimed the great trust,
appointed him as Chief Clerk of the Garrison Army.
He himself thought that as a senior figure of reputation,
his position and treatment were extremely important.
Yet later, those like Xiè Hùn,
whom he had once associated with,
now stood shoulder to shoulder with him as equals.
He often felt discontented and lost.
Later, he was indeed exiled to Xìn'ān."
Yīn Zhòngwén, having long enjoyed fame and prestige,
believed he would certainly assist in governing the court.
Suddenly appointed as Administrator of Dōngyáng,
he felt deeply discontented.
*Records of Jìn Āndì* states:
"Later, Zhòngwén was sent to Dōngyáng,
growing even more resentful and aggrieved.
He conspired with Huán Yǐn to rebel,
and was subsequently executed.
Once, Zhòngwén looked in a mirror and could not see his head,
and soon disaster befell him."
When he reached his commandery,
arriving at Fùyáng,
he sighed with emotion:
"Looking at these mountains and rivers,
surely another Sūn Bófú will arise!"
Sūn Cè
was from Fùchūn.
Hence, he sighed at this.
Hé Qiáo was extremely frugal by nature.
His family had fine plum trees,
and Wáng Wǔzǐ asked for some,
but was given only a few dozen.
Wáng Wǔzǐ took advantage of Hé's being on duty,
leading a group of young men who could eat a lot,
carrying axes to the garden.
After eating their fill together,
they cut down the trees,
and sent a cartload of branches to Hé.
He asked:
"How do these compare to your plums?"
After receiving them,
Hé only laughed.
*Praises of Jìn Nobles* states:
"Qiáo's nature was unyielding;
his household wealth rivaled that of princes and dukes,
yet he was extremely frugal,
risking a reputation for violating righteousness."
*Forest of Conversations* states:
"When Qiáo's younger brothers went to the garden to eat plums,
he would even count the pits and charge them.
That is why his brother-in-law Wáng Jì cut down the trees."
Wáng Róng was frugal and stingy.
When his nephew got married,
he gave him a single-layered robe as a gift,
but later demanded it back.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Róng's nature was extremely frugal;
he could not provide for himself adequately,
and his wealth never left his household.
People of the time said it was an incurable disease."
The Minister of Education, Wáng Róng,
was both noble and wealthy.
His estates, servants, and herds,
as well as his fertile fields and water-powered trip-hammers,
had no equal in Luòyáng.
Deeds and documents piled up in disorder;
he and his wife would often spread out counting rods by candlelight to calculate their accounts.
*Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn* states:
"Róng's nature was simple and direct;
he did not cultivate an imposing demeanor.
He treated himself very meagerly,
yet his property and assets were excessively abundant.
Commentators believed this diminished the gravitas expected of a high minister."
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Róng was fond of managing his livelihood;
his gardens and fields were spread all over the empire.
The old couple
would often use ivory counting rods to calculate their family wealth day and night."
*Jìnyáng Qiū* states:
"Róng amassed much wealth and valuables,
yet often acted as if it were not enough.
Some said Róng intentionally used this to conceal his true self."
Dài Kuí discussed this, saying:
"Wáng Róng maintained obscurity and silence during times of peril and disorder,
thereby avoiding worry and calamity.
Being both intelligent and wise,
he succeeded in this.
Some said:
'Is this truly the way a high minister should apply his mind?'
Kuí said:
'Circumstances have their dangers and ease;
times have their darkness and clarity.
If it were as you say,
then figures like Qú Yuàn
and Jì Zhá
would all be at fault.
Looking at it from ancient times,
how could it be just Wáng Róng alone?'"
Wáng Róng had some fine plum trees.
When he sold the plums,
he feared others would obtain the seeds,
so he always bored holes in the pits.
Wáng Róng's daughter married Péi Wěi
and borrowed tens of thousands in cash from him.
When his daughter returned home,
Róng looked displeased.
His daughter promptly repaid the money,
and only then did he relax.
When Wèi, the Governor of Jiāng Province, was in Xúnyáng,
*Yǒngjiā Liúrén Míng* states:
"Wèi Zhǎn, styled Dàoshū,
was from Ānyì in Hédōng.
His grandfather was Liè,
Protector of Péngchéng.
His father was Sháo,
Magistrate of Guǎngpíng.
Zhǎn, in the early Guāngxī period, was appointed General Soaring Eagle and
Governor of Jiāng Province."
An old acquaintance sought him out,
but he paid him no attention at all,
only sending him
one *jīn* of "Wangbuliuxing" herb.
This person, upon receiving the gift,
immediately ordered his carriage and left.
*Běncǎo* states:
"Wangbuliuxing grows on great mountains.
It treats metal wounds,
dispels wind.
Taken over a long time,
it lightens the body."
Lǐ Hóngfàn heard of this and said:
"My maternal uncle is so harsh and ungenerous,
he even puts plants to such use!"
*Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Lǐ Guǐ, styled Hóngfàn,
was from Jiāngxià.
He served up to the position of Gentleman in the Imperial Secretariat."
According to the record, Guǐ
was the nephew of the Liú family.
This should refer to Hóngdù,
not Hóngfàn.
Chancellor Wáng Dǎo practiced frugality.
The sweet fruits under his tent
overflowed and were not distributed.
When spring arrived, they rotted and spoiled.
The military supervisor reported this,
and the Duke ordered them discarded,
saying:
"Be careful not to let the Eldest Young Master know."
This refers to Wáng Yuè.
During Sū Jùn's rebellion,
Grand Marshal Yǔ Liàng fled south and went to see Duke Táo.
Duke Táo greatly admired and valued him.
Táo's nature was frugal and stingy.
When they ate,
they ate *xiè* (Chinese scallions).
Yǔ therefore left the white bulbs.
Táo asked:
"What are you using these for?"
Yǔ said:
"They can still be planted."
Thereupon, Táo greatly admired Yǔ, saying he was not only refined and cultured,
but also practical in managing affairs.
Duke Xī Chāo amassed great wealth,
accumulating tens of millions in cash.
His son, Jiābīn (Xī Chāo), held a very different view.
He would often pay his morning respects.
According to the Xī family rules,
younger generation members did not sit in his presence.
So, leaning against something, they conversed for a long time,
and the topic eventually turned to wealth and goods.
Duke Xī said:
"You simply want my money, that's all!"
He then opened his treasury for one day,
allowing him to use the money as he wished.
Duke Xī initially thought he would only spend a few million or so.
But Jiābīn, in that single day, requested money to give to relatives and friends,
and nearly exhausted it all.
Duke Xī heard of this
and was so shocked and astonished he could not stop himself.
*Zhōngxīng Shū* states:
"Chāo, from youth, was outstanding and unrestrained,
possessing a magnanimity rare in his generation."
Shí Chóng, whenever he invited guests to a banquet,
would often have beautiful women serve wine.
If a guest did not finish his wine,
he would have eunuchs take turns beheading the serving woman.
Chancellor Wáng Dǎo and General-in-Chief Wáng Dūn once went together to visit Chóng.
The Chancellor normally could not drink,
but he forced himself each time,
until he was thoroughly drunk.
But when it came to the General-in-Chief,
he firmly refused to drink,
to see what would happen.
After three women had already been beheaded,
his expression remained unchanged,
and he still would not drink.
The Chancellor reproached him,
but the General-in-Chief said:
"He's killing his own household people;
what business is it of yours?"
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Shí Chóng, as Governor of Jīng Province,
plundered, robbed, and killed people,
thereby amassing enormous wealth."
*Wáng Chéngxiàng Déyīn Jì* states:
"The Chancellor was always highly regarded by his uncles.
Wáng Jūnfū (Wáng Kǎi) once asked Wáng Dūn:
'I hear your cousin is a fine man
and also understands music.
I wish to have some musicians perform;
can you bring him along?'
So they went.
A flute player had a minor memory lapse.
Jūnfū heard it
and had a eunuch beat him to death under the steps.
His expression did not change.
When the Chancellor returned,
he said:
'I fear this gentleman, in his conduct in the world,
is bound to have affairs like this.'"
The two accounts differ,
so they are recorded in detail here.
Shí Chóng's toilet
always had over ten maidservants standing in attendance,
all dressed in beautiful garments and adorned with ornaments.
They had items such as jiǎjiān powder
and chénxiāng juice prepared,
leaving nothing incomplete.
Moreover, they would give guests new clothes to wear upon exiting.
Many guests were too embarrassed to use the toilet.
When General Wáng Dàjiāngjūn went,
he removed his old clothes,
put on the new ones,
and his expression was haughty.
The maidservants said to each other:
"This guest is certainly capable of becoming a rebel."
The Forest of Tales says:
"Liú Shí visited Shí Chóng,
and when he went to use the toilet,
he saw a large bed with crimson gauze curtains,
mattresses and cushions that were extremely luxurious,
and two maids holding brocade incense pouches.
Shí immediately turned and fled,
then said to Chóng:
'I mistakenly entered your inner chamber just now.'
Chóng said:
'That was the toilet.'"
Emperor Wǔ once visited Wáng Wǔzǐ's home.
Wǔzǐ served a feast,
using only glassware.
There were over a hundred maidservants,
all dressed in silk trousers and skirts,
who carried food and drink in their hands.
The steamed suckling pig was exceptionally rich and delicious,
different from the usual taste.
The emperor found it strange and asked about it.
He replied:
"It was fed with human milk."
The emperor was very displeased,
and before finishing the meal,
he left.
Wáng and Shí did not know how to make such skirts.
An alternative character is bǎi.
Wáng Jūnfū used malt sugar paste to wash his pots,
while Shí Jìlún used candles as fuel for cooking.
Jūnfū made a purple silk cloth screen with a green silk lining stretching for forty lǐ,
and Shí Chóng made a brocade screen stretching for fifty lǐ to rival it.
Shí used pepper to make mud for plastering,
while Wáng used red stone paste to plaster his walls.
The Praise of the Jin Nobles says:
"Wáng Kǎi, styled Jūnfū,
was from Dōnghǎi
and was the son of Wáng Sù.
Although he lacked restraint in conduct,
he gained fame from a young age for his talent and ability,
and was praised for his public service.
As a member of the imperial family by marriage,
and with the Jin dynasty's lenient governance,
coupled with his extremely extravagant nature,
according to old regulations,
the zhèn bird was not allowed to cross the river,
because if its feathers fell into wine,
it would certainly kill people.
When Kǎi served as Yìjūn,
he obtained a zhèn bird from Shí Chóng and raised it.
It was as large as a goose,
with a beak over a chǐ long,
and fed solely on snakes and vipers.
The Sīlǐ official submitted a report impeaching Kǎi
and Chóng, but the emperor pardoned them both,
and the bird was burned in the capital's streets.
Kǎi indulged his desires and displayed his arrogance,
without any fear or restraint.
He served as Hòujūn Jiāngjūn
and upon his death, was given the posthumous title 'Chǒu' (Ugly)."
Shí Chóng would prepare bean porridge for guests,
and it would be ready in an instant.
He could always obtain leek and water mallow pickles even in winter.
Also, although his oxen were inferior in appearance and strength to Wáng Kǎi's oxen,
when he went out with Kǎi,
even if they set out very late,
and raced to enter Luòchéng,
Chóng's oxen, though dozens of steps behind,
would speed like flying birds,
and Kǎi's oxen, running at full speed, could not catch up.
Kǎi often felt frustrated over these three matters.
So he secretly bribed the overseer in Chóng's household and the chariot driver,
asking for the reasons.
The overseer said:
"Beans are extremely difficult to cook,
so we pre-cook them and grind them into powder.
When guests arrive,
we make plain porridge and add the powder to it.
The leek and water mallow pickles are made by pounding leek roots,
mixed with wheat sprouts."
He also asked the driver why the oxen were so fast.
The driver said:
"The oxen are not inherently slow;
it's just that the driver does not control them properly.
In urgent situations, if you let them lean to one side of the shaft,
they will run faster."
Kǎi followed all these methods,
and thus vied for superiority.
When Shí Chóng later found out,
he killed all those who had revealed the secrets.
The Praise of the Jin Nobles says:
"Chóng had a chivalrous nature
and competed with Wáng Kǎi in showing off."
Wáng Jūnfū had an ox
named
"Eight Hundred Lǐ Bó,"
and he often polished its hooves and horns.
Wáng Wǔzǐ said to Jūnfū:
"My archery is not as good as yours,
but today I propose a wager with your ox:
I will stake ten million against it."
Jūnfū, relying on his quick hands,
and thinking that such a fine creature would not be killed,
agreed.
He let Wǔzǐ shoot first.
Wǔzǐ hit the target with his first shot,
then sat back in his folding chair,
shouting to his attendants:
"Quickly, bring me the ox's heart!"
In a moment,
the roasted heart arrived,
and he took one bite and left.
The Classic of Ox Physiognomy says:
"The Classic of Oxen originated from Nìng Qī,
and was passed down to Bǎilǐ Xī.
During the Hàn dynasty, Xuē Gōng of Héxī obtained the book
and used it to judge oxen,
with almost no errors.
Originally, it was meant for selecting oxen to carry heavy loads over long distances,
the text was not widely circulated.
By the Wèi dynasty,
Gāotáng Shēng passed it on to Jìn Emperor Xuān,
and later Wáng Kǎi obtained the book."
I note that according to this Classic of Physiognomy:
"If the yīn rainbow connects to the neck,
it can run a thousand lǐ."
The annotation says:
"The yīn rainbow refers to
two white tendons from the tailbone connecting to the neck,
which is what Nìng Qī described."
Kǎi's ox
likely also had a yīn rainbow.
Nìng Qī's Classic says:
"The head should be held high,
the body should be compact,
large flanks and sparse ribs make chewing difficult,
and a dragon-like head with protruding eyes indicates a tendency to jump.
Also, the horns should be slender,
the body short,
and the shape should be like a scroll."
Wáng Jūnfū once punished a person for not wearing extra undergarments.
He then directly placed him inside a winding pavilion with multiple layers,
not allowing anyone to take him out.
The person starved for days,
becoming disoriented and not knowing where to go.
Later, through some chance, he was on the verge of death,
and only then was he released.
Shí Chóng and Wáng Kǎi vied in extravagance,
both exhausting all means of splendor and beauty
to adorn their carriages and attire.
The *Continuation of the Records of Literary Figures* states:
"Chóng's accumulated assets amounted to tens of millions in gold.
His residences, carriages, and horses
usurped the standards of royalty.
His kitchen provisions invariably included the rarest delicacies from land and water.
His rear chambers housed hundreds of women,
all trailing fine silk embroideries,
wearing gold and jade earrings,
while the musicians among them
were the finest selections of the age.
He built pavilions and dug ponds,
exhausting all human ingenuity.
With noble relatives such as Yáng Xiù
and Wáng Kǎi and their ilk, he competed in extravagance and luxury,
and Chóng stood as the foremost among them.
Xiù and others often felt ashamed and envious,
believing they could not match him."
Emperor Wǔ,
who was Wáng Kǎi's maternal nephew,
often assisted Kǎi.
Once, he bestowed upon Kǎi a coral tree
about two feet tall.
Its branches and stems were luxuriant and well-spread,
rarely matched in the world.
Kǎi showed it to Chóng.
After looking at it,
Chóng struck it with an iron *rúyì* scepter,
and it shattered at the touch.
Kǎi was both regretful
and thought Chóng was jealous of his treasure,
so his tone and expression became very severe.
Chóng said:
"Do not be troubled;
I will now repay you."
He then ordered his attendants to bring out all his coral trees.
There were some three or four feet tall,
with branches and trunks unparalleled in the world,
six or seven of them so dazzlingly brilliant they overwhelmed the eyes,
and many others comparable to Kǎi's.
Kǎi was left bewildered and crestfallen.
The *Records of Strange Things from Southern Regions* states:
"Coral grows in the Great Qin Kingdom.
There is an island in the swelling sea,
about seven or eight hundred *li* from that country,
named Coral Tree Island.
At the bottom lies a flat rock,
with water over twenty *zhang* deep.
Coral grows upon the rock.
When first growing, it is white
and soft, resembling a mushroom.
The people of that country ride large boats,
carrying iron nets,
which they first sink underwater.
After one year, coral grows within the meshes of the net,
its color still yellow,
with branches and stems interlocking,
reaching three or four feet in height,
the larger ones over a foot in circumference.
After three years, it turns red.
They then use iron rakes to uproot it,
tie the iron net to the boat,
and use a windlass to lift the net, then cut and chisel it at will.
They work freely as they wish.
If they do not chisel it in time,
it withers and becomes infested with worms.
The larger pieces are delivered to the royal palace,
while the finer ones are sold."
The *Extensive Records* states:
"Large coral
can be used as cart axles."
Wáng Wǔzi was reprimanded
and moved his residence to the foot of Běimáng.
The *Praise of the Various Dukes of Jin* states:
"Jì was at odds with his elder cousin Tián.
Jì was appointed Governor of Hénán,
but before he could assume office,
while passing by the royal palace,
his attendants did not promptly clear the road.
Jì whipped them in front of the carriage,
and the authorities reported this, leading to his dismissal.
Commentators considered Jì lacking in magnanimity.
Soon after, he was transferred to the position of Grand Coachman,
but by then Wáng Tián had already gained favor and appointment,
so Jì was eventually relegated to a provincial post."
At that time, the population was dense and land was expensive.
Jì was fond of horseback archery,
so he bought land to make a racecourse,
and lined the entire perimeter of the course with strung coins.
People of the time called it
"the Golden Moat."
Some texts record "moat" as "racecourse."
Shí Chóng often went with Wáng Dūn to the school to play.
Seeing the portraits of Yán
and Yuán (the *Family Sayings of Confucius* states:
"Yán Huí, styled Zǐyuān,
was from Lǔ.
He was twenty-nine years younger than Confucius,
yet his hair turned white early,
and he died prematurely at thirty-two.")
Yuán Xiàn has been mentioned previously.
He sighed and said:
"If I could ascend the hall of Confucius alongside them,
why would there be any gap between me and others?"
Wáng said:
"I do not know about the others,
but Zǐgòng is somewhat closer to you."
The *Records of the Grand Historian* states:
"Duānmù Cì, styled Zǐgòng,
was from Wèi.
He once served as Prime Minister of Lǔ,
accumulated a fortune of a thousand gold,
and died in Qí."
Shí sternly said:
"A gentleman should ensure both his person and his reputation are secure and prosperous.
Why must one speak to others of living behind a broken jar window!"
Yuán Xiàn used a broken jar as a large window.
Prince Péngchéng had a swift ox,
which he cherished deeply.
Zhū Fèng's *History of Jin* states:
"Péngchéng Prince Mù, Quán,
styled Zǐyú,
was the son of Kuí, younger brother of Emperor Xuān.
He was enfeoffed in the first year of the Tàishǐ era."
Grand Commandant Wáng went shooting with him
and won it as a wager.
Prince Péngchéng said:
"If you wish to ride it yourself, that is one matter;
but if you intend to eat it,
I will replace it with twenty fat oxen.
This way, you do not miss out on eating,
and my beloved is also spared."
Wáng then had it killed and eaten.
When Wáng Yòujūn was young,
he sat in the lowest seat at Zhōu Hóu's gathering
and was served ox heart to eat.
From this, people's view of him changed.
It was customary to consider ox heart a delicacy,
so Xīzhī was served it first.
Wèi Wǔ had a singing girl
whose voice was exceptionally clear and lofty,
but whose temperament was extremely vile.
He wanted to kill her but cherished her talent;
he wanted to keep her but could not endure her.
So he selected a hundred girls and trained them all at once.
After a short while,
indeed, one girl's voice matched hers,
so he killed the one with the vile temperament.
Wáng Lántián had an impatient temperament.
Once, while eating an egg,
he tried to stab it with chopsticks
but failed.
He became greatly enraged,
picked it up, and threw it to the ground.
The egg rolled on the ground without stopping,
so he stepped down and tried to crush it with the teeth of his clogs,
but again failed.
Furious,
he picked it up from the ground, put it in his mouth,
bit it, and immediately spat it out.
Wáng Yòujūn heard of this and laughed heartily, saying:
"Even if Ānqī had such a temperament,
he would still be utterly unworthy of mention,
let alone Lántián!"
The *Records of the Restoration* states:
"Shù was noble, pure, simple, and upright,
seldom yielding to others,
only burdened by his impatient temperament."
Ānqī
was Shù's father.
He was renowned for his virtue,
as previously mentioned.
Sīzhōu Wáng once traveled through snow to visit Wáng Chī.
Wáng Húzhī
and Wáng Tián have both been mentioned previously.
Tián's childhood name was Chīhǔ.
Sīzhōu's words and tone were slightly at odds with Chī,
so Chī's expression turned displeased.
Sīzhōu sensed the hostility,
so he moved his seat closer,
grasped Chī's arm, and said:
"How could you ever be worthy of contending with your elder brother?"
According to the *Genealogy of the Wáng Clan*:
Húzhī was Tián's elder cousin from the same paternal grandfather.
Chī brushed his hand away and said:
"Cold as a ghost's hand,
forcing yourself to grab someone's arm!"
Wáng Xù repeatedly slandered Yīn Jīngzhōu (Yīn Zhòngkān) to Wáng Guóbǎo,
and Yīn was deeply troubled by this,
so he sought a strategy from Wáng Dōngtíng (Wáng Xún).
Wáng said:
"You simply need to visit Wáng Xù frequently,
and each time you go, have others leave the room,
then discuss other matters.
In this way,
the friendship between the two Wángs will be broken."
Yīn followed his advice.
Guóbǎo saw Wáng Xù and asked:
"Lately, what have you been discussing with Zhòngkān in private?"
Xù replied:
"It's just our usual interactions,
nothing else was discussed."
Guóbǎo believed Xù was hiding something from him,
and indeed, their affection grew increasingly distant,
and the slander ceased.
Note: Guóbǎo gained favor with Prince Kuàijī,
and it was through Xù that he advanced.
They were evildoers seeking each other out,
like merchants in a market,
yet they ultimately faced execution and extermination,
without ever betraying each other.
How could Zhòngkān's slight intervention
have created such a rift?
Emperor Wén of Wèi was jealous of his younger brother, Rènchéng Wáng Cáo Zhāng, for his bravery and vigor.
Once, while playing weiqi together in Biàn Tàihòu's chamber,
they were eating dates.
Emperor Wén placed poison in the stems of some dates.
He selected the edible ones for himself and offered them,
but the prince, unaware,
ended up eating the poisoned ones as well.
After being poisoned,
the empress dowager sought water to save him.
The emperor had previously ordered his attendants to destroy all bottles and jars,
so the empress dowager ran barefoot to the well,
but had nothing to draw water with.
After a short while,
he died.
The *Wèi Lüè* states:
"Rènchéng Wēi Wáng Zhāng,
courtesy name Zǐwén,
was the second son of Tàizǔ and Biàn Tàihòu.
He was bold and courageous with a yellow beard.
When campaigning north in Dàijùn,
he alone broke through enemy lines with over a hundred of his men and escaped.
Tàizǔ heard of this and said:
'My yellow-bearded son can be of use!'"
The *Wèi Zhì Chūnqiū* states:
"In the third year of Huángchū,
Zhāng came to court.
Earlier, Zhāng had inquired about the imperial seal and ribbons,
showing rebellious intentions,
so when he came to court, he was not immediately granted an audience.
It was due to this anger and fear that he died suddenly."
The emperor also wanted to harm Dōng'ē (Cáo Zhí),
but the empress dowager said:
"You have already killed my Rènchéng,
you must not kill my Dōng'ē as well."
The *Wèi Zhì·Fāngjì Zhuàn* states:
"Emperor Wén asked the dream interpreter Zhōu Xuān:
'I dreamed of grinding the inscriptions off coins,
but the more I tried to erase them, the brighter they became.
What does this mean?'
Xuān was troubled and did not reply.
The emperor pressed him,
and Xuān said:
'This concerns Your Majesty's family matters.
Although you wish to act,
the empress dowager does not consent,
which is why the attempt to erase them only makes them brighter.'
The emperor wanted to punish his brother Zhí,
but under pressure from the empress dowager,
he only demoted and reduced his noble rank."
Wáng Hún's later wife
was a woman from the Yán family of Lángyé.
At the time, Wáng was the governor of Xúzhōu.
After the wedding ceremony was completed,
Wáng was about to return the bow,
but the onlookers all said:
"You are a marquis and a regional general,
while the bride is a commoner of the region.
It is likely inappropriate for you to return the bow."
So Wáng stopped.
Wǔzǐ (Wáng Jì) believed that because his father did not return the bow,
the ceremony was incomplete,
and they might not be considered husband and wife.
He did not bow to her,
calling her merely Concubine Yán.
The Yán woman felt ashamed.
But because of the family's high status,
she ultimately did not dare to leave.
The rites of marriage
are of great importance to human relations.
How could a single failure to bow reduce someone to the status of a concubine?
The words of the *Shì Shuō*
are thus erroneous.
Lù Píngyuán (Lù Jī) was defeated at Héqiáo,
slandered by Lú Zhì,
and executed.
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* states:
"Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng campaigned against Chángshā Wáng Yì,
appointing Lù as the commander of the vanguard forces."
The *Lù Jī Biézhuàn* states:
"Lú Zhì, the senior administrator of Chéngdū Wáng,
had different inclinations from Lù Jī's brother, Lù Yún.
Additionally, the eunuch Mèng Jiǔ requested from Yǐng to be appointed as the magistrate of Hándān.
Yǐng instructed that the matter be handed to Yún,
who was then the Left Sima.
Yún said:
'A castrated person
should not govern the people!'
Upon hearing this, Jiǔ resented Yún,
and together with Zhì, slandered them daily.
When Jī suffered a major defeat at Qīlǐ Jiàn,
Jiǔ falsely accused Jī of causing it through rebellion,
so Yǐng sent Qiān Xiù to execute Jī.
Before this,
Jī dreamed at night of a black curtain wrapping around his carriage,
and no matter how he tried, he could not open it with his hands,
which he considered ominous.
The next morning,
Xiù's soldiers suddenly arrived.
Jī asked for his military attire,
but ended up wearing a robe and cap to meet Xiù.
His demeanor was calm and composed,
and he was then killed.
He was forty-three years old at the time.
None of the soldiers failed to shed tears.
On that day, heaven and earth were shrouded in fog,
a great wind broke trees,
and snow piled a foot high on level ground."
Gān Bǎo's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Earlier,
when Lù Kàng executed Bù Chǎn,
he exterminated the entire family of one hundred people,
which was criticized by those with insight.
When Jī
and Yún were killed,
their three clans were wiped out without exception."
Facing execution, he sighed:
"I wish to hear the cranes cry at Huátíng again—
but can that ever happen?"
The *Bā Wáng Gùshì* states:
"Huátíng
was a villa in the outskirts of Yóuquán County in Wú,
with clear springs and lush forests.
After Wú was pacified,
Lù Jī and his brother roamed there together for over ten years."
The *Yǔ Lín* states:
"When Jī was the commander of Héběi,
he heard the sound of warning horns
and said to Sūn Chéng:
'Hearing this is not as good as the cry of cranes at Huátíng.'
That is why he sighed thus when facing execution."
Liú Kūn was skilled at recruiting followers
but poor at comforting and controlling them.
Although thousands might join him in a single day,
just as many would flee and scatter.
Thus, he ultimately achieved nothing.
Dèng Chàng's *Jìn Jì* states:
"Kūn served as the governor of Bìngzhōu,
forming alliances,
leading military campaigns,
but failing to comfort the people within his territory.
This led to the loss of his army and followers,
and he achieved no success."
Jìng Chè notes:
"Kūn became the governor of Bìngzhōu in the first year of Yǒngjiā.
At that time, Jìnyáng was an empty city,
with bandits attacking from all sides.
Yet he was able to gather followers
and resist Liú Yuān
and Shí Lè. Over ten years,
he suffered defeats but could recover.
If he truly could not comfort and control his people,
how could he have achieved this?
During times of famine,
with no smoke from cooking fires for miles around,
how could thousands of people join him in a single day?
If thousands left him in a single day,
how could he have endured a decade of great hardship?"
When Wáng Píngzǐ (Wáng Chéng) first went down to the east,
the Prime Minister (Wáng Dǎo) said to the Grand General (Wáng Dūn):
"We cannot let that Qiāng man go east again."
Píngzǐ's face resembled that of a Qiāng person.
Note: Wáng Chéng was ultimately killed by Wáng Dūn.
The Prime Minister was a man of reputation and virtue;
how could he have uttered such words?
When the Grand General Wáng Dūn raised his rebellion,
Chéngxiàng Wáng Dǎo and his brothers went to the palace to apologize.
Zhōu Hóu (Zhōu Yǐ) was deeply concerned for the Wáng family,
and when he first entered,
he wore a very worried expression.
Chéngxiàng called out to Zhōu Hóu, saying:
"I entrust the lives of my entire clan to you!"
Zhōu walked straight past without responding.
Once inside,
he strenuously worked to protect and save them.
After they were released,
Zhōu was greatly pleased,
and drank wine.
When he came out, the Wáng brothers were still at the gate.
Zhōu said:
"This year, when we kill all those rebel scoundrels,
we should take a gold seal as big as a dipper and tie it behind our elbows."
When the Grand General arrived at Shítóu,
he asked Chéngxiàng:
"Is Zhōu Hóu fit to be one of the Three Dukes?"
Chéngxiàng did not answer.
He asked again:
"Is he fit to be Shàngshū Lìng?"
Again, he received no response.
Thereupon, he said:
"If that's the case,
then we have no choice but to kill him!"
Again, there was silence.
Later, when Zhōu Hóu was killed,
Chéngxiàng later learned that Zhōu Hóu had saved him,
and sighed, saying:
"I did not kill Zhōu Hóu,
yet Zhōu Hóu died because of me.
In the netherworld, I have wronged this man!"
Yú Yù's *Jìn Shū* states:
"When Dūn captured the capital,
his cānjūn Lǚ Yī persuaded Dūn, saying:
'Zhōu Yǐ
and Dài Yuān
both enjoy great fame and prestige,
enough to mislead the masses.
Judging by their recent words,
they show no signs of shame or fear.
If they are not eliminated,
our campaign will not cease.'
Dūn immediately agreed with him,
and subsequently killed Yuān
and Yǐ. Earlier,
when Yī was a Táiláng,
Yuān, having taken up his official post,
was by nature arrogant,
and treated Yī as a petty man.
Therefore, Yī now promoted his proposal."
Wáng Dǎo and
Wēn Qiáo both had an audience with Emperor Míng.
The Emperor asked Wēn about the reasons why their predecessors had gained the empire.
Wēn did not answer.
After a moment, Wáng said:
"Wēn Qiáo is young and not yet fully acquainted with these matters;
allow your servant to explain them to Your Majesty."
Wáng then gave a full account of how Xuānwáng (Sīmǎ Yì) began the enterprise,
exterminating famous clans,
and favoring and promoting those who were like-minded.
He also spoke of events at the end of Wénwáng's (Sīmǎ Zhāo's) time,
namely the affair of Duke Gāoguìxiāng.
(Regarding) Xuānwáng's founding of the enterprise,
he executed Cáo Shuǎng,
and appointed men like Jiǎng Jǐ.
The affair of Duke Gāoguìxiāng
has already been mentioned above.
When Emperor Míng heard this,
he covered his face, laid it on the bed, and said:
"If it is as you say,
how can our dynasty's blessings last long!"
Grand General Wáng once said in front of a gathering:
"None of the Zhōu clan members have ever held the position of one of the Three Dukes."
Someone replied:
"Only Zhōu Hóu (Zhōu Yǐ) had five horses leading but could not win."
The Grand General said:
"I and Zhōu
met in Luòxià,
and with one meeting, we understood each other completely.
But encountering a time of turmoil,
things have come to this!"
And he wept.
Dèng Càn's *Jìn Jì* states:
"A cānjūn of Wáng Dūn's
was playing chūpú in Dūn's presence.
Just as he was about to complete his set,
his horse piece was killed.
He thereupon said:
'The Zhōu family for generations has enjoyed fine repute,
yet none reached the position of the Three Dukes.
Bórén (Zhōu Yǐ) nearly achieved it but did not succeed,
rather like this official's horse piece.'
Dūn sighed with emotion and wept, saying:
'When Bórén was a youth,
I served together with him in the Eastern Palace.
We met just once,
and with open hearts, I already promised him the position of the Three Dukes.
Who could have foreseen such misfortune,
that he would be condemned by the royal law?
The depth of my sorrow and regret—
how can words express it!'"
When Wēn Gōng (Wēn Qiáo) first received orders from Minister over the Masses Liú Kūn to urge the Prince of Lángyá to ascend the throne,
his mother, née Cuī, firmly tried to detain him.
Qiáo tore his robe and left.
The *Wēn Shì Pǔ* states:
"Qiáo's father, Wēn Chān,
married the daughter of Cuī Cān of Qīnghé."
Even after he achieved high rank and honor,
his local evaluation still did not pass.
Every time he was enfeoffed, an imperial edict had to be issued.
Yú Yù's *Jìn Shū* states:
"When Emperor Yuán ascended the throne,
he appointed Wēn Qiáo as Sànqí Shìláng.
Qiáo, because his mother had died,
and he was pressed by the rebels,
could not go to attend her burial,
firmly declined.
An edict stated:
'Qiáo, because he has not yet buried (his mother),
and court opinions are also rather divided,
has not accepted the appointment.
Let the Eight Ministers deliberate,
and I will decide the matter.'"
Yǔ Gōng (Yǔ Liàng) wanted to summon Zhōu Zǐnán (Zhōu Shào) to office.
Zǐnán held to his refusal all the more firmly.
Whenever Yǔ went to visit Zhōu,
Yǔ would enter through the south gate,
and Zhōu would leave through the back door.
Once, Yǔ went straight in and arrived suddenly,
and Zhōu had no time to leave.
They faced each other the whole day.
Yǔ asked Zhōu for food.
Zhōu brought out vegetarian fare.
Yǔ also forced himself to eat,
and they were extremely joyful.
They also discussed the affairs of the world,
and agreed to recommend each other,
to share the responsibility of assisting the age.
After Zhōu took office,
he reached the rank of General with a salary of two thousand shi.
The *Xúnyáng Jì* states:
"Zhōu Shào, styled Zǐnán,
lived in seclusion with Zhái Tāng of Nányáng on Mount Lú in Xúnyáng.
When Yǔ Liàng came to Jiāngzhōu,
he heard of the reputations of Zhái
and Zhōu,
fastened his belt, put on his shoes, and went to visit them.
Hearing that Yǔ had arrived,
they turned to avoid him.
Liàng later went secretly,
and found Shào shooting birds in the woods.
He therefore went forward and spoke with him.
Upon returning, he said:
'This man can be summoned to office.'
He immediately promoted him to Zhèn Mán Hùjūn
and Tàishǒu of Xīyáng."
His collected works contain a letter to Shào, which says:
"The commandery of Xīyáng
has a fairly substantial population.
If one is not truly pure in following the Way,
how can one pacify its drifting and fleeing people?
Consulting both court and commoners,
all say it should be you.
I have now prepared a memorial to the throne,
requesting that you govern it.
Do not decline."
But (Zhōu) was not satisfied.
In the middle of the night, he sighed with emotion, saying:
"A great man like me has been sold out by Yǔ Yuánguī (Yǔ Liàng)!"
With one sigh,
he developed a carbuncle on his back and died.
Ruǎn Sīkuàng was devoted to the great Dharma,
and his reverence and faith were profound.
His eldest son, not yet twenty years old,
suddenly fell gravely ill.
The Ruǎn Clan Genealogy states:
"Ruǎn Yǒu, styled Yànlún,
was Ruǎn Yù's eldest son.
He served as a Registrar of a province."
Since this son was particularly beloved and cherished by him,
he prayed to the Three Jewels on his behalf,
diligently day and night without cease.
Believing that utmost sincerity could evoke a response,
he was certain the boy would receive divine protection.
Yet the son ultimately did not survive.
Consequently, he harbored resentment toward Buddhism,
and completely abandoned his belief in karma.
Given Ruǎn Sīkuàng's wisdom and understanding,
he surely should not have succumbed to such a fallacy.
If this account is not mistaken,
how could he have been so deluded?
Even King Wén reached his destined end,
and his sage son could not prolong his years;
when the Śākya clan was massacred,
divine power could not extend their lives.
Therefore, karma has fixed limits,
and retribution cannot be altered.
To pray and expect efficacy,
then upon failing to see proof, suddenly reject the Way—
such are merely the narrow-minded and ignorant.
How can they be spoken of as possessing the wisdom of divine understanding?
When Huán Xuānwǔ faced Emperor Jiǎnwén,
he struggled to find words.
After deposing Hǎixī,
he felt he should explain himself,
so he prepared hundreds of words in advance,
outlining his reasons for the deposition.
But when he met Emperor Jiǎnwén,
the Emperor simply shed tears in streams.
Huán Xuānwǔ, feeling ashamed and remorseful,
could not utter a single word.
Huán Gōng once said while lying down:
"To live in such obscurity,
I will be laughed at by [Emperors] Wén and Jǐng!"
Then he suddenly sat up and said:
"Since I cannot leave a fragrant name for posterity,
is it not enough to leave a stench for ten thousand ages?"
The Continued Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Huán Wēn, having dominated the court with his martial prowess,
held both military and civil authority.
His disloyal heart
was evident in his words and actions.
Once, lying down facing his close aides,
he patted his pillow and rose, saying:
'To live like this in obscurity,
I will be laughed at by [Emperors] Wén and Jǐng!'
None dared respond."
Grand Tutor Xiè was traveling by boat in the east.
The servants rowing the boat
were sometimes slow, sometimes fast,
sometimes stopping, sometimes waiting,
and even let the boat drift recklessly,
bumping into people and hitting the shore.
The Grand Tutor initially did not scold or reprimand them.
People said he was usually without anger or joy.
Once, returning from his elder brother Zhēngxī's funeral,
Zhēngxī
was Xiè Yì.
As dusk fell and rain poured,
the servants were all drunk,
and could not be managed.
The Grand Tutor then, from within his carriage,
took the carriage pillar in hand and struck the driver,
his voice and expression extremely stern.
Consider that water's nature is deep and gentle,
yet when forced into narrow straits, it rushes and churns.
Comparing this to human emotions,
we know that in constrained circumstances,
one cannot preserve one's calm and purity.
The Mèngzǐ says:
"Swift water,
channeled east flows east,
channeled west flows west.
If you strike it and make it leap,
it can go over your forehead;
if you dam it and force its course,
you can make it flow uphill.
Is this water's nature?
So too can man be made to do what is not good;
his nature is also like this."
Emperor Jiǎnwén saw paddy rice but did not recognize it,
asking what grass it was.
His attendants replied it was rice.
Emperor Jiǎnwén returned
and did not emerge for three days,
saying:
"How can one rely on its tip [the grain]
yet not recognize its root [the plant]?"
Duke Wén planted vegetables,
Zēngzǐ herded sheep—
even if one does not recognize rice,
why such excessive regret!
This story must be fictitious.
Chariot-General Huán was hunting at Shàngmíng.
A dispatch arrived from the east,
reporting a great victory on the Huái River.
He said to his attendants:
"The young men of the Xiè clan
have greatly defeated the enemy."
Thereupon he fell ill and died.
Commentators considered this death
nobler than yielding Yángzhōu for Jīngzhōu.
The Continued Jìnyáng Qiū states:
"Huán Chōng originally believed that the roles of general and minister differed,
and their talents and uses were not the same.
Reflecting on his own virtue and capacity,
he felt inferior to Xiè Ān,
so he relinquished Yángzhōu to yield to Ān.
Considering himself experienced in military commands,
upon becoming Governor of Jīngzhōu,
he heard that Fú Jiān personally led troops toward the Huái and
Féi, and grew deeply concerned for the capital's security.
He dispatched three thousand elite troops from his personal guard to the capital.
At that time, Ān had already deployed various armies,
and wishing to outwardly display calm and leisure,
he ordered Huán's troops to return.
Huán was greatly alarmed, saying:
'Xiè Ān may have the capacity for court governance,
but he is unfamiliar with military strategy.
I reckoned the enemy would surely take Xiāngyáng,
then concentrate forces at Huái and
Féi. Now the great enemy has indeed come,
yet he idly chats to show leisure,
sending inexperienced youths,
who are actually few and weak.
Who in the realm knows this?
We shall be barbarians!'
Soon hearing of the great victory,
he died in shame and anguish."
When Huán Gōng first received news of defeating Governor Yīn of Jīngzhōu,
Zhōu Zhī's Lóng'ān Record states:
"Yīn Zhòngkān, seeing popular sentiment leaning toward Huán Xuán,
suspected the court intended to replace him with Xuán.
He sent the monk Sēng Qiān with treasures to bribe the Prince's favorites,
matchmaking nuns,
and attendants,
to accuse Xuán of crimes.
Xuán learned of the plot
and attacked and destroyed him."
[Huán Xuán] was once lecturing on the Analects,
reaching
"Wealth and honor are what men desire,
but if they are not obtained in the proper way, they should not be held."
Kǒng Ānguó's Commentary states:
"If wealth and honor are not obtained in the proper way,
then the benevolent do not hold them."
Xuán's expression and demeanor turned very unpleasant.
When Wáng Dūn first married the princess,
Dūn married Emperor Wǔ's daughter, the Princess of Wǔyáng,
styled Xiūhuī.
Going to the toilet,
he saw a lacquered box containing dried dates,
originally meant to block the nose.
Wáng thought fruits were also served in the toilet,
and ate them all.
Upon returning,
a maid held a golden basin of water,
and a glass bowl containing bath beans.
He then poured them into the water and drank it,
thinking it was dried rice.
All the maids could not help but cover their mouths and laugh at him.
After the great mourning for Wáng Dà,
court discussions suggested
"Guóbǎo should be appointed to Jīngzhōu."
The "Jìn Āndì Jì" states:
"When Wáng Chén died,
the Prince of Kuàijī intended to have Guóbǎo replace him.
During the Xiàowǔ period,
an edict appointed Zhòng Kān instead,
and the matter was dropped."
Guóbǎo's secretary sent a sealed report overnight,
saying:
"The matter of Jīngzhōu has been settled."
Guóbǎo was overjoyed,
and immediately opened his gatehouse,
summoned his administrators to discuss the situation.
Although he did not get to become Governor of Jīngzhōu,
his expression and demeanor were very pleased.
At dawn, he sent someone to inquire,
only to find there was no such thing.
He immediately summoned his secretary and reprimanded him, saying:
"How could you mislead people like this?"
Lady Zhēn of Wèi was kind and beautiful.
She was first the wife of Yuán Xī,
and was greatly favored.
When Lord Cáo sacked Yè,
he ordered her to be summoned quickly.
His attendants reported:
"The General of the Household for All Purposes has already taken her away."
Lord Cáo said:
"This year's defeat of the enemy was precisely for this woman."
The "Wèi Lüè" states:
"During the Jiàn'ān era,
Yuán Shào married his second son, Xī, to the daughter of Zhēn Huì.
After Shào's death,
Xī went out to Yōuzhōu,
while Lady Zhēn remained to serve her mother-in-law.
When Yè city was captured,
the General of the Household for All Purposes entered Shào's residence,
saw Lady Zhēn frightened,
with her head bowed on her mother-in-law's lap.
The General said to Shào's wife, Lady Yuán:
'Help Lady Zhēn to raise her head.'
Seeing her extraordinary beauty,
he praised her.
Tàizǔ, hearing of his intent,
then had her welcomed and married,
and she enjoyed exclusive favor for several years."
The "Shìyǔ" states:
"When Tàizǔ captured Yè,
Wéndì first entered Yuán Shàng's residence,
saw a woman with disheveled hair, a dirty face, and weeping,
standing behind Shào's wife, Lady Liú.
Wéndì asked,
learned she was Xī's wife,
had her hair tidied,
and wiped her face with his sleeve,
revealing peerless beauty.
After he left,
Liú said to Lady Zhēn:
'You will not die now.'
He then took her in,
and she was favored."
The "Wèishì Chūnqiū" states:
"When the General of the Household for All Purposes took Xī's wife,
Kǒng Róng wrote to Tàizǔ, saying:
'King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and gave Dájǐ to the Duke of Zhōu.'
Tàizǔ, considering Róng learned,
truly thought it was recorded in historical texts.
Later, seeing Róng, he asked him about it,
to which Róng replied:
'Judging the past by the present,
I imagine it was so.'"
Xún Fèngqiàn and his wife were deeply devoted.
In winter, when his wife had a fever,
he went out into the courtyard to chill himself,
then returned to press his body against hers to cool her.
After his wife died,
Fèngqiàn also died a short while later.
For this, he was ridiculed by the world.
The "Càn Biézhuàn" states:
"Càn often held that a woman's intelligence and talent were not worth discussing,
and that beauty should be the primary consideration.
General of Agile Cavalry Cáo Hóng's daughter was beautiful,
so Càn married her.
Her appearance, attire, and bed curtains were exquisite,
and she enjoyed his exclusive affection.
After some years, she fell ill and died.
Before the burial,
Fù Gǔ went to console Càn,
who did not weep but was deeply grieved.
Gǔ asked:
'For a woman, both talent and beauty
are rarely found together.
In your marriage,
you overlooked talent and kept beauty,
which is not hard to find.
Why such profound grief?'
Càn said:
'A beautiful woman is hard to find again!
Although the deceased did not possess extraordinary, city-toppling beauty,
she was still not easily encountered.'
His sorrow and mourning were endless.
A little over a year later, he also died.
He was twenty-nine at death.
Càn was aloof and noble,
not associating with ordinary people,
his friends being the outstanding talents of the time.
On the evening of his burial,
only a dozen or so attended,
all famous scholars of his own generation.
They wept for him,
moving passersby with their grief.
Although Càn was narrow-minded,
and brought ruin upon himself through his devotion to love,
discerning people still regretted his eloquence."
Fèngqiàn said:
"A woman's virtue is not worth praising;
beauty should be the main consideration."
Péi Lìng heard this and said:
"This is just a spur-of-the-moment remark,
not the words of great virtue.
I hope later generations do not misunderstand this saying."
Hé Shào commented on Càn, saying:
"Confucius said
'Those with virtue have words.'
But Xún Càn fell short of this;
though his words were abundant in force and care,
his insight was insufficient."
Regarding Jiǎ Gōnglǘ, the "Chōng Biézhuàn" states:
"Chōng's father, Kuí,
had a son late in life,
so he named him Chōng,
styled Gōnglǘ,
meaning there would surely be the distinction of filling the gatehouse in the future."
His later wife, Lady Guō, was fiercely jealous.
They had a son named Límín,
who was just a year old.
When Chōng returned from outside,
the wet nurse was holding the child in the courtyard.
The child, seeing Chōng, happily jumped,
and Chōng kissed him in the wet nurse's arms.
Guō saw this from afar,
thought Chōng favored the wet nurse,
and immediately killed her.
The child wept in grief and longing,
refusing to drink any other milk,
and eventually died.
Guō later had no more sons.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" states:
"Lady Guō was the mother of Empress Jiǎ.
She was noble and intelligent by nature.
Knowing the Empress had no son,
she was very concerned and fond of Mǐnhuái,
often urging and encouraging him.
On her deathbed,
she admonished Empress Jiǎ,
telling her to devote herself to the Crown Prince,
her words extremely earnest.
She said that Zhào Chōnghuá and Jiǎ Mì's mother
should not be allowed to enter the palace.
She also said:
'These will both ruin your affairs!'
The Empress did not heed her,
and ultimately met with execution and extermination."
Your subject notes:
Considering Fù Chàng's words,
Lady Guō was a wise and virtuous woman.
Had Empress Jiǎ heeded her and shown affection to Mǐnhuái,
how could she have indulged her jealousy and ferocity,
leading to the death of her own son?
Thus, perhaps people differ,
or feelings change with age and maturity?
Sūn Xiù surrendered to Jìn,
and Jìn Wǔdì generously favored and cherished him.
The "Tàiyuán Guōshì Lù" says:
"Xiù, styled Yǎncái,
was from Wú County in Wú Commandery.
He served as the commander of Xiàkǒu,
wielding great authority and kindness.
Sūn Hào feared him and sought to eliminate him,
so he sent General Hé Dìng to sail up the river,
under the pretext of hunting three thousand deer for the imperial kitchen.
Xiù anticipated the plot in advance,
and thus came to submit.
Shìzǔ was pleased with him,
appointing him as General of Agile Cavalry
and Governor of Jiāozhōu."
He was married to his maternal cousin's younger sister, Kuǎi Shì,
and their marital relationship was very affectionate.
Once, his wife grew jealous
and scolded Xiù,
calling him a "raccoon dog."
The "Jìnyáng Qiū" says:
"Kuǎi Shì was from Xiāngyáng.
Her grandfather, Liáng,
served as Minister of Personnel.
Her father, Jūn,
was the Grand Administrator of Nányáng."
Xiù was greatly displeased,
and thereafter stopped entering her chambers.
Kuǎi Shì deeply regretted and blamed herself,
seeking help from the Emperor.
At that time, a general amnesty was in effect,
and all the ministers were in audience.
After they had left,
the Emperor detained Xiù alone,
and leisurely said to him:
"The world is now in a state of leniency and pardon;
might Lady Kuǎi also be granted such clemency?"
Xiù removed his cap and apologized,
and thereafter they resumed their harmonious relationship as husband and wife.
Hán Shòu possessed handsome features and graceful demeanor.
Jiǎ Chōng recruited him to serve as an assistant.
Whenever Chōng held gatherings,
his daughter would watch from behind the green lattice screen,
and upon seeing Shòu,
she became enamored with him.
Constantly thinking of him,
her feelings found expression in song and verse.
Later, a maidservant went to Shòu's home,
and fully recounted the situation,
also mentioning the girl's radiant beauty.
Upon hearing this, Shòu was moved in his heart,
and so requested the maidservant to secretly convey messages.
When the appointed time came, he went to stay overnight.
Shòu was exceptionally agile and nimble,
leaping over the wall to enter,
with no one in the household aware.
The "Jìn Zhūgōng Zàn" says:
"Shòu, styled Dézhēn,
was from Zhěyáng in Nányáng.
His great-grandfather, Jì,
served as Minister of Works under Wèi,
and was of noble character."
Shòu upheld his family's traditions,
and his nature was loyal and honest—
how could there be such an affair?
No other texts mention it;
it is only seen in the "Shì Shuō,"
and thus cannot be considered credible.
From then on, Chōng noticed that his daughter was diligently adorning herself,
and her cheerful demeanor was unusually bright.
Later, when meeting with his officials,
he noticed that Shòu carried a rare and exotic fragrance,
which was a tribute from foreign lands.
Once it clung to a person,
it would linger for months without fading.
The "Shízhōu Jì" says:
"During the reign of Hàn Wǔdì,
the king of Yuèzhī in the Western Regions sent an envoy to present four ounces of incense,
as large as sparrow eggs,
and black as mulberries.
When burned,
its fragrant aroma would linger for three months without dissipating."
This was likely the same incense.
Chōng reckoned that Wǔdì had only bestowed this incense upon himself and Chén Qiān,
and no other households possessed it.
Suspecting that Shòu was involved with his daughter,
yet the walls were thick and secure,
and the gates tightly guarded—
how could this have happened?
So he pretended there had been a theft,
and ordered the walls to be inspected.
The messenger returned and said:
"There is nothing unusual elsewhere,
only at the northeast corner there appear to be traces of someone.
But the wall is high,
and no ordinary person could have scaled it."
Chōng then interrogated the maidservants attending his daughter,
and they immediately confessed the truth.
Chōng kept it secret,
and married his daughter to Shòu.
The "Guō Zǐ" states that the one who had an affair with Hán Shòu
was actually Chén Qiān's daughter,
and she was married to Shòu,
but she died before the wedding.
Shòu then married a woman of the Jiǎ family,
which is why later generations mistakenly believed it was Chōng's daughter.
Wáng Ānfēng's wife
often addressed Ānfēng as "qīng."
Ānfēng said:
"For a wife to address her husband as 'qīng'
is disrespectful according to propriety;
do not do so again."
His wife replied:
"Because I am intimate with you and love you,
I call you 'qīng';
if I do not call you 'qīng,'
who else should?"
Thereafter, he always allowed it.
Chancellor Wáng had a favored concubine surnamed Léi,
who frequently interfered in government affairs and accepted bribes.
Duke Cài referred to her
as "Minister Léi."
The "Yǔ Lín" says:
"Léi was greatly favored,
and gave birth to Tián
and Qià."
Sūn Xiù harbored resentment against Shí Chóng for not giving him Lǜzhū,
as Gān Bǎo's "Jìn Jì" records:
"Shí Chóng had a courtesan named Lǜzhū,
beautiful and skilled at playing the flute.
Sūn Xiù sent a messenger to request her.
Chóng was at his villa north of Běimáng,
just then ascending a cool pavilion,
overlooking clear waters,
when the messenger informed him.
Chóng brought out several dozen of his maids and concubines, showing them and saying:
'Choose whichever you wish.'
The messenger said:
'The one I was ordered to seek
is specifically Lǜzhū.
I do not know which one she is?'
Chóng flared up and said:
'Lǜzhū
is my beloved;
she cannot be obtained!'
The messenger said:
'Your Lordship is learned in the past and understands the present,
perceptive of the distant and discerning of the near.
I hope you will reconsider thrice.'
Chóng remained unmoved.
The messenger left but returned again,
yet Chóng ultimately refused."
Sūn Xiù also resented Pān Yuè for having treated him disrespectfully in the past.
Later, when Xiù became Zhōngshū Lìng,
Yuè saw him within the ministry
and called out to him, saying:
"Sūn Lìng,
do you remember our past interactions?"
Xiù replied:
"I hold it deep in my heart;
how could I forget it for a single day?"
Yuè then knew for the first time that he could not avoid disaster.
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Yuè's father, Wéndé,
was the governor of Lángyé.
Sūn Xiù served as a minor clerk under him.
Yuè often kicked and trampled Xiù,
not treating him as a human being."
Later, when Shí Chóng and
Ōuyáng Jiānshí were arrested,
Pān Yuè was arrested on the same day.
"Jìnyáng Qiū" records:
"Ōuyáng Jiàn, styled Jiānshí,
was from Bóhǎi.
Talented and eloquent,
contemporaries said of him:
'Bóhǎi is illustrious,
thanks to Ōuyáng Jiānshí.'
Earlier, when Jiàn was governor of Féngyì,
and Prince Zhào Lún served as General of the West,
with Sūn Xiù as his confidant,
they disrupted Guānzhōng.
Jiàn often tried to rectify matters,
thus creating enmity between them."
Wáng Yǐn's "Jìn Shū" states:
"Shí Chóng and
Pān Yuè were on friendly terms with Jiǎ Mì.
After Mì was deposed,
fearing eventual danger,
they conspired with the Prince of Huáinán to kill Lún.
The plot was exposed,
and Chóng along with all his relatives within the mourning degree were executed.
Earlier, Yuè's mother had admonished him about the principle of knowing when to stop.
Upon his arrest,
he bid farewell to his mother, saying:
'I have failed you, Mother!'
Chóng's family was north of the river.
When the arresting officers arrived,
he said:
'I am merely to be exiled to Jiāozhōu or
Guǎngzhōu!'
Only when the cart reached the eastern market
did he sigh and say:
'These slaves coveted my family's wealth.'
The arresting officer said to Chóng:
'If you knew wealth brings harm,
why did you not distribute it earlier?'
Chóng could not reply."
Shí was sent to the market first,
and they were unaware of each other's fate.
Pān arrived later.
Shí said to Pān:
"Ānrén,
have you also come to this?"
Pān replied:
"It can be said
'we return together, white-haired.'"
"Yǔ Lín" records:
"Pān and
Shí were executed together at the eastern market.
Shí said to Pān:
'The world kills heroes;
what are you doing here?'
Pān replied:
'Outstanding men fill the ditches,
and the ripples reach others.'"
Pān's poem from the "Jīngǔ Collection" says:
"Entrusting my fate to a stony friend,
we return together, white-haired."
Thus, it became a prophecy fulfilled.
When Liú Yú and his brother were young, they were hated by Wáng Kǎi.
Once, Kǎi summoned the two to stay overnight,
intending to silently eliminate them.
He ordered a pit dug.
When the pit was finished,
he was about to harm them.
Shí Chóng had always been on good terms with Yú and
Kūn.
Hearing they were staying at Kǎi's,
he knew something was amiss.
So he went to visit Kǎi at night,
asking where the two Liús were.
Kǎi, caught off guard, could not conceal it,
and replied:
"They are sleeping in the rear study."
Shí then went straight in,
pulled them out himself,
and left with them in the same carriage.
He said to them:
"Young men,
why do you lightly agree to stay at others' homes?"
Liú Càn's "Jìn Jì" states:
"Kūn and his elder brother Yú were both renowned,
moving among the powerful and noble.
Their contemporaries considered them heroes."
General Wáng Dūn captured Prince Mǐn of Sīmǎ,
and at night sent Shìjiàng to carry the prince in a carriage and kill him,
something not widely known at the time.
The *Jìnyáng Qiū* says:
"Sīmǎ Chéng, styled Yuánjìng,
was the son of Prince Qiáo, Sīmǎ Xùn.
He served as Xiāngzhōu Governor for Emperor Yuán.
Passing through Wǔchāng,
Wáng Dūn held a banquet for him.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Dūn said to Chéng:
'Your Highness is a sincere and excellent scholar,
but not a talent for leading armies.'
Chéng replied:
'How do you know a leaden knife cannot make one cut?'
Dūn was plotting rebellion.
He summoned Chéng to serve as Army Marshal.
Chéng sighed and said:
'I am surely going to die!
The land is barren, the people scattered,
I am isolated with no hope of aid.
To go to my lord's aid in his distress is loyalty;
to die in my sovereign's service is righteousness.
To die for loyalty and righteousness,
what more could I seek?'
He then sent urgent dispatches to the various commanderies,
rallying them to the righteous cause.
Dūn sent his maternal cousin Wèi Yì to attack Chéng.
Wáng Yì had bandits waylay him,
and he died in the carriage.
After Dūn was destroyed,
Chéng was posthumously awarded the title of General of Agile Cavalry,
and given the posthumous name Prince Mǐn."
Even within Prince Mǐn's own household,
not everyone knew the full details,
