and Wújì and his brothers were all young.
The *Biography of Wújì* says:
"Wújì, styled Gōngshòu,
was the son of Chéng.
He possessed both talent and capability,
with civil and military prowess.
He inherited the title of Prince of Qiáo,
and served as General of the Guards."
Wáng Húzhī and Wújì
became very close as they grew older.
Once, when Húzhī was visiting,
Wújì went in to tell his mother,
asking her to prepare food.
His mother wept and said:
"In the past, Wáng Dūn brutally murdered your father,
using Shìjiàng as his instrument.
The *Genealogy of the Sīmǎ Clan* says:
'Chéng married a daughter of the Zhào family of Nányáng.'
The *Biography of Wáng Yì* says:
"Yì, styled Shìjiàng.
His grandfather was Lǎn,
his father was Zhèng.
Yì was lofty, brilliant, bold, and straightforward.
Once, when Wáng Dǎo and Yǔ Liàng were boating at Shítóu,
Yì happened to arrive.
That day, a strong wind filled the sails,
and Yì leaned against the cabin, letting out a long whistle,
his spirit and bearing very carefree.
Dǎo said to Liàng:
'Shìjiàng still understands the joy of things.'
Liàng replied:
'That's just enough to express his carefree nature.'
By nature, he was arrogant and haughty.
He would reject to their face anyone who did not suit him,
and thus was resented by others.
He was promoted to General Who Pacifies the South,
and then died.'
The reason I have not told you for all these years
is that the Wáng family's power was great,
and you brothers were still young.
I did not want this matter to become widely known,
in order to avoid disaster!"
Wújì cried out in shock and alarm,
drew his blade, and rushed out,
but Húzhī had already gone far away.
When Yìng Zhènnán took up his post in Jīngzhōu,
Wáng Yǐn's *Jìn Shū* says:
"Yìng Zhān, styled Sīyuǎn,
was a man of Nándùn, Rǔnán,
and the great-grandson of Yìng Qú.
He was magnanimous, far-sighted, and possessed depth,
adorned with literary talent.
Minister Hé Chōng sighed in admiration:
'Truly what is called a gentleman of both refinement and substance!'
He rose through the ranks to become Governor of Jiāngzhōu
and General Who Guards the South."
Wáng Xiūzài
and Prince Qiáo's son Wújì both went to Xīntíng to see him off.
There were many guests present,
and they did not realize both men had arrived.
One guest remarked:
"Prince Qiáo Chéng met his disaster
not by General Wáng Dūn's intention,
but was precisely the doing of Píngnán (Wáng Yì)."
Wújì then seized the sword of the Adjutant in Charge of Guards,
and was about to strike.
Xiūzài fled and threw himself into the water.
People on a boat pulled him out,
and he escaped.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"When Chǔ Póu was in Jiāngzhōu,
Wújì drew his blade during a gathering intending to kill him.
Póu and Huán Jǐng together managed to avoid it.
The Censor submitted a memorial that Wújì intended premeditated murder.
An imperial edict ruled he could redeem himself by payment."
The previous section already stated Wújì's mother told him,
and this section again mentions a guest relating the affair.
Moreover, Wáng Yì's murder of Sīmǎ Chéng
was known far and wide.
How could the Xiūlíng brothers
possibly not know?
Fǎ Shèng's words
are all factual records."
The Right Army General Wáng Xīzhī had always looked down upon Lántián (Wáng Shù).
In his later years, Lántián's reputation and esteem grew,
which made the Right Army General especially resentful.
When Lántián was in mourning in Kuàijī,
he halted at Shānyīn to conduct the funeral.
The Right Army General was acting as the commandery governor.
He repeatedly spoke of going to offer condolences,
but for days did not actually go.
Later, he went to the door and announced himself.
After the host (Shù) had performed the mourning rites,
Xīzhī did not go forward to pay respects but left,
intending to insult him.
From then on, great enmity was created between them.
Later, when Lántián was appointed to oversee Yángzhōu,
the Right Army General was still in the commandery.
Upon first hearing the news,
he sent an aide to the court,
requesting that Kuàijī be split off to form Yuèzhōu.
The messenger misunderstood his intent,
and this became a great laughingstock among the worthies of the time.
Lántián secretly ordered his assistants to enumerate the various unlawful acts of Xīzhī's commandery.
Because there was prior enmity,
he told Xīzhī to handle it appropriately himself.
The Right Army General then pleaded illness and left his post,
and died from indignation and resentment.
The *Zhōngxīng Shū* says:
"Xīzhī and Shù had different ideals and aspirations,
and were mutually incompatible.
When Shù was Governor of Kuàijī,
he observed mourning within the commandery.
Wáng Xīzhī later became governor.
He merely offered condolences once and that was all,
never paying a formal visit again,
which Shù deeply resented.
After the mourning period ended,
Shù was summoned and appointed to Yángzhōu.
Upon receiving the summons,
he toured the entire commandery,
but did not visit Xīzhī.
As he was about to depart,
he merely bid a single farewell and left.
Xīzhī initially said to his friend:
'Once Wáng Huáizǔ's mourning is over,
he might just become a Minister.
In his old age, he might become a Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
To hope for Kuàijī
is now far beyond him.'
After Shù received his prominent appointment,
he also inspected Kuàijī Commandery,
seeking out its faults.
The officials were exhausted from answering his inquiries.
Xīzhī, feeling ashamed and indignant,
pleaded illness and left his post.
Before his father's tomb, he swore an oath never to serve again.
The court, considering his oath solemn,
did not summon him again."
Wáng Dōngtíng spoke with Xiàobó,
and later gradually became estranged.
Xiàobó said to Dōngtíng:
"You have become truly unfathomable!"
He replied:
"Wáng Líng contended at court,
while Chén Píng followed in silence—
it only matters how things ultimately turn out."
The *Book of Hàn* states:
"When Empress Lü wanted to enfeoff the various members of the Lü clan as kings,
she asked the Right Chancellor Wáng Líng,
who considered it unacceptable.
She asked the Left Chancellor Chén Píng,
and Píng said:
'It is acceptable.'
After leaving, Líng reproached Píng,
and Píng said:
'In openly opposing and contending at court,
I am not as good as you;
but in preserving the altars of state,
and securing the Liú clan's rule,
you are not as good as I.'"
The *Annals of Āndì of Jìn* states:
"Initially,
when Wáng Gōng went to the imperial mausoleum,
he wanted to execute Guóbǎo.
Wáng Xún firmly advised against it,
and he desisted.
Later, Gōng said to Xún:
'Looking at you today,
you resemble Hú Guǎng.'
Xún said:
'Wáng Líng contended at court,
Chén Píng followed in silence—
it only matters how things ultimately turn out.'"
After Wáng Xiàobó died,
his head was hung on the Great Bridge.
Grand Tutor Sīmǎ had his carriage driven to the place where it was displayed,
gazed intently at the head,
and said:
"Why were you in such a hurry
to kill me?"
The *Continued Chronicles of Jìnyáng* states:
"Wáng Gōng deeply feared calamity,
and raised troops in defiance of the court.
Thereupon, Left General Xiè Yǎn was sent to attack Gōng.
Gōng was defeated,
fled to Qū'ē,
and was captured by the Captain of Húpǔ.
Initially, Dàozǐ had been on good terms with Gōng,
and wanted to bring him to the capital,
to confront and reproach him face-to-face.
Upon hearing that the western army was pressing near,
he ordered him beheaded at Értáng,
and his head displayed on the eastern bridge."
When Huán Xuán was about to usurp the throne,
Huán Xiū wanted to take advantage of Xuán being at his mother's place to ambush him.
Lady Yǔ said:
"You are close to me,
and have accompanied me in my remaining years.
I raised him,
and cannot bear to see you carry out such an act."
The *Genealogy of the Huán Clan* states:
"Huán Chōng later married the daughter of Yǐngchuān's Yǔ Miè,
whose courtesy name was Yáo."
The *Annals of Āndì of Jìn* states:
"Xiū was often slighted by Xuán in his youth,
and Xuán's words often belittled him.
Xiū deeply resented this,
and secretly harbored intentions to plot against Xuán.
Xiū's mother said:
'Língbǎo regards me as a mother;
how can you bear to plot against your own flesh and blood!'
Xiū then desisted."
